Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 1 (part 1 of 3):

4. Surat an-Nisa' (The Women).

It is Medinan according to the sound view. Al-Nahhas claimed that it is Meccan, relying on the fact that the words of Allah, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you...﴾, the verse, were revealed in Mecca by general agreement, concerning the key of the Ka'bah. Al-Suyuti responded to this that this is a weak basis, because the revelation of one verse or several verses in Mecca from a long surah most of which was revealed in Medina does not necessitate that the surah be Meccan, especially since the more likely view is that whatever was revealed after the Hijrah is Medinan. Whoever examines the occasions of revelation of its verses will recognise the refutation of this. Among the things that also refute it is what al-Bukhari transmitted from A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "Surat al-Baqarah and Surat an-Nisa' were not revealed except while I was with him (ﷺ)," and his (ﷺ) consummating the marriage with her was after the Hijrah by general agreement. It has also been said that it was revealed at the time of the Hijrah. The number of its verses according to the Syrians is one hundred and seventy-seven, according to the Kufans one hundred and seventy-six, and according to the rest seventy-five. The points of disagreement in it are two verses: the first is ﴿lest you go astray from the path﴾, and the second is ﴿then He will punish them with a painful punishment﴾. The Kufans count the first only as a verse, the Syrians count the second as well, and the rest say that they are both parts of a verse.

The aspects of its connection to Al 'Imran include several matters. Among them: Al 'Imran concluded with the command to piety (taqwa), and this surah opens with it. This is among the most emphatic aspects of connection in the arrangement of the surahs, and it is a type of rhetorical ornamentation (badi') which in poetry is called tashabuh al-atraf (resemblance of the extremities), and some people call it al-tasbigh (completion). An example is the saying of Layla al-Akhyaliyyah:

When al-Hajjaj alights in a sick land,
he seeks out its deepest illness and cures it.
He cured it of the deadly disease that was in it,
a youth who, when he shakes the spear, quenches its thirst.
He quenched it and gave it drink from its buckets
of the blood of men, wherever it reached its inner parts.

[p. 179]

Among them: Al 'Imran contains the story of Uhud in full, and this surah contains its tail end, which is His saying, ﴿Why have you become two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾, for it was revealed concerning matters related to that battle, as you will hear, if Allah wills, as narrated from al-Bukhari, Muslim and others. Among them: Al 'Imran contains mention of the expedition that followed Uhud, as we indicated in His saying, ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger﴾ and so on, and it is alluded to here in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And do not falter in pursuit of the people﴾, the verse. By these two aspects it becomes known that placing An-Nisa' after Al 'Imran is more fitting than placing it before it, as in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, because what is mentioned here is an appendix to what was mentioned there and a follower of it, so delaying it is more fitting. Whoever looks carefully will find much of what is mentioned in this surah detailing what was mentioned before it, and then the greater connection and the utmost interlocking will become clear.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. ﴿O people﴾: an address that encompasses the responsible persons from the time of its revelation until the Day of Resurrection, as its verification has passed. Regarding the inclusion of such a form of address for slaves in the legal sense, so that the ruling covers them, there is a difference of opinion. Most scholars held that it includes them, because a slave is among "the people," for example, and so he enters the general address concerning him with certainty, and his being a slave is not a valid obstacle to this. Some held that it does not include them. They said: It has been established by consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement) that the benefits of the slave belong to his master, so if he were addressed as responsible, that would mean assigning his benefits to someone other than his master, and that is a contradiction. Consensus is therefore followed and the apparent meaning is set aside. Also, slaves are excluded from the address concerning jihad, Friday prayer, 'Umrah, Hajj, voluntary charity, acknowledgements (iqrar) and similar matters, and if the address included them by way of generality, specification (takhsis) would be required, and the default is that there is none. The answer to the first argument is that we do not accept that his benefits belong to his master in every respect. Rather, this may be excepted at the time when acts of worship become pressing, such that if his master commanded him at the end of the time of Zuhr, and if he obeyed him the prayer would be missed, then prayer becomes obligatory upon him, and his benefit at that time is not assigned to the master. Once this is established, then being obligated to worship does not contradict their saying that benefits belong to the master. The answer to the second argument is that his exclusion is due to an indicator that required his exclusion. This is like the exclusion of the sick, the traveller and the menstruating woman from the general texts that establish the obligation of fasting, prayer and jihad. That does not indicate that the texts do not cover them by agreement. At most it is contrary to the default, and it is undertaken because of an indicator, and that is permissible.

Then, the correct view is that the nations that passed before the revelation of this address have no share in it, because commands and prohibitions are specific to those from whom compliance can be conceived. And how could they comply, when they are beneath the layers of the earth and will not rise until the Trumpet is blown?

Some scholars allowed that the address is general in such a way that they are included in it. Then he said: "It is not far-fetched that the command that is to come is general for them as well, in relation to the eternal speech that subsists in the Essence of Allah, exalted is He, even if its being in Arabic is incidental for this community." And this is open to examination, because what is considered is the rulings of the Qur'an after its revelation. Otherwise the call and all the direct address within it would be metaphorical, and no one holds that. So reflect.

In any case, the word "people" (al-nas) includes males and females without dispute. Regarding whether a form such as His saying, ﴿Fear your Lord﴾, includes females, there is a difference of opinion. Most hold that females do not enter such a form apparently, in contrast to the Hanabilah (Hanbalis). The first group argued: It has been narrated from Umm Salamah that she said: "O Messenger of Allah, the women say: We do not see that Allah has mentioned anything but men, so their mention was revealed." She denied their mention absolutely. Had they been included, her denial would not have been valid, and he (ﷺ) would not have approved her denial. Also, the grammarians have agreed that a form like this is a masculine plural, and that it is for the plural of the singular, and the singular is masculine. Also, the parallel of this form is "the Muslims" (al-muslimun), and had the meaning of "the Muslim women" (al-muslimat) been included in it, the conjunction in His saying, ﴿Indeed the Muslim men and the Muslim women﴾ would not be fitting except by way of emphasis (ta'kid), while establishing a new ruling (ta'sis) is better than emphasis. The others said: What is known among the people of the language is the prioritising (taghlib) of the masculine over the feminine when they are combined, by agreement. Also, if the females were not included in that, they would not share in the rulings, since most rulings are established by a form like this, and the consequence is negated by agreement, as in the rulings of prayer, fasting and zakat. Also, if someone bequeathed a hundred dirhams to men and women, and then said: "I bequeathed to them such and such," the women would enter without any indicator, and this is the meaning of the literal sense (haqiqah), so it is literal in regard to men and women, apparent in both, and this is what is sought.

It was answered: As for the first, it only shows that the usage is correct when all are intended, and the majority say so, but it is then figurative (majaz) and it does not follow that it is apparent. This is where the dispute lies. As for the second, we deny the implication. Yes, it follows that they do not share in the rulings by such a form, but what prevents them from sharing by an external proof? And that is the case, which is why they do not enter into jihad or Friday prayer, for example, because there is no external proof there. As for the third, we deny that the understanding there is without a contextual indicator (qarinah), for the earlier bequest is an indicator showing the intention. So the correct view is that females do not enter apparently. Yes, the better view here is that they enter by way of prioritisation. Some claimed that there is no prioritisation, and that the command is for men only, as the apparent form requires, and the entry of women into the command to piety is by an external proof. It is not hidden that this requires restricting the word "people" to some of its members, because keeping it in its generality in that case is something that sound taste rejects. The command is either to guard oneself in a way that covers avoiding disbelief, sins and all other ugly acts, and includes observing the rights of people as it includes observing the rights of Allah, exalted is He; or it is guarding oneself against violating the rights that must be preserved among the servants. This meaning corresponds to what is in the surah concerning the care of orphans, maintaining the ties of kinship, justice in marriage and inheritance, and similar matters in particular. The first, by contrast, corresponds to them only in terms of generality.

In mentioning the title of Lordship together with its attribution to the pronoun of those addressed, there is what is not hidden of confirming the command and emphasising the obligation to comply. Likewise in describing the Lord with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Who created you from a single soul﴾, because the usage is that the attribute upon which a ruling is made dependent is an effective cause (illah) requiring it, or a motive prompting it and calling to it. It is not hidden that what is here is like that, because what is mentioned indicates great power or great blessing. Undoubtedly the first necessitates piety absolutely, out of caution against the great punishment, and the second calls to it, in fulfilment of the due gratitude. And the creation from one origin being a reason for guarding oneself is very evident on the second interpretation. In the mentioned attribute there is an alert that the addressees know what has been mentioned, which requires adorning oneself with piety, and in it there is complete rebuke for whoever misses that.

By "the single soul" is meant Adam, peace be upon him. What the majority of jurists and hadith scholars, and those who agree with them, hold is that there is no one other than one Adam, who is the father of humanity. The author of Jami' al-Akhbar among the Imamiyyah mentioned in the fifteenth chapter a long report in which he narrated that Allah created thirty Adams before our father Adam, with a thousand years between each Adam and Adam, and that the world remained in ruin after them for fifty thousand years, and then it was populated for fifty thousand years, and then our father Adam was created, peace be upon him. Ibn Babawayh in Kitab al-Tawhid also narrated from al-Sadiq, in another long hadith, that he said: "Perhaps you think that Allah did not create any human other than you. Yes, by Allah, He created a thousand thousand Adams, and you are at the end of those Adamites." Al-Maytham, in his large commentary on the Nahj, said, citing Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir, that he said: "There passed before Adam, who is our father, a thousand thousand Adams, or more."

[p. 181]

Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, in his Futuhat mentioned what by its apparent meaning indicates that before Adam, forty thousand years earlier, there was another Adam. In Kitab al-Khasa'is there is something from which plurality may almost be understood now, where it is narrated from al-Sadiq that he said: "Allah, exalted is He, has twelve thousand worlds, each world of which is greater than seven heavens and seven earths. No world among them sees that Allah, mighty and majestic, has a world other than them. How could there be a proof against them? Perhaps this and its like, from the land of Simsimah, Jabarsa and Jabalqa, if it is sound, is to be understood as the world of the image ('alam al-mithal), not this world in which we are. Understanding the plurality of Adam in that world is also not far-fetched. As for holding to the apparent meaning of these reports, that is something that the People of the Sunnah and the Congregation do not accept. Indeed Zayn al-'Arab has explicitly declared the one who believes in plurality to be a disbeliever.

Yes, this Adam of ours, peace be upon him, is preceded by other creations such as the angels, the jinn, many animals and other things that none knows except Allah, exalted is He. But he is not preceded by creatures like himself. And he is originated both in kind and in person, unlike some philosophers who claimed the eternity of the human species. Many of us held that from his time until the time of the mission was six thousand years, and that the age of the world is seven thousand years, and they narrated many reports on this. But the truth in my view is that he came into existence after he was not, and will not cease to exist after he has come into existence. As for when he came into being and when he will cease to be, that is something none knows but Allah, exalted is He. The reports are contradictory in this matter, so one can hardly rely upon them.

The view that the universal soul (al-nafs al-kulliyya) sits once every seven thousand years to judge between the particular souls, and that the Hour's arrival after the completion of a thousand years from the mission is to be understood in that light, is something I do not accept as religion nor choose as certainty. The address in "your Lord" (rabbakum) and "who created you" (khalaqakum) is directed to those who were commanded, and generalizing it so that it includes earlier nations, while the preceding address remains not inclusive, is based on the view that the all-encompassing lordship of God the Exalted and His creation of all is more complete in confirming the preceding command. Yet this involves a disruption of the structure, which is unnecessary, because God's creation of those addressed from the very self of Adam, peace be upon him, since they came about through the fathers and mothers between him and them, means that mentioning their creation implicitly includes the right of all the intermediaries. Likewise, mentioning His lordship over them implicitly includes His lordship over all their origins, especially since the speech is followed by the words of God the Exalted: ﴿And from it He created its mate﴾, which is coordinated with (khalaqakum) and is included together with it within the scope of the relative clause. The verb is repeated to show the difference between the two creations: the first is by way of branching from the origin, and the second by way of origination from the material. The meaning of "its mate" is Eve, who was created from the left rib of Adam, peace be upon him, as has been narrated from Ibn 'Umar and others. Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated: "Treat women well, for they were created from a rib, and the most crooked part of the rib is its upper part. If you try to straighten it, you will break it, and if you leave it, it will remain crooked."

Abu Muslim denied her creation from the rib, because He, glory be to Him, is able to create her from dust, so what is the benefit in creating her from that? He claimed that the meaning of "from it" is "from its kind," and the verse is in the manner of His saying (He made for you mates from yourselves). Some agreed with him, claiming that saying what was mentioned leads to saying that Adam, peace be upon him, used to marry parts of himself, and in this there is an abhorrence that is not hidden. Some claimed that Eve was a houri created from what the houris were created from after Adam was made to dwell in the Garden. Both opinions are false. As for the second, there is nothing in the verses or the hadiths that could be taken to indicate it, let alone state it explicitly. Moreover, it may be said against it: the houris were created from the saffron of the Garden, as stated in some reports. If Eve were created from what they were created from, as the claimant's own words state, then between her and Adam, peace be upon him, who was created from the dust of this world, there is a total distance, nearly amounting to a divergence in the kind that the verse may seem to imply, and this would require the remoteness of procreation occurring between them in this life. If she were created from what Adam was created from, then this, despite contradicting the text of his statement, returns against him: this is a statement in agreement with what Abu Muslim said, or else it is close to it. As for the first, if the matter were as he mentioned, then people would have been created from two selves, not from one self, which contradicts the text. Moreover, it contradicts what the sound reports have stated from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and this also refutes the second.

As for the view that asks what the benefit is of creating her from a rib when God the Exalted is able to create her from dust, it may be answered: the benefit of this, apart from the wisdom which is hidden from us, is to show that He, glory be to Him, is able to create a living being from a living being not by way of procreation, just as He is able to create a living being from inanimate matter. And if the ability to create from dust prevented creation from anything else because there is no benefit in creating all from dust without an intermediary, then since He, glory be to Him, is as able to create Adam from dust, He is also able to create all individual humans from it. So what is your answer about the creation of people from one another when He is able to create them as He created Adam, peace be upon him? Our answer about the creation of Eve from Adam when He is able to create her from dust is the same. As for the claim that this leads to what involves an abhorrence, what is there to say about it? Because this particular individuation that came to that part, such that no apparent trace of its original individuation remains, removes the abhorrence, which has no basis except pure imagination, especially since wisdom requires that marital union of that kind.

Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned that when Eve was separated from Adam, she filled the place from him by the carnal desire through which intercourse took place, for the sake of the manifestation of procreation and reproduction. The air that went out and filled the place of her body at her emergence, since there is no void in the world, sought its place which Eve had taken with her particular individuality, so it moved Adam to seek its place, and he found it filled by Eve, so he came upon her. When he had intercourse with her, she conceived from him and bore offspring. After that it remained a continuing custom among the animals of the children of Adam and others by nature. But man is the comprehensive word and the copy of the world; everything in the world is a part of him, and man is not a part of any one thing in the world. The cause of the separation and the bringing into existence of this first separated part was the seeking of intimacy with what is similar in the kind, which is the more specific species, and so that in the world of bodies, through this natural joining, there would be for the perfect human, in the form which God the Exalted willed, something resembling the Supreme Pen and the Preserved Tablet, which are expressed by the First Intellect and the Universal Soul. End of quotation.

It is understood from their words that this creation did not occur in this way except between these two spouses, not among the rest of the mates of animals, and I have not found in this anything that satisfies the thirst. Yes, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, that the spouse of Iblis, may the curse of God be upon them both, was created from his left flank. The "khalf," as stated in al-Sihah, is the shortest of the ribs of the side, and al-Dahhak interpreted it in this sense in this context. The explanation of the creation of the spouse was delayed after the explanation of the creation of those addressed because mentioning their creation is more effective in achieving the intended purpose, which is to move them to comply with the command, than mentioning the creation of her. The prepositional phrase was placed first to give attention to explaining Adam's, peace be upon him, priority of origin for her, and the sense of anticipation that fronting creates for what comes later. The title "spouse" was chosen as a preparation for what follows of procreation.

Some verifying scholars held that it is permissible to coordinate this clause with an implied element that the context indicates, because the branching of branches from a single origin necessarily requires the origination of that origin, as if it were said: He created you from one self which He created first, and from it He created its mate, etc. This implied element is either a resumptive statement serving to establish the unity of the origin and explain the manner of their creation from it by detailing what was summarized first, or it is a qualifier of "self" conveying this. Some made this implied element necessary on the supposition that the address in what preceded is general to the species. Perhaps this is because, without the implied element in that case, this together with His saying (and He scattered from both of them) — that is, He spread and dispersed from that self and its mate, by way of procreation and reproduction, many men and women — would be a repetition of His saying (who created you), since their meaning is one, and it would not be an explanation of the first, because it would be coordinated with it on the absence of the implied element. It would also give the impression that men and women are not among those created from one self, and that they are separately created from it and from its mate, whereas people were created only from one self without any role for the mate. This does not follow on coordination. The addressee in (khalaqakum) was made to be those to whom the Prophet, peace be upon him, was sent, since then (and He scattered from both of them, etc.) would apply to those other than the addressed people among the earlier nations, which is restriction and an assumption that is far-fetched. Likewise, it does not follow on the supposition of omitting the coordinated element, and the address being made general, because that omitted element and what is coordinated with it would be an explanation of the manner of creation from that self, and among people there are those who claimed that there is no obstacle to making the address general without need for an implied coordinated element along with it. To this view went the author of al-Taqrib. The objection they mention is not valid, because from the creation of the children of Adam from one self it is not understood that its mate was created from it, nor that men and women were created from both origins together. The coordinated clause carries the explanation of that.

Many have mentioned that what is required in coordination is the difference of the coordinated items, even if only in one respect, and here it is certainly present without doubt, as is not hidden. The variation in (rijalan wa nisa'an) is for multiplication. (Kathiran) is an adjective of (rijalan), emphasizing what the indefiniteness conveys. The singular form is in view of the meaning of plurality, or of number, or to observe the pattern of (fa'il). Abu al-Baqa' reported that it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "scattering, many," and for this reason it is singular. Making it an adjective of (hin), as it has been said, is a crude artifice. The meaning of "men and women" is not adult males and females only, but males and females in general, by figurative usage. Perhaps the preference of these two over "males and females" is to emphasize the abundance and the exaggeration in it by singling out each individual of the scattered ones as the origin of others. It has been said: he mentioned the elders among them, because the context concerns those charged with piety. He suffices with describing the men as numerous instead of describing the women with it, because wisdom requires that they be more numerous, since a man may take more than one wife, unlike a woman. This was stated by al-Khatib. Some used the verse as evidence that what comes into being comes only from a prior material, and that the creation of a thing from pure nothingness is impossible. It was answered: it does not follow from bringing a thing into existence in one form from matter, for a wisdom, that bringing into existence must depend on matter in all forms. Moreover, the verse does not indicate more than the creation of us and the creation of the spouse from what was mentioned, and this is not sufficient for the claim.

It was also read (wa khaliqun wa batthun) by omitting the subject, because it is a relative clause coordinated with a relative clause, so it can only be a nominal sentence, unlike the example "Zayd rode and is going," meaning: and He is the Creator and Scatterer.

﴿And fear God, by whom you ask one another﴾: this is a repetition of the first command and an emphasis on it, and the addressees are again those to whom the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, was sent, as already passed. It was said: the addressees here and there are the Arabs, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, because their custom was this mutual invoking. It was said: the addressees there are all those to whom he was sent, and here the Arabs specifically, and the generality of the beginning of the verse does not prevent the specificity of its end, nor the reverse; and what this involves of disjunction is not hidden. Placing the Name of Majesty in place of the pronoun indicates all the attributes of perfection, ascending after the attribute of lordship, as if it were said: fear Him for His lordship and His creation of you as a wonderful creation, and because He deserves all the attributes of perfection.

In attaching the judgment to what is within the relative clause there is an indication of another of the requirements of compliance: when one says to his companion, "I ask you by God, and I implore you by God the Exalted," as a plea for compassion, this requires guarding against violating His commands and prohibitions. "Tasa'alun" is either in the sense of "some of you ask others," so the reciprocal form retains its literal meaning, or in the sense of "you ask," as is read. Tafa'ala comes in the sense of fa'ala when its subject is multiple, and its original form in the well-known reading is "tatasa'alun" with two tas, one of which was omitted for heaviness. Nafi' and Ibn Kathir and the rest of the people of Kufa read "tassa'alun," assimilating the ta of the reciprocal form into the sin, because they are close in voicelessness.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 1 (part 3 of 3):

﴿And the wombs﴾ is read in the accusative (naṣb), and it is coordinated (ma'ṭūf) either with the place (maḥall) of the preposition and its object, if the place belongs to both of them, or with the place of the object alone, if the place belongs to it alone. The construction is like "I passed by Zayd and ʿUmar." This is supported by the reading (*tasā'alūna bihi wa-bil-arḥām*, "you ask one another by Him and by the wombs"), and by the fact that they used to join the wombs with God Most High in asking and in adjuration, saying: "I ask you by God Most High, and by God, glory be to Him, and by the womb." This is related by more than one transmitter from Mujahid. It is also the view preferred by al-Farisi (Abu ʿAli) and ʿAli ibn ʿIsa. Or it is coordinated with the Majestic Name (al-ism al-jalil, i.e., God), meaning: "Fear God Most High and the wombs, and maintain them and do not sever them, for severing them is among the things that must be guarded against." This is the transmission of Ibn Humayd from Mujahid, and of al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas, and of Ibn al-Munthir from ʿIkrima. It is related from Abu Jaʿfar, may God be pleased with him, and it is preferred by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. Al-Wahidi permitted the accusative as an incitement (al-ighra'), meaning: "Hold fast to the wombs and maintain them."

Hamza read it in the genitive (jarr). In the well-known explanation, this is treated as coordination with the pronominal object (al-ḍamīr al-majrūr). Most grammarians criticized this, on the ground that the attached pronoun is like part of the word, because it is so closely joined to it. Just as one does not coordinate with part of a word, one does not coordinate with it.

The first to criticize Hamza for this reading was Abu al-ʿAbbas al-Mubarrad, to the point that he said: "The recitation with it is not permissible." Others followed him in this, including Ibn ʿAṭiyya, who claimed that two considerations refute it. The first is that mentioning the wombs as something by which people ask one another has no meaning in urging the fear of God Most High, and there is no benefit in it beyond the report that the wombs are something by which people ask one another, and this detracts from eloquence. The second is that mentioning them in this way establishes asking by them and swearing by their sanctity, and the authentic hadith refutes that. The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related from him, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace: "Whoever swears, let him swear by God Most High or keep silent."

You know that Hamza did not recite this way on his own, but took it, indeed the whole Qur'an, from Sulayman ibn Mihran al-Aʿmash, from the Imam Ibn Aʿyan, from Muhammad ibn Abi Layla, and from Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq, who was righteous, scrupulous, and trustworthy in hadith, of the third generation.

Imam Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, and Yahya ibn Adam said about him: "Hamza surpassed the people in recitation and in the laws of inheritance (al-fara'id)." Several took from him and became his students, among them the Imam of Kufa in recitation and Arabic, Abu al-Hasan al-Kisa'i, who is one of the seven readers whom the pillars of the religion said have a recitation transmitted mutawatir (by an uninterrupted, multiply-attested chain) from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace. Yet he did not recite this alone; rather, a group outside the Seven recited it too, such as Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi, al-Hasan al-Basri, Qatada, Mujahid, and others, as Ibn Yaʿish reported. So the condemnation of this Imam is extremely shameful, the height of audacity and ugliness, and it may even be feared that it leads to disbelief.

What has been mentioned about the prohibition of coordinating with the genitive pronoun is the doctrine of the Basrans. We are not bound to follow them. Abu Hayyan prolonged the discussion in *al-Bahr* in refuting them, and claimed that what they held is not correct; rather the correct view is that of the Kufans, which is permissible, and it occurs in the speech of the Arabs in prose and verse. Ibn Malik also held this view.

As for the claim that mentioning the wombs in this way has no meaning in urging the fear of God Most High, it falls away from the argument, because if by "fear" is meant specifically the fear that concerns the rights of people, which includes maintaining the ties of kinship, then asking by the wombs is undoubtedly among what it requires. If the broader sense is meant, then it is included within it. As for the suspicion that mentioning them establishes asking by them and swearing by their sanctity, and that the hadith refutes this because it forbids swearing by other than God Most High, it has been answered: we do not grant that swearing by other than God Most High is absolutely forbidden. What is forbidden is only that which is done with the belief that one must be bound by the oath. As for swearing for emphasis, for example, there is no harm in it. In the report: "He has prospered, by his father, if he is truthful."

Some have mentioned that when a person says to another, "I ask you by the womb to do such and such," his purpose is nothing but to move the other to compassion. It is not like the saying of one who says, "By the womb, I will certainly do such and such," or "I have certainly done such and such," so it is not the object of the prohibition in any respect. The claim that the intended meaning here is a report of what they used to do in the Jahiliyya is not hidden in its defect, so understand.

Ibn Jinni explained this reading in another way. He said in *al-Khasa'is*: "A chapter on the fact that when the omitted element is indicated by evidence, it has the status of what is actually pronounced. Among examples: 'A trace of a house I stood at its remains' (i.e., 'many a trace of a house'). When Ruba was asked, 'How did you wake up?' he would say, 'Good, may God keep you well'" (i.e., "with good"), omitting the preposition because the situation indicates it. In this manner, Hamza's reading is, for us, to be understood. In the commentary on *al-Mufassal* it is stated that the preposition in this reading is omitted because its mention preceded it. Al-Zamakhshari also followed this in his *Ahajiyy*. The author of *al-Kashf* mentioned that it is closer than the first explanation according to most of the Basrans, because the omission of the preposition is established in such expressions as "By God, I will certainly do it," and in the saying: "What ʿAbdullah and his brother did not impersonate, saying: 'That is.'" Taking the matter according to what is established is the proper course. It is also reported from some that the *wāw* is for oath, as in: "Fear God Most High, for by God He is watching you," with the *fa'* (then) omitted, because the resumption (al-istiʾnaf) is the stronger of the two original options. This is a good explanation.

Ibn Zayd read (*wa-l-arḥāmu*) in the nominative, as the subject of an omitted predicate, meaning: "and the wombs are likewise," i.e., they are among what must be guarded, by the indication of "fear" (*ittaqū*), or among what is asked by, by the indication of (*tasā'alūna*). Ibn ʿAṭiyya estimated the predicate as "deserving to be joined," and Ibn Jinni as "what you must join and be careful about." Perhaps the clause then is parenthetical (muʿtariḍa), since otherwise coordination is obscure. God, glory be to Him, by joining the wombs to His own name, has indicated that their maintenance has a place with Him, Exalted. The two Shaykhs related from Abu Hurayra who said: the Messenger of God, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, said: "God Most High created creation, and when He had finished with them, the womb stood up and said: 'This is the station of one who seeks refuge in You from severance.' He said: 'Yes. Are you not pleased that I join whoever joins you, and sever whoever severs you?' She said: 'Indeed.' He said: 'Then that is for you.'" Al-Bazzar related with a good chain: "The womb is a branch attached to the Throne, speaking with a slippery tongue: 'O God, join whoever joins me, and sever whoever severs me.' God Most High says: 'I am the Merciful (al-Raḥmān), I am the Compassionate (al-Raḥīm); I have derived the womb from My name. Whoever joins it, I join him; whoever cuts it off, I cut him off.'"

Imam Ahmad related with an authentic chain: "Among the most usurious forms of usury is oppression without right. This womb is a branch from the Merciful; whoever severs it, God Most High forbids him Paradise."

The reports on this subject are numerous. The term "womb" (raḥim) refers to relatives, and it applies to everyone with whom you share a kinship, however distant. It is also applied to relatives through women. Restricting it, in the matter of maintaining ties, to those who trace back to the mother's womb is unsupported, since a command to show kindness to relatives has come in general terms. ﴿Indeed God has been watching over you﴾ (1), i.e., a guardian (ḥafīẓ), as Mujahid said. It derives from *raqiba*, in the sense of "guarded," as al-Raghib stated. It may also be explained as "the one who oversees," and from this comes *al-marqab*, the high place overlooking something from which one observes what is below. For this reason Ibn Zayd explained it as "the knowing one." In any case, it is *faʿīl* in the sense of *fāʿil*. The sentence is in the position of giving the reason for the command and the obligation to obey it. The Majestic Name is made explicit to emphasize it, and the preposition is placed first to observe the rhyme (fawāṣil).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And give the orphans their property.﴾ This begins the detailed account of the means of safeguarding (al-ittiqa'), in the most complete manner. He began with what concerns the orphans, to show the full extent of care for their affairs, and because they are bound to the addressees by ties of kinship. The address is to the guardians (al-awsiya') and the custodians (al-awliya'), and guardianship is rarely entrusted to a stranger.

The orphan (yatim), in the case of a human, is one whose father has died. In the case of other animals, it is one who has lost its mother. It derives from *al-yutm*, which means being alone. From this root, the term is applied to anything whose equal is rare, such as the unique pearl (al-durra al-yatima).

[Page 186]

It is pluralized as *yatama*, although *fa'il* does not take the plural *fa'ala*; rather, its plurals are *fi'al* (as *karim* → *kiram*), *fu'ala'* (as *karim* → *kuruma'*), and *fu'ul* (as *nadhir* → *nudhur*), and *fa'la* (as *marid* → *marda*). This is either because it has been treated as a noun, which is why it rarely functions as an adjective for a described noun, so it was pluralized as *yatayim* (as *afil* → *afayil*). Then it was inverted, so it became *yataamii* with a kasra, then it was lightened by changing the kasra to a fatha, and the *ya'* became an *alif*. It has come in its original form in the verse:

"Are these the ruins of beauty at al-Barraq, the orphaned ones? Peace upon the stones that were once the ancient ones."

Or it is because it was first pluralized as *yutma*, and then as *yataama*, by analogy with the category of afflictions and ailments, since *fa'il* in that category is pluralized as *fa'la*, and *fa'la* is pluralized as *fu'ala'*, just as *asir* (prisoner) is pluralized as *asra*, and then *usara'*. The point of resemblance is the humiliation and painful brokenness found in it. It has also been said that the point of resemblance is the bad manners that it entails, which are likened to afflictions. Etymologically, its application to both young and old would be valid, but the Law, and likewise custom, have restricted it to the young. The hadith, "There is no orphanhood after reaching puberty (ihtilam)," is a teaching of the Law and not a definition of the meaning of the word.

The meaning of "giving them their property" is leaving it intact and unharmed, not subjected to any abuse. This is a metaphor used for its necessary consequence, since property is not "given" unless it is in that condition. The subtle point of this expression is to indicate that the purpose of refraining from interfering with it should be the delivery of the property to those mentioned, not merely the avoidance of interference with it. On this basis, it is valid to take "the orphans" to mean the young, as is the immediate understanding. The command is specific to whoever is in charge of their affairs among the guardians and custodians. The extension of this ruling to the guardians of one who was adult at the time the verse was revealed is by way of implication (dalala) and not by way of explicit expression (ibara).

It is also valid to take "orphan" in a more general, metaphorical sense, as applying to anyone who was an orphan at some point, whether he was so at the time of revelation or was adult. Thus the command includes the guardians of both groups. It is a verbal form that obligates upon them what has been mentioned: refraining from touching the property, and not breaking the seal to consume it. As for the obligation to hand it over to adults, it is derived from what will come later about the command to do so.

It has also been said: the meaning of "giving" (ita') is actual handing over in deed, and "orphans" is either in its original linguistic meaning, in which case it is a real (haqiqa) usage in accordance with the original language, or it is metaphorical, based on what was earlier because of the recency of the state of being young. The indication is toward the obligation to hasten to hand their property over to them, as if the name "orphan" still remains and has not ceased. This meaning is called in the principles of jurisprudence "indication of the text" (isharat al-nass), which is when speech is directed toward one meaning and another meaning is included within it. In this respect, it is analogous to the preceding category of "approaching" (al-mushārafa).

It has also been said: it is permissible to take "orphans" to mean the young, and there is no metaphor in making the ruling conditional, as if it were said: "Give them when they reach maturity." This has been refuted: al-Taftazani said in al-Talwih (a work by Sa'd al-Din al-Taftazani on the principles of jurisprudence) that the meaning of the Exalted's words, "And give the orphans their property," is the time of puberty, taking into account what they were, since the relevant consideration is the state of the relationship, not the state of speaking. Thus the verse applies to the adult in every case.

Some of the scholars of verification said: estimating the condition does not dispense with metaphor, because the ruling applied to what the attribute expresses implies that the subject is characterized by the attribute at the time the attribute is attached to it, and at the time the giving is attached to him he is an orphan. So there must be an interpretation along the lines already mentioned. This was answered: although this question is mentioned in al-Talwih, it is not accepted without challenge, and al-Sharif (al-Jurjani) hesitated about it in his glosses. The verification is that in such a case there are two relations: a relation between the condition and the consequence, which is the conditional relation (al-ta'liqiyya), which is actual now and does not depend on the existence of its two parts in the external world; and an attributive relation in each of the two ends, which is not actual at present but future, and the intended one is the first. During the time of that relation they were orphans in actuality. Do you not see that they say, in examples such as "I pressed this vinegar last year," that it is a real statement, even though at the time of pressing it was juice (asir) and not vinegar? This is because what is intended is the relation that is subordinate between the demonstrative and its follower, not the relation of action between it and the pressing, as one of the learned men verified. The reference to this was already made at the beginning of al-Baqara, so reflect on it, for it is subtle.

[Page 187]

It has also been said: the meaning of "giving" is what is more general than giving in the present or giving in the future, and "orphans" includes the young and the old by way of generalization (taghlib). The address is general to the guardians of both groups. Whoever among them has reached maturity, his guardian is commanded to hand over to him in deed, and whoever has not yet reached maturity, his guardian is commanded to hand over to him upon his reaching maturity and sound judgment (rushd). Many have preferred the first view, because of the Exalted's words after several verses: "And test the orphans" (etc.), for this is like evidence that the first verse is an exhortation to preserve it for them so that they may hand it over to them when they reach maturity and sound judgment. And the second verse is an exhortation to actual giving when maturity and sound judgment are attained. The use of "giving" here and "handing over" there hints at this. Also, the following of this verse by the Exalted's words:

"And do not substitute the bad for the good, and do not consume their property along with your own property" supports this. All of this is a discipline for the guardian as long as the property is in his hand and the orphan is in his care. As for the other views, the outcome of this verse and what comes after it will be like one thing, in that both contain the command to give in actuality. Whoever holds this view makes the first verse like a general statement and the second like a clarifying statement of the condition of giving, namely maturity and the perception of sound judgment. The last of the views is also open to objection: it involves a difficulty that is not hidden. The preferred view is not open to the objection that Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that a man from Ghatafan had a large amount of property belonging to a young orphaned nephew of his. When the nephew reached maturity he demanded the property, but his uncle refused him. So he brought the case before the Prophet (ﷺ), and the verse "And give the orphans" was revealed. This indicates that the meaning of giving is handing over in deed, especially since al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi narrated from Muqatil and al-Kalbi that when the uncle heard it, he said: "We obey Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ). We seek refuge with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from the great sin (hawb kabir)." Because they said: the lesson is in the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause. Perhaps the uncle did not understand the command to give to be explicit in the wording, but understood it from something else, so he said what he said.

This is the case, and the substitution of one thing for another, and exchanging it for it, means taking the first in place of the second after the second had been in one's possession or was about to come into possession. Both verbs are always used such that they lead to what is possessed by themselves, and to what is lost by means of the particle *bi*, as in the Exalted's words: "And whoever substitutes disbelief for faith" (etc.), and His words: "Do you exchange what is lower for what is better?" As for *tabdil* (replacement), it is sometimes used in the same way, as in the Exalted's words: "And We replaced for them their two gardens with two gardens" (etc.), and at other times in the reverse, as in your saying: "I replaced the ring with the signet ring," when you melted it and made it a signet ring, and "I replaced the signet ring with the ring," when you melted it and made it a ring. Al-Damiri restricted himself to the first, and al-Azhari transmitted the second from Tha'lab, and the verse of al-Tufayl when he became Muslim attests to it:

"And he replaced my ill omen with good fortune."

At other times it is used with its object directly, as in the Exalted's words: "Those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds" and "Then we wished that their Lord would replace them with one better than him," meaning that He will make good deeds in place of evil deeds and give them in place of what they had something better than it. Sometimes it is transitive to one object, as in *baddaltu al-shay'* (I changed the thing), meaning I altered it, and the Exalted's words: "And whoever changes it after hearing it." Al-Tibi mentioned that the meaning of *tabdil* is alteration, which is general, covering taking one thing and giving another, and seeking what one does not have and leaving what one has. This is the meaning of al-Jawhari's statement: "*Tabdil* of a thing is changing it, even if no replacement comes." The meaning of *tabaddul* is *istibdal* (exchanging), and *istibdal* is seeking a replacement. So every *tabaddul* is *tabdil*, but not every *tabdil* is *tabaddul*. Some distinguished between *tabdil* and *ibdal*: the former is changing a thing while its essence remains, and the latter is removing a thing and putting another in its place. So one says, "I replaced the signet ring with the ring," when you remove this and put that in its place. They have spoken at length on this point, and what has been mentioned is sufficient for our purpose.

The meaning of "the bad" and "the good" is either the unlawful and the lawful, and the meaning is: do not exchange the property of orphans for your own property, or do not leave your lawful property and consume the unlawful from their property. Thus the prohibited thing is exchanging an orphan's property for their own property in every way, or consuming his property in place of their own property, which is either actual or estimated. The first view was taken by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. It has also been said: the meaning is, do not exchange the bad matter, which is taking the orphan's property, for the good matter, which is safeguarding that property. In any case, the expression of that as "the bad" and "the good" is to deter them from what they took and to encourage them toward what they gave. Or the meaning is "the inferior" and "the superior," and the object of the prohibition is then what the guardians used to do: taking the superior from the orphan's property and giving the inferior from their own property. Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi that he said: one of them would take the fat sheep from the orphan's flock and put in its place the lean sheep, saying, "A sheep for a sheep." He would take the good dirham and put in its place the counterfeit one, saying, "A dirham for a dirham." This is the view of al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, and Ibn al-Musayyib. Restricting this transaction to the prohibition is because it came out in that manner according to custom, not to permit anything else. Therefore there is no implicit meaning (mafhum) in it, since its condition was lost, according to the one who holds this view.

Objection was raised against this: the more fitting reading then would be "substitution," or the substitution of the good by the bad, according to what the preceding discourse requires. The reply is that if the guardian gives a poor-quality item and takes a good one from the orphan's property, it is true to say that he has exchanged the poor for the good on behalf of the orphan and exchanged for himself. The apparent sense of the verse is that the exchange intended is the one on behalf of the orphan, because guardians are the ones who manage the property of orphans; so they were forbidden to sell at a loss, whether to themselves or to others, and what resembles this. There is no harm in an exchange for himself too, under another consideration, because what comes first to the understanding is the prohibition of any dealing for the sake of the orphan that is harmful, whether the guardian deals with himself or with someone else. Al-Zamakhshari, who was unaware of the difference in consideration, interpreted it in a way that the wording does not suggest. In any case, the meaning of the verse is the prohibition of taking the orphan's property in the specific manner, after the implicit prohibition of taking it in general. The word "eating" in the last prohibition means any kind of benefit and disposal; it was expressed by this because it is the most common of its uses. The meaning is: do not eat their property added to your property, that is, do not spend the two together and do not treat them as equal, while this is lawful and that is unlawful. So "ilā" is connected to an implied element that takes it, and it has come as a circumstantial phrase; Abu al-Baqa' estimated it as "joined to." It is permissible for it to be connected to "eating" by implying the meaning of joining. Some have preferred that it means "with," as in "the camel is to the camel," and by "being with" is meant merely the equalizing of the two properties in use, whether separately or together with their own property. From the "Kashshaf" it is understood that "being with" indicates the extreme ugliness of their act, since they ate their property while being free of need for it; and in this there is a public condemnation of what they used to do. Therefore it does not follow for the one who holds the argument of contrary implication that eating their property alone is permitted, and the objection is resolved by this.

You know that the objection does not arise needing an answer if the substitution of the bad by the good is explained as exchanging the orphans' property for one's own and eating it in its place, because then that is a prohibition against eating it alone, and this is a prohibition against combining it. The first is not absolute, so that the question would arise as to what benefit there is in this after the absolute prohibition has come. In the "Kashf": if the ending in "ilā" is taken in its original sense, the prohibition would be against eating it while their property remains, because their property being made the goal would achieve emphasis and an escape from the excuse. The apparent sense of this prohibition is the impermissibility of eating any part of the orphans' property, though the equivalent of the wage is excepted when the guardian is poor; and that this is from the orphan's property is not hard to see. So the saying that there is no need for specification, because what the guardians take as wage is their own, and eating it is not eating their property together with their property, is not free from obscurity.

"Innahu" [it]: that is, the eating understood from the prohibition. It was said: the pronoun refers to the substitution; and it was said: it refers to both, and it is treated as a demonstrative in that sense. "Kana huban" [was a great sin]: that is, a sin or an injustice; both are from Ibn Abbas, and they are close in meaning. Al-Tabarani related that Rafi' ibn al-Azraq asked him, may Allah be pleased with him, about "hub," and he said: it is sin in the language of Abyssinia. He said: "Do the Arabs know that?" He said: "Yes, have you not heard the saying of al-A'sha:

"Indeed I, and what you have burdened me with of your affairs,
it will be known who among them becomes more disobedient and more sinful."

Some restricted it to a great sin. Al-Hasan read "hawban" with a fatha on the ha', which is the verbal noun of "haba yahubu hawban." "Haban" was also read, and it too is a verbal noun, like "qawl" and "qal." On the well-known reading it is a noun rather than a verbal noun, contrary to some; and its tanwin is for magnification, meaning a great sin. It is described by His saying, exalted is He: "a great sin," for the emphasis on the terrifying nature of what is forbidden, as if it were said: it is one of the great sins, not one of their lesser kinds.

(Commentary of al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 4, verse 3, part 1 of 4)

﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly toward the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women﴾ — a beginning of the prohibition of another wrong which they used to commit, one that concerns the persons of orphans primarily and their wealth secondarily, coming right after the prohibition concerning what relates to their wealth exclusively. Its delay after that prohibition is due to the rarity of the forbidden act's occurrence with respect to wealth, and its placement after it is like the placement of the compound after the simple, although the intended meaning of "orphans" here is a category of what was intended by it earlier. That is because they used to marry those women among the orphan girls who were lawful to them, who were under their guardianship, but without any desire for them, rather for their wealth; they would mistreat them in companionship, and they would wait for them to die so that they could inherit from them. So they were admonished about this. This is the statement of al-Hasan. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related it from ʿAʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, and these same narrators, by another route, as did al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Nasa'i and al-Bayhaqi in his "Sunan," from ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr that he asked ʿAʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, about this verse, and she said: "O son of my sister, this is the orphan girl who is in the care of her guardian, who shares with her in her wealth, and he is attracted by her wealth and her beauty, so he wants to marry her without being just regarding her dowry, giving her what others would give her. So they were forbidden to marry them unless they act justly toward them and bring them up to the highest level of their dowry, and they were commanded to marry what seemed good to them of women other than them." So the intended meaning of "orphans" is those who are married, and the indication of this is that answer, for it is explicit in it and the connection requires it. "Women" means other than orphans, as ʿAʾisha, the Red-cheeked (al-Humayra'), clearly stated, due to the indication of meaning and the allusion of the word "women" to it.

"Al-iqsat" means justice and fairness. If the hamza in it is taken to denote removal, then its basic meaning becomes the removal of qusut, i.e., injustice and inequity. Al-Nakha'i read "tuqsitu" with a fatha on the ta'. It is said: it is from qasata, meaning "he deviated and wronged," and from it is ﴿And as for the qasitun, they will be fuel for Hell﴾, and the lam is extra, as in His saying ﴿so that he may not know﴾. It is also said: it means the same as aqsata, for al-Zajjaj related that qasata without a hamza is used in the same way as aqsata.

"Al-yatama" is the plural of "yatima," by inversion, as it is said "ayama" (widows); the original form was "ayaʾim" and "yataʾim." It is applied to males as it is applied to females. The meaning of "fear" here is knowledge; it is expressed by that to signal that what is known is feared and dreaded, not its literal meaning, because what the answer is attached to is knowledge of the occurrence of the oppression that causes fear, not fear of it; otherwise the command would not include the one who endures oppression without fearing it. "Inna" and what follows it are in the sense of a verbal noun. If "an" is not taken as governing "man," and the verb reaches it directly, then if "an" is considered, two options are permissible: the accusative according to Sibawayh and the genitive according to al-Khalil. "Ma" is either a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun, and what follows it is its relative clause or its qualifier. It was preferred over "man" with the consideration of the attribute, such as virgin or non-virgin, for example. "Ma" is specific to, or predominantly used for, non-rational beings when the essence is intended; when the attribute is intended, it is not so, as you say: "What is Zayd?" in a question, meaning "Is he virtuous or noble?" and "Honor whatever men you wish," meaning the noble or the base.

It is related from al-Farra' that here it is a verbal (masdariyya) particle, and that the verbal noun determined by it and by the verb is determined by the active participle, i.e., "marry the good [one]" from women. This is an unnecessary affectation. It is also said: its being preferred over "min" is based on the fact that females among the rational beings are treated like non-rational beings, because it is reported regarding them that they are deficient in intellect and religion. But this is objectionable, as it undermines the station of encouraging them. "Min" is explanatory; it is also said to be partitive. What is meant by "what seems good to you" is what your souls incline to and find pleasant. It is also said: what is lawful for you. This is reported from ʿAʾisha, and al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and Abu Malik said the same. Al-Imam objected to this, saying that it amounts to "permit what is permitted," and also it entails vagueness, since what is permitted is not known from the verse. He preferred the first interpretation, though it entails specification, and considered it preferable to vagueness. The meticulous scholar in "al-Kashf" replied that if the prohibition explained in His saying ﴿Prohibited to you are your mothers﴾ and so on was revealed earlier, there is neither vagueness nor specification, because the relative clause functions like a definite with the article, and reading it as a reference to a known referent is the proper approach in such a case. Otherwise, vague matter whose explanation is deferred is preferable to specification by something not concurrent, because deferring the explanation of the vague is permissible according to both groups, while deferring the explanation of specification is not permissible according to most Hanafis.

Some verifying scholars said: "what seems good to you" means what you are not troubled by, because it is in contrast to the one troubled by orphans, and this is not without merit. In any case, to refer to foreign women with this title contains an exaggeration in attracting them and encouraging them that is not hidden. The secret of this is attention to turning the addressees away from marrying orphans when fearing unjustness, out of consideration for their orphanhood and to console their brokenness. Because of this concern, the command to marry foreign women was preferred over the prohibition of marrying them, although the prohibition is the primary intent. This is for the greater gentleness in drawing them down, for the soul is naturally inclined to desire what it is forbidden. The implicit prohibition aims at the anticipated marriage, although the cause of revelation is the actual marriage, as some understood from the reports. The hadith of al-Bukhari from ʿAʾisha indicates this: "A man had an orphan girl whom he married, and she had a date-palm, and he would hold on to her with it, and he had no share of his own in her, so Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And if you fear﴾" and so on, because it hastens to avert evil before it occurs, for many an occurrence cannot be lifted. And there is exaggeration in stating the condition of the actual marriage, for the prohibition of the anticipated one is because of the anticipated injustice in it, so the prohibition of the actual one, with injustice certainly present in it, is more fitting.

Ibn Abi ʿAbla read "man ṭāba" [with "man"]; and in some copies of the Qur'an, as in "al-Durr al-Manthur," it is "mā ṭība lakum" with a ya'. On this interpretation, the verse indicates the permissibility of marrying an orphan girl, meaning a young one, since its permissibility is implied except when there is fear of injustice.

The matter has been extensively discussed in the books of jurisprudence concerning the guardian of marriage. The school of Imam Malik holds that a young orphan girl is not married off, since she has no consent. Within his school there is disagreement about a guardian (wasi) marrying her if her father gave him the right of compulsion (ijbar) or he understood that from him, and the prevailing view is that he has that right. Accordingly, the orphans in the verse are understood as those newly reaching puberty. The name "orphan" is as we indicated earlier.

﴿Two, three, or four﴾ — accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the hidden subject of "tāba," or from its referent. Al-ʿAllama permitted it to be a state from "women" on the assumption that "min" is explanatory. Abu al-Baqa' went to its being a substitute (badal) for "ma," and the Basrans went to its being a state, which is the preferred view, while the Kufans did not permit this because they regard these numerals as definite; they required in this context what Abu al-Baqa' stated. They are diptote (not declined with tanwin) according to the correct view, although al-Farra' permitted declining them. The reported reasons for their being diptote are four:

First: the statement of Sibawayh, al-Khalil and Abu ʿAmr, that it is due to "ʿadl" (derivation by deviation) and attributive quality. This was objected to on the basis that attributiveness in numerals is incidental and does not prevent declension. It was answered that although it was incidental in its origin, it was transferred from it after considering the incidental attribute, so it became original in this case rather than in its origin. This is not free from scrutiny.

Second: the statement of al-Farra': they are diptote due to ʿadl and definiteness by the intention of the article, which is why they cannot be annexed or preceded by the article.

Third: what is transmitted from al-Zajjaj, that they are derived from "ithnayn ithnayn" (two two), "thalatha thalatha" (three three) and "arba'a arba'a" (four four), so they deviated from the forms of numbers and from the feminine to the masculine, so there are two derivations, and these are two causes.

Fourth: what Abu al-Hasan transmitted from some grammarians, that the preventing cause is the repetition of ʿadl in it, since "mathna," for example, is derived from "ithnayn" in form and meaning, because it is not used where "ithnayn" is used; it does not govern operators, and it only occurs after a plural, either as predicate, state or attribute, and it is anomalous for it to govern operators or to be annexed.

Al-Safaqisi added a fifth cause to the prevention: ʿadl from a source other than ʿadl, because the rule of ʿadl is that it occurs in definites, and this is ʿadl in indefinites. And a sixth: ʿadl and plurality, because it requires repetition, so it became like the meaning of plurality. He said: Ibn al-Sa'igh in "Sharh al-Jumal" added these two. Also attested are "ahad" and "muwahhad," "thunaʾ" and "mathna," "thulath" and "mathlath," "rubaʿ" and "marbaʿ." Nothing beyond that was heard, as Abu ʿUbayda said, except in the verse of al-Kumayt:

"And your ṭāhir (spear-shaft?) did not conceal you until you cast above men qualities 'ishār'..."

For this reason they found fault with al-Mutanabbi's saying:

"Is it 'uhad' or 'sudas' in a single one, for our night bound to the summons?"

Some people permitted "khumas" and "mukhammas" up to the end of the decade by analogy, but this is nothing.

The repetition and the conjunction with "waw" were chosen so that the verse conveys that each of the addressees may choose from these listed numbers whatever number he wishes, since that is what is intended, not that some of them are for some and others for others. Had you listed the numbers without repetition, it would be understood to permit combining those numbers without distribution. Had they been mentioned with "aw" (or), the permission of variation in number would be lost, such that one man marries two and another three or four. As for what is said, that the mind does not turn to it because no one holds it, the reply is that the discussion concerns the apparent meaning, which is the point of the deviation. Some verifying scholars claimed that if the numerals were used without indicating repetition, it would not be valid to make them a state, explaining that all lawful good things are not in the state of being two, nor in the state of being three. Likewise, if one said: "Divide this wealth, which is a thousand dirhams, into a dirham, two, three and four," it would not be valid to make the number a state of the wealth which is a thousand dirhams, because the state of a thousand is not that; this differs from when it is repeated, for then the intent is detail in the matter of distribution, as if it were said: "Marry the good women for yourselves, detailed and divided into two two, three three, four four." And: "Divide this wealth, which is a thousand dirhams, detailed and divided into a dirham a dirham, two two, three three, four four." By this, the invalidity of the claim becomes clear that there is no difference between "ithnayn" and "mathna" in the validity of the state, because the sense of distribution is evident from the second and not the first, as is not hidden. And that He used "waw" rather than "aw" only to convey that the divisions are in these kinds without going beyond them to what is above them, not that they are one of these kinds without combining two of them. This rests on the premise that the state is an explanation of the manner of the action, and the restriction in the statement negates its opposite, while "waw" is not for one of two options as "aw" is. By this, the view of some who permitted nine is refuted, relying on the claim that "waw" is for combination, so two, three and four, which total nine, would be allowed. This is because whoever marries five or more has not kept to the restriction, namely the manner of marriage, which in this case is that it be distributed as detailed, but has exceeded it to beyond. Perhaps this is what al-Qutb meant by his statement: when God concluded the numbers at four, there was no room for them to exceed it, otherwise their marriage would be five and five; so the statement of some of them:

The argument that this is a restriction is invalid, because the speech does not indicate restriction. If a man tells his son, "Do whatever you wish: go to the market, to the school, and to the orchard," this is an explicit delegation to him of the reins of choice in general, and the lifting of restraint from him. It is not a restriction of the permission to those things mentioned. Rather, it is a permission for what was mentioned and for other things as well. The same applies here. Moreover, mentioning all the numbers is impossible, so if some numbers are mentioned after ﴿Marry what seems good to you of women﴾, that would be an indication that permission is granted for all numbers. This is a statement that is out of place, and there is a clear difference between what we are discussing and the example just given.

Imam al-Razi mentioned the argument of those who permit marriage with any number desired, and he extended his discussion on this point. However, he did not offer anything that would ease the heart or relieve the mind. He said: "A group of outliers (shudhdhadh) went to the permissibility of marrying any number and argued from the Qur'an and the Report (khabar). As for the Qur'an, they held to this verse in three respects. The first: the word of Him, glorified is He, ﴿Marry what seems good to you of women﴾ is an unrestricted statement covering all numbers, as evidence that there is no number which cannot be made an exception from it, and the ruling of an exception is to exclude what would otherwise have been included. The second: ﴿two, three, and four﴾ is not suitable to specify that generality, because specification by some does not negate the ruling's establishment for the remainder. The third: the waw (and) is for absolute conjunction, so ﴿two, and three, and four﴾ conveys the permissibility of the whole group, which is nine, or rather eighteen. As for the Report, it is in two respects. The first: it is established by mass transmission (tawatur) that the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, died leaving nine wives, and then Allah, exalted is He, commanded us to follow him, saying, ﴿and follow him﴾, and the least level of a command is permissibility. The second: the sunnah of a man is his way, and marrying more than four is the way of the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, so that is a sunnah for him. Then the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'Whoever turns away from my sunnah is not of me.' The apparent meaning of the Hadith requires that blame be directed at whoever abandons marrying more than four, so at the very least the basic permissibility is established." Then he said: "Know that the reliance of the jurists in establishing the restriction (al-hasr) is on two matters. The first is the Report, which is what is narrated: that Ghaylan embraced Islam while he had ten wives, and the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'Keep four and separate from the rest of them.' This route is weak for two reasons. The first: since the Qur'an indicates non-restriction, if we were to establish restriction by this Report, that would be abrogation (naskh) of the Qur'an by a solitary report (khabar al-wahid), and that is not permissible. The second: perhaps he, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, only commanded keeping four and separating from the rest because combining four with the rest is impermissible, either due to kinship or due to fosterage. In sum, this possibility exists in this Report, so the Qur'an cannot be abrogated by something like it. The second matter is the consensus (ijma') of the jurists of the major cities that it is not permissible to exceed four. This is the reliance, but there are two objections to it. The first: consensus cannot be abrogated by it, so how can it be said that consensus abrogated this verse? The second: among the Umma there are groups of outliers who do not hold that exceeding four is forbidden, and consensus is not formed when one or two dissent." End of quotation. I answer the first objection: consensus reveals that an abrogating (nasikh) matter existed in the time of the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him. And I answer the second: the dissenter from this consensus is among the people of innovation (ahl al-bid'ah), so his dissent carries no weight, and it does not harm the formation of consensus."

It is not hidden what is problematic in the outliers' argument from the verse, and this will be known from reflection on what we have mentioned.

As for the argument from the Report, it is also worthless, because consensus has occurred that exceeding four is one of the particularities (khususiyyat) of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, while we are commanded to follow him and to desire his sunnah, peace be upon him, in matters other than those known to be among the particularities. As for matters known to be among them, we are not so commanded. As for the two matters on which the jurists relied in this context, they are in the utmost firmness.

[Page 193]

The first objection to the first of the two matters is that the Imam's statement in it, "Since the Qur'an indicates non-restriction," etc., is disputed. How can that be, when what indicates restriction has already been understood from it? And even if it does not indicate restriction, it does not indicate non-restriction. At most it is ambiguous between the two, and then it is mujmal (ambiguous, requiring clarification), and clarifying the mujmal by a solitary report is permissible, as has been explained in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh). As for what was mentioned in the second objection, the two grounds of weakening, namely that the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, perhaps only commanded keeping four and separating from the rest because combining is impermissible, either due to kinship or due to fosterage, this is hardly acceptable given the indefinite form of "four" (arba'an) and the establishment of the phrase "choose four of them" as in some sound narrations of the Hadith of Ghaylan. Likewise in the Hadith that Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Nahhas narrated from Qays ibn al-Harith al-Asadi, who said: "I embraced Islam and I had eight wives, so I informed the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and he said: 'Choose four of them and release the rest,' and I did so." This indicates undoubtedly that the intention is to retain any four, not four specific ones. So the possibility mentioned by the Imam is merely a potential (qa'id), not an actual (qa'im) objection. If such a possibility were considered a defect in evidence, no evidence would remain on the face of the earth.

Yes, the Hadith poses a difficulty for the position of the Imam al-A'zam (Abu Hanifah), as transmitted by Ibn Hubayrah regarding a man who embraced Islam while having more than four wives: if the marriage contracts were concluded with them all in a single instance, it is void; and if they were in separate contracts, the marriage in the first four is valid, and then he has no choice. The three Imams disagreed with him on this, but that is another issue, and we are not concerned with it here.

The strongest of the two matters relied upon for restriction is consensus. It has occurred, and the era of those who formed the consensus passed before any dissenter appeared. Consensus does not require the agreement of the entire Umma from the time of his mission, peace be upon him, until the Hour, as the words of Imam al-Ghazali seem to imply; otherwise no consensus would exist at all. With this we dispense with what Imam al-Razi mentioned, which is one of the positions on the matter: that the dissenter from this consensus is among the people of innovation, so his dissent is disregarded. Rather, the truth from which there is no escape is that exceeding four is forbidden. This is the view of the Imamiyyah (Twelver Shi'ah), who narrated from al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him: "It is not lawful for a man's water to flow into more than four wombs." What is widespread from them is the opposite of this, but perhaps this is an anomalous view among them.

Furthermore, the legitimacy of marrying four is specific to free men, and slaves are not included in this address, because it applies to a person when a woman is lawful to him and he is able to marry her, whereas the slave is not in this position, since his marriage is not permissible without the permission of his master, based on the word of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him: "Whichever slave marries without the permission of his master, he is an adulterer (ahir)." Also, executing his marriage involves a defect for him, since marriage is a defect in him, so he does not possess it without the master's permission. Also, the subsequent word of the Exalted, ﴿And if you fear that you will not be just, then one, or what your right hands possess﴾, cannot include slaves, since they do not own. Since they are not included in this address, they are not included in the first address either, because these addresses came in succession in a single sequence, and it is unlikely that something would be included in the earlier address but not in the later one. Likewise, they cannot be included in the word of the Exalted: ﴿And if they give you willingly some of it, then consume it with satisfaction and ease﴾, because a slave does not possess, so what he has belongs to his master.
