Imam Malik disagreed on this, and included the slaves in the address, and permitted them to marry four like free men, without their marriage depending on permission, because they possess divorce, and so they possess marriage. Some jurists claimed that the apparent meaning of the verse includes them, but that this generality is specified by analogy, because slavery has an effect in diminishing the rights of marriage, such as divorce and the waiting period ('iddah). And since the number is among the rights of marriage, it is necessary that the slave be given half of what the free man has in this as well.

They differed regarding the command to marry. It was said that it is for permissibility, and the word ﴿seems good﴾ (tayyaba) is not idle if it means "permitted," because the meaning becomes: "What is permitted here is permitted to you," since the point of benefit lies in the restriction, namely the mentioned number. It was also said that it is for obligation, i.e., the obligation to limit oneself to this number, not the obligation of marriage itself. Imam al-Nawawi said: "No one is known to have made marriage obligatory except Dawud and those who agree with him among the Zahiris, and a report from Ahmad, for they said: it is binding on him, if he fears sin (al-'anat), to marry or to take a concubine. They said: it is obligatory for him only once in his life. Some did not stipulate the fear of sin. The Zahiris said: he is only obliged to marry, but not obliged to have intercourse . . . The scholars differed on whether marriage or abstaining from it is better. Al-Nawawi mentioned that people in this matter are of four categories: one whose soul yearns for it and who finds the means, for whom marriage is recommended; one who does not yearn and does not find the means, for whom it is disliked; one who yearns but does not find the means, for whom it is also disliked, and this one is commanded to fast to suppress the desire; and one who finds the means but whose soul does not yearn, and the school of al-Shafi'i and the majority of the Shafi'is hold that for this person, abstaining from marriage and devoting himself to worship is better. It is not said that marriage is disliked, but rather that abstaining from it is better. The view of Abu Hanifah and some of the companions of Malik and al-Shafi'i is that marriage is better for him." End of the intended quotation.

You know that what is stated in the books of our masters the Hanafis, both texts and commentaries, differs from what this Imam mentioned in verifying the school of the Imam al-A'zam, may Allah be pleased with him. In "Tanwir al-Absar" and its commentary "al-Durr al-Mukhtar," in the Book of Marriage, the text reads: "It becomes obligatory when desire is strong. If one is certain that he will fall into fornication without it, it becomes an obligation, as in "al-Nihayah." This applies if he possesses the dower and the maintenance; otherwise there is no sin in abandoning it, as in "al-Bada'i'." It is a confirmed sunnah in the more correct view, so he is sinful for abandoning it and rewarded if he intends chastity and offspring, in the state of moderation, meaning the capacity for intercourse, dower, and maintenance."

"Al-Nahr" preferred that it is obligatory, because of the constant practice of it and the censure of whoever turns away from it, and that it is disliked out of fear of injustice; but if one is certain of injustice, it is forbidden." End of quotation. However, regarding the evidence for obligation according to what the author of "al-Nahr" stated, there is an argument from the opponents, and the full discussion belongs in its proper place.

[Page 194]

This is a commentary passage; I translate it as it stands.

Furthermore, it has been said regarding the noble verse that the intended meaning of "women" here also includes orphans, and that the meaning is: "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans reared in your guardianship, then marry what is good for you of the orphan women of your relatives." This view was held by al-Jubba'i, and it is as you see. It has also been said that when the verse concerning orphans and the great sin of consuming their property was revealed, the guardians began to shrink from their guardianship out of fear that the sin of failing to act justly would befall them. Yet they were not scrupulous about failing to be just in the rights of women, for a man among them might have ten wives. So it was said to them: "If you fear failing to be just in the rights of orphans, and you are scrupulous about that, then fear also failing to be just among women, and reduce the number of those you marry, for whoever shrinks from a sin, or repents of it while committing its like, is neither scrupulous nor repentant of it." This view was held by Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, Qatadah, al-Rabi', al-Dahhak, and Ibn 'Abbas in one of the reports from him. It has also been said: they were not scrupulous about adultery, yet they were scrupulous about guardianship of orphans, so it was said: "If you fear sin regarding the rights of orphans, then fear adultery, and marry what is lawful to you of women, and do not hover around what is forbidden." An analogous case is that of one who persists in prayer but does not give zakah: you tell him, "If you fear sin in neglecting prayer, then fear sin in neglecting zakah." Something close to this was held by Mujahid.

The scholar Shaykh al-Islam critiqued these two views, saying: "It is not hidden that the eloquence of the noble composition does not support them, since they rest on the earlier revelation of the first verse and its wide circulation among people, and on the evident dependence of its ruling on what follows it, from His exalted saying: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾ up to His glorified saying: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Reckoner﴾." It is also understood from the words of some verifying scholars that the more apparent view regarding the verse is that related by al-Shaykhan and others from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, rather than these two views. This is because the verse according to that report corresponds to His exalted saying: ﴿They ask you concerning women. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and what is recited to you in the Book concerning orphan women to whom you do not give what is prescribed for them, yet you desire to marry them﴾, so the two verses agree. This is not possible under the two views; rather, there is no connection between the two verses on them, because their implication is that the discussion concerns orphans in general, not orphan women. Moreover, the two views are weakened by the fact that the condition is not connected to the answer with them except through a general aspect. As for the first: injustice toward women in respect of their rights is like injustice toward orphans, in that each is an injustice. As for the second: adultery is forbidden, just as injustice toward orphans is forbidden, and many forbidden things share with them in prohibition, so there is no particular link tying the condition and the answer as there is in the former case. Furthermore, the apparent sense of His glorified saying: ﴿Two, three, or four﴾ is that it comes in the form of widening [latitude] for them with a kind of restriction, as if it were said: "If you fear [wrong] in marrying orphans, then there is ample room in other women up to such-and-such." On the first of the two views, the intent would be restriction, for its outcome would be: "If you fear injustice toward women, then take precaution by reducing the number of those you marry." This contradicts what the context implies of widening, and is far from the eloquence of the revelation, as is not hidden.

It has been said that a man would marry four, five, six, or ten, and say, "What prevents me from marrying as so-and-so married?" Then when his wealth ran out, he would take from the property of the orphan in his custody and spend it. So the guardians of orphans were forbidden to exceed four, so that they would not need to take the orphan's property. This is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah. According to this, the intended sense of "orphans" is more general, covering males and females, and likewise on the two views before it.

It was objected to this that it implies the permissibility of exceeding four for one who does not need to take the orphan's property, and that this contradicts the consensus. Also, the intended sense of this command would be restriction, and that, as you know, contradicts what the context implies, which is emphasized by His exalted saying: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly, then [marry] one﴾. It is as if, when He widened [the permission] for them, He informed them that widening may lead to fear of inclination; so the obligation then is to be cautious by limiting, and to confine oneself to one.

The intended meaning is: "If you fear that you will not be just among these counted [wives], even in the smallest of the numbers mentioned, as you feared [injustice] regarding orphans, or as you have not been just toward them, then choose; or adhere to one, and leave off all of them entirely."

Ibrahim read "wuluth wa ruba'" (thuluth and rubu') with the short vowel form instead of "thalath wa rubaa'". Abu Ja'far read "fa-wahidatun" (fa-wāḥidatun) with the nominative, meaning: "then the sufficient [option] is one," or "then one suffices," or "then what suffices you is one," or "then the one who is married is one."

﴿Or what your right hands possess﴾: that is, of the concubines, of whatever age they may be, as is taken from the context. The contrast with "one" and its coordination with "one" [implies] that obligation and choice here are by way of concubinage, not by way of marriage, as in what is coordinated with it. This is because marriage applied to a right of ownership would entail the marital bond falling upon the ownership of the right hand, given the unity of the addressees in both places. They have said: a master may not marry his female slave, nor may a woman marry her male slave, because marriage was legislated only to produce shared fruits between the two spouses, and slavery contradicts ownership, so the fruit cannot be realized in a partnership. This is unlike what His glorified saying will mention later: ﴿And whoever among you is not able to afford to marry free believing women, then [marry] from what your right hands possess of your believing young women﴾, for the one commanded to marry there is other than those addressed as owners by right of possession. Some scholars supply in the coordinated term "then marry" (fankihu), since the beginning of the sentence indicates it, and this is coordinated with it in the sense of "confine yourselves to what your right hands possess." The statement is in the manner of his saying:

"I fed her straw and cold water."

The particle "aw" here denotes equivalence, and the single free woman and the concubines are made equal in ease and facility, without restriction, because of the small burden of their dependents, the lightness of their maintenance, and the non-obligation of equal division among them. Some claimed that this is coordinated with "women," meaning: "then marry what is good for you of women or of what your right hands possess," but its remoteness is not hidden. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "man malakat" (whoever they possess). The well-known reading uses "ma," for the attribute is intended, and since the owned thing is for buying and selling, and most of what is sold is non-rational, the expression with "ma" is more apparent. The attribution of ownership to the right hand is because its usual cause is the transaction made with it. It was also said: because it is first obtained through jihad and capture, which requires their labor; and this is well known regarding slaves, especially their females, which is what is intended here, in keeping with the contrast between it and the marital ownership applied to free women. It was also said: the right of ownership is called "right hand ownership" only because it is distinguished by excellence, and there is in it an omen of good fortune (yumn). Some reported that a bedouin was asked: "Why have you made the names of your clients beautiful, rather than the names of your sons?" He said: "The names of our clients are for us, and the names of our sons are for our enemies." So let this be understood.

Ibn al-Faras claimed that the verse refutes those who hold marriage to be obligatory upon every individual, because He, exalted is He, gave a choice in it between marriage and concubinage, and concubinage is not obligatory by consensus; and if marriage were obligatory, He would not have offered a choice between it and concubinage, since in the science of legal theory, it is not valid to give a choice between an obligatory act and something else, as this would lead to nullifying the reality of obligation, and its abandoner would not be sinful. This does not refute the one who says: "The obligatory is one of two things." Nor does it contradict the consensus that concubinage is not obligatory in general. So reflect.

Some claimed that the verse contains evidence for prohibiting marriage to jinn women, because He, exalted is He, singled out women for mention. But you know that the argument from opposite implication (mafhum al-mukhalafa) is not considered valid here according to its proponent, because the wisdom behind singling out women for mention and its purpose is evident.

Imam al-Suyuti claimed that the verse contains an allusion to the permissibility of looking before marriage, because it is by this that the good (al-tayyib) is known. It is not hidden that the allusion may be sound, but restriction (al-hasr) is disputed, and this solution is established in more than one hadith. In Sahih Muslim: "He (ﷺ) said to a man who was marrying a woman of the Ansar: 'Did you look at her?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'Go and look at her, for there is something in the eyes of the Ansar.'" This is the view of the majority of scholars. It is reported from some people that they disliked it, but they are refuted by the hadith and by the consensus on the permissibility of looking out of need in buying, selling, testimony, and the like. Then, looking is permitted only to the face and the two palms. Al-Awza'i said: to the places of flesh. Dawud said: to her whole body, and this is a manifest error, opposed to the foundations of the Sunnah and consensus. Is the woman's consent required or not? The majority hold that consent is not required; rather the man may look even while she is unaware and does not consent. Malik reported disliking looking while she is unaware, and in one weak report from him: it is not permitted to look at her except with her consent. Many have found it commendable that this looking take place before the proposal, so that if he dislikes her he may leave her without causing harm, unlike if he leaves her after the proposal, as is not hidden.

Some said: the verse also contains an allusion to the recommendation of exceeding one wife for one who does not fear failing to be just, because He, exalted is He, put the command to marry more first and tied the command to one to the fear of not being just. How sweet is the plurality of wives if they agree, and the plural of feminine nouns after the dual is correctly declined with a damma among all the other vowels! But this, by my life, is further than the Pleiades (al-'Ayyuq) and rarer than red sulphur and the eggs of the Anuq bird:

"Not everything a man wishes for does he attain; the winds blow in ways the ships do not desire."

"That" (dhalika) refers to the choice of one, or to concubinage, or to all of them, and the last is the better; this is indicated by the words of Ibn Abi Zayd. "Closer to not being unjust" ('awl): in origin, 'awl means perceptible inclination; one says: "the scale inclined (ala al-mizan 'awlan)" when it tilted. Then it was transferred to moral inclination, which is injustice, and from it: "the ruler became unjust (ala al-hakim)" when he acted unjustly. The intended meaning here is forbidden inclination, the opposite of justice; that is, what has been mentioned, namely choosing one or concubinage, is nearer, compared with what is other than them, to your not inclining in forbidden inclination, since it is entirely absent in the first case because its locus is absent, and its danger is absent in the second, unlike choosing a number in multiple marriages, for forbidden inclination is expected there, since both its locus and danger are present. Some verifying scholars held this view. Others allowed that the reference is to three things: reducing the number of wives, choosing one, and concubinage; that is, these three are nearer than all that is other than them. The first is more apparent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 3 (part 4 of 4):

It has been related from the Imam al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, that he explained ﴿ألا تَعُولُوا﴾ (an tʿaʿulū, "that you not be unjust" / "that you not have many dependants") as meaning "that your dependants not be many." Al-Shihab (al-Alusi) mentions that he was considered to have erred in this, and many of the earlier scholars (al-mutaqaddimin) held him to be above that, because it is only said of one whose dependants have increased: aʿala yuʿilu iʿalatan (أعال يُعيل إعالة), and they did not say ʿala yaʿulu (عال يَعُول). It is answered that al-Imam al-Shafi'i, in this explanation, followed the path of metonymy (al-kinaya). He, may Allah be pleased with him, took the verb in the verse to be from ʿala al-rajulu ʿiyalahu yaʿūluhum (عال الرجل عياله يعولهم), like your saying māna-hum yamūnu-hum (مانهم يمونهم) when he spent on them. Whoever has many dependants is obliged to support them, so he used "spending" and meant its necessary consequence, which is the multiplicity of dependants. It is objected that ʿāla in the sense of māna and anfaqa has no indication of great expense, so that it could be used metonymically for a large number of dependants. It is answered that al-Raghib mentioned that the original meaning of al-ʿawl is heaviness; one says ʿālahu, meaning he bore the burden of his expense, and heaviness occurs with much spending, not with little. So what is intended by ﴿لا تَعُولُوا﴾ is the great amount of spending, by the indication of the context and the setting, because the intended meaning is not the negation of expense and dependants altogether, since whoever marries one wife is a supporter (ʿaʾil) and bears expense. Thus the speech is almost explicit in this, and the use of the root meaning of the verb for an increase in it is not rare, so there is no dust (no difficulty).

It is mentioned in al-Kashf that there is no need for the original answer concerning the Imam al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, for al-Kisa'i transmitted from the eloquent Arabs that ʿāla yaʿūlu when his dependants increased, and among those who transmitted it are al-Asma'i and al-Azhari. This explanation was transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim from Zayd ibn Aslam, who is among the great Successors (ajillat al-tabi'in). The reading of Tawus, an tu'ilū (أن لا تُعيلوا), supports it, so there is no basis for the censure of those who censured the Imam while being ignorant of the languages and reports. Al-Duri, the imam of the readers (imam al-qurra'), transmitted that it is the dialect of Himyar, and he recited:

"Indeed death seizes every living being, without doubt, even if he walks [with much livestock] and has many dependants (wa-ʿālā)."

That is, even if his livestock and his dependants are many.

As for what is said, that ʿāla in the sense of "his dependants increased" is from the ya' (yāʾī), and in the sense of "oppressed" (jāra) is from the waw (wāwī), the objection is not to the use of ʿāla for the increase of dependants, but to the failure to distinguish between the two roots. This was also answered by what the words of some imply: that ʿāla has meanings: to incline, to oppress, to become poor, to have many dependants, to spend, and to be unable (aʿjaza). One says ʿālanī al-amr, meaning it overcame me, and its present tense is yaʿīlu and yaʿūlu, so it is of the waw and ya' roots according to the differing meanings. Then the meaning of "dependants" according to this explanation may be the wives, as we have pointed out, and the non-multiplicity of wives in choosing one is clear, and likewise in reducing [to one] if we say it is included in what is referred to. As for not having many concubines (tasarri), it is by the consideration that this applies to having none at all.

It may also be that the dependants are the children, and that not having many of them in choosing one (wife) and likewise in reducing is also clear. As for not having many of them through concubines, it is by the consideration that this is a likely cause of few children, since the custom is that a man does not restrict himself to lying with concubines and does not refuse withdrawal (ʿazl) from them. This is unlike the free wives (mahāʾir), for the custom is that a man restricts himself to lying with them and refuses withdrawal from them. Although withdrawal from them, like withdrawal from concubines, is permitted by the Shari'a, with or without permission, according to the well-known position of the school of al-Shafi'i. In some commentaries on al-Kashshaf there is something indicating that there is disagreement on this among the Shafi'is, so some of them forbade it, as is the position of Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna that he explained ﴿ألا تَعُولُوا﴾ as "that you not become poor." We have already mentioned that ʿāla comes in the sense of "became poor," and from its usage in this sense is his saying:

"The poor man does not know when his wealth will come, and the rich man does not know when he will become needy (yaʿīlu)."

However, the verb in the verse is of the ya' root and not the waw root as in the verse, and the matter here is easy, as you have come to know. According to all the other explanations, the sentence is a new clause (mustaʾnifa), running in relation to what precedes it in the manner of a reason clause (ta'lil).

**[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 4 (part 1 of 2)]**

﴿And give the women their dowers﴾, i.e., give the women whom it has been commanded to marry them their *ṣadaqāt* (dowries). *Ṣadaqāt* is the plural of *ṣadaqah* with a fatḥah on the ṣād and a ḍammah on the dāl. It is like *ṣadāq* (dowry), meaning the *mahr* (bridal gift). It has also been read as *ṣadaqātihinna* with a fatḥah on the ṣād and a sukūn on the dāl, and its origin is with a ḍammah on the dāl, which was lightened by making it sukūn. It has also been read as *ṣudqātihinna* with a ḍammah on the ṣād and a sukūn on the dāl, the plural of *ṣudqah* on the pattern of *ghurfah*. And it has been read as *ṣudqatahunna* with a ḍammah on both the ṣād and the dāl, in the singular, and its origin is *ṣudqah* with a ḍammah on the ṣād and a sukūn on the dāl, and the dāl was given a ḍammah to match the ḍammah of the first letter, just as it is said *ẓulmah* and *ẓulmah*.

﴿*Niḥlah*﴾ means *farīḍah* (an obligation), as stated by Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Jurayj and Qatādah. It is in the accusative as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier, i.e., a state-accusative) of *al-ṣadaqāt*, meaning: give them their dowers in the state of being an obligation from Allah Most High upon them. Al-Zajjāj and Ibn Khālawayh said: *tadayyunan* (as a religious duty). Its accusative then is as an object of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*), meaning: give them out of religious observance and law. Al-Kalbī said: a gift and a grant from Allah and a favour from Him Most High upon them. Its accusative is then likewise as a *ḥāl* of *al-ṣadaqāt*. It has also been said: a gift from the husbands to them, and its accusative is then as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), or as a *ḥāl* of the pronoun in *ātū* (give), or of *al-nisāʾ* (the women), or of *ṣadūqātihinna*.

It has been objected that the *ḥāl* is a qualifier of the governing verb, so here the giving would be a qualifier of the giving, and a thing cannot qualify itself. The answer is that *niḥlah* is not the absolute giving but a type of it, namely giving out of goodwill. The meaning is: give them their dowers, being content in giving, or giving willingly out of goodwill. On this reading, the verbal noun specifies the type.

If you say: *niḥlah* also includes in its meaning the absence of a return, so how can the dower be without return when it is in exchange for the sexual relation and enjoyment of her? The answer: since the wife in intercourse has the like of what the husband has, or more, and she has additional benefit through the obligation of maintenance and clothing, the dower was a gift in return for enjoyment that is greater than it. It has also been said that the dower in the law of those before us was due to the guardians, as evidenced by the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿I intend to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine﴾ (28:27), etc. Then it was abrogated (*nusikha*, i.e., naskh, abrogation, the replacement of a ruling by a later one), and it became a gift specified for them, and so it was called *niḥlah*. Several scholars supported the statement of al-Kalbī: that what the word *niḥlah* was originally set for is a gift without return, as the Rummānī and a group of others held. From this sense was derived: *niḥlah* as religious obligation, since it is like the *niḥlah* (gift) of Allah Most High; and *naḥl* (bee) for the hive, because of the honey it gives; and *nāḥil* for the emaciated, because it takes its flesh little by little, as if it gives it without return; and *manḥūl* for poetry that is attributed (falsely) to a poet, since it is a poet's gift of what is not his.

Given this, whoever interprets *niḥlah* as *farīḍah* (obligation) looks at the fact that this giving is an obligation. The address, according to what is most apparent, is to the husbands. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās and a group, and al-Ṭabarī, al-Jubbāʾī and others preferred it. It was said: a man would marry without a dower, saying: "I inherit from you and you inherit from me?" She would say: "Yes." So they were commanded to hasten to give the dowers. It has also been said that the address is to the guardians of the women. Ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū Ṣāliḥ that he said: when a man married off a widow (*ayyim*), he would take her dower instead of her. So Allah Most High forbade them from this, and the verse ﴿And give the women their dowers﴾ etc. was revealed. Al-Jārūd from the Imāmiyyah reported this from al-Bāqir, may Allah be pleased with him. This is the custom of many Arabs today, and it is forbidden, like the husbands' consuming any portion of the women's dowers without their consent.

﴿And if they remit to you anything of it willingly﴾. The pronoun refers to the *ṣadaqāt*, and it is masculine because it is treated as the *dhālika* (that), since it is often pointed to with this for a plurality, as in the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something better than that?﴾ (3:15), after the mention of the enumerated desires. It has been reported from Abū ʿUbayda that he said: I said to Ru'bah about his saying:

*There are in it lines of black and white,*
*as if on the hide is the spotting of leprosy.*

"If you mean the lines, then say *ka-annahā* (as if they), and if you mean the black and the white, then say *ka-annahumā* (as if both)." He said: "I mean *ka-anna dhālik*, woe to you!" Or, the *ṣadāq* (dowry) occupying its place: *ṣadaqātuhunna* is as if it were said: "Give the women their dowers." Interpreting by meaning is common, and among it is the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿so that I may give charity and be among the righteous﴾ (63:10), where it is conjoined to what is implied by what was mentioned and occupies its place. Or the pronoun refers to the dower that is implicit in the plural, since the meaning is: give each of the women a dower. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the giving (*itāʾ*). This is objected to: it is only correct if by it is meant the thing given, and a pronoun referring back to a verbal noun that is understood is not free from remoteness, and interpreting that verbal noun in the sense of the object is also somewhat remote. The *lām* (in *lakum*) is connected to the verb, and likewise *ʿan* (in *ʿan shay'in*) by including in it the sense of turning away and withdrawing; otherwise its basic usage for such a meaning would be with *bāʾ*, as in the saying:

*And he hardly willingly accepts parting from his soul.*

*Min* (in *min shay'in*) is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of *shay'* (a thing), meaning: existing from the dowers. In this is an incitement to them to reduce what is given, to the point that it is reported from al-Layth that their giving is not permitted except for a small amount. There is no difference between what has been received and what is still owed, except that the first is a gift and the second is a release. For this reason people have dealt with compensation in it, so that the disagreement is removed.

﴿*Nafsan*﴾ is a specifier (*tamyīz*, the accusative that specifies the meaning of a noun or clause) for the explanation of the kind, and for this it is in the singular. The clarification of this, according to what some verifiers said, is that the *tamyīz*, as the grammarians say, if its meaning agrees with what it specifies, the agreement is required, as in *karuma al-zaydūna rijālan* (the Zaydūn were noble, men), like the predicate, the qualifier and the circumstantial. Otherwise, if it is singular and not plural, it must be singular, as in *karuma banū fulānin abban* (the sons of so-and-so were noble, as a father), since the meaning is that their origin is one, characterized by nobility. If it is plural and there is ambiguity, it must be followed by an apparent noun, as in *karuma al-zaydūna ābāʾan* (the Zaydūn were noble, as fathers), when it is meant that each of them has a noble father, since if it were in the singular it would be imagined that they were from one father, and that is not the intent. If there is no ambiguity, both are permitted. The justification for the singular is the absence of ambiguity, as here, since it is not imagined that they have one single soul. Its preference is that it is the original form, with lightness, and its agreement with the pronoun in *minhu* (from it), which is a noun of kind (*ism jins*), and the purpose here is to specify the kind, and the singular indicates it, as when you say: *ʿishrūna dirhaman* (twenty dirhams). The meaning is: if they give you some of the dower with their souls detached from it, pure, not corrupted, by which they are not compelled to give out of the harshness of your character and the badness of your treatment. The noble text was chosen over the formulation *fa-in wahabna lakum shay'an minhu ʿan ṭībin nafsin* (if they give you something of it out of goodwill) to indicate that the essence of the matter is goodwill of the soul and the soul's complete detachment from what is given, since that was made the beginning and a pillar of the sentence, not a supplement, as in the hypothetical structure.

﴿Then consume it﴾, i.e., consume that thing from which their souls have been content to part, and dispose of it by taking possession. The specification of consumption by mention is because it is the greatest form of financial disposal.

﴿With enjoyment and ease﴾. These are two qualifiers of *hanua al-ṭaʿām yahnuʾu hanāʾatan* and *maruʾa yamruʾu marāʾatan*, when the food is not heavy on the stomach and goes down it pleasantly. In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*, quoting al-Akhfash, it is said: *hanuʾa* and *hanuʾa*, and *maruʾa* and *mariʾa*, just as it is said *faqaha* and *faqiha* with a kasrah and a ḍammah on the qāf. It is said: *hanaʾanī al-ṭaʿām yuhannʾunī* and *yahnaʾunī*, and there is no parallel to it in the hamzated verbs (*hanaʾa* and *hanuʾa*). You say: *hanaʾtu al-ṭaʿām*, i.e., I enjoyed the food. Likewise it is said: *maraʾanī al-ṭaʿām yamraʾu marʾan*. Some said: *amraʾanī*. Al-Farrāʾ said: it is said *hanaʾanī al-ṭaʿām* and *maraʾanī* without an alif. When they separate it from *hanaʾanī*, they say: *amraʾanī*. It was also said: *al-hanīʾ* is what the eater finds pleasant, and *al-marīʾ* is what its outcome is praised for. It was said: it is what slides smoothly along its passage, which is the *marīʾ* (gullet), like *amīr*, and it is the head of the stomach, and the tripe adjacent to the windpipe; it was named after it because food passes through it, i.e., its smooth sliding.

Their accusative, as al-Zamakhsharī said, is because they are two qualifiers of the verbal noun, meaning: eating that is pleasant and easy. The verbal noun is described by them, as al-Saʿd said, by figurative attribution (*isnād majāzī*), since the pleasant thing in its strict sense is the thing eaten. Or they are two states of the pronoun in the accusative, meaning: eat it while it is pleasant and easy. It may be stopped at *kulūhu* and begin *hanīʾan marīʾan* as a supplication, and as two qualifiers placed in the position of two verbal nouns, as if it were said: *hanaʾan maraʾan*. This was objected to, with the fact that supplication does not come from Allah Most High, until they interpreted it as a distortion of the grammarians' statements and a contradiction of them. For they make the accusative of *hanīʾan* a state, and *marīʾan* either a state or a qualifier. What refutes the view that al-Zamakhsharī derived, and confirms the correctness of the grammarians' statement, is that apparent nouns come in the nominative after *hanīʾan marīʾan*. Had they been accusative in the manner of verbal nouns meant as supplication, it would not be permitted for them, just as one cannot say *fī saqyan laka wa-raʿyan* (in "may you be watered and pastured") as "the watering of Allah Most High to you and the pasturing of Allah to you", although that is permitted in its verb form.

The evidence for the permissibility of the nominative of the apparent nouns after the two is the saying of Kuthayyir:

*"Hanīʾan marīʾan," other than a disease infiltrating*
*to ʿIzzah from our honour, what has it made lawful.*

For *mā* (what) is nominative, governed by what preceded it from *hanīʾan* or *marīʾan*, by way of working (*iʿmāl*). The working was permitted in this issue, even though there is no conjunction between them, because *marīʾan* in most cases is not used except as following *hanīʾan*, so they became as if they were connected for that reason. It was refuted that Sībawayh said: *hanīʾan marīʾan* are two qualifiers whose accusative is like the accusative of verbal nouns called for by a verb not used in its pronunciation, which is omitted because the speech indicates it. In this there is no explicit statement in favour of what al-Zamakhsharī took, since it is possible that he meant that they are two qualifiers in the accusative as states, and the governing element in them is an omitted verb that the speech indicates, like the verbal nouns called for in that they are governed by an omitted verb that the speech indicates. This is supported by his saying after that: "As if they said: that became pleasant, *hanīʾan*," for this is what is said on the assumption that they stand in the place of the verbal noun. From here al-Safāqisī said: the view of Sībawayh and the majority is that they are a state in the accusative, governed by an omitted verb that is necessarily elided because they stand in its place, like your saying: *aqāʾiman wa-qad qaʿada al-nās* (are you standing while people are seated?). This is objected to in light of what came before, namely the possibility of making them a state of the pronoun in the accusative in *kulūhu*, for on that view they would be from another clause that has no connection with *kulū* in terms of grammatical analysis.

I was asked to translate a passage of Ruh al-Ma'ani. Here is the translation.

Another objection was raised against using the verse of poetry as evidence for the raising of the noun (al-Zahir) by the two (ma and hanian), namely that the argument is not complete, because "ma" may be in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted ('izzah khabaruhu), or it may be in the nominative by a verb that is implied (fi'l muqaddar). Whichever is the case, His saying, glorified is He, "that" (dhalika) is an expression for permissibility, for exaggeration in allowing it, and for removing any responsibility.

In the Book of al-'Ayyashi, from the Imamiyyah, it is transmitted with a raised chain (marfu') to 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that a man came to him and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I have a pain in my belly." He said: "Do you have a wife?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Ask her to give you something of her property, one whose soul is content with it, then buy with it honey, then pour upon it rain water, then drink it, for I heard Allah, glorified and exalted, say in His Book: ﴿And We send down from the sky blessed water﴾, and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿There comes forth from their bellies a drink of varying colors, in which there is healing for mankind﴾, and He, mighty is His affair, said: ﴿And if they are content for you to give up to you something of it willingly, then consume it with satisfaction and ease﴾." So when blessing, healing, wholesome satisfaction and ease are gathered together, he will be healed, if Allah wills. The man did so, and he was healed.

'Abd ibn Humayd and others from our companions transmitted from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, something close to this, with the wording: "If one of you falls ill, let him ask his wife for three dirhams or thereabouts, then let him buy with them honey, and let him take water from the sky, and it will be gathered into wholesome, easy, healing and blessed (drink)."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Hadrami that some people used to feel sinful if one of them took back anything of what he had given to his wife, so this verse was revealed. In it is evidence of the narrowness of the path in this matter and the obligation of caution, since the condition is built upon the contentment of the soul, which is rarely realized. For this reason, 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, wrote to his judges that women give out of desire or fear, so whichever woman gives and then wishes to take back, it is hers to do so.

al-Sha'bi related that a man came with his wife to Shurayh regarding a gift she had given him, and she was asking to take it back. Shurayh said: "Return it to her." The man said: "Has not Allah said: ﴿If they are content for you﴾?" He said: "If her soul had been content with it, she would not have taken it back." And from him: "I will dismiss for her what she gave, and I will not dismiss it for him, for they are deceived." What the Hanafis hold is that if a wife gives something to her husband, she has no right to take it back. Rather, Ibn Hubayrah mentioned the consensus of the four Imams that neither of the spouses has the right to take back what he gave to the other.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 5 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And do not give the foolish your property⟩ This is a return to explaining the remaining rulings concerning the property of orphans, and a detailing of what was stated in summary earlier, namely the condition for handing it over and its manner. This comes right after explaining the rulings concerning persons, namely marriage, and explaining some of the rights concerning non-relatives, both in respect of their persons and in respect of their property, digressively. For the address, as the words of Ikrimah indicate, is to the guardians. He and Ibn Jubayr explicitly stated that by "the foolish" is meant the orphans, and by "your property" is meant their property. The property was attributed to the pronoun of the guardians who are addressed, treating its exclusive belonging to its owners as if it were exclusive to them. So their property is as if it were their own property, because of the kind of unity, both generic and relational, between them, as an exaggeration in urging them to preserve it. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not kill yourselves⟩, for the meaning is: let none of you kill another, but He expressed their kind by "yourselves" as an exaggeration in deterring from killing, to the extent that their killing is as if it were the killing of themselves. This is reinforced by what is indicated by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿which Allah has made for you a means of support⟩, where He expressed making it the means of subsistence of its owners by making it the means of subsistence of the guardians. The first object of "made" is omitted, and it is the pronoun referring to the properties, and by "support" is meant that by which one stands and lives. Expressing it thus is an added exaggeration, and it is the second object of "made". It has also been permitted that the omitted element alone be the object, and this be a circumstantial state of it. It was also said: the properties were attributed to the pronoun of the guardians in view of their being under the guardians' authority.

It was objected that although this is sound in itself, since attribution for the slightest connection is established in their speech, as in his saying:

When the star of al-Kharqa rises at the dawn near Suhayl, she has scattered her spun wool among the relatives.

However, it is not valid, because the properties are described by what follows them as an attribute. It was also said: the property was attributed to their pronoun because the intended meaning of "property" is its genus, that by which people make a living, and its relation to each person is like its relation to another, due to the generality of the relation. What is specific to one rather than another is the individual property itself, so it is permissible for it to be attributed in reality to the guardians, just as it is attributed to its owners. This is supported by its being described by what does not specifically belong to one property rather than another. It was objected that this is far from making the guardians preserve it as mentioned, for how so, when the genus-unity of wealth is not specific to what lies between the properties of orphans and the properties of guardians, but is realized between their properties and the properties of strangers? So there is no basis at all for considering it.

It is narrated that al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about this attribution, and it was said to him: how were their properties our properties? He said: when you are their heirs. This has two possibilities: the first is that it is an allusion to what we mentioned first in explaining the attribution. The second is that this is of the metaphorical kind of the first. It is objected, then, after saying that the attribution to al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, is false, that the first is not realized, rather custom in most cases is contrary to it, and taking it as an optimistic expectation is something a sound taste finds distasteful.

Allamah al-Tibi mentioned that the properties were attributed to the orphans in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And give the orphans their property⟩, and it was not attributed to them here, although in both cases the properties belong to them, so as to indicate that the ruling is consequent upon the attribute in both. For calling them orphans there suits cutting off greed, and thus it yields exaggeration in returning the properties to them, so this required saying: "their property". As for the attribute here, it is foolishness, so it suited that they should not be given any share of ownership, lest they get entangled with the properties. For this reason their property was not attributed to them, and it was attributed to the guardians. End quote. It is not hidden that this is an explanation of the cause that favours attributing the properties to the mentioned parties, and the cause that makes it valid should be what has just passed.

Then the orphans were described as foolish in view of the lightness of their judgement and the instability of their opinions, due to their youth and lack of training. The root of safah is lightness and movement; one says: "the wind made the tree foolish" (tasaffahat al-rihu al-shajar), meaning it swayed it. Dhu al-Rummah said:

They ran as spears "swayed" (tasaffahat) by their tips, as the gusting winds sway them.

And he also said:

Upon the back of a swift she-camel whose halter is light.

That is, its reins are light. Because this attribute is one from which the squandering and loss of property arises, harming the orphan's condition, it suited that it be made the basis for this ruling. The foolish have been explained as those who actually squander from among the orphans, and the majority of later scholars went to explaining the verse as we have mentioned. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Masud and others that by "the foolish" is meant women and children, and the address is to everyone, whoever they may be, and the meaning is a prohibition against giving his property to those among these who lack sound judgement. It was also said that by them is meant women specifically. It is narrated from Mujahid and Ibn Umar, and it is narrated from Anas ibn Malik that he said: "A black woman, sharp of speech, with a sharp tongue, came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: My father and mother be your ransom, O Messenger of Allah, say something good about us just once, for it has reached me that you say every evil about us. He said: What did I say about you? She said: You called us the foolish. He said: Allah, exalted is He, called you the foolish in His Book. She said: And you called us the deficient. He said: It is enough deficiency that you leave five days each month in which you do not pray. Then he said: Is it not enough for one of you that when she conceives she has the reward of one who guards the frontier in the way of Allah, and when she gives birth it is as one who writhes in his blood in the way of Allah, and when she nurses, for each sip she has the reward of freeing a slave from the descendants of Ishmael, and when she stays awake at night, for each night she spends awake she has the reward of freeing a slave from the descendants of Ishmael? And that is for the believing women who are humble, patient, and who do not deny their husbands' kindness. The black woman said: What a virtue, were it not for the condition attached to it."

It was also said that "the foolish" is general to every fool, whether a child, an insane person, or one placed under interdiction for squandering. Close to this is what is narrated from Abu Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: the fool is the drinker of wine and whoever is like him. He also made the address general to the guardians and to all people. The attribution in "your property" does not indicate anything but exclusivity, and this includes exclusivity of ownership and exclusivity of disposal. Those who went to the majority view supported it by saying that it suits the preceding and following verses, while whoever went to other views made the mention of this ruling a digression, and whether that would harm the excellence of the noble arrangement is open to reflection.

Nafi and Ibn Amir read "qiyaman" without an alif. As Abu al-Baqa said, there are three possibilities in it. The first: it is a verbal noun like al-hawl and al-iwad. The analogy would have been for the waw to remain, as it is protected by being in the middle, as it was retained in al-iwad and al-hawl; but they changed it to ya', taking it as analogous to qiyam, and because of its being altered in the verb. The second: it is the plural of qimah, like dimah and diyam, and the meaning is that wealth is like the values of souls, since their subsistence is by it. Abu Ali said: this is not valid, because it has been read in His saying: ﴿a upright religion, the religion of Abraham⟩ and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, as a means of support⟩, and the meaning of "value" is not valid in those two places. The third: the original is qiyaman, and the alif was dropped as it was dropped in khiyam; this is the view of some researchers, and it was made like 'uwadhan and 'iyadhan.

Ibn Umar read "qiwaman" with a kasrah on the qaf, with a waw and an alif. In it there are two possibilities. The first: it is the verbal noun of qawamtu, qiwaman, like lawadhtu, liwadhan, so the waw was retained in the verbal noun as it was retained in the verb. The second: it is a noun for that by which a matter is sustained, not a verbal noun. It was also read in the same way but without an alif, and it is a verbal noun whose middle radical is sound and which retains its original form, like al-iwad. It was read with a fatha on the qaf, with a waw and an alif. In it there are two possibilities: one, that it is a verbal noun like al-salam, al-kalam, and al-dawam; the other, that it is a dialect form of al-qiwam, which means stature. One says: a girl of good qiwam and qawam. The meaning is that which Allah, exalted is He, made the cause of the survival of your stature. In all the other readings of the verse there is an allusion to praising wealth. The predecessors used to say: wealth is the weapon of the believer; and "that I leave wealth for which Allah will call me to account is better than that I should need people." Abdullah ibn Abbas said: dirhams and dinars are the seals of Allah on earth; they are not eaten or drunk, but wherever you intend them, you satisfy your need. Qays ibn Sad said: O Allah, grant me praise and glory, for there is no praise except through deeds, and no glory except through wealth. It was said to Abu al-Zinad: Why do you love dirhams, when they bring you near to the world? He said: Though they bring me near to it, they have preserved me from it. In "Manthur al-Hikam": whoever is independent is honoured among his family. In it also: poverty is abandonment, wealth is joy, misery is contemptibility, and begging is humiliation. They used to say: trade and earn, for you are in a time when, if one of you is in need, the first thing he consumes is his religion. Abu al-Atahiyah said:

People exalted you when you attained wealth, and every rich man is esteemed in the eyes.
When the world inclines toward a man, it makes him desirable, and people incline wherever it inclines.
Wealth is nothing but the wealth that adorns a youth, in the evening when he entertains guests or in the morning when he bestows.

People have said much in praise of wealth and differed over preferring wealth or poverty, each supporting his claim with what this place cannot contain. For our teacher Ala al-Din, may Allah exalt his rank in the highest of the high:

They said: some people became rich, and we see that you, the flag, are poor in wealth.
I said: the wealth of the soul is the perfection of wealth, and poverty, all of poverty, is the loss of perfection.

Also by him:

They said: men have gathered wealth, and you have not reached this attainment through any perfection.
I said: they gained a part of its parts, but I have gained the whole of perfection.

﴿And provide for them therein and clothe them⟩: that is, make them the place of their provision and clothing, by trading and profiting, so that their expenses come from the profits and not from the principal, lest spending consume it. This is what the making of the properties themselves a container for the provision and clothing requires. Had it said "from them", the spending would be from the property itself. Some have permitted that "in" (fi) here means "from" in the partitive sense.

﴿And speak to them a kind word⟩: that is, words by which their hearts are made content, such as the guardian saying to the orphan: "Your property is with me and I am trustworthy over it; when you reach maturity and become rightly guided, I will give you your property." Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj explained "a kind word" as a fair promise of kindness and gift. Ibn Abbas said: it is like saying: "If I profit on this journey, I will do for you what you deserve, and if I gain booty in my campaign, I will give you a share." Al-Zajjaj said: teach them, along with feeding and clothing them, the matters of their religion that concern knowledge and practice. Al-Qaffal said: if he is a child, the guardian informs him that the property is his, and that when his childhood passes, the property will be returned to him; and if he is a fool, he admonishes him, urges him to pray, and informs him that the outcome of squandering is poverty and need.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) related from Ibn Zayd concerning the verse, "if he is not of your offspring, nor of those for whom it is obligatory upon you to spend, then say to him: 'May God keep us and you safe, and may God bless you.'" It is not hidden that this is contrary to the apparent sense, because the apparent sense indicates that the address in this clause is not to the guardians.

In sum, whatever the soul finds comfortable because of its goodness, legally or rationally, of speech or action, is ma'ruf (recognized good), and whatever the soul rejects because of its ugliness, legally or rationally, is munkar (reprehensible). Said by more than one scholar. This is not an indication of the two positions regarding goodness and ugliness, whether they are legal (shar'i) or rational ('aqli), as has been claimed, since there is no disagreement between us and those who hold the rational view of goodness and ugliness regarding the attribute that suits the purpose and the attribute that is repugnant to it, and that some of these have their source in reason, though the law may also bring them. The disagreement lies only in that to which praise and blame are attached in this world, and reward and punishment in the next: is its sole source the law, or reason? This is settled in the books of usul (principles of jurisprudence).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 6 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿And test the orphans﴾ This begins the specification of the time for handing over the orphans' property to them, and the condition for doing so, after the general command to give it to them and the prohibition against doing so when their owners are *sufaha'* (foolish). This is what Shaykh al-Islam said. It is evident if *sufaha'* is taken to mean those among the orphans who are actually squandering their property. But if it is taken to mean orphans in general, and their being described as foolish is in regard to what was indicated earlier, then there is some obscurity in it. It has also been said that this is a return to explaining the rulings concerning orphans' property, not a new beginning. This view rests on the premise that what came before was mentioned by way of digression, and that the address is to the guardians. *Ibtila'* (testing) means examination. The meaning is: test those among you who are orphans by observing their conditions, to see whether they are guided to preserving property and managing it well, and try them with what suits their state. Restricting it to this guidance is the opinion of Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, also takes into account piety in religion. Ibn Jubayr adopted this view, and it is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan.

The two Imams, may Allah be pleased with them both, agreed that this testing takes place before puberty. The apparent wording supports them, because of what the limit (*ghayah*) implies. Imam Malik said it takes place after puberty. Imam al-A'zam (Abu Hanifa) deduced, on the premise that the testing takes place beforehand, that the transactions of a discerning minor (*'aqil mumayyiz*) are valid with the permission of the guardian, because such testing can only occur if he is permitted, for example, to buy and sell. Al-Shafi'i said that testing does not imply permission to act, because it depends on handing the property to the orphan, and that depends on the two conditions (guidance and maturity), which only become realized afterwards. Rather, testing occurs without that, according to what suits the situation. So the son of a merchant, for example, is tested in buying and selling up to the point where the matter depends on a contract, and then the guardian contracts if he wishes. The same analogy applies.

﴿until, when they reach marriageable age﴾ That is, when they reach the limit of puberty (*bulugh*). This is either by wet dreams (*ihtilam*) or by age. The age is fifteen years according to al-Shafi'i, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad, and this is also a narration from Abu Hanifa. It is the ruling followed by the Hanafis, because it is the widespread custom that boys and girls become fit for marriage and for its fruits during this period and do not lag behind it. The use of the report that al-Bayhaqi transmitted in *al-Khilafiyyat* on the authority of Anas, "When a child completes fifteen years, his deeds are recorded, for and against him, and the prescribed punishments apply to him," is weak, because al-Bayhaqi himself stated that its chain of transmission is weak.

It is widely reported from Imam al-A'zam that the age for a boy is completing eighteen years, and for a girl completing seventeen years. For this he relies on the words of Allah, ﴿until he reaches his maturity (*ashudd*)﴾, and the *ashudd* of a child is eighteen years. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said, and al-Qutabi followed him. This is the lowest figure stated, so the ruling is based on it for certainty. However, females grow and mature faster, so for them we reduced one year, because it includes the four seasons, one of which necessarily suits their temperament. There is also a report from him that for a boy it is nineteen years, meaning that he enters his nineteenth year and completes eighteen. It has been said that there is a difference in the narrations because of the phrase "until he completes nineteen years."

It is widely reported from Imam al-Shafi'i that he made the growth of pubic hair (*inbat*) a sign of puberty only among polytheists (*mushrikin*). Ibn Hazm the Misguided (*al-Dall*) criticized this severely. What the Shafi'is mention is that if a near-pubescent (*murahiq*) is captured and it is not known whether he has reached puberty, he is treated as adults are treated, with killing, grace, ransom in exchange for prisoners, either for free or for property, or enslavement. If he is not pubescent, he is treated as children are treated, in terms of enslavement. His private parts are examined, and if he has grown pubic hair, he has the ruling of men, and if not, not. This is done to him because he does not tell the Muslims that he has reached puberty, for fear of being killed. By contrast, a Muslim does not need to be known to have reached puberty in this way. It is not hidden that this is not a fitting subject for criticism. At most, he made growth of hair a cause for applying the rulings of men to him in this matter, because there is no means of knowing puberty in it, and its suitability in general as a sign for that is clear. As for the claim that he holds that growth of hair is one of the proofs of puberty, like wet dreams, impregnating or being impregnated, menstruation, and pregnancy, this applies to unbelievers only, not to Muslims.

﴿if you perceive﴾ That is, if you sense. This is the statement of Mujahid. The original meaning of *istinas* (perceiving), as al-Shihab said, is looking from a distance with the hand placed over the eyes toward an approaching traveler or the like, from whom one feels at ease. Then its usage became general in their speech. A poet said:

"A cry startled her, and the hunter [*al-qannas*] frightened her in the afternoon, when evening was approaching."

Then it was borrowed to mean clarity, that is, knowing a thing clearly. Some have claimed that its original meaning is seeing in general, and that it is derived from *insan al-'ayn*, the pupil of the eye, which is the part by which one sees. Here it is possible that either the figurative or the literal meaning is intended. Ibn Mas'ud read *ahastum*, with a fatha on the *ha'* and a sukun on the *sin*. Its original form is *ahsastum* with two *sin*s. The vowel of the first was transferred to the *ha'* and the *sin* was deleted because two consonants met, one of them being deleted contrary to the usual analogy. It has been said that this is the dialect of Sulaym, and that it applies regularly to the middle radical of every doubled verb when the pronoun of the subject, *ta'* or *nun*, is attached to it, as in the words of Abu Zayd al-Ta'i:

"Except that the noble she-camels among the mounts, *ahsin bihi* [how well they perceive him], those that are fast to him are fierce."

﴿from them, maturity (*rushd*)﴾ That is, guidance (*ihtida'*) toward preserving property and managing it well. It has also been said it means righteousness in their religion and preservation of their property. The placement of the prepositional phrase *minhum* first is for a reason already mentioned more than once. *Rushdan* was read with two fathas, and also *rushdan* with two dammas. Both mean *rushd*. It has been said that *rushd* with a damma refers to worldly and otherworldly affairs, while with a fatha it refers only to otherworldly ones. *Rashid* and *rashid* are both used of a person who has *rushd*.

﴿then hand over to them their property﴾ That is, without delaying beyond the limit of puberty, as the *fa'* indicates. The choice of *daf'* (handing over) rather than *ita'* (giving) at the beginning of the command indicates, according to what some have held, a difference in meaning between them. This subject has already been discussed.

The structure of the verse is as follows. *Hatta* is the particle that is followed by full sentences, as in the line:

"I traveled with them until their mounts became weary, and even the swift horses were not driven by reins."

It is called an *ibtida'iyyah* (initiating) *hatta* in this case. It does not lose the meaning of limit (*ghayah*), as the grammarians state in most of their books, and as many of the jurists (*usuliyyun*) mention, contrary to whoever has made a mistake about this. What follows it is a conditional sentence, made the limit of the testing. The conditional verb is *balaghu* (they reach), and its answer is the second conditional clause, as several grammarians have verified. The explanation of this is that Ibn 'Aqil in *Sharh al-Tashil* mentions that when two or more conditions follow one another, as in your saying: "If you come to me, if I promise you, I will be good to you," the answer "I will be good to you" belongs to the first condition, "if you come to me," and dispenses with an answer to "if I promise you." Ibn Malik claimed that the second condition qualifies the first, serving as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), as if it were said: "If you come to me while I promise you." The correct view on this question is that the answer belongs to the first, and the answer to the second is omitted, because the first condition and its answer indicate it. So if you say: "If you enter the house, if you speak to Zayd, if he comes to you, then you are free," then "you are free" is the answer to "if you enter the house." "If you enter the house" and its answer indicate the answer to "if you speak to Zayd." "If you speak to Zayd" and its answer indicate the answer to "if he comes." The answer that is meant in meaning is a response, and the answer comes later. Thus the third condition is first, and likewise the second. It is as if it were said: "If he comes, then if you speak, then if you enter, then you are free." So he is not freed unless all occur. This is the sequence: coming, then speaking, then entering. This is the view of al-Shafi'i. Al-Jassas mentioned that there is a disagreement on this between Muhammad and Abu Yusuf, and that it is not only the view of al-Shafi'i. The usage of the speakers supports it. The poet said:

"If you seek our help, if you are frightened, you will find from us the bonds of honor, which generosity adorns."

It is also the usage of the modern eloquent writers (*fusaha' al-muwallidin*). Some jurists said: the answer belongs to the last condition, and the last condition with its answer is the answer to the second condition, and the second condition with its answer is the answer to the first. On this view, he is not freed until all of them occur in this order: entering, then speaking, then coming. Some said:

"When they are combined, the freeing occurs without any order."

This applies when the sequence is without a conjunction. If it is joined by *aw* (or), the answer belongs to one of them without specification, as in "if you come to me, or if you honor Zayd, I will be good to you." If it is joined by *wa* (and), the answer belongs to both. If it is joined by *fa'* (then), the answer belongs to the second, and it and its answer are the answer to the first. Thus the *fa'* falls outside of coordination, and in what we are discussing, the *fa'* attached to the answer serves as a linking particle for the answer, like the second *fa'*.

What we have explained is what was accepted by a group including al-Zamakhshari. The view of al-Zajjaj and some grammarians, and the burden on it is lighter, is that *hatta* which precedes this sentence is a preposition (*harf jarr*), and *idha* is purely temporal, with no conditional meaning in it. The governing element, on the first explanation, is what is derived from the meaning of its answer. The meaning is: test the orphans until the time they reach puberty. Their entitlement to having their property handed over to them is conditional on perceiving maturity in them. The word for puberty is expressed with *idha* and the word for perceiving with *in*, to show the difference between them in clarity and obscurity.

The apparent meaning of the noble verse is that property is not handed over to them even if they reach puberty, unless maturity has been perceived in them. This is the view of al-Shafi'i and the position of the two Imams, and Mujahid also held this. Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from him that he said: "Property is not handed over to an orphan, even if he has gray hair, unless maturity has been perceived in him." This is also attributed to al-Sha'bi.

Imam al-A'zam said: when he exceeds the age of puberty by seven years, which is a period that is significant for the change of conditions, since the child discerns after it and is commanded to worship, as in the hadith, his property is handed over to him even if maturity has not been perceived, because the restriction was for the hope of his being disciplined. When he reaches that age and has not become disciplined, that hope generally ends, so there is no point in restriction after that. This is in *al-Kafi*.

Imam al-A'zam also relies on the words of Allah, ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾, and what is meant is after puberty. So this is an explicit statement on the obligation to hand over property after puberty. However, withholding his property before this period was agreed upon by consensus (*ijma'*). There is no consensus here, so handing over the property is required by the text. Conditioning a ruling on a condition does not imply its absence when the condition is absent, according to us. Moreover, the condition "maturity" is indefinite (*nakirah*), so when the condition is in some respect existent, its consequence becomes obligatory. The first stages of puberty may be accompanied by foolishness in terms of the lingering effect of childhood, and the persistence of its effect, just as its substance persists. When time passes and experience and trial appear, the effect of childhood no longer remains, and some kind of maturity necessarily comes into being, because it is the state of the full development of his intellect. It is reported from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "A man's intellect reaches its completion when he reaches twenty-five." The people of medicine (*ahl al-tiba'*) said: whoever reaches twenty-five years has reached his maturity (*ashudd*). Do you not see that at this age he may become a healthy grandfather? The minimum period of puberty is twelve lunar years, and the minimum period of pregnancy is six months. In this period it is possible for him to have a son, and then at double this age, his son may have a son.

[Page 207]

You know that the inference drawn from the verse in the manner mentioned is clear, on the basis that the meaning of *al-iytaʾ* (giving) in it is *al-dafʿ* (handing over). This has already been discussed. It has been objected to his statement, "that the condition etc." (*ʿala annahu al-shart ilakh*), that if some degree of *rushd* (sound judgment) suffices, as the indefinite form (*al-tankir*) implies, and if that is certainly present at that age, as is the clear sense of his words, and the proof he cites is adduced for it, then *al-dafʿ* would be due upon the appearance of *rushd*. This is the position of al-Shafiʿi and the view of the two Imams. Therefore it is not correct to say that the position of the Imam (Abu Hanifa) is that the wealth of the orphan must be handed over to him whether or not *rushd* is observed in him. The most that can be said is that a disagreement remains between the Imam and others about what kind of *rushd* is required as a condition for handing over in the verse, and that is another matter beyond what has spread from the Imam, may Allah be pleased with him, in this question.

Furthermore, if by this kind of *rushd* indicated by the *tanwin* is meant *rushd* in the management of property, then its necessarily being attained at the age of twenty-five falls within the scope of the prohibition. And if what is meant is *rushd* in any form whatsoever, then even granting that it is attained at that time, it is of no benefit, since the verse is almost explicit in requiring the first kind.

Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: "There is no doubt that what is meant by the testing of orphans, which is commanded, is testing them in matters related to the preservation of property. And after that command Allah the Exalted said, ﴿Then if you perceive in them sound judgment﴾. So it must be that what is meant is: if you perceive in them *rushd* in the management of their affairs. For if this were not what is meant, the composition would come apart, and some parts would have no connection to others. And once this is established, we know that the condition required in the verse is the attainment of *rushd* in looking after the affairs of property, not 'some kind of *rushd* however it may be.'" Then he said: "Clear analogy (*al-qiyas al-jali*) strengthens the inference from the verse, because a child is denied his property only because of lack of the intellect that guides to the proper preservation of property and the proper way of benefiting from it. So if this meaning is present in the young man and the old man, they are in the same position as the child." Therefore it is obligatory that handing over property to them be prevented if *rushd* is not perceived in them. From this one knows the flaw in the earlier reasoning, namely their statement, "because the prohibition was for the hope of discipline," etc., from the standpoint of examination.

Because the opponent's argument in this question is strong, the misguided Ibn Hazm, as is his habit with all the leading scholars of the religion, reproached the Great Imam, may Allah be pleased with him, and the foolish among the Shiites followed him in this, such as Yusuf al-Awali and others. It should not be overlooked that the question is one of the subsidiary rulings (*furuʿ*), and how many of Ibn Hazm's followers' violations of the Book and the Sunnah there are in it, while they hold to what is weaker than the spider's web.

Whoever reflects carefully on what the Imam held will know that his view on this matter, may Allah be pleased with him, is subtle. For when the orphan has reached the status of men, and his faith and disbelief are taken into account, and he becomes the recipient of divine addresses and legal obligations, and Allah the Exalted has entrusted him with himself to dispose of by his own choice, upon which praise and blame, reward and punishment are based, then withholding his property from him and the disposal of it by others is most like injustice. Then, although this requires handing over the property to him after maturity without delay until he reaches the age of twenty-five, in the case of one who reaches maturity without being sound in judgment, we have delayed the handing over until that period for discipline and in hope of sound judgment, and for restraint from foolishness and from what squanders and ruins property. A parallel to this in terms of seizing the property of rebels and withholding it from them until they return to obedience is found. The addition of seven years was considered because, as previously stated, it is a period that is significant in the change of conditions. Ten years, for example, although also significant, as his words (ﷺ) indicate: "Command your children to pray when they are seven years old, and strike them for it when they are ten years old, and separate them in their beds," nevertheless we took the lesser figure because it is generally sufficient for the purpose. It cannot be objected that the prohibition revolves around foolishness, because we do not concede that it revolves around foolishness absolutely, but rather around the foolishness of childhood, and we do not concede its continuation after that period. Moreover, making the ruling dependent on a condition does not necessitate its non-existence when the condition is absent, according to us. So the basic premise of revolving (*al-dawaran*) is then disputed, and on this basis there is no point in reproaching the Great Imam, may Allah be pleased with him, for what he held.

His position is also supported by the Exalted's words: ﴿And do not consume them wastefully and in haste lest they grow up﴾. For this indicates that the property of the orphan is not withheld from him when he grows up. The meaning is: do not consume their property wastefully and hastily, anticipating their growing up, by being negligent in spending it and saying, "We will spend as we wish before the orphans grow up, so that they will snatch it from our hands." But the adulthood was measured, for one who reaches maturity foolish, by what has been mentioned for what has been mentioned, so understand this, and may Allah the Exalted guide you.

*Al-israf* (wastefulness) originally means exceeding the permitted limit into what is not permitted. It may occur in excess, and it may occur in deficiency. However, when it is in excess one says *asrafa yusrifu israfan*, and when it is in deficiency one says *sarafa yasrafu sarafan*. It is also used in the sense of forgetfulness and error, but that is not intended here at all. *Al-mubadara* is hastening, and it is the original sense of the act here. The form of mutual action (*al-mufaʿala*) is valid in it, in that the guardian hastens to take the orphan's property while the orphan hastens to snatch it from him. Its root, as has been said, is from *al-bidar*, which means fullness, and from it comes *al-badr* (the full moon) for its fullness with light, *al-budra* (a purse of money) for its being filled with money, and *al-baydar* (threshing floor) for its being filled with food. The two conjoined nouns are in the accusative as circumstantial accusatives (*hal*), as we have indicated. It has also been said that they are accusatives of purpose (*maful lahu*), and the sentence is conjoined to *ibtalu* (test), not to the answer of the conditional, because the first would then be after maturity and this before it, which corrupts the meaning.

*Yakbaru* with a fatḥa on the *ba'* from the pattern *ʿalima* is used of age. As for *yakburu* with a ḍamma, it is used of power and nobility. When the second is transitive with *ʿala*, it denotes hardship, as in *kabura ʿalayhi kadha* (this was hard for him).

The specification of eating, which is the foundation of benefit and in which need is most frequent, by the prohibition indicates the prohibition of other uses by a stronger implication. Within the sentence there is also an emphasis on the command to hand over property, a confirmation of it, and a preparation for what follows it in the Exalted's words:

﴿And whoever is wealthy, let him abstain﴾, etc. That is: whoever among the guardians and executors is possessed of wealth, let him restrain himself from consuming the orphan's property, and let him benefit from what Allah the Exalted has given him of wealth. So *al-istiʿfaf* is restraint, and it is more emphatic than *al-ʿaff*. In *al-Mukhtar* it is said: "He refrained from the forbidden, *yaʿiffu* with a kasra, ʿiffatan, ʿaffan, ʿafafatan, meaning he restrained himself, so he is *ʿaff* and *ʿafif*. A woman is *ʿaffa* and *ʿafifa*. Allah the Exalted made him chaste (*aʿaffahu*), and he sought to abstain from asking (*istaʿaffa*), meaning he refrained. *Taʿaffafa* means he exerted himself to be chaste." Interpreting it as purity of conduct, as some commentators indicate, is an explanation of the sense of the meaning.

﴿And whoever is poor﴾, from among the guardians and executors, ﴿let him consume in a reasonable manner﴾, according to his urgent need, to satisfy hunger and cover nakedness. This was said by ʿAtaʾ and Qatada. Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The poor man who takes charge of an orphan's property may eat according to the measure of his management of it and the benefit to him, so long as he does not waste or squander." Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasaʾi and Ibn Majah narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that he asked the Prophet (ﷺ), saying: "I have no property, and I am the guardian of an orphan." He said: "Eat from your orphan's property, without extravagance, and without accumulating wealth, and without protecting your property with his property." Is that considered a wage or not? There are two opinions. Our school holds the second, as al-Jassas explicitly stated in *al-Ahkam*. From Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Abu al-ʿAliya, al-Zuhri, ʿUbayda al-Salmani, al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with them all, and others, it is related that the poor guardian may eat from the orphan's property to the extent of sufficiency by way of a loan; when he becomes affluent he repays what he borrowed. This is the meaning of eating in a reasonable manner. This is supported by what ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Shayba and others narrated through various chains from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I have placed myself, with regard to Allah's property, in the position of an orphan's property: if I am rich I refrain, and if I am in need I take from it in a reasonable manner, and when I am well-off I repay." Abu Dawud and al-Nahhas, both in *al-Nasikh*, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated through ʿAtaʾ from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "﴿And whoever is poor﴾, the verse was abrogated by ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾" etc. (*naskh*: abrogation, the replacement of a ruling by a later one). Some people held that eating is permitted but not clothing, and this is related from ʿIkrima from Ibn ʿAbbas. Others claimed that the verse was revealed concerning the orphan, who is to be spent upon from his own property according to his condition.
