This was attributed to Yahya ibn Saʿid, but it is rejected, because the Exalted's words ﴿let him abstain﴾ do not convey that meaning, and dividing the composition in this way is not fitting for the noble text.

﴿When you hand over﴾, O guardians and executors, ﴿to them﴾, that is, to the orphans, after observing what has been mentioned to you, ﴿their property﴾ which is under your control. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the direct object is for emphasis on it. ﴿Then call witnesses against them﴾, by their having received it and your obligations being discharged from it, because that is further from suspicion, more effective in preventing disputes, and more fitting for trustworthiness. This is recommended (*mandub*) according to us. Al-Shafiʿiyya and al-Malikiyya held that it is a command of obligation, and they used this to argue that the custodian is not believed in his claim of having handed over the property without evidence.

﴿And Allah suffices as a reckoner﴾, that is, as a witness, as al-Suddi said. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that the meaning of "and Allah suffices as a reckoner" is that there is no witness better than Allah the Exalted between you and them. This agrees with our position that evidence is not obligatory. It was also said that the meaning is: and He, the Exalted, suffices as a reckoner for you, so do not oppose what you were commanded, and do not transgress what has been set as a limit for you. The fitness of the word "reckoner" here is not hidden, because the executor is held to account for what is in his hand. Regarding the subject of *kafa* (suffices), as Abu al-Baqa said, there are two possibilities: first, that it is the divine name, and the *ba* is additional, entering to indicate the sense of command, so the meaning is "be content with Allah the Exalted." Second, that the subject is a pronoun, and the meaning is "the contentment with Allah the Exalted suffices," so *bi-Allah* in this case is in the accusative place as the object, and *hasiban* is a circumstantial accusative. It was also said to be a specifying accusative (*tamyiz*). According to al-Samin, *kafa* is transitive to one object, and the meaning is "and Allah has sufficed you as a reckoner." According to Abu al-Baqa it is transitive to two objects, and the meaning is "and Allah has sufficed you their evil" and similar.

* * *

Furthermore, from the sphere of allusion (*al-ishara*): ﴿O people, fear your Lord﴾, that is, beware of Him from acts of disobedience and from looking at other than Him, and hold fast to the covenant of pre-eternity, when He made you witness against yourselves, ﴿who created you from a single soul﴾, which is the Muhammadan Reality. It is also expressed as the Universal Rational Soul, which is the heart of the cosmos, and as the True Adam, who is the father of Adam. To this the sultan of lovers, Ibn al-Farid, may his secret be sanctified, alluded in his words, speaking in the voice of that Reality:

"Though I am the son of Adam in form,
Within me there is a meaning that witnesses to my fatherhood."

[Part 3 of 3]

﴿And He created from it its mate﴾: that is, the *tabi'ah* (nature), or the animal soul (*al-nafs al-hayawaniyyah*) that arises from it. She was created from the side that faces the world of generation (*'alam al-kawn*), namely the left rib, as mentioned in the report. She was singled out for this because she is weaker than the side that faces the Truth. ﴿And from both of them He spread forth many men﴾, that is, perfect ones who incline toward their father, ﴿and women﴾, deficient ones who incline toward their mother. ﴿And fear God, through whom you ask one another﴾: so do not establish for yourselves an existence alongside His existence, for He is the One who manifested your determinations after you were not a thing worth mentioning. ﴿And [fear] the wombs﴾, that is, avoid opposing My friends (*awliya'i*) and failing to love them, for whoever joins them, I join with him, and whoever severs them, I sever from him. The true wombs are thus the kinship of the lofty origins. ﴿Indeed God is ever a Watcher over you﴾, observing your hearts and aware of what is in them. When He sees in them an inclination toward the crooked and ill opinion of the people of His presence (*hadrah*), the mounts of His lights depart from them, and they remain desolate wastes in whose corners the owls call to one another.

﴿And give the orphans﴾, who are the orphans of the spiritual faculties (*al-quwwa al-ruhaniyyah*), cut off from the nurture of the Holy Spirit (*al-Ruh al-Qudsi*), who is their father, ﴿their property﴾, which is their rights to perfections (*al-kamalat*). ﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾: by giving the good of the attributes and making it subordinate, and taking in its place the bad of them and becoming characterized by it. ﴿And do not consume their property along with your own property﴾: by mixing the truth with falsehood. ﴿Indeed, that is a great sin﴾, that is, a great veil. ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly﴾, that is, that you will not be equitable in the nurture of the orphans of the strong, ﴿then marry what seems good to you of women, two, or three, or four﴾, so that your desires may diminish and you may guard your chastity, and thereby be aided in the nurture by what you gain of purification from immorality. ﴿And if you fear that you will not be just﴾ among the women, ﴿then [marry] one﴾, which suffices you in attaining your aim. ﴿And give the women their dowries﴾, their marriage gifts, ﴿as a gift﴾, a bounty and favor from God. In this is an indication of emptying oneself of stinginess and treachery and adorning oneself with fidelity and generosity, and this is among what one is nurtured by as one who is strong. ﴿And if they willingly give you a part of it, then consume it with ease and satisfaction﴾: and do not disdain or behave arrogantly regarding that. This too is a kind of nurture, for in it is emptying oneself of pride and haughtiness, and adorning oneself with humility and compassion.

﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾, that is, do not entrust your secrets and sciences to those who fall short of the ranks of perfection, ﴿which God has made for you a means of support. And provide for them from it﴾, that is, nourish them with some of it, ﴿and clothe them﴾, that is, adorn them, ﴿and speak to them kindly﴾, so that they may submit to you and surrender themselves into your hands.

﴿And test the orphans﴾, that is, examine them. Perhaps this is an indication of testing those among the wayfarers who are deficient. ﴿Until, when they reach marriageable age﴾, and become fit for guidance and nurture, ﴿and you perceive in them maturity﴾, that is, uprightness on the path and absence of inconstancy, ﴿then deliver to them their property﴾, which they deserve, of the secrets that are entrusted only to the free.

[Page 210]

What is meant is the commitment of the perfect among the shaykhs to appoint successors and to authorize for guidance whoever among the disciples who travel under their guidance is fit for it. ﴿And do not consume it﴾, that is, do not benefit from that property to the exclusion of them, ﴿wastefully and hastily, before they grow up﴾ by taking up guidance, for that is among the greatest diseases of the soul and deadly poisons. ﴿And whoever is wealthy﴾ among you, ﴿in God﴾, who does not turn to the necessities of life at all, ﴿let him abstain﴾ from what belongs to the disciple. ﴿And whoever is poor﴾, who cannot bear need, ﴿let him eat﴾, that is, let him benefit from what belongs to the disciple, ﴿in a reasonable manner﴾, which is what is in proportion to necessity. ﴿And when you deliver to them their property, then call God to witness against them﴾, the Exalted, and the spirits of the people of the presence, and take from them a covenant to observe the rights, both with the Truth and with creation. ﴿And God suffices as a Reckoner﴾, for He is the true Existent and the Observer who knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal. He is our sufficiency, and how excellent a Guardian He is.

Page 211 begins at the marked point in the commentary.

﴿For men there is a share of what the parents and the close relatives leave behind﴾. This begins the explanation of the rules of inheritance, after the explanation of the property of orphans that passes to them by inheritance. "Men" here means the male children. Or "men" is more general, covering both adults and minors. "The close relatives" means those who are inherited from. "The parents" means those without an intermediary. The grandfather and grandmother are included under "the close relatives." The mention of "the children" [walad] alongside them, although they are also included, is to give them special attention. It is also permitted that "the parents" be understood more generally, covering those with or without an intermediary, so that it includes the grandfather and grandmother. It has been objected that this would require the inheritance of grandchildren in the presence of children. The answer is that the absence of inheritance in this case is known from another matter that is not hidden. "Naṣīb" means share, like "naṣb" with a kasra, and its plurals are "anṣibāʾ" and "anṣibah." The word "min" in "mimmā" [from what] is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of the indefinite noun before it, meaning: "a share existing from what was left." It is also permitted that it be connected to "naṣīb."

﴿And for women there is a share of what the parents and the close relatives leave behind﴾. "Women" here means daughters in general, or females in general. The rule for them is stated independently rather than being included within the rules of those mentioned earlier, by saying, "For men and women there is a share, etc.," for the sake of giving attention to them and signaling their independent entitlement to inheritance, as Shaykh al-Islam said. Also, from the outset there is an indication of the difference between the two shares and an emphasis on nullifying the judgment of the pre-Islamic period (jāhiliyyah). They did not give inheritance to women and children, and they said: "Only one who fights and defends the territory inherits." In response to them this verse was revealed, as Ibn Jubayr and others said. It is narrated that Aws ibn Thābit, and it is said Aws ibn Mālik, and it is said Thābit ibn Qays, and it is said Aws ibn al-Ṣāmit, but this is an error, because he died during the caliphate of ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him. He died leaving two daughters, a young son, and his wife Umm Kuḥḥah, and it is said Bint Kuḥḥah, and it is said Umm Kuḥlah, and it is said Umm Kulthūm. Then his paternal cousins, Khālid or Suwayd, and ʿArfaṭah or Qatādah, and ʿArfajah, came and took all his inheritance. His wife said to them: "Marry the two daughters," and they had a disfigurement, so they refused. She then came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him of the matter. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I do not know what to say." Then this verse was revealed: "For men there is a share," and so on. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then sent for the two paternal cousins and said: "Do not touch anything of the inheritance, for something has been revealed to me about it, and I have been informed that the male and the female have a share." Then after that this was revealed: "They ask you concerning women," up to His words: "All-Knowing." Then this was revealed: "Allah instructs you concerning your children," up to His words: "And Allah is All-Knowing, Forbearing." Then he (ﷺ) called for the inheritance, gave the wife the one-eighth, divided what remained among the children, with the male receiving the equivalent of the share of two females, and he gave the two paternal cousins nothing. In some of its transmissions it is that the deceased left a wife, two daughters, and two paternal cousins, and the Prophet (ﷺ) gave the wife the one-eighth, the two daughters the two-thirds, and the paternal cousins what remained.

In the report there is evidence for the permissibility of delaying the explanation (bayān) of a general address. Whoever generalizes "men" and "women," and says that "the close relatives" is general to those related by lineage and by cause, makes the verse include the ruling for husband and wife and the entitlement of each of them to inherit from the other.
Page 211

And whoever does not go this way, and says that "the close relatives" is specific to those related by lineage, makes the understanding of entitlement like the understanding of the quantity to be inherited, from the verses that will come. He gives as the reason for limiting the mention here to sons and daughters the greater concern for the matter of orphans. The Ḥanafiyyah and the Imāmiyyah (Twelver Shiʿa) argued with this verse for the inheritance of distant kin (dhawū al-arḥām, relatives through female links). They said: because the paternal aunts, maternal aunts, and the children of daughters are among the close relatives, it is obligatory for them to be included under His words: "For men," and so on. The most that can be said is that the quantity of that share is not mentioned in this verse, but we establish that they are entitled to the basic share by it. As for the quantity, it is derived from other evidences. The Imāmiyyah alone hold that the prophets, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, are inherited from like others. It will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, shortly, that its refutation is given in the most complete way.

﴿Of what is little of it or much﴾. This is a substitute (badal) for the last "mā," by repeating the governing element before it. Perhaps they did not consider the prepositional phrase to be a substitute for the prepositional phrase, because that would require substituting "min" for "min," and the unity of the wording in a substitute is not customary. Abu al-Baqāʾ permitted that the prepositional phrase be a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the pronoun omitted in "taraka," meaning: whatever he left, little or much, or established from what is little. A condition like this is considered in the first clause, though it is not stated explicitly there, relying on its mention here. Its benefit is to rule out the suspicion that some property is specific to some heirs, such as horses and weapons being for men. By this, it refutes the Imāmiyyah, because they assign the eldest son of the deceased from his estate the sword, the Qurʾan, the ring, and personal clothing without compensation, according to most of them. This is strange, as is their not giving the wife any share of the real estate, although the verse indicates that each of the two groups has a right in everything great and small. Placing the little before the much is like His words: "It leaves out nothing small or great without enumerating it."

﴿A share ordained﴾. It is in the accusative either because it is an absolute verbal noun (maṣdar muʾakkad) by interpretation as "a gift" or similar meanings of the verbal type; otherwise it is a fixed noun. It is reported from some that it is a verbal noun. Or it is in the circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the hidden pronoun in "qalla" and "kathura," or from the prepositional phrase that is a qualifier, or from "naṣīb," since its being described by the adverbial phrase allowed the circumstantial to come from it, or from the hidden pronoun in the prepositional phrase that is a predicate, because the meaning is: a share was established for them as ordained. In that case it is a preparatory circumstantial (ḥāl muwaṭṭi'ah), and the true circumstance is its description. It is said that it is in the accusative as an object of an omitted verb, the estimate being "He ordained for them a share." It is said that it is in the accusative by an implied "aʿnī" (I mean). Its accusative as a case of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ) according to the well-known meaning is something Abu Ḥayyān denied, because they explicitly stated the condition that the noun in the accusative of specification must not be indefinite.

The word "fard" is like "ḍarb," meaning to set a limit (tawqīt). From it is His saying: "Whoever ordains the pilgrimage (ḥajj) in them" [Q 2:197]. Carving into a thing is like "tafrīḍ." What Allah the Exalted has made obligatory is called "mafrūḍ" like something ordained. It was so named because it has markers and limits. It is also used with the meaning of cutting. From it is His saying: "I will surely take from Your servants an ordained share" [Q 4:118], meaning a portion cut off and defined, as in the Ṣiḥāḥ. So "mafrūḍan" here is either in the sense of a portion cut off and defined, as in that verse, or in the sense of what Allah the Exalted has made obligatory, meaning a share that Allah the Exalted has made obligatory for them.

The Ḥanafiyyah distinguished between fard and wājib by saying: the act, apart from the abstention that is related to it, is a command to perform an act such that abandoning it at any time becomes a cause of punishment, if it is established by a definitive text. So a fard is like reciting the Qurʾan in prayer, established by His words: "So recite what is easy of the Qurʾan" [Q 73:20]. If it is established by a probable text, then it is the wājib, like the specification of al-Fatiḥah, established by His saying (ﷺ): "There is no prayer except with the Opening of the Book (al-Fātiḥah)," and this is a solitary report (āḥād). Negation of excellence is a clear probable meaning. The Shafiʿiyyah held that the two are synonyms, and each side argued for its claim with what it argued. The dispute, as verified in the principles of jurisprudence, is verbal, as said by more than one scholar. Some researchers said: Al-Shafiʿi has no dispute about the difference between the two concepts of fard and wājib in linguistic usage, nor about the difference between what is established by definitive evidence, like the ruling of the Book, and what is established by probable evidence, like the ruling of a solitary report in the Sharʿ. The one who denies the first is an unbeliever, but not the one who denies the second. The one who abandons acting by the first while interpreting it is a sinner, but not the one who abandons the second. What he claims is that fard and wājib are two terms that are synonymous, transferred from their linguistic meanings to a single meaning, namely what its doer is praised for and its abandoner is blamed for in the Sharʿ, whether it is established by definitive or probable evidence. This is merely a technical convention, so there is no point in arguing that the difference between the Book and a solitary report requires a difference between their meanings, or that fard linguistically means "determination" while wājib means "falling," so that the fard is known with certainty to be determined upon us, and the wājib is what fell upon us by way of probability, and what is probable is not determined, nor is what is definitive fallen upon us. Moreover, the opponent may say: even if the linguistic meaning is considered, we do not accept that it is impossible for something to be established as determined upon us by a probable evidence, and as fallen upon us by a definitive evidence. Do you not see that their saying "fard," meaning the prescribed (mafrūḍ, the determined) in wiping the head, is a quarter? Also, the truth is that wājib linguistically means "established," while the verbal noun of wājib in the sense of "fallen" and "agitated" is "wajbah" and "wajīb." Then the usage of fard for what is established by probable evidence, and wājib for what is established by definitive evidence, is common and widespread, like their saying: "Witr is fard," and "the regulation of the postures is fard," and similar, and it is called "practical fard." Like their saying: "Prayer is wājib," and "zakat is wājib," and similar. From here it becomes known that the argument of some Shafiʿiyyah is invalid in rejecting the Ḥanafiyyah's use of what has passed to prove the inheritance of distant kin, by saying that wājib for the Ḥanafiyyah is what is known to be established by probable evidence, and fard is what is known by decisive evidence, and the inheritance of distant kin is not of this kind by consensus. So we know that it is not intended by the verse. The basis of the invalidity is clear and needs no explanation.

Some argued with the verse that if an heir renounces his share, his right is not forfeited. This is the position of the Imam al-Aʿẓam (Abu Ḥanīfah), may Allah be pleased with him.

﴿And when the division [of the estate] is attended﴾, i.e., the division of the inheritance (*tarikah*, the estate of the deceased) among its owners. It is the object (*maf'ul bihi*) and has been placed first because it is the subject under discussion, and because the agent (*al-fa'il*) is plural in number. If the normal word order were observed, the interlinking of the parts of the sentence (*tajadhub atraf al-kalam*) would be lost. It was also said: it was placed first so that it would be in front of those present in the wording, just as it is in front of them in reality. This is a rhetorical point for the fronting, which I have not seen mentioned by the scholars of rhetoric (*'ulama al-ma'ani*).

﴿the near of kin﴾, from among those who do not inherit, either because they are an agnatic relative (*'asib*) who is excluded (*mahjub*), or because they are of the uterine relatives (*dhawu al-arham*). The indication that this is intended is the mention of the heirs before it. ﴿and the orphans and the needy﴾, from among the strangers (*al-ajanib*). ﴿then provide them from it﴾, i.e., give them something of the wealth, or of the divided property indicated by the division. It was also said: the pronoun refers to *ma* (the estate), and this is a command of recommendation (*amr nadb*), which the adult heirs are charged with, to comfort the hearts of those mentioned and to give charity to them. It was also said: it is a command of obligation (*amr wujub*), and scholars have differed about its abrogation (*naskh*, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one). In some narrations from Ibn 'Abbas, he said there is no abrogation and the verse is muhkam (not abrogated). This is also reported from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her.

Abu Dawud reported in his *al-Nasikh* and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through the chain of 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: ﴿And when the division is attended﴾ up to the end of the verse was abrogated by the verse of inheritance, so that each person was given his share of what was left, whether it was little or much.

It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that the intended meaning of ﴿the near of kin﴾ here is the heirs, and by ﴿the orphans and the needy﴾ are meant non-heirs; that His saying, glorified is He, ﴿then provide them from it﴾ refers to the first group, and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and speak to them a kind word﴾ refers to the last group. This is very far-fetched. The apparent meaning is what was mentioned first. This statement [*and speak to them a kind word*] is addressed to the recipients from those mentioned. The kind word (*al-qawl al-ma'ruf*) means that they should pray for them, belittle what they have given them, apologize for it, and not remind them of it as a favour.

[Page 213]

The saying of Him, glorified is He: ﴿And let those fear who, if they were to leave behind them weak offspring, would fear for them.﴾ Concerning this there are several opinions.

The first: it is a command to guardians (awsiya', sing. wasi) to fear God Most High, or to fear for their own children, and so to treat the orphans in their care as they would wish their weak offspring to be treated after their death. The words of Ibn 'Abbas point to this. Ibn Jarir reported from him that he said concerning the verse: "It means a man who dies leaving small, weak children, whom he fears will suffer poverty and destitution, and he fears that after him those in charge of them will not treat them well. So he says: if one is in charge of orphans like his weak offspring, let him treat them well, and let him not devour their property wastefully and hastily before they grow up." According to this, the verse is connected to what precedes it, because His saying ﴿for men﴾ etc. is in the sense of a command to the heirs, that is, give them their due, repelling the custom of the Jahiliyya (the Age of Ignorance). The guardians should preserve what has been given to them and fear for them as they fear for their own children. It has also been said regarding the connection: this is an injunction to guardians to protect the orphans, after mentioning the heirs, both young and old, by way of completion (tatmim). It has also been said that the verse is connected to His saying ﴿and test the orphans﴾.

The second: it is a command to those who attend the sick person (al-'uwwad, the visitors) at the time of making a bequest, that they should fear their Lord, or fear for the sick person's children, and show them the compassion they show their own children, so that they do not allow him to harm them by diverting the property away from them. Something similar has been attributed to al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Something in support of this has also been related from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi reported from him that he said concerning the verse: "It means a man whom death is approaching, and it is said to him: give charity from your property, free slaves, and give from it in the way of God. So they (the attendants) were forbidden to command him to do that. That is, whoever among you attends a sick man at the time of death, let him not command him to spend of his property on manumission, or on charity, or in the way of God. Rather, let him command him to state what he owns and what debts he has, and to bequeath from his property to his relatives who do not inherit, bequeathing to them a fifth or a quarter. He says: Does not one of you, when he dies, leave behind weak children, that is, small children, whom he would not be content to leave without property, so that they would become a burden on people? So it is not fitting for you to command him to do what you would not be content with for yourselves and your children. But say the truth concerning that." According to this, the beginning of the speech is addressed to the guardians and what follows is addressed to the heirs, and this (the verse) is for strangers, that they should not let him (the sick man) harm them, or command him to do what harms them. So the verse is connected to what precedes it as well.

The third: it is a command to the heirs to show compassion toward the weak relatives, orphans and needy who are present at the division (of the estate), picturing to themselves that if they had been their own children who were left behind them as weak as they are, would they permit their deprivation? The connection of the speech on this view with what precedes it is evident, because it urges giving to them and commands them to fear depriving them, just as they fear depriving their own weak offspring.

The fourth: it is a command to the believers to consider the heirs, so that they do not exceed the bounds in bequests. It has been related from the early generation (al-salaf) that they used to recommend that a bequest should not reach a third, and they would say: a fifth is better than a quarter, and a quarter is better than a third. A report supporting this has also come. On this view, by "those" is meant the sick and the owners of bequests, and He commanded them not to be excessive in bequests out of fear for their weak offspring. The indication for this is that they are the ones approaching that state. The warning about devouring the property of orphans after that is a warning against taking what exceeds the bequest, so it relates to it. It also connects to what precedes it as a completion of the command to guardians and heirs with the command concerning the sick among the believers. This is the most remote of the views. And more remote than it is what has been said: that it is a command to whoever attends the sick man to show compassion to the near relatives, by not saying to the sick man, "Do not make a bequest to your relatives, and keep it for your offspring." And more remote than that view is the claim that it is a command to those who divide the estate to be just among the heirs in the division, by not favouring the eldest, giving him the best of the estate, and not paying attention to the young, even if it is in what is contained in the relative clause (silat al-mawsul), as several have said. Since the relative clause must be a known matter to the addressee, established for the relative pronoun like an attribute, they said: here too it is so, and the meaning is: "let those fear whose condition and attribute is that, if they were about to leave behind weak offspring, they would fear for them loss."

Al-Ujhuri and others went to the view that "law" (law) here means "in" (in), so it turns the past into the future, and they made the verb "left" (taraku) necessarily refer to approaching (al-musharafa), so that "feared" (khafu) may validly be the response (jaza') to it, since there is no fear after the actual occurrence of death and the heirs' leaving. In the ordering of the command upon the described attribute mentioned in the relative clause, which implies causation (al-'illiyya), there is an indication that the purpose of the command is that they should not neglect orphans, so that their own children are not neglected. In it there is also a threat to them that if they do so, God will cause their children to be lost; and it hints that if they observe the command, God Most High will preserve their children.

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Shaybani, who said: "We were in Constantinople during the days of Maslama ibn 'Abd al-Malik, and among us were Ibn Muhayriz, Ibn al-Dayhami and Hani' ibn Kulthum. We began to discuss what will happen at the end of time, and I was greatly distressed by what I heard. So I said to Ibn al-Dayhami: 'O Abu Bishr, I wish that I might never have a child.' He struck my shoulder with his hand and said: 'O my nephew, do not do that. For there is no soul (nasama) that God has decreed should come out of a man's loins except that it will come out, whether he wills or not.' Then he said: 'Shall I not direct you to a matter which, if you attain it, God will save you from it, and if you leave a child after you, God will preserve them for your sake?' I said: 'Yes.' So he recited ﴿And let those fear who﴾ — the verse."

Describing the offspring as "weak" (diafa') arouses compassion. The apparent view is that "from behind them" (min khalfihim) is an adverbial complement (zarf) for "leave" (taraku). Explicitly stating it adds emphasis to the frightfulness of that situation. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial term (hal) from "offspring" (dhurriyya) and "weak" (diafa'), as Abu al-Baqa' said. "Weak" (diafa') is read with the full (tafkhim) pronunciation according to the original form, and with imala (inclination) because of the kasra. This is permitted despite the presence of the emphatic letter (harf al-isti'la'), since it is a preceding kasra, so there is a descent (infihar). Likewise "fear" (khafu) is read with the full pronunciation according to the original form, and with imala, because the kha' is pronounced with kasra in some cases, namely khifta. It is also read ḍu'afa', ḍa'afa and ḍu'afa, like sakara and sukara.

﴿Then let them fear God﴾ in that matter. The fa' (then) indicates the consequence of what follows upon what precedes it. God commanded them to be mindful of Him (taqwa), which is the ultimate of fear, after He had commanded them to fear, observing both the beginning and the end. Since the first is of no benefit without the second, He did not limit Himself to it, although it normally implies it. ﴿And let them speak﴾ to the orphans, or to the sick man, or to those present at the division, or let them speak in the bequest, ﴿a fitting word﴾. So the guardian speaks to the orphan what he would say to his own child, of gracious speech that guides him to good manners and noble conduct. The visitor of the sick man says what reminds him of repentance, of uttering the testimony of faith, of good opinion of God, and what restrains him from excess in bequeathing, which would harm the heirs. The heir speaks to those present at the division what removes their loneliness or increases their joy. The testator, in his bequest, says what does not lead to exceeding a third.

"Sadid" (fitting), according to al-Tabarsi, is the correct, just, lawful speech, agreeing with the Shari'a. It has also been said that it is that in which there is no flaw. It is said: his speech "sadda" (sadda, yasiddu, with kasra in the present) when it becomes sadid, and "innahu la-yusiddu fi al-qawl" (indeed he is precise in speech), so he is "musidd" when he hits the mark (al-sadad), that is, the aim. A matter is sadid, and "asadd," that is, aimed. "Sadad" with a fatha means uprightness and correctness, and likewise "sadad" is its shortened form. As for "sidad" with a kasra, it means sufficiency and what is used to plug something. From it is the saying: "fihi sidad min 'awaz" (it has a sufficiency against want). This was said by more than one. In "Durrat al-Ghawwas fi Awham al-Khawass" it is stated that people say "sadad min 'awaz" with a fatha on the sin, and this is a solecism, the correct form being with a kasra. Ibn Barri criticized this, saying it is an error, for Ya'qub ibn al-Sikkit equated the fatha and kasra in "Islah al-Mantiq," in the pattern fi'al and fa'al with the same meaning, and said: "It is said sidad min 'awaz and sadad." Likewise Ibn Qutayba related it in "Adab al-Katib," and similarly in "al-Sihah," except that it added: "and the kasra is more eloquent." Yes, it is mentioned in it that "sidad" of a bottle and "sidad" of a gap (al-thaghr) are with a kasra only. It recited the verse of al-'Arraj:

They abandoned me, and what a youth they abandoned for a day of distress and a plug for a gap.

So let this be noted.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), brought to confirm what has been detailed of commands and prohibitions. The word ﴿unjustly﴾ (ẓulman) may be a circumstantial accusative (ḥal), meaning "being unjust," or an accusative of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi). It has also been said that it is in the nature of an absolute object (maṣdar), meaning "consuming of injustice," i.e., consuming in a manner that is unjust. It has also been said that it is a specifier (tamyīz). The threat was attached to consuming in this manner because a person may consume an orphan's property on a basis of entitlement, such as a wage or a loan, for example, and then it is not injustice, nor is the consumer unjust. It has been said: the mention of injustice is for emphasis and clarification, because consuming an orphan's property is never anything but injustice, and whoever takes an orphan's property as a loan or a wage has consumed his own property and not the orphan's property. And in this there is a clear objection.

﴿They consume only a fire into their bellies﴾: that is, filling their bellies. This expression became common for this meaning, and it seems to be based on the principle that the true sense of the adverb of place (ẓarfiyyah), as understood from it, is encompassing, such that the container is not larger than what is contained. So eating "in" the belly means filling the belly, while eating in part of the belly means less than that, and this is what is meant in the verse of the poet:

"Eat in part of your bellies, and you will be spared, for your time is a time of hunger."

This is not contradicted by the statement of the jurists of usul: that when a noun of place is introduced by fī, it is not entirely a container, unlike the implied sense of it; so "I traveled on Thursday" refers to all of it, while "in Thursday" refers to something other than it. ʿIṣām al-Millah said: this is the position of the Kufans, while the Basrans do not distinguish between the two, as explained in grammar. Shihab al-Din said: the apparent meaning is that what the jurists of usul mentioned applies to what may be governed by fī and put in the accusative as a place, and this is not so, because one does not say "he ate his belly" meaning "in his belly"; so it is not among what the jurists of usul mentioned at all. It is like "I placed the goods in the house," which is true whether it fills it or not; but the first principle is as they stated.

It is also permitted that the mention of bellies is for emphasis and exaggeration, as in His saying: ﴿They say with their mouths what is not in their hearts﴾, where speech is only with the mouth; and His saying: ﴿But it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind﴾, where the heart is only in the breast; and His saying: ﴿Nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾, where a bird flies only with a wing. They have said that the purpose of all of this is emphasis and exaggeration. Then the container here is the object, i.e., the thing eaten, not the subject. The verification of this, as transmitted from al-Tumurtashi in the book on oaths, is that when an adverb of place is mentioned after a verb that has a subject and an object, as when you say: "If I strike Zayd in the house, or in the mosque, then such-and-such," if both are in it, the matter is clear; if the subject is in it but not the object, or the reverse, then if the verb's effect appears on the object, such as striking, killing, or wounding, the condition is that the object be in it; and if its effect does not appear on the object, such as insulting, the condition is that the subject be in it. For this reason some jurists said: if he says, "If you insult him in the mosque, or throw at him," the condition of breaking the oath is that the subject be in it; and if he says, "If you strike him, or wound him, or kill him, or throw at him," the condition is that the object be in it. Throwing in the first case is among what shows no effect on him, because it means shooting an arrow from the bow with intention; that does not show an effect on the place and does not depend on the arrival of the subject's action. In the second case it shows an effect, because it means sending the arrow, or something similar, in a way that reaches the one aimed at, wounding him, or causing him pain and suffering. There is no doubt that what we are dealing with belongs to this latter category, and the completion of the discussion on this will come, God willing, later.

The prepositional phrase is connected to "they consume," and this is the apparent reading. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to ﴿fire﴾ (nāran), i.e., what leads to it. Thus "fire" is a metonymy (majāz mursal), mentioning the effect and meaning the cause. It has been permitted in this that it is a metaphor, by likening what is consumed of orphans' property to fire, for its destruction of what it contains. Some researchers considered this remote, and some held that it may be taken in its literal sense. It is related from ʿUbayd Allah ibn Jaʿfar that he said: Whoever consumes an orphan's property will be seized by his lip on the Day of Resurrection, his mouth will be filled with burning coals, and it will be said to him: "Eat what you ate in this world," then he will enter the Great Blaze.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) told me about the night of his Night Journey, saying: 'I looked, and behold, there were people who had lips like the lips of camels, and someone was assigned to them who seizes their lips, then places in their mouths a rock of fire, which is cast into their bellies until it comes out from their lower parts. They have a moaning and a screaming. I said: O Jibril, who are these? He said: Those who consume the property of orphans unjustly.'"

﴿And they will burn in a blaze﴾: that is, they will enter a fierce fire, of undefined description. Ibn ʿAmir and Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read the imperfect prefix with a ḍammah (yuṣlawna), and the rest read it with a fatḥah (yaṣlawna). It was also read as "wa-sa-yaṣallawna" with a shaddah on the lam. In the Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: "ṣalaytu al-laḥma wa-ghayrahu uṣlīhi ṣalyan," like "ramaytuhu ramyan," when you roast it; and "ṣalaytu al-rajul nāran" when you cause him to enter it and make him endure its heat; but if you throw him into it, casting him as though you intend burning, you say "aṣlaytuhu" with alif, or "ṣallaytuhu taṣliyatan." It is also said: "ṣallā bi-al-amr" when he endures its heat and intensity. al-Ṭuhawi said:

"Their valor will not wear out, even if they endure the war for a time after time."

Some researchers said: the original meaning of ṣalī is nearness to fire, and it is used here metaphorically for entering. The apparent sense of some statements is that it is transitive by itself, while it has been said that it takes the preposition bi, as in "ṣaliya bi-al-nār." al-Raghib mentioned that it is sometimes transitive with bi and sometimes by itself, perhaps with two meanings, as indicated by what is in the Ṣiḥāḥ. "Saʿīr" is an adjective in the sense of a passive participle, from "saʿʿartu al-nār," when you kindle and set it ablaze. Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Ibn Jubayr that al-Saʿir is a valley from the intense heat of Jahannam. The apparent meaning of the verse is that this ruling is general for everyone who consumes an orphan's property, whether a believer or a polytheist. Ibn Jarir related from Zayd ibn Aslam that he said: This verse is for the people of polytheism, when they would not give inheritance to the orphans, that is, they would consume their property. It is not hidden that if he means the ruling of the verse is specific to the people of polytheism only, this is not accepted; and if he means it was revealed concerning them, there is no harm in that, since the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion. In some reports: "When this verse was revealed, it weighed heavily on people, and they guarded entirely against mixing with orphans, so the matter became difficult for the orphans, and then the statement of God Most High was revealed: ﴿If you mix with them...﴾ [Qur'an 2:220]."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 11 (part 1 of 5):

﴿Allah enjoins you﴾ This begins the explanation of what was left general in His words, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿For men there is a share﴾ and so on. "Wasiyyah (bequest, injunction) is, as al-Raghib said, that something which one is to act upon be presented to another accompanied by admonition, from the phrase 'a land wasiyah' (a land whose vegetation is continuous)." In reality it is a command to do what one has been charged with. So the meaning is: Allah commands you and imposes upon you. With the second sense, [the lexicographer] al-Fayruzabadi explained it in al-Qamus, and [the author] turned away from "command" to "enjoining" because it is more eloquent and more indicative of concern and of seeking swift fulfilment.

﴿concerning your children﴾ That is, concerning the inheritance of your children, or concerning their affairs; and this was supposed so that the sense of the adverbial (zarfiyyah) would be correct. It was also said that "fi" here carries the meaning of "li" (for), as in the report: "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat" (inna imra'atan dakhalat al-nara fi hirrah), meaning "for it," as the grammarians have explicitly stated. As for the addressee, it was said to be the believers, and between the two correlatives there is an omitted noun: i.e., "He enjoins you concerning the children of your deceased," because it is not permissible to address the living regarding the division of inheritance among his children. It was also said the address is to those who have children, in the sense of "He enjoins you concerning their inheritance if you die," and then there is no need to posit an omitted noun, just as if "yuwassikum" were explained as "yubayyinu lakum" (makes clear to you). Allah began with the children because they are the nearest of the heirs to the deceased and the most enduring after the one who bequeaths. The occasion of revelation is what we pointed to earlier. Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) visited me while I was ill, and I said: 'How should I divide my property among my children?' He did not answer me at all, and then this was revealed: ﴿To the male is the equivalent of the share of two females﴾."

It is in the position of detailing and explaining the bequest, so the clause has no place in terms of grammatical analysis. Abu al-Baqa' placed it in a position of accusative as an object of "yuwassi," taking it as having the sense of saying, prescribing, or legislating; but this is strained. The meaning is that each male is given the share of two females when the two categories of males and females are together and the direction of their inheritance is unified; so the male's share is doubled. Thus it has been said, and the apparent meaning is that the intent is to state the ruling for the joint presence of son and daughter in general.

In the clause there must be an omitted pronoun referring to the children, relying on its being evident, as in the saying "Ghee is two manas for a dirham"; and the implied sense here is "for the male among them," so reflect. The singling out of the male for explicit mention of his share, although the verse, according to the well-known account, was revealed to explain inheritances in refutation of their practice of giving inheritance only to males and not to females, suggests attention to females; and one might say "for the two females is the equivalent of the share of the male," because the male is more excellent, and because mentioning good qualities is more fitting for the Wise than otherwise. This is why He, glorified is He, said: ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own selves, and if you do evil, it is against them﴾, where He put forward the mention of good and repeated it, but not evil. It also contains an alert that doubling is sufficient for preference; so it is as if, since they used to give inheritance to males and not to females, it was said to them: "It suffices the males that the females' share has been doubled for them, so the females are not deprived of inheritance entirely, given that both are equal in the direction of inheritance."

The use of the names "male" and "female" instead of what was mentioned first, "men" and "women," is to make explicit that the adult and the young of both groups are equal in entitlement, with no bearing of puberty or maturity on this whatsoever, as was the claim of the people of ignorance, who did not give inheritance to children any more than to women. The wisdom in His, may He be exalted, making the females' share of the wealth less than the males' is the deficiency of their intellect and religion, as came in the report; together with the fact that their need for wealth is less, because their husbands spend on them, while their desire is greater, so wealth may become a cause of increased immorality in them. Among what is well known:

"Youth, leisure and wealth are a corruption to a man, what a corruption!"

And it is narrated from Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that Hawwa', peace be upon her, took a handful of wheat and ate it, took another and hid it, then another and gave it to Adam, peace be upon him. When she made her own share double the man's share, the matter was reversed upon her, and the woman's share was made half the man's share. This was mentioned by some, and I have not found its authenticity established.

Then the place of inheritance applies if no impediment exists, such as slavery, killing, and difference of religion, as is not hidden. The inheritance from the Prophet (ﷺ) was excepted from the general rule, on the basis of the view that he (ﷺ) is included in the general statements revealed through his tongue, which in linguistic terms encompass him; and the evidence for the exception is his saying (ﷺ): "We, the company of the prophets, are not inherited from." The Shia adopted the generality without exception and used this to criticize Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, because he did not give inheritance to al-Zahra', may Allah be pleased with her, from the estate of her father (ﷺ), to the point that, according to their claim, she said to him: "O son of Abu Quhafah, you inherit from your father, and I do not inherit from my father? What justice is this?" They also said: the report was narrated by him alone, and even granting that others narrated it too, it is not mutawatir but solitary (ahad), and it is not permissible to specify the Book by a solitary report. The proof is that Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, rejected the report of Fatimah bint Qays that she was given neither residence nor maintenance, because it would have specified the verse "House them (askinuhunna)"; he said: "How can we abandon the Book of our Lord and the Sunnah of our Prophet (ﷺ) for the word of a woman?" So if it were permissible to specify the Book by a solitary report, he would have specified it by it and would not have rejected it, nor would his being a woman's report together with its contradiction to the Book have been a barrier to accepting it. Also, the general, which is the Book, is definitive, and the specific, which is the solitary report, is speculative, so it would entail abandoning the definitive for the speculative. They also said: among what indicates the falsity of the report is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Solomon inherited David﴾ and His saying, glorified is He, reporting from Zakariyya, peace be upon him: ﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir﴾ ﴿who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾; for this is explicit that prophets inherit and are inherited from.

The answer is that this report was also narrated by Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Abu al-Darda', Abu Hurayrah, al-Abbas, Ali, Uthman, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. Al-Bukhari also narrated, from Malik ibn Aws ibn al-Hadathan, that Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said in the presence of the Companions, among them Ali, al-Abbas, Uthman, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas: "I adjure you by Allah, by whose leave heaven and earth stand: Do you know that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'We are not inherited from; what we leave is charity'?" They said: "Indeed, O Allah, yes." Then he turned to Ali and al-Abbas and said: "I adjure you both by Allah, do you know that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said that?" They both said: "Indeed, O Allah, yes." So the claim that the report was narrated only by Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, is not to be heeded. The books of the Shia also support it: al-Kulayni narrated in al-Kafi from Abu al-Bakhtari, from Abu Abd Allah Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets, for the prophets did not bequeath a dirham or a dinar, but bequeathed hadiths; whoever takes some of them has taken a copious share." The word "innama" (only) is definitively restrictive by the acknowledgment of the Shia, so it is known that the prophets do not bequeath anything but knowledge and hadiths.

It is also established by the consensus of the people of biographies, histories and hadith scholars that a group of those regarded as infallible by the Shia and as protected by Ahl al-Sunnah acted upon its ruling; for the estate of the Prophet (ﷺ), when it came into their hands, they did not give al-Abbas, nor his sons, nor the pure wives, anything from it; and had inheritance applied to that estate, they would certainly have shared it with them. So when from the totality of what we have mentioned mutawatir transmission is established, all the better; for specifying the Qur'an by a mutawatir report is permissible by agreement, and even if it is not established and the report remains solitary, we say: specifying the Qur'an by a solitary report is permissible according to the sound view, and the four Imams held to its permissibility. Its permissibility is shown by the fact that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, were specified by it without objection, so it was a consensus. From this is His saying: ﴿And lawful for you is what lies beyond that﴾, which includes marrying a woman together with her paternal aunt or maternal aunt, and it was specified by his saying (ﷺ): "Do not marry a woman together with her paternal aunt, nor together with her maternal aunt." The Shia too have specified many general statements of the Qur'an by solitary reports, for they do not give the wife inheritance from the land, and they specify the eldest son of the deceased from his estate by the sword, the Qur'an, the ring and the garment without compensation, as we pointed out earlier; and they rely in this on solitary reports which they alone transmitted, although the generality of the verses is contrary to that. The argument against permissibility of specification by the report of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, is answered by the fact that Umar only rejected the report of the daughter of Qays because of his doubt about her truthfulness or falsehood; for this reason he said: "a woman's word, we do not know whether she spoke truth or lied." So he gave as the reason for rejection the doubt about her truthfulness and falsehood, not that it was a solitary report. As for the claim that specification entails abandoning the definitive for the speculative, it is rejected on the ground that the specification occurred in the indication, for it is a removal of the indication in some instances; so it does not entail abandoning the definitive for the speculative, but rather it is abandoning the speculative for the speculative. As for what they claimed from the indication of the two verses they cited on the falsity of the report, it is extremely weak, because the inheritance in them is inheritance of knowledge, prophethood and inner perfections, not inheritance of possessions and wealth. Among what indicates that the inheritance in the first verse is of this kind too is what al-Kulayni narrated from Abu Abd Allah: that Solomon inherited David and that Muhammad inherited Solomon; for inheritance of wealth between our Prophet (ﷺ) and Solomon, peace be upon him, is inconceivable in any way. Also, David, peace be upon him, according to what the historians mention, had nineteen sons, and all of them would have been heirs in the sense the opponent claims; so there is no point in singling out some of them over others in the inheritance of wealth, since they all share in it without any particularity for Solomon, peace be upon him, in it, unlike the inheritance of knowledge and prophethood. Also, describing Solomon, peace be upon him, with that inheritance is not something that entails perfection nor requires distinction, because the righteous and the wicked
