He would inherit from his father. So what is the purpose of mentioning this general inheritance in describing this Prophet's virtues and merits, peace be upon him?

Another indication that the inheritance in the second verse is likewise not material is that if "inheritance" there meant the inheritance of wealth, the speech would be akin to sophistry. For "the family of Ya'qub" would then mean either his own noble person, which would imply that Ya'qub's property remained undivided until the time of Zakariyya, with about two thousand years between them, and that is clearly absurd. Or it would mean all his sons, which would imply that Yahya inherited from all the Children of Israel, both living and dead, and this is even more abominable than the first. Or it would mean some of his sons, or "Ya'qub" would refer to someone other than the one who is apparent, namely the son of Ishaq, peace be upon them both. In that case one asks: what benefit is there in describing this guardian, when Zakariyya asked God, by saying that he inherits from his father and inherits from some of his relatives? A son is the heir of his father and of those close to him in all religious laws. Moreover, this inheritance is understood from the word "guardian" without any strain, and the context is not one of emphasis. Furthermore, in the lofty outlooks and the aspirations of holy souls, which have severed their ties to this perishing world and joined the presence of the true holiness, there is no inclination toward worldly goods even the weight of a gnat's wing. So it is not fitting that Zakariyya, peace be upon him, should ask for a son to whom his wealth would pass and into whose hands his possessions would come, nor should he show grief and fear over the loss of that. For this clearly indicates complete love and attachment of the heart to this world and what is in it, and that is far from his lofty sanctuary and holy aspiration. Also, there is no sense in Zakariyya's fear that his paternal cousins would misuse his wealth after his death. If the disposal were in obedience, it is obvious. If it were in disobedience, then when a man dies and the property passes to the heir who spends it on sins, there is no blame upon the deceased and no reproach, and this fear could have been averted easily by spending it and giving it in charity in the way of God before his death, leaving his heirs in greater ease and avoiding the risk of sudden death.

The inability to do this does not hold against the Shi'ah, for in their view the prophets know the time of their death. So the meaning of that Prophet's inheritance, peace be upon him, is nothing but the inheritance of spiritual perfections, knowledge, and prophethood, which qualifies him for the rank of rabbinical leadership (hubur). For he, peace be upon him, feared that the wicked among the Children of Israel would distort the divine rulings and the lordly laws, would not preserve his knowledge, would not act upon it, and that this would be a cause of great corruption. So he asked for a son to implement the rulings of God after him, to propagate the law, and to be a resting place for prophethood. Such a wish is a cause of multiplied reward and continuous recompense, and desire for the like of this is characteristic of those with holy souls and pure, sanctified hearts.

If it is said: inheritance in the sense of inheriting knowledge is a metaphor, while in the sense of inheriting wealth it is literal, and turning a word from its literal meaning to a metaphorical one is not permitted without necessity, so what is the necessity here? I answer: the necessity here is to preserve the words of the infallible one from being called false. Moreover, we do not accept that inheritance is literal only for wealth. Rather, through the predominance of usage in custom it became specific to wealth, whereas in its original linguistic application its use for the inheritance of knowledge, wealth, and rank is correct. This use is its linguistic literal meaning. Even if we grant that it is a metaphor, this metaphor is so well established and well known that it is equal to the literal meaning, especially in the usage of the Glorious Qur'an. Among such examples is God's saying: ﴿Then We gave the Book as inheritance﴾ and "They were made to inherit the Book," and there are several other verses.

Among the Shi'ah, some have raised a point here: if the Prophet ﷺ did not bequeath anything to anyone, why were his pure wives given their chambers? The answer is that this is a fallacy, because the assignment of the chambers to the wives was only because they were owned by them, not by way of inheritance. Rather, the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, built each chamber for one of them, so the gift together with taking possession was realized, and this necessarily brings about ownership. The Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, did the same for Fatimah, may God be pleased with her, and Usamah, and handed them over to them. Whoever possessed anything the Messenger of God ﷺ had built for him would dispose of it as an owner did during his lifetime, peace be upon him. What confirms what has been mentioned is that it is established by the consensus of the People of the Sunnah and the Shi'ah that when the Imam al-Hasan, may God be pleased with him, was on his deathbed, he asked permission from A'ishah al-Siddiqah, may God be pleased with her, and requested that she give him a place for burial beside his grandfather, the chosen one ﷺ. For if the chamber were not the property of the Mother of the Believers, there would be no meaning in asking permission and requesting it. The Qur'an also contains a kind of indication that the purified wives owned those chambers, when He, glorified be He, said: ﴿And stay in your houses﴾, attributing the houses to them, and did not say "in the houses of the Messenger."

Among the People of the Sunnah, some have responded to the basis of the argument by saying that after the death of the Prophet ﷺ, the property became in the status of an endowment (waqf) for all Muslims. So the ruler of the time may give preference to whomever he wishes with whatever he wishes, just as al-Siddiq gave the Commander of the Faithful, may God honor his face, a sword, a coat of mail, and a white mule called Duldul. The Commander of the Faithful, may God honor his face, did not inherit from the Prophet ﷺ in any way. It is also established that al-Siddiq gave al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam and Muhammad ibn Maslamah some of the property the Prophet ﷺ left behind. But he, may God be pleased with him, did not give Fatimah, may God's blessings be upon her father and her and may He grant them peace, Fadak, even though she requested it as an inheritance. Her contentment was disturbed by the refusal, by consensus, and she turned from that to claiming a gift. She brought Ali, al-Hasan and al-Husayn, and Umm Ayman as witnesses, but according to the Shi'ah her claim did not stand firm. It was not implemented because of religious and worldly considerations which the caliph of that time saw, as al-Aslami mentioned in al-Tarjamah al-Abqariyyah wa al-Sawlah al-Haydariyyah, and he elaborated on it at length.

The essence of the discussion on this point is that Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, restricted the verse on inheritance by what he heard from the Messenger of God ﷺ. A report from the Prophet, peace be upon him, concerning those who heard it from him directly, without intermediary, gives definite knowledge without doubt, and acting upon what one has heard is obligatory for him, whether or not others heard it. The scholars of the principles of jurisprudence from both the People of the Sunnah and the Shi'ah have agreed that the division of reports into mutawatir (widely transmitted) and other categories applies to those who did not witness the Prophet ﷺ and heard his report through narrators, not to those who saw the Prophet ﷺ and heard from him directly. Thus the report "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from" is, for Abu Bakr, definitive, because for him it is like the mutawatir, and even higher in rank. A definitive report restricts a definitive text by consensus. There is no contradiction between this report and the verses which attribute inheritance to the prophets, peace be upon them, for the reason you have understood. Fatimah's claim to Fadak on the basis of inheritance does not prove that the report is false, but only that she had not heard it. This does not detract from her station, her elevated rank, or her great knowledge. Likewise, the purified wives taking their chambers does not indicate that, for the reason already explained and clarified. Her turning to a claim of gift is not established according to us. What is established is her claim of inheritance. Even if we grant that she made a claim of gift, we do not accept that she brought those pure ones as witnesses. This is because it is agreed that a gift is not complete except by taking possession, and Fadak was not in the possession of al-Zahra, may God be pleased with her, at any time, so there was no urgent need to request witnesses. And even if we grant that those pure ones testified, we do not accept that al-Siddiq rejected their testimony. Rather, he did not rule by it. There is a difference between not ruling here and rejecting. The latter means not accepting it on account of an accusation of lying, for example, while the former means not enforcing it due to the absence of some conditions that are required beyond justice. The deviation of al-Zahra's contentment was one of the requirements of human nature. Moses, peace be upon him, became angry with his elder brother Aaron until he seized him by the beard and head, and that did not diminish the rank of either of them in the slightest. Moreover, Abu Bakr sought her pleasure, may God be pleased with her, asking Ali, may God honor his face, to intercede with her, and she was pleased with him, as is recorded in Madarij al-Nubuwwah, Kitab al-Wafa, Sharh al-Mishkat by al-Dahlawi, and others. In Mahajj al-Salikin and other reliable Imami books there is something that supports this section, for they narrate that when Abu Bakr saw Fatimah, may God be pleased with her, she withdrew from him, shunned him, and did not speak about the matter of Fadak after that. This weighed heavily upon him, so he wanted to win her pleasure. He came to her and said: "You have spoken truly, daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ, in what you claimed. But I saw the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, distributing it, giving to the poor, the needy, and the wayfarer, after setting aside from it your sustenance. So what will you do with it?" She said: "I will do with it what my father, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, used to do with it." He said: "God has given you the right that I do with it what your father used to do." She said: "By God, will you truly do so?" He said: "By God, I will surely do that." She said: "O God, bear witness," and she was pleased with that, and she took a covenant from him. So Abu Bakr would give them their sustenance from it and distribute the remainder among the poor, the needy, and the wayfarer.

What remains is the reason why she, may God be pleased with her, was not enabled to dispose of it. The purpose was to remove confusion and to close the door of demands which would lead to breaking many hearts, or to avoid making the matter difficult for the Muslims. It has been reported: "When the believer is tested with two afflictions, he chooses the lighter of them." Moreover, the later contentment of al-Zahra, may God be pleased with her, with al-Siddiq closed the door of criticism against him, whether he was right in refusing or not. Glory be to Him who grants success to what is right, and who protects His prophets from error in decisive speech.

﴿If they are women﴾: the pronoun refers to the children in general, and the statement conveys meaning without any need for interpretation. The fact that the feminine is given precedence over the masculine does no harm, because this is among what scholars have explicitly permitted for the sake of agreement with the preceding statement and for harmony with it. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the female offspring or the daughters who are included within the general category of children. The meaning would then be: if the offspring or daughters are women, purely female with no male among them. This interpretation gives a meaningful sense, otherwise the subject and predicate would be identical and would convey nothing. Furthermore, if His saying ﴿more than two﴾ is taken as a qualifier of "women," then it is the place of benefit. Abu Hayyan insisted on this, and did not permit what many others allowed, namely that it be a second predicate, supposing that it would not then convey any benefit. This is part of conjecture, as you know. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that kāna be a complete verb, and the pronoun be ambiguous, explained by the accusative following it as a specification (tamyiz). The grammarians did not approve of this, because kāna is not one of the verbs whose subject is a pronoun explained by what follows it, since that is specific to the construction of ni'ma (how excellent). The interplay (tanazu') is as al-Shihab said. The intended meaning of superiority is an increase in number, not literal superiority in position. The benefit of mentioning this is to make clear that the meaning is not restricted to one number rather than another, that is, if they are women more than two, of whatever age they reach.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 11 (part 3 of 5):

﴿Then for them are two-thirds of what he left.﴾ That is, of what the deceased among you left; it is elided because the context points to it, and such ellipsis is common and permissible. ﴿And if she (i.e., the female child implied by the discourse) is one﴾ — that is, one woman, with no brother or sister alongside her. Nafi' and the people of Madina read ﴿wāḥidatun﴾ (wahidatun) with a damma, on the basis that kāna is complete (tāmmah) and the noun after it is its subject (fā'il). The reading with the fatha (wahidatan) was preferred on the ground that it is more consistent with what precedes. Ibn Tamjid said: the reading with the damma is preferable and more suitable to the structure of the verse, because the reading with the fatha appears, on the surface, to disrupt the structure. For if the pronoun of kāna refers to the children, the meaning is corrupted, as is evident; and if it refers to the female child, as they have said, it requires a pronoun before its referent. Both difficulties are removed in the reading with the damma, since the meaning is: "and if one girl of those children is found." The scholars of verification do not deny such an elision, as you have learned just now. ﴿Then for her is the half﴾ — that is, (of what he left); "what he left" is omitted, relying on the first occurrence. The word nisf (half) may be pronounced with three vowels, as in the Qamus, meaning one of the two halves of a thing. Zayd ibn Thabit read ﴿al-nuṣf﴾ with a damma on the nun, which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and he mentioned that it is more regular (aqyas), because you say: al-thuluth (the third), al-rub' (the quarter), al-khums (the fifth), and so on, all of which begin with a damma.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, took the apparent sense of the verse, so he assigned two-thirds to what exceeds two daughters, like three or more, and he assigned to two daughters a half, like the share of one. The majority of the Companions, the scholars, and the Imamiyya held otherwise, ruling that two or more daughters receive two-thirds, and that the half is only for a single daughter. The basis for this, according to al-Qutb, is that since it has been shown that the male with a female receives two-thirds (for the male has the equivalent of the share of two females), there must be a case in which two daughters receive two-thirds; otherwise the male would not have the equivalent of the share of two females, since two-thirds is not a share for them at all. But that case cannot be a case of the combination (of two daughters with a son), since there is no case in which two females combined with a male would receive two-thirds. Therefore it must be the case of their being alone. This was indicated by al-Sayyid al-Sanad in his commentary on al-Sirajiyya, and he raised the objection that the argument is circular (dawri), because knowing that the male receives two-thirds in the stated case depends on knowing the share of the two females, since nothing is known from the verse except that the male has the equivalent of the share of two females; so if knowledge of the share of two females were derived from the share of the male, circularity would follow. It is answered that what is derived is the specific share assigned to the two females, namely two-thirds, while what is required to know the male's share is knowledge of the share of two females in general, so there is no circularity. Because of the strain in this answer, some verifiers abandoned it, and it was mentioned that the ruling for two daughters is understood from the text by way of indication (dalalah) or allusion (isharah). This is because of what Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah related from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The wife of Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: O Messenger of Allah, these are the two daughters of Sa'd; their father was killed at Uhud, and their paternal uncle took their property and left them no property, and they cannot be married unless they have property. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Allah will decide concerning that.' Then the verse of inheritance was revealed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent to their uncle and said: 'Give the two daughters of Sa'd two-thirds, give their mother one-eighth, and what remains is yours.'" This shows that the ruling is grasped from the text by one of the two ways, since he ruled by it after the revelation of the verse. Its explanation is that since the two daughters were entitled to a half together with a male, it is known that if they are alone without him they are entitled to more than that; for when one woman is alone she takes a half, having previously taken a third when with him. Their share must be what the male takes in general, which is two-thirds, since he takes it together with a daughter. Thus His saying, "And if they are women..." etc., is an explanation of the share of one woman, and of more than two after He had stated their share; that is why He placed it as a consequence (with the fa'), since if there were nothing before it indicating the share of females, the fa' would not be in its proper place. This is beyond dispute. It was also said that the ruling for two daughters is established by analogy (qiyas) to a daughter with her brother, or to two sisters. As for the first: since a daughter receives a third with a brother, then with daughters (two) it is by a stronger reasoning. As for the second: He mentioned the ruling for one daughter and for three or more daughters, and did not mention the ruling for two daughters; and in the inheritance of sisters He mentioned the ruling for one sister and for two sisters, and did not mention the ruling for many sisters. So the ruling for two daughters is known from the inheritance of sisters, and the ruling for sisters from the inheritance of daughters. For since the share of two sisters is two-thirds, two daughters are more entitled to it; and since the share of many daughters does not exceed two-thirds, by a stronger reasoning the share of sisters does not exceed that. Many later scholars went this way. Al-'Allama Nasir al-Din made it a supporting argument, not an independent proof, since it is dispensed with by what preceded; and because it was said that analogy does not operate in the fixed shares and measures. Some scholars criticized the first analogy, saying that a single daughter does not receive a third with a brother, but rather receives half of his share, and that it being a third is by coincidence. But its weakness is not hidden. It was also said: it may be said that the two daughters are joined to the group, because the description "women" exceeds two, to draw attention to the lack of difference between one number and another; and two daughters share with the group in plurality, and it is known that few or many does not make a difference; so the apparent conclusion is to join the two to the group on the basis of plurality, while the distinction of few and many is not considered for one alone, because there is no common basis between them.

It was also said: the meaning of the verse is "if they are women, two or more," but He placed mention of "more than" before "two," as is related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said: "A woman should not travel a journey of more than three days unless with her husband or a mahram of hers." Its meaning is: do not travel a journey of three days or more. To this view went those who said that the minimum of plurality is two. It was objected against Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that if from His saying "more than two" it is derived that the status of two is not the status of the group, based on the concept of the adjective (mafhum al-sifah), then it is countered by the derivation from "one" that their status is not the status of one, based on the concept of number (mafhum al-'adad), and this has been said. It was answered by distinguishing between them: "women" is apparent in what is more than two, so when it is emphasized by it, it becomes definitive in the restriction, unlike "And if she is one." It was objected to this that this holds only if the adverbial phrase is a confirmatory adjective, not a predicate after a predicate. It was answered that His saying "women" is apparent in its being more than two, so that not being sufficient by itself, and bringing a predicate after it, indicates clearly that the ruling is restricted to it and does not go beyond it. Also, among what supports the view of Ibn 'Abbas is that when the two evidences conflicted, the matter of the two daughters lay between two-thirds and one-half; the certain is the half, and the excess is doubtful and not established, so it is necessary to resort to it. It is not hidden that the sound hadith which preceded demolishes the reliance on such supports; perhaps it did not reach him, may Allah be pleased with him, as it has been said, so he said what he said. In the commentary on Yanbu' (Sharh al-Yanbu'), citing al-Sharif Shams al-Din al-Armuni, who said in his commentary on the Faraid of al-Wasit: "The retraction of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, from that is authenticated, and so it became a consensus." Accordingly, it is possible that the hadith reached him, or that he reflected deeply on the verse and understood from it what the majority holds, and so returned to their agreement. As for the report of al-Nizam from him, may Allah be pleased with him, in the book al-Nukat, that he said: "For two daughters is a half and a qirat, because one woman has a half, and what exceeds two has two-thirds, so it should be that two daughters have what lies between them," this is something that hardly holds. So understand.

﴿And for his parents﴾ — that is, the deceased, whether male or female; the noble structure changes (to the parents) because the ruling for them is not restricted to what precedes of cases, but rather it is in reality the beginning of the inheritance of ascendants after mention of the inheritance of descendants. By "parents" is meant the father and mother, by way of giving precedence to the word "father." It is not permissible to say "two sons" for a son and a daughter, due to the possibility of confusion; but if no confusion is caused, it is permissible, as al-Zajjaj said. ﴿For each one of them﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿and for his parents﴾, with the repetition of the governing particle, and it is placed between the subject, which is His saying, "from them is the sixth," and the predicate, which is "for his parents." Ibn al-Munir claimed that "there is a problem in parsing it as a substitute, because on this supposition it would be a substitution of a thing for a thing when both refer to one and the same entity, and the original sentence would be: 'and the sixth for his parents, for each one of them,' and the implication of restricting it to the substituted element is the sharing between them in the sixth, as He, glorified is He, said: '...if they are women, more than two, then for them are two-thirds of what he left,' which implies their sharing in it; and the implication of a substitute, were the first element discarded, would be the individual allotment of the sixth to each of them and no sharing, and this contradicts the reality of this type of substitute, since it requires that what is substituted and the substitute be one in what they convey, and their purpose is only emphasis by the combined two names without additional meaning. Once the difference between them is established, the stated substitution is impossible; nor is it a substitution of division either under this parsing, since that would require additional meaning in the substitute. Therefore the correct view is to posit an elided subject, as if it were said: 'and for his parents is the third'; then when it mentioned their share in summary, it detailed it by saying: 'for each one of them is the sixth.' Omitting the subject is permissible because the detail indicates it, since it is necessarily implied from each one's entitlement to the sixth that both together are entitled to the third." Abu Hayyan refuted this, saying: "This is a substitution of part from whole, and that is why the pronoun is used; it is not to be supposed that it is a substitution of a thing for a thing when both are one entity, because one may say 'your parents do such-and-such,' but it is impossible to say 'your parents, each one of them, do such-and-such'; rather one says 'he does such-and-such.'" However, an objection was raised against making ﴿li-abawayhi﴾ the predicate of the subject, that in such cases it is the substitute, not the substituted element, that is the predicate, as in the example. Al-Halabi responded that there is room for consideration in this objection, because if you are asked, "What is the grammatical position of li-abawayhi?", you are compelled to say that it occupies a nominative position as a fronted predicate,

and it is he who transferred the predicate-status to each of them, not to li-abawayhi. This wording was chosen rather than saying "and for each one of his two parents is the sixth," because the first contains a generality and then the detail, which is more apt to come to mind than the second; and rather than saying "for his parents are two sixths," to make explicit that the two parents are equal in the first, while the second does not make this explicit, since it allows for inequality; and that it departs from the apparent sense does no harm, since it suffices as a rhetorical point for the deviation.

Al-Hasan and Na'im ibn Maysarah read ﴿al-sudus﴾ with the lightened form, and likewise al-thuluth, al-rub' and al-thumn.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 11 (part 4 of 5):

﴿After the bequest﴾ is connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun resting in the adverbial phrase, which refers back to the subject. The governing element is the stable predicate (al-istiqrār), meaning: being from what the deceased has left, ﴿if he has a child﴾, male or female, one or more. The child of a son is likewise. Then, if the child is a male, the remainder is his. If they are males, the remainder is theirs equally. If they are males and females, then ﴿to the male is the equivalent of the portion of two females﴾. If the child is a daughter, she has half, and to one of the two parents (ummah and abb) a sixth, or to both of them two sixths, and the remainder returns to the father if he exists, but by way of agnatic residuary status ('aṣabah) and the multiplicity of the directions (of inheritance), it is treated as the multiplicity of persons. If there is only a mother and a daughter, then the remainder after the shares of the mother and the daughter is returned to them both. The Imamiyyah (Twelver Shi'a) claimed, in the case of two parents, or a father, or a mother and a daughter, that the remainder after each one takes his fixed share is returned to the daughter and to one of the two parents, or to both of them, in proportion to their shares.

﴿But if he has no child﴾, and no child of a son, ﴿and his two parents inherit from him﴾ alone, and this is derived from the specification of the male (the sense that the parents alone inherit), as the implication (fahwā) indicates. ﴿Then to his mother is a third﴾ of what he has left, and the remainder is for the father. It was not mentioned because there is no need for it, since, when it was stipulated that the heirs are restricted to his two parents, and the share of the mother was specified, it became known that the remainder is for the father, and this is something upon which the Muslims have unanimously agreed. It was said: it was not mentioned because the aim is to change the share, and in this case only the share of the mother changes, while the share of the father remains as it is; the father takes the remainder after his share, and the mother's share, by way of agnatic residuary status, so this is not the context of the father's share. There is room for reflection in this, because the apparent meaning is that the father's taking of the remainder after the mother's fixed share is by way of agnatic residuary status, and the jurists of inheritance (al-Furūḍiyyūn, specialists in the fixed shares) have explicitly stated this. The specification of the mother's side by mention, and the leaving of the father's side to indication from the context, while the explanation also occurs by the reverse, is for that reason too; and because her share is shorter and her entitlement is more complete and abundant. This applies when neither of the spouses is with them. But if one of the spouses is with them, these two cases are called al-Gharrawān (the two famous ones), al-Gharībatān (the two strange ones), and al-'Umariyyatān (the two of 'Umar). Then the mother has a third of what remains after the fixed share of one of them, according to the majority of the Companions and the jurists, not a third of the whole, unlike Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who argued that He, exalted is He, first made her a sixth of the estate when there is a child, by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And to his parents, to each one of them is a sixth of what he has left, if he has a child﴾, then it was mentioned that she has a third when there is no child, by His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿But if he has no child, and his two parents inherit from him, then to his mother is a third﴾. So it is understood from this that the intended meaning is a third of the original estate as well.

This is supported by the fact that all the fixed shares are calculated in relation to their original base after the bequest and the debt. To this view the Imamiyyah went. Abu Bakr al-Asamm used to say that she has, with the husband, a third of what remains of his share, and with the wife, a third of the original estate. It is attributed to Ibn Sirin, because if a third of the entire wealth were given to her along with the husband, the share of the mother would exceed the share of the father, since the problem would then be from six, due to the combination of half and third: the husband has three, the mother two on that assumption, and one remains for the father; and in this there is a preference of the female over the male. If she is given a third of what remains of the husband's share, she has one and the father has two. And if she were given a third of the original estate with the wife, that preference would not arise, since the problem would be from twelve, due to the combination of a third and a quarter; so when the mother takes four, five remain for the father, and there is no preference for her over him. The doctrine of the majority was preferred over the doctrine of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, because it avoids
[p. 225]
leading to the preference of the female over the male who is equal to her in degree and nearness, but rather the male is stronger than her in inheritance, as shown by his taking double her share when the two of them are alone without one of the spouses, and by his being both a holder of a fixed share and an agnatic residuary, and that is contrary to the disposition of the Law. This preference is evident in the first problem, and by this reasoning Zayd ibn Thabit justified his ruling in it, differing from Ibn 'Abbas. For 'Abd al-Razzaq and al-Bayhaqi related from 'Ikrimah, who said: Ibn 'Abbas sent me to Zayd ibn Thabit to ask him about a husband and two parents. Zayd said: For the husband is half, for the mother is a third of what remains, and for the father is the rest of the estate. Ibn 'Abbas sent to him: Do you find this in the Book of Allah, exalted is He? He said: No, but I dislike preferring a mother over a father. It should not be unknown that this does not suffice as a preponderant argument for the doctrine of the majority over the doctrine of al-Asamm. Hence al-Sayyid al-Sanad and others, in supporting their doctrine, departing from the path we have taken, said: The meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if he has no child, and his two parents inherit from him, then to his mother is a third﴾, is that she has a third of what the two of them inherited, whether that is the whole estate or part of it. This is because if a third of the original estate were intended, the statement would have been sufficient for the explanation. The verse says: ﴿But if he has no child, then to his mother is a third﴾, as He, exalted is He, said regarding daughters: ﴿And if she is one, then she has half﴾, after His saying, glorified is He: ﴿But if they are more than two females, then for them is two thirds of what he has left﴾. So it would follow that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and his two parents inherit from him﴾ would be devoid of benefit. If it is said: we will interpret it as meaning that the inheritance is for the two of them alone, we say: there is no indication in the expression that inheritance is restricted to them, and even if that is granted, then the verse gives no indication, in that case, regarding the case in dispute, neither negating nor affirming it. So it returns, regarding these two, to the principle that the two parents among the ascendants are like the son and daughter among the descendants, because the cause for the inheritance of the male and the female is one, and each of them is connected to the deceased without an intermediary. Therefore what remains of the fixed share of one of the spouses is divided between them in thirds, as in the case of the son and daughter, and as in the case of the two parents when they alone inherit. So the mother's share does not exceed half the father's share, as analogy requires. Therefore there is no room for what al-Asamm adopted either, on this basis. Would that he had heard this, so let him understand.

They also differed regarding the mother's share in the case where a paternal grandfather takes the place of the father, and the rest of the problem remains as it is. The view of Ibn 'Abbas, and one of the two narrations from al-Siddiq, and the people of Kufah related this from Ibn Mas'ud in the case of the husband alone, is that the mother has a third of the entire estate. And the opinion of Abu Yusuf, which is the other narration from al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, is that she has a third of the remainder, as with the father. On this narration, the grandfather is treated like the father, so he makes the mother an agnatic residuary as the father would. The way, according to the first narration, as the Furudiyyun have stated, is that it abandons the apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then to his mother is a third﴾ regarding the father, and it is interpreted as explained above, so that it does not lead to preferring her over him while they are equal in nearness and rank. The interpretation is supported by the statement of most of the Companions. But as for the grandfather, it is applied to its apparent meaning, because there is no equality in nearness, and the disagreement among the Companions is strong. There is no impossibility in preferring a female over a male when there is a difference in degree, as when a man leaves a wife, a full sister, and a paternal half-brother. The wife has a quarter, the full sister has half, and the paternal half-brother has the remainder. Here the female is preferred because of her greater nearness than the male. Furthermore, the mother has the actual bearing (ḥaqīqat al-wilād) just as the father does, so he makes her an agnatic residuary, whereas the grandfather has the ruling of bearing but not its reality, so he does not make her an agnatic residuary, since there is no agnatic residuary status where the causes differ, but rather where they agree.

﴿But if he has brothers, then to his mother is a sixth﴾. The majority hold that the intended meaning of "brothers" is a number of those who have brothers, without considering the sense of three, whether they are brothers or sisters, and whether they are from both parents or from one of them. Ibn 'Abbas differed in this, for he held that three of the brothers and sisters block the mother, but not two. So with two, she has a third according to him, on the basis that the word "brothers" is a plural form, so it does not include the dual. 'Uthman argued with Ibn 'Abbas on this basis, may Allah be pleased with them both. Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Ibn 'Abbas that he entered upon 'Uthman and said: Two brothers do not turn the mother away from the third, and he recited the verse, then said: And two brothers are not "brothers" in the language of your people. 'Uthman said: I cannot reverse what was before me, which has continued in the regions, and by which people have inherited. The majority said: The ruling for two in the matter of inheritance is the ruling for a group. Do you not see that two daughters are like daughters, and two sisters like sisters, in the entitlement to two thirds? So likewise in blocking. Also, the general meaning of plurality is shared between two and what is above them, and this context calls for indicating general plurality, so the word "brothers" indicates it. Indeed a group said: the plural form is literally applied to two, just as it is to what is above them in the speech of the Arabs. Al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Zayd ibn Thabit that he used to block the mother with two brothers. They said to him: O Abu Sa'id, Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿But if he has brothers﴾, and you block her with two brothers. He said: The Arabs call two brothers "brothers." This contradicts the earlier report from Ibn 'Abbas, which is explicit that the plural form is not said of two in the language of the Arabs. 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, accepted that, but argued that the application of "brothers" to the more general case was a consensus. Hence people differed about what the plural form literally signifies. Some of the Usuliyyun (scholars of legal theory) stated that in inheritance and bequests, the plural form applied to two is attached to the literal meaning, whereas the grammarians hold otherwise. Ibn 'Abbas also differed concerning the inheritance of a sixth for the mother together with female full siblings, because "brothers" is the plural of "brother," so it does not include a sister except by way of the masculine taking precedence, and the pure females have no males with them, so they do not take precedence. This is a sound argument, but in practice the matter follows the consensus on that interpretation, which existed before the emergence of Ibn 'Abbas's dissent. Breaking a consensus is forbidden only for one who did not exist at the time it was formed.

The Zaydiyyah and the Imamiyyah held that brothers from the mother alone do not block her, unlike others, for the blocking here has a rational meaning, as the words of Qatadah indicate: if there are brothers from both parents or from the father, the father's dependants increase, so he needs more wealth for maintenance. This meaning does not exist where the brothers are from the mother alone, since their maintenance is not upon the father. The majority held that there is no difference, because the term is literal for the three categories, and this ruling is one whose reason is not understood, established by the text. Do you not see that they block the mother after the father's death, though he bears no maintenance obligation after his death, and that they block her even when they are adults, though their maintenance is not upon him either? Furthermore, what is widely known and established from outside (the text) or, in one opinion, from the verse itself, is that the brothers block the mother with a reduction (ḥajb nuqṣān, blocking that reduces her share), and if they are themselves blocked by the father, they are blocked with exclusion (ḥajb ḥirmān, blocking that removes entitlement altogether). The sixth they blocked her from returns to the father. This is also the doctrine of the majority of the Companions. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that it goes to the brothers, because they blocked her from it only so that they could take it, for a non-heir is not blocked, as when the brothers are unbelievers or slaves. This may be supported by the mursal report of Tawus that "upon him be blessings and peace gave the brothers a sixth alongside the two parents."

and for the majority, as al-Sharif said, the beginning of the statement indicates that his mother has a third and the remainder goes to the father; so likewise is the case at its end. It is as if it were said: "If he has siblings and his parents inherit from him, then his mother has a sixth and his father has the remainder." Moreover, the condition of the one who blocks (al-hajib) is that he be an heir with respect to the one he blocks, and a Muslim brother is an heir with respect to the mother, unlike a slave or a disbeliever. So the siblings block her, and they are blocked by the father. Do you not see that they inherit nothing alongside the father when the mother is absent, because they are kalala (collateral relatives), so there is no inheritance for them alongside a parent? The status of the siblings alongside the mother is no stronger than their status when she is absent. It has been narrated from Tawus that he said: "I met the son of a man from among the brothers whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave a sixth alongside the two parents, and I asked him about that, and he said: 'That was a bequest (wasiyyah), and at that time the hadith becomes evidence for the majority, since there is no bequest to an heir.'" The apparent view is that this narration from Ibn 'Abbas is not sound, because it agrees with al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) on the blocking of the grandfather by the siblings, so how could he say that they inherit alongside the father? So said al-Imam al-Sarakhsi in his "Sharh." And in "al-Durr al-Manthur" it is related that Ibn Jarir, 'Abd al-Razzaq,
page 227
and al-Bayhaqi related it from him. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (fa-li-ummihi) with a kasrah on the hamzah, following the kasrah of the lam. It is also said that it is an imitation of the kasrah of the mim, but this was deemed weak, because it involves imitating an original vowel with an incidental vowel, namely the i'rabi (case-ending) vowel. It is also said that it is a dialectal form for "umm" (mother), but al-Shihab rejected this. In al-Qamus: "al-Umm (and it may be kasrah-ed) is the mother. It is said for the mother: ummah and ummahah, and it is pluralized as ummat and ummahat; the latter is for rational beings, and ummat for non-rational beings." This is also reported in al-Sihah from some of them.

﴿min ba'di wasiyyatin﴾ ("after a bequest") is connected to "yusikum" (enjoins you). The speech contains an omitted modifier, on the basis that what is meant by the bequest is the property bequeathed, and the meaning is: these shares for the heirs are after the removal of a bequest. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) of "the sixth," the implied sense being "established after that," and the governing element is the prepositional phrase functioning as predicate because it is dependent; and for what precedes it, its equivalent is implied, as in the case of tanazu'. It is also said that it is connected to a general verb omitted, i.e., "that is established for these after a bequest which the deceased enjoins."

Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (yusa) in the passive, lightly stressed, and it has been read as (yusi) in the active, with shaddah. The clause is a descriptor of "wasiyyah." The purpose of the description is to encourage the bequest and recommend it. It is also said: the generalization, because a bequest is not except something bequeathed.

﴿aw dayn﴾ ("or debt") is conjoined to "wasiyyah." However, it is not restricted by what the earlier descriptor restricted it with, so the removal of the debt does not depend on its being bequeathed; rather it is absolute, encompassing what is established by evidence and by acknowledgment during health. The choice of "aw" (or) rather than the waw (and) is to signal their equality in obligation, and that both precede the division, whether together or separately. Mentioning the bequest before the debt, though the debt precedes it in ruling, is as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ decided in what 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) related, and a group transmitted it from him, to show complete care for executing it, because it is a place of negligence in its payment, since it is taken like inheritance without compensation, so it would burden them; and because all of it is recommended when there is no obstacle, unlike the debt, according to the well-known view, though its rarity or the rarity of delaying it until death is noted. Ibn al-Munir said: "In the verse, the order established by the Law is not violated, because the first thing one begins with is the removal of the debt, then the bequest, then the division among the heirs. Observe how the removal of the inheritance came last, right after the removal of the bequest, and the bequest right after the debt. So it agrees with our statement that the division of inheritances is after the bequest, and the debt is the actual form in the Law. Had it been dropped and mentioned afterward, and the speech were 'Remove the inheritance, the bequest, and the debt,' the aforementioned question could arise, and this is of great eloquence."

﴿Your fathers and your sons—you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit﴾. The address is to the heirs. "Abaukum" (your fathers) is the subject, "wa-abna'ukum" (and your sons) is conjoined to it, and "la tadrun" (you do not know) with what is in its scope is its predicate. "Ayyu" is either interrogative, a subject with "aqrabu" as its predicate, and the verb is suspended from it, so it takes the place of the two objects; or it is relative, with "aqrabu" as a predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause is the relative clause; the relative pronoun is the first object, built on a dhamma because it is attached to something, with the initial element of its relative clause omitted, and the second object is omitted. "Naf'an" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), transferred from the subject sense. The clause is parenthetical, emphasizing the obligation to execute the bequest.

"Fathers" and "sons" are expressions for the heirs of the ascendants and descendants, so it includes daughters, mothers, grandfathers, and grandmothers: that is, your ascendants and descendants who die before you, you do not know which of them is most beneficial to you: whether one who bequeaths part of his property, thereby exposing you to the reward of the Hereafter by executing his bequest, or one who does not bequeath, thereby providing you with the goods of this world in abundance. The intent is not, as Shaykh al-Islam said, to deny their knowledge, to explain that the matter is confused for them, or that the greater benefit of each of the first and second lies within the realm of possibility for them without preference of one over the other. For that would have nothing to do with conveying the aforementioned emphasis or the encouragement to execute the bequest, but rather with establishing the greater benefit of the first within the implicit reproach that they believe the second is more beneficial, based on their lack of knowledge. This is indicated where he expressed "more beneficial" as "nearer in benefit," to remind them of the basis of their assumption, to specify the source of their error, and as emphasis in the aforementioned encouragement by portraying the deferred right in the form of the immediate, since human natures are inclined to love present good. It is as if it were said: "You do not know which of them is more beneficial to you, so you judge by the apparent situation and nearby gain, that the second is more beneficial, though the matter is otherwise. For what results from the first is lasting reward in the Hereafter, and what results from the second is transient goods in this worldly life. The first, because of its permanence, is the nearest and most proximate; the second, because of its perishing, is the farthest and most remote." Many of the researchers chose that the clause is a parenthetical emphasizing the matter of division, and the address is directed to the testators. Its rationale: He, exalted, had earlier explained the shares of children and parents, and the shares were varied, and minds cannot be guided to the quantity of that. So a person might think that if the division had occurred in a different manner, it would have been more beneficial and better, as the people of the Jahiliyyah were accustomed to, when they would give inheritance to strong men and not to young boys and weak women. So God rejected what such thoughts might occur to them, and pointed to the deficiency of their minds. It is as if He said: "Your intellects do not encompass your interests, so you do not know which of those who inherit from you among your ascendants and descendants is more beneficial to you in your present and future. So leave off estimating the inheritances by amounts that you find pleasing with your minds, and do not intend to prefer some and deprive others. Be obedient to God's command in these estimates that He, glorified, has set, for He is the Knower of unseen matters and their outcomes, and the wisdom in what He has decreed and arranged, and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise." Benefit in this sense is more general than worldly and otherworldly, and one party's benefit from another in this world is through supporting them, raising them, and defending them, for instance, while their benefit in the Hereafter is through intercession. Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When a man enters Paradise, he will ask about his parents, his wife, and his children. It will be said: 'They have not reached your rank.' He will say: 'O Lord, I did good deeds for myself and for them.' So he will be commanded to have them join him." Al-Hasan (may Allah have mercy on him) adopted this view. Mujahid restricted benefit to the worldly, and some restricted it to the otherworldly.

It has been mentioned that the meaning is: you do not know which of the fathers, among the parents and mothers, and which of the sons, among the sons and daughters, is nearer to you in benefit, so that you may elevate them in rank in the Hereafter. And when you do not know, then uphold what God has ordained and apportioned, and do not say: "Why did He place the father after the son? And why did the son take everything to the exclusion of the mother and the daughter?" It has been objected that this is not explained by benefit, such that what was mentioned would be complete, and that it indicates that whoever is given precedence among the heirs, or whose share is doubled, is more beneficial, which is not so. The response is that it is meant that since benefits were hidden from your understanding, you believed in a benefit that your intellects do not reach, which is far-fetched because it is not understood from the context. Something similar may be raised against what the majority chose. It may be said: the meaning is that you do not know which of the ascendants and descendants is nearer to you in benefit, let alone the benefit itself, so how can you judge the division according to benefit when it is entirely hidden from your understanding? The discourse is directed to refute what was in the Jahiliyyah. For the people of the Jahiliyyah, as al-Suddi said, did not give inheritance to girls or to weak boys, and a man would not inherit from his son except one who was able to fight. And from Ibn 'Abbas: they would give the inheritance to the eldest, then the eldest. This suggests that their basis for inheritance was benefit together with kinship. So God refuted them, saying that you do not know benefit, so how do you consider it? The purpose of this is an argument ad hominem, not an explanation that benefit is regarded in itself while they simply do not know it. Perhaps on this view the earlier objection does not apply, so reflect. It is also said that the meaning of the verse is: you do not know which of the heirs and the testators will die more quickly, so that the one will inherit from the other; therefore do not wish for the death of the one who is inherited from, nor hasten it. This is attributed to Abu Muslim, and its remoteness is not hidden.

﴿a duty from Allah﴾

page 229
It is an absolute verbal noun (masdar muakkid) for itself, in the manner of "this is my son, truly." Because it follows a sentence that admits no other interpretation, its governing verb is obligatorily omitted; i.e., "He decreed that as a duty from Allah." It is also said that it is not a verbal noun but a passive participle functioning as a circumstantial clause (hal), and the sense is: these portions for these heirs, being prescribed by God, Exalted. It is also said that it is indeed a verbal noun, but emphasizing its verb, namely "yusikum" ("He enjoins you") previously, though not in its exact wording, since the meaning is "He prescribes for you." Isam al-Milla objected to this: when a verbal noun is attached to its agent or object, or is connected to it, its verb must be omitted, as Radi explicitly stated, unless a distinction is made between the explicit verbal noun and what it implies. But this requires evidence, and we have not come across it.

﴿Indeed Allah is ever All-Knowing﴾, i.e., of the interests and the ranks, ﴿All-Wise﴾ in everything He decrees and ordains, so the rules of inheritance enter into this primarily. The position of this sentence here is like His saying, exalted, to the angels: ﴿Indeed I know what you do not know.﴾ Describing God, exalted, with such expressions, as Khalil said, is like reporting a present or future state, since He, exalted, is far above being subject to time. Sibawayh said: the people, when they witnessed knowledge, wisdom, grace, and kindness, marveled, so it was said to them: "Indeed Allah was such," i.e., He has always been characterized by these attributes. Therefore there is no need to hold that "kana" is redundant, as some have claimed.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 12 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave﴾ if you have not had intercourse with them, ﴿if they have no child﴾, male or female, one or many, from you or from others. For this reason He, glory be to Him, said "for them" (lahunna) and did not say "for you." There is no difference whether the child is from the wife's womb or from the loins of her sons or her sons' sons, to whatever extent God Almighty wills. ﴿But if they have a child﴾, according to the detail mentioned. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that a son's son does not block (the share). The fa' (then) is for the sequence of what follows upon what precedes, for mentioning the supposition of there being no child and explaining its ruling entails the supposition of its existence and the explanation of its ruling. ﴿Then for you is a quarter of what they leave﴾ of the property, and the remainder in both cases belongs to the rest of the heirs, from among the sharers (ashab al-furud) and the agnates (asabat), or the distant kindred (dhawu al-arham), or to the public treasury (bayt al-mal) if there is no other heir. ﴿After any bequest they make or debt﴾ is connected to both cases, not to what immediately precedes it alone. The discussion of the purpose of the qualifier, and likewise of the placing of the bequest first in mention, has already passed, so there is no benefit in repeating it. ﴿And for them﴾, that is, the wives, whether they are many or one, ﴿is a quarter of what you leave if you have no child﴾, according to the detail previously given. ﴿But if you have a child, then for them is an eighth of what you leave, after any bequest you make or debt﴾. He assigned to the man, by the right of marriage, double what He assigned to the woman, as in lineage, because of his superiority over her; and for this reason he was singled out with the honour of direct address, and the mention of the ruling on his inheritance was placed first. Thus is the analogy for every man and woman who share the same direction and nearness of kinship. Excepted from this are only the uterine siblings and the freed male and female slave, because male and female are equal among them.

﴿debt. And if a man﴾ — "a man" refers to the deceased, and it is the subject of kana (was). ﴿Is inherited﴾ — in the passive form, from the triliteral warratha, is the predicate of kana, and the meaning is that he is inherited from, for warratha is transitive with min, and it is often omitted. ﴿Kalalah﴾ — it is originally a verbal noun meaning kalal, which is exhaustion. al-A'sha said:

So I swore I would not show pity for her, because of kalala, nor because of a loving one, until I meet Muhammad.

Then it was borrowed and used in the manner of true meanings for kinship other than that of parent and child, because of its weakness in relation to their kinship, and it is applied to one who leaves behind neither parent nor child, and to one who is neither parent nor child among those left behind, in the sense of "one who has kalala," just as "kinship" is applied to relatives. Some of them considered that to be of the category of naming by the verbal noun. Others allowed that it be an adjective, like hajajah for the fool. The poet said:

Hajajah, chosen of heart, as though he were an ostrich in a valley.

It is also used of inherited property from one who is neither parent nor child, but this usage is not common. In all of these meanings it is neither dualized nor pluralized. Many chose that its origin is from takallalahu al-nasab, since kinship surrounds him, and from this comes al-iklil (the crown), because it surrounds the head, and al-kull (the whole), because it surrounds the number. Al-Husayn ibn 'Ali al-Maghribi said: The origin of kalala in my view is what a person leaves behind his back, taking it from kall, which is the back and the nape.

It is in the accusative in one of several ways: as an object of purpose, meaning it is inherited from him because of the aforementioned kinship; or as a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in "is inherited," meaning while he is one with kalala, which al-Zajjaj preferred; or as the predicate of kana, with "is inherited" as an attribute of "a man," meaning if a man is inherited from who has kalala, neither parent nor child. Abu al-Baqa' mentioned the possibility that kana is complete, with "a man" as its subject, "is inherited" an attribute of it, and "kalala" a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in "is inherited." Its accusative on this possibility as an object of purpose is also apparent. It was also allowed that it be in the nominative as an attribute or as a substitute for the pronoun, but no one is known to have read with it, so it is not permissible to recite with it at all. Its accusative was also construed, in the uncommon usage, as a second object of "yuratha."

It is read "yuratha" and "yurithu," with lightness and with emphasis, in the active form, so the accusative of "kalala" is either as a circumstantial accusative from the verb's subject with the object omitted, meaning he bequeaths his heir while being one with kalala; or as a direct object, meaning he bequeaths one with kalala; or as an object of purpose, meaning he is inherited for the sake of kalala, so they say. Then, what the people of Kufa and a group of the Companions and Successors hold is that kalala here has the third meaning. It is related from others, among them Ibn Jubayr, and a report is authenticated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that it has the second meaning. We have not seen the attribution of the other two views to any of the early scholars. The first of these two is not far-fetched, and the second is permissible, though it has a remoteness, as is not hidden.

﴿Or a woman﴾ — a conjunction upon "a man," restricted by what he is restricted by. It is often sufficient to restrict the conjoined by restricting the one conjoined to, so no further restriction is needed. Perhaps the separation of her mention from his is to signal her nobility and her原 standing in rulings. It was said: because the occasion of revelation was to explain her ruling, based on what is related from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to me while I was ill and I said: 'How is inheritance, when only kalala inherits from me?' Then the verse of the inheritance shares was revealed for this." ﴿And he has﴾, that is, the man, and the singular pronoun is used because it is required in what follows, or so that what came contrary to this is interpreted by the majority, as in His words: ﴿If he is rich or poor, God is more entitled to both of them﴾. He used the masculine for the choice between giving precedence to the conjoined or to the one conjoined to in such a case, and the masculine has been observed here because of its precedence in mention and its nobility. It is permissible that the pronoun refers to one of the two, and that the masculine is for predominance. It was allowed that it refers to the deceased, or to the one inherited from, and because of the precedence of what indicates it. He who allowed that it refer to the man was further removed. The pronoun of the woman is omitted, and the meaning is "and he has or she has": ﴿a brother or a sister﴾, that is, from the mother alone. The majority of the exegetes hold this, to the extent that some reported a consensus on it.

Many reported from Sa'id ibn Abi Waqqas that he used to read "and he has a brother or a sister from a mother." And from Ubayy: "from the mother." This reading, though irregular, was relied upon by many scholars, on the basis that an irregular reading whose chain is sound is like a single report (khabar al-wahid) in the obligation to act upon it, contrary to some of them. What also points to this qualification is that the rulings on full siblings and paternal siblings are those that come at the end of the blessed surah. Also, what is assigned here to each of the brother and the sister, and to the majority, which is the sixth, while the third is the mother's share, so it is fitting that this belongs to the children of the mother, who are called half-siblings by the mother (ikhwat akhyaf) and sons of the mother (banu al-akhyaf). The construction is an explanatory genitive. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "is inherited," or from "a man," on the assumption that "is inherited" is its attribute, and its purpose is to depict the case. He mentioned "kalala" to confirm that the stated ruling applies, even though with the one mentioned there are other heirs through the kinship of kalala. It does no harm, according to those who do not hold the argument from implication, that it applies in the case of the mother or the grandmother, though their kinship is not through kalala. Likewise it does no harm according to the one who holds it either, because of the consensus on that. ﴿Then for each one of them﴾, that is, the sister and the brother, ﴿is a sixth﴾ of what he left, without preferring the male over the female. Perhaps he turned from "then he has a sixth" to this in order to avert the misconception that what is mentioned is the brother's ruling, and to omit the sister's ruling because it is known from it that she has half the brother's share by the rule of femininity. The wisdom in God's Lawgiver equalizing them is their equality in their descent to the deceased by pure femininity.

﴿But if they are more than that﴾, that is, the siblings and half-siblings from the mother implied by what came before, and the masculine is for predominance, ﴿than that﴾, that is, than the stated number by one, or more than it. The expression by the demonstrative rather than "one" is because one does not say "more than one," so that if it were said, "the first," the meaning would be that it exceeds it. Some scholars undertook this interpretation here too, since there is no comparison after the state of the referent is revealed. Perhaps the expression by the demonstrative then emphasizes the indication that the matter is one of fixed shares. The fa' (then) is because of what has passed: that mentioning the possibility of being alone entails mentioning the possibility of plurality. ﴿Then they are partners in the third﴾, sharing it among themselves equally. There is no disagreement about this among any of the Community. The remainder goes to the rest of the heirs, from among the sharers and the agnates. The Shi'a disagree on this. Here some people allowed that "yuratha" in the well-known reading be passive from "awratha," on the basis that the meaning is "the heir," and the sense is: if a man is made an heir because of kalala, or one with kalala, that is, neither parent nor child, and for this heir there is a brother or a sister, then for each of that heir or his brother or his sister is a sixth. If they are more than that, that is, more than two, by being three or more, then they are partners in the third distributed between the two, to which nothing is added. It is not hidden that the discussion on this is deficient in explaining the ruling for the case where the heir stands alone apart from a brother and a sister, and it implies that the consideration for the heirs' entitlement to the stated share is the siblings of each other from the mother alone, and this is an unprecedented manner. There is also in it what there is. Our master Shaykh al-Islam, may his secret be sanctified, clarified this with what admits no addition.

﴿After any bequest that is made or debt, not harmful﴾, that is, without harm to his heirs. So he does not acknowledge a right that is not upon him, nor bequeath more than a third. This was said by Ibn Jubayr. So the debt here is restricted like the bequest. In "yusa" there are two canonical readings, in the passive and in the active. "Ghayr" in the first reading is a circumstantial accusative from the subject of a verb in the active voice, hidden, indicated by what was mentioned, and what was omitted from the conjoined is relied upon by it. Its parallel is His words: ﴿He is glorified therein at morning and evening by men﴾, in the reading "yusabbaha" in the passive. And the poet's verse: "Let Yazid weep, a suppliant for a dispute, and one stumbling in what the calamities cast down." On the second reading it is a circumstantial accusative from the subject of the mentioned and omitted verb, sufficed by it. On this, there is no need to separate the circumstantial from its owner by a foreign element, as is not hidden. That is: he bequeaths what was mentioned of the bequest and the debt, while being one who is not harmful. It is not permissible that it be a circumstantial accusative from the omitted subject of the passive, because he has been left in a state where he is not regarded, so a circumstantial from him is not valid. It was allowed that it be an attribute of a verbal noun, that is, a bequeathing not harmful. Some preferred making it a circumstantial accusative from "bequest" or "debt," meaning: after the discharge of a bequest or debt not harmful to that one. He made the masculine for predominance, and that is nothing. This person also allowed that the meaning be

in accordance with what has preceded, not harming himself by committing an act contrary to the Shariah, namely by exceeding the third. This is valid in itself, but the first (meaning) is the one that comes immediately to mind, and Mujahid and others hold it. It is possible, as a group has said, that the meaning is one who does not intend harm but rather seeks nearness to God (qurbah). Isam al-Millah (ʿIṣām al-Milla) mentioned that what is understood from the verse is that a bequest or an acknowledgment of debt made with the intention of harming the heirs does not deserve to be executed. This is so, but proving the intention is difficult, unless it is known through his own acknowledgment. The apparent meaning is that the intention of harm, not of nearness to God, is what matters in bequeathing a third or less, and so it does not prevent execution. Ibn Abi Shaybah reported from Muʿadh ibn Jabal, who said: "God, exalted is He, has granted you charity from a third of your wealth as an increase in your lives. Yes, that is forbidden beyond any doubt. But not every forbidden act is non-executory, for something like manumission (ʿitq) or endowment (waqf) done for show and reputation is forbidden by consensus, yet it is still valid. Whoever claims that this ruling is restricted to bequests bears the burden of proof and must establish the evidence." From Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, it is reported that harming through a bequest is one of the major sins (al-kabāʾir). Ahmad, Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi reported from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, in a raised (marfūʿ) report: "A man may do the deeds of the people of good for seventy years, but when he makes a bequest he deviates in it, so his life ends with the evil of his deeds, and he enters the Fire. And a man may do the deeds of the people of evil for seventy years, but then he acts justly in his bequest, so his life ends with the good of his deeds, and he enters Paradise."

﴿A bequest from God﴾ is an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar muʾakkad), meaning: God enjoins this upon you as a bequest. The tanwīn (nunation) on wasiyyatan is for magnification (tafkhīm). The word min is connected to a deleted element that occurs as a descriptive modifier of an indefinite noun, emphasising its grandeur. A parallel is ﴿a duty from God﴾. Perhaps the reason each of these two terms is assigned to its own place is what the Imam (al-Razi) said: "The word farḍ (duty) is stronger and more emphatic than the word waṣiyyah (bequest). So he concluded the explanation of the inheritance of children with mention of the obligatory nature (al-farḍiyyah), and concluded the explanation of the inheritance of the kalālah with the bequest, to show that although all of it must be observed, the first category, the case of observing the rights of children, takes precedence." It has also been said that the bequest is stronger than the duty, because it indicates desire and a wish for quick attainment. So he concluded the explanation of the inheritance of the kalālah with it, because such relatives are distant and their matters may not be attended to, so he urged attention to them by mentioning the bequest, which is not the case with what came before.

Alternatively, ﴿ghayra muḍārrin﴾ is in the accusative governed by a deleted verb, and wasiyyatan is either: (a) an object of the verb, by supposition, meaning "the people of God's bequest"; or (b) an exaggerated (mubālagha) object, because harm is not done to the bequest itself but to its people. This is like the expression "O thief of the night, the people of the house" (yā sāriqu al-laylata ahla al-dār). The harm to them is the violation of their rights and the reduction of what is due to them through what has been mentioned of a bequest exceeding a third, or through a bequest of a third or less made with intent to harm rather than nearness to God, or through an acknowledgment of a false debt.

By "the people" (ahl) here is meant the heirs mentioned in this context. It occurs in some expositions that what is meant is God's bequest concerning children. Perhaps what is meant by them is all heirs, by way of expressing the universal through its most common individuals, as one expresses the general notion of benefiting from property by "eating" it. Otherwise this would not fit. The word muḍārr governs the direct object because it is an active participle (ism fāʿil) relying on a preceding element (dhū al-ḥāl), or because it is negated in meaning, and so it governs the explicit object. This possibility is supported by the reading of al-Hasan, ﴿ghayra muḍārri wasiyyatin﴾ with the genitive construction (idāfah). Abu al-Baqāʾ mentioned two possibilities for this reading. The first: the intended meaning is "not harming the people of a bequest," with the noun deleted. The second: the intended meaning is "not harming at the time of a bequest," with the time deleted, which is the attribution of an adjective to a time noun. This is close to the saying "he is a knight of war," meaning a knight in war, and "he is the knight of his age," meaning in his age. The majority do not admit the genitive construction with the meaning of "in." The Durr al-Masun mentions the possibility that it is in the accusative by way of exception (ʿalā al-khurūj), without explaining what is meant by this. Hamʿ al-Hawāmiʿ says regarding the direct object that the Kufans treat it as accusative by way of exception, but it also does not explain this. Al-Shihab said: "It seems that they mean it lies outside the two ends of the predication, so it is like their saying 'a superfluous element' (faḍlah). So let this be considered."

﴿And God is Knowing﴾ of the one who causes harm and of others. It has been said: of what He has ordained for His creation of the obligatory shares. ﴿Forbearing﴾: He does not hasten punishment, so let not the one who causes harm be deceived by the reprieve, or let not whoever opposes Him concerning the obligations He has explained be deceived by this. The use of the pronoun in place of the noun is to create awe and to cultivate reverence.

Know that God, glorified is He, has presented the categories of heirs in these verses in the best arrangement. The heir either connects to the deceased directly, without an intermediary, or connects to him through an intermediary. If the connection is direct, its cause is either kinship (nasab) or marriage (zawjiyyah). Three categories result. The noblest and highest is the connection arising initially from kinship, which is the relationship of birth (qarābat al-wilādah), and it includes children and parents. The second is the connection arising initially from marriage. This category is inferior in nobility to the first, because the first is essential (dhātī) and the second is accidental (ʿaraḍī), and the essential is nobler than the accidental. The third is the connection through an intermediary, which is called kalālah. This category is posterior to the first two for several reasons. First: children, parents, husbands and wives are not liable to be entirely excluded, whereas the kalālah may be entirely excluded. Second: the first two categories each relate to the deceased directly, whereas the kalālah relates through an intermediary, and what is established directly is nobler than what is established through an intermediary. Third: a person's association with parents, children, spouses and wives is more frequent and complete than his association with the kalālah, and frequent association is the basis of affection and tenderness, which necessitates intense concern for their conditions. For these reasons and similar ones, God, glorified is He, delayed the mention of the inheritance of the kalālah after the mention of the first two categories. How excellent is this arrangement, and how well it accords with the principles of rational thought, as the Imam has said.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 13:

﴿Those﴾, i.e., the rulings mentioned concerning orphans, inheritances, and other matters. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, restricted it to the inheritances. ﴿Are the limits of Allah﴾, i.e., His laws, or His obedience, or His detailed provisions, or His conditions. They are called "limits" (ḥudūd) because of their resemblance to the boundaries (ḥudūd), in that the responsible person may not go beyond them to something else.

﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ in what He has commanded of the rulings, or in what He has made obligatory of the obligations. The use of the explicit noun in place of a pronoun is due to the reference that has already been mentioned. ﴿He will admit him into gardens﴾: it is in the accusative as an adverb of place (ẓarfiyya) according to the majority (al-Jumhur), and as a direct object (mafʿūliyya) according to al-Akhfash.

﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾, i.e., beneath its trees and its buildings, and the discussion of this has already passed. ﴿The rivers﴾, i.e., their water. ﴿Abiding therein﴾ is a presumptive circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddara) from the object of (yudkhilhu), because abiding follows entering. It is like your saying: "I passed by a man with a falcon with him, hunting with it tomorrow." The plural form is used in consideration of the meaning of (min), just as the singular pronoun is used in consideration of its wording. ﴿And that﴾, i.e., entering the gardens in the manner mentioned, ﴿is the great triumph﴾, i.e., the success and the attainment of good, ﴿great﴾ in itself, or in comparison with obtaining the inheritance, as has been said. The sentence is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 14:

﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ in what He commanded of the rulings, or in what He made obligatory of the obligations. Ibn Jurayj said: whoever does not believe in what He, glory be to Him, explained of the inheritance shares. The same is related from Ibn Jubayr.

﴿and transgresses His limits﴾ which His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought. Among them is what He related to us earlier. Or it means that he transgresses His limits concerning the aforementioned division, considering it lawful (istihlal), as related from al-Kalbi. ﴿He will admit him﴾: Nafi' and Ibn Amir read it with the nun (nahn) in both places. ﴿into a Fire﴾, meaning a great, terrifying one. ﴿abiding therein﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), as has passed.
