It is stated in the singular here and in the plural there, because the people of obedience are the people of intercession, and when one of them intercedes for another, that other enters with him. The people of disobedience do not intercede, so no one enters with them, and they remain alone (furada). Or it is because abiding in the abode of reward is expressed in the plural, which is more conducive to intimacy, while abiding in the abode of punishment is expressed in the singular, which is more effective in producing loneliness. Al-Zajjaj and al-Tabrizi permitted that "khalidin" there and "khalidan" here be qualifiers (sifatan) of "jannat" or "nar." It was objected that if this were so, the pronoun would have to be made explicit, because they apply to other than those they belong to. Abu Hayyan responded that this is according to the school of the Basrans, whereas the school of the Kufans permits the adjectival use in such a case and there is no need to make the pronoun explicit, since there is no ambiguity. ﴿And for him is a punishment﴾, meaning a great one that cannot be fathomed, ﴿humiliating﴾, meaning degrading to him. The clause is circumstantial. The intent is to combine two punishments for the sinful transgressors: a physical punishment and a spiritual punishment. We ask Allah, exalted is He, for well-being.

Whoever claims that the believing sinner is eternally abiding in the Fire has taken proof from this verse. The answer is that it does not apply to him, either because it refers to the disbeliever, as you have heard from al-Kalbi, Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Jurayj, or because the intended meaning of "the limits of Allah" is all of His limits, given the validity of the exception (istithna'), and the believing sinner stands at the limit of monotheism (tawhid), or because that is conditional on the absence of pardon, just as, according to the claimant, it is conditional on the absence of repentance. Concluding the verses on inheritance with this verse is an indication of the gravity of the matter of inheritance, the necessity of caution, diligence, and avoiding injustice in it. Ibn Majah narrated from Anas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever cuts off an inheritance that Allah and His Messenger have made obligatory, Allah will cut off his inheritance from Paradise."

Abu Mansur narrated similarly from Sulayman ibn Musa, and al-Bayhaqi from Abu Hurayra. al-Hakim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that the Hour will not come until no inheritance is divided and no one rejoices in the spoils of an enemy. It seems that the non-division is either due to laxity in religion, indifference, and widespread injustice among people, or due to the spread of ignorance and the absence of anyone who knows the obligatory shares. It is reported from Abu Hurayra, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that "the knowledge of the obligatory shares is the first thing to be removed from the Ummah." al-Bayhaqi and al-Hakim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Learn the obligatory shares and teach them to the people, for I am a soul that will be taken, and knowledge will be taken away, and trials will appear, until two people dispute over an obligatory share and find no one to judge between them." Perhaps the first possibility is the more apparent.

This is what we have. We have closed the door of allusion (isharah) in the verses, because opening it involves artificiality, and we have left it to its people.

[p. 234]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 15:**

﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness﴾ This begins the explanation of some rulings concerning men and women, following the explanation of the rulings on inheritance. *Allati* (those who) is the plural of *allati* (she who) in an irregular form. It has been said that it is a noun formulated for the plural, and its position is nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence. *Al-fahisha* (lewdness) is that whose ugliness is intense. It is often used for fornication (*zina*), since it is among the most ugly of ugly deeds, and this is the intended meaning here according to the correct view. *Al-ityan* (coming) is originally arrival. In *al-Sihah* it is said: "I came to him (*ataytuhu*) *atyan*," and the poet said:

*So choose for yourself before the coming of the army.*

*Atawtuhu atwatan* is a dialectal form of it, and from it is the saying of the Hudhali:

*Whenever I came to him from an absence...*

In *al-Qamus*: "*Atawtuhu atwatan* and *ataytuhu atyan*, *ityanan* and *ityanatan* with a kasra on both, and *ma'atatan* and *itiyyan* like *i'tiyyan*; it is also pronounced *ji'tuhu*." It may be used metaphorically, like *al-majiʾ* (coming), *al-rahaq* (overtaking) and *al-ghishy* (covering), for the act itself, and this has become widespread until it became a customary literal meaning. This is the intended meaning here. So the meaning is: they commit fornication, i.e., they commit *zina*. The expression with this word is for added condemnation. Ibn Mas'ud recited *ya'tina bil-fahisha* (they bring lewdness), in which case *al-ityan* keeps its well-known original sense. The phrase *min* (of) is connected to a deleted element that occurs as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of the subject of *ya'tina*. The intended meaning of "women" is, as al-Suddi said and Ibn Jarir reported from him, and as Ibn Jubayr also said: the women who have been married and have become chaste.

﴿then call for the testimony﴾, i.e., ask that they testify ﴿against them﴾ regarding their coming to lewdness, ﴿four of your men﴾, i.e., four of the men of the believers who are free. Al-Zuhri said: "The sunna from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the two caliphs after him was that the testimony of women is not accepted in the hudud (prescribed punishments)." The requirement of four witnesses for fornication was imposed as a strictness toward the accuser and as a concealment for the servants of Allah. It has been said: so that the quorum of testimony is complete against each of the two fornicators, like all other rights, but its weakness is not hidden. The sentence is the predicate of the subject, and the *fa'* (then) is added to it because it contains the meaning of a condition. Predication with this was permitted because the speech has taken on the status of a condition, since the relative *allati* has been joined to the verb. This was stated by Abu al-Baqa', who mentioned that when this is the case, the accusative by *al-ishtighal* (occupation of the verb) is not good, because it is not permissible to supply the verb before the conditional particle, and supplying it after the relative clause requires supplying a verb other than *fastashhidu*, because the accusative cannot govern *allati*. This is unnecessary given the soundness of the nominal construction. Some people permitted the accusative with a deleted verb whose supposed form is "intend those who" or "deliberately target those who." It has also been said that the predicate is deleted, and the supposed meaning is: "concerning what is recited to you is the ruling of those who." So the prepositional phrase and its object are the predicate, and *hukm* (ruling) is the subject, and both are deleted, because of the indication of *fastashhadu*, since it is the ruling recited to them. The address has been said to be to the judges, and it has been said to be to the husbands.

﴿Then if they testify﴾ against them regarding the coming (to lewdness),

﴿then confine them﴾, i.e., imprison them as a punishment for them, ﴿in houses﴾ and make them a prison for them, ﴿until death takes them﴾. The intended meaning of *tawaffi* (taking in full) is its original sense, i.e., full receipt, and it is taking hold. You say: "I took (*tawaffaytu*) my money from so-and-so," and "I received it in full" when you take it. Attributing it to death is by considering it as resembling a person who does that, so there is a metaphor within a metaphor (*isti'ara bil-kinaya*), and the speech is with an omitted modifier. The meaning is: until death takes their souls. It is not permissible to intend by *tawaffi* its well-known meaning, since then the speech would be equivalent to "until death causes them to die," and that has no meaning unless a modifier is supposed to which the verb is attributed, i.e., the angels of death, or the attribution is made a figurative attribution of what belongs to the real agent to the effect of its act.

﴿Or God makes for them a way﴾, i.e., an exit from confinement by what He prescribes of a *hadd* (prescribed punishment) for them. Ibn Jubayr said this. Al-Imamayn al-Shafi'i and Ahmad and others related from Ubada ibn al-Samit, who said: "When revelation descended upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he was distressed by it, and his face would turn pale." In a wording of Ibn Jarir: "He would be seized by something like a swoon, because of what he felt of the weight of it. Then it was revealed to him one day, and when it was lifted from him he said: 'Take from me, Allah has made for them a way: the married (*thayyib*) gets one hundred lashes and stoning with stones, and the virgin (*bikr*) gets one hundred lashes and then exile for one year.'" Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Jubayr that he said: "At the beginning of Islam, if four Muslim upright witnesses testified against a woman for fornication, she was imprisoned. If she had a husband, he would take her dowry from her, but he would spend on her without divorce, and she had no *hadd* and he did not have intercourse with her."

Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi: "At the beginning of Islam, when a woman committed fornication she was confined in a house, and her husband took her dowry, until the *hudud* came and abrogated it." The narration of abrogation (*naskh*) has come through more than one chain from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, and was also reported from Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with both of them. According to some, the abrogating text is the verse of flogging in Surat al-Nur. According to others, the verse of confinement was abrogated by the hadith, the hadith is abrogated by the verse of flogging, and the verse of flogging by the evidence of stoning. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is permissible that the verse is not abrogated, by leaving out mention of the *hadd* because it is known from the Book and the Sunna, and it enjoins keeping them in houses after they have been punished, to protect them from what befell them because of going out of houses and exposing themselves to men. The way in this case would be marriage that makes one independent of illicit intercourse." Shaykh Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi said in *Ma'alim al-Sunan*: "Abrogation has not occurred in the verse or in the hadith. The verse indicates that keeping them in houses is extended until the point where Allah makes a way for them. Then that way was general, so when the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Take from me,' up to the end of what is in the hadith, that became an explanation of what is in that verse, not an abrogation of it, and it became a specification of the generality of the verse of flogging. You have already been given earlier in Surat al-Baqara what will benefit you in verifying this matter, so remember it."

[Page 235]

[Page 236]

**"And those two of you who commit it"** (﴿واللَّذانِ يَأْتِيانِها مِنكُمْ﴾): they are the adulterer and the adulteress, by way of *taghlib* (the grammatical convention of giving the masculine precedence over the feminine). This was said by al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jubayr. What is meant by the two is the unmarried pair (*al-bikran*), who have not been muhsan (married or previously married). What supports this is that their punishment is lighter than indefinite confinement (*al-habs al-mukhallad*). By this reading the apparent repetition is avoided, but the ruling for the adulterer who is muhsan remains unclear.

Ibn Kathir read ﴿واللَّذانِ﴾ with a doubled nun (*tashdid al-nun*). This is a dialectal form (*lughah*). It is not restricted to the dual with alif, as has been said. Rather, it also occurs with ya', and it stands in place of the elided ya' of *alladhi*, since its analogical form would be *al-ladhiyan*. The meeting of the two unvoweled letters here follows its usual rule, as in *dabbah* and *shabbah*.

**"Then cause them harm"** (﴿فَآذُوهُما﴾): that is, after four witnesses have testified against them to the act of penetration. The mention of this is omitted, relying on what was stated just before.

Scholars differed about the meaning of *idha'* (harm) on two views. According to Ibn 'Abbas, it is by reproach and beating with sandals. According to al-Suddi, Qatadah and Mujahid, it is by reproach and rebuke only.

**"Then if they repent"** (﴿فَإنْ تابا﴾) of the immorality they committed, by means of the harm, as the *fa'* (then) indicates.

**"And reform"** (﴿وأصْلَحا﴾), that is, their conduct.

**"Then turn away from them"** (﴿فَأعْرِضُوا عَنْهُما﴾): that is, pardon them and refrain from harming them.

**"Indeed Allah is ever Accepting of repentance, Merciful"** (﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ كانَ تَوّابًا رَحِيمًا﴾): *tawwab* means intensely accepting of repentance, and *rahim* means of vast mercy. The sentence comes in the position of giving a reason for the command to turn away. The address here is to the judges (*hukkam*). It is also permissible that it is addressed to the witnesses who stood over their act. By harm (*idha'*) is meant blaming and reproaching them, threatening them with referral to the judges and dragging them to the rulers, and opening the door of evil against them. By turning away from them is meant refraining from confronting them in this way. The first view is the well-known one.

The ruling on it is abrogated (*mansukh*) by the prescribed punishment (*al-hadd al-mafrud*) mentioned in Surat al-Nur as well, according to al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, Ibn Jubayr and others. This view was held by al-Balkhi, al-Jubba'i and al-Tabari. Al-Farra' said that this verse abrogated the verse before it. This cannot stand on the view that the relative pronoun refers to the unmarried pair, as is not hidden.

Abu Muslim held that neither verse is abrogated. Rather, the first verse concerns the lesbians (*al-sahhaqat*), who are women who gain sexual pleasure from one another, and their punishment is confinement. The second verse concerns the two male sodomites (*al-lata'*), whose punishment is harm only. As for the ruling on fornicators, it will come in Surat al-Nur.

This view has been rejected on the grounds that no one has said it. It has also been rejected on the grounds that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, differed about the ruling on the sodomite, and none of them relied on this verse. Their not relying on it, despite their great need for a text indicating the ruling, is evidence that the verse does not concern that matter.

Furthermore, making confinement in the house the punishment for lesbianism is meaningless, because it is not something that depends on going out, unlike fornication. If the intended meaning were lesbians, the punishment for them would be that they not mix with one another, not confinement and prohibition of going out. Since confinement was made their punishment, this shows that the intended meaning of those women who commit the immorality is fornicators.

Abu Muslim replied that this is the view of Mujahid, who is one of the great early exegetes. Many have said: "If an interpretation from Mujahid reaches you, that is enough for you." It is also established in the principles of jurisprudence that devising a new interpretation of the verse which the earlier scholars did not mention is permissible.

It has also been rejected on the grounds that the goal of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, was to know the punishment for the sodomite and its quantity, and there is no indication in the verse about this, either by negation or affirmation. Mere harm is not suitable as a prescribed punishment (*hadd*) nor as an explanation of the quantity, which is why they differed.

Abu Muslim also argued that the meaning of keeping them in houses (*imsakihinna fi al-buyut*) is confining them there and making the house a prison for them. The condition of a prisoner is that he is prevented from anyone who wants to enter to him, and that he is not allowed to mix with others. Thus the statement amounts to: "Prevent them from mixing with one another," with the confinement mentioned being a prescribed punishment, and the intent of it being nothing but deterrence and exemplary punishment.

His view is supported by the pure feminine form in the first verse and the masculine form in the second verse, and taghlib goes against the original usage. What distances this view further is the word *minkum* (of you), since what is understood from it is "of your men," as in the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿أرْبَعَةً مِنكُمْ﴾ ("four of you").

Also, if each of the two verses were about fornication, it would follow that one thing is mentioned twice in the same place, which is a repetition with no justification. Moreover, on this assumption there is no need to posit abrogation in either verse, and the ruling of each one would remain established as it is. On what the others have said, one must posit abrogation, which goes against the original usage. Also, on their view the Book would be empty of an explanation of the ruling on lesbianism and sodomy, whereas on our view it contains that, which is more fitting for its status. God, Glorified is He, said: ﴿ما فَرَّطْنا في الكِتابِ مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ ("We have neglected nothing in the Book"), and ﴿تِبْيانًا لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ ("an exposition of everything").

It is answered that we do not accept that this is a view of Mujahid. In *Majma' al-Bayan* it is stated that he took "those two who commit it" to mean the two male fornicators. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him that they are the two who commit the act. This is not an explicit statement that they are the two sodomites.

Moreover, the reading of *al-lati* (the feminine relative) in the first verse as referring to lesbians has no sound narration from him. Rather, they have reported from him what is clearly contrary to it. Adam and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* reported from him, regarding that verse, that he had ordered them to be confined, and then it was abrogated by: ﴿الزّانِيَةُ والزّانِي فاجْلِدُوا﴾ ("The adulterous woman and the adulterous man, lash each of them").

What has been mentioned about the addition is accepted. But this interpretation is remote, because there is no sense in the dual form in the second verse. Promise and threat are customarily expressed either by the plural, to include individuals, or by the singular, since it indicates the category. There is no point in departing from that here on Abu Muslim's reading. Rather, the fitting form on his reading would have been the plural, so that the sodomy verse would be like the lesbianism verse.

This objection does not apply to what the majority established, because according to them the first verse is for married women who commit fornication, and the second verse is for an unmarried male and an unmarried female who commit fornication. So the two expressions are varied, due to the strong difference between the two cases. It is also possible that on their view the difference is meant to signal how rare the fornication of an unmarried person is compared with the fornication of a married person, because an unmarried woman fears disgrace more than others, owing to the visible trace of fornication, which is the loss of virginity, whereas a married woman is not in that situation.

It is not possible to apply a point like this to the difference on Abu Muslim's view, since we do not accept that sodomy among men is less common than lesbianism among women. Rather, the matter may be the reverse.

The claim that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, sought to know the punishment for the sodomite and its quantity, and that harm is not suitable as a prescribed punishment or as an explanation of quantity, is not valid. This is shown by the fact that some of them did not impose anything on him at all, and said: his punishment is deferred to the Hereafter. The Imams, may Allah be pleased with them, adopted this view. Moreover, what prevents harm from being considered a prescribed punishment, since it is mentioned in the context of the prescribed punishment and its manner is left to the opinion of the Imam, who then does to the sodomite what deters him, short of killing him?

Finally, that the statement amounts to "prevent them from mixing with one another" is extremely obscure, as is not hidden.

Yes, what is in the matter of the addition is acceptable. What has been said, that taghlib goes against the original usage, is accepted. But it is found in the Mighty Qur'an more than can be counted. Its application in *minkum* follows its application in *al-ladhani*. Mentioning a similar thing before without taghlib may even support applying taghlib here, in order to differ from the first, so that mentioning it afterwards has greater benefit. Do you not see how the testimony requirement was dropped from the second verse, although it is a condition by consensus, relying on what was mentioned in the first verse, because the two cases share the same testimony?

The claim that repetition in the same place is necessary on the majority's view is not valid, as we indicated in our explanation of the verse. The claim that abrogation must be posited does no harm, because abrogation is a familiar matter in many rulings. A group of the Companions and Successors explicitly stated here that the making obligatory of the prescribed punishment in the first verse is an abrogation, and there is a dispute about that, which is known from what we presented in al-Baqarah. If ﴿أوْ يَجْعَلَ اللَّهُ لَهُنَّ سَبِيلًا﴾ ("or Allah makes for them a way") is taken as relevant to the second verse, it is omitted from it, relying on what is in the first, as the report of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit indicates: "The matter was discussed in the two verses."

The necessity that the Book be empty of an explanation of the ruling on lesbianism and sodomy, on the majority's view, is not a problem. This applies whether lesbianism and sodomy are called fornication, in which case it is obvious, or they are not called that, in which case mentioning what can be analogised to them counts as an explanation of their ruling. Many rulings have been left unstated in the Book, relying on analogy, such as the ruling on nabidh (date wine) and the ruling on the grandfather (*al-jadd*) and others, relying on an explanation of what can be analogised. This does not contradict its being an exposition of everything and that it has neglected nothing.

Whoever claims that all religious rulings are stated explicitly in the Qur'an without any consideration of analogy has gone too far and spoken in error.

In sum, what is relied upon is the view of the majority, and the hand of Allah is with the community. Abu Muslim's view, although it is not without corruption, is not relied upon, and it has not gained acceptance. This is what I have in my verification of the matter, and in Allah, Glorified is He, is refuge.

When He, glorified is He, described Himself as the Oft-Returning (al-Tawwab), the Most Merciful, He followed this with an explanation of the condition for the acceptance of repentance, by His saying, exalted is His majesty:

﴿Repentance is only upon Allah﴾. That is, the acceptance of repentance is upon Allah. Although ʿalā (upon) is used to indicate obligation, so that some have cited this as evidence that it is obligatory upon Him, the meaning is that it is necessary and absolutely certain to occur, by virtue of the prior promise, so that it is as if it were one of the obligatory matters, as one says "wājib al-wujūd" (the Necessarily Existent, lit. "that whose existence is obligatory"). It was also said that ʿalā here means min (from), and it was said that it means ʿinda (with). Al-Tabarsi held this view, meaning: repentance is only with Allah. ﴿for those who do evil﴾, that is, sin, whether minor or major. Repentance (al-tawbah) is the subject (mubtada'), "for those who" (lilladhīna) is its predicate (khabar), and "upon Allah" is connected to what the predicate is connected to of stability (al-istiqrār). Alternatively, it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of the subject concealed in the element connected to the predicate, according to the view of those who permit placing the circumstantial clause before its implicit governing element when it is an adverbial phrase. Some have construed it on the pattern of "busran aṭyabu minhu ruṭaban" (unripe dates that are better than ripe ones). It is also permitted that "upon Allah" be connected to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of repentance, meaning: repentance which is upon Allah, and "for those who" is the predicate. This is clear according to the view of those who permit omitting the relative pronoun together with part of its relative clause. Abu al-Baqa' mentioned the possibility that "upon Allah" is the predicate, and "for those who" is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause from the concealed pronoun in the element connected to the predicate. It is also possible that it is connected to what the predicate is connected to. It is not hidden that the context of the verse supports taking "for those who" as the predicate, as is not hidden to anyone who does not force an interpretation.

﴿out of ignorance﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "they do" (yaʿmalūna), meaning: they do evil while engaged in it through ignorance. Or it is connected to "they do," and the preposition bāʾ is causal. By ignorance (al-jahālah) is meant ignorance and foolishness, committing what is unbecoming of a rational person, not the lack of knowledge, contrary to al-Jubbaʾi, for one who does not know does not need repentance. Ignorance in this sense is a true usage found in the speech of the Arabs, as in his saying:

*Ah, let no one among us act ignorantly, lest we act more ignorantly than the ignorant ones.*

Hence Mujahid said, as al-Bayhaqi reported from him in *al-Shuʿab* and others: "Everyone who disobeys his Lord is ignorant until he desists from his disobedience." ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah that he said: "The companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) agreed that everything disobeyed through it is ignorance, whether deliberately or otherwise." Similar was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him. Abu ʿAbd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Every sin that the servant commits, even if he knows, he is ignorant in it when he risks himself in disobedience to his Lord." Allah related the saying of Yusuf (peace be upon him) to his brothers: ﴿Do you know what you did with Yusuf and his brother when you were ignorant?﴾ So He attributed to them ignorance for their risking themselves in disobedience to Allah. Al-Farrāʾ said: the meaning of His saying, glorified is He, ﴿out of ignorance﴾ is that they do not know the reality of the punishment in disobedience. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of that is their choosing fleeting pleasure over lasting pleasure.

﴿Then they repent soon﴾, that is, within a near time, which is before the arrival of death, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He, which will come: ﴿until, when death approaches﴾ etc. It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said at the end of a sermon he gave: "Whoever repents a year before his death, Allah will accept his repentance." Then he said: "Indeed a year is long. Whoever repents a month before his death, Allah will accept his repentance." Then he said: "Indeed a month is long. Whoever repents a day before his death, [Page 239] Allah will accept his repentance." Then he said: "Indeed a day is long. Whoever repents an hour before his death, Allah will accept his repentance." Then he said: "Indeed an hour is long. Whoever repents when his soul has reached this point," and he pointed with his blessed hand to his throat, "Allah will accept his repentance." Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhi reported from Ibn ʿUmar, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah accepts the repentance of the servant as long as he has not begun the death rattle." Ibn Abi Shaybah reported from Qatadah that he said: "We were with Anas ibn Malik, and Abu Qilabah was present, and Abu Qilabah narrated: 'When Allah cursed Iblis, he asked Him for respite, so He granted him respite until the Day of Judgment. He said: By Your might, I will not remove from the heart of the son of Adam for as long as the spirit is in him. He said: By My might, I will not veil repentance from him for as long as the spirit is in him.'" Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The near time is what lies between him and seeing the Angel of Death." Similar was narrated from al-Ḍaḥḥāk. From ʿIkrimah: "The whole of this world is near." From Imam al-Qushayri: "The near time, according to the people of knowledge, is before death, and according to the people of practice, is before the soul becomes accustomed to evil and it becomes for it like a nature." Perhaps their intent is that if it is so, it is far from acceptance, though the acceptance of his repentance is not impossible. The word min (from) is partitive, as if he made the period between the occurrence of the sin and the arrival of death a near time, so that whatever part of this period he repents in, he is a penitent in some part of a near time. Some made it denote the starting point of the limit. The first view was preferred on the grounds that min, when it denotes the starting point, does not enter upon time according to the well-known opinion, and what denotes the starting point for time is mudhu and mundhu. The mention of thumma (then) indicates the vastness of His pardon, exalted is He.

﴿Those﴾, that is, those characterized by what has been mentioned, and what is in it of the sense of distance, in consideration of their being, by the conclusion of their mention, in the status of the distant. It is also permitted that this is an indication of the elevation of their rank and the high status of their affair, in that they are penitents. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to be addressed. The fāʾ (so) indicates causality. The demonstrative noun is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah will accept their repentance﴾. The repetition of the predication in it is for strengthening the ruling. This is a promise to fulfill what He, glorified is He, promised earlier, so there is no repetition. The verb (yatūb) is construed with the meaning of yaʿṭifu (turn toward with compassion), and therefore it takes ʿalā. It is also permitted that this is from the theological method, as if it were said: repentance is like what is obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, and everything that is like what is obligatory upon Him, exalted is He, must necessarily occur; so repentance is a matter that will necessarily occur. Thus the first verse stands as the minor premise, the major premise is implied, and the second verse stands as the conclusion.

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing﴾, so He knows the sincerity of the one who repents, ﴿Wise﴾, so He does not punish the penitent. The sentence is a parenthetical clause confirming the content of what precedes it. The explicit mention of the divine name in the place of the pronoun is to indicate the reason for the ruling.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 18:

﴿And repentance is not [accepted] from﴾ those ﴿who do evil deeds﴾, that is, sins. The word is in the plural because of the repeated occurrence of these acts over a long period of time, not because it is meant to cover all their kinds. The evil mentioned earlier is one type of them. ﴿Until, when death comes to one of them﴾, by witnessing the states in which return to the world is no longer possible in any way, seeing the Angel of Death, and the rope of hope being cut, ﴿he says: "Indeed I repent now"﴾. That is, this present time. [The word] "now" is mentioned to specify the time further, and the choice of "he says" over "he repents" is to remove this [statement] from the rank of consideration and to avoid calling it repentance, even though he emphasised it and was eager for it. The reason for this may be that this state most resembles the Hereafter, indeed it is the first station of its stations, while this world is a house of action without recompense and the Hereafter is a house of recompense without action. "Until" (hatta) is a particle of beginning, and the conditional clause after it is the limit of what precedes it. That is, repentance is not for those who do evil deeds up to the presence of their death and their saying such-and-such.

﴿Nor for those who die while they are disbelievers﴾. It is coordinated with the relative clause before it, meaning: acceptance of repentance is not for these, nor for those. The purpose of mentioning these [disbelievers], although they have no repentance at all, is to emphasise the non-acceptance of the repentance of those who procrastinate, and to indicate that its existence is like its non-existence. Moreover, the repetition of the negative particle in the coordinated clause, as has been said, implies a hidden indication that the state of those who procrastinate, in failing to bring about any benefit, is stronger than the state of those who die in disbelief. Most of the people of knowledge hold that the intended meaning of "those who do evil deeds" includes both the wicked and the disbelievers, while "those who die" and so on refers to disbelievers only. It is also permitted that both relative clauses refer to disbelievers specifically, or to the wicked alone, the designation of them as disbelievers in the circumstantial clause being for intensification. It is also permitted that both refer to both groups together, in which case the designation is by way of predominance. Ibn Jarir reported from al-Rabi' and Ibn al-Mundhir from Abu al-Aliyah that the first verse was revealed concerning the believers, the second concerning the hypocrites, and the third concerning the polytheists. Placing the middle [verse] on the hypocrites gives them further censure, since it makes their doing of evil deeds, in comparison with their other deeds, as though it were nothing, so that it is as if they did these deeds and no one else did. On this view the subtlety of the expression in the plural with regard to their deeds, and in the singular regarding the believers, is clear. However, this view has been criticised on the ground that if "the hypocrites" means those who persist in hypocrisy, then they have no repentance, which would not need to be negated; and if not, then they and others are equal.

This verse has been cited as evidence that the repentance of one in despair is not accepted, just as his faith is not accepted. There is a difference of opinion on this matter. It has been said that the repentance of one in despair is accepted, but not his faith, because hope remains, and regret and resolution to abandon sin are valid along with it. Also, repentance is a renewal of covenant with the Lord, may He be glorified, whereas faith is the establishment of a covenant that did not exist before, and there is a difference between the two matters. In al-Bazzaziyya it is stated that the correct view is that it is accepted, unlike the faith of one in despair. And if intercession is accepted on the Day of Resurrection, which is a state of despair, then this is more fitting. Al-Qadi Abd al-Samad al-Hanafi declared in his Tafsir that the position of the Sufis is that faith too benefits [a person] at the witnessing of punishment. This is supported by the fact that our master, the Greatest Shaykh (may his secret be sanctified), declared in his Futuhat the validity of faith at the time of compulsion. And from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, [it is reported]: "If a polytheist gasps [his last breath] while embracing Islam, I would hope for much good for him."

Some have supported the view that the repentance of a disbeliever at the moment of witnessing [death] is accepted by what Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Tarikh, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Dharr, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah accepts the repentance of His servant, or forgives His servant, so long as the veil has not fallen." It was asked: "And what is the falling of the veil?" He said: "The soul departs while it is associating [others with Allah]."

It is not hidden that the verse is clearly in favour of the view taken by the people of the first opinion. Some of the scholarly investigators answered regarding it that its import is that the acceptance of the repentance of the procrastinator and the persistent one is not established, and the negation of establishment is not the establishment of negation. So the matter concerning both of them remains somewhere in between. Allah, exalted is He, if He wills, pardons them, and if He wills, He does not pardon. The verse ﴿Indeed Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ shows that He, glorified is He, does not will forgiveness for the persistent disbeliever, and the repentant one at the time of death, for whatever sin he committed, remains under the Will [of Allah].

Some have claimed that there is no genuine repentance in the middle verse to be accepted; rather, all that is in it is the statement "Indeed I repent now," which is a sign of the absence of sincere repentance. For this reason, [the verse] did not say: "Repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death comes to one of them, he repents." Even on the assumption that the expression by way of saying has some other purpose, it entails the view that the restriction to "now" indicates that the conditions of repentance have not been fulfilled, because in it there is an allusion to the absence of resolve not to return to the sin he was in during the times that follow, if it is possible for him to remain alive. And one of the conditions of valid repentance is that. So reflect.

﴿Those﴾, that is, those mentioned from both groups, whose condition has reached the ultimate extreme of horror, ﴿for them We have prepared﴾, that is, We have made ready for them. It was also said: "We have prepared" (a'dadna), and the dal was changed into ta'. ﴿a painful punishment﴾, that is, causing pain and agony. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the direct object is to show concern that the punishment is made ready for them. The indefinite form is for magnification, and the repetition of the predication is for what has passed. The Mu'tazilah used this verse as evidence for the obligation of punishment for believers who die without repentance after committing major sins. It is answered that the preparation of punishment is the creation of the Fire with which they will be punished, and the verse does not state that Allah, exalted is He, will definitely cause them to enter it. That Allah, exalted is He, causes those who die in disbelief to enter it is known from other than this verse. It is also possible that the intended meaning is: "We have prepared for them a painful punishment if We do not pardon," as the texts indicate. It is reported from al-Rabi' that the verse is abrogated (mansukh) by His words, exalted is He: ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾.

It has been objected that "We have prepared" is a report, and there is no abrogation in reports. It has been said that "those" (ulaika) refers to "those who die while they are disbelievers," so there is no difficulty, just as if it were taken to refer to both groups, with the first meaning the hypocrites and the second meaning the polytheists.

﴿O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion﴾. When Allah, glory be to Him, forbade, in what preceded, the customs of the people of ignorance (jahiliyyah) concerning orphans and property, He followed this with a prohibition against adopting one kind of their practices concerning the women themselves or their property. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "When a man died and left a slave-girl, his kinsman would cast his garment over her, thereby preventing her from others. If she was beautiful, he would marry her; if she was plain, he would keep her confined until she died, so that he could inherit her." In the narration of al-Bukhari and Abu Dawud: "When a man died, his guardians had a greater right over his wife. Some of them would marry her if they wished, or they would give her in marriage if they wished, or they would not give her in marriage if they wished. They had a greater right over her than her own family. So this verse was revealed concerning that." Ibn al-Mundhir related from ʿIkrimah, who said: "This verse was revealed concerning Kubaysha bint Maʿn ibn ʿAsim of the Aws. She was married to Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat, and when he died, his son took an interest in her. She came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'I have neither been inherited as my husband's property, nor have I been left free so that I may be married.' Then this was revealed." Something similar is related from Abu Jaʿfar. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "The people of Yathrib, when a man among them died in the Jahiliyyah, whoever inherited his property would inherit his wife. He would keep her confined until he married her himself or gave her in marriage to whomever he wished. So Allah, exalted is He, forbade the believers from this."

It is related from al-Zuhri that the verse was revealed concerning a man who keeps a woman with him although he has no need of her, waiting for her death so that he may inherit her.

As for the word "the women" (al-nisaʾ): it may be the second object (maf'ul thani) of "you inherit" (tarithu), with the sense that the women themselves are the things inherited. "By compulsion" (karhan) is a verbal noun (masdar) in the accusative, functioning as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "the women." It has also been said that it is a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in "you inherit" (tarithu), and the meaning would then be: "It is not lawful for you to take the wives of your deceased by way of inheritance, as you claim, just as it is lawful for you to take property, while they are unwilling to that or are compelled to it, or while you are compelling them." Or "the women" may be the first object (maf'ul awwal) of the verb, and the meaning would be: "It is not lawful for you to take from the women, by way of inheritance, their property by compulsion." What is intended by this is that the husband should divorce a woman whose company he dislikes, and not keep her by compulsion until she dies so that he may inherit her wealth.

Hamzah and al-Kisai read "kurhan" with a damma in all its occurrences; ʿAsim, Ibn ʿAmir and Yaʿqub agreed with them in al-Ahqaf. The rest read it with a fatha in all of these places. The two forms have the same meaning, like "daʿf" and "duʿf" (weakness). It has also been said that "kurh" with a damma means compulsion, and with a fatha means dislike. It was also read "lā tahillu" with the feminine ta', because "an tarithu" (that you inherit) carries the sense of inheritance, just as it was read, "Their trial was not but that they said" (6:23), because it carries the sense of a statement. This is the reverse of masculinizing a feminine verbal noun, since it is interpreted as an "an" clause with a verb. Both are in use in the eloquent language.

﴿And do not restrain them in order to take away part of what you have given them﴾. The root meaning of ʿadl is constriction and confinement. From it comes ʿadalat al-mara'ah bi-waladiha, meaning that the woman had difficulty with her child in childbirth; it is also used as aʿdalat, so she is muʿdil and muʿaddil. It is said: ʿadala al-mara'ah yaʿdiluha, with each of the three vowels, ʿadlan, ʿidlan and ʿidlanan with the vowel of the ʿayn, and ʿaddalaha: the husband prevented her unjustly. ʿAdalat al-ardu bi-ahliha means the land became choked with its people. Aws said:

"You see the land around us in the open plain sick, *constricted* by us with a numerous, mighty army."

[p. 242]

The "lā" (not) may be a prohibitive (nahiyah), as has been said, and the verb is jussive (majzum) by it. The clause is then a new sentence (mustaʾnifah), as Abu al-Baqa said. Or it is conjoined (maʿtufah) to the preceding clause, on the basis of the permissibility of conjoining a prohibitive clause to a declarative clause, as is attributed to Sibawayh. Or it is based on the view that the first clause has the sense of a prohibition, since its meaning is: "Do not inherit women by compulsion," for that is not lawful for you. Or "lā" may be a negation that is an extra particle for emphasis of the negation, and the verb is in the accusative by conjunction with "tarithu" (you inherit), as if it were said: "The inheritance of women by compulsion is not lawful, nor is their restraint." This is supported by the reading of Ibn Masʿud: "wa-la an taʿduluhunna." As for making "lā" a negation that is not extra, with the verb conjoined to the accusative noun before it, some have rejected this, saying: when a negated verb with "lā" is conjoined to an affirmed verb, and both are in the accusative, the rule is that the accusative particle is to be understood after the conjunction particle, not after "lā." If one were to posit it here after the conjunctive particle according to that estimate, the meaning would be corrupted, as is not hidden.

The address in the two conjoined clauses is either to the heirs other than the husbands, for they used to prevent the widow from marrying so that she would ransom herself with what she had inherited from her husband, or she would give them a dowry she had taken, just as they used to inherit women by compulsion. What is meant by "what you have given them" in this case is what their kind has given, for otherwise the sentence would not cohere, since the heirs had given them nothing. Or the address is to the husbands. For just as they did what was mentioned before, they used to keep women without any need for them, and would harm them and constrict them, so that they might take away part of what they had given them, by having the women ransom themselves with their dowries. Much of the exegetes went to this view, and it is what is related from Abu Jaʿfar, may Allah be pleased with him. Its coherence with the context is evident. It is also permitted that the first address is to the heirs, and this address is to the husbands, and the speech is complete with His words, glory be to Him, "by compulsion." Thus there is no objection to it, once the rule is accepted that two persons are not addressed in a single speech without a vocative. So one does not say, "Stand and sit," addressing Zayd and ʿAmr, but rather, "Stand, O Zayd, and sit, O ʿAmr." It has also been said that this is an address to the husbands, but after they have separated from their wives. Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Zayd, who said: "The Quraysh in Mecca: a man among them would marry a woman of noble birth, and perhaps she would not be agreeable to him, so he would divorce her on condition that she not marry anyone without his permission. He would bring witnesses, and this would be written against her. Then if a suitor proposed to her, if she gave him [the husband] something and satisfied him, he would permit her; otherwise he would restrain her."

What is meant by His words, glory be to Him, "in order to take away," and so on, is that they should hand over to you part of what you gave them, and you take it from them. The reason the verse does not mention their action is that, since it proceeds from them under compulsion, it is considered as nonexistent. He expressed this by "taking away" (adhhab) rather than "taking" (akhdh). The use of "taking away" is for emphasis in denouncing it, by clarifying that it includes two matters, each of which is forbidden and abominable: taking and taking away, for it is an expression for going away while accompanied by it. He mentioned "part" so that it would be known that taking away the whole is still more abominable.

﴿Except that they commit a manifest immorality﴾. It is in the form of the active participle (fa'il) from among the intransitive verb (lazim) meaning "became clear," or the transitive verb, and the object is omitted, meaning "manifesting" (mubayyinah) with its agent as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read "mubayyanah" in the form of the passive participle (maf'ul). From Ibn ʿAbbas, he read "mubayyinah" in the form of the active participle from abana, intransitive meaning "became clear" or transitive. What is meant by "immorality" (fahishah) here is rebelliousness (nushuz) and bad character, as said by Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Ibn ʿAbbas and others. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "except that they behave immorally toward you." In "al-Durr al-Manthur" this reading is attributed to Ubayy and Ibn Masʿud without "ʿalaykum" (toward you). Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan that what is meant by it is fornication. This is reported from Abu Qilabah and Ibn Sirin. As for the exception, it has been said that it is disjunctive (munqati'), and it has been said that it is connected (muttasil), and it is then an adverbial expression of general time, meaning: "Do not restrain them at any time except the time of giving them," and so on; or of general circumstance, meaning: "Do not restrain them in any circumstance except in this circumstance"; or of general cause, meaning: "Do not restrain them for any cause except for giving them." This does not preclude mentioning the specific cause, since it is permissible that the general is intended, that is, for taking away and other things, and mention of one instance of it is for a particular reason, or because the cause mentioned is a final cause (ghayyiyyah), while the general implied cause, which motivates the act, precedes it in existence.

In the verse is the permissibility of khulʿ (divorce initiated by the wife through compensation) at the time of nushuz (rebelliousness), since the excuse is established by the existence of the cause on their part. [p. 243]

It is related from al-Asamm that the permission to take property from them was before the hudud (prescribed penalties), as a punishment for them. Something similar is related from ʿAta'. Abd al-Razzaq and others related from him: "When a man's wife committed immorality, he would take what he had given her and expel her, and this was abrogated (nasakha) by the hudud." Abu ʿAli al-Jubba'i and Abu Muslim held that this relates to restraint (ʿadl) in the sense of confinement and keeping, and there is no reference to taking property in it. So in it is the permission of confining them if they commit immorality, which is fornication according to the first view and lesbianism (sihaq) according to the second. The verse is thus similar to His words, exalted is He: "So confine them in the houses" (4:15).

﴿And live with them in kindness﴾, that is, treat them well (ʿasharu), ﴿in kindness﴾ (bil-maʿruf), which is what neither the Law (shar') nor good manners (muruwwah) rejects. What is intended here is equity in division and maintenance, and general kindness in speech and action. It has been said: kindness is that he does not strike her, does not speak harshly to her, and is cheerful in his face toward her. It has also been said that it is that he adorns himself for her as she adorns herself for him. Whoever held that they are obligated to be served when they are of those who do not serve themselves relied on its generality. The address is to those who treat their wives badly. Some have linked it to what preceded at the beginning of the surah, His words, glory be to Him: "And give the women their dowries graciously" (4:4), but this is far-fetched.

﴿And if you dislike them﴾, that is, you dislike their company and keeping them according to the demands of natural disposition, without there being anything from their side that requires it, ﴿then perhaps you dislike a thing﴾ such as the companionship and keeping.

﴿While Allah places in it much good﴾, such as a child, or the affection that comes after dislike. Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said this. This clause is the cause (ʿillah) of the consequent (jaza'), and it has been placed in its position as an announcement of the strength of its implication, for "ʿasa" (perhaps), because it is for the inception of hope (tarajji), is not suitable as a response, and it is complete, lifting what follows it and needing no predicate. The meaning is: "If you dislike them, then be patient with them, and do not separate from them merely because of your own dislike, for perhaps in what you dislike is much good for you." The self often dislikes what is praiseworthy and loves what is contrary to it. So let the aim of consideration be what contains good and righteousness, not what the souls desire. He made "a thing" and "good" indefinite and described them with what he described, for emphasis in urging against separation, and for generalizing the guidance. For this reason the verse has been used as evidence that divorce is disliked (makruh). It was also read "wa-yajʿalu" (and He places) in the nominative, on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause is a circumstantial qualifier, meaning: "And He (that thing) — Allah places in it much good." It has been said that its estimate is "and Allah, He places," with the apparent noun placed in the position of the pronoun, so the "wa" is then circumstantial. Concerning its entry upon the imperfect verb there are three positions. The first: its prohibition from entering upon it except with an estimated subject. The second: its permissibility absolutely. The third: a distinction, that if it contains a nuance, such as removing the appearance of being a qualifier, it is good, otherwise not. It is not hidden that estimating a subject here is contrary to the apparent sense.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 20:

﴿And if you wish to replace a wife﴾, O husbands, ﴿with another wife﴾, meaning to take in marriage a woman you desire ﴿in place of a wife﴾, that is, a woman you turn away from by divorcing her, ﴿and you have given﴾, that is, one of you has given, ﴿one of them﴾, that is, one of the wives, for the intended sense of "wife" is the generic category, which is true of the plural and suits the plural address. By "giving" (itaʾ, lit. "bringing") is meant, as al-Karkhi said, commitment and guarantee, as in His words, ﴿when you hand over what you have given﴾, that is, what you have committed to and guaranteed. The condition's implied opposite is not intended, as some verifiers have stated; it was mentioned because that situation might be imagined to involve taking back, so they were alerted to its ruling. The clause is a circumstantial clause with an implied qad (meaning "while" or "and indeed"), or it is conjoined to the condition, that is, "and you have already given the one you wish to divorce and substitute for another," ﴿a heap of gold﴾, that is, a great amount of wealth, and the opinions about it have already been mentioned. ﴿Then do not take back from it﴾, that is, from the heap given, ﴿anything﴾
Page 244
small, that is, much less than the large amount.

﴿Would you take it﴾, that is, the thing, ﴿by slander and manifest sin?﴾ This is a resumed statement, brought to confirm the prohibition, and the interrogation is for denunciation and rebuke. Both nouns are in the accusative as circumstantial states, in the sense of a descriptive phrase: "Would you take it while being slanderers and sinners?" It is also possible that they are accusative as causal objects. In this matter there is no difference between a final cause and a motivating cause, and what is under discussion here is the second kind, as in "I held back from the war out of cowardice," since taking it occurs because of their slander and their commission of sins. It has been said: when one of them wanted a new wife, he would slander the wife he had by accusing her of immorality, until she was compelled to ransom herself from him with what he had given her, so that he could turn to marrying the new one. So they were forbidden from this. "Buhtan" (slander) is the lie that stuns the one it is told about. Al-Zajjaj said: it is falsehood whose falseness leaves one bewildered. Here it is interpreted as injustice, and according to Mujahid it is sin, so "sin" is conjoined to it for explanation, as in the verse of the poet:

*And he found her words to be lies and falsehood.*

It has been said that the meaning here is the denial of ownership (of the dowry). "Manifest" means clear and evident.

[Page 245]

"How can you take it back?" is a denial following a denial. It has been emphasised in the same way as in "How can you disbelieve?" (2:28), which came earlier. It has also been said that it is an expression of wonder from Allah, the Exalted, meaning: indeed your taking it is a strange thing. "When one of you has gone in unto the other" is a metaphor (kinayah, euphemism) for sexual intercourse, as related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi. It has also been said that what is meant is genuine seclusion (al-khalwah al-sahihah), even without intercourse. Al-Farra' preferred this view, and Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, held it. It is one of the two opinions of the Imamiyyah (the Twelver Shi'ah). In the *Tafsir al-Kalbi*, from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, "al-ifda'" (going in unto) means being together with her under a single covering, whether or not he had intercourse with her. The first view is preferred on the ground that the expression is clearly a metaphor, and the Arabs use such expressions only for things that are shameful to mention, such as intercourse. Seclusion is not shameful to mention, so it would not need a metaphor. Also, the use of "ila" with "ifda'" indicates the meaning of reaching and joining, which is more suitable to intercourse. Those who took the second view said: seclusion was called "ifda'" because the man reaches the place of intercourse through it. It is not granted that seclusion is not shameful to mention. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of "you take it," serving to emphasise the rebuke and confirm the sense of wonder, meaning: in what state, or in what way, do you take it, when what has happened between you has happened? "And they have taken from you a solemn covenant" means a firm pledge. "Solemn" means strong. Qatadah said: it is what Allah took on behalf of women against men. "Then either retain them with kindness or release them with good treatment" (2:229). He then said: this covenant used to be taken at the time of the marriage contract, where it was said: "By Allah, you must either retain her with kindness or release her with good treatment." This was related from al-Dahhak, Yahya ibn Abi Kathir and Kathir. From Mujahid: the solemn covenant is the words of marriage by which they made lawful their private parts.

The verse has been used as evidence by those who prohibit khul' (divorce initiated by the wife, with compensation to the husband) absolutely, and who said that it abrogates the verse in al-Baqarah. Another said that it is abrogated by that verse. This was related from Abu Zayd. A group said: it is neither abrogating (nasikhah) nor abrogated (mansukhah), and the ruling in it is taking without the goodwill of the soul. Some, as Ibn al-Faras said, used it as evidence for permitting excessive bridal gifts (mahr). Abu Ya'la related from Masruq that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, forbade that bridal gifts be increased beyond four hundred dirhams. A woman from Quraysh objected to him and said: "Have you not heard what Allah has revealed: 'and you had given one of them a qintar' (4:20)?" He said: "O Allah, forgive me! Every person knows more than ʿUmar." Then he went back, mounted the pulpit and said: "I had forbidden you to increase women's bridal gifts beyond four hundred dirhams. Whoever wishes to give from his wealth what he likes, let him do so." The Shi'ah have used this report to criticise ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, for his ignorance of this matter and for the way he silenced the woman. They said: ignorance is incompatible with the imamate. It is answered that the verse is not a clear text permitting the giving of a qintar. It is like your saying: "If Zayd comes to you, and he has killed your brother, then pardon him." This does not show that killing one's brother is permitted. Suppose we grant that the verse shows the permissibility of giving a qintar; we still do not grant that giving it as a bridal gift is permitted. It may be that what is meant is giving jewellery and other things, not by way of bridal gift but by way of gift. A husband may not retract his gift to his wife, especially if he has upset her by separating from her. Allah's words "and you had given" do not specify that what was given was a bridal gift. Suppose we grant that it was a bridal gift; we still do not grant that avoiding excess is less excellent than it.

Ibn Hibban related in his *Sahih*, from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the best of women is the one whose bridal gift is easiest." And from ʿA‘ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, from him (ﷺ): "The blessing of a woman is the easing of her affair in her bridal gift." Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi related it as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report: "The greatest of women in blessing is the easiest of them in bridal gift." So the Commander of the Believers' prohibition of excess may be understood as being for ease, and as an inclination towards what is better, and a desire for what he (ﷺ) pointed to by word and deed. His departure from that, and his not rebutting the Qurashi woman, was a way of encouraging the pursuit of the meanings of the Qur'an and the drawing out of its subtleties. Showing the great scholar being overcome by the small ignorant one is an encouragement to the small one, a delight to him, and an urging upon him and his like to occupy themselves with knowledge and to attain what will overcome others. Thus his saying, may Allah be pleased with him, "O Allah, forgive me! Every person knows more than ʿUmar" was a way of humbling himself, of modesty and good character, and what prompted him to it prompted him. Yet with all this he did not command them to excess. The most he did was to lift the prohibition from them and leave them to choose between the better and the lesser, and there is no sin upon them in doing either of the two as they wish. Suppose we grant that this matter had escaped the notice of his noble mind; we still do not grant that this is an ignorance that harms the rank of the imamate. Something similar happened to the Commander of the Believers ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, who is the imam of both groups. Ibn Jarir and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: a man asked ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, about a matter, and he gave an answer. The man said: "It is not like that, but rather such and such." The Commander said: "You are right and we were wrong. 'And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows' (12:76)." Something has also happened to Dawud, peace be upon him, which Allah related to us in His Book, in His saying: "And Dawud and Sulayman, when they judged concerning the tilth" (21:78), until He said, Mighty is the Speaker: "So We gave understanding of it to Sulayman" (21:79). Since that did not diminish the rank of prophethood and the caliphate referred to in His saying, "O Dawud, indeed We have made you a khalifah (vicegerent) upon the earth" (38:26), it does not diminish the rank of the imamate, as is not hidden. Whoever is fair will make this event among the virtues of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, not among his faults. But there is no remedy for the disease of hatred and obstinacy. "And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide" (39:23).

[p. 245]

﴿Do not marry what your fathers married of women﴾ begins the explanation of which women are forbidden for marriage and which are not, after the explanation of how wives are to be treated. According to some scholars it is connected to His words, glorified is He: ﴿It is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾. This marriage was singled out for prohibition and not included among the list of the forbidden marriages that follow, to emphasize the strictness of the prohibition, since it was a common practice among them in the Jahiliyyah. Ibn Sa'd related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: "When a man died leaving his wife, his son had the greater right to her, to marry her if he wished, provided she was not his mother; or he could marry her to whomever he wished. When Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat died, his son Hisn inherited the marriage to his wife, did not spend on her, and did not give her any of the property. She came to the Prophet ﷺ and told him of this, and he said: 'Go back, perhaps Allah will reveal something concerning you.' Then ﴿Do not marry﴾ was revealed, and also ﴿It is not lawful for you﴾ and so on." Al-Wahidi and others mentioned that it was revealed concerning the aforementioned Hisn, concerning al-Aswad ibn Khalaf who married his father's wife, concerning Safwan ibn Umayya ibn Khalaf who married his father's wife Fakhita bint al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, and concerning Manzur ibn Rayyan who married his father's wife Mulayka bint Kharija. The term "fathers" (ābā') includes grandfathers, however they may be, on the basis of a meaning that covers both linguistically, not on the basis of combining literal and figurative meaning. In the *Nihaya* it is stated that the indication of "father" for "grandfather" is through one of two ways: either "father" is meant as "origin," or it is by consensus (ijma'). It is not hidden that the indication by consensus is meaningless. Yes, for the prohibition of whomever the grandfather married, there is a clear meaning by consensus, so the prohibition of what they married is established both by explicit text and by consensus. In establishing this prohibition, the marriage itself, I mean the contract if it is valid, is sufficient, and consummation is not required. Ibn 'Abbas held this view, for Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi related from him that he said: "Every woman your father married, whether he consummated with her or not, is forbidden to you." This was also related from al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Rabah. If the marriage was invalid, then for establishing the prohibition there must be intercourse (wat') or what is similar to it, such as kissing or touching with desire, for example. Indeed, that is what is forbidden in reality, so that if any of these occurred through ownership by right of the hand (slave concubinage), it would also establish the prohibition. By the forbidden means, the prohibition is established according to us, and the Imamiyya agree with this, while the Shafi'iyya disagree regarding the forbidden. The clarification of this is that people differed about the linguistic meaning of *nikah* (marriage). It was said that it is a homonym (mushtarak lafzi) between intercourse and contract, and this is the apparent view of many lexicographers. It was said that it is literal for the contract and figurative for intercourse, and this is the view of the Shafi'iyya. It was said that it is the reverse, and this is the view of our companions. This is not contradicted by their statement that it is literal for "joining" (ḍamm), because intercourse is one of its instances, and what is coined for the more general meaning is literal for each of its instances, as the earlier scholars stated. The use of *nikah* in each of these meanings is attested. For intercourse there is his ﷺ saying: "I was born from a *nikah*, not from *sifah*," meaning from lawful intercourse, not unlawful intercourse. And his, peace be upon him, saying: "For a man, from his menstruating wife, everything is permitted except *nikah*." And the poet's verse:

"And of a widow whom our spears have *ankahat* (taken by force), and another left grieving between an uncle and a paternal uncle."

And another's verse:

"And a *mankuha* (a woman lain with) who was not given a dowry."

And al-Farazdaq's verse:

"When Allah gave drink to a people with the rain of Adiya, may Allah not give drink to the land of Kufa the rain.
Those who leave their wives in purity, and those who *al-nākiḥīn* (lie with them), at the two banks of the Tigris, the cattle."

In *al-'Iqd* there is al-A'sha's verse:

"So do not approach a neighbor woman, for her secret is forbidden to you, so *fankiḥan* (lie with her) or remain celibate forever."

In the more general meaning is the saying of the speaker:

"I pressed to my chest the perfumed body of her chest, as the mother of the boy *nakaḥat* (embraces) her child."

And Abu al-Tayyib's verse:

"I *ankaḥtu* (made to join) the hard stones of its... with the hoof of a swift she-camel, which carried me over the plain and the mountain."

So the proponent of the homonymy says: usage is established, and the original is literal meaning. The second says: that it is figurative in one and literal in the other, where possible, is preferable to homonymy. Then he claims that when the word *nikah* is used, the contract is understood before intercourse, and he deems the understanding of intercourse from it to depend on a context. In the first hadith, the mention of *sifah* as a conjunction supports this, though it is also possible to take *nikah* there as the contract, even though birth in itself comes from intercourse. In the second, the woman is attributed to the man's pronoun, since his wife is the one contracted with, so it necessitates that the intended meaning of the excepted *nikah* is intercourse, otherwise the meaning is corrupted, for it would become: from her who is contracted with, everything is permitted except the contract. In the verses, the attribution to cattle, the denial of dowries, and the ascription to spears indicate that the intended meaning is intercourse with cattle and captives. The answer is: the claim that the contract is understood upon the unqualified use linguistically is denied; rather, that is in the legal technical sense. We do not accept that understanding intercourse in what was mentioned depends on a context, even if a context is present, for the presence of a context that supports the intended literal meaning is something that is established alongside the intended literal meaning, so it does not necessitate that the meaning is figurative. Rather, what is considered is merely looking at the context: if it is known that without it the word would not indicate what is meant, then it is figurative; otherwise it is not. In these cited materials we understand intercourse before seeking a context, and the examination of how it indicates... [p. 246] ...the mode of its indication, so the word is literal, even if it is accompanied by what, when examined, calls for that meaning. Do you not see that what they claimed as evidence that it is literal for the contract and figurative for intercourse, from al-A'sha's verse, has a context that also indicates the contract? For his saying: "So do not approach a neighbor woman" is a prohibition of fornication, as is shown by "her secret is forbidden to you," so it necessitates that his saying "so *fankiḥan*" is a command to the contract, i.e. "marry," if fornication is forbidden to you, or "remain celibate," i.e. be wild like the beasts toward human women, so that you do not approach them as a wild animal does not approach them. This does not prevent the word from being literal for the contract according to them in the verse, since they do not say it is figurative in it. As for the claim that in the hadith it means the contract, this necessitates a figurative use in attributing the birth to it, because the contract is only the cause of the cause. So there is a claim of literal meaning by departing from a literal meaning, and this is preference without a preponderant factor if both were equal. How much more so, when the more fitting reading is that it refers to intercourse, so that the contrast between it and *sifah* is established, for the meaning becomes "from lawful intercourse, not unlawful intercourse," so it refers to a specific kind of intercourse. The indicator of the specificity is also the word *sifah*. Thus it has been established up to here that we have not added to the establishing of the mere occurrence of usage anything that must be taken into account. It is also known that the use in the sense of joining (ḍamm) is established, so if it is literal in that sense, it is a general shared meaning (mushtarak ma'nawi) with intercourse and contract as its instances, if we consider joining more general than joining of body to body or of word to word, or if we consider it only intercourse. Then it would be figurative for the contract, because when it stands between figurative and homonymous meaning, the figurative is preferable unless the contrary is explicitly established. But this transfer has not been established. Rather, they said: al-Mubarrad transmitted from the Basrans, and the slave of Tha'lab from the Kufans, that it means gathering and joining. Then, the apparent meaning of the word joining is that it relates to bodies and not to words, because they are accidents, the first of which vanishes before the second exists, so the second does not meet what it joins. Therefore it must be figurative for the contract. Thus [states] *Fath al-Qadir*.

When you know this, we say: the Shafi'iyya understood *nikah* in the verse under discussion as the contract, not intercourse, and they used it as evidence for the prohibition of the one contracted with even if she was not consummated. They held that prohibition is not established by fornication. Some of our companions understood it as the contract, and used it as evidence for the prohibition of marrying the wives of fathers and grandfathers, and for the establishing of the prohibition of affinity by fornication. They made the prohibition of the contract established by consensus. Then they said: if it is understood as the contract, the prohibition of intercourse is established by way of a fortiori.

It has been objected that one should not say: the prohibition of the one consummated is established by the verse, and of the one contracted with but not consummated by consensus, because if the ruling is prohibition by mere contract, and the word of the proof is suitable for it, then it is undoubtedly intended by it. For consensus follows the text, since analogy derives from one of them. And if it were from necessary knowledge that Allah creates in them, it would be established thereby that this ruling is intended from the speech of the Lawgiver, if it is possible. Others understood it as both intercourse and contract together. Al-Zayla'i said: the verse encompasses the wife of the father, both by intercourse and by valid contract. Combining literal and figurative meaning does no harm, because the statement is a negation, and in negation it is permitted to combine them, just as it is permitted that a homonym encompass all its meanings. Sa'di Afandi also transmitted from the *Wasaya* of the *Hidaya* the permissibility of combining the meanings of a homonym in a negation. In that case there is no difficulty in the verse being evidence for the prohibition of the consummated and the one contracted with, as is not hidden.

It has been objected to what al-Zayla'i said that it is weak in the principles of jurisprudence, and the correct view is that it is not permitted to combine literal and figurative meaning, neither in negation nor in affirmation, nor is a homonym general in all cases. In *al-Akmal* it is said: the truth is that negation is like what affirmation requires; if affirmation requires combining the two meanings, then negation is likewise, and otherwise not.

As for the matter of the oath mentioned in *al-Mabsut*: one who swears that he will not speak to his *mawali* (clients/freedmen/relatives), and he has higher and lower ones, so whichever of them he speaks to, he breaks the oath. This is not due to the generality of a homonym in negation, as some have supposed, but rather because the literal meaning of the statement has been left by the indication of the oath toward a figurative meaning that encompasses them. In *al-Bahr* it is said: the better view is that *nikah* in the verse is the contract, as is the consensus, and the establishing of the prohibition of affinity by unlawful intercourse is derived from another proof, so let this be understood.

*Ma* (what) is a relative noun referring to one who understands, and there is no discussion about that according to the view of those who permit it absolutely, and likewise according to the view of those who permit it when a particular quality is intended from it. It is said that it is a verbal noun (maṣdariyya), intending the object of the verbal noun, i.e. "the wives your fathers married." Al-Tabari chose to keep the verbal noun in its verbal sense, meaning the prohibition of every marriage that was invalid for them, i.e. "Do not marry the like of the marriages of your fathers," but this is not the preferred view.

﴿From women﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from *ma*, or from the pronoun returning to it. According to al-Tabari it is connected to *nakaḥa*. More than one scholar mentioned that it is an explanation of what is on the two aforementioned views. Its apparent sense is that it is explanatory (bayaniyya), and it is possible that it is partitive (tab'iḍiyya) while the explanation is by meaning. Its point, despite not needing it, since those who are married are only women, is generality, as if it were said: whatever woman it was. The possibility that it removes the assumption of a predominance of the male in "your fathers," and makes it more general than the mothers, so that it indicates that a daughter is forbidden to marry the husband of her mother, is not free from obscurity.

﴿Except what has passed﴾, i.e. died, as this was related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b. According to the preferred view it is a continuous exception (istithna' muttaṣil) from *mā nakaḥa*, for the sake of emphasis on the prohibition and comprehensiveness. The statement is then in the manner of affirming a thing by what resembles its opposite, as in the saying of al-Nabigha:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords, with them, are notched from the clashing of the battalions."

The meaning is: "Do not marry those whom your fathers married, except what has already passed." The purpose is to close the door of permission entirely, because it involves attaching a matter to something impossible, as in His saying, ﴿until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾, and what is attached to the impossible is itself impossible. It has also been said that it is a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*) from what the prohibition implies, and what direct engagement with the forbidden act entails, namely punishment.
