It is as if it were said: "You deserve punishment for marrying what your fathers married, except what has already passed and gone, for that is pardoned." By this interpretation the objection is dispelled that the prohibition concerns the future, while what has already passed is past, so how could it be excepted from it? Some of the verifying grammarians (*muhaqqiqin al-nuhat*) made the exception a disconnected one (*istithna' munqati'*) from what has entered into the ruling of the implied meaning (*dalalat al-mafhum*), and so they judged this case to be disconnected. The meaning then is: "But what has passed, there is no blame for it, so you will not be reproached for it, because Islam wipes out what came before it, and thereby the rulings of lineage and other matters are established, and that is not counted as fornication (*zina*)." Al-Balkhi mentioned that not every marriage that God Most High has forbidden is fornication, because fornication is a specific act that does not follow a constant path or a continuous custom. For this reason, the polytheists in the Jahiliyyah were not called children of fornication, nor are the children of the People of the Covenant (*ahl al-dhimmah*), for example, when that arises from a contract among them that they recognize. Some people claimed, on the assumption of disconnection, that the meaning is: "But what has passed is something you (all) acknowledge." It is related that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) allowed them to keep the wives of their fathers for a period, and then ordered them to separate from them, and he did this so that the removal of them from this vile custom would occur gradually. Al-Balkhi said: "This contradicts the ijma' (scholarly consensus), and whatever is known from the religion of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the claim to it is an error." The most reliable of the opinions is the first, because of His words, glorified is He:

( إنَّهُ ) i.e., the marriage to what the fathers married, ﴿was an indecency and hateful﴾. This is a reason for the prohibition and an explanation that the forbidden thing is at the extreme of ugliness, as the report that it is an "indecency" indicates, being extremely despised and belittled, to the point that it is as if it were the very essence of hatred, as the report that it is "hateful" indicates. It has not ceased, in the ruling and knowledge of God Most High, to be described by this, even if it was permitted to one nation among the nations, as the phrase "kana" (was) requires according to what 'Ali ibn 'Isa and others mentioned. This does not suit placing between the two something that diminishes its gravity, namely dropping blame for what has passed of it, as al-Zamakhshari indicated and as a group of the verifying scholars approved. Some people inclined to take this sentence as a predicate (*khabar*) under the assumption of disconnection, but that is not the apparent sense. Others interpreted "fahisha" here as fornication, but that is nothing. This marriage was called in the Jahiliyyah "the marriage of hatred" (*nikah al-maqt*), and a child born from it was called *maqti*, and also *maqit*, meaning despised and belittled. Among those who practised this marriage, according to what al-Tabarsi mentioned, were al-Ash'ath ibn Qays and Mu'ayt, the grandfather of al-Walid ibn 'Uqba.

﴿and an evil way﴾, i.e., evil is the path, the path of that marriage. In "sa'a" (was evil) there is an unspecified pronoun (*damir mubham*) which the following phrase explains, and the object of dispraise is omitted. The path is dispraised as an intensification in censuring its traveller and as a metonymy for him. It is also permissible, and al-Layth preferred this, that "sa'a" be like other verbs, so that it contains a pronoun returning to what the pronoun in "bihi" refers to. "Sabilan" is a *tamyiz* (specifying accusative) transferred from the subject. The sentence is either a new, independent sentence with no place in i'rab, or it is conjoined to the predicate of "kana" and is reported by an implied verb of saying, which is in reality the conjoined element, i.e., "and said of it, that ruling in every age."

Imam al-Razi said: "The degrees of ugliness are three: rational ugliness (*al-qubh al-'aqli*), legal ugliness (*al-qubh al-shar'i*), and customary ugliness (*al-qubh al-'adi*). God, glorified is He, has described this marriage with all of these. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿indecency﴾ is an indication of the degree of its rational ugliness; His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and hateful﴾ is an indication of the degree of its legal ugliness; and His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿and an evil way﴾ is an indication of the degree of its customary ugliness. Whatever combines these degrees has reached the furthest degree of ugliness." You know that His saying, Exalted is His majesty, ﴿and hateful﴾ being an indication of the degree of its legal ugliness is evident if the intended meaning of "hateful" is hateful in the sight of God Most High, but if the intended meaning of "hateful" is hateful in the sight of people of honour, then it is not evident. From here it has been said that His saying, Majestic is His glory, ( fahisha ) (indecency) is an indication of legal ugliness, ﴿hateful﴾ is an indication of rational ugliness in the sense of repugnance (*al-munafarah*), and ﴿an evil way﴾ is an indication of customary ugliness. In my view each has its aspect, and perhaps the Imam's ordering is better in some respects, as is not hidden. Among what indicates the gravity of this matter is what 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from al-Bara', who said: "I met my maternal uncle, and with him was the banner. I said: 'Where are you going?' He said: 'The Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent me to a man who married his father's wife after him, and he ordered me to strike off his neck and take his property.'"

﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brothers' daughters, and your sisters' daughters﴾. The intended meaning is not the prohibition of their persons, because prohibition (ḥurma) and its related terms apply only to the actions of accountable persons. So the statement contains an omitted modifier (muḍāf), understood by rational implication (dalālat al-ʿaql). The intended meaning is the prohibition of marrying them, because marriage is the chief purpose for which they are sought, because it is the meaning that comes first to the mind, and because what precedes and follows the verse concerns marriage. If this were not the intended meaning, such as if an unrelated element had intervened between them without any purpose, then there would be no ambiguity in the verse, contrary to al-Karkhi's view. The sentence is performative (inshāʾiyya), and it is not intended to inform about a prohibition in past time. Some verifiers said: There is no objection to its being informative (khabariyya), and the past-tense verb in it is like the verb in the definitions, such as: "The noun (ism) is what signifies a meaning in itself and is not joined to any of the tenses; the verb (fiʿl) is what signifies and is joined [to a tense]." For they stated explicitly that the past-tense clause there is informative. Otherwise it would not be valid for it to be a relative clause (ṣila) of a relative pronoun, even though the verb in it is not intended to signify only past time. Otherwise it would follow that the state of the defined term would be in the present time, and the future would not be that state. He put the verb in the passive form, because it is not doubtful that the one who prohibits is Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Your mothers﴾ includes the grandmothers, however they may be, since "mother" is originally the root in the root, as in "the Mother of the Book" and "the Mother of the Towns." Thus the prohibition of grandmothers is established by the lexical meaning of the word and its literal sense, since "mother" in this sense is among the gradational (mushakkik) terms. Some have held that applying "mother" to a grandmother is figurative (majāz), and that the prohibition of grandmothers is established by consensus (ijmāʿ). The verified view is that "mother" is intended in the sense of origin in every case. For if it is used in that sense literally, it is clear; and if not, it must be judged to be intended figuratively, so grandmothers enter into the general scope of the figurative meaning. What indicates that this is intended in the text is the consensus on their prohibition.

[Page 250]

By "daughters" is meant those whom she has borne or who have borne those whom she has borne. Calling the second [generation] "daughter" is literal, on the basis that "daughter" is used to mean descendant, as has been said. Thus the text covers her literally, or figuratively according to some, or according to all. Whoever prohibits applying "daughter" to a descendant in every case said: The prohibition of the daughters of sons is established by consensus. The prohibition of grandmothers and of the daughters of sons may also be inferred from the implication of the text that prohibits paternal aunts, maternal aunts, brothers' daughters, and sisters' daughters. As for the first: the full siblings among them are children of grandmothers, so the prohibition of grandmothers is more fitting, since they are closer. As for the second: the daughters of sons are closer than the daughters of brothers. Furthermore, the apparent text indicates that a man's daughter from fornication is prohibited to him, since she is his daughter. The address is in the Arabic language, as long as no conventional transfer (naql) has been established, as with the word ṣalāt (prayer) and similar terms, which becomes a legal technical term (manqūl sharʿī). On this, Imam al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, differed. He said: A created being from the water of fornication is lawful to the fornicator, because she is a stranger to him, since no inheritance or other legal rights of kinship are established for her. He also relied on the Prophet's saying, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: "The child belongs to the bed," and this requires restricting lineage to the bed (marriage).

Some Shafiʿis said: She is prohibited if a prophet, such as ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, informs him at the time of his descent that she is from his water. It was answered: The Lawgiver has cut off her lineage from him, as has been established, so there is no consideration for her being from the water of his illicit intercourse. The opponents of the prohibition raised an objection against those who hold prohibition, namely that they must either establish that she is his daughter on the basis of literal reality, because she was created from his water, or on the basis of the Lawgiver's ruling. The first is invalid according to their own school, both in inclusion and exclusion. As for the first: if he bought a virgin, deflowered her, and kept her until she gave birth, this child is clearly created from his water, yet his lineage is not established except by acknowledgment (istilḥāq). As for the second: if an easterner married a westerner, and a child was born to her while they did not meet, and there was a barrier between east and west between them, then he establishes the lineage while being certain that she was not created from his water. The second is invalid by the consensus of the Muslims, since a child of fornication has no lineage from the fornicator; and if he claimed to be his father, the judge must prevent this.

It was answered by choosing the first option, since there is no disagreement among the people of the language that a being created from a person's water is his daughter, whether that water was from a lawful union or from fornication. The partial relation (juzʾiyya) is established in both cases. The apparent meaning is that this is the basis of the prohibition of marriage. Do you not see how the prohibition on a woman's child from fornication is established by consensus? The distinction between the two cases is that in the second case the child is part of her and separated from her as a human being, whereas in the first case the daughter is not like that, since she was separated from him only as semen, which indicates nothing except that the partial relation is more evident in the second case. As for the claim that [the fornication case] negates the partial relation in the first case, it does not, because they call a child separated as semen from its father a piece of flesh (buḍʿa), which implies partiality. So they say: "So-and-so is a piece of flesh, and so-and-so is a piece of flesh of so-and-so." Denying the existence of partiality in both cases is obstinacy. The non-establishment of inheritance, for example, between a girl created from the water of fornication and the owner of the water is not due to the absence of partiality and her not being his daughter in reality, but due to consensus on that matter. Were it not for that, she would inherit from him, just as the child of fornication inherits from its mother.

As for what was mentioned in refuting the inclusive rule, namely that if he bought a virgin, deflowered her, and kept her, and she gave birth, the child is certainly created from his water, though his lineage is not established except by acknowledgment, this was taken from the jurists' statement regarding a slave-woman who gives birth in her master's possession: the lineage of her child from him is not established unless he acknowledges it, and it is not sufficient that he had intercourse with her and she gave birth. However, in al-Hidaya and others it is said that this is a legal ruling. As for the religious obligation between him and Allah, exalted is He, what is narrated from Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, is that if at the time he had intercourse with her he did not withdraw from her and he secured her against suspicions of fornication, then he is obligated by Allah, exalted is He, to claim the child, by consensus, because the apparent situation at that time is that it is from him, and acting on the apparent is obligatory. If he withdrew from her, and he had secured her first or did not secure her, [the rule is the same].

But if he did not secure her, and left her to come and go without a trustworthy guardian, it is permissible for him to deny the child. For this apparent sign, namely that it is from him, is based on the apparent fact that a Muslim woman does not commit fornication, and it is opposed by another apparent sign, namely that it is from someone else, due to the existence of one of

[Page 251]

the two indicators, namely withdrawal or failure to secure her. There are two other reports on this from Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, which he mentioned in al-Mabsut. He said: From Abu Yusuf: If he had intercourse with her and did not verify her condition afterward until she gave birth to a child, then he must claim it, whether he withdrew from her or not, and whether he secured her or did not, in order to improve the assumption about her and to treat her affairs as righteous, unless the contrary becomes clear. This is like the view of the majority, because what is apparent through its cause becomes his state until the contrary is clarified. From Muhammad: He should not claim her child if he does not know that it is his, but he should free the child. In al-Iḍāḥ, both views are mentioned in the language of recommendation. He said: Abu Yusuf said: "I like him to claim it," and Muhammad said: "I like him to free the child." In al-Fath, after a discussion, he said: Based on this, it follows that if he confesses and says: "I had intercourse with her with the intention of having a child," then when she gives birth, the lineage of what she bore is established, even if he does not say "It is my child," because its establishment by his saying "It is my child" is based on the premise that his intercourse at that time was for the purpose of a child. On this, one of the eminent scholars of the lesson said: It follows that if he acknowledges that he did not withdraw from her and that he secured her, then his lineage is established without his claim being required. And although we require him in this situation to acknowledge it, there is no need to require him to acknowledge it so that he acknowledges and his lineage is established; rather his lineage is established from the beginning. I think there is no difficulty in ruling according to the school on this basis, end of quotation. In al-Mabsut: When much time has passed, the child is attributed to him, because the lapse of time is evidence of his acceptance, since at that time there occurs from him what indicates acceptance, such as accepting congratulations and similar things, so it is as if he had explicitly acknowledged it.

From the totality of what has been mentioned, one knows what is in the objector's statement, and that the opponent may refuse to accept it. But in al-Baḥr, while criticizing, it was mentioned: Some eminent scholars thought that it is not valid to rule according to the school on this basis, since its adherents explicitly stated the opposite. The text of al-Badaʾiʿ was quoted on this. Then he said: If he intends establishment before the judge in the outward sense, they explicitly stated that a claim is necessary in every case. If he intends [establishment] between himself and Allah, exalted is He, then al-Hidaya and others explicitly stated that what we mentioned about the requirement of a claim applies only to judicial matters, to the end of what we mentioned. However, in al-Mujtaba: The manumission and tadbīr (conditional emancipation) of an insane person are not valid, but his istilād (making a slave-woman a mother of a child, which secures her freedom upon his death) is valid. If this is correct, it is excepted from the ruling, and it is problematic, end of quotation. Based on this, one says regarding the case the objector raised: The child born is in fact the master's child, because he was created from his water, and the child of fornication is likewise, with an addition, since acknowledgment has been added to that. Allah, glorified is He, made the basis of prohibition to be filiation (bunuwwa), and it is realized in our case. So how is marriage lawful in reality? The non-establishment of inheritance and similar matters, as we said, is a matter of consensus. The non-establishment of acknowledgment by judgment without a claim is a different matter beyond the realization of filiation in reality. For many things realized in reality are not judged by, and many things judged are not realized in reality, as in the report about the horse that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, bought from a Bedouin, and Khuzayma testified for him when the Bedouin denied the sale. The matter has been fully investigated in the discussion of istilād in Fath al-Qadir and other extensive books of that school. As for what was mentioned in refuting the reverse, namely the case of the easterner marrying a westerner, we do not concede certainty in it that the child was not created from his water, because the miracles (karamāt) of saints and the [supernatural] services (istikhdāmāt) are established. So it is conceivable that the husband possessed a power of leaping (khuṭwa) or was a jinn, and that he went to the west and had intercourse with her. Were it not for the existence of this possibility together with the existence of the marriage, the child would not be attributed to him. Do you not see how the companions said: If the wife of a boy gives birth to a child, the lineage is not established from him, because such a thing is not conceivable there, and conceivability is a condition. The mere existence of the marital bed is not sufficient according to the correct view. Perhaps the consideration of this filiation is judicial. Otherwise, since the child was not created from his water, it is not said of him that he is the husband's child in reality. Rather they considered that, despite the weakness of the possibility, to cover free women and to protect the child from loss. Close to this is the view of al-Shafiʿi, Malik, and Ahmad, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on them, in the chapter on istilād: that if a slave-girl bears a child, the child's lineage from the master is established if he acknowledges intercourse with her even with withdrawal, just as it is established without withdrawal. Indeed, if he had intercourse with her in her anus, the child is attributed to him according to Malik, and similarly from Ahmad, and this is a weakened aspect for the Shafiʿis.

[Page 252]

It has been said: There is between this issue and the issue of the easterner marrying a westerner a distance as great as the distance between east and west, because intercourse here is realized in general without needing to cross deserts and wastelands, whereas it is not so there. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

"Banāt" (daughters) is the plural of bint (daughter) according to the well-known view. It has been deemed sound that its radical letter is a waw, like ukht (sister). The deleted letter was restored in "akhawāt" (sisters) but was not restored in "banāt," treating each of the two plurals as analogous to its masculine singular. The masculine of banāt does not have its deleted letter restored; rather they say for it "banūn" with a nūn. The masculine of akhawāt has its deleted letter restored, so for the plural of akh (brother) they say: "ikhwa" and "akhawāt." Al-Danawshari has versified the question, saying:

O virtuous, discerning one, be so kind as to give an answer by which my guidance will be [...]

The word *ukht* (sister) and the word *bint* (daughter), when they are put in the sound plural form, do not become corrupted:
So *ukht* is allowed for a mother's [side], but as for *bint*, no. Clarify my meaning.
Along with the replacement of the omitted lām by a *tā'* in both of them, may I never leave those I rely on.

He, may God Most High have mercy on him, answered that in his words:
The word *ukht* has a *ḍamma* on its first letter, which suits the *wāw*, and so it takes on the returning [to its original form].

Abū al-Baqā' said: the *tā'* in it is not the feminine marker, because the feminine *tā'* does not have the letter before it made quiescent, and it turns into a *hā'* when pausing. So *banāt* is not the plural of *bint*, but of *binh*. The *bā'* was vowelled with a *kasra* to signal the deleted letter, as al-Farrā' said. Others said: its origin is the *fatḥa*, and its plural came upon that, and so did its masculine counterpart, which is *banūn*. The Basrans went to this view. As for *ukht*, the *tā'* in it is a replacement for the *wāw*, because it comes from *ikhwa* (siblings). *Akhawāt* (sisters) covers the sisters from the three directions. The same goes for the rest, because the term includes them all, and it enters into the paternal and maternal aunts, and the children of grandfathers and grandmothers, however far up they go. Likewise the paternal aunt of his grandfather and his maternal aunt, and the paternal aunt of his grandmother and her maternal aunts, whether from father and mother, or from father alone, or from mother alone. All of that is by consensus. In *al-Khāniyya*: the paternal aunt of his paternal aunt (from father and mother, or from father alone) is likewise [forbidden]. As for the paternal aunt of his paternal aunt from the mother's side, she is not forbidden. In *al-Muḥīṭ*: as for the aunt of the aunt, if the nearer aunt is an aunt from father and mother or from father alone, then the aunt of the aunt is forbidden, because when the nearer one is the sister of his father from father and mother or from father alone, her aunt will be the sister of the grandmother of his father's father, and the sister of his father's father is forbidden, because she is his aunt. If the nearer one is an aunt from the mother's side, then the aunt of the aunt is not forbidden to him, because the father of the aunt will be the husband of his father's mother, so her aunt will be the sister of the wife of the grandmother, the mother of the father. The sister of the husband of the mother is not forbidden, so the sister of the husband of the grandmother is even more so not forbidden. As for the maternal aunt of the maternal aunt: if the nearer maternal aunt is a maternal aunt from father and mother or from the mother's side, then her maternal aunt is forbidden to him. If the nearer one is a maternal aunt from the father's side, then her maternal aunt is not forbidden to him, because the mother of the nearer maternal aunt will be the wife of the grandfather, the father of the mother, not the mother of his mother. So her sister will be the sister of the wife of the father, and the sister of the wife of the grandfather is not forbidden to him. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that just as it is forbidden for a man to marry any of those mentioned, it is forbidden for a woman to marry the equivalent of those mentioned.

The apparent meaning is that this prohibition which the verse indicates did not hold for all of those mentioned in all the religions. Yes, they mentioned that the prohibition of mothers and daughters was established even in the time of Ādam, peace be upon him, and the permissibility of marrying them was never established in any of the religions. It was said that Zoroaster, the prophet of the Magians according to their claim, said it was permissible. Most of the Muslims agreed that he was a liar. The fact that molten brass did not harm him, because of medicines with which he smeared his body, and we have seen someone who carries fire in his hand after smearing it with particular medicines, and it does not harm him, and in that case it would not be fit to be a miracle.

As for the permissibility of marrying sisters, it has been said that it was permitted in the time of Ādam, peace be upon him, out of necessity, and Ḥawwā', peace be upon her, used to give birth to a male and a female in each pregnancy, and the male of the second pregnancy would take the female of the first pregnancy. Some Muslims deny that and say: He [God] sent the ḥūr from Paradise so that the sons of Ādam, peace be upon him, married them. It is refuted that this offspring would then not be purely the children of Ādam, and that is false by consensus.

*And your mothers who have nursed you, and your sisters through fosterage* — this is conjoined to what came before. *Ar-raḍāʿa* with a *fatḥa* on the *rā'* is the verbal noun of *raḍaʿa*, like *samiʿa* and *ḍaraba*. Similarly *ar-riḍāʿa* with a *kasra*. *Ar-ruḍʿ* with a quiescent or vowelled *ḍād*, and *ar-riḍāʿ* like *as-saḥāb*, and *ar-raḍiʿ* like *al-katif*. They have reported *raḍuʿa* like *karuma*, and *riḍāʿan* like *qitāl*. Its *ḍād* may be replaced by a *tā'*. And *ruḍāʿan* like *suʾāl*. But the form with a *ḍamma*, like *al-murāḍaʿa*, implies sharing. It is said: the woman *arḍaʿat*, so she is *murḍiʿ*, if she has a child whom she is nursing. If you describe her by the nursing of the child, you say *murḍiʿa*. Its meaning linguistically is sucking the breast, and in the sacred law it is the suckling of the infant from the breast of a human female at a specific time. By this they meant the arrival of milk from the woman's breast into the inside of the little one, through his mouth or his nose, within the period that follows, whether sucking occurred or did not occur. They mentioned the sucking only because it is a cause of the arrival, so they used the cause and meant the effect. In *al-Khāniyya* it is explicitly stated that there is no difference between sucking, snuffing, and the like. They restricted it to a human female, so as to exclude a man and an animal. Imam al-Bukhārī stood alone, and this was the cause of his trial, in one opinion, in the case where a boy and a girl suckled from the breast of a sheep, going to the view that the prohibition occurs between them. The verse is unrestricted so as to include the virgin and the non-virgin, the living and the dead. We restricted it to the mouth and the nose, so as to exclude what is delivered by dropping into the ear, the urethra, a wound that penetrates into the body, or an enema, according to the apparent narration. What is excluded by the word "arrival" is the case where a woman puts the nipple of her breast into the mouth of a suckling infant and she does not know whether the milk entered his throat or not. The marriage is not forbidden, because there is doubt about the impediment.

God, glorified is He, has made suckling take the place of lineage, to the extent that the nursing woman is called the mother of the suckling infant, and the one who nurses is called a sister. Likewise the husband of the nursing woman is his father, her parents are his grandparents, and her sister is his paternal aunt. Every child born to him from another woman, before the suckling or after it, is his brothers and sisters from his father. The mother of the nursing woman is his grandmother, and her sister is his maternal aunt. Every child she has from this husband is his brothers and sisters from his father and mother, and whoever is born to her from another [man] is his brothers and sisters from his mother. From here the Prophet, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, said, as narrated by al-Bukhārī and Muslim from the ḥadīth of ʿĀ'isha and Ibn ʿAbbās, may God Most High be pleased with them: "What is forbidden by lineage is forbidden by suckling." Many of the scholars of verification, such as Mawlānā Shaykh al-Islām and others, went to the view that the ḥadīth applies in its generality. As for the mother of his brother from the father, the sister of his son from the mother, the mother of his son's maternal grandmother, the mother of his uncle, and the mother of his maternal uncle from the father, their prohibition is not from the side of lineage, so that the generality of the ḥadīth is compromised by the necessity of their permissibility in the case of suckling. Rather it is from the side of marriage by affinity. Do you not see that the first is the one who has had intercourse with his father, the second is the daughter of his one who has had intercourse, the third is the mother of his one who has had intercourse, the fourth is the one who has had intercourse with his grandfather in a valid marriage, and the fifth is the one who has had intercourse with his grandfather in an invalid marriage? In the words of some of them there occurs an exception that is formed after the ḥadīth is cited. Al-Ṭūrī, in *al-Baḥr*, brought the exceptional cases to eighty-one cases, and he spoke at length on this point and brought a wondrous marvel.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that there is no difference between a small amount of suckling, which is what is known to reach the inside, and a large amount, in regard to the prohibition. As for the report of Muslim, "A single sucking or two suckings do not forbid," and what indicates a measure, it has been abrogated. Ibn ʿAbbās, may God Most High be pleased with them both, explicitly stated its abrogation when it was said to him: "People say that a single suckling does not forbid." He said: "That was [the case], then it was abrogated."

It is reported from Ibn Masʿūd, may God Most High be pleased with him, that he said: "The matter of suckling has come to the point that its small amount and its large amount forbid." It is reported from Ibn ʿUmar that a small amount forbids. And from him it is reported that it was said to him: "al-Zubayr says there is no harm in one suckling or two." He said: "The decree of God Most High is better than the decree of Ibn al-Zubayr," and he recited the verse. Al-Shāfiʿī, may God have mercy on him, according to what our companions quoted from him, said: the prohibition is not established except by five full suckings at five separate times recognized by custom. There are two reports from Aḥmad, one like our view and one like his view. The argument for this is what Ibn Ḥibbān narrated in his *Ṣaḥīḥ* from the ḥadīth of al-Zubayr, that he said: The Prophet, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, said: "A single sucking or two suckings do not forbid, nor a single swallowing or two swallowings." The argument from this is that the single sucking is included in the two suckings, and the single swallowing in the two swallowings. Their sum is: two suckings do not forbid, nor two swallowings, so the prohibition is negated for four, and it follows that it is established by five.

Ibn al-Humām objected to this, saying: "It is nothing. First, because the school of al-Shāfiʿī is not prohibition by five sucks but by five full [feedings] at times. Second, because the sucking is an action of the suckling, and the swallowing is the feeding, an action of the nursing woman. The sum of the meaning is that the Prophet, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, negated that both acts were prohibiting from him and from her. Then he verified that what is in this narration should not be one ḥadīth, because swallowing is not the true prohibiting factor but its necessary consequence from suckling. So the prohibition of swallowing is negated as a negation of a prohibition that is its necessary consequence. Therefore the sum is not: 'Two swallowings do not forbid' except 'their necessary consequence, which is the two suckings, does not forbid.' If they were combined in one ḥadīth, the sum would be 'Two suckings do not forbid, and two [swallowings] do not forbid,' and it would follow that it could only be meant as 'two suckings,' not four. On this it is necessary that the narrator, who is al-Zubayr, may God Most High be pleased with him, intended to combine the words of the Prophet, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, which he heard from him at two times, as if he said: 'The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "A single sucking or two suckings do not forbid,"' and he also said: '"A single swallowing or two swallowings do not forbid."'" It was said regarding the argument another route, which is that the ḥadīth negates what Imam al-Aʿẓam, may God Most High be pleased with him, held, so the school of Imam al-Shāfiʿī, may God Most High have mercy on him, is established by it, since there is no one who holds a distinction. It was objected that the one who holds a distinction is Abū Thawr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Dāwūd, and Abū ʿUbayd, and these are imams of ḥadīth, and they said: "What forbids is three sucklings." The claim that their view is not to be considered is a prohibition on account of the strength of its argument compared with the argument of al-Shāfiʿī's view.

Some of his companions argued for this point with what Muslim narrated from ʿĀ'isha, may God Most High be pleased with her, who said: "Among what was revealed of the Qur'an were ten known sucklings that forbid; then they were abrogated by five known sucklings that forbid. Then the Prophet ﷺ died, and they were in what is recited from the Qur'an..." In another narration: "It was in a sheet under my bed. When the Messenger of God, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, died, we were occupied with his death, and tame animals entered and ate it."

And by what is also narrated from ʿĀ'isha, she said: "Sahla bint Suhayl, the wife of Abū Ḥudhayfa, came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'O Messenger of God, I see in the face of Abū Ḥudhayfa the entering of Sālim, who is his ally.' He ﷺ said: 'Suckle Sālim five times, and you will become forbidden to him by them.'" The answer is that all of that has been abrogated, as Ibn ʿAbbās explicitly stated, as has passed. What indicates the abrogation of what is in the first report of ʿĀ'isha is that if it were not abrogated, some of the Qur'an that was not abrogated would be lost, and God Most High has guaranteed its preservation. What is in the narration does not contradict abrogation, since it may be said: she, may God Most High be pleased with her, meant that it was written and had not yet been washed away because it was recent, until tame animals entered and ate it. The claim that what is mentioned necessarily implies the abrogation of the recitation, so the recitation may be abrogated while the ruling remains, like "the old man and the old woman, if they commit adultery, stone them," is nothing, because the claim that the ruling of the indicator remains after its abrogation requires evidence; otherwise the principle is that the abrogation of the indicator lifts its ruling. What it was compared to would only be so if it were not known from the sunna, and consensus has not been established by it. Then what we are certain of in the ḥadīth of Sahla is that the Prophet, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, did not intend that Sālim be fed to satiety five times at five separate times while hungry, because a man is not satisfied with milk by a pound or two pounds. So where would you find in the breast of a human female

[Page 256 of the printed edition is not reproduced here; the passage continues from the preceding section.]

the amount that satisfies him, but this is ordinarily impossible. So the apparent meaning is that the counted five feedings, if it is established that they are from the report, are the sucklings (al-massāt). Then how is it permissible for him to put his lips to her private part? Perhaps the intended meaning is that she milks for him an amount equal to five feedings, and he drinks it, as al-Qadi said. Otherwise it is problematic. "It may be said" that it is abrogated (mansūkh) in another respect, because it indicates that suckling in adulthood establishes the prohibition, since Salim was then a man. No one among the Four Imams has said this. The period of suckling by which prohibition is established is thirty months according to Imam Abu Hanifa, and two years according to his two companions, whose evidence is very strong. The three other imams also took this view. From Malik there are these reports: two years and a month; in another narration two months; in another two years and some days; and in another, as long as the infant needs milk and is not weaned from it. Zufar said three years. Some said fifteen years, and others said forty years. Dawud said that suckling in adulthood also establishes prohibition, with no limit on the period. This is related from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, and when she wished that any man should enter upon her, she would order her sister Umm Kulthum, or one of her sister's daughters, to nurse him. Muslim related from Umm Salama and the rest of the wives of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that they opposed Aisha in this. The main basis of those who held her view in this matter is the report of Sahla, although the sound reports are contrary to it. It is established both as a marfu' (prophetic) and a mawquf (companion) report that "There is no suckling except what occurs within two years." This is in the Muwatta' and in Sunan Abi Dawud, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, that a man asked Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, saying: "I sucked milk from my wife's breast and it went into my stomach." Abu Musa said: "I do not see her except as having become forbidden to you." Ibn Mas'ud said: "Look at what you give as a fatwa to the man." Abu Musa said: "Then what do you say?" Ibn Mas'ud said: "There is no suckling except within two years." Abu Musa said: "Do not ask me about anything as long as this scholar is among you." Also in it, from Ibn Umar: a man came to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "I had a slave-girl, and I used to have intercourse with her. My wife intended to her and nursed her, and then she entered upon her and said: 'Take her, by Allah, I have nursed her.'" Umar said: "Return her, and go to your slave-girl, for suckling is only the suckling of infancy." At-Tirmidhi related, and said it is a sound hadith, from the hadith of Umm Salama that he said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "Nothing is prohibited by suckling except the rupture of the intestines at the breast, and that was before weaning." In Sunan Abi Dawud, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, raising it: "Nothing is prohibited by suckling except what makes the flesh grow and strengthens the bone." Even Aisha herself, may Allah be pleased with her, related what contradicts her practice. In the two Sahihs, from her, she said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, entered upon me while a man was with me. He said: 'O Aisha, who is this?' I said: 'My brother by suckling.' He said: 'O Aisha, look at who your brothers are, for suckling is only from hunger.'" Her narration was taken into account, but not her opinion, because of the clear oversight in it and because her reasoning did not hit the mark. For this reason it was said: it seems she returned to the ruling as Abu Musa did, when abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of an earlier ruling by a later one) became clear to her. Many scholars understood the report of Sahla to mean that it is specific to her and to Salim, and they also regarded the pardon for direct contact with the private part as among the special privileges.

This, and among the strange things I came upon concerning this verse, is a passage from a maqama of the scholar al-Suyuti, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, which he named "The Celestial Revolution Against Ibn al-Kurki." In it he addresses the aforementioned virtuous man with the following text: "What did you do with the important question that circulated in the land and that no one answered: the difference between His saying, ﴿And your mothers who have nursed you﴾, and what would be said if it were: 'And those who have nursed you, your mothers,' since five feedings are established as a requirement in the first, while with the second one feeding would suffice? This came to me and was brought to me, but I did not write on it, although its answer is before my eyes and ready with me, nothing stands between it and me, so that I might see whether there is any rightly guided man, or anyone who has a lofty castle of knowledge. Why did you not bring forth in it a well-aimed answer, and vary in it the diverse paths, and take with it support and backing for your claim to knowledge? Now for about two years no one has adorned it with a letter, nor has any observer glanced at it, nor has anyone of refined taste placed in it a single refined thing. If I wished, I would have written on it a number of works, and inscribed on it five compositions: a concise, well-guarded one, a medium, uncomplicated one, a brief abridgement, a versified work of fine composition, and a maqama of composition as if it were refined gold." End of his words.

I say: Perhaps the difference is that when He, glorified is He, mentioned "mothers" (ummahatukum) in this verse, coupled with what precedes it in the previous verse, in which the mothers are made forbidden, the mind remained stretched out toward an explanation of the distinction between these mothers and those mothers. So He, glorified is He, came with His saying, ﴿who have nursed you﴾, as an explanation of that, averting the suspicion of repetition. Thus the clause of suckling, which occurs as a relative clause, was given the utmost attention. Among what follows from this attention is its being considered wherever it is taken into account. It has been taken into account five times in the verse. The first: when it came as a verb. The second: when it was attributed to the agent, namely the pronoun of the women. The third: when it was connected to the object, namely the pronoun of the addressees. The fourth: when the part of the sentence occurring as the relative clause was made a component of the relative. The fifth: when "those who" was made an attribute of "your mothers," because its being an attribute of them is, without doubt, by way of the relative clause. So these are five considerations of suckling in this construction, pointing out that what brings about motherhood is five feedings. This is one of the secrets of choosing this construction, even though other constructions were possible, some of which may be more concise. Often in the Qur'an there occur constructions and expressions that point to real matters, having a correspondence between them and those expressions, like what occurs in His saying: ﴿And they have rights similar to their duties, according to what is reasonable﴾, which is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device of omitting in each of two parts what is mentioned in the other), pointing to the harmony between the spouses. And what occurs in His saying: ﴿Or if he is unable to dictate himself, then let his guardian dictate﴾, which involves idgham (assimilation) in yumill (the form of the verb), pointing to the state of the agent, who is the mute, whose tongue is tied, according to many views. And what occurs in His saying: ﴿each in an orbit﴾, which involves the absence of impossibility when reversed, pointing to the sphericity of the orbits according to one opinion, and to other things beyond counting. This is not a matter of inference, but of allusion that strengthens it. Do you not see that none of those who held the requirement of five feedings derived it from this verse? Rather, they derived it from the occurrence of five feedings in the reports. To this the words of the Jalal al-Suyuti, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, point. This allusion is absent in the hypothetical wording, "And those who have nursed you, your mothers," because the conjunction in it does not suggest repetition, since no similar expression has preceded it. So the mind is not stretched toward what is mentioned afterward, as it was stretched toward what was mentioned before. Therefore there is no reason to take it into account wherever it occurs, as was the case there. Rather, it suffices to take it into account once, which is the least by which the category is realized. Especially since it is mentioned after "your mothers," and it is in apposition, and the apposition, as they say, is the intended element in relation to the intention, by way of repeating the governing word, which serves to establish the meaning of the speech and emphasize it. This emphasis also indicates the unity of suckling, because prohibition by a single feeding is almost improbable and so needs to be emphasized, unlike multiple feedings.

I have seen in some copies of the commentary on Sahih Muslim by the Imam al-Nawawi, after his mention of Imam Malik's evidence for the claim that prohibition is established by a single feeding, from His saying, ﴿And your mothers who have nursed you﴾, where no number is stated, the following text: "The companions of al-Shafi'i objected to the Malikis, saying: 'The indication would only be yours if the verse were: "And those who have nursed you, your mothers."'" End of quotation. He, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, did not explicitly state that the verse which Malikis used as evidence indicates five; rather, he confined himself to saying that the indication of one is not established by it, and he meant that the strong indication of plurality that we pointed to rejects taking the category to mean the least that it is realized by. In some copies of that commentary it reads: "The companions of al-Shafi'i objected to the Malikis, saying: 'The indication would only be yours if the verse were: "And those who have nursed you and your mothers," with a conjunction between "who have nursed you" and "your mothers."' The apparent view is that this is a scribal error, and holding to its justification is forced; we have seen leaving it as the better gain.

[Page 257]

This is what appeared to my limited view and my weak thinking. I have asked, gently, about this distinction a group of the scholars of my age, and I consulted for the explanation of that text all the virtuous scholars included in the margins of an Egyptian edition. But I did not find anyone who spoke a word, nor anyone who claimed knowledge in resolving that difficulty, although among them are those before whom necks have bowed and whose virtues have spread through the horizons. It was not manly of me to give them time until the trumpet is sounded, or to wait for the daughters of their thoughts until the mule gives birth to the ʿAqūr al-Bāqūr. So I wrote what you see, and I am not certain that it is the most fitting and the most correct, so consider it carefully. For the path of the mind has breadth, and the truth is more deserving of being followed.

﴿And the mothers of your wives﴾: the beginning of an explanation of the prohibitions arising from marriage (musāharah, affinity), following the explanation of the prohibitions arising from suckling, which has a kinship like the kinship of lineage. By "women" is meant those who have been married, without restriction, whether or not they have been consummated with, and this is agreed upon among the Four Imams. However, it is required that the marriage be valid. As for a corrupt marriage, the mother is not forbidden unless he has had intercourse with her daughter. Al-Bayhaqi related it in his Sunan and others, through the chain of ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said: "If a man marries a woman, it is not lawful for him to marry her mother, whether he has entered upon the daughter or not. And if he marries the mother and has not entered upon her, then divorces her, he may marry the daughter if he wishes." To this view a group of the Companions and the Successors went. There are two reports from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn al-Mundhir related from him that he said: "Women are general (mubhamah): if a man divorces his wife before entering upon her, or she dies, her mother is not lawful to him." He also related from Muslim ibn ʿUwaymir that he said: "I married a woman but did not enter upon her until my paternal uncle died, leaving her mother. I asked Ibn ʿAbbas, and he said: 'Marry her mother.'" There are also two reports from Zayd ibn Thabit. Malik related from him that he was asked about a man who married a woman and then separated from her before touching her: is her mother lawful to him? He said: "No. The mother is general (mubhamah), there is no condition in it; the condition is only in the stepdaughters (rabaʾib)."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 23 (part 4 of 5):

It is related by Ibn Jarir and a group [of transmitters] from him (Ibn 'Abbas) that he used to say: If a man's wife dies while he is with her and he takes her inheritance, it is disliked for him to marry her mother. And if he divorces her before he has consummated [the marriage] with her, then there is no harm in his marrying her mother. It is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud that he used to issue a legal ruling permitting the mother of a woman [to be married] when he had not consummated [the marriage] with her daughter, and then he retracted that. Malik related from him that he was asked in Kufa about marrying the mother after the daughter, when the daughter had not been touched, and he permitted it. Then he came to Madina and was asked about it, and he informed [them] that it is not as he had said, and that the condition [of consummation] applies to the stepdaughters. So he returned to Kufa, and he had not reached his house until he came to the man to whom he had given that ruling and ordered him to separate from her. Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he was asked about a man who marries a woman and then divorces her, or she dies, before he has consummated [the marriage] with her: is her mother lawful for him? He said: She is in the position of the stepdaughter. Ibn al-Zubayr and Mujahid also held this view. The term "mothers" includes paternal and maternal grandmothers, however high they go. And if the man's wife is a slave-woman, her mother is not forbidden except by intercourse or its preliminaries, because the word "women," when it is attributed to husbands, means free women, as in zihar and ila'.  It is also read: "and the mothers of your women with whom you have consummated [the marriage]."

﴿And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship﴾. Al-Rabaʾib (the stepdaughters) is the plural of rabība, and rabb, and ruba are of the same meaning. Al-Rabib is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'ul (passive). When it was attached to the non-derived nouns, the attachment of the ta' to it was permitted; otherwise, fa'il in the sense of maf'ul is equal for masculine and feminine, and this is the meaning of their saying that the ta' is for transferring [the word] to the category of nouns. Al-Rabib is the child of a woman by another man, and it was named so because he generally raises him as he raises his own child. Al-Hujur is the plural of hijr (with fatha or kasra), and it means in language the lap of a person, that is what lies below his armpit down to the flank. And they say: "So-and-so is in the hijr of so-and-so," meaning in his protection and safeguard, and this is what is meant in the verse. The description of the stepdaughters as being in [the men's] laps is given as a generally occurring case and a custom, since it generally happens that the daughter is with her mother in the husband's house. Its purpose is to strengthen the cause of the prohibition, just as it is the reason for mentioning them by the name "stepdaughters" rather than "daughters of the women." It is also said: this was mentioned to censure them, similar to [the verse] "Do not consume usury, doubled and redoubled" (3:130). Had it not been mentioned, permission would have held when that [condition] is absent, by the indication of the wording outside the place of utterance, according to those who consider the concept of contrariety (mafhum al-mukhalafa); and by reference to the original state, which is permission, according to those who do not consider the concept, because departure from it to prohibition is restricted by a condition, and when the condition is absent it reverts to the original state, not by the indication of the wording. It is related from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he used to say that a stepdaughter is lawful when she is not in [the husband's] guardianship. Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim related with a sound chain from Malik ibn Aws, who said: "I had a wife, and she died after having borne me children, and I was grieved over her. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah ennoble his face, met me and said: 'What is the matter with you?' I said: 'The woman has died.' He said: 'Does she have a daughter?' I said: 'Yes, and she is in al-Ta'if.' He said: 'Was she in your guardianship?' I said: 'No.' He said: 'Marry her.' I said: 'Then what about His saying, "and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship"?' He said: 'She was not in your guardianship; that applies only when she is in your guardianship.'" Dawud also held this view, while the first is the view of the majority, and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, returned to it. The prohibition includes the daughters of the stepdaughter and of the stepson, however far down they go, because the name includes them, unlike [the case of] sons and fathers, since it is a term specific to them. For this reason it is permitted to marry the mother of a son's wife and her daughter, and it is permitted for a son to marry the mother of his father's wife and her daughter.

Some of the verifiers said: The establishment of the prohibition of the mentioned persons is by consensus (ijma').

﴿from your women with whom you have consummated [the marriage]﴾. The prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial clause (hal) modifying "stepdaughters" or its pronoun residing in the adverbial phrase, meaning: those who have settled in your laps, being of your women, etc. And "who" (allati) is an attributive modifier of the "women" mentioned before it, and it is for specification, since the stepdaughter of a wife with whom consummation has not taken place is not forbidden. It is not permissible for the prepositional phrase to be a circumstantial clause modifying "mothers" as well, or modifying what it is attached to, because being a circumstantial clause from "stepdaughters" or its pronoun requires that "min" be for origin, while being a circumstantial clause from "mothers" or from "your women" requires that it be explanatory. The claim that it is for connection, as in the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying, "You are to me as Aaron was to Moses," and the line of poetry: "If you attempt wrongdoing against Asad, I am not from you and you are not from me," is a meaning that encompasses origin and explanation, so it covers the connection of mothers with women, since they are their parents, and with the stepdaughters, since they are their offspring. Or the relative clause is made a description of both "women" while their governing elements differ, because the "women" that is attached as a genitive to "mothers" is governed by the genitive construction, and the one governed by "min" with it is very remote; indeed, the sanctity of revelation should be protected from it. As for the reading, its transmission is weak, and if it is granted to be sound, it is interpreted as abrogation, as Shaykh al-Islam said. The "ba'" in "bihinna" is for transitivity, and it carries the sense of accompaniment, or it means "with," that is, you entered with them behind the curtain. It is a metaphor for intercourse, like "he built upon her" and "he drew the veil over her." Many people say "bana biha" (he built with her), and al-Hariri considered this a mistake, but it is a mistake.

Touching and its counterparts are, according to Imam al-A'zam, may Allah be pleased with him, equivalent to intercourse. Some scholars have objected that his position has no basis, because the explicit sense of the verse is definitely not intended, but rather the commonly known figurative meaning; and what he said, if established by analogy, contradicts the explicit meaning of the condition; and if it is established by a hadith, which is not well-known, it does not agree with his principles. It is answered that it is from the explicit text, because the preposition "ba'" of association is explicit in it, since it is said: "He entered with her" when he held her and brought her into the house. If you say: Granted that the figurative sense does not require a preventing indicator against the literal meaning, yet it necessarily entails that it is intended, as has been verified in the science of meanings, so the verse has no indication of it. It is answered: even if it does not necessarily entail that it is intended, there is no impediment to it when an indicator for its intention exists, and the traditions suffice as an indicator. Among them is what is related through the chain of Ibn Wahb, from Abu Ayyub, from Ibn Jurayj, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning the man who marries a woman and then fondles her, without going beyond that: he must not marry her daughter. This report is mursal and munqati' (broken in its chain), but this does not harm it in our view when the transmitters are trustworthy; therefore they included it within the implication of the wording. It is related from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "If a man has intercourse with a woman, or kisses her, or touches her with desire, or looks at her private part with desire, then his father and his son are forbidden to her, and her mother and her daughter are forbidden to him."

If you say: Granted that he includes touching in its explicit sense, how does its counterpart enter into it? It is answered: it enters by the indication of the text (dalalat al-nass). What was mentioned about contradicting the explicit condition is based on accepting the concept of the condition, and we do not hold it, and moreover it is not general; and granting its generality, it is not far-fetched to say that it is specified. So reflect.

Adultery with a woman's private part is forbidden in our view. Whoever commits adultery with a woman, her daughter becomes forbidden to him. This is contrary to al-Shafi'i, who held that adultery does not establish the prohibition of affinity, because affinity is a blessing and therefore is not obtained through something forbidden; and because of his saying (ﷺ): "What is forbidden does not make the lawful forbidden." Our argument is that intercourse is a cause of offspring, so the prohibition attaches to it, by analogy with lawful intercourse; and the attribute of lawfulness has no bearing on the ground of the ruling, for intercourse with a jointly owned slave-woman, the slave-woman of a son, a mukatabah (a slave under a contract of manumission), a woman one has made unlawful by zihar and her slave-woman, a Magian slave-woman, a menstruating or postpartum woman, and intercourse during ihram or fasting, are all forbidden, and the stated prohibition is established by them. This shows that what is considered in the original ruling is the act of intercourse itself, without regard to whether it is lawful or unlawful. It is related that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, I committed adultery with a woman in the Jahiliyya; may I marry her daughter?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I do not see that; it is not right that you marry a woman whose daughter sees from her what you see from her." Although this has both irsal and inqita' in it, we bring it against their report, and the scholars of hadith have criticized it. 'Abd al-Haqq related it from Ibn 'Umar and then said: "Its chain includes Ishaq ibn Abi Farwa, who is abandoned (matruk). Moreover, it is not to be taken according to its apparent meaning. Consider: if someone urinated or poured wine into a small amount of water, would it not be unlawful, even though its use is forbidden? So it must be that the meaning is that the unlawful does not become unlawful by virtue of being unlawful." And in that case we say in accordance with its implication, since we do not hold that adultery establishes the prohibition of affinity by virtue of being adultery, but by virtue of being intercourse. The author of al-Hidaya answered their statement in explaining why adultery does not establish the prohibition of affinity, that it is a blessing and therefore not obtained through something forbidden, saying: "Intercourse is prohibited insofar as it is a cause of offspring, not insofar as its essence (dhatuhu) and not insofar as it is adultery." In Fath al-Qadir it is said that this statement is "a fallacy, for the blessing is not the prohibition insofar as it is a prohibition, since prohibition is restriction; that is why the lawfulness was broadened for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as a blessing from Allah, the Exalted. Rather, the blessing is what results from affinity, insofar as it results from affinity. The true blessing is affinity, because it is what makes the stranger a close relative, a support and an arm, one whose concerns are your concerns. Affinity through adultery does not exist. So the in-law (sihr), such as the husband of a daughter, is not from adultery with a man's daughter, and thus the relationship of in-law is negated, and its benefit as well, since a man recoils from one who committed adultery with his daughter, so he does not become acquainted with him but rather opposes him; how then would he benefit from him?" The transmitted reports are equally balanced, so the reference is to analogy, and we have shown in it the cancellation of an attribute additional to its being an attribute. The full discussion is in the extended works of our imams.

﴿So if you have not consummated [the marriage] with them﴾, i.e., previously, ﴿with them﴾, i.e., with those women, the mothers of the stepdaughters, ﴿then there is no blame﴾, i.e., no sin, ﴿upon you﴾, absolutely, ﴿in marrying their daughters if you have divorced them or they have died.﴾ This is an explicit statement of what the preceding indicated, and in it is the removal of the misconception that the condition of consummation is like the condition of being in the laps. The first fa' is for the ordering of what follows upon what precedes, in the manner already mentioned. And in restricting the explanation of the negation of prohibition to the negation of consummation, there is an indication that what counts for the prohibition is only the consummation, and not the stepdaughters being in the laps; otherwise it would have been said: "So if you have not consummated with them and they are not in your laps," or "if you have not consummated with them or they are not in your laps," following the usage of attaching the negation of a ruling to the negation of a complete compound cause or one of its recurring parts. And although it is valid to attach it to the negation of its specific part, that is contrary to the consistent usage.

﴿And the wives of your sons﴾, i.e., their wives, plural of halilah; the wife is so called because she is lawful (tahillu) [to her husband]

with his wife in a single bed; or because she is lawful to him wherever he is. So she is a *fa'ilah* in the sense of *fa'ilah* (a feminine form with active meaning), and similarly the husband is called *halil*. It has also been said that the two words derive from *al-hall* (untying), because each of them unties the other's waist-wrap (*izar*). It has also been said that they derive from *al-hill* (lawfulness), since each is lawful to the other, so the form is *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive). The ta' in *halilah* is because it is treated as one of the nouns that are not derived (*jamid*). If *fa'il* were taken in the case of the husband in the sense of *fa'il*, and in the case of the wife in the sense of *maf'ul*, there would be a subtle refinement that is not hidden. The verse clearly prohibits only the wife. As for the prohibition on one whom the son has had intercourse with who is not a wife, it is based on another proof. Ibn al-Humam said: "If *halilah* is taken from *hulul al-firash* (the settling on the bed) or *hall al-izar* (untying the waist-wrap), it includes the woman had through ownership by right of the hand, or by a doubtful union, or by fornication, so all of them become forbidden to the fathers, and this is the established ruling according to us... It does not include the woman to whom a son or his sons, however far down, have contracted marriage before intercourse and before obligation, because by the mere contract she becomes forbidden to the fathers, and this is considered from *al-hill* with a kasra. The proof has been established for the forbiddenness of a woman fornicated with by the son upon the father, so it is necessary to consider it in what is more general than *al-hill* and *al-hall*. Then by 'sons' are meant descendants, so the wife of a son however far down is forbidden to the highest grandfather." Likewise the son of a daughter, however far down. The apparent meaning of the words of the lexicographers is that *halilah* is the wife, as we have indicated. Some have chosen the more general meaning which includes ownership by the right hand, so that the secret of using this term here rather than *azwaj* or *nisa'* is that a man may think that the slave-girl of his son is his own slave-girl, on the basis that the son and his property belong to his father; so he is not concerned about having intercourse with her, and if the son has had intercourse with her. So they drew attention to her prohibition by a designation that truly applies to her and to the wife, the general term applying to its individuals, to indicate that there is no difference between them. Reflect on this. The ruling on those who have been touched and the like is the ruling on those whom the sons have had intercourse with.

﴿Those from your loins﴾: this is a qualifier of "the sons," and it was mentioned to exclude the wife of an adopted son. It is narrated from 'Ata' that it was revealed when the Prophet ﷺ married the wife of Zayd ibn Harithah, may Allah be pleased with him, and the polytheists spoke about that. The purpose of this is not to exclude the wife of a son by nursing, for she is also forbidden, just like the wife of a son by lineage. Some have mentioned a disagreement on this with al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, but what is well known from him is agreement on this.

﴿And that you combine two sisters﴾: in the place of raising, it is a conjunction upon what precedes it of the forbidden things. The intended meaning is combining them in marriage, not in ownership by the right hand. There is no difference whether the two are sisters by lineage or by nursing, so much so that they said: if he had two nursing wives who were nursed by a stranger, their marriages are void. It is related from al-Shafi'i that only the second marriage is void, and it is not forbidden to combine two sisters in ownership by the right hand. However, combining them in intercourse by ownership by the right hand is attached to it by way of implication, because they are united in the same circle, so it is forbidden according to the majority, and Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, and 'Ammar ibn Yasir, may Allah be pleased with them, held this. The reports from 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, differed. Al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Abi Shaybah related from him that he was asked about a man who had two slave-girls who were sisters, and he had intercourse with one of them, then wished to have intercourse with the other. He said: "No, until he removes her from his ownership." Both of them related through Abu Salih from him that he said concerning two sister slave-girls: "One verse permits them and another verse forbids them, and I do not command, nor forbid, nor make lawful, nor make forbidden, nor do I do it, nor do my household." 'Abd ibn Humayd related from Ibn 'Abbas that combining them is something with no harm, and the like was related from 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him. From 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I do not like to permit combining them," and he forbade the questioner about it. Some have claimed that the apparent meaning is that those among the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, who held it lawful returned to the opinion of the majority. If we say there was no return, then the subsequent consensus (*ijma'*) removes the earlier disagreement, and this is only complete if the dissent of the people of the literal school (*Ahl al-Zahir*) is not taken into account. If that is not the case, then the preferred view when there is conflict is prohibition. If he marries the sister of his slave-girl whom he has had intercourse with, the marriage is valid, but intercourse with either of them is forbidden until he makes the one he has had intercourse with forbidden to himself by one of the causes, and then he may have intercourse with the one he married, since the combining no longer exists, as in sale, wholly or partly, and the valid marriage, the gift with delivery, manumission wholly or partly, and the contract of *kitabah* (manumission by contract). If he marries the sister in an invalid marriage, the slave-girl he has had intercourse with does not become forbidden to him unless he has consummated the marriage with the one he married; then the one he has had intercourse with becomes forbidden, because the combining between them actually exists. Ihram, menstruation, postpartum bleeding, and fasting do not affect this, and likewise mortgage, hire, and *tadbir* (conditional manumission upon death), because her private part is not made forbidden by these causes. If the one he has had intercourse with returns to his ownership after being removed, whether by annulment or a new purchase, it is not lawful to have intercourse with either of them until he makes the slave-girl forbidden to himself by a cause as before. The apparent meaning of their statement "intercourse is not lawful until she is made forbidden" is that the marriage is valid, and they have stated this and given as its reason that it proceeds from its people attached to its place. It has been objected to this that the one married is considered to have been had intercourse with, by their acknowledgment, so by the marriage he becomes one who combines intercourse in a legal sense, and that is void. From this, some Malikis went to the view of invalidity. It is answered that the necessity of combining them in intercourse legally is not necessary, because it is in his hand to remove it, so it does not harm the validity, and it prevents intercourse after it, because it is then present. The prohibition is attributed to the combining, not to the second, by saying: "and the sisters of your women," in order to avoid conveying permanent prohibition as with the earlier forbidden things; and because it is not concerned with conveying the prohibition of combining in simultaneity. The combining between a woman and her paternal aunt or maternal aunt and similar relations also shares this, for the ground of the prohibition on combining two sisters is that it leads to severing what Allah has commanded to be joined, unlike what is in *al-Mabsut*, as is shown by what al-Tabarani related from his saying, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him: "If you do that, you will sever your kinship ties," and what Abu Dawud related in his *Marasil* from 'Isa ibn Talhah, who said: "The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, forbade a woman to be married upon her relative, for fear of severance." That is realized in combining those we have mentioned, rather more so, for the paternal aunt and maternal aunt are in the position of the mother. So his saying, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, emphasizing the explanation of the prohibition: "A woman shall not be married upon her paternal aunt, nor upon her maternal aunt, nor upon her brother's daughter, nor upon her sister's daughter," is, according to some verifiers, a statement of explanation rather than a statement of expression. Others said: the hadith is well known, for it is established in the *Sahihs* of Muslim and Ibn Hibban, and Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i related it, and the early generation received it with acceptance from the Companions and the Successors, and a great multitude related it from them: Abu Hurayrah, Jabir, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. So it is permissible to specify the generality of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾. Indeed, even if it were of the solitary reports (*akhbar al-ahad*), specification by it would be permissible without depending on it being well known. Ibn al-Humam said: "The apparent meaning is that it is necessary to claim it is well known, because the hadith's place is abrogation (*naskh*), not specification, and he explained this in *Fath al-Qadir*, so refer to it."

﴿Except what has already passed﴾: this is a disjunctive exception. The aim of intensifying and emphasizing here is not appropriate for the closing with His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾, because forgiveness and mercy are not suited to emphasizing the prohibition. What is meant by "what has passed" is what occurred before the prohibition, for they used to combine two sisters by it. Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it as good), and Ibn Majah related from Fayruz al-Daylami that Islam reached him while he had two sisters under him, and the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "Divorce whichever of them you wish." 'Ata' and al-Suddi said: its meaning is except what came from Ya'qub, peace be upon him, when he combined two sisters, Layya, the mother of Yahudha, and Rahil, the mother of Yusuf, peace be upon him. The closing does not support this, because what Ya'qub, peace be upon him, did, if it is sound, was lawful in his law. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the people of the Jahiliyyah used to forbid what Allah had forbidden except the wife of the father and combining two sisters. The like was related from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, who said: "Do you not see that He followed the prohibition concerning each of them with His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿except what has already passed﴾?" This, as Shaykh al-Islam said, points to the exception being in both on one pattern, and the difference in what follows them rejects this.

The fourth part of the Tafsir of Ruh al-Ma'ani; it is followed by the fifth part, which begins with: ﴿And the married women among women﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 24 (part 1 of 2):

Page 2

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿And the married women, except those whom your right hands possess⦆ is a conjunction with what precedes it of the prohibited women.

According to the well-known view, what is meant by them (al-muhsanat) is those who are married (dhawat al-azwaj), whom marriage has protected (ahsanahunna al-tazawwuj), or the husbands, or the guardians, meaning that they are prevented from falling into sin. The reciters agreed, as Abu 'Ubayda said, on the vowel fath on the ṣād here. The narration of fath from al-Kisa'i is not sound. The well-known narration of this reading is from Talha ibn Musarrif and Yahya ibn Wathhab, and on this reading it is an active participle (ism fa'il), because they have guarded their chastity (furuj) from other than their husbands, or they have guarded their husbands.

It is said that the form is also active according to the first reading. Ibn al-A'rabi said: every af'al has its active participle with kasra except three letters: ahsana, and alfaja when his property is gone, and asshaba when his speech is abundant.

The same is related from al-Azhari. Tha'lab said: every chaste woman is muhsana and muhsina, and every married woman is muhsana with fath only and no other. It is said: the woman was ḥuṣina (with ḍamm) ḥuṣnan, meaning she was chaste, so she is ḥāṣin and ḥaṣnān with fath, and ḥaṣnā' also, clearly chaste. A horse is ḥiṣān with kasra, clearly protected and guarded.

It is said that it was named ḥiṣān because it withheld its water and did not mount except a noble mare; then this became so common that they called every male of the horses ḥiṣān.

The word iḥṣān regarding a woman occurs in the language and is used in the Qur'an with four meanings: Islam, freedom, marriage, and chastity. Al-Rafi'i added reason ('aql), because it prevents from immoral acts.

The prepositional phrase is related to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from (al-muḥṣanat), meaning: the married women are forbidden to you, being from among the women. Its benefit is to emphasize their generality. It is said: to remove the suspicion that it includes men, on the basis that it is an adjective of the souls (anfus), which includes males and females. But this is nothing, as is not hidden. The meaning of the verse is obscure, to the extent that Mujahid said: "If I knew who would explain it to me, I would travel to him by the livers of camels." Ibn Jarir related it from him. Ibn Abi Shayba related from Abu al-Sawda, who said: I asked 'Ikrima about this verse, ﴿And the married women⦆ etc., and he said: I do not know. The earlier scholars had sayings about it. One of them: what is meant by them is the married women, as we have mentioned.

What is meant by possession (milk) is only possession by captivity (al-sabi), for it is that which necessitates annulling the marriage and making them lawful to the captor and no other. This is the view of 'Umar, 'Uthman, the majority of the Companions, the Successors, and the four imams. However, there is a dispute: is captivity alone what makes it lawful, or is it the capture of them alone?
