According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, captivity alone necessitates separation and makes marriage lawful. According to Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, it is the capture of them alone, so that if they are captured together with him, they are not lawful to the captor. The proponents of this view argued with what Muslim related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "We captured captives on the day of Awtas, and they had husbands. We disliked having intercourse with them, so we asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the verse was revealed, so we made them lawful to us." This narration from him is more sound than the other narration that it was revealed concerning the emigrant women. It was objected that this is restricting a general text to its occasion of revelation, which contradicts what is established in the principles that the specificity of the cause is not considered. It was answered that this is not restriction of that kind at all; rather it was specified because it conflicts with another proof, namely the well-known hadith from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that when she bought Barira, who was married, she freed her, and the Prophet ﷺ gave her the choice. So if the sale of a slave-girl were a divorce, he would not have given her the choice. Thus the general text is then restricted to its specific cause. Since other kinds of transfer besides sale are like sale in that they are voluntary possession that follows an earlier possession, unlike captivity, which is a new, compulsory possession, nothing else is attached to it. So it is said. The followers of al-Shafi'i objected by applying the verse and the report to the Imam al-A'zam, may Allah be pleased with him, and made this an argument against him in what he held. Al-Shihab answered that the application is not accepted: in the reports it is related that on the day of Awtas the men joined the mountains, and took the women, and the Muslims said: "How shall we do, when they have husbands?" So Allah revealed the verse. Likewise at Hunayn, as the historians of the campaigns mentioned. Thus it is established that there were no husbands with them. If they argue from the generality of the wording, it is said to them: we agree that it is not general, and that separation is not required by the renewal of possession. When this is not so, we know that the separation is for another reason, namely the difference of abodes (ikhtilaf al-darayn), so it is necessary to restrict it to the captive women alone, and captivity is not the cause of separation. The proof is that if she came out Muslim or a dhimmi and her husband did not join her, separation occurs without dispute.

Allah has judged this regarding the emigrant women in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And do not hold to the marriage ties of disbelieving women⦆. So what was raised is not an objection.

Second: what is meant by the married women is what we have mentioned, and by possession is absolute possession of the right hand, so whoever comes to possess a slave-girl by sale, gift, captivity, or otherwise, and she was married, that transfer necessitates her divorce and her lawfulness to the one to whom she has passed. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and a group of the Companions, and the majority of the Imamiyya went to it.

Third: the married women are more general than the chaste, the free, and those with husbands, and possession is more general than possession of the right hand and possession of enjoyment through marriage. So the meaning of the verse returns to the prohibition of fornication and the prohibition of every foreign woman except by contract or possession of the right hand. Ibn Jubayr, 'Ata' and al-Suddi went to this, and it is related from some Companions, and Malik chose it in the Muwatta'.

Fourth: that what is meant by the married women are the free women, and by possession the absolute kind, and the aim is the prohibition of free women after the four. 'Abd al-Razzaq and others related from 'Ubayda that he said about this verse: "Allah the Exalted made four lawful to you at the beginning of the sura, and forbade marriage to every married woman after the four, except what your right hand possesses." Something similar was related from many.

Shaykh al-Islam said: what is meant by the married women are those with husbands, and the relative pronoun is either general according to the generality of its clause, and the exception is not to exclude all individuals from the ruling of prohibition by way of the comprehensiveness of negation, but by way of negating comprehensiveness, which entails excluding some, meaning: the married women are forbidden to you absolutely, except the married women whom you possess, for they are not among the absolutely prohibited; rather among them are some whose marriage is not forbidden in general, namely the captive women whose husbands are not with them, or absolutely, according to the difference of the two schools. Or it is specific to the captive women, so the meaning is: the married women are forbidden to you except those who were captured, for their marriage is legislated in general, that is, to others than their owners. As for their being lawful to them by the ruling of possession of the right hand, it is understood by the indication of the text, due to unity of the ground (ittihad al-manat), not by its expression, because the context of the noble arrangement is to explain the prohibition of enjoying the prohibited women listed by the ruling of the possession of marriage, and the prohibition of enjoying them by the ruling of possession of the right hand is by way of indication of the text, and exception definitely does not apply to that. As for counting them among the married while separation from their husbands is certain, by the difference of the two abodes or by captivity, that is based on the belief of people, since they were unaware of the separation, as the report of Abu Sa'id indicates. And there is no indication in the ruling of the verse, following the revelation, that the verse was addressed to it, for that depends only on it being understood by some way of the modes of indication, not on it being understood by way of expression or the like.

It was objected that this involves departing from the apparent meaning without any reason, and there is no barrier, even on the assumption that the context of the noble arrangement is to explain the prohibition of enjoying the prohibited women listed by the ruling of the possession of marriage only, to say that the exception is by way of the necessary consequence of the prohibition of marriage, which is the prohibition of intercourse. So it is as if it were said: marriage with the married women is forbidden to you, so intercourse with them is not permitted to you except what your right hands possess, for it is permitted to you to have intercourse with them. So consider.

﴿The decree of Allah⦆ is an emphatic infinitive: Allah the Exalted has prescribed ﴿upon you⦆ the prohibition of these as a decree. The addition does not contradict this, as was supposed. The sentence emphasizes what precedes it, and ﴿upon you⦆ is connected with the omitted verb. It was also said: ﴿decree⦆ is in the accusative as an incitement (al-ighra'), meaning: hold to the Book of Allah. ﴿Upon you⦆ is connected either with the infinitive or with an omitted element occurring as a circumstantial clause from it. It was said: it is another incitement emphasizing what precedes it, and its object is omitted because of what precedes it. It was also said: it is accusative by ʿalaykum, and they used this as evidence for permitting the fronting of the object in the case of incitement, but this is nothing.

Abu al-Sammaqa read: "Kutub Allah" with the plural and nominative, meaning these are the obligations of Allah upon you, and "Kataba Allah" with the verb form.

﴿And it is made lawful for you⦆: Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read it in the passive, and the rest in the active. Al-Zamakhshari made it, on the first reading, conjoined with "were made unlawful," and on the second reading conjoined with the implied "decreed." Abu Hayyan criticized him, saying that the distinction he chose is not preferred, because the clause "decreed" is for emphasis of what precedes it, while this one is not emphatic, so it should not be conjoined with the emphatic clause, but with the founding clause, especially since they correspond in permission and prohibition. Al-Halabi considered this, and perhaps the basis of the consideration is that permitting what is other than that is emphatic in meaning for its prohibition, and what was mentioned is an aesthetic matter, observing a clear correspondence.

﴿Beyond that for you⦆: a reference to the prohibited women mentioned earlier, meaning: marriage with others than them is made lawful for you, singly and in plurality. Preferring the demonstrative over the pronoun indicates that those who are in the sense of the mentioned ones share in the ruling of prohibition with the mentioned ones, so the prohibition of combining a woman and her paternal aunt is not an objection, nor is combining any two women of whom, if one were male, the other would not be lawful to her, as is explained in the branches of law, because the prohibition of those mentioned falls within what preceded by way of indication, as the reference of some verifiers pointed to. The hadith specifying this generality by the Book and the Sunna is well known.

﴿That you seek⦆ is an object of purpose for what the speech implies, meaning: He made clear to you the prohibition of the mentioned prohibited women and the permission of others, desiring and seeking that you seek. The object is omitted, meaning you seek women, or it is left, meaning you perform the seeking with your wealth, by spending it on their dowries, or it is a substitution of inclusion for "beyond that," with the object of the verb being a pronoun.

Some allowed that "ma" refers to the act, such as marriage and nikah, and made this an apposition of whole to whole. What is related from Ibn 'Abbas is to generalize the statement so that it includes spending wealth on dowries and prices.

﴿Chaste⦆ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "seek." What is meant by iḥṣan here is chastity and guarding oneself against falling into what does not please Allah, the Exalted.

﴿Not fornicating⦆ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun attached, or from the hidden pronoun, and in reality it is an emphatic circumstantial clause. Sifah means fornication, from safh, which is pouring water. Zina was named by it because the fornicator has no aim but to pour out the drop, not offspring. From al-Zajjaj: al-musafiha and al-musafih are the two fornicators who do not refrain from anyone. It is said of a woman who fornicates with one man: she has a lover (dhat khidn). The object of the two descriptions is omitted, meaning: guarding your private parts or your souls, not fornicating with prostitutes. The apparent meaning of the verse is evidence for those who went to the view that the dower must be...

Page 5

Al-Imam al-A'zam (may Allah be pleased with him) held this view, and some of the Shafi'is said: there is no proof in that, because specifying wealth (māl) is due to it being the most common and customary case, so marriage is permissible for something other than wealth. This is supported by what al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Sahl ibn Sa'd: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked a man who had proposed to a woman who had given herself to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'What do you have of the Qur'an?' He said: 'I have such-and-such surahs,' and he counted them. He said: 'Can you recite them by heart?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Go, I have married her to you for what you have of the Qur'an.'" The point of the support is that if the verse contained a proof, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would not have contradicted it.

It is answered that the Qur'an being with him does not necessitate that it is the consideration (badal), and teaching is not mentioned in the report, so it is possible that his intention (ﷺ) was: "I have married you out of reverence for the Qur'an and because of what you have of it." This was said by some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin), and perhaps the report contains an indication of it.

﴿So whomever you have enjoyed of them﴾: "mā" is either an expression for the women, or for what relates to them of actions. On both, it is either conditional (shartiyyah) or relative (mawsulah). In either case it is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate, on the conditional reading, is the conditional verb, its response, or both; on the relative reading it is the Almighty's words: ﴿give them their due wages﴾, and the fa' is because the relative pronoun includes the meaning of a condition. Then, on the reading where it means the women, with the implicit returning pronoun to the subject being the object pronoun in (fa-ātūhunna), and "min" is explicative (bayaniyyah) or partitive (tab'idiyyah), in a position of accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in (bihi). The use of "mā" for rational beings is because a quality (wasf) is intended by it, as has passed more than once. The pronoun was treated first according to the wording and last according to the meaning. The sīn is for emphasis, not for request. The meaning: "So whichever individual you have enjoyed, being of the kind of women or some of them, give them their wages." On the reading where it is an expression for what relates to them, "min" is initial (ibtida'iyyah) and connected to the enjoyment in the sense of enjoying, and "mā" is for what does not reason, and the returning pronoun to the subject is omitted, meaning: "whatever action you have enjoyed from them of the actions mentioned, give them their wages for it or in exchange for it." What is meant by the wages is the dowries (muhur), and the dowry was called a wage because it is a substitute for a benefit and not for a substance. ﴿An obligation﴾ is a circumstantial state (hal) from the wages, in the sense of "obligated," or an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a obligatory giving, or an emphatic verbal noun, meaning: that was made obligatory as an obligation, so it is like qati'ah in the sense of cutting. ﴿And there is no blame﴾, meaning no sin, ﴿upon you in what you mutually agree upon﴾ of reducing the dowry, or waiving it, or increasing above what was stipulated. There is no blame in increasing the increase, since "no blame" does not fit when the address is made to the husbands by way of predominance; for taking an increase is a likely cause for the negated thing to apply to the wife. ﴿After the obligation﴾, meaning the fixed amount. It was said: ﴿in what you mutually agree upon﴾ refers to maintenance and the like, and it was said: to residence or separation. Shaykh al-Islam objected to this by saying that the mention of the obligation does not support it, since they have no connection with it, unless separation is by way of khul' (mutual separation for compensation). It was said: the verse concerns mut'ah, which is marriage for a known term of a day or more, and the meaning is: ﴿there is no blame upon you in what you mutually agree upon﴾ of entering into another contract after the end of the term set in the mut'ah contract, such as the man increasing the wage and the woman extending the term. The Imamiyyah went to this view, and the verse is one of their proofs for the permissibility of mut'ah. They supported their reasoning from it by saying that it is in the reading of Ubayy: "So whomever you have enjoyed of them, for a named term," and Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with them) read likewise. The discussion on this is well known. There is no dispute among us that it was made permissible and then prohibited. Qadi 'Iyad mentioned a lengthy discussion on this, and the correct and preferred position is that the prohibition and permission occurred twice: it was lawful before the day of Khaybar, then prohibited on the day of Khaybar, then permitted on the day of the Conquest of Makkah, which is the day of Awtas, due to the proximity of the two, then prohibited on that day after three days, as a permanent prohibition until the Day of Resurrection, and the prohibition continued. It is not permissible to say that permission is restricted to what was before Khaybar, and the prohibition on the day of Khaybar was for perpetuity, and that what was on the day of the Conquest was merely a confirmation of the prohibition without any prior permission on the day of the Conquest, since the authentic hadiths reject that, and in Sahih Muslim there is what is sufficient.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) that he used to say it was lawful, then he retracted when 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) said to him: "You are a confused man; the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade mut'ah." Thus it is said, but in Sahih Muslim there is what indicates that he did not retract when 'Ali said that to him. For he narrated from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr that 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with him) stood in Makkah and said: "Some people whom Allah has blinded in their hearts as He has blinded their sights are issuing fatwas on mut'ah," alluding to a man, meaning Ibn 'Abbas, as al-Nawawi said. So he called out to him and said: "You are a coarse, dry boor. By my life, mut'ah was practised in the time of the Imam of the pious," meaning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ibn al-Zubayr said to him: "Then test yourself, for by Allah, if you do it I will stone you with your stones." This occurred during the caliphate of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, after the death of 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face). Thus it is established that he consistently held the view of its permissibility and did not return to the statement of the Commander (Amir, i.e. 'Ali). This was also the view of the scholar Ibn Hajar in his commentary on al-Minhaj. Therefore it is better to judge that he returned after that, based on what al-Tirmidhi, al-Bayhaqi and al-Tabarani narrated from him that he said: "Mut'ah was only at the beginning of Islam. A man would come to a town where he had no acquaintances, so he would marry a woman for as long as he thought he would stay, and she would guard his goods and look after his affairs," until the verse was revealed: ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾, so every other private part is unlawful. This may be understood to mean that he came to know that the matter was only in this manner, so he returned to it and related it. It is also related from him that he only permitted it in cases of necessity and severe hardship during journeys. It is narrated from Ibn Jubayr that he said: "I said to Ibn 'Abbas: your fatwas have traveled with the caravans, and the poets have spoken about them." He said: "And what have they said?" I said: "They said:

I said to the elder when his sitting grew long: O companion, are you interested in the fatwa of Ibn 'Abbas?
Are you interested in the concession of a young woman of the wayfarers, who would be your abode until the people depart?"

He said: "Subhan Allah! I did not issue fatwas with this. It is nothing but like carrion, blood and pig's flesh, and it is lawful only for the one under compulsion." From here al-Hazimi said: he (ﷺ) did not permit it for them while they were in their homes and homelands, but only permitted it for them at times according to necessity, until he finally prohibited it for them with a permanent prohibition. As for what is narrated that they used to practise mut'ah in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr and 'Umar, until 'Umar forbade it, it is to be understood that the one who practised it had not reached the news of abrogation, and 'Umar's prohibition was to make it known, since mut'ah had spread among those who had not reached the prohibition of it. As for the meaning of "I forbid it" in his statement, if it is authentic: it means "I make its prohibition manifest," not "I originate it," as the Shi'ah claim. This verse does not indicate permissibility, and the claim that it was revealed concerning mut'ah is an error, and some people's interpretation of it in that way is not acceptable, because the structure of the noble Qur'an rejects it, since Allah, glorified is He, first clarified the forbidden women, then said, exalted is His majesty: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that, that you seek with your wealth﴾, and this contains a condition in meaning, so the legitimizing of the private part and its lending is invalid, though the Shi'ah have held both. Then He, majestic and exalted, said: ﴿chaste, not fornicating﴾, and this contains an indication of prohibiting the intention to be merely the fulfilment of desire, pouring out water and emptying the vessels of semen. Thus mut'ah is invalidated by this condition, since the goal of the one who enjoys it is nothing but that, not marriage, begetting children, protecting honour and family. Hence you find the one who enjoys it each month under a companion and each year in the lap of another playmate. Chastity is not at all present in the woman of mut'ah. For this reason the Shi'ah say: the one who enjoys without marrying, if he commits zina, is not stoned.

Then He, glorified is He, based on the state of marriage the words of the Mighty One: ﴿So when you have enjoyed﴾, which indicates that the intended enjoyment is intercourse and consummation, not enjoyment in the sense of mut'ah which the Shi'ah maintain. The reading they transmit from earlier Companions is anomalous.

What indicates prohibition, such as the verse ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾, is definitive, so do not contradict it. Moreover, when two proofs are equal in strength and conflict regarding permissibility and prohibition, prefer the proof of prohibition. The Shi'ah may not say that the woman enjoyed is a slave, for the falsity of that is self-evident, nor a wife, for all the necessary consequences of marriage are absent, such as inheritance, the waiting period, divorce and maintenance. Their own scholars have stated this.

Abu Nusayr among them narrated in his Sahih from al-Sadiq (may Allah be pleased with him) that he was asked about the woman of mut'ah: is she among the four? He said: "No, nor among the seventy." This is explicit that she is not a wife, for otherwise she would be counted among the four. In sum, using this verse as proof for the permissibility of mut'ah is worthless, as is not hidden. There is no dispute now among the Imams and scholars of the regions, except the Shi'ah, regarding its impermissibility. The attribution of permissibility to Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) is an error with no basis; rather, there are two reports from him regarding the punishment for one who enjoys mut'ah, and the view of most is that he is not subject to the hadd (prescribed punishment) because of the shubhah of contract and the shubhah of disagreement. The source of disagreement, as al-Nawawi said, is the disagreement of the jurists of usul regarding whether consensus after disagreement removes the disagreement and the matter becomes agreed upon. Some said it does not remove it, rather the disagreement persists and the matter never becomes agreed upon thereafter; this was the view of Qadi Abu Bakr al-Baqillani. Others said that a later consensus removes an earlier disagreement, and its full treatment is in the books of usul. Some have reported from Zufar that he said: whoever marries with a mut'ah marriage, his marriage becomes permanent, and the mention of a term is among the invalid conditions in marriage, which are disregarded. The well-known position in the books of our companions is that he said this regarding the time-limited marriage, and whether it is the same as mut'ah marriage is open to investigation. Some held that witnesses are required for the time-limited marriage and not for mut'ah, and that the wording of marriage or nikah is used in the former, while "astamtiʿu" or "atamattaʿu" is used in the latter. Others said the time-limited marriage is one type of mut'ah. Ibn al-Humam mentioned that marriage is not concluded with the word mut'ah even if the valid permanent marriage was intended and witnesses were present, because it is not suitable as a metaphor for the meaning of marriage, as he explained in al-Mabsut. Remaining is the case where one marries unconditionally while intending not to remain with her beyond a period he intends: is that a valid, lawful marriage or not? The majority hold the former, and the Qadi even reported consensus on it, though al-Awza'i deviated and said: it is mut'ah marriage, and there is no good in it; therefore it is appropriate not to intend that. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing﴾ of what sets right the affairs of creation, ﴿Wise﴾ in what He has legislated for them, and among that is the marriage contract which safeguards wealth and lineages.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 25 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And whoever among you is not able﴾ (man) is either a conditional particle, and what follows it is its condition, or a relative pronoun, and what follows it is its relative clause. (minkum) is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun in (yastati') [is able]. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿tawlan﴾ [means of marrying free women] is the direct object of (yastati'). Making it an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), with an elided noun, gives the sense: "for lack of means (li-'adami tawl)" — an elaboration without substance.

It means wealth and ample means. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid interpreted it this way. Its root meaning is superiority and surplus, and from it comes ṭā'il (abundant wealth). Some interpreted it as elevation and attainment, from their saying ṭultuhu, meaning "I attained it." From this is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"Indeed al-Farazdaq is a compact rock, too high for the mountain goats to reach."

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿to marry believing free women [al-muhsanat al-mu'minat]﴾ means the free women (al-hara'ir). The evidence is that they are contrasted with the slave women (al-mamlukat). He described them this way because their freedom guarded them (ahsanathunna) from the deficiency of slave women. The phrase may be connected to (tawlan), meaning: "and whoever is not able to attain the marriage of free women." Or it may be taken with an implied (ila) or (li), and the prepositional phrase occupies the position of an adjective for (tawlan), meaning: "and whoever is not able to find wealth leading to marrying them, or for marrying them." Or [it is taken as] that tawl means ability, as al-Zajjaj said. The position of (an) after the elision is genitive or accusative, according to the well-known disagreement. This estimation is the view of al-Khalil, and al-Kisa'i adopted it. Abu al-Baqa' allowed that it may be a substitute for (tawlan), a substitution of one thing for another, both referring to the same thing, on the basis that tawl is ability or surplus, and marriage is strength and surplus. It was also said that it may be the object of (yastati') with (tawlan) being an emphatic infinitive for it, since istita'a is tawl, or a specifier (tamyiz), meaning: "and whoever among you is not able with an ability," or "in respect of means and wealth," that is, not in respect of natural disposition and temperament, since that has no connection to the context.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then from what your right hands possess﴾ is the answer of the condition, or the predicate of the relative. The fa' has come for the reason mentioned more than once. (ma) is a relative pronoun in the genitive position after the partitive (min), and the prepositional phrase is connected to an elided verb whose object is omitted; in reality it is connected to an elided element that functions as an adjective of that object, meaning: "let him marry a woman who is part of the type that your right hands possess." Abu al-Baqa' allowed that (min) is extra, meaning: "let him marry what your right hands possess."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from your believing slave girls [fatayatikum al-mu'minat]﴾ means your believing female slaves (imaikum). It is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from the elided pronoun referring to (ma). It was also said that (min) is extra and (fatayatikum) is the object of the elided verb mentioned before, and (mimma malakat) is connected to the verb itself, with (min) indicating the starting point; or it is connected to an elided element functioning as a circumstantial qualifier of this object, and (min) is partitive. (al-mu'minat) in all these views is an adjective of (fatayatikum). It was also said that it is the object of that elided verb, but this is distant.

The apparent meaning of the verse indicates the impermissibility of marrying a slave woman for one who is able, by the implication of the condition (mafhum al-shart), as Shafi'i held. It also indicates the impermissibility of marrying a scripturally-following (kitabiyya) slave woman absolutely, by the implication of the qualifier (mafhum al-sifa), as is the view of the people of the Hijaz. Imam al-A'zam (may Allah be pleased with him) permitted both, on the basis of the unrestricted indication from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿marry what seems good to you of women﴾ and ﴿lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾, so nothing is excluded from it except by what necessitates specification. What was cited does not stand as a valid proof. First, the two implications, that is the implication of the condition and the implication of the qualifier, are not proofs according to him (may Allah be pleased with him), as established in the principles of jurisprudence. Second, even granting them as proofs, their implication is the absence of the permission that is established when the permitting condition exists, and the absence of permission is more general than the establishment of prohibition or disapproval, and a general term does not indicate a more specific one in particular. Therefore disapproval may be established when the free woman's means are present, just as prohibition may be established equally, and disapproval is the lesser, so it is determined, and we hold by it. Disapproval is stated explicitly in al-Bada'i'. Some explained the impermissibility of marrying a slave woman, given that the condition is not fulfilled, by the exposure of the child to slavery, so that the prohibition is established by analogy to many principles, or so that one of the two particulars of the general, which is the absence of permission, namely prohibition, is intended by the general.

It was objected that if they mean that it involves exposing a child described as free to slavery, we accept that this entails prohibition, but the existence of the description is denied. There is no one here described as free being exposed to slavery; rather, the descriptions of freedom and slavery accompany the existence of the child with respect to its mother: if she is free, the child is free, or if she is a slave, the child is a slave. If they mean by it the exposure of the child who will come into existence to the simultaneous occurrence of slavery in existence, not enslaving it, we accept its existence but deny that it influences prohibition, rather it influences disapproval. This is because it was possible for a child to come into existence at all through marrying a woman past childbearing age and the like, so it is more so possible for it to come into existence as a slave after being Muslim, since the primary purpose of procreation is to multiply those who affirm Allah, exalted is He, in His oneness and divinity, and what must be acknowledged of Him, and this is established through the Muslim child. Freedom beyond that is a perfection most of which pertains to a worldly matter. It is agreed that a slave may marry two slave women, although there is in that an exposure of the child to slavery at a point where it is unnecessary and there is no necessity; and the slave being a father has no effect on establishing the child's slavery, for if he marries a free woman, his child is free. The preventing factor is only understood as being the slavery itself, since it is what necessitates the deficiency which they made a prohibition, not together with the condition of the father's freedom. Therefore, if that reasoning were valid, slave and free would be equal in this ruling. This was stated by Ibn al-Humam, and there is some discussion in it, so consider it.

In this verse there is something that indicates the weakness of the Shi'a's use of the preceding verse as evidence for the permissibility of mut'a, because Allah, exalted is He, commanded in it to be content with marrying slave women when there is no means for marrying free women. Had He permitted mut'a in the preceding discourse, He would not have said after it: ﴿And whoever is not able﴾ etc., since mut'a in the case of the absence of the stated means is not deficient in fulfilling the need for intercourse; rather, by the rule that every new thing is more pleasurable, it would be more delightful and better. Moreover, mut'a is lighter in cost and less burdensome, since it is a matter for which a dirham or two suffices. What necessity then would call for marrying slave women?! By my life, saying so is an extremely far-fetched notion, as will not be hidden from one who has been freed from the noose of blind imitation.

﴿And Allah knows best your faith﴾ is a parenthetical clause, brought in to comfort their hearts and remove aversion from marrying slave women, by showing that the basis of distinction is faith, not lineage or ancestry, and many a slave woman's faith surpasses the faith of many free women.

The meaning is that He, exalted is He, knows better than you the degrees of your faith, which is the axis in both abodes, so let it be the aim of your attention. It was said that it was brought to indicate that outward faith suffices for the validity of marrying a slave woman, and that knowledge of faith need not be certain knowledge, since there is no way to comprehend realities except for the Knower of the unseen. ﴿You are of one another﴾ means you and your slave girls are alike, either in religion or in lineage. On the second view it is another parenthetical clause emphasizing comfort from another angle; on the first it is an explanation of their similarity in that respect following an explanation of their difference in it. Either way, (ba'duhum) is the subject, and the prepositional phrase is connected to an elided element functioning as its predicate. Some claimed that (ba'duhum) is the subject of the elided verb; it was said that in the statement there is inversion, and the intended meaning is: "let some of you marry some of the slave girls." But the noble Book of Allah should not be taken in that direction.

﴿So marry them with the permission of their people﴾ is consequent upon what precedes it, and therefore it is introduced with fa'. That is: when you have arrived at the clear matter, ﴿marry them﴾ etc. The command is repeated although it is understood from what precedes, for the added encouragement to marry them, or because what is understood from it is permission, whereas this is for obligation.

By "their people" (ahl) is meant their masters (al-mawali). The jurists interpreted this as one who has the authority to marry, even if not an owner. They said: the father, grandfather, judge and guardian have the right to marry off an orphan's slave woman. However, in al-Zahiriyya: if a guardian marries an orphan's slave woman to his own slave, it is not permitted. In Jami' al-Fusuliyyin: the judge has no right to marry off the slave woman of an absent person. In Fath al-Qadir: a partner in full partnership may marry off a slave woman, but a partner in limited partnership, a mudarib, or a licensed slave may not, according to Abu Hanifa and Muhammad; Abu Yusuf said they have that right. This permission is a condition for the permissibility of marrying a slave woman according to us, so marrying her without permission is not permitted. Impermissibility here means lack of enforceability, not lack of validity; rather it is suspended, like the contract of one acting without authority (fudul). Malik held this view, and it is a narration from Ahmad. The marriage of a slave also falls under this. They cited for the impermissibility in both cases what Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi transmitted from the hadith of Jabir, and al-Tirmidhi said it is a hasan hadith, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "Any slave who marries without the permission of his master is an adulterer (ahir)." Ahr means fornication, and it is interpreted as applying when he has intercourse, not merely by the contract; this is legal (shar'i) fornication, not juristic (fiqhi) fornication, so it does not entail the obligation of the prescribed punishment, since that is attached to juristic fornication, as explained in the branches of law. They also argued that enforcing the marriage of both involves causing them defect, since marriage is a defect for them, so they cannot undertake it except with the permission of their masters. It is attributed to Imam Malik, but not soundly, that he permitted a slave to marry without his master's permission, because he has the right to divorce, so he has the right to marry. This was answered by the distinction that divorce is the removal of a defect from himself, unlike marriage. Ibn al-Humam said: it may not be said that the slave's confession against himself regarding the prescribed punishment and retaliation is valid, although it involves his destruction, let alone causing him defect; because we say: what is subject to the divine address, commands and prohibitions, such as prayer, ritual washing, fasting, fornication, drinking and others, does not fall under the master's ownership, except where the Lawgiver is known to have dropped it from him, such as Friday prayer and Hajj. Then these rulings are required as a consequence of committing a prohibited act in the law; so the Lawgiver removed him from the master's ownership in that respect, in which He had placed him by a different consideration, as a deterrent against corruption and grave defects. End quote.

Some Hanafis claimed that the verse indicates that slave women may conclude the contract themselves, since the permission of masters is required, not their contracting. This was objected to: non-requirement does not necessitate requirement of absence, so perhaps the contracting party is the master or the agent, and therefore it does not necessarily follow that their contracting is permissible, as is not hidden. If the slave woman is jointly owned by two persons, for instance, her marriage is not permitted without the permission of all. In al-Zahiriyya: if one of two masters marries off his slave woman and the husband consummates with her, the other has the right to annul it; if he annuls it, he has half the proper dower, and the husband has the lesser of half the proper dower and half the stated dower. The ruling for a partially freed slave is the ruling for a fully enslaved one according to Imam al-A'zam (may Allah be pleased with him). According to the two disciples, his marriage is permitted without permission, since he is a free person in debt.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 25 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And give them their wages (ujur)﴾ means: pay them their dower (mahr, the marriage gift), with the permission of their guardians. This condition is omitted because it was mentioned earlier, not because coordination (ʿatf) requires the coordinated term to share the condition of the term it is coordinated with. It is possible that the sentence contains an elided noun, meaning "give to their guardians," and what preceded serves as an indication of it. It has been said, on the authority of some verifying scholars, that the reason for choosing "give them" (ātūhunna) over "give them" (ātūhum) despite the earlier mention of the guardians (ahl) is that it emphasizes the obligation of the dower and signals that it is their right in this respect, whereas the masters (mawālī) take it by way of ownership of the right hand (milk al-yamin). What drives all this is that, according to most jurists, the dower belongs to the master, since it is the compensation for his right.

Imam Malik said: the verse is to be taken at face value, and the dower belongs to the slave woman. This necessitates that the slave woman has ownership, although the slave (ʿabd) has no ownership. Therefore she must have a kind of possession of it, like the licensed slave (ʿabd al-mapplication) permitted to trade, because making her a spouse is a license for her. So it is obligatory to hand it over to them, as is the apparent meaning of the verse. If the wages are interpreted as maintenance (nafaqat), then there is no need to consider the estimation at the beginning or end, and likewise if the words of His exalted saying are interpreted in this way.

﴿in a fair manner﴾ means: in accordance with what is known by the Sharia regarding the permission of the masters. The fair manner (al-maʿruf) is connected grammatically to "give them" (ātūhunna). The meaning is: pay them without procrastination or harm. It may also be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while they are clothed in what is fair, not delayed. Or it may be connected to "marry them" (ankiḥūhunna), meaning: so marry them in the fair manner, that is, with the permission of their guardians and a dower of the like of their kind. ﴿chaste (muḥṣanāt)﴾ is a circumstantial clause, either from the object of "give them," in which case it means "married," or from the object of "marry them," in which case it means "chaste." Interpreting it as "Muslims" is permissible, especially according to the view of the majority who do not permit marrying a Scripturary slave woman. However, this condition was already mentioned in His saying: ﴿from your believing slave women﴾, so repeating it has little benefit. The well-known interpretation here is that muḥṣanāt means chaste. So His saying: ﴿not fornicating (musāfiḥāt)﴾ is an emphasis of it, and the meaning is: not openly committing adultery, as Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said. ﴿nor taking secret lovers (akhdān)﴾ is coordinated with "fornicating," and "nor" (walā) reinforces the negative sense contained in "not" (ghayr). Akhdān is the plural of khidn, which means companion. Here it refers to one whom a woman takes as a friend to commit adultery with her, and the plural is used for contrast. The meaning is: nor those who keep adultery secret.

In the pre-Islamic era, adultery was divided into the secret and the public. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that the people of the Jahiliyya used to forbid what was public, saying it was baseness, and would permit what was hidden, saying there was no harm in it. To forbid both kinds, His saying was revealed:
[Page 11]
﴿And do not approach the indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden﴾.

﴿Then when they are chaste (uḥṣinna)﴾ means: by marriage, as Ibn ʿAbbas and a group said. Ibrahim recited it as aḥṣanna, in the active voice, meaning: they guarded their private parts and their spouses. ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated that it was recited thus. Then he said: their chastity is their Islam. Many scholars held that on the first recitation too, the meaning of chastity is Islam and not marriage. Some who took it this way said: a slave woman is not punished for adultery unless she has married a free man. This is narrated as a view of Ibn ʿAbbas. It is also reported that there is no hadd (prescribed punishment) before marriage, from Mujahid and Tawus. Al-Zuhri said: in this context it means marriage.

The hadd is obligatory for a Muslim slave woman if she has not married, because of what is in the two Sahihs, from Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani, that the Prophet ﷺ was asked about a slave woman who commits adultery and is not chaste. He said: "Flog her; then if she commits it again, flog her; then if she commits it again, flog her; then sell her even for a braided rope." So a married slave woman is punished by the Qur'an, and the other by the Sunna. This interpretation is preferred because He, glorified is He, made Islam a condition with His saying: ﴿from your believing slave women﴾. Thus taking what is here to mean something else is more complete in benefit, although it is possible that it is an emphasis because of the length of the speech.

Some verifying scholars mentioned that interpreting chastity as Islam is evident according to the view of Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, because marrying a slave woman does not require that she be Muslim, and disbelievers are not addressed with the branches of law. This is problematic according to those among the Shafiʿis who hold the concept of the conditional implication (mafhum al-sharṭ), for it implies that a disbelieving slave woman who commits adultery is not flogged. That is not his position, for he establishes the hadd against disbelievers. ﴿If they commit an indecency (fāḥisha)﴾ means: if they do an indecency, which is adultery, and it is established. ﴿then upon them﴾ means: it is established upon them by the Sharia ﴿is half of what is upon the chaste (muḥṣanāt)﴾ means: the free virgins ﴿of the punishment (ʿadhāb)﴾ means: the hadd, which is one hundred lashes, so half of it is fifty. There is no stoning for them, because it cannot be halved. This is a rebuttal of the supposition that the hadd for them increases through marriage, which would cancel using this verse as evidence, and also of the view that they have no hadd before marriage, as was narrated from those mentioned earlier.

Al-Shihab said: From the explanation of their condition, the condition of slaves (ʿabid) is known by indication of the text. So there is no basis for what has been said, that this is contrary to what is customary, because it is customary for women to fall under the ruling for men by subordination. It seems the reason is that the motives for adultery are stronger in them. This is not an inclusion by domination and mention by way of subordination, so that what was mentioned would hold. The objection to the view of specification is that if it were so, it would not indicate the ruling for slaves. Rather, the reason is that the discussion concerns marrying slave women, so this is what the context requires. End of quote.

The apparent meaning is that what is known by indication of the text is the condition of male slaves when they commit an indecency, not in every respect, for the condition of male slaves is not the condition of slave women in the matter of marriage in every way, as explained in the books of jurisprudence. ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Mujahid that it was recited: ﴿If they (males) commit it, and they (females) commit an indecency﴾. This is the explanation. The fa' in "if they commit" is the answer to "when," and the second is the answer to "if." The second condition with its answer follows from the existence of the first. ﴿of the punishment﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase, and the governing element for it is the one governing its referent. Abu al-Baqa said: it cannot be a circumstantial clause from "what" (ma), because it is in the genitive by annexation, so there is no governing element for it.

﴿For whoever among you fears hardship (ʿanat)﴾ means: for whoever fears adultery because desire has overwhelmed him. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Nafiʿ ibn al-Azraq asked him about ʿanat. He said: sin. Nafiʿ said: Do the Arabs know that? He said: Yes, have you not heard the poet's saying:
[Page 12]
You see that you seek my hardship and strive
along with the one who runs against me without cause.

It was also said: the root of ʿanat is the breaking of a bone after it has been set, so it is used for every hardship and harm that befalls a person after his condition was sound. No harm is greater than falling into sins by committing the most vile abominations. From the speech of many lexicographers it is understood that it is literally used for sin, and likewise for exertion and hardship. From this comes ʿanūt, meaning a hill difficult to climb. Al-Zajjaj interpreted it here as ruin, but what most scholars hold is what was mentioned earlier, and this is also transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. It was also said that it refers to the hadd, because if he desires her he fears he will commit it and be punished. The first view is preferred because of the number of those who held it, along with the indication that what is befitting the state of a believer is fear of adultery that leads to punishment. In this there is an implication that what he fears is the hadd and not what makes it obligatory. Whichever is the case, it is another condition for the permissibility of marrying slave women according to al-Shafiʿi, may God have mercy on him. The school of the great Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, is that it is not a condition at all, but only guidance toward what is better. ﴿And that you be patient﴾ means: and your restraint from marrying slave women while being chaste.

﴿is better for you﴾ than marrying them, even though it has been permitted for you, because the masters' right over them is stronger, so they are not purely devoted to their husbands as free women are, since the masters can make use of them while traveling and at home, and sell them to those in town and in the desert. In this there is great hardship for the husbands, especially when children have been born to them from these women. Also, they are humiliated, degraded, and go out and come in, and this is abasement and disgrace that spreads to the one who marries them, and a jealous man can hardly bear that. Also, marrying them exposes the child to slavery.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and others narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "If a slave marries a free woman, he has freed half of himself; and if a free man marries a slave woman, he has enslaved half of himself." Saʿid ibn Mansur narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "The one who marries a slave woman has not turned away from adultery except a little." It is similarly narrated from Abu Hurayra and Ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Abi Shayba narrated from ʿAmir who said: "Marrying a slave woman is like carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine; it is not permitted except for one in dire necessity."

In the Musnad of al-Daylami and the Firdaws, from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Free women are the goodness of the house, and slave women are the ruin of the house."

The poet said:
Whoever does not have in his house a housekeeper,
that house is ruined, may you have no father.

Another said:
When there is no free woman in a man's house
to manage it, the affairs of his home are lost.

﴿And Allah is Forgiving﴾ means: abundant in forgiveness, so He forgives whoever does not restrain himself from marrying them. He expressed it this way to make it repugnant, as if it were a sin. ﴿Merciful﴾ means: abundant in mercy, and for this reason He permitted for you what He permitted.

* * *

Furthermore, among the allusive indications in some of the preceding verses: when He, glorified be He, said ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married﴾, He alluded to the prohibition of dealing with the lower (suflīyyāt) things, which are the mothers, in which the upper paternal (ʿulwiyya) forces have already acted, except what has passed of the divine arrangement in the pairing of spirits, for the necessities of perfections. Indeed, inclining toward the lower world calls down the hatred of the Truth, glorified be He.

And by the prohibition of the chaste women (muḥṣanāt), He alluded to the prohibition of matters toward which souls incline, meaning that the seeker should not desire a station that another has attained, while he has no capacity to attain it. From here the speech was met with a swoon when he (Moses) asked to see Allah, and the poet of the Muhammadan reality said:
I do not wish to return; you will never see Me, nor am I a mountain that the splitting should move me.
[Page 13]

And my master Ibn al-Farid said, speaking in her voice:
And when I ask you to see you in reality,
listen, and do not make my answer "you will never see."

And one of the veiled ones spoke well when he said:
If you cannot do something, leave it,
and pass beyond it to what you are able to do.

Al-Nisaburi said: The chaste women among the women of this lower world, Allah the Exalted made forbidden to the sincere among His servants, and He permitted for them, by His saying ﴿except what your right hands possess﴾, the handling of necessary matters such as food and drink, ﴿chaste (muḥṣinīn)﴾ meaning free from this world and what is in it, ﴿not fornicating﴾ in seeking the waters of faces. Then He commanded them, when they enjoy something of that, to render its rights of thankfulness, obedience, and remembrance, for example. The rest of the verses follow this pattern. However, I have not found clear understanding regarding the daughters, sisters, paternal aunts, maternal aunts, daughters of a brother, daughters of a sister, foster mothers, foster sisters, stepdaughters, and combining two sisters, that would open the heart and gladden the inner conscience. I have no doubt that Allah, the Exalted, has servants who know Him with true knowledge, but they are in the corners, and how many hidden things are in the corners. And Allah speaks the truth, and He guides to the path.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 26:

﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence that confirms what came before) that reaffirms the rulings already mentioned. This kind of construction occurs in early Arabic speech. The grammarians, as al-Shihab said, explained it in several ways. It was said that the object of "desires" is omitted, meaning the permitting of what He permitted and the forbidding of what He forbade, and similar. The lam here indicates purpose or consequence, meaning: this is for the sake of making clear. This view is attributed to Sibawayh and the majority of the Basran grammarians, so the desiring is distinct from the making clear. They adopted this because otherwise the verb would reach its object, which comes after it, by means of the lam, and that is either impossible or weak.

It was said that if emphasis is intended, this is permissible without weakness, and emphasis on the futurity that necessarily belongs to desire is intended here, but with regard to the connection (of the desire to the making clear). Otherwise, Allah's desire is eternal. The author of al-Lubab named this lam "the lam of completion" (lam al-takmilah) and set it in contrast with "the lam of transitivity" (lam al-ta'diyah).

Some Basran grammarians held that the verb is interpreted as a verbal noun without an intervening particle (sabk), as was said of the proverb: "Hearing of al-Mu'aydi is better than seeing him." On this view, the verbal noun is the subject, and the prepositional phrase is its predicate, meaning: My desire is for the purpose of making clear. This is strained.

The Kufan grammarians held that the lam itself is the particle that puts the verb in the subjunctive without the need for an implied "an" (that), and that the lam with what follows it is the object of the preceding verb. Their reason is that the lam may stand in place of "an" with verbs of desire and command. The Basrans reject this and say: the function of the lam is to govern in the genitive, and the subjunctive is produced by an implied "an" after it. On some of the views, the object of "yubayyina" (to make clear) is omitted, meaning: (to make clear to you) what is hidden from you of your welfare and of the excellent deeds, or what He has made you worship, or something similar.

It was permitted that the phrase "li-yubayyina" (to make clear) and His words ﴿and guide you﴾ both govern the phrase ﴿the ways of those before you﴾, meaning: the paths of those prophets and righteous people who came before you, so that you may follow their traces and pursue their conduct. The intended meaning is not that the ruling was the same for the earlier nations, as some have said. Rather, what is meant is that what has been mentioned is of the same kind as the ways of the rightly guided predecessors and of the same sort in making clear what is beneficial.

﴿and to turn to you in forgiveness﴾ is coordinated with what came before. Since repentance is the abandoning of sin together with regret and the resolve not to return to it, and since attributing this to Allah is impossible, the commentators interpreted it in this context in one of several ways.

It was said that repentance here means forgiveness, by metonymy (majaz), because forgiveness results from it. Or it means guidance toward what prevents sins, by metaphor of the subsequent kind (isti'arah tab'iyyah), because repentance prevents sins, just as His guidance does. Or it is a metaphor for His urging people toward it, because He is its cause, the reverse of the first. Or it means guidance toward what expiates it, also by way of comparison (tashbih). Al-Baydawi, Nasir al-Din, pointed to all of these.

The scholar al-Tibi established that this is the placing of the effect in the position of the cause. The verb "wa-yatuba" (and turn in forgiveness) is coordinated with "wa-yahdiyakum" (and guide you) as an explanatory sequence, as if it were said: "to make clear to you, to guide you, and to direct you to acts of obedience." So "wa-yatuba 'alaykum" was placed in its position. As for the objection, in some of the interpretations, that the purpose would differ from the desire, which is a complete cause, this is answered by the fact that the address is not general to all those obligated, but to a specific group in whom this repentance occurred.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾: exaggerated in knowledge of things. He knows what He has legislated for you of rulings, what the rightly guided people of earlier nations followed, and what benefits or harms His believing servants. ﴿All-Wise﴾: in all His actions He observes wisdom and benefit. So He makes clear to whom He wills, guides whom He wills, and turns in forgiveness to whom He wills. He is not questioned about what He does, while they will be questioned.

صفحة 14

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 27:

﴿And Allah wishes to turn (in forgiveness) to you.﴾ Some (scholars) have said that this is a repetition of what came before, for emphasis and intensification. This is evident if the meaning of "turning" (tawbah) is one and the same thing both here and there. But if "yatuba" is first interpreted as accepting repentance and guidance, for example, and second as doing what makes one deserving of acceptance, then it is not a repetition. Moreover, this only works out if (li-yubayyina lakum, "that He may make clear to you") is the object (of the verb), otherwise there is also no repetition; for the attachment of the will to turning in the first case is in the manner of causation (ʿillah), and in the second it is in the manner of objecthood (maf'uliyyah), and through this the difference inevitably arises.

﴿But those who follow their desires wish that you should deviate (into) a tremendous deviation.﴾ This means the wicked (fasaqah), because they go along with the desires of their own souls without restraining themselves from them. It is as if, by their immersion in them, the desires had commanded them to follow them, and they obeyed their command and followed them. This is a figurative (tamthiliyyah) metaphor. As for one who indulges in what the Sharia has permitted of them, and not otherwise, he is following the Sharia, not the desires.

This was related from Ibn Zayd. Mujahid narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that they are the fornicators (al-zunat). Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi that they are the Jews and the Christians. It has also been said that they are specifically the Jews, since they claimed that a paternal sister is lawful in the Torah. And it has been said that they are the Magians, since they used to permit marriage to sisters through one father, because they were not joined by a womb (rahim), and (permitted) daughters of a brother and of a sister by analogy with the daughters of a paternal aunt and maternal aunt, on the common ground that their mothers are not lawful. So they wished to lead the believers astray by what has been mentioned, saying: "Why did you permit those and not permit these?" Then (this verse) was revealed. The two sentences were separated (by the particle "wa" in some readings) in order to distinguish between the will of Allah, exalted is He, and the will of the deviators ﴿that you should incline﴾ away from the truth by agreeing with them, so that you become like them. And from Mujahid: that you commit fornication as they commit it.

It was also read with the yaʾ (third person, "they wish"), in which case the pronoun refers to those who follow the desires ﴿a tremendous inclination﴾, relative to the inclination of one who commits a sin rarely, acknowledges that it is a sin, and does not deem it permissible.

﴿Allah desires to lighten [the burden] for you﴾: that is, in the obligations concerning women and marriage, by permitting marriage to slave-women. This is the view of Tawus and Mujahid. It was also said that He lightens the obligations in general, for He has lightened for this Community what He did not lighten for other earlier nations. It was also said that He lightens [the burden] by accepting repentance and granting success in it. The clause is a new sentence (mustaʼnafah) with no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis).

﴿And man was created weak﴾: that is, in the matter of women, unable to be patient with them. This is the view of Tawus. In a report: "There is no good in women, and no patience toward them. They overcome the noble man, and the base man overcomes them. So I love to be a noble man who is overcome, and I do not love to be a base man who overcomes." It was also said: his desire and appetite sway him, and his fear and grief agitate him. It was also said: he is unable to oppose his desire and to bear the hardships of obedience. It was also said: he is weak in judgment, and does not perceive secrets and wisdoms except by a divine light.

It is related from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, that the intended meaning is weak in creation, pained by the least misfortune that befalls him. The weakness of the context in supporting these two meanings is not hidden, for the clause is an explanatory addition (i'tiraḍ tadhyīlī), brought to affirm what precedes it of lightening through the concession of marrying slave-women. The weakness of judgment or of physical constitution has no bearing on this. That it is an allusion to the ignorance of the Magians in their analogy based on the first of the two views is not worth considering.

"Weak" (ḍaʻīfan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). It was also said that it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, meaning "from weakness," and that by it is meant clay or the drop [of semen]. Both of these, as you see, are [weak views]. Ibn Abbas read: "and He created man," in the active voice, with the pronoun referring to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Al-Bayhaqi related in Shuʻab al-Iman from him that he said: Eight verses were revealed in Surat al-Nisa', which are better for this Community than everything upon which the sun rises and sets:

The first: ﴿Allah desires to make [things] clear to you and to guide you to the ways of those before you, and to turn to you in forgiveness. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾.

The second: ﴿And Allah desires to turn to you in forgiveness﴾, to its end.

The third: ﴿Allah desires to lighten [the burden] for you﴾, to its end.

The fourth: ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you to an honorable entrance﴾.

The fifth: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong [anyone] by the weight of an atom﴾.

The sixth: ﴿And whoever does wrong or wrongs himself, then seeks Allah's forgiveness, will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

The seventh: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating others with Him, but He forgives what is less than that﴾, to its end.

The eighth: ﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers and do not make distinction between any of them, those – He will give them their rewards﴾, the verse.

O you who believe, do not consume one another's wealth wrongfully (﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لا تَأْكُلُوا أمْوالَكم بَيْنَكم بِالباطِلِ﴾). This is an explanation of some of the prohibitions concerning wealth and persons, following the explanation of the prohibition of women in ways other than the lawful ones. It also indicates the great concern with the ruling mentioned. By "consuming" (al-akl) is meant all kinds of disposal of wealth, and it is expressed by it because it is the greatest of benefits. The meaning is: "Let none of you consume the wealth of another." By "wrongfully" (bil-batil) is meant what contradicts the Sharia, such as usury (riba), gambling (qimar), defrauding (bakhs), and injustice (zulm). This was said by al-Suddi, and it is also transmitted from al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him. And from al-Hasan: it is what is taken without entitlement by way of exchange.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him (al-Suddi? no, from al-Baqir/al-Hasan as above) and from Ikrimah that they both said: "A man would scruple to eat at the house of any of the people because of this verse, so that was abrogated (nusikha) by the verse in Surat al-Nur: ﴿nor upon yourselves that you eat from your houses﴾ (24:61), and so on." The first opinion is stronger, because what is eaten in the manner of noble conduct is not eating wrongfully. Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani transmitted with a sound chain from Ibn Mas'ud that he said concerning the verse: "It is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated); it has not been abrogated and will not be abrogated until the Day of Resurrection."

"Between you" (baynakum) is in the accusative either as an adverb of place (zarfiyya) or as a circumstantial qualifier (hāliyya) of "your wealth."

﴿Except that it be trade by mutual consent from you﴾ (illa an takuna tijaratan 'an taradin minkum). This is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati', an exception not of the same kind as what precedes). Abu al-Baqa' related the view that it is connected (muttasil) and rejected it. "From" ('an) is related to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of "trade," and "from you" (minkum) is a qualifier of "consent" (taradin). The meaning is: except that the trade be a trade proceeding from a consent that exists from you, or except that the wealth be wealth of trade. The accusative reading is that of the people of Kufa; the rest read it in the nominative, with "kana" (was/be) as a complete verb.

The summary of the meaning: Do not intend to consume wealth wrongfully; rather, intend that there be an occurrence (wuqu') of trade (by mutual consent). Or: do not consume it in that manner, for that is forbidden, whereas the existence of trade by mutual consent is not forbidden. Trade is singled out from among the other causes of ownership because it is the most frequent occurrence and the most suitable for people of honour. Al-Asbahani transmitted from Mu'adh ibn Jabal who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The best earnings are the earnings of merchants, who, when they speak, do not lie; when they promise, do not break it; when they are entrusted, do not betray; when they buy, do not disparage; when they sell, do not praise excessively; when they are owed, do not delay; and when they owe, do not make it difficult."

Sa'id ibn Mansur transmitted from Nu'aym ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Azdi who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Nine-tenths of provision is in trade, and the tenth is in livestock."

It is permissible that by it (trade) be meant the transfer of property from another by a lawful means, whether it be trade, inheritance, gift, or other than that, by the use of the specific to mean the general. It was also said: the intended prohibition is the prevention of spending wealth on what Allah the Exalted does not approve, and by trade is meant spending it on what He approves. This is more remote than what preceded it. By "mutual consent" (al-taradi) is meant the mutual satisfaction of the two parties to the sale with what they contracted upon at the time of offer and acceptance, according to us (the Hanafis), and according to Imam Malik; according to al-Shafi'i, it is at the time of separation from the contract session. It was also said: mutual consent is the option (takhyir) after the sale. Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Abu Zur'a that he sold a horse of his and said to his companion: "Choose," and he gave him the option three times; then he said to him: "Give me the option," and he gave him the option three times. Then he said: "I heard Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, say: 'This sale is by mutual consent.'"

﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ (wa la taqtulu anfusakum), that is, let not some of you kill others. The prohibited killing of one another is expressed by "selves" for the sake of emphasis in restraint. It has been reported in the hadith: "The believers are like a single soul." This is the view of al-Hasan, 'Ata', al-Suddi, and al-Jubba'i. It was also said: the meaning is: do not destroy yourselves by committing sins, such as eating wealth wrongfully and other disobediences, for which you deserve punishment. It was also said: what is meant is the prohibition of a person killing himself in a state of anger or distress; this is related from al-Balkhi.

It was also said: the meaning is: do not risk your selves in fighting, so that you fight those you cannot withstand. This was narrated from Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him. It was also said: what is meant is: do not trade in the lands of the enemy, lest you isolate yourselves; Malik used this as evidence for the disapproval of trade to the lands of war. It was also said: the meaning is: do not cast yourselves into destruction. This is supported by what Ahmad and Abu Dawud transmitted from 'Amr ibn al-'As, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) sent me in the year of Dhat al-Salasil, I had a wet dream on a night that was very cold, and I feared that if I bathed I would perish. So I performed tayammum and then led my companions in the dawn prayer. When I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), this was mentioned to him, and he said: 'O 'Amr, you led your companions in prayer while you were in a state of major impurity (janub)?' I said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah, I had a wet dream on a night that was very cold, and I feared that if I bathed I would perish, and I remembered His saying: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ (4:29), so I performed tayammum and then prayed.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laughed and said nothing."

'Ali, may Allah honour his face, read: (wa la tuqattilu), with the doubled letter for intensification (lil-taksir). The combination of the admonition to preserve wealth and the injunction to preserve the self is not hidden as being fitting, since wealth is the twin of the self, in that it is the cause of its sustenance, the attainment of its perfections, and the fulfilment of its virtues. The harmony between the two prohibitions, according to the view of Malik, is more complete. The first prohibition is mentioned first because of the frequency of encountering what it prohibits.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Merciful to you﴾ (inna Allaha kana bikum rahima). This is a reason (ta'lil) for the prohibition. The meaning is that He, the Exalted, has always been exceedingly merciful; and from His mercy to you is His prohibition of you from consuming the unlawful and destroying the selves. It was also said: its meaning is: indeed He has been merciful to you, O community of Muhammad, since He did not impose upon you the killing of selves in repentance, as He imposed that upon the Children of Israel.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 30:

﴿And whoever does that﴾ — i.e., the killing of a soul alone; or that together with what precedes it, namely devouring wealth falsely; or the totality of the prohibited acts mentioned earlier, from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion﴾; or from the beginning of the surah up to here. There are several opinions.

The first of these was narrated from ʿAṭāʾ, and it is perhaps the most apparent. The remoteness implied in the demonstrative (dhālika, "that") is an indication of the monstrousness of killing a soul and of its remoteness in rank in corruption. The use of the singular demonstrative, despite the plurality of what it refers to, is because it is interpreted as referring to what has preceded.

﴿Transgressively﴾ — i.e., excessively going beyond the limit. It is also read ʿidwānan with a kasra on the ʿayn. ﴿And wrongfully﴾ — i.e., committing an act for which one does not deserve [the consequence]. It has been said: both have the same meaning, and the conjunction is for explanation. It has also been said: by transgression is meant encroaching upon others, and by wrongdoing is meant wronging oneself by exposing it to punishment. Whichever it is, both are in the accusative, either as circumstantial qualifiers (ḥāl) or as causal (ʿilla). It has been said that inadvertence (sahw), error (ghalaṭ), and mistake (khaṭaʾ), and whatever its path is ijtihād (independent juristic reasoning) in legal rulings, are excluded by these two. ﴿Then We will cause him to enter the Fire﴾ — i.e., We will make him enter it and burn him with it. The clause is the response (jawāb) of the conditional.

Page 17
It is also read nuṣallīhi with tashdīd (doubled lām), and naṣlīhi with a fatḥa on the nūn from ṣallāhu, a dialectal form like aṣlāhu; and yuṣlīhi with the yāʾ (third-person), in which case the pronoun refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, or to that (the act), and the attribution is metaphorical, of the kind that attributes an effect to its cause.

﴿And that﴾ — i.e., his being made to burn in the Fire on the Day of Resurrection — ﴿is for Allah easy﴾ — effortless, with no preventer hindering Him from it, no repeller turning it away from Him, and no intercessor interceding for him except by His permission. The manifestation of the Glorious Name instead of a pronoun is by way of iltifāt (shift of grammatical person), to instill awe and to emphasize the independence of the concluding parenthetical statement (iʿtirāḍ tadhyīlī).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 31:

﴿If you avoid﴾, i.e., you keep away from, ﴿the major sins (kaba'ir) that you are forbidden﴾, i.e., that Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ) forbid you, i.e., from committing them, of those mentioned and of those not mentioned. It was also read as (kabir) in the singular, taken in the generic sense, which conforms to the well-known reading. It was said that it may be understood to refer to shirk (associating partners with Allah). ﴿We will remove﴾, i.e., We will forgive and erase. The choice of wording that indicates greatness, by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), is an exaltation of the magnitude of that forgiveness. It was also read as (yughfar), with the yaa' (third person). ﴿From you﴾, O those who avoid, ﴿your misdeeds (sayyi'at)﴾, i.e., your minor sins (saghair), as al-Suddi said. The scholars differed over the definition of the major sin (kabira) and gave several opinions:

The first: it is that for which its perpetrator is specifically threatened with severe punishment by an explicit text of the Book or the Sunnah. This was the view of some Shafi'is.

The second: it is every act of disobedience that makes the hadd (prescribed legal punishment) obligatory. This was the view of al-Baghawi and others.

The third: it is everything the Book explicitly prohibits, or for whose type a hadd is required.

The fourth: it is every transgression that indicates little concern on the part of its perpetrator for the religion and weakness of piety. This was the view of al-Imam.

The fifth: it is what makes the hadd obligatory or is subject to a threat of punishment. This was the view of al-Mawardi in his Fatawa.

The sixth: it is everything forbidden in its very essence, prohibited for a meaning inherent in itself. This was related with a detailed explanation, to be found in its proper place, from al-Halimi.

The seventh: it is every act that the Book explicitly prohibits using the word "prohibition" (tahrim).

Al-Wahidi said: The correct view is that the major sin has no limit by which the servants can recognize it; otherwise people would rush into the minor sins and make them lawful. Rather, Allah the Exalted concealed this from the servants so that they would strive to avoid everything forbidden, in the hope that the major sins would be avoided. A parallel to this is the concealment of the middle prayer (al-salat al-wusta), the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr), and the hour of acceptance of supplication. End of quotation.

Shaykh al-Islam al-Barizi said: The verified position is that a major sin is every sin that is accompanied by a threat, a hadd, or a curse in an explicit text of the Book or the Sunnah; or whose corruption is known to be like the corruption of what is accompanied by a threat, a hadd, or a curse, or greater than its corruption; or that indicates the perpetrator's negligence in his religion in the way the least of the explicitly mentioned major sins does, such as if one kills a person protected by sanctity and it then becomes evident that he deserved to be killed, or if one has intercourse with a woman thinking she was an adulteress with him but she turns out to be his wife or his slave-girl.

Some said: All the limits that have been mentioned were intended only as approximations, and otherwise they are not comprehensive definitions. How can one control what there is no hope of controlling? A group of scholars went to define them by counting rather than by a definitional limit. According to Ibn 'Abbas and others, they are what Allah the Exalted mentioned from the beginning of this surah up to this point. It was also said that they are seven, and this is supported by the report in the two Sahihs: "Avoid the seven destructive sins: associating partners with Allah the Exalted, sorcery, killing a soul which Allah the Exalted has forbidden except by right, consuming the property of orphans, consuming riba (usury), fleeing on the day of battle, and slandering chaste, believing, unwary women." In a narration of both of them: "The major sins are: associating partners with Allah the Exalted, sorcery, disobedience to parents, and killing a soul." Al-Bukhari added: "and the perjurious oath (al-yamin al-ghamus)." Muslim replaced it with: "and false speech." The answer is that this is understood to mean that the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned them intentionally to explain what was needed at the time of mention, not to restrict the major sins to them.

Among those who explicitly stated that the major sins are seven were 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, 'Ata', and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr.
