It was also said they are nine, based on what 'Ali ibn al-Ja'd transmitted from Ibn 'Umar, that when he was asked about the major sins he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'They are nine: associating partners with Allah the Exalted, slandering a chaste woman, killing a believing soul, fleeing from the battle line, sorcery, consuming riba, consuming the property of an orphan, disobedience to parents, and violating the sanctity of the Sacred House, your qibla, in life and in death.'"

It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that they are three, and from him also that they are ten, and it was said fourteen, and it was said fifteen, and it was said four. 'Abd al-Razzaq related from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked: "Are the major sins seven?" He said: "They are nearer to seventy." Ibn Jubayr related that he said to him: "They are nearer to seven hundred than to seven," except that there is no major sin with seeking forgiveness and no minor sin with persistence.

A group of the imams denied that there are minor sins among the sins. They said: rather, all acts of disobedience are major sins. Among them were Ustadh Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini, al-Qadi Abu Bakr al-Baqillani, Imam al-Haramayn in al-Irshad, and Ibn al-Qushayri in al-Murshid. Indeed, Ibn Furak related it from the Ash'aris and chose it in his tafsir, saying: "All of Allah the Exalted's acts of disobedience are major sins according to us; the terms minor and major are applied to some of them only in relative terms." He interpreted the verse in a way that its apparent meaning rejects. The Mu'tazila said: sins are of two kinds: minor and major. This is not correct. End of quotation.

It is sometimes claimed that there is consensus among the companions (al-ashab) on what was mentioned, and al-Taqi al-Subki relied on this. Al-Qadi 'Abd al-Wahhab said: It is not possible to say of an act of disobedience that it is minor, except in the sense that it becomes minor when the major sins are avoided. This statement is supported by what al-Tabarani related from Ibn 'Abbas, though it is disconnected (munqati'), that the major sins were mentioned in his presence and he said: "Everything that Allah the Exalted has forbidden is a major sin." In another narration: "Everything in which Allah the Exalted is disobeyed is a major sin." This was stated by the scholar Ibn Hajar, who mentioned that the majority of scholars hold to the division (into minor and major), and that there is no disagreement between the two camps regarding the meaning; the disagreement is only over the naming and the general application. This is because everyone agrees that acts of disobedience include those that impair uprightness (al-'adala) and those that do not. The earlier scholars (al-awwalun) avoided the naming, disliking to call disobedience to Allah the Exalted "minor," out of consideration for the greatness of Allah the Exalted and the severity of His punishment, and out of reverence for Him, Mighty and Majestic, against calling His disobedience minor, since, compared to the dazzling greatness of Allah the Exalted, it is major, and what a major sin it is. The majority did not consider this, because it is known. Rather, they divided sins into two categories, as the explicit verses and reports require, especially this verse. The meaning of "If you avoid major sins" being what you were forbidden in this surah of unlawful marriages, consuming property, and other things mentioned earlier, and "We will remove from you" being what was committed of them in the past, is very far-fetched. Likewise, a parallel in the revelation: "Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them," is far-fetched in the extreme.

For this reason, the Proof of Islam al-Ghazali said: It is not fitting to deny the distinction between minor and major sins, since both are known from the sources of the Shari'a. Yes, it may be said of a single sin that it is major and minor from two perspectives, because sins vary in this according to persons and circumstances. From here the poet said:

A high-ranking man does not belittle a small slip
in which there are excuses for a lowly person.

So the major sins of a small man are minor,
and the minor sins of a great man are major.

Sayyidi Ibn al-Farid, may Allah sanctify his secret, said:

Even if a desire for other than You
crossed my mind by mere heedlessness, I would judge myself an apostate.

Whoever alluded to this variation said: "The good deeds of the righteous are the misdeeds of those brought near (to Allah)."

That said, this verse has been found problematic together with what is in
[p. 19]
the hadith of Muslim, where the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The five prayers expiate what lies between them, as long as major sins are avoided." The difficulty is that if the prayers expiate, nothing remains for other things to expiate, and so the content of the verse is not realized. It has been answered with various responses, the soundest of which, according to al-Shihab, is that the verse and the hadith have one meaning, because his (ﷺ) saying "as long as ... is avoided" and so on indicates an explanation of the verse; for whoever does not pray has committed a major sin, and what a major sin it is. So reflect.

﴿And We will admit you to a noble entrance (mudkhal)﴾. The majority read the mim with a damma. Abu Ja'far and Nafi' read it with a fatha. The damma form is either a verbal noun (masdar), with the object of "We will admit you" omitted, meaning: We will admit you into the Garden with admission; or it is a place, accusative as an adverbial of place (zarf) according to Sibawayh, and as a direct object according to al-Akhfash. Likewise every place-noun after "entered" is subject to this disagreement. With the fatha form, it was said it is accusative by an implied verb, meaning: "We will admit you, so you enter an entrance," and its accusative is as already discussed. It was also permitted that it is like His saying: ﴿And He produced you from the earth as a growth (nabat)﴾. It was preferred to take it as a place, because it is described by His saying, Glorified and Exalted is He: ﴿noble (karim)﴾, i.e., good. The Glorious Qur'an has described a place with this word, for He, Glorified is He, said: ﴿and a noble station (maqam)﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 32:

﴿And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others.﴾ Al-Qaffal said: When Allah the Exalted forbade the believers from consuming one another's wealth falsely and from killing souls, He followed this with a prohibition against what leads to coveting their wealth. It was also said: He first forbade them from encroaching upon their wealth with their limbs, then from encroaching upon it with the heart through envy, so that their outward and inward deeds would be purified. The meaning, then, is: "do not wish for" what Allah has given some of you, and distinguished it "by it" over you, of wealth, standing, and everything in which rivalry takes place. For that is a distribution issued by the All-Wise, the All-Aware. Each of those who are given less must be content with what has been allotted to him, and must not wish for the portion of the one who has been favoured, nor envy him. For that resembles objecting to the One who perfected everything, made it firm, and governed the world with His far-reaching wisdom and ordered it.

"The most wrongful of Allah's creatures is the one who spends the night envious of the one who spends the night turning about in His blessings."

This interpretation was adopted by Ibn 'Abbas and Abu 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with them both). It has been related from them concerning the verse: "Let none of you say: 'Would that what Fulan was given of wealth, blessing, and a beautiful woman were mine!' For that would be envy. Rather, let him say: 'O Allah, give me the like of it.'" From this it is understood that the wish mentioned is a metonymy (kinaya) for envy. Some scholars made the reason for prohibiting it that it is a means (dhari'a) to envy. Each has its own direction.

Al-Balkhi claimed that the meaning is: it is not permissible for a man to wish that he were a woman, nor for a woman to wish that she were a man, because Allah the Exalted does only what is best, so he would be wishing for what is not best. Shaykh al-Islam related that when Allah made the male's share equal to the share of two females, the women said: "We are more in need of having two shares and men having one share, because we are weak and they are strong, and more capable of seeking livelihood than we are." So the verse was revealed. He then said: This is the most fitting explanation for the reason given for the prohibition in His words:

﴿For men there is a share of what they have earned, and for women there is a share of what they have earned.﴾ This is explicit in showing that the wishing occurs between the two groups of men and women. Perhaps the masculine form in the prohibition is used because the pronoun referring to the women is expressed by "some" (ba'd). The meaning is: for each of the two groups, in inheritance, there is a share of fixed quantity from what has fallen to it according to its capacity. He expressed this by "earning" (iktisab) in the manner of a sequential metaphor (isti'ara tab'iyya), based on a comparison that its state required between its share and its earning of it. This is to affirm that each of them deserves its share, and to strengthen its exclusivity, such that it does not overstep to another. For this is among the things that require refraining from the wishing mentioned. End of quotation.

This meaning he has given for the verse is related from Ibn 'Abbas. However, the report that he transmitted, following al-Zamakhshari, concerning the occasion of revelation, we have not found with any chain of transmission. What al-Wahidi mentioned on this matter are three reports:

The first: what he related from Mujahid, who said: "Umm Salama said: 'O Messenger of Allah, men go out to fight and we do not fight, and we only have half of the inheritance.' So Allah revealed the verse."

The second: what he related from 'Ikrima, that the women asked for jihad, saying: "We wish that Allah had made fighting for us, so that we might obtain the reward that men obtain." So it was revealed.

The third: what he related from Qatada and al-Suddi, who said: "When His words were revealed, ﴿For the male is the like of the share of two females,﴾ the men said: 'We hope to be favoured over women in our good deeds as we were favoured over them in inheritance, so that our reward will be double the reward of women.' And the women said: 'We hope that the burden upon us in the Hereafter will be half of what is upon men, just as we have half their share of inheritance in this world.' So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And do not wish for...﴾ to the end of it."

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned something similar in al-Durr al-Manthur. It is not hidden that the report he transmitted clearly carries the wish prohibited to be envy. The first and second reports that al-Wahidi related are not like that, since upon them it is permissible to take it as envy, or as what is a means to it. It may appear that understanding it according to the second is more evident when considering both of them. As for the third report, the meaning of the verse rejects it, whether the wishing is a metonymy for envy or a means to it, except with a very far-fetched strain. The meaning of the verse according to the first two is that each of the men and the women has a share of reward according to what Allah the Exalted has imposed upon them of acts of obedience, through His excellent arrangement. So do not wish for what contradicts this arrangement.

This is related from Qatada. In it, the use of iktisab for good is found, though it is also used for evil, and kasb is used for good in His words: ﴿For it is what it has earned, and against it is what it has merited.﴾ It is also related from Muqatil and Abu Jarir that they said: "What is meant by 'what they have earned' is the sin they have earned." In this case there is the use of the preposition lam with evil rather than 'ala, which contradicts what is in the verse. It was also said: what is meant is: "for each," and upon each of the two groups there is an amount of reward and punishment according to what the Wise has ordained for their actions. However, this view dispensed with lam in place of 'ala, and with iktisab in place of kasb. This is, as you see, far-fetched. What refutes these meanings is that the noble composition does not support them, since it is connected with inheritance and the excellences of men. Perhaps those who adopt them consider the verse a parenthetical insertion.

Some have mentioned that the meaning of the verse according to the first view related from Abu 'Abd Allah and Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them) is that each group of men and women has a share determined from eternity in the world's bounties, through trade, agriculture, and other means of earning. So let them not wish for what has been allotted to them otherwise.

﴿And ask Allah of His bounty.﴾ This is coordinated with the prohibition after establishing the cessation by the reasoning, as if it were said: "Do not wish for the share of others, and do not envy those who have been favoured over you, and ask Allah the Exalted for His abundant grace and His multiplied favour, for His treasuries are full and never run out." The object is omitted to indicate generality, meaning: ask for whatever you wish, for He, glorified is He, will give it to you if He wills. Or, because it is known from the context, meaning: ask for its like. This is called ghibta. It was also said: min (of) is extra, meaning: ask Allah the Exalted for His bounty. It has been reported in a hadith: «Let none of you wish for the wealth of his brother, but let him say: "O Allah, provide for me, O Allah, give me its like."» Some scholars, as in al-Bahr, went to the prohibition of wishing for the like of another's blessing, even without wishing for its removal, because that blessing may be corrupting for him in his religion and harmful to him in his worldly life. So it is not permissible for him to say: "O Allah, give me a house like the house of Fulan, nor a spouse like his spouse." Rather, he should say: "O Allah, give me what will be good for me in my religion, my worldly life, my return, and my livelihood," and not refer to the one who has been favoured over him.

This has been attributed to the careful scholars (al-muhaqqiqun), and they are refuted by the hadith, unless they do not accept its authenticity. It was also said: the meaning is: do not wish for the world, but ask Allah the Exalted for the worship that brings you near to Him. Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Sirin took this view. Ibn al-Mundhir related from the second that when he heard a man wishing for the world, he would say: "Allah the Exalted has forbidden you from this," and recite the verse. The apparent meaning is generality. And from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: «Ask Allah the Exalted of His bounty, for Allah the Exalted loves to be asked, and among the best of worship is waiting for relief.» Ibn 'Uyayna said: He, glorified is He, only commanded asking so that He might give. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing.﴾ For this reason He favoured some people over others according to the degrees of their capacities and the differences in their receptivities.

It may be that the meaning is that He, the Exalted, has always been and still is Knowing of everything, so He knows what you conceal of envy and will requite you for it,

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 4, verse 33:**

﴿And for every one We have appointed heirs (mawali) of what the parents and the nearest relatives leave behind.﴾ The phrase "for every one" requires the supplying of a genitive noun (mudaf ilayhi), meaning: for every person, or for every people, or for every property or estate. On this basis, al-Shihab (may Allah illuminate his resting place) mentioned several possibilities:

**The first:** On the first supposition, the meaning is: For every person who is inherited from, We have appointed heirs (mawali), i.e., inheritors, of what he left behind. Here the sentence is complete. Thus "of what he left behind" is connected to "heirs" (mawali), or to an implied verb, and "mawali" is the first object of "ja'ala" (appointed), in the sense of "sayyara" (made), while "li-kull" ("for every one") is its second object. It was placed before it to emphasize comprehensiveness and to dispel the assumption that the appointing applies to some but not others. The subject of "taraka" (left behind) is the pronoun referring to "kull" (every one). "Al-walidan" ("the parents") is in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, as though it were said: "Who are the heirs?" and it was answered: "They are the parents and the nearest relatives."

**The second:** The supposition is: For every person who is inherited from, We have appointed inheritors of what that person left behind. Then that person is specified by His words: "al-walidan" (the parents), as though it were said: "Who is this inherited-from person?" and it was answered: "the parents and the nearest relatives." Its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is as before, except that the difference between the two is that "the parents and the nearest relatives" in the first are inheritors, while in the second they are the ones inherited from. On these two readings, the statement consists of two sentences.

**The third:** The supposition is: For every inheritor of what "the parents and the nearest relatives" left behind, We have appointed heirs, i.e., those who are inherited, so "mawla" means the one who is inherited. "Al-walidan" is in the nominative, governed by "taraka" (left behind), and "ma" is in the sense of "min" (from). The preposition-phrase is a qualifier of "ma," to which "kull" is added as a genitive. The statement is one single sentence.

**The fourth:** On the second supposition, the meaning is: For a people whom We have made "heirs" (mawali), there is a share of what their parents and relatives left behind. Thus "li-kull" is the predicate of an implied "nasib" (share), placed after it. "Ja'alnahum" (We made them) is a qualifier of "qawm" (people), and the returning pronoun is the omitted pronoun which is the object of "ja'ala." "Mawali" is either a second object or a circumstantial state (hal). "Mimma taraka" is a qualifier of the omitted subject, whose qualifier remains like the qualifier of the genitive noun, and the returning pronoun is omitted from it.

A parallel to this is your saying: "For everyone whom Allah the Exalted has created as a human being, from the provision of Allah the Exalted", i.e., for each one whom Allah the Exalted has created as a human being, there is a share from the provision of Allah the Exalted.

**The fifth:** On the third supposition, the meaning is: For every property or estate ("mimma taraka al-walidan wal-aqrabun" – of what the parents and the nearest relatives left behind), We have appointed heirs, i.e., inheritors who take charge of it and possess it. "Li-kull" is connected to "ja'ala," and "mimma taraka" is a qualifier of "kull."

It has been objected to the first and second that in them the noble structure of the verse is broken up, and that "mawla" seems originally to be a noun of place rather than an adjective, so how can "min" be a relative complement to it? It was answered that this is because it includes the meaning of a verb, as has been indicated. Moreover, that "mawla" is not an adjective contradicts the words of al-Raghib, for he said that it has the meaning of the active and passive participle, i.e., "al-mawali" and "al-mawla." However, the pattern maf'al for an adjective has been rejected by some people, and Ibn al-Hajib said in his commentary on al-Mufassal that it is rare. So either it is classed as a rare usage, or it is a case where an adjective is expressed by a noun of place figuratively, because it is firmly established and settled in what it describes. It is also possible to class it under the usage of "al-majlis al-sami" (the exalted assembly, a form of honorific address).

The third has been objected to as being far-fetched, and the fourth on the grounds that it involves omitting a subject described by a preposition-phrase and placing that phrase in its position, which is rare; and that for every people among the heirs there is the whole of what the parents and relatives left behind, not a share, since the share belongs to each individual.

As for the first objection, it was answered that this usage is established despite its rarity, as in His words: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ and ﴿And among us are those beneath that﴾.

*(Page 22)*

As for the second, it was answered that what the people deserve is only part of the estate, because the expenses of burial, debts and bequests take precedence, if there are any. As for taking "min" to be explanatory of the omitted element, that is very far-fetched.

Al-Shihab criticized the answer to the first objection on two grounds:

First, the example cited is no evidence for it, because the grammarians have established that when a qualifier is a sentence or an adverbial phrase, it may take the place of the noun it qualifies, on condition that the noun qualified is part of what precedes it governed by "min" or "fi." Otherwise, it may stand in its place only in poetry. What was cited falls under this rule, but the verse does not.

Second, the intended meaning of its standing in its place is not that it is literally a subject; rather, the subject is omitted, and its explanation is as indicated in the exposition. So there is no basis for regarding it as far-fetched. Yes, what they stated, though well known, is not accepted without question, for Ibn Malik explicitly disagreed with it in al-Tawdih, and he permitted omitting the qualified noun in ordinary usage without that condition. So the truth is that it is a general tendency, not an absolute rule.

The fifth has been objected to on the ground that it involves separating the qualifier from the qualified by a clause that governs the qualified, as in: "With every man I passed a Tamimi." Its permissibility is questionable. It was answered that it is permissible, as in His words: ﴿Say: Shall I take other than Allah as a protector, the Originator of the heavens and the earth?﴾ Here "Originator" (fatir) is a qualifier of the divine name, and it is separated from it by "atakhidhu" (shall I take), which governs "ghayr" (other than). So this is more appropriate. As for the answer that the governing word was not interposed, but rather the governed element was moved forward, so that the interposition arose from that, and thus it is not weakened, since the governed element ought to come after its governor, then the qualified noun would be connected with its qualifier in an artificial way, which is unnecessary.

A group of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) preferred this fifth and the one before it, and they considered the sentence to be an independent sentence confirming what precedes it. They objected to the first supposition on the ground that it excludes the children, because they are not included among "the nearest relatives" by common usage, just as the parents are not included among them. If the lexical meaning is intended, it includes both parents. It was answered that this objection is shared by all readings. Moreover, it has been answered that the children are omitted because their circumstances are clear from the verses on inheritance, just as the spouses are omitted for the same reason; or that the parents are mentioned for their nobility and to indicate concern for their affairs, so there is no harm from this aspect. Reflect.

**﴿And those whom your oaths have bound﴾** are the "mawali al-muwalah" (clients by alliance).

Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Qatada, who said: In the pre-Islamic period a man would make a covenant with another man, saying: "My blood is your blood, my ruin is your ruin; you inherit from me and I inherit from you; you seek vengeance for me and I seek vengeance for you." So he was given a sixth of all the property in Islam, and then the heirs would divide their inheritance. Then that was abrogated (naskh) later in Surah al-Anfal by His words: ﴿And those of blood relationship are more entitled to one another﴾.

This was also narrated by various routes from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), and likewise from others. The school of Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) holds that if a man embraces Islam at the hand of another man, and they make a contract that the one will inherit from the other and pay his blood-money (aql) on his behalf, it is valid; the other is then obliged to pay his blood-money, and he is entitled to inherit from him if the latter has no heirs at all. The report of the abrogation mentioned does not stand as proof against this position, since there is no indication in what is claimed as abrogating that the ally does not inherit, especially since he inherits only when there are no agnatic heirs (asabat) or relatives by blood (ulu al-arham).

Here "al-aymanu" is the plural of "yamin" (right hand), and the attribution of the "contract" (aqd) to it is because they used to place their hands in agreements; or it means "oath." That "aqd" here means the marriage contract is contrary to the apparent meaning, since its attribution to the right hand is not known in that usage.

The Kufans read "'aqadat" without an alif, and the rest read "'aqadat" with an alif. It was also read with shaddah. In all the readings the object is omitted, meaning "their covenants" ('uhudahum). The omission is gradual so that the omitted returning pronoun is in the accusative, as is most common and regular. There are several possibilities of i'rab for the relative clause:

**The first:** That it is the subject, and the sentence ﴿then give them their share﴾ is its predicate; the "fa" was added because the subject includes the sense of a conditional.

**The second:** That it is in the accusative by "ishtighal" (the verb being occupied with a pronoun), and it was said that it should preferably be the chosen construction, so that a command does not fall as a predicate; but they did not choose it, because such a construction rarely occurs except in exclusive contexts, and that is not appropriate here. It was objected that, "Zaydan darabtuhu" (Zayd, I struck him) – if the governing verb is supposed to be after it, it conveys exclusivity; if it is supposed to be before it, it does not convey that. And there is no doubt that the apparent supposition is that it is before, so exclusivity does not follow.

**The third:** That it is conjoined to "al-walidan" (the parents). If it is meant that they are inherited from, then the pronoun in "fa-atuhum" returns to "mawali"; and if it is meant that they are inheritors, then it is permissible for it to return either to "mawali" or to "the parents" and what is conjoined with them. It was said that the stopping at "al-aqrabun" (the relatives) and not at "aymanukum" (your oaths) is a well-known pause, which weakens this.

**The fourth:** That it is in the accusative by conjunction with "mawali," and this is far-fetched.

In a report from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), recorded by al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and a group, he said concerning the verse: "When the emigrants (muhajirun) came to Medina, the emigrant would inherit from the Ansari (helper) to the exclusion of his blood relatives, because of the brotherhood which the Prophet (ﷺ) established between them. Then when ﴿And for every one We have appointed heirs﴾ was revealed, this was abrogated. Then He said: ﴿And those whom your oaths have bound, then give them their share﴾ – of assistance, support and counsel – and inheritance has gone, but a bequest may be made to him." It was also narrated from Mujahid something similar. The apparent meaning of this is that the conjunction is not permissible, for whoever conjoins it intends: "Then give them their share of inheritance."

**﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, Witness﴾**, i.e., He, glorified is He, has never ceased to be knowing of all things, aware of them, whether manifest or hidden. So He is aware of the giving and the withholding, and He recompenses each of the one who withholds and the one who gives according to his action. Thus in general there is both promise and warning.

﴿Men are in charge of women﴾, that is, it is their role to be in charge of them, like the authority of rulers over subjects in commanding and forbidding and the like. The choice of the nominal sentence together with the intensive form (qawwamun) indicates their firm establishment and deep rootedness in the attribute ascribed to them. The statement also alludes to the reason men deserve the greater share in inheritance, just as the preceding verse hints at the differing degrees of entitlement. He, glorified is He, grounded the ruling in two matters, one bestowed and one earned, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿because Allah has made some of them excel over others﴾. The bā' (because of) denotes causation, and it is connected to (qawwamun) just as ʿalā is. There is no objection at all. It is also permitted that it be connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of its pronoun, and the bā' is then causal or denotes accompaniment, and mā is a verbal noun (maṣdariyya). The plural pronoun refers to both groups by way of predominance. That is: they are in charge of them because Allah, exalted is He, has given them preference over them, or they deserve this because of the preference, or they are characterised by the preference. He turned away from the pronoun, so He did not say, "because Allah has given them preference over them," to indicate that the matter is so evident that there is no need to state explicitly the one preferred and the one over whom preference is given. It was also said that the vagueness is intended to point out that some women are better than many men, but this is not valid. Likewise, He, glorified is He, did not state what the preference consists of, as an allusion that it is too clear to require detail.

It has been reported that women are deficient in intellect and religion, and men are the opposite of them, as is well known. For this reason, men alone were given prophethood and messengership according to the most well-known view, as well as the great and lesser imamate, the establishing of the rites such as the call to prayer, the iqama, the sermon, the Friday prayer, and the takbirs of tashriq according to our greatest Imam, the exclusive right to divorce and to marriage according to the Shafi'is, testimony in major matters, the extra share in inheritance, and ta'sib (the status of residual heir), and other things besides.

﴿and because they spend of their wealth﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it, so the bā' is connected to what the first bā' is connected to. Mā is either a verbal noun or a relative pronoun whose returning pronoun is omitted. Min is either partitive or initial, connected to (anfaqu) or to an omitted element occurring as a state of the omitted returning pronoun. By "what is spent," as Mujahid said, is meant the dower. It is also permitted that what is meant by what they spent be what includes it and the maintenance of women.

The verse, as narrated from Muqatil, was revealed concerning Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' ibn 'Amr, who was one of the nuqaba' (chiefs), and concerning his wife Habiba bint Zayd ibn Abi Zuhayr, because she rebelled against him, and he struck her. Her father set out with her to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said, "I gave my noble daughter to him as a spouse, and he struck her." The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Let her take retribution from her husband." So she left with her father to take retribution from him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Return, for this is Jibril (peace be upon him), who came to me and Allah revealed this verse," and he recited it. Then he said, "We desired one thing and Allah desired another, and what Allah desired is better."

Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' and his wife Khawla bint Muhammad ibn Maslama, and he mentioned the story. Some of them said: it was revealed concerning Jamila bint 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and her husband Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, and something close to it was mentioned.

The verse was cited as evidence that the husband has the right to discipline his wife and to prevent her from going out, and that she must obey him except in disobedience to Allah, exalted is He. In a report: "If I were to order anyone to prostrate to anyone, I would order the woman to prostrate to her husband."

It was also cited as evidence by those who permit annulling the marriage when the husband is unable to provide maintenance and clothing. This is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i, because when he ceases to be her qawwam (one in charge of her), he has departed from the purpose intended by marriage. According to us, there is no annulment, because of His saying: ﴿and if someone is in difficulty, then let there be respite until a time of ease﴾.

It was also cited as evidence by those who held that the husband has the right of restraint (hajr) over his wife concerning her person and her property, so she may not dispose of it except with his permission, because He, glorified is He, made the man qawwam using the intensive form, and qawwam means one who watches over a thing and guards it.

﴿So the righteous women﴾, that is, among them, ﴿are obedient﴾: this begins the detailing of their conditions and the manner of being in charge of them according to the differences in their circumstances. The meaning is: the righteous among them are obedient to Allah, exalted is He, and to their husbands. ﴿guarding in the absence [of their husbands]﴾, that is, they guard themselves and their chastity in their husbands' absence. Al-Thawri and Qatada said: or they guard in their husbands' absence what must be guarded regarding the self and property. So the lam is in the sense of fi (in), and al-ghayb is in the sense of al-ghayba (absence), and the alif-lam is a substitute for the genitive complement according to one opinion. It is also permitted that what is meant is: guarding what is obligatory in the absence, that is, what they must guard during the absence, so the lam retains its literal sense. It was also said that what is meant is: guarding the secrets of their husbands, that is, what occurs between them and their wives in privacy, including rivalry, quarrelling, and the slap mentioned in the report, and in that case there is no need for what was said about the lam, nor for interpreting al-ghayb as absence. However, what Ibn Jarir, al-Bayhaqi, and others reported from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The best of women is she who, when you look at her, pleases you, when you order her, she obeys you, and when you are absent from her, she guards you in your property and in herself." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾ up to ﴿guarding in the absence﴾. This weakens this view, and some people claimed that it is more suitable given the occasion of revelation.

﴿by what Allah has guarded﴾, that is: by what Allah, exalted is He, has guarded for them in their dowers and in obligating their husbands to maintain them. This was said by al-Zajjaj. It was also said: by Allah's guarding of them and His protection of them, and had Allah not guarded and protected them, they would not have guarded. So mā is either a relative pronoun or a verbal noun. Abu Ja'far read (bi-mā ḥafiẓa Allāha) with the accusative, and on this reading an omitted noun must be supposed, such as "the religion of Allah" or "the right of Allah," because no one can guard His essence. Mā is either a relative or a descriptive pronoun. Several scholars rejected its being a verbal noun, because ḥafiẓa would then lack an agent, since it should have been said: "by what Allah guarded them." It was answered that its agent may be a singular pronoun referring back to the plural of females, since it has the sense of a genus, as if it were said: "so from the guarding of Allah." Ibn Jinni treated it like the poet's saying: "Verily the calamities have destroyed them." Yet the strain of this is not hidden, and the omission of the feminine marker, and the like of it, does not befit the noble text, as is not hidden. Furthermore, the sound plural form here indicates multitude. As for the definite, it is evident, and as for the indefinite, it is because it is treated as the definite, so it must agree with it in multitude, otherwise it would not apply to all its instances. This has been explicitly stated in al-Durr al-Masun.

Ibn Mas'ud read: (fa-al-ṣawāliḥu qawāniqu ḥawāfiẓu lil-ghayb bi-mā ḥafiẓa Allāhu fa-aṣliḥū ilayhinna), and Ibn Jarir reported from him the addition (fa-aṣliḥū ilayhinna) alone.

﴿And those [women] from whom you fear rebellion﴾, that is, their rising above obeying you and their disobedience to you. Nushuz, with the shin either vowelled with a sukun or a fatha, is an elevated place, and it can mean elevation. ﴿admonish them﴾, that is, advise them, and say to them: "Fear Allah, and return from what you are upon." The apparent meaning of the verse is that this is ordered upon the fear of rebellion, even if it has not occurred, for otherwise it would have said "who rebel," and perhaps this is not intended. For this reason, al-Tayseer glossed (takhāfūna) as (taʿlamūna, you know), and al-Farra' said so too, as al-Tabarsi quoted from him, and fear is used in this sense, as in the Qamus. It was also said that what is intended is: you fear the continuation of their rebellion or its furthest degree, such as fleeing from them in bed.

Al-Bahr chose that there is an omitted element in the speech, and its origin is: "And those from whom you fear rebellion and who have rebelled, then admonish them," and this is an address to husbands and guidance to them on the way of being in charge of them. ﴿and forsake them in the beds﴾, that is, the places of lying down. The meaning is: leave them alone separately in their beds, so do not let them under the covers, and do not make physical contact with them, so the statement is a metaphor for abstaining from intercourse with them. Ibn Jubayr adopted this view. It was also said: what is intended is: forsake them in the bed by turning your backs to them in it, and do not turn to them. This was reported from Abu Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, and perhaps it is also a metaphor for abstaining from intercourse. It was also said: al-madajiʿ means the places of sleeping, that is: forsake their rooms and the place where they sleep. It was also said: fi is causal, that is: forsake them because of the beds, that is, because of their avoidance of lying together. This is what Ibn 'Abbas's statement indicates, in what Ibn Abi Shayba reported from him through Abu al-Duha. Thus abandonment (hijran) in this sense is with speech, and 'Ikrima said: by speaking to her harshly. Some claimed that the meaning is: compel them to intercourse and bind them, from "hajara al-ba'ir" when he tied the camel with a halter rope (hijar). Al-Zamakhshari criticised this, saying that it is an interpretation of the dull-witted. Ibn al-Munir said: perhaps this interpretation is supported by His saying: ﴿then if they obey you﴾, for it indicates a prior compulsion in some matter, and the context of the beds points to its being intercourse. Al-Zamakhshari's excessive censure of this interpreter is [thus unwarranted], end of quote.

I think that if this were presented to al-Zamakhshari, he would have placed its proponent in the same category as that interpreter, and would have considered leaving it out to be negligence. It was also read as (fi al-muḍṭajaʿ) and (al-maḍja').

﴿and strike them﴾, meaning a blow that is not severe, as Ibn Jarir reported from Hajjaj, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The non-severe blow was explained as one that does not cut flesh or break a bone. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it is striking with a siwak (tooth-stick) or the like.

What the context and the rational indication show is that these three matters are sequential: when a woman's rebellion is feared, she is admonished, then forsaken, then struck, since if the order were reversed, the stronger would make the weaker unnecessary. Otherwise, the conjunction wa does not indicate sequence, and likewise the fa in (fa-ʿiẓūhunna) does not indicate more than the sequence of the whole. So the claim that it is the clearest evidence for sequence is not evident. In al-Kashf: the sequence is derived from the conjunction of parts that differ in severity and weakness, arranged under one comprehensive command, for the text itself is what indicates the sequence.

Furthermore, some of our companions stated that the husband may strike his wife for four matters, and what is equivalent to the four: neglecting adornment when the husband desires her, refusing to respond when he calls her to his bed, neglecting prayer (according to one report), neglecting ritual washing, and going out of the house except for a legitimate excuse.

It was also said: he may strike her whenever she angers him. It is related from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, that she said: "I was the fourth of four women with al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam, may Allah be pleased with him, and whenever he became angry with one of us, he would strike her with a tent-pole until he broke it upon her." It is not hidden that bearing the harm of women and patience with them is better than striking them, except for a strong reason. Ibn Sa'd and al-Bayhaqi reported from Umm Kulthum bint al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "Men were forbidden to strike women, then they complained of them to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he let men have their way in striking them. Then he said: 'Your best will never strike.'"

Al-Sha'rani, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned that when a man strikes his wife, he should not hasten to have intercourse with her after the striking. It seems he derived this from what al-Shaykhan and a group reported from 'Abd Allah ibn Zam'a, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Does one of you strike his wife as a slave is struck, and then have intercourse with her at the end of the day?"

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 4, verse 34 (part 2 of 2):

Abd al-Razzaq narrated from ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, with the wording: "Does not one of you feel shame that he beats his wife as a slave is beaten, beating her at the beginning of the day and then lying with her at its end?" There is another possible understanding of the report, which is not hidden.

﴿Then if they obey you﴾, i.e., if they agree with you and submit to what Allah, exalted is He, has made obligatory upon them of obedience to you in this matter, as is the apparent meaning, ﴿then do not seek a way against them﴾, i.e., do not seek a means or path to transgress against them, or do not wrong them by any way whatsoever, whether by verbal reproach, physical harm, or otherwise, and treat what has passed from them as if it had not occurred. Thus, "al-baghy" may mean "seeking" (talab), with "sabilan" as its object and the prepositional phrase "ʿalayhinna" connected to it; or it may be a modifier of the indefinite noun ("sabilan") placed before it. Or it may mean "wronging" (zulm), with "sabilan" in the accusative by the removal of the preposition. It is reported from Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah that the intended meaning is: do not burden them with love. The sum of the meaning is: when their outward conduct is upright for you, do not find fault with them for what is in their inward selves.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted and Great﴾, so beware of Him; for His power over you is greater than your power over those under your hands among them. Or, He, exalted is He, despite the loftiness of His station and the perfection of His essence, overlooks your misdeeds and turns to you when you repent; so you too should overlook the misdeeds of your wives and pardon them when they repent. Or, He, exalted is He, is able to take vengeance upon you and is not pleased with anyone's wronging; or, He, glorified is He, despite His absolute loftiness and majesty, has not burdened you except with what you can bear; so likewise do not burden them except with what they can bear.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 35:

﴿And if you fear a breach between the two⦆ The address is, as Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and others said, directed to the rulers (hukkam). It comes in a form that builds the command upon an unstated supposition, to indicate that this is something that should not be presumed to occur, namely the non-compliance (ʿadm al-iṭāʿa). It has also been said that the address is to the people of the two spouses, or to the spouses themselves; this was narrated from al-Suddi. The meaning is: "If you know," as Ibn ʿAbbas said, or: "If you suspect," as has been said.

﴿a breach between them⦆ That is, between the two spouses. Although they are not explicitly mentioned, they are implicitly present, since the word nushuz (disobedience), which is the wife's disobedience to her husband, and the men and women upon whom it falls, indicate them. The shiqaq (breach) is opposition and enmity. Its derivation is from shiqq (side), because each of two opponents is on a side other than the side of the other. The word bayn (between) is among the spatial adverbs of place, whose usage is limited. Its annexation to shiqaq is either to treat the adverb as if it were an object, as in his saying: "O thief of the night, the people of the house," or as if it were a subject, as in their saying: "He fasted his day." The original phrasing is "shiqaqan baynahuma," meaning that one of them opposes the other. Because of the association between the adverb and what it contains, it was placed in the position of a subject or object and was likened to one of them; then it was treated in its annexation as such. It has also been said that the annexation is in the sense of "in" (fi). It has also been said that bayn here means the connection existing between the spouses, namely companionship (muʿashara), and that it is not an adverb. The statement of Abu al-Baqaʾ points to this, but the verifying scholars did not approve of it.

﴿So send⦆ That is: direct and dispatch, to the spouses, for the reconciliation of their situation, ﴿an arbiter (ḥakam)⦆ that is, a just man, knowledgeable, of good judgment and insight into achieving the benefit ﴿from his family⦆ that is, the husband's. The phrase "from" (min) is either connected to "send," in which case it indicates the starting point, or it is connected to an omitted element that functions as a qualifier of the indefinite noun, in which case it is partitive. ﴿And an arbiter⦆ another, in the same description as the first, ﴿from her family⦆ that is, the wife's. The family is specified because they are more inclined to reconciliation and better acquainted with the inner state of affairs; the soul is at rest with them, so they become aware of what is in the heart of each of love, hatred, intention, and companionship or separation. This is by way of recommendation (istihbab). If they are chosen from strangers, it is permissible. It has been disputed whether the two arbiters have the authority to unite or separate if they see fit. It has been said: they do, and this was reported from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, and Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and one of two reports from Ibn Jubayr, and al-Shaʿbi said the same. Al-Shafiʿi related in al-Imam, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan, and others, from ʿUbayda al-Salmani, who said: A man and a woman came to ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, and each of them had a group of people with them. ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, ordered them to send an arbiter from his family and an arbiter from her family. Then he said to the two arbiters: "Do you know what is incumbent upon you? If you see that you should reconcile, reconcile; and if you see that you should separate, separate." The woman said: "I am content with the Book of Allah, the Exalted, with what is upon me and what is mine in it." The man said: "As for separation, no." ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, said: "You have lied, by Allah, until you acknowledge the like of what she acknowledged."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said concerning this verse, "And if you fear..." etc.: this is about the man and the woman when what is between them has deteriorated. Allah commanded that they send a righteous man from the man's family and a man like him from the woman's family, and they look at which of them is the wrongdoer. If the husband is the wrongdoer, they prevent him from his wife and compel him to provide maintenance; if the wife is the wrongdoer, they compel her to her husband and prevent her from maintenance. If their decision agrees upon separating or uniting, then their decision is permissible. If they see fit to unite, and one spouse is pleased while the other dislikes it, and then one of them dies, the one who was pleased inherits from the one who disliked it, and the one who disliked does not inherit from the one who was pleased. It has also been said: they have no such authority; this was reported from al-Hasan.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and others related from him that he said: The two arbiters are only sent to reconcile, and to bear witness against the wrongdoer for his wrongdoing; as for separation, it is not in their hands. Al-Zajjaj went to this view, and it was attributed to the Great Imam (Abu Hanifa). The action of ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, was answered by saying that he was an imam, and an imam may do what he sees as beneficial; perhaps he saw the benefit in what was mentioned, so he delegated the two arbiters to act as they saw fit. Moreover, his statement contains what indicates that the execution of the command is conditional upon consent, since he said to the man: "You have lied until you acknowledge the like of what she acknowledged."

You know that this, for all that it contains, is not suitable as an answer to what was reported from Ibn ʿAbbas; perhaps the matter is one of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning), and the statement of one mujtahid is not a proof against another. The Imamiyya went to the view of al-Hasan, and it seems that the report from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, was not established for them.

From al-Shafiʿi there are two reports on the matter, and from Malik that the two may effect a khul (separation by the wife's compensation) if they find it beneficial. It has been transmitted from some of our scholars that if the wrongdoing is from the husband, they separate the two, and if it is from the wife, they separate them in exchange for part of what she was given as dower. The apparent view is that whoever holds that their ruling is executed made them agents (wakilan) who judge by that.

Ibn al-ʿArabi said in al-Ahkam: They are judges, not agents, for the term ḥakam is a technical name in the Shariʿa for them.

﴿If they intend⦆ that is, the two arbiters, ﴿reconciliation⦆ that is, between the spouses, and harmony, ﴿Allah will bring about agreement between them⦆ so that their word is united and their aim is achieved. The pronoun here also refers to the two arbiters, and this was the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi.

It is permissible that both pronouns refer to the spouses: that is, if they intend to reconcile what lies between them of breach, Allah will create between them affection and accord. It is also permissible that the first refers to the arbiters and the second to the spouses: that is, if they intend to reconcile the situation and their intention is sound and their hearts are sincere for the sake of Allah, Allah, glorified is He, will create between the spouses affection and love, and place in their souls agreement and companionship. And it is permissible that the first refers to the spouses and the second to the arbiters: that is, if the spouses desire reconciliation and agreement, Allah, exalted is His majesty, will bring about agreement between the arbiters so that they act with righteousness and seek it.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing, Acquainted⦆ with the apparent and the hidden, so He knows the intentions of the servants, their benefits, and all their circumstances. The scholar Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, used this verse as evidence against the Kharijites in their denial of arbitration (tahkim) in the story of ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, which is one of three matters that had taken root in their minds, and he refuted them all, may Allah be pleased with him. Twenty thousand of them returned to the side of the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah ennoble his face.

And in it, as Ibn al-Furs said:
A refutation of those among the Malikis who denied sending two arbiters for the spouses, and who said: the woman goes out to the house of a trustworthy person, or a trustworthy person stays with her.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 36:

﴿Worship God and associate nothing with Him.﴾ This is a fresh statement, brought to guide toward qualities that comprise the highest matters, following the guidance given to each of the two spouses toward good treatment and the removal of enmity and harshness should they arise between them. It also affirms the observance of the right of marriage and teaches how to deal with all kinds of people. The command concerning the rights of God, exalted is He, is placed first, because those are the greatest foundation. This also contains an allusion to the elevated standing of what has been arranged in that same string. Worship is the utmost degree of submission. And "shay'an" (anything) is either a direct object, meaning: do not associate with Him anything at all of things, whether an idol or otherwise, so the tanwin here is for generalization.

Isam al-Din (Isam al-Din) preferred that it be for belittlement, so that there would be a severe rebuke, meaning: do not associate with Him anything insignificant, given that His greatness is boundless, since everything in comparison to the greatness of Him, glory be to Him, is the most insignificant of the insignificant. The relation of the possible to the Necessary Being is farther than the relation of the non-existent to the existent, since the non-existent is the possibility of the existent. Where is possibility from necessity? They are two opposites, separated by the greatest separation. Or it is a verbal noun, meaning: do not associate with Him, exalted is His station, from association (ishrak), openly or secretly. The prohibition against associating is conjoined to the command to worship, although refraining from association is necessary for worship under this interpretation, since the utmost submission cannot be conceived for one who has a partner. The submission to One who has no partner is greater than the submission to one who has a partner. The prohibition against association is for that which the Law made the sign of the utmost submission, or it is a rebuke with utmost ignorance, since they do not perceive this necessity. Thus it has been said. But the clearer view may be that this prohibition is an indication of the command to sincerity, as if it were said: "Worship God, sincere to Him." This reverts, as the Imam pointed out, to the fact that He, glory be to Him, first commanded what includes monotheism and other acts of the heart and limbs, then followed it with what is understood from it as monotheism, which God, exalted is He, does not accept any deed without. So the conjunction is of the type of conjoining the specific to the general.

﴿And to parents, good treatment.﴾ That is: and be good to both of them, good treatment. So the prepositional phrase is attached to a verb understood. It is permitted that it be attached to the verbal noun. It is placed first for emphasis. "Ahsana" (to be good to) is transitive with bi, ila, and li. It has been said that it is transitive with bi only when it implies the meaning of kindness (atf).

The good treatment commanded is that one attends to their service, does not raise one's voice over them, does not speak harshly to them, and strives to achieve their needs and spend upon them according to one's capacity. The completion of the discussion regarding them will come, God willing, exalted is He.

﴿And to the near of kin.﴾ That is: to the companion by kinship, such as brother, paternal uncle, maternal uncle, and the children of each, and the like. The preposition bi is repeated here and was not repeated in al-Baqarah. Al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) said: because this is a charge to this community, it was given care and emphasis, and that was for the Children of Israel.

﴿And orphans and the needy﴾ from among strangers, ﴿and the neighbor who is near﴾ that is: the one whose neighborhood is near, ﴿and the neighbor who is far﴾ that is: the distant, from janabah (remoteness), the opposite of kinship. This meaning is spatial. It may be that by "the neighbor who is near" is intended one who, together with neighborhood, has nearness and connection by lineage or religion, and by "the neighbor who is far" is intended one who has no kinship, even if he is a polytheist.

Abu Nu'aym and al-Bazzar narrated from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abdullah, and in it is weakness, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Neighbors are of three kinds: a neighbor who has three rights: the right of neighborhood, the right of kinship, and the right of Islam; a neighbor who has two rights: the right of neighborhood and the right of Islam; and a neighbor who has one right: the right of neighborhood, and he is the polytheist from among the People of the Book."

And al-Bukhari narrated in al-Adab (al-Adab al-Mufrad), from Abdullah ibn Umar, that a sheep was slaughtered for him, and he began saying to his servant: "Did you send a gift to our Jewish neighbor? Did you send a gift to our Jewish neighbor? I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'Jibril ceaselessly enjoined me concerning the neighbor, until I thought he would make him an heir.'"

Page 29

The apparent view is that the basis of neighborhood is custom. It is narrated from al-Hasan, as in al-Adab, that he was asked about the neighbor and said: forty houses in front of him, and forty behind him, and forty to his right, and forty to his left. The like of it is narrated from al-Zuhri. It has been said: forty cubits. One begins with the nearest and then the nearest. From Aisha, may God be pleased with her, she said: "I said: 'O Messenger of God, I have two neighbors, to which of them should I send a gift?' He said: 'To the one whose door is nearer to you.'" It was also read: "wal-jara dha al-qurba" (and the neighbor who is near) in the accusative, meaning: and I single out the neighbor. In this is an admonition concerning the greatness of the right of the neighbor.

The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Abu Shurayh al-Khuza'i that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him be good to his neighbor." What Abdullah heard suffices. The two Shaykhs and Ahmad also narrated it from the hadith of Aisha, may God be pleased with her.

﴿And the companion at the side﴾, and he is the companion on a journey, or the one who attaches himself to you hoping for your benefit and gift. Both opinions are from Ibn Abbas. It has been said: the companion in a good matter, such as learning, trade, craft, or travel. They counted among this the one who sits beside you in a mosque or assembly and the like, of any lesser companionship that unites you and him. A group found this view good because of its generality.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ali, may God ennoble his face: "The companion at the side is the woman." The neighbor (al-jar) is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial state of the companion, and the governing element of it is the understood verb. ﴿And the wayfarer﴾, and he is the traveler or the guest.

﴿And those whom your right hands possess.﴾ Muqatil said: from your male slaves and your female slaves. He, may God bless him and grant him peace, used to enjoin concerning them often. Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Anas, who said: "The most general of the will of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), when death came upon him, was: 'The prayer, and those whom your right hands possess,' until he began to gurgle them in his chest, and his tongue could hardly express them." Then the good treatment toward these categories varies in levels, according to what befits each and what is fitting.

﴿Indeed God does not love one who is self-conceited﴾, that is: one who has arrogance and pride, who disdains his relatives and neighbors, for example, and does not turn to them, ﴿boastful﴾, who counts his virtues over them, out of haughtiness and self-magnification. The sentence is a reason for the preceding command.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas who said: "I was with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he recited this verse: 'Indeed God...' etc., and he mentioned pride and magnified it, so Thabit wept. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: 'What makes you weep?' He said: 'O Messenger of God, indeed I love beauty, to the extent that it pleases me that the strap of my sandal be fine.' He said: 'You are among the people of Paradise. Indeed, it is not pride that you beautify your riding beast and your saddle, but pride is one who belittles the truth and looks down upon people.'" The reports on this subject are numerous.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 37:

﴿Those who are stingy and enjoin stinginess upon people﴾ In it there are several grammatical possibilities (i'rab):

The first: it is a substitute (badal) for (man) in the sense of a substitute of the whole from the whole (badal kull min kull).

The second: it is an attributive (sifah) of it, according to the view of those who permit a relative clause (mawsul) to be described (mawsuf), a view held by al-Zajjaj.

The third: it is in the accusative (nasb) by way of censure (dhamm).

The fourth: it is in the nominative (raf') by way of censure.

The fifth: it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), i.e., "they are the ones who."

The sixth: it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, i.e., "they are hated," or "they deserve every reproach," and similar to that, which is taken from the context. The predicate was omitted so that the listener's mind may go every way, and its estimation after the completion of the relative clause is preferable.

The seventh: it is, as Abu al-Baqa' said, a subject (mubtada'), with (alladhina) coming later being conjoined to it, and the predicate being (inna Allah la yazlim), in the sense of: He does not wrong them. This is very far-fetched.

Al-Tibi distinguished between its being a predicate and its being a subject, saying that on the first it is connected to what precedes it, because this is of the kind of their attributes by which they are known, and on the second it is disconnected, brought for the explanation of their conditions. He mentioned that the preferred view is connection, and he elaborated at length on it.

Regarding al-bukhl (stinginess) there are four dialectal readings (lughat):

Opening of the kha' and the ba', and with it Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read.

Vowelling both with damma, and with it al-Hasan and Isa ibn Umar read.

Opening of the ba' and sukun of the kha', and with it Qatadah read.

Damma of the ba' and sukun of the kha', and with it the majority (al-Jumhur) read.

﴿And they conceal what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾ i.e., of wealth and riches, or of His attributes, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him.

﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾ i.e., We have prepared that for them. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun, to indicate that whoever has this condition is a disbeliever in the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, and whoever is a disbeliever in His blessings, for him is a punishment that humiliates him, just as he humiliated the blessings by stinginess and concealment. It is also permissible to take disbelief in its literal sense. The pronoun of majesty (damir al-ta'zim) was mentioned for the sake of awe, because the punishment of the Great is great, and the anger of the Forbearing is grave. The clause is a concluding parenthetical insertion (i'tiraq tadhyili), confirming what precedes it.

The occasion of revelation of the verse is what Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated with a sound chain, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Kardam ibn Zayd, the ally of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and Usamah ibn Habib, and Nafi' ibn Abi Nafi', and Bahri ibn 'Amr, and Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut used to come to men of the Ansar, advising them sincerely, and they would say to them: 'Do not spend your wealth, for we fear poverty for you in its loss, and do not hasten in spending, for you do not know what will happen.' So Allah, the Exalted, revealed: ﴿Those who are stingy﴾ up to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And Allah was ever Knowing of them﴾."

It is also said: it was revealed concerning those who concealed the description of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others. Abd ibn Humayd and others narrated from Qatadah that he said concerning the verse: "They are the enemies of Allah, the People of the Book, who were stingy with the right of Allah upon them, and concealed Islam and Muhammad (ﷺ), while they find him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel."

According to this narration, stinginess is apparent as stinginess with wealth, and Ibn Jubayr stated this in one of the two narrations from him; in the other narration, it is stinginess with knowledge. Their commanding people to it, i.e., their followers to it, may be understood literally, and may be understood figuratively, treating them as those who command it because of their knowledge of their followers' obedience to them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 38:

﴿And those who spend their wealth to be seen by people﴾ means: for boasting and for what people say, not for the sake of God, the Mighty, the Exalted. The relative clause (al-mawsul) is coordinated (ʿatf) with its counterpart, or with "the disbelievers." They are associated with them in blame and threat because stinginess (bukhl) and extravagance (israf), which is spending not in the proper manner, are two extremes, one of excess and one of deficiency, and they are equal in ugliness and in drawing blame. It is also permissible that it be a new sentence (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is omitted, meaning: their companion is Satan, as the following statement indicates.

رِئاءَ (riʾaʾa) is a verbal noun (masdar) in the accusative, functioning as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun in يُنْفِقُونَ (yunfiqun). Its genitive construction (idafa) to النّاسَ (al-nas) is an idafa of the verbal noun to its object, meaning: showing off to people.

﴿And they do not believe in God﴾, who is able to reward and punish, ﴿nor in the Last Day﴾ on which the obedient are rewarded and the disobedient are punished. They intend by their spending what its branches bear leaves for and what its fruit is gathered from. They are the Jews, as is related from Mujahid, or the polytheists of Mecca, or the hypocrites, as has been said.

﴿And whoever has Satan﴾, by which is meant Iblis and his helpers, both those within and those outside his tribe, and the people who follow him, or the carnal faculties and desire, and the company of evil people, or the soul and the animal faculties, and the devils of mankind and jinn, ﴿as a companion﴾, that is, a friend and intimate in this world, ﴿then evil is he﴾, that is, how wretched is the Satan or the companion.

﴿as a companion﴾ because he calls him to disobedience that leads to the Fire. سَاءَ (saʾa) has been transferred to the category of نِعْمَ (niʿma) and بِئْسَ (biʾsa), the verbs of praise and blame (bab niʿma wa biʾsa), so it is treated as a rigid (non-inflecting) verb, which is why it is joined with the فاء (fa). It is possible that it remains in its original sense, with قَدْ (qad) implied, as in His words, glorified is He: ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed, their faces will be overturned into the Fire﴾ (27:90). The purpose of this sentence is to alert that Satan is their companion, and so he led them to that and adorned it for them. It is also permissible that it is a threat to them, that Satan will be joined with them on the Day of Resurrection in the Fire, and they will curse and hate one another, and regret will stand over them upon a leg.

[Page 31]

And what would it have cost them ﴿وماذا عَلَيْهِمْ﴾? That is: what harm or loss would befall them?

﴿لَوْ آمَنُوا بِاللَّهِ واليَوْمِ الآخِرِ وأنْفَقُوا﴾ "Had they believed in God and the Last Day and spent," on those among the groups mentioned, seeking the Face of God, as the context indicates and the discourse implies, ﴿مِمّا رَزَقَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ "out of what God had provided them" of wealth. The intent is not to ask about the harm that results from belief and from spending in the way of God, as the apparent sense would suggest, since there is no harm in that for which they could be questioned. Rather, the intent is to rebuke them for their ignorance of where the benefit lies and for their belief in a thing contrary to what it is, and to urge them to turn their thought toward reaching the answer, which may lead them to knowledge of what is in that, which is more beneficial than the splitting of the staff (of community). It also serves to alert them that one who is called to a matter that involves no harm should respond out of caution, so how much more so when benefits flow from it! This is a wonderful stylistic device, which the Arabs often used in their speech. Among that is the saying of one who said:

*What harm would it have done you had you bestowed a favor? Indeed a young man may bestow it while he is furious and enraged.*

In the statement there is also a refutation of the Jabriyya (the determinist school), since such a phrase is not said to one who has no choice and no effect at all on the act. Do you not see that one who says to the blind man, "What would it cost you had you been sighted?" or to the short man, "What would it cost you had you been tall?" is rebuking him for what he dislikes?

Those who hold that the faith of the muqallid (one who follows authority without independent proof) is valid also cited this verse, since it indicates that faith is extremely easy, and if independent reasoning (istidlal) were obligatory, it would be extremely difficult. It was answered, after granting the indication, that the difficulty lies in the details, which are not obligatory, whereas the proofs in summary form are easy, and these are what is obligatory. The ﴿لَوْ﴾ (law, "had") is either on its own usage, and the statement is understood according to its meaning, i.e., had they believed, it would not have harmed them; or it has the meaning of *an* (the verbal particle), as Abu al-Baqa' said. In both cases there is no new, independent sentence (isti'naf).

It has also been permitted that the clause be a new, independent sentence whose response is implied, i.e., happiness would have been theirs, or something similar. Faith is mentioned first here and placed later in the preceding verse, because there the discourse concerns the explanation of what preceded, namely their placing their expenditures in their worldly life in other than their proper place, whereas here the purpose is exhortation, so one should begin with what is most important and then what is next. Had it been said that faith is delayed there and spending is placed first, because that spending was in the sense of extravagance, which is the counterpart of stinginess, so faith was delayed lest it come between the two counterparts, that would have a valid basis, especially if we adopt the view of conjunction (ʿatf).

﴿وكانَ اللَّهُ بِهِمْ عَلِيمًا﴾ "And God is ever Knowing of them": a statement that carries a threat and an alert to the evil of their inner states, and that He, exalted is He, is aware of what they concealed within themselves, and will requite them for it. It was also said that it contains an indication of His, exalted is He, reward for them had they believed and spent. There is no harm in taking it to mean "He is knowing of them" and of their actual and hypothetical conditions, so that He punishes for the first and rewards for the second, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 40:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong (anyone) by an atom's weight﴾. Al-mithqal (the weight) is on the pattern mif'al, from ath-thiql (heaviness). It is applied to a known measure which, as has been said, did not differ in the Jahiliyyah and in Islam. It is, as Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, twenty-four qirat, and it is also applied to measure in general, which is what is meant here. For this reason al-Suddi said: that is, the weight of an atom (dharrah), which is the small red ant that is barely seen.

This was also reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd. And from the first (al-Suddi) it is also reported that it is the head of an ant. Also from him, that he put his hand in the dust, then blew on it, and said: each one of these is an atom (dharrah). Close to this is what has been said: that it is a part of the particles of dust seen in a sunbeam through a window. It has also been said: it is the mustard seed. What supports the first view is what Ibn Abi Dawud related in al-Masahif, through the chain of 'Ata', from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he recited: (mithqala namlah) (the weight of an ant).

He, glory be to Him, did not mention the atom to restrict the ruling to it, but because it is the smallest thing that enters human imagination, or because it is the most frequently used expression when describing smallness. He, glory be to Him, did not express it by "measure" or the like, but expressed it by "mithqal" to point to what is understood from it of heaviness, by which greatness and magnitude are expressed, as in His saying: ﴿As for him whose scales are heavy﴾. Yet although it is insignificant, it is great in terms of its unit.

Its accusative case is either as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), like the object: that is, wronging in the amount of an atom's weight, so the verbal noun and its adjective are omitted and the genitive noun that follows is put in their place. Or it is a second object of (yazlimu): that is, He does not wrong anyone, or does not wrong them by an atom's weight.

Al-Samin said: It seems they took (yazlimu) to include the meaning of "seizes" or "diminishes", so they made it transitive to two objects.

Al-Raghib mentioned that wronging, according to the lexicographers, is placing a thing in other than its proper place, whether by deficiency, by excess, or by deviating from its time or place. Accordingly, the statement contains an indication that the diminishing of reward and the increasing of punishment do not occur from Him, the Exalted, at all. In this there is an exhortation to faith and to spending, and indeed a guidance that everything He has commanded is something that should be done, and everything He has forbidden is something that should be avoided.

The Mu'tazilah used the verse to argue that wronging is possible in itself, but that He, exalted is He, does not do it because it is impossible in wisdom, not because it is impossible in power. For He, glory be to Him, praised Himself for abandoning it, and there is no praise for abandoning an ugly act unless it is from ability. Do you not see that the impotent man is not praised for abstaining from fornication? This was objected to by His saying: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾, for it is mentioned in the context of praise, although sleep is not possible for Him, glory be to Him. In al-Kashf it is said: This is not a valid objection, for it is praise for the negation of deficiency from His sanctified essence, and it is like saying: the Creator, exalted and high, is neither a body nor an accident. As for what we are dealing with, it is praise for abandoning an act, and abandonment is praiseworthy only when it is by choice. Yes, the opponent may refuse to concede that He, exalted, was praised for abandonment, but rather (the praise is) from the standpoint of indicating deficiency, because necessity of existence contradicts the permissibility of being characterized by wronging. Its verification according to their school is that placing a thing in other than its rightful place is possible in itself, and the power of the Truth, majestic is His affair, encompasses all possibilities, but wisdom, which is bringing the possible in a manner of perfection and as it should be, prevents it. On this basis they said: the wise does not do except the good among the possibilities, unless a need compels him, and the one free from needs, the Gathering, exalted above doing ugliness. We say: He, mighty is His name, neither diminishes from the reward nor increases in punishment, based on His binding promise, for breaking the promise is impossible in Him, since it is a deficiency contrary to divinity and perfect self-sufficiency. In this sense it may be called wronging, though wronging in the true sense cannot be conceived from Him, exalted, because He is the absolute Owner. So increase and decrease are possible in themselves, and breaking the promise is impossible in itself. That breaking the promise is impossible in itself with respect to the Necessary Being does not entail that its object is likewise, exalted and sanctified is He. This is similar to what has been established in the question of obligation to the impossible: that Allah's report about the non-faith of the persistent disbeliever, and the necessity of the truth that accompanies it, does not take the act out of being within the capacity of the obligated person, rather it confirms His power over it. So let this be retained, for it is important.

﴿And if it is a good deed﴾. The hidden pronoun in the defective verb refers to (mithqal). It was made feminine in consideration of the meaning, because it is in the sense of (and if the weight of an atom is a good deed). It has also been said: because the genitive noun may acquire the feminine from the noun it is attached to when it is part of it, as in the line: "as the spear's shaft was reddened with blood." Or it is an adjective of it, as in (no soul will benefit from its faith) in the reading of the one who read with the upper ta'. The quantity of a thing is an adjective of it, just as faith is an adjective of the soul. It has also been said: the pronoun was made feminine because the predicate is feminine. It was objected that the feminine predicate is only for agreement with the feminine subject, so if the subject's femininity were due to it, it would be circular. It was answered that this is when its being an attribute is intended, but (hasanah) has come to be dominated by nounhood, so it is joined to the solid nouns for which agreement is not observed, as in: "the speech is the sentence."
