Its admitting of good is in the meaning of "give us respite and look upon us," or "wait for us, and we will speak to you." Its admitting of evil is by taking it as an insult. In **al-Taysir**: "**Ra'ina**" itself is one of the words they use to revile each other, and it is for describing someone as foolish. It was also said that it resembles an insulting word among them in Hebrew or Syriac, which is **ra'īnā**. It was also said: rather, they lengthened the vowel of the kasra on the 'ayn, and meant, may Allah curse them, that he (and far be it from him, ﷺ) is in the position of their servants and the shepherds of their flocks. They used to say this while showing respect and reverence, while concealing what makes them deserve Hell, "and wretched is the destination."

This is a kind of hypocrisy, and it is not contradicted by their explicit statement of disobedience, because it was said that all the disbelievers address the Prophet (ﷺ) with disbelief, but they do not address him with insult, blame, or curse against him, upon him be prayers and peace. It was objected: in that case there is no reason to mention the hearing and disobedience together with the distortion and the throwing of ambiguous speech as a stratagem. It was answered: it may be said that the intention in this view is to enumerate their blameworthy attributes, not merely the distortion and stratagem. So it is as if it were said: they distort their Book, and openly deny the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ).

It was also said: their saying "we hear and we disobey" was not in his presence, upon him be prayers and peace, but was among themselves, so it does not contradict their hypocrisy in the two statements in his presence (ﷺ).

It was also said: the statement, regarding the first clause, is circumstantial (ḥālī), and regarding the last two clauses, verbal (lisānī). It was also said that the first is also two-faced like the last two, since it may be that what they mean is: "We obey your command and disobey the command of our people," and it may be that what they mean is what has already been stated.

Some people permitted that the distortion of words means inclining them away from their places, whether those were places that Allah the Exalted placed them in, or places that the context and custom have made suitable for them. Then the meaning is: they are a people whose custom is distortion, and His saying, glory be to Him, **"and they say"** (﴿وَيَقُولُونَ﴾) and so on, is an enumeration of some of their distortions. What is meant is: they say to you, "We hear," and among their own people they say, "We disobey," and they say such and such, so they show you one thing and conceal its opposite.

**"Twisting their tongues"** (﴿لَيًّا بِألْسِنَتِهِمْ﴾). **Layy** may mean turning, deviating, or bending from one direction to another, and it may mean folding one strand of a rope over another.

Its meaning here is either diverting the speech from the side of good to the side of evil, or joining one of the two matters to the other. Its root is **lawā**, the waw was changed to a yā' and assimilated. Its accusative is as an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu) of **"they say"** (﴿يَقُولُونَ﴾), considering its connection to the last two statements. It was also said that it is connected to all the statements. Or it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning: "twisting." Similar to it is His saying, the Exalted: **"and slander against the religion"** (﴿وَطَعْنًا في الدِّينِ﴾), meaning: disparagement of it by mockery and ridicule. Each of the two adverbial phrases is connected to what is nearest to it.

**"And if they had"** (﴿وَلَوْ أنَّهُمْ﴾), when they heard something of the commands and prohibitions of Allah the Exalted, **"said"** (﴿قالُوا﴾) by verbal speech, as is apparent, or with it and with the tongue of the state, as has been said, **"we hear"** (﴿سَمِعْنا﴾) with the hearing of acceptance, in place of their saying "we hear" which means the hearing of rejection, **"and we obey"** (﴿وَأطَعْنا﴾), in place of their saying "we disobey," and **"hear"** (**isma'**), in place of their saying "hear, without being heard."

**"And look upon us"** (﴿وَانْظُرْنا﴾), in place of their saying **"ra'ina"** (﴿راعِنا﴾), **"it would have been better for them"** (﴿لَكانَ خَيْرًا لَهُمْ﴾), and more beneficial than their saying that, **"and more upright"** (﴿وَأقْوَمَ﴾), meaning: more just in itself. The comparative form is either on its own pattern, with the basic meaning of the verb considered in the comparison, on the basis of their belief, or by way of sarcasm (tahakkum). Or it has the meaning of the active participle, and then there is no need to estimate "min" (than).

In placing the state of the saying in relation to them before its state in itself, there is an indication that the aspirations of the Jews, may Allah curse them, are inclined toward what benefits them. The construction formed from **an** (that) and what follows it is the subject of the omitted verb **"was established"** (**thabata**), indicated by **an** itself, meaning: "If their saying 'we hear' and so on were established." This is the view of al-Mubarrad. It was also said that it is a subject without a predicate, and it was also said that its predicate is omitted.

**"But Allah cursed them for their disbelief"** (﴿وَلَكِنْ لَعَنَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِكُفْرِهِمْ﴾), meaning: but they did not say what is more beneficial and more upright, and they persisted in that. So Allah the Exalted forsook them and removed them far from guidance because of their disbelief. **"So they do not believe"** (﴿فَلا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾) afterward, **"except a few"** (﴿إلا قَلِيلا﴾).

The great scholar chose the second view: that the exception is from the pronoun object in (cursed them). That is, "But Allah cursed them, except for a small group among them, for He did not curse them, and therefore those among them believed, such as Abdullah ibn Salam (may Allah be pleased with him) and his like." It was also said that the exception is from the subject of (they believe). On this view, it is necessary that the correct reading becomes the nominative as a substitution (badal, substitution of one noun for another), because it comes after a non-affirmative statement. Yet the readers (qurra') agreed on the accusative, and it is unlikely that they would agree on what is not preferred. Moreover, this view implies that the belief of one whom Allah cursed and forsook would occur, unless ﴿Allah cursed them for their disbelief﴾ is taken to mean the cursing of most of them. This is as you see. It was also said that the phrase is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: except a little belief, because they affirmed Oneness (tawhid) but disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) and his law. Here, belief is in the sense of affirmation (tasdiq), not legal belief (al-iman al-shar'i). On this view, it is permissible that by "little" is meant "nonexistence," as in his saying:

Little complaining when a calamity befalls him,
much desire, scattered are his journeys and paths.

The meaning is that they do not believe except with a nonexistent belief. This is either in the sense of ﴿They will not taste death therein, except the first death﴾, meaning: if what is nonexistent is belief, then they bring about some portion of belief, which is an instance of conditioning on the impossible. Or it means that what they produced of it, since it did not include what is necessary, was nonexistent in the way the whole is nonexistent through its part. The first is the correct view.

Page 49

[p. 49]

"O you who have been given the Book" (﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتابَ﴾). It was revealed, as al-Suddi said, concerning Zayd ibn al-Tabut and Malik ibn al-Sayf.

Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* and others related on the authority of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke with the leaders of the rabbis of the Jews, among them Abdullah ibn Suriya and Ka'b ibn Asad. He said to them: 'O assembly of Jews, fear Allah and submit. By Allah, you know that what I have brought you is the truth.' They said: 'We do not recognize that, O Muhammad.' So Allah, exalted is He, revealed concerning them the verse."

It is not hidden that the lesson lies in the general wording of the expression, which encompasses those whose states and sayings are recounted and others as well. The address was directed specifically to the first group by way of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person or address). Describing them once by being given the Book and another time by being given a portion of it is, in order to give each situation its due, a very remote interpretation.

Since the detailed account of these states and sayings is among the means by which those addressed may be turned away from the error they are in, He (glorified is He) followed it with a command to hasten to take the path of guidance, accompanied by warning, intimidation, and severe threat against opposition. So He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Believe﴾, a legal (*shar'i*) belief, ﴿in what We have sent down﴾, that is, in what We sent down from Our presence upon Our Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), of the Qur'an, ﴿confirming what is with you﴾ of the unaltered Torah. The manner in which the Qur'an confirms that has already been explained. He expressed the Torah by the description mentioned, to indicate their complete acquaintance with the reality of the situation, which leads to knowledge that the Qur'an confirms it. ﴿Before We obliterate faces﴾: this is connected to the command, conveying the urgency of hastening to comply with what it contains of threat, which is stated in the most forceful and emphatic manner. It did not make the occurrence of the threatened matter conditional upon opposition, nor did it explicitly state its occurrence in that case. This is to alert that this matter is certain and needs no announcement, and that it is at the point of occurring and directed toward those addressed. Indefinite *wujuh* (faces) conveys the magnitude of the affair together with gentleness and a fitting invitation.

The original sense of *tams* is the obliteration of a thing's trace. The intended meaning is: believe before We erase what the Creator has inscribed with the pen of His power on the pages of the faces, namely the nun of the eyebrow, the sad of the eye, the alif of the nose, and the mim of the mouth, so that We make them like the sole of a camel or the hoof of an animal. This was related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Al-Farra', al-Balkhi, and Husayn al-Maghribi said: the meaning is: believe before We make the faces places of hair growth like the faces of monkeys ﴿and turn them back upon their backs﴾, that is, make them in the form of their backs and nape, obliterated like them, since what lies behind the face has no features and is also the place of hair growth. The conjunction with *fa* (then) is either on the supposition of an implied "We wish to obliterate," or the conjunction is of the detailed upon the general.

From Ata al-Awfi it is related that the intended meaning is: We reverse them after obliteration, by placing the eyes that are in them and what is with them at the back of the head. Thus the conjunction with *fa* is apparent. It was also said: the intended meaning of "faces" is the dignitaries, with *tams* meaning any change; that is, before We change the conditions of their dignitaries, stripping them of their status and their favour, and clothing them in humiliation and retreat, or returning them to where they came from, which is Adhri'at in Syria. Thus the intended meaning is the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir. Ibn Zayd went to this interpretation, but it was judged weak, since it does not suit the context of intensifying the threat and generalizing the warning to all.

Scholars have differed over whether this threat was to be fulfilled in this world or in the Hereafter. A group said it was to be fulfilled in this world, and this is supported by what Ibn Jarir related from Isa ibn al-Mughira, who said: "We discussed in the presence of Ibrahim the Islam of Ka'b, and he said: Ka'b embraced Islam in the time of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. He came, intending Bayt al-Maqdis, and passed by Madina. Umar came out to him and said: 'O Ka'b, embrace Islam.' He said: 'Do you not read in your Book: ﴿The likeness of those who were charged with the Torah, then did not bear it, is like the likeness of a donkey carrying books﴾?' And I have borne the Torah." [p. 50] So Umar left him. Then he went out until he reached Homs, and he heard a man of its people reciting this verse, and he said: "My Lord, I have believed; my Lord, I have submitted," fearing that its threat would befall him. Then he returned, came to his family in Yemen, and brought them back as Muslims.

It is also related that Abdullah ibn Salam, when he came from Syria and had heard this verse, came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) before reaching his family and embraced Islam, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I did not think I would reach you until my face was turned back upon my nape."

Then they differed. Al-Mubarrad said: it is still awaited, and there must be an obliteration and transformation among the Jews before the Hour. This was supported by the indefinite *wujuh* and by the use of the third-person pronoun in what follows. Shaykh al-Islam objected that the turning away of the promised punishment from their forebears, who are those who directly engaged the causes of its descent and the reasons for its arrival, since they witnessed the signs of prophethood in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then denied them, and in the Torah, then altered it, and persisted in disbelief and error, and to whom the address of direct speech with the threat was directed, and then its descent upon those who came after them, many years later, who went astray by their misguidance and acted upon the rules of error they had laid down, is remote from the wisdom of the Mighty, the Wise.

The answer: Allah's custom, glorified is He, has been with the Jews that He takes vengeance upon their descendants for what their forebears did. Even if the wisdom in this is not known, on the assumption of accepting it, it does not remove the remoteness in this case.

Al-Barsi said: this threat was directed at them had none of them believed; but some of their rabbis believed, so it did not occur, and it was lifted from the rest. It was objected also that if the embracing of Islam by some was not a cause for the affirmation of the descent of punishment upon the rest, since they intensified denial and obstinacy after the truth had become clearer and the proof had been established against them by the testimony of their upright noble men, then at least it should not be a cause for lifting it from them.

It was also said in reply: if it is permissible for Him, glorified is He, to send down affliction upon a people because of the disobedience of some of them, as His statement, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿And guard against a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have done wrong﴾, then it is all the more permissible that He lift it from all because of the obedience of some. For He, glorified is He, is the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, whose mercy has preceded His wrath.

Reports have come that indicate this occurred, and the claim of distinct groups is hardly free from difficulty. It was also said that the threat was of one of the two matters, as His statement, exalted is He, expresses: ﴿Or curse them as We cursed the People of the Sabbath﴾. If the first matter did not occur, there is no dispute that the second occurred, for the Jews are cursed in every tongue and in every age. So the curse is in its apparent meaning, and the intended sense of the comparison with the cursing of the People of the Sabbath is exaggeration in describing it.

It was objected that the curse which befell them is what the tongues circulate, and it is far from being fit to serve as a ruling for this threat or as a deterrent from opposing the obstinate. So cursing here means humiliation through transformation, making them apes and swine, as Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Dahhak, and Ibn Jarir from al-Hasan. The apparent sense of the comparison supports this. There is no indication in its being conjoined with the obliteration and the turning back upon their backs that this is intended, since it is a different expression from what it is conjoined with. The argument that the curse differs from transformation by His statement: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse as recompense from Allah? Those whom Allah cursed and upon whom He became angry and made of them apes and swine﴾ yields no more than that it differs from transformation in that verse.

Al-Balkhi and al-Jubba'i went to the view that the threat was only to be fulfilled in the Hereafter, at the gathering, and one of the two matters or both will occur there in a distributed manner.

As for what was related from the two rabbis, the apparent meaning is that it is in this world. It is answered that this is grounded in caution and the predominance of fear that befits its matter. It has been reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to frequently enter and leave the chambers, and he would hardly settle when the wind grew strong, saying: "I fear the Hour may come," even though he knew, (ﷺ), that before its coming there would be the Mahdi, Isa (peace be upon him), the Dajjal (may the curse of Allah be upon him), the beast, and the rising of the sun from its west, and other things which he (ﷺ) related to us. Some allowed, on the supposition that the threat is to be fulfilled in the Hereafter, that by the obliteration and the turning back upon the backs is meant the sealing of the eyes and mouth and the stamping upon them, for Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And had We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾ and ﴿This day We seal their mouths﴾. Some who claimed that this is in this world allowed something similar, saying: the meaning is: believe before We obliterate faces by blinding the eyes from reflection, deafening the ears from listening to the truth by sealing, and turning them back from guidance to error.

This was related from al-Dahhak, and Abu al-Jarud related it from Abu Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him. The truth is that the verse is not explicit as to whether this is in this world or the Hereafter. Rather, what is understood from it according to the context is that it is in this world, since that is more effective in deterrence, and the reports from the two rabbis are based on this.

However, since the occurrence of this is obscure, and there is the possibility that it occurred but has not reached us, according to what is in *al-Taysir*, which is not to be considered, the possibility that it is in the Hereafter was preferred. Whatever the case, perhaps the secret in singling them out with this punishment among punishments, as Shaykh al-Islam said, is to observe the correspondence between it and what necessitated it from their crime, which is distortion and alteration. The doer and the one who is content are equal. The pronoun in the accusative in ﴿nalanahum﴾ refers to the people of the faces, or to ﴿those who﴾, by way of *iltifat*, since after the completion of the vocative the apparent form requires direct address, whereas before it the apparent form is third person. Address is permissible but is not eloquent, as in the verse:

"O you whom it is hard for us to part from, our finding every thing after you is nothing."

Or it refers to the faces if by it is meant the dignitaries.

﴿And the command of Allah was done﴾: that is, the bringing about of some thing of things. By "command" its well-known meaning is intended, and it may be that by it is meant one of the matters. This is perhaps the more apparent: that is, His threat, or what He decreed and judged, was an effective, actual act occurring now, or certainly to occur in the future. What was threatened against you is included in this first and foremost. The sentence is a concluding parenthetical statement confirming what preceded. Placing the majestic Name in place of the pronoun by way of *iltifat* is for the reason already mentioned more than once.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 48 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾. This is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf) confirming the threat mentioned before it, and emphasizing the obligation of complying with the command to believe, since there is no forgiveness without it, as the Jews claimed. Its indication is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then there succeeded them an heir who inherited the Book, grasping the goods of this lower world and saying, "It will be forgiven us."﴾ It also contains the removal of their fear of the evil of the major sins committed earlier, if they believe.

Shirk (association of partners with Allah) may mean the belief that Allah, exalted is His glory, has a partner, either in divinity (ulluhiyyah) or in lordship (ruburriyyah), and it may mean disbelief (kufr) in general, which is what is intended here, as Ibn ʿAbbas indicated. Thus the disbelief of the Jews is included in it by primary inclusion, for the Law has explicitly stated the association of all the People of the Book, and has decreed the eternal abode of all categories of disbelievers, however they may be. The revelation of the verse concerning the Jews, according to what is narrated from Muqatil, does not necessitate restriction to their disbelief; rather, being included within what the general wording implies suffices. The well-known view is that it was revealed in unrestricted form.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated, from Abu Mijlaz, who said: "When the saying of the Exalted was revealed: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves...﴾ the verse, the Prophet (ﷺ) stood upon the pulpit and recited it to the people. A man rose to him and said: 'And association with Allah?' He remained silent. Then he rose again and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, and association with Allah, the Exalted?' He remained silent, two or three times, and then this verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ etc."

The meaning is that Allah, the Exalted, does not forgive disbelief to one who is characterized by it without repentance and faith; because He, glorified be He, has decided the judgment of its eternal punishment, and His judgment does not change; and because the legislative wisdom requires closing the door of disbelief, which is why no prophet was sent except to close it; and permitting its forgiveness without faith would lead to opening it.

It has been said: because its sin does not have its effect erased from it, so it is not prepared for pardon, unlike others. It is not hidden that this is based on the premise that the act of Allah, the Exalted, follows the readiness of the locus, and this is the view of most of the Sufis and all of the philosophers.

The word (yushraka) is in the accusative position as an object. It has been said that the object is omitted, and the meaning is: He does not forgive on account of its being associated with Him any of the sins; thus it indicates that the non-forgiveness of shirk is all the more so. What the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) hold is the first view.

﴿And He forgives what is less than that﴾: it is coordinated (ʿatf) upon the predicate of (inna) and not a resumed statement. "That" refers to shirk, and in it is an announcement of the remoteness of its rank in ugliness, i.e., He forgives what is below it of sins, however great they are, even if they were like the sands of ʿAlij, and it was not repented of, by His grace and beneficence from Himself.

﴿For whomever He wills﴾: that He forgives him, from among those characterized by what has been mentioned only. So the prepositional phrase is connected to the affirmative (yaghfiru), and the verse is evident in distinguishing between shirk and what is below it: that Allah, the Exalted, never forgives the former, and forgives the latter for whomever He wills. The majority say this regarding non-repentance, so they interpreted the verse accordingly, by the indication of the verses and hadiths that show the acceptance of repentance in both of them and their forgiveness upon it, without disagreement from anyone.

The Mu'tazilah held that there is no difference between shirk and what is below it of major sins, in that both are forgiven by repentance and are not forgiven without it. So they interpreted the verse, as has been said, to mean: Allah does not forgive association for whomever He wills not to forgive him, who is the non-repentant, and He forgives what is below it for whomever He wills to forgive him, who is the repentant. They made (liman yashaʾ) connected to both verbs, and restricted the negated by what the affirmed was restricted by, according to the rule of tanazuʿ (competition of governors). But (man yashaʾ) in the first refers to the persistent by agreement, and in the second to the penitent, to satisfy the requirement of antithesis. This is not using a single word in two opposite meanings, because what is mentioned relates only to the second, and its like is understood for the first, and the meaning is one; but the object of the will in the first is understood as non-forgiveness, and in the second as forgiveness, by the indication of prior mention. It is not hidden that considering this as tanazuʿ with differing objects of the will is something no scholar would utter, nor would any complete person accept it. Moreover, there is no basis for restricting each of the two qualifiers to what it was restricted to, because shirk is also forgiven for the penitent, and what is below it is not forgiven for the persistent according to them, without any distinction between them; while the context of the verse calls for distinction, and restricting the forgiveness of what is below that to repentance is something for which there is no evidence, since the generality of the verses of threat is not more deserving of preservation than the verses of promise.

Al-Amidi mentioned in Abkar al-Afkar that the verses of promise are preferable over the verses of threat in consideration from eight aspects, which he enumerated there. He claimed that if they were not restricted, and it was said that forgiveness is permissible for one who did not repent, it would necessitate that Allah incites the servant to sin, since it would then be easy for him; and inciting to that is ugly, which is impossible for Allah, glorified be He. This is not a valid argument.

First: because it is based on the view that good and evil are rational, which has been refuted in its proper place.

Second: because even if granted, it would entail that pardon is ugly by analogy with the witness (shahid), which contradicts the consensus of the sensible.

Third: because it is refuted by repentance, for they said that its acceptance is obligatory, and it is not hidden that this too makes it easy for the disobedient to undertake disobedience, trusting in repentance, just as he trusts in forgiveness, and even more so, inasmuch as repentance is within his power, unlike forgiveness. So his repentance should not be accepted, because of the incitement in it; and that is contrary to consensus. If they say: he is not confident of being granted time for repentance, we reply: he is not confident of forgiveness either, due to the ambiguity of the relative pronoun. The claim that if repentance were not stipulated it would necessitate favoritism by Allah in forgiveness toward some and not others, and favoritism is not permissible for Him, is baseless; for Allah is a bestower of grace, and a bestower of grace may bestow upon one people and not another, and one person and not another, and He is just in punishing whom He punishes; and neither reason nor law prevents grace and justice, as is not hidden.

Among the Mu'tazilah there is one who said: forgiveness has come to mean the postponement of punishment without its removal, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the evil before the good, though exemplary punishments have already passed before them. Indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾. Here it is not valid to interpret it as removal of punishment, because the verse concerns disbelievers and punishment is not removed from them by consensus. And the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving, Possessor of mercy. If He were to seize them for what they have earned, He would hasten for them the punishment﴾, which is explicit that forgiveness here means the postponement of punishment. Therefore, in what we are discussing, it should be interpreted accordingly, by the indication that Allah addressed the disbelievers and warned them of hastened punishment for abandoning faith, then the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ etc. So the meaning would be: Allah does not postpone the punishment of shirk, but hastens it, and postpones the punishment of what is below it for whomever He wills. Thus the verse does not stand as evidence for what is the point of dispute. Moreover, even if it is granted that forgiveness in it means removal of punishment, the purpose is still not achieved; for it is either that removal of each individual type of punishment is intended, or removal of the totality of punishments, or removal of some types of them. The first is not possible, since the wording does not indicate it. The remaining two possibilities stand. On the first of them, it does not follow from His not punishing with all types of punishment that He does not punish with some of them; and on the second, it does not follow from removing some types the removal of others.

It is answered that interpreting forgiveness as removal of punishment is preferable to interpreting it as postponement, for three reasons:

The first: that it is the meaning that comes immediately to mind from the unrestricted use of the word.

The second: that if the word forgiveness in the verse were interpreted as postponement, it would necessitate a restriction in the statement that Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him; because the punishment of shirk is postponed in the case of many polytheists, indeed they may be in the most comfortable and pleasant living compared to the living of some believers; and in such a case there would be no distinction between shirk and what is below it. This is avoided by interpreting it as removal.

The third: that the community of the early generations, before the appearance of opponents, continually agreed on interpreting the word forgiveness in the verse as the falling away of punishment, and what the consensus has settled upon is correct, and its opposite cannot be correct.

As for their statement: the objective is also not achieved if it is interpreted so, for it is either that is intended... We say: rather what is intended is the removal of each individual one. Its explanation is that the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ is a negation of forgiveness. So if what is understood from forgiveness is the removal of punishment, then negating forgiveness is negating the negation, which is an affirmation, and its meaning is the establishment of punishment. At that point, it is either that what is understood is establishment of all types of punishments or of some of them. The first is not possible, because of the impossibility of combining opposing punishments, and because that is not a condition regarding disbelievers by consensus. So only the second remains, and it follows from that that forgiveness in what is below shirk is by removal of every punishment; otherwise the distinction between shirk and what is below it would not be realized.

Among them is one who fell into utter confusion over this verse, to the point that he claimed that (wa) and (yaghfiru) are coordinated upon the negated, the negation extends over both, and the verse is for equating between shirk and what is below it, not for distinguishing. It is not hidden that this is a distortion of the words of Allah, the Exalted, and placing them in other than their proper positions.

Among the group is one who said in refuting the Mu'tazilah: the restriction by will contradicts the obligation of punishment before repentance and the obligation of pardon after it. Sahib al-Kashf criticized him, saying it did not proceed from a firm basis; for obligation by wisdom reinforces the will according to them. Also, al-Zamakhshari indicated in this context that the will means entitlement, and it entails obligation and reinforces it, so what was mentioned does not arise at all.

Furthermore, this verse is used as a refutation against the Mu'tazilah, just as it is used as a refutation against the Kharijites, who claimed that every sin is shirk and its perpetrator is eternal in the Fire. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned that it also contains a refutation of the Murji'ah, who said that the people of major sins among the Muslims are not punished.

Ibn al-Duraysi and Ibn ʿAdi narrated, with a sound chain, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: "We used to refrain from seeking forgiveness for the people of major sins until we heard from our Prophet (ﷺ) ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ the verse, and he said: 'I have saved my supplication and my intercession for the people of major sins from my community.' So we refrained from much of what was in our hearts, then we spoke and hoped." The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, rejoiced greatly at this verse, so much so that ʿAli, may Allah honor his face, said, as narrated from him by al-Tirmidhi who graded it sound: "The verse most beloved to me in the Qur'an is ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, and He forgives what is below that for whomever He wills﴾."

﴿And whoever associates partners with Allah﴾: a resumed statement hinting at the reason for the non-forgiveness of shirk, and the mention of the Glorious Name in place of the pronoun

It is for the sake of adding grandeur and increasing the ugliness of association (shirk) and the horror of the state of one who is characterized by it. That is: "And whoever associates others with Allah, the Exalted, who combines all the attributes of perfection, of beauty and majesty, in any form of association whatsoever, ﴿has indeed fabricated a tremendous sin﴾." That is, he has committed what makes all other sins appear insignificant in comparison, so that forgiveness definitively does not attach to him.

The root of al-iftira' (fabrication, slander) is from al-fara (فرى), which means cutting. Since cutting something is generally a corruption of it, the word came to be dominated by the sense of corruption. In the Qur'an it is used to mean lying, associating partners with Allah, and wrongdoing, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani, d. 502 AH) has stated. Thus it means committing what is not fit to be said or done, and so it applies to the invention of falsehood and the commission of sin, and this is the meaning intended here.

Is it a homonym shared between the invention of falsehood and the fabrication of what is not fit, or is it a literal meaning in the first case and a figurative usage (majaz mursal or isti'arah) in the second? There are two opinions, and the more apparent of them according to some is the second. There is no necessity of combining the literal and the figurative, because shirk is more general than the verbal and the active; the intended meaning is a general sense, namely committing what is not fit.

In Majma' al-Bayan, a distinction is made regarding the original meaning between faraytu (فَرَيْتُ) and afraytu (أَفْرَيْتُ): it is said that faraytu al-adim (فَرَيْتُ الأَدِيمَ) means when you cut the hide in a manner of improvement, and afraytuhu (أَفْرَيْتُهُ) means when you cut it in a manner of corruption.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 49:

﴿Have you not seen those who ascribe purity to themselves?﴾ al-Kalbi said: It was revealed concerning "men of the Jews who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with their children, and said: 'O Muhammad, do these children of ours bear any sin?' He said: 'No.' They said: 'By Him by whom oaths are sworn, we are in no different state from them. No sin do we commit by day but it is expiated for us by night, and no sin do we commit by night but it is expiated for us by day.' This is what they ascribed to themselves as purity."

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan that it was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians, when they said: ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾, and said: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾. The meaning is: look at them and marvel at their claim that they are pure before Allah, despite what they are upon of disbelief and great sin! Or [marvel] at their claim that Allah expiates their nightly and daytime sins, despite the impossibility that any disbeliever should be forgiven any of his disbelief or his disobedience! And in the same category is one who ascribes purity to himself and praises himself for no sound purpose, such as speaking of a blessing and the like. ﴿Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills﴾ is a negation of their ascribing purity to themselves, and an affirmation of Allah's ascribing purity.

That this is a turning away from censuring them for that self-ascribed purity to censuring them for stinginess and envy is far, both in wording and in meaning. The clause is a conjunction with an implied understood matter to which the speech leads, as if it were said: they do not in reality purify themselves; rather, Allah purifies whom He wills of His servants among the believers who deserve it, since He is All-Knowing, All-Aware. The root of tazkiyah (purification) is cleansing and freeing from what is ugly, in speech, as is evident, or in deed, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾ and ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow﴾.

﴿And they will not be wronged a [fraction as much as] fatil﴾ is a conjunction with a clause that has been omitted, relying on the state's indication of it and signalling that it is independent of mention; that is, they will be punished for that abominable act, and they will not be wronged in that punishment the least and smallest wrong, which is what is meant by fatil: the thread that lies in the split of a date-stone. It is often used as a proverb for paucity and insignificance, like the naqir (the pit in the back of the date-stone) and the qitmir (its thin skin). It is also said that fatil is what comes out between your two fingers and palms of dirt; this is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Malik, and al-Suddi, may Allah be pleased with them.

It is also permitted that the clause ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), with the pronoun referring to ﴿man﴾ according to its meaning; that is: and the state is that they will not have any of their reward diminished at all, rather they will be given it in full on the Day of Resurrection, despite what Allah has purified and praised them for in this world.

It is also said that it is a resumptive sentence, and the pronoun refers to the two relatives: the one who ascribes purity to himself and the one whom Allah purifies; that is, neither this one's reward will be diminished nor that one's punishment. The first is more fitting to the context of warning. The accusative of fatil is as a second object, like your saying: "I wronged him his right." 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: It may also be a specification (tamyiz), like your saying: "I poured out sweat."

Page 55

﴿Look how they invent lies against God!﴾ In their claim that they are pure (azkiya') before God Most High, which entails their claim that God accepts them and is pleased with them. Because of the monstrousness of this, since it attributes to Him what is utterly impossible for Him, the attention was directed to the manner of it (kayfiyyah), to intensify the condemnation and to emphasize the amazement that the speech indicates. Otherwise, they are also inventing lies against themselves by claiming to possess attributes whose opposite is what they actually possess. The word (kayfa, "how") is in a position of accusative, either by analogy with an adverb of time (zarf) or as a circumstantial accusative (hal), according to the well-known difference of opinion between Sibawayh and al-Akhfash. The verb is (yaftaruna, "they invent"), and (bihi, "against Him") is connected to it.

Abu al-Baqa' allowed that it could be a circumstantial clause (hal) from (al-kadhib, "the lie"). It has also been said that (bihi) is connected to it, and that the clause is in a position of accusative after the removal of the preposition, and that the verb of seeing (al-nazar) is suspended by that. The explicit mention of "lie," even though inventing (iftira') is never anything but a lie, is for the sake of exaggerating the ugliness of their state.

﴿And sufficient is it as a manifest sin﴾, that is, sufficient is their inventing, and it has been said: sufficient is this specific lie, ﴿a manifest sin﴾, whose being a sin among their sins is not hidden. This is an expression for its being great and abominable. The sentence, as 'Isam al-Millah said, is in the position of a circumstantial clause with the implied (qad), meaning: how do they invent lies, while the state is that this contradicts its content, since it is a manifest sin, and one who is guilty of a manifest sin, not refraining from it despite its clear wrongness, cannot be the son of God, glory be to Him, nor His beloved, nor can he be pure before God Most High. The accusative of (ithman, "a sin") is a specification (tamyiz).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 51:

﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book, believing in jibt (idols or sorcery) and taghut (false deities)?﴾ This is an expression of wonder at another state of theirs. Describing them with what lies within the relative clause (silah) serves to intensify the reproach and to emphasize the wonder, and a parallel to this has already been discussed. The verse was revealed, as narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, concerning Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf along with a group of Jews. They went out to Makkah after the Battle of Uhud to form an alliance with the Quraysh against the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and to break the covenant that was between them and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Ka'b descended upon Abu Sufyan, and he hosted him generously, while the Jews lodged in the houses of the Quraysh. The people of Makkah said: "You are people of a Book, and Muhammad ﷺ is a man of a Book, so we cannot be sure this is not a deception from you. If you want us to go out with you, then prostrate to these two idols and believe in them." And he did so.

Then Ka'b said: "O people of Makkah, let thirty of you come and thirty of us, and we will press our livers against the Ka'bah, and we will pledge to the Lord of the House that we will exert ourselves in fighting Muhammad ﷺ." They did so. When they had finished, Abu Sufyan said to Ka'b: "You are a man who reads the Book and knows, while we are unlettered and do not know. Which of us is better guided on the path and nearer to the truth, we or Muhammad?" Ka'b said: "Present your religion to me." Abu Sufyan said: "We slaughter camels for the pilgrims, we give them milk to drink, we host the guest, we free the captive, we keep the ties of kinship, we maintain the House of our Lord and circumambulate it, and we are the people of the Sacred Precinct, whereas Muhammad ﷺ has abandoned the religion of his forefathers, severed the ties of kinship, and left the Sacred Precinct. Our religion is ancient, and the religion of Muhammad is new." Ka'b said: "By Allah, you are better guided on the way than those whom Muhammad follows." Then Allah the Exalted revealed the verse concerning this.

Jibt originally is the name of an idol, and then it was used for every object of worship other than Allah the Exalted. It was also said that its root is jibs, which, as al-Raghib said, is the base thing that has no good in it, and its sin was changed into a ta', as in the saying of Amr ibn Yarbu': "shirar al-nat" (the worst of people), meaning the people. Qutrub also took this view. Taghut is applied to every falsehood, whether a deity or otherwise.

Al-Firyabi and others narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Jibt is the sorcerer, and taghut is the devil."

Ibn Jarir narrated through several chains from Mujahid something similar, and through the route of Abu al-Layth from him he said: "Jibt is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and taghut is the devil, who was in the form of a human being."

From Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "Jibt is the sorcerer in the language of Abyssinia, and taghut is the soothsayer."

Ibn Humayd narrated from Ikrimah that jibt is the devil in the language of Abyssinia, and taghut is the soothsayer, and this is a narration from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father.

In another narration: jibt is Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and taghut is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf.

In another: jibt is the idols, and taghut is those who stand before them and express falsehood through them in order to mislead people.

The meaning of believing in them is either affirming that they are deities and associating them with Allah the Exalted in worship, or obeying them and agreeing with them in the falsehood they are upon, or the common element between the two meanings, such as veneration for example. The first meaning is the more immediately apparent, i.e., that they affirm the divinity of these two falsehoods, associate them with the true God in worship, and prostrate to them.

And "wa-yaquluna lilladhina kafaru" (and they say to those who disbelieved): the lam here means "for the sake of them" and "concerning them," so the lam is not the object of the verb of saying, for otherwise it would have said "antum" (you) instead of His words "ha'ula'" (these), i.e., the disbelievers from the people of Makkah.

﴿Are more rightly guided than those who believe as to the way?﴾ That is, more correct in religion and more upright in path. It was said: the apparent meaning is that they used the elative form without considering the sense of sharing in it, or they said this in mockery because of their disbelief. The mention of the Prophet ﷺ and his followers by the title of belief did not come from the speakers but from Allah the Exalted, to acquaint them with a beautiful description and to rebuke those who preferred over them those characterized by the most shameful vices.

﴿Those﴾ are the speakers, who are far removed in misguidance, ﴿whom Allah has cursed﴾, meaning He has removed them far from His mercy and expelled them. The demonstrative ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ (ism al-ishara, demonstrative pronoun) is a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence), and the relative pronoun ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ (al-mawsul, relative pronoun) is its khabar (predicate). The sentence is a mustaʾnafah (independent resumptive clause) that explains their condition and reveals their final fate. ﴿And whoever Allah curses﴾, meaning whom He removes far from His mercy, ﴿you will not find for him any helper﴾, meaning any supporter who can prevent punishment from him, whether worldly or otherworldly, whether by intercession or by other means. This indicates their deprivation of the benefit they sought by seeking help from the polytheists of Makkah, and it hints at the promise to the believers that they are the ones who will be victorious, since they were the opposite of these people. They are the ones whom Allah has brought near, and whomever Allah brings near, you will not find for him any forsaker.

As for the use of the particle ﴿لَنْ﴾ (lan, a negative particle of emphatic future negation), the addressing of the discourse to every one who is fit for it, the indefinite singular form of ﴿نَصِيرًا﴾ (nasir, helper), and the expression of its absence by "not finding", which indicates a prior seeking, attributed to the general addressee, there is clearly an indication of their everlasting deprivation of attaining, completely, what they hoped for. If the intensive form in ﴿نَصِيرٍ﴾ (nasir, helper, in the intensive pattern) is taken as directed toward the negation, as has been said regarding His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to [His] servants﴾, then the strength of this indication is increased.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 53:

﴿Or do they have a share of the dominion?﴾ This begins the detailing of another of their vile qualities. The particle (am) here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), so it is to be construed as (bal) (rather) together with the interrogative hamzah, meaning: "Rather, do they have..." The intent is to deny that they have any share of the dominion, and this is a rejection of what the Jews claim, namely that dominion will return to them at the end of time.

It is related from al-Jubba'i (al-Jubba'i) that the intended meaning of "dominion" here is prophethood, i.e., they have no share of prophethood such that people would be obliged to follow and obey them. But the first interpretation is more apparent, because of His exalted statement: ﴿Then they would not give the people﴾, meaning: anyone at all, or the poor, or Muhammad (ﷺ) and his followers, as was related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) ﴿a speck﴾, meaning: something very little. Its original sense is what we have pointed out just now.

Ibn Jarir related, through the chain of Abu al-'Aliyah, from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) that he said: "This is the naqir," and he placed the tip of the thumb on the inside of the index finger and then flicked it. The summarized meaning, as it has been said, is: they have no share of dominion not because they do not deserve it, but because they deserve to be deprived of it, since if they were given a share of it they would not give people even the smallest amount of it. Whoever is given dominion ought to give, and they are not like that. So the fa' in (fa-idhan) is for causation and consequence, answering an elided condition, namely: "If they were to obtain a share... no" (or: "if they had a share," as al-Zamakhshari estimated), because the fa' does not occur in the answer to law (if), especially with (idhan) and the present-tense verb. It is also permissible that the fa' be conjunctive (atifah), with the hamzah for denying the whole of the conjoined and the conjoined-to together, in the sense that it is not fitting that this which has occurred should be the case, namely that they have been given a share of dominion, since they had wealth, gardens, and lofty palaces like kings, and following it from them is stinginess even with the smallest amount. The benefit of (idhan) is to increase the denial and rebuke, since they make the establishment of the share, which is the cause of giving, a cause for withholding. The difference between the two aspects is that the denial in the first is directed at the first clause and means denial of occurrence, while in the second it is directed at the combination of the two matters and means denial of what has actually happened. (Idhan) in both aspects is inactive (mulghah), though it is permissible to make it operative, because it has been stipulated for its operation that it be at the head of its clause; so when it is viewed as being at the head of its clause it operates, and when it is viewed in terms of conjunction and being subordinate to something else it is made inoperative. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with them) read: (fa-idhan la yu'tuna al-nas), with the accusative, on the basis of operation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 54:

﴿Or do they envy the people﴾ This is a transition from rebuking them for stinginess to rebuking them for envy (hasad), which is the most vile of the destructive vices, for whoever is characterized by it in this world and the next. Mentioning it after the previous matter is by way of ascent (taraqqi). The "am" here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and the hamzah of interrogation implied after it is for denying what is actually happening. By "the people" is meant their chief, indeed the chief of all creation without exception, Muhammad (ﷺ). This was the view of Ikrimah, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Abu Malik, and Atiyyah.

Ibn Abi Hatim related, through al-Awfi, from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: "The People of the Book said: 'Muhammad claims that he has been given what he has been given with humility, yet he has nine wives, and his only concern is marriage. What kingdom is greater than this?' So Allah revealed this verse."

Qatadah, al-Hasan, and Ibn Jurayj held that by them is meant the Arabs. It is reported from Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd Allah that they are the Prophet and his family, upon whom be the most excellent blessings and the most complete peace.

It has been said: by them is meant all the people to whom the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, of every color, black and red; that is, "Or do they envy them for what Allah has given them of His bounty," meaning prophethood and the permission of nine wives, or the sending of the Prophet (ﷺ) from among them, the revelation of the Qur'an in their tongue, or gathering for them perfections that hopes fall short of, or preparing the cause of their guidance by sending the Prophet (ﷺ) to them. Envy in this sense is metaphorical, because when the Jews disputed with him regarding his prophethood (ﷺ), which is guidance for all people, it is as though they envied them all collectively. ﴿Indeed We gave﴾ This is a reason for the denial and condemnation, and the speech is conducted in the manner of majesty by way of iltifat, to show complete care for the matter. The fa' here, as has been said, is fasihah (expressive), meaning: if they envy the people for what they have been given, they have erred, since giving is no novelty from Us, for We gave before this ﴿the family of Ibrahim the Book﴾, that is, its kind, meaning the Torah and the Gospel, or both along with the Psalms, ﴿and the wisdom﴾, that is, prophethood, or mastery of knowledge and action, or the secrets deposited in the Book; these are sayings.

﴿And We gave them, in addition to that, a great kingdom﴾ which its extent cannot be measured. It is also permissible that the meaning is that they gain no benefit from this envy, for We gave these what We gave despite the many tyrant envious ones such as Nimrod, Pharaoh, and others; the envier gained nothing and the envied was not harmed. It may also be intended that their envy here is extremely ugly and baseless, for We gave previously to the forefathers of this envied Prophet (ﷺ) and the sons of his paternal uncle what We gave them, so how do they find it strange that he be a prophet, and envy him for being given it?! The repetition of "gave" corresponds to what the context of detail requires, along with indicating the difference between kingdom and what precedes it. The meaning of "giving" is either giving directly, or what is more general than that and includes giving through an intermediary. On the first, the family of Ibrahim means the prophets of his offspring, and some of them are meant by the pronoun returning to them in "We gave them." Thus Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "The kingdom among the family of Ibrahim is the kingdom of Yusuf, Dawud, and Sulayman (peace be upon them)." al-Suddi restricted it to what was made lawful to Dawud and Sulayman of women; the first had ninety-nine wives, and his son had three hundred wives, and an equal number of concubines. From Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: "It reached me that Sulayman (peace be upon him) had three hundred wives and seven hundred concubines." On the second, the intended are all his offspring, for honoring some with what has been mentioned is an honoring of all, since they share in the blessings of that and draw light from its illuminations.

Some people interpreted "wisdom" as knowledge, and "great kingdom" as prophethood; this is attributed to al-Hasan and Mujahid. It is not hidden that applying "great kingdom" to prophethood is far-fetched, and that taking the words in their evident sense is preferable.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 55:

﴿Among them﴾ i.e., of the kind of these envious people and their forefathers, ﴿is one who believed in it﴾, i.e., in what was given to the family of Ibrahim (Abraham), ﴿and among them is one who averted﴾, i.e., turned away, ﴿from it﴾, and did not believe in it. This, according to one opinion, is a narration of what proceeded from their predecessors after the occurrence of the narrated event, without it having any bearing on obligation. It has been said that it has a bearing on this, by showing that if envy were not ugly, their predecessors would have unanimously agreed upon it, and none of them would have believed, just as they unanimously agreed upon it and none of them believed. But this is nothing. It has also been said that its meaning is: ﴿So among the family of Ibrahim is one who believed in it, and among them is one who disbelieved﴾, and that this did not weaken his affair; likewise, the disbelief of these people does not weaken your affair. According to this, the pronouns in (in it) and (from it) refer to Ibrahim, and in this there is consolation for him, peace be upon him. The pronouns referring to Muhammad (ﷺ), and making the discourse a consequence of His words, Exalted is He, ﴿O People of the Book﴾, or of His words, Glorified is He, ﴿Have you not seen those who...﴾ etc., is extremely remote.

Likewise, making the two pronouns refer to what was mentioned of the story of the family of Ibrahim. ﴿And sufficient is Hell as a blaze﴾, i.e., a fire kindled and ignited with intense fire. That is: if some of the punishment is averted from them in this world, then what has been prepared for them of the blazing fire of Hell in the Hereafter is sufficient for them.

[p. 58]

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved in Our signs, We will surely cause them to enter the Fire﴾: this is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new sentence that is not grammatically tied to what precedes it), which functions as an explanation and confirmation of what came before it. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) may refer either to those who disbelieved in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to a broader group that includes them and others who disbelieved in all the other prophets (peace be upon them). Those who disbelieved in the Messenger (ﷺ) enter this category first and most directly. On the first reading, "signs" (al-aya) may mean either the Qur'an, or what includes all of it and part of it, or what includes all his miracles (peace and blessings be upon him). On the second reading, "signs" means what includes the aforementioned signs and all the other proofs that the prophets (peace be upon them) brought in support of their claims. As Sibawayh said, "sawfa" (سوف, "surely/will") is a word used to express threat and warning, and the letter "sin" (السين) takes its place, as in the Almighty's words: ﴿I will cause him to enter Saqar﴾. It may also be used to express promise, as in His words: ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied﴾, and in the words: ﴿I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you﴾. Often both "sawfa" and "sin" serve to emphasise a warning. The indefinite form of "nar" (fire) is for magnification, meaning: they will certainly enter a terrifying fire.

﴿Every time their skins are roasted through﴾: that is, they are burned, scorched, and destroyed. It derives from nadija (نَضِجَ), said of fruit and meat, nadjan and nudjan, when it becomes fully ripe. "Kullama" (كلما, "every time") is an adverb of time, and the element that governs it is ﴿We will replace them with other skins﴾. That is, in place of every skin that is burned, at the moment of its burning, We will give them a new skin that differs from the burned one in form, even though its original material still exists, by having the burning removed from it. So it cannot be objected: how is the second skin punished when it did not disobey? This is because it is the one that disobeyed, considering its origin, since only its attribute was changed. In my view, however, this objection is one that no intelligent person would hardly raise, let alone a learned one. This is because the disobedience, obedience, suffering, and pleasure of the skin are not conceivable, since in its essence it makes no difference from the rest of inanimate things in lacking perception and awareness, and it is most like an instrument. Thus the hand of one who unjustly kills a soul, for example, is an instrument for him, like the sword with which he killed. There is no difference between them except that the hand carries the spirit and the sword does not. This alone is not sufficient as a cause for restoring the hand itself and burning it without restoring the sword and burning it, because that carrying is not voluntary. Therefore the truth is that punishment falls upon the sensitive soul, whatever body it inhabits and whatever skin it is in, and the same is said regarding bliss. This is supported by the fact that among the people of the Fire is one who fills a corner of the corners of Jahannam, that the tooth of a dweller of Jahannam is like Mount Uhud, and that the people of Paradise will enter it at the height of Adam (peace be upon him), sixty cubits, with a width of seven cubits. There is no doubt that the two groups did not carry out evil and good with those bodies. Rather, whoever is just sees that the parts of bodies in this world do not remain the same in quantity through youth and old age. The fact that the quiddity (mahiyyah) is one does not help, because in what we are discussing we have not claimed that the second skin differs from the first skin as an accident differs from a substance, or a human from a stone, but rather as the difference between Zayd who is obedient and 'Amr who is disobedient, for example. Furthermore, if it were said that the disbeliever is punished first with a body of iron inhabited by the spirit, and then with a body of other material, it would likewise not be proper for anyone to say: the iron did not disobey, so how was it burned by the fire? Were it not known from religion by necessity that the bodily resurrection is such that denying it is disbelief, it would not be rationally far-fetched to say that the bliss and punishment are spiritual only.

Since the matter rationally depends on establishing the existence of bodies at all, and it should not be imagined from this that I say the restoration of what has ceased to exist is impossible (God forbid), rather I say there is no need for its restoration, even though it is possible.

The texts on this subject are contradictory. Some indicate the restoration of the very same bodies after their annihilation, and others indicate the creation of their likeness and the passing away of the first. I see no harm, after affirming the bodily resurrection, in believing either of the two matters. The discussion of the verses whose apparent meaning indicates the restoration of the very same [bodies] will come later, God willing, such as the words of the Glorified: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do﴾, and what is in al-Safiri's commentary on al-Bukhari, that there will never cease to be disputes among people until the spirit and the body dispute on the Day of Resurrection. The spirit will say to the body: "You did it, and I was only a wind, and without you I could not have done anything." The body will say to the spirit: "You commanded, and you incited, and without you I would have been like a fallen trunk, not moving a hand or a foot." Then Allah the Exalted will send an angel to judge between them, and he will say to them: "Your similitude is that of a paralysed man who can see and a blind man who entered a garden. The paralysed one said to the blind one: 'I see fruit here, but I cannot reach it.' The blind one said to him: 'Mount me, and pick it.' So which of them is the transgressor?" They will say: "Both of them." The angel will say to them: "Then you have both judged against yourselves." I do not consider this sound, because the differences between the example and what it exemplifies are clear. In what we are discussing, the bearer has no choice, and no awareness in any way, except that there may be some awareness which we are not aware of. Perhaps we will return to this, God willing, to investigate this station. Moreover, this change, however it is, happens many times in a single hour.

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "This verse was recited in the presence of 'Umar, and Ka'b said: 'I have its interpretation. I read it before Islam.' 'Umar said: 'Bring it, O Ka'b. If you bring it as it was heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), we will believe you.' He said: 'I read it before: "Every time their skins are roasted through, We replace them with other skins, in the same hour, a hundred and twenty times."' 'Umar said: 'That is how I heard it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah and others narrated from al-Hasan who said: "It has reached me that one of them is burned seventy thousand times in a day. Every time the Fire cooks them and consumes their flesh, it is said to them: 'Return,' and they return."

﴿That they may taste the punishment﴾: that is, so that its tasting may continue and not cease. It is like saying to someone dear: "May Allah honour you." The expression of perceiving punishment by tasting is either because it does not diminish through the continuation of contact, or to indicate its bitterness together with its pain, or to draw attention to the intensity of its effect, since the faculty of taste is the most affecting of the senses, or to indicate its penetration into the inner self. Perhaps the secret in the replacement of skins, although He is able to keep the perception and taste of punishment in a state, even with burning or with their bodies kept safe from it, is that the soul may imagine that perception ceases by burning, and it does not at all find it unlikely that it may be protected from pain and punishment as its body is protected from burning. This was said by our master Shaykh al-Islam.

It is also said: the secret in that is that in the roasting and the replacement there is a kind of despair for them and a renewal of grief upon grief. Some denied the roasting of skins in the commonly understood sense and their replacement, claiming that the replacement is only of the garments (sarabil) which Allah the Glorified and Exalted mentioned: ﴿Their garments will be of pitch﴾, and that the garments were called skins by association. But in this there is abandonment of the apparent meaning, and it is close to being contrary to what is known necessarily. Also, garments are not described as being roasted. It seems that nothing prompted him to this claim except finding the apparent meaning unlikely, and it is not far from the power of Allah the Glorified and Exalted. ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Mighty﴾: that is, He has never ceased to be unassailable, and nothing can resist or prevent Him. It is also said: He is powerful, and nothing He wills is impossible for Him, of what He has promised or threatened. ﴿Wise﴾ in His management, His determination, and in punishing whoever He punishes. The clause is a justification for what precedes it, namely the burning and the replacement. The mention of the Glorious Name here is to justify the ruling, along with what has passed many times.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 57 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾: having mentioned the bad condition of the disbelievers, he follows it with the good condition of the believers, to complete the contrast between displeasure and delight. He begins with the condition of the first group because the discussion concerns them. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) may refer either to the believers in our Prophet (ﷺ), or to them together with all who believed among the nations of the prophets (peace be upon them). The meaning is: those who believe in what must be believed and do good deeds, ﴿We will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾.

Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) read (sa-yudkhiluhum) with the letter ya', the pronoun referring to the Name of Majesty (Allah). The letter sin in it emphasizes the promise. The significance of using it here, and of using (sawfa) in the verse about disbelief, is not hidden.

﴿Abiding therein forever﴾: this is for magnifying the favor. It is a predicated circumstantial clause (hal muqaddara) from the object pronoun in (sa-nudkhiluhum). The verse continues: ﴿For them therein are pure spouses﴾, meaning pure from menstruation, postnatal bleeding, all other defects and impurities, bad character and base natures. They do nothing that would repel their husbands, and nothing is found in them that would turn their husbands away. This phrase is in the accusative position, either as a circumstantial clause of (gardens), or as a second circumstantial clause of the object pronoun, or as an adjective of (gardens) following another adjective. It may also be in the nominative position, as a predicate of the relative pronoun following another predicate.

The intended meaning is many spouses, as the traditions indicate. ﴿And We will admit them into a shade, deep and extended﴾, meaning abundant shade with no hardship in it, lasting shade that the sun does not abrogate, and a temperate state with no heat or cold. May Allah grant us to rest in it by His mercy, for He is the Most Merciful of the merciful. This may be understood literally, the absence of the sun not preventing it, or as an indication of complete and lasting blessing. The word (zalil) is an adjective derived from the word (zill, shade) for emphasis, as is their habit in expressions such as "a day that is extremely day (yawm ayyam) and a night that is extremely night (layl alyal)."

Al-Imam al-Marzuqi said: it is merely a word that follows what it is derived from, and it has no independent meaning. It is like (basan) in your saying "hasan basan" (good and well-formed). It was also read (yudkhiluhum) with the letter ya', coordinated with (sa-yudkhiluhum). This is not because it is different from the first admission in essence, but in its designation, as in His saying: ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and We saved them from a severe punishment﴾.

* * *

Furthermore, among the allusions in the verses is: ﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying﴾. This is an address to the believers of knowledge, and a prohibition for them from conversing with their Lord or approaching the station of presence and intimate communion with Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, while they are intoxicated with the wine of passion and love of the world, or in the sleep of heedlessness. They should wait until they become sober and do not occupy themselves with other than their Master. The intended meaning is the prohibition of occupying the heart with anything other than the Lord.

It has also been said that this is an address to the people of love and passion, whom the drink of Layla and the wine of Mayy have intoxicated, so they remain bewildered and dazed, unable to distinguish the living from the dead, unable to know the times, and unable to perform the conditions of the prayers. It is as if they were told: O you who know Me and My attributes and My names, you who are intoxicated with the drink of My love, the spring of My intimacy, the Tasnim of My nearness, the ginger of My closeness, the wine of My passion, and the elixir of My contemplation: when I reveal to you My beauty and make you intimate in the station of My lordship, do not burden your souls with performing the outward observances, for you are in the garden of My contemplation, and there is no restriction in the garden. When you sober up from your intoxication and become sober by the attribute of firm establishment (tamkin), then perform what I have made obligatory for you: ﴿And stand before Allah in devout obedience﴾.

The summary of this is the lifting of obligation from those who are drawn away and drowned in the seas of contemplation until they come to reason and sober up. On this interpretation, faith is understood as the faith of direct sight, but the first meaning is more appropriate to the allusion.

﴿Nor in a state of major impurity﴾, meaning: do not approach prayer while you are far from the Truth because of the intense inclination toward the self and its pleasures. ﴿Except those passing through [a place]﴾, meaning travelers along one of the paths of its enjoyments to the extent of necessity, like passing along the path of nourishment through food and drink to relieve hunger, or clothing to ward off the need of heat and cold and to cover the nakedness, or intercourse to preserve offspring. ﴿Until you have washed﴾ and purified yourselves with the waters of repentance, seeking forgiveness, and sincerely disavowing and apologizing. ﴿And if you are ill﴾ with the diseases of vices, ﴿or on a journey﴾ in the desert of ignorance and bewilderment, seeking desires, ﴿or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself﴾, meaning from occupation with the filth of wealth, soiled by love for it, ﴿or you have contacted women﴾, meaning you have clung to the souls and engaged with them in fulfilling their desire, ﴿and you find no water﴾, meaning knowledge that guides you to free yourselves from that, ﴿then perform tayammum with clean earth﴾, meaning aim for the earth of your readiness, or return to the guides who are masters of readiness. ﴿Then wipe your faces and your hands﴾, meaning wipe your essences and attributes with what rises from the lights of their readiness, adopt their characters, and follow their ways, until those dispositions that destroy you are wiped away and your souls remain pure. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning﴾, pardoning what has come from you in accordance with those dispositions, ﴿Forgiving﴾, concealing the blemish with beauty.

﴿Have you not considered those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾, meaning a part of it, which is their acknowledgment of the Truth together with their veiling by seeing creation. ﴿They purchase error﴾, abandoning true tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness). ﴿And they want﴾ along with that ﴿that you should lose the way﴾, the Truth, which is pure tawhid and not seeing other things, so that you would become like them. ﴿And Allah is most knowing﴾ of your enemies. By them he means those described above. The cause of their enmity toward them is the difference in the outward names among them, and for this reason they wished to make them disbelievers. ﴿And sufficient is Allah as an ally﴾, who manages your affairs by granting success on the path of tawhid. ﴿And sufficient is Allah as a helper﴾, who helps you against your enemies, so they cannot harm you or turn you back from the Truth you are upon.

﴿Among those who are Jews﴾, who turned back from the requirement of readiness, which is the negation of other than God, toward what their souls embellished for them, what their thoughts deduced, what their views supported, and what their formal sciences called for. ﴿They distort words from their places﴾. It is possible that "words" means their apparent meaning: they interpret everything whose apparent sense indicates unity according to their own wishes, claiming that it is impossible for anything other than that to be intended by Allah, the Exalted, neither directly nor indirectly, neither by expression nor by allusion. It is also possible that by "words" are meant these possible things, since they are the words of Allah in the sense of signs pointing to Him, or His word in the sense of the traces of His word, namely "Be" (kun), which is repeated according to the multiplicity of the objects of the will.

The meaning of distorting them from their places is turning them away from what Allah placed them for, namely being manifestations of His names, so they affirm for them an existence other than the existence of Allah, the Exalted. ﴿And they say: We hear﴾ what indicates unity, or: we hear what is said about these possible things, ﴿and we disobey﴾, so we do not say what you say and do not believe what you believe. They also say, in the course of addressing the knower, belittling and mocking him: ﴿And hear﴾ what contradicts what you claim, ﴿without being heard﴾, meaning may Allah not let you hear. ﴿And [they say]: Ra'ina﴾, meaning they intend to ascribe to him foolishness, which is stupidity, ﴿twisting their tongues and defaming the religion﴾ by which the knower of his Lord is guided.

﴿O you who were given the Scripture﴾, meaning those who understood its outward sense but did not understand what it pointed to of the knowledge of the inner meaning. ﴿Believe in what We have sent down﴾ upon the hearts of My friends of the knowledge bestowed directly from Us, ﴿confirming what is with you﴾ of the knowledge of the outward, for every inner meaning that contradicts the outward is false. ﴿Before We obliterate faces﴾, which are the faces of the hearts, with blindness, ﴿and turn them back on their heels﴾, looking toward the world and its adornments, after they were originally, in the nature of creation, turned toward what is in the first covenant. ﴿Or curse them as We cursed the companions of the Sabbath﴾, so that We transform their spiritual forms as We transformed the physical forms of the Jews. It is also possible that this is an address to those given the Book of readiness, commanding them to true faith and threatening them with the removal of their readiness, their return to the lowest of the low, and their distancing through transformation.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him﴾, except with repentance from it, because of His intense jealousy. ("There is no one more jealous than Allah.") ﴿But He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾, whether he repents or does not repent. They have mentioned that association has three levels, and each level has its own repentance.

The first is manifest association in persons, which belongs to the common folk, such as worshipping idols and stars for example. Its repentance is the manifestation of servanthood in affirming lordship, confirmed in both secret and public.

The second is hidden association in attributes, which belongs to the elite. It is explained as a mixture of servanthood with turning toward other than lordship. Its repentance is turning away from that turning.

The third is the most hidden association, for the elite of the elite, and it is egoism (ananiyya). Its repentance is through unity (wahda), which is the annihilation of the human nature (nasut) in the subsistence of the divine nature (lahut).
