﴿And whoever associates with Allah﴾, of any kind of association among the levels, ﴿has indeed fabricated﴾ and committed, according to his level, ﴿a great sin﴾ whose magnitude cannot be measured. ﴿Have you not considered those who claim purity for themselves?﴾, like the scholars of evil among the people of the outward, who gained from their knowledge nothing but conceit, arrogance, envy, rancor, and all other base attributes. ﴿But Allah purifies whom He wills﴾, like the knowers of Him, who see no action for themselves. It is also possible that this is an expression of wonder at one who purifies himself by himself, travels the paths of the people according to his own opinion without relying on a guiding teacher who is a perfect saint, nor on a remnant of divine knowledge, like some philosophers among the practitioners of spiritual exercises.

﴿Look how they invent lies against Allah﴾, by claiming to have purified their souls of their attributes when they have not been purified, or by ascribing the attributes of Allah to themselves while their selves still exist. ﴿And sufficient is it as a manifest sin﴾, evident and without any concealment. ﴿Have you not considered those who were given a portion of the Scripture﴾, a part of it, ﴿the comprehensive Book﴾, and by this is meant the knowledge of the outward. ﴿They believe in jibt﴾, meaning the jibt of the soul, ﴿and taghut﴾, meaning the taghut of desire, so they incline with their souls and their desires. ﴿And they say of those who disbelieve﴾, meaning for the sake of those who concealed the Truth, ﴿These are better guided than those who believe﴾ with true faith ﴿in the way﴾. ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed﴾, meaning He has distanced them from knowledge of Him and nearness to Him. ﴿And whoever Allah curses﴾, meaning whom Allah distances from that, ﴿you will not find for him a helper﴾ who guides him to the Truth.

﴿Or do they have a share in dominion? Then they would not give the people even a speck﴾. This is a censure of them for stinginess, which is the greatest blemish according to the people of Allah, the Exalted. ﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty?﴾, namely the knowledge, their honor among His creation, and their guidance of those who seek guidance. ﴿We had already given the family of Abraham﴾, who are those who follow his religion from among the people of love and intimate friendship, ﴿the Scripture﴾, meaning the knowledge of the outward, or the comprehensive Book that includes it and the knowledge of the inward, ﴿and wisdom﴾, the knowledge of the inward, or the inmost inward. ﴿And We gave them a great dominion﴾, which is arrival at the essence and not stopping at the trace. ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved in Our signs﴾, meaning they were veiled from the manifestations of Our attributes and actions, or they denied Our friends who are the manifestations of the signs, ﴿We will drive them into a Fire﴾, a great Fire, which is the fire of subjugation and veiling, or the fire of envy. ﴿Every time their skins are roasted﴾, and the wishes of their commanding souls and the demands of their desires are cut off, ﴿We will replace them with other skins﴾, through the renewal of another kind of manifestation of subjugation, or through the renewal of other blessings that appear upon Our friends whom they envied and denied. ﴿That they may taste the punishment﴾ for as long as they remain immersed in the states of vices.

﴿But those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾, meaning the deeds by which they become fit to receive the manifestations, ﴿We will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾, of the water of wisdom, the milk of innate nature, the wine of witnessing, and the honey of unveiling, ﴿abiding therein forever﴾, for the continuance of their spirits.

the spreading (over them) of what refreshes them... 

Let me render the passage properly:

"...that which cools them [i.e., the spreading over them of what refreshes them]. ﴿For them therein are spouses﴾ of the manifestations (tajalliyat) in which they take delight. ﴿Purified﴾ from the stain of deficiency. ﴿And We shall admit them into a shade, deep and extended﴾, and it is the shade of Existence and the divine attributes, and that is by the effacement of human nature (al-bashariyyah) from them. We ask God Most High for His bounty; there is no bounty but His.

Then, glory be to Him and exalted is He, He guided the believers, in the most eloquent manner, to some of the foremost (ummahat) righteous deeds, and the Mighty One, the Speaker, said:"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 58:

﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render the trusts (amanat) to their rightful owners﴾. Ibn Mardawayh transmitted, through al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, he summoned Uthman ibn Abi Talhah. When he came to him, he said: 'Show me the key.' He brought it to him, and when he extended his hand toward it, al-Abbas stood up and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, may my father and mother be your ransom, give it to me along with the siqaya (the provision of water for pilgrims).' Uthman withdrew his hand. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Show me the key, O Uthman.' He extended his hand to give it, and al-Abbas said the same words as his first statement, so Uthman withdrew his hand again. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O Uthman, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day, then give me the key.' He said: 'Take it, in the trust of Allah, the Exalted.' So he stood, opened the Ka'bah, and found in it the image of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) with arrows (qidah) by which he sought decisions by divination. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'May Allah fight the polytheists! What has Ibrahim to do with the arrows?' He removed that, and took out the Station of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), which had been inside the Ka'bah. Then he said: 'O people, this is the qiblah.' Then he went out and circumambulated the House. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) descended to him, as it has been related to us, with the command to return the key. So he summoned Uthman ibn Abi Talhah and gave him the key, and then said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you﴾, the verse."

In the narration of al-Tabarani, it is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when the key was given to him, said: "Take it, O sons of Talhah, as a perpetual and inherited possession, which none will take from you except a wrongdoer," meaning the sidanah (custodianship) of the Ka'bah.

In the tafsir of Ibn Kathir: Uthman then handed the key to his brother Shaybah ibn Abi Talhah, and it has remained in the hands of his descendants until today. Al-Tha'labi, al-Baghawi and al-Wahidi mentioned that "Uthman refused to give the key to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Had I known that he was the Messenger of Allah, I would not have withheld it.' Then Ali, may Allah honor his face, twisted his hand and took it from him. The Prophet (ﷺ) entered the Ka'bah and prayed two rak'ahs. When he came out, al-Abbas asked him to combine the sidanah and the siqaya for him, and then the verse was revealed. He commanded Ali, may Allah honor his face, to return the key and apologize to him, and that became a cause of his (Uthman's) conversion to Islam, and the revelation came that the sidanah would remain in his descendants forever."

What we have mentioned is more worthy of consideration.

Firstly: al-Ashmuni said that it is well known among the people of biography (ahl al-siyar) that Uthman ibn Talhah embraced Islam earlier, at the truce of al-Hudaybiyah, together with Khalid ibn al-Walid and Amr ibn al-As, as mentioned by Ibn Ishaq and others, and Ibn Abd al-Barr in al-Isti'ab, al-Nawawi in his Tahdhib, al-Dhahabi and others affirmed this as certain.

Secondly: because this narration contradicts what Ibn Kathir mentioned, and they have stated that his account is the sound one.

Thirdly: because according to this account the key would not be considered a trust, since Ali, may Allah honor his face, took it from him by force, and what is of this nature is usurpation (ghasb), not a trust. The claim that it is called a trust because Allah did not intend to remove it from him, or to indicate that the usurper should be like the trustee in intending to return it, or that Ali, may Allah honor his face, when he took it intending good, and that by the command of the Prophet (ﷺ), was treated as a trustee in that he bears no blame, is far-fetched.

Whatever the case, the address is general to everyone, and the trusts (amanat), which is the plural of amanah, is a verbal noun used as a designation for the object (mafʿul). Yes, the rights attached to people's obligations, whether rights of Allah or rights of the servants, whether they are actions, statements or beliefs, are included. The generality of the ruling does not negate the specificity of the cause (sabab). Narrations indicating the generality have been related from Ibn Abbas, Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Bara' ibn Azib, Abu Ja'far and Abu Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with them all, and most scholars adopted this view. From Zayd ibn Aslam, and al-Jubba'i and others chose it, that this is an address to the rulers (wulat al-amr) that they should take care of the subjects and direct them to what the religion and the Shariah require. They counted among this the appointment of positions to those deserving them, and they regarded the following address as also directed to them.

Concerning the opening of the statement with (inna), which indicates certainty, the mention of the sublime Name, and the presentation of the command in the form of a report, there is, in grandeur, in emphasizing the obligation to comply, and in indicating the great care given to its matter, nothing further to add. For this reason it has come in the hadith of Thawban, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no faith for one who has no trustworthiness."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Four things, if they are in you, then you will not mind what you have missed of this world: guarding a trust, truthfulness in speech, good character, and chastity in earning (iffat tu'mah)."

He also related from Maymun ibn Mihran: "Three things are to be rendered to the righteous and the wicked: kinship ties are to be maintained, whether the one is righteous or wicked; the trust is to be rendered to the righteous and the wicked; and the covenant is to be fulfilled for the righteous and the wicked."

Muslim related from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three are the signs of one who is a hypocrite even if he fasts, prays and claims to be a Muslim: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, and when he is entrusted he betrays." The reports on this are numerous.

It has been recited as (al-amanata) in the singular, and the intended meaning is the genus, not a specific known trust, i.e., He commands you to render any trust whatsoever.

﴿And when you judge between people, that you judge with justice﴾. This is a command to deliver the rights attached to the obligations of others to their owners, following the command to deliver the rights attached to your own obligations. The waw is for coordination (ʿatf), and the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is connected to what follows (an), and it is coordinated with (an tu'addu), and the prepositional phrase is connected to it, or to an implied element that functions as a circumstantial clause (hal) from its subject. That is: and He commands you (that you judge) with equity and fairness, or while being characterized by that when you decide between people, from among those whose command is binding upon you or who accept your judgment. This is based on the view of one who considers it permissible for the adverbial element that is the complement of what is within the relative particle's scope to precede it, and the separation between the conjunctive particle and the conjoined element by the adverbial phrase. In al-Tashil: separating the conjunction from the conjoined by an adverbial or prepositional phrase, when the element is not a verb, is permissible and is not a necessity; this differs from Abu Ali. Because of the existence of disagreement on this question, Abu Hayyan held that the adverbial phrase is connected to an implied element which the mentioned element explains, that is: and that you judge, when you judge between people, that you judge, so that it is free of what has preceded. It is not permissible for it to be connected to what precedes it, because the sense would not be sound: rendering the trust is not the time of judgment. The meaning of judgment here is that which is by general or specific authority, and they included in this what is by arbitration (tahkim).

In some reports it is related that two boys brought a dispute before al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, son of Ali, may Allah honor his face, concerning two writings they had written, and they made him the arbiter in this, so that he would judge which of the two writings was better. Ali, may Allah honor his face, saw him and said: "O my son, look how you judge, for this is a judgment, and Allah will hold you accountable for it on the Day of Resurrection."

﴿Indeed, how excellent is what Allah admonishes you with﴾. This is a resumptive sentence (jumlah mustaʾnafah) confirming the content of what precedes it, containing further kindness toward those addressed and a good encouragement to them to comply. The mention of the greatest Name is to cultivate awe. It is the subject of (inna), and the sentence (nimmā yaʿiẓukum) is its predicate. (Ma) is either in the sense of "thing" as a complete definite (maʿrifah tammah), and (yaʿiẓukum) is an attribute of an omitted noun, which is the one praised (al-makhsus bi-al-madh): that is, an excellent thing is the thing with which He admonishes you. It is also permissible to read: "excellent is He," i.e., the thing is an excellent thing with which He admonishes you, and the one praised is omitted. Or (ma) is in the sense of "that which," and what follows it is its relative clause, and it is the agent of (niʿma), and the one praised is also omitted, that is: how excellent is that which He admonishes you with, the rendering of trusts and judging with justice, as Abu al-Baqa said. This has been examined: it is established that the agent of niʿma, when it is explicit, must be preceded by the definite article of the genus or be a genitive construction, as in al-Mufassal. It was answered that Sibawayh permitted the entry of (ma), when it is a complete definite, into its place, and Ibn al-Sarraj also permitted the relative (ma), since it has the sense of the definite with al-. It has been objected to the view that (ma) is a distinguishing element (tamyiz) by saying that it is equivalent to the pronoun in vagueness, so it cannot specify it, because the distinguishing element serves to clarify the genus of what it distinguishes. It was answered by denying that it is equivalent to it, because the intended meaning of it is a great thing, and the pronoun does not indicate that. Among the strange views is what has been said: that (ma) is a restrictive particle (kaffah). So consider this. The discussion of the recitation variants regarding (nimmā) has already been mentioned.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing﴾ of all that is heard, including your statements, ﴿Seeing﴾ of everything, including your actions. Thus there is in general a promise and a warning. It has been related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ali, may Allah honor his face: "Treat the two litigants equally in your glance and in your speech."

O you who believe! After commanding those in authority, whether generally or specifically, to discharge trusts and to rule with justice, He, glorified and exalted is He, commanded people to obey them as part of obeying Him, may He be glorified and exalted, and obeying His Messenger (ﷺ). He, mighty is the One who speaks, said: ﴿Obey Allah﴾, meaning: adhere to His obedience in what He has commanded you and forbidden you. ﴿And obey the Messenger﴾, the one sent to convey His rulings to you, in everything he commands you and forbids you, likewise.

It is related from al-Kalbi that the meaning is: obey Allah in the obligatory duties (al-fara'id) and obey the Messenger in the recommended practices (al-sunan). The first view is preferable. The verb was repeated, although obedience to the Messenger is linked with obedience to Allah, the Exalted, in order to give importance to his station, peace be upon him, to cut off the misconception that it is not obligatory to comply with what is not in the Qur'an, and to indicate that he has an independent authority in obedience that was not granted to anyone else. For this reason, the verb was not repeated in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and those in authority among you﴾, indicating that they have no independent authority in such matters as the Messenger, peace be upon him, has. There has been disagreement about who is meant by them. It was said: they are the commanders of the Muslims during the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) and after him, and the caliphs, sultans, judges and others are included among them. It was also said: they are the commanders of the expeditionary detachments (al-sara.ya), and this was narrated from Abu Hurayrah and Maymun ibn Mihran.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, and Ibn Asakir related from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid in a detachment, and Ammar ibn Yasir was among them. They set out towards the people they intended, and when they reached near them they camped at night. Dhu al-'Uyaynatayn came to them and informed them, and in the morning they had all fled except one man, who told his family to gather their goods. Then he walked through the darkness of the night until he reached Khalid's camp, asking about Ammar ibn Yasir. He came to him and said: 'O Abu al-Yaqzan, I have embraced Islam and I testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. When my people heard of you, they fled, but I remained. Will my Islam benefit me tomorrow, or else I shall flee?' Ammar said: 'Rather, it will benefit you, so stay.' He stayed. When they awoke, Khalid attacked and found no one except that man, so he seized him and took his property. The news reached Ammar, and he came to Khalid and said: 'Release the man, for he has embraced Islam and is under my protection.' Khalid said: 'And why do you grant protection?' They quarrelled and raised the matter to the Prophet (ﷺ). Khalid said: 'O Messenger of Allah, will you leave this slave, the cropped-eared one, to revile me?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O Khalid, do not revile Ammar, for whoever reviles Ammar, Allah reviles him; whoever hates Ammar, Allah hates him; and whoever curses Ammar, Allah curses him.' Ammar became angry and stood up. Khalid followed him until he caught hold of his garment and apologized to him, and he was pleased. Then Allah revealed this verse."

The specification on this view is that failing to obey them, when there is neither ruler nor centre of authority, causes great corruption. It was also said: those meant are the people of knowledge. This was narrated by more than one authority from Ibn Abbas, Jabir ibn Abd Allah, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ata', and a group. Abu al-Aliyah cited as evidence His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those who derive it from them would have known it﴾, for the scholars are those who derive and extract the rulings. Many commentators, and this is not far-fetched, interpreted it to include all of them, because the term covers them all: the commanders have the management of the army and warfare, and the scholars have the preservation of the Shari'ah and of what is permissible and what is not.

The meaning of the scholars is considered problematic because of His saying: ﴿And if you dispute concerning anything﴾, for the address therein is general to the believers absolutely, while "anything" is specific to matters of religion, as indicated by what follows. The meaning is: if you dispute, O believers, you and those in authority among you, concerning a matter of the affairs of religion, ﴿then refer it﴾, return to it, ﴿to Allah﴾, that is, to His Book, ﴿and the Messenger﴾, that is, to his Sunnah. There is no doubt that this fits only the interpretation of "those in authority" as the commanders, not the scholars, because the common people may dispute with the commanders in some matters, but they have no right to dispute with the scholars, since the intended ones are the mujtahids (qualified jurists, those capable of independent reasoning), and others do not dispute with them over their rulings.

Some of them made the address in this clause directed to "those in authority" by way of iltifat (a shift in address), so that the intention of the scholars would be valid, because mujtahids may dispute with one another through argument and debate, and the meaning becomes: He commanded them to hold to what the evidence requires. It was said: on the interpretation of the broader meaning, the address may be to the believers, and the dispute between them and those in authority is considered with respect to some individuals, namely the commanders. Furthermore, obedience to them is obligatory as long as they are upon the truth, so it is not obligatory to obey them in what contradicts the Shari'ah.

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no obedience to any human being in disobedience to Allah." He, and Ahmad, and the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), and Abu Dawud, and al-Nasa'i related from him also, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a detachment and appointed over them a man from the Ansar, and he commanded them to listen to him and obey him. They angered him over something, and he said: 'Gather wood for me.' They gathered wood for him. He said: 'Light a fire.' They lit a fire. He said: 'Did the Messenger (ﷺ) not command you to listen to me and obey me?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then enter it.' They looked at one another and said: 'We only fled to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the Fire.' So his anger subsided and the fire was extinguished. When they returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they mentioned that to him, and he, peace be upon him, said: 'If they had entered it, they would never have come out of it. Obedience is only in what is good (al-ma'ruf).'"

As for whether this includes what is permissible (al-mubah), there is disagreement. It was said: it is not obligatory to obey them in it, because it is not permitted for anyone to forbid what Allah has made lawful, nor to make lawful what Allah has forbidden. It was also said: it is obligatory, as al-Haskafi and others explicitly stated. Some of the verifying scholars of the Shafi'is said: obeying the Imam in his command and prohibition is obligatory, so long as he does not command something forbidden. Others said: what appears is that what he commands that contains no general benefit is obligatory to comply with only outwardly, whereas what contains such benefit is obligatory inwardly as well. The same applies to what is permissible but harmful to the one commanded. Then, is the consideration in the permissible and the recommended (mandub) matter that is commanded according to the belief of the commander? So if he commands something permissible which in his view is a Sunnah but in the view of the one commanded it is not, is it obligatory to comply outwardly only, or inwardly as well? And the reverse, and this is reversed accordingly. Each is a possibility. The apparent generality of their statements in the matter of the Imam commanding people to fast for a second rain-prayer (istisqa') is that they did not distinguish between whether the fast commanded there is recommended in the view of the commander or not. This is supported by what they established in the chapter on following the Imam (al-iqtida'), that the consideration is the belief of the follower (ma'mum), not of the Imam. I have not come across what our companions said on this question, so let it be examined.

Furthermore, whoever denies qiyas (analogical reasoning) has cited this verse, because Allah, exalted is He, made the return to the Book and the Sunnah obligatory and not to qiyas. The truth, however, is that the verse is evidence for establishing qiyas, indeed it includes all the legal sources, for the meaning of obedience to Allah is acting upon the Book, the meaning of obedience to the Messenger is acting upon the Sunnah, and the meaning of returning to them is qiyas, because returning a disputed matter, which is not known from the explicit text, to what is explicitly stated is done only by way of analogy and building upon it, and qiyas is nothing beyond that. It is known from His saying, glorified is He: ﴿if you dispute﴾ that when there is no dispute, one acts upon what has been agreed upon, which is ijma' (scholarly consensus).

﴿If you believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ is connected to the final command mentioned in the place of dispute, since it is that which requires warning against opposing it. The response to the condition is omitted according to the majority of the Basran grammarians, relying on what is mentioned indicating it, and the statement is like (if you are my son, then obey me). Belief in Allah, the Exalted, necessitates complying with His command, and likewise belief in the Last Day, because of the punishment for disobedience therein. ﴿That﴾, that is, the return commanded, ﴿is best﴾, of great importance. And if it were understood, as some have said, to refer to all that has preceded, by way of consequence, it would be fitting.

Al-Tabarsi said: it is a reference to what has preceded of the commands, that is: obedience to Allah, obedience to His Messenger (ﷺ) and to those in authority, and the return of the disputed matter to Allah and the Messenger, peace be upon him, ﴿is better﴾ for you and more right, ﴿(and more excellent)﴾, that is, more praiseworthy in itself, ﴿in outcome﴾, that is, in consequence (ta'wil). This was said by Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd. The superlative in both places is to give the sense of perfection contrary to its literal form. The reason for placing the first before the second is that people's attention generally fixes upon what benefits them. It was also said: the meaning is "better" for you in this world, and "more excellent in outcome" in the Hereafter, and the reason for placing it first is more evident.

It is related from al-Zajjaj that the meaning of "more excellent in interpretation" is more excellent than your own interpretation of it, without returning it to a root in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet (ﷺ). Ta'wil (interpretation) may mean either returning to the outcome and consequence, or explaining the intended meaning of a word that is not apparent from it. Both are literal meanings, though the second has become predominant in common usage, and for this reason it stands in contrast to tafsir (exegesis).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 60:

﴿Have you not seen﴾ is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) and an expression of wonder directed at him, peace be upon him; that is, "Have you not looked, or has not your knowledge reached, [concerning] those who ﴿claim﴾." Za'm (claim) is, as in the Qamus, a word with three vowel patterns for its verbal form, meaning: truth, falsehood, and lie (it is an opposite term), and it is most often used for what is doubtful; from this it has been said that it is "a saying without evidence." Its use has nevertheless become frequent in the sense of a true statement. In a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Gabriel claimed (za'ama)," and in the hadith of Dimam ibn Tha'labah (may Allah be pleased with him): "Your messenger claimed (za'ama)." Sibawayh in his Kitab frequently uses the phrase "al-Khalil claimed (za'ama al-Khalil) that such-and-such," in matters he accepts. In Nawawi's commentary on Muslim it is stated that za'ama in all of this carries the meaning of "said," and what is meant here is simply assertion, that is, they assert ﴿that they have believed in what has been sent down to you﴾, meaning the Qur'an:

﴿And what was sent down﴾ to Musa (peace be upon him) ﴿before you﴾, which is the Torah. They are described with this assertion to emphasise the wonder and to intensify the rebuke and the condemnation. It is also read as (anzala) and (unzila) in the passive/active forms. ﴿They desire to take their judgement to the Taghut﴾ is an explanation of the locus of the wonder, following the pattern of its counterparts.

Al-Tha'labi and Ibn Abi Hatim related, through several chains, from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): "A man from the hypocrites, called Bishr, had a dispute with a Jew. The Jews invited him to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the hypocrite invited him to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. Then they both took their dispute to the Prophet (ﷺ), who ruled in favour of the Jew, but the hypocrite was not satisfied and said: 'Come, let us take it to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.' The Jew said to 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ruled for us, but he did not accept his judgement.' So he said to the hypocrite: 'Is that so?' He said: 'Yes.' 'Umar said: 'Stay where you are until I come out to you.' 'Umar went in, took up his sword, then came out and struck the neck of the hypocrite until he died. Then he said: 'This is how I judge for one who does not accept the judgement of Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ).' Then it was revealed."

In some reports: Gabriel (peace be upon him) said: "Indeed 'Umar distinguished between truth and falsehood," and the Prophet (ﷺ) named him al-Faruq (the Distinguisher), may Allah be pleased with him.

According to this, the Taghut is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and applying it to him literally is based on its being in the sense of one who is extremely tyrannical (kathir al-tughyan), or that it is a name given to him as a title, like al-Faruq for 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). Perhaps it is in contrast to the Taghut itself. Included in its meaning is everyone who judges by falsehood and prefers it for their own sake. It is also possible that the Taghut means Satan, and applying it to al-Akhass ibn al-Ashraf is either a metaphor or a literal usage. The figurative element lies in attributing the act of seeking judgement to him, through the relation of the act to its object by means of an intermediary.

It has also been said that seeking judgement from him is seeking judgement from Satan, insofar as he is the one who drives them to it, so transferring it from Satan to him is by way of metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal).

Al-Tabarani related, with a sound chain, also from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "Abu Barzah al-Aslami was a soothsayer who judged between the Jews in what they disputed, so some Muslims went to him for judgement, and Allah revealed the verse concerning them."

Al-Suddi related, through Ibn Jarir: "Some people from the Jews of Qurayzah and al-Nadir had embraced Islam, and some of them were hypocrites. There was a dispute among them over a slain man, and the hypocrites among them refused except to take it to Abu Barzah. They set out to him and asked him, and he said: 'Increase the morsel (i.e., the bribe).' They said: 'For you, ten wasqs.' He said: 'No, rather a hundred wasqs.' They refused to give him more than ten, so Allah revealed concerning them what you hear."

On this basis, the verse contains an indication of the monstrousness of the act of seeking judgement itself, which is not hidden. It also better suits the description of the hypocrites with the claim of believing in the Torah. The report of al-Tabarani can be read in this light, by taking the Muslims in it to mean the hypocrites from among those of Qurayzah and al-Nadir who had embraced Islam.

﴿And they were commanded to reject it﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (yuridun). It contains emphasis for the wonder, like the preceding description. The pronoun in the genitive refers to the Taghut, and this is evident if it is intended to mean Satan; otherwise it refers to it in respect of its description rather than its essence, that is: they were commanded to reject one who is extremely tyrannical or resembles Satan. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the seeking of judgement understood from (yatahakamu), but this is remote.

Abbas ibn al-Mufaddal read (bihā), and it has also been read (bihinna). The pronoun here too refers to the Taghut, since it can be used for the singular and the plural; when the plural is intended it is feminine in terms of the meaning of a group, as has already been mentioned.

﴿And Satan desires to lead them astray with far-reaching error﴾ is coordinated with the circumstantial clause and falls under the ruling of wonder. In it, according to some possibilities, the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, with the meaning "they desire to take their judgement to Satan," and he is intent on their misguidance, whereas they do not desire to take their judgement to you, while you are intent on guiding them. (Ḍalālan) is either an infinitive emphasising the verb mentioned with the augmentation removed, on the pattern of what has been said about ﴿He brought you forth from the earth as a growth﴾; or it is an emphasis of its verb implied by what is mentioned, that is, (fa-yaḍillūna ḍalālan). Describing it with "far" (al-bu'd), which is the attribute of what it qualifies, is for intensification.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 61:

﴿And when it is said to them﴾, i.e., to those claimants, ﴿"Come to what Allah has revealed"﴾ in the Qur'an of rulings, ﴿and to the Messenger﴾, who was sent to judge by it, ﴿you see﴾, i.e., you perceive or know, ﴿the hypocrites﴾, and they are the claimants. The explicit mention in place of the pronoun serves to record hypocrisy against them, to censure them for it, and to indicate the reason for the ruling, i.e., "you see them, because of their hypocrisy," ﴿turning away﴾, i.e., they turn aside, ﴿from you with a turning away﴾, i.e., with what a turning away it is. It is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing its verb, and its tanwin is for magnification. It has been said that it is a noun for the verbal noun which is the ṣadd (ṣadd), and this is attributed to al-Khalil. The more apparent view is that it is a verbal noun of the intransitive (ṣadda), while ṣadd is the verbal noun of the transitive. As for the claim that (yaṣuddūna) here is transitive with its object omitted, i.e., "they hinder those who seek judgment," meaning they prevent them from what they have no need of, this sentence completes the matter of wonder by clarifying their turning away from that within the act of seeking judgment from the Taghut.

Al-Hasan read (taʿālaw) with a ḍamma on the lām, on the basis that the lām of the verb was elided irregularly (iʿtibāṭan), as they say: mā bālaytu bihi bālatan, and its original form is bāliyah like ʿāfiyah; and as al-Kisa'i said regarding (āyah) that its original form is āyiyah like fāʿilah, so the lām became like the lām [of the word], and it was ḍammed to match the wāw. From this is the saying of the people of Makkah: taʿālī with a kasra on the lām for a woman, and it is an attested dialect, which Ibn Jinni established; so no heed is paid to one who committed a grammatical error, like Ibn Hisham al-Hamdani,
in it, where he says:

Ayā jārataā mā anṣafa al-dahru baynanā
taʿālī uqāsimki al-humūma taʿālī

and there is no need to say that the first (taʿālay) has a fatḥah on the lām while the second has a kasrah for the rhyme, as is not hidden.

The original meaning of this verb is the request to come up to a high place,

Then it was generalized: "So how [will it be] when a disaster befalls them," that is, strikes them, "a calamity" (nakbah) that exposes their hypocrisy, "because of what their hands have put forward," meaning because of the transgressions they committed, such as seeking judgment from the false deity (al-taghut) and turning away from your ruling. "Then they come to you" to make excuses. This is a conjunction (atf) upon "befalls them," and the purpose is to magnify what has overtaken them. It was also said that it is upon "they turn away" (yasuddun), and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD). "Swearing" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "they come to you," meaning: swearing to you by Allah, "We intended only" (in aradna) that is, we did not intend by our seeking judgment from others than you, "except goodness" (ihsanan) toward the disputants "and conciliation" (tawfiqan) between them. We did not intend, by resorting to other than you, a dissatisfaction with your ruling, so do not hold us accountable for what we did.

This is a threat against them for what they did, and that they will regret when regret will not benefit them, and they will make excuses when excuses will not avail them. It was also said: the people of the slain man came seeking his blood, and said: "If we intended, by seeking judgment from ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), only that he would show goodness to our companion and reconcile him with his adversary..." Thus "idha" here is for mere temporal sense (zarfiyyah) and not for the future (istiqbal).

It was also said: the one meant by the verse is ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy, and the calamity is what befell him and his companions of humiliation upon their return from the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq, which is the expedition of Muraysi', when Surat al-Munafiqun was revealed, so they were compelled to humility and apology, as will be mentioned in its proper place, if Allah the Exalted wills. They said: "We intended by the speech between the two disputing parties in that expedition nothing but good," or [it was] the calamity of death, when he humbly implored the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for pardon and forgiveness, and asked him to grant him his garment so that he might shield himself with it from the Fire.

﴿Those﴾, that is, the hypocrites mentioned, ﴿whom Allah knows what is in their hearts﴾, of the kinds of evil that contradict what they showed you of (banat ghayr, an idiom meaning "lies," lit. "daughters of other than..."), and what they brought of (adhunay 'anaq, an idiom meaning "fabrications," lit. "ears of a she-goat").

﴿So turn away from them﴾ since their state is such, ﴿from them﴾, that is, from accepting their excuse. This necessarily entails turning away from demanding the blood of the slain, since it is forfeited (hadar). It was also said: from punishing them, for a benefit in sparing them. And do not show them your knowledge of what is in their corrupt inner selves, so that they remain upon the fires of dread.

﴿And admonish them﴾ with your tongue and restrain them from hypocrisy, ﴿and speak to them in their souls﴾, that is, speak to them privately, with no one present with them, for this is more conducive to the acceptance of counsel. This is why it was said: "Advising in front of people is reproach." Or: speak to them concerning the matter of their own selves, and its meaning, ﴿a far-reaching word﴾, effective, reaching the very core of the intended meaning, corresponding to what it was driven toward of the aim. The adverbial phrase, under both interpretations, is connected to the command.

It was also said: it is connected to (far-reaching). This is evident according to the school of the Kufans, while the Basrans do not permit it, because the complement of an adjective, in their view, does not precede the modified noun, since a complement precedes only where its governing element may precede. 

It was said: this is permissible only if it is an adverbial phrase, and some have strengthened this. It was also said: it is connected to an omitted element which the mentioned word explains, but this is far-fetched. The meaning under the connection is: "Speak to them a far-reaching word in their souls," effective in them, by which they are greatly grieved, and from which they sense fear, namely the threat of killing and extermination, and the notification that what their corrupt hearts harbor of evil and hypocrisy is in the sight of Allah the Exalted and within His hearing, not hidden from Him, glorified is He, and that this necessitates what makes foreheads turn gray. This leniency and delay are only for their showing faith and concealing disbelief. And if they display discord and emerge with their persons from the tunnel of hypocrisy, then the spears and swords will entertain them, and the wide plains will become narrow upon them with the tremendous affliction.

The first verse has been used as evidence that a calamity may befall a person because of sins he has committed. Then the scholars differed on this. Al-Jubba'i said: this occurs only as punishment for the repentant. Abu Hashim said: it occurs as a lutf (divine kindness that draws one toward obedience).

Qadi Abd al-Jabbar said: it may be a lutf, and it may be a recompense, and this depends on evidence.

[p. 70]

Al-Alusi's commentary on Surah 4, verse 64:

﴿We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by Allah's permission.﴾ This is a preface to explaining their error, which lies in their occupying themselves with covering the fire of their crime with the dry, worthless straw of their false excuses, and in not extinguishing it with the water of repentance. The meaning is: We did not send any messenger among the messengers, for any purpose, except that he be obeyed by the permission of Allah, the Exalted, and by His command to those to whom he was sent that they obey him. This is because he conveys on behalf of Him, mighty is His majesty; so his obedience is obedience to Him, and his disobedience is disobedience to Him. Or it means: by His facilitating and enabling, glorified is He, their obedience to him. The significance of turning from the pronoun to the sublime Name is not hidden.

The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) cited this verse as evidence that Allah wills only good, and that evil runs contrary to His will. The author of al-Taysir (a commentary) answered this by saying that the meaning is: "except that the one whom He has permitted to obey him, and whom He has willed to obey him, obeys him. As for the one whom He has not permitted, He wills his non-obedience; therefore he does not obey him, and he is a disbeliever." Or he answered that what is intended is the imposition of obedience, i.e., "We did not send a messenger except to impose obedience to him upon people, so that whoever submits is rewarded and whoever takes the path of obstinacy is punished. Thus their claim cannot stand as proof for their position."

It was also cited as evidence by those who affirm purpose (gharad, final cause) in the acts of Allah, the Exalted, which is clear. This cannot be interpreted as meaning an end (ghayah) rather than a purpose, because the obedience of all people does not follow from the sending of messengers, unless it is said that the end is that he be obeyed by permission, not that all be obeyed; for whoever has no permission does not obey. The discussion of this question has already preceded.

﴿And if, when they had wronged themselves﴾ by hypocrisy and by seeking judgment from the false deity (ṭāghūt), and thereby exposing themselves to ruin, ﴿they had come to you﴾ immediately after their wrongdoing, without delay, seeking your intercession, repenting of their crime, not combining (in their coming) worthless straw and poor measure, with their false excuses and their wicked oaths, ﴿and asked Allah for forgiveness﴾ for their sins, and desisted from what they were engaged in, and regretted what they had done.

﴿And the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them﴾ and asked Allah, the Exalted, to accept their repentance and forgive their sins. The expression "asked forgiveness (istaghfara)" rather than "you asked forgiveness (istaghfarta)" etc. is a glorification of the rank of the Messenger of Allah (may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him), in that it turns away from addressing him directly to what is among his great qualities, in the manner of "the commander ruled thus" in place of "you ruled." It is also an exaltation of his asking forgiveness (peace be upon him), in that it attributes it to a term that indicates the loftiness of his station.

﴿they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance, Merciful﴾. That is: they would have known Him to be One who accepts their repentance, bestowing on them favor by overlooking the sins that had passed. Whoever interprets "finding" (wijdān) as "encountering" (muṣādafah) makes the first attribute a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), and the second a substitute (badal) for it, or a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in it or of its like. And placing the all-encompassing Name in the position of the pronoun indicates the magnitude of acceptance and mercy.

**[p. 71]**

﴿So no, by your Lord﴾: that is, *fa-wa-Rabbika* (so by your Lord). The *la* (لا) is an extra particle (*mazidah*, "redundant") used to emphasise the sense of the oath (*qasam*), not to emphasise the negation in its answer, namely His words, exalted is He: ﴿they do not believe﴾. This is because it is also inserted with affirmation, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿So no, I swear by the positions of the stars﴾. This is what al-Zamakhshari and those who followed him chose regarding the *la* that is mentioned before an oath.

It has also been said that it is a rejection of an assumed statement, meaning: the matter is not as you claim. Al-Tabrisi chose this view. It has also been said that it is extra to emphasise the negation in the answer, and to emphasise the oath if there is no negation. Ibn al-Munir said: "The apparent view to me is that here it is a preparatory particle (*tawti'ah*) for the negation sworn about." Al-Zamakhshari did not mention any obstacle to this except that it comes in affirmation for a different meaning. He does not deny its coming in negation in the other sense of preparation. Moreover, it has not come in the Qur'an except with an explicit verb of oath, and with an oath by other than Allah, the Exalted, such as: ﴿I swear by this city﴾, ﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾, ﴿So I swear by the twilight﴾, intending to emphasise the oath
**[p. 71 continued]**
and to magnify what is sworn by, since one swears by a thing only out of magnifying it. So it is as if by its insertion he is saying: "My magnifying of these things by swearing by them is [as though it were] no magnification at all," meaning that they deserve greater veneration than that. This is not fitting in an oath by Allah, the Exalted, since there is no suspicion to be removed. Its extra use has not been heard with an oath by Allah except when the answer is negative. This shows that with it, it is an extra, preparatory particle for the negation occurring in the answer. You will hardly find it outside the Mighty Book entering upon an affirmative oath. The entry of this particle upon an oath whose answer is a negation is common, as in his saying:

*So no, by your father, daughter of al-Amiri,*
*the people do not claim that I flee.*

And his saying:

*Did not Umamah call out with departure*
*so as to grieve me? No, by you, I do not care.*

And his saying:

*He saw a flash and urged on a young camel above a stallion,*
*so no, by you, it neither flowed nor rained.*

And [there are] countless others. From this the difference between the two contexts is known. As for the answer to their saying that there is no difference between them, reflect on that, for it deserves reflection.

﴿until they make you a judge (*yuhakkimuka*)﴾: that is, they make you an arbiter (*hakam*) or a judge (*hakim*). Shaykh al-Islam said: "they take their disputes to you and bring them before you." The form of *tahkim* was used even though he, ﷺ, is a judge by the command of Allah, to indicate that what is fitting for them is that they make him, upon him be blessings and peace, an arbiter among them, and accept his ruling, even if his being a judge in absolute terms is set aside. ﴿in what is disputed among them﴾: that is, in what has come into disagreement and confusion among them of matters. From this comes *al-shajar* (tree), because its branches intertwine. It is also said that a dispute is called *tashajur*, because the disputants' opinions differ and their claims conflict, and some of them become mixed with others.

﴿then they do not find﴾: this is a conjunction (*'atf*) upon an implied element to which the speech leads, meaning: "so you judge between them, then they do not find" ﴿in their souls﴾ and hearts ﴿any discomfort (*haraj*)﴾: that is, doubt, as Mujahid said; or constriction, as al-Jubba'i said; or sin, as is related from al-Dahhak. Some of the verifiers chose to interpret it as constriction of the breast, due to a trace of aversion and refusal, since some disbelievers were certain of the signs without doubt, yet they denied them out of injustice and arrogance, and so they were not believers. What is related from al-Dahhak can be referred to whichever of the two meanings you wish. The negation of finding discomfort is more eloquent than the negation of discomfort itself, as is not hidden. It is the direct object of *yajidu* (they find). The adverbial phrase (*zarf*) is said to be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from it, or to be connected to what is before it.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿of what you have decided﴾ are connected to an omitted element that functions as an adjective to *haraj* (discomfort). Abu al-Baqa' permitted its connection to *haraj* itself. The word *ma* may be a relative pronoun, an indefinite noun with a descriptive clause, or a verbal-masdar particle, meaning: "of that which you decided," that is, "you decided concerning it," or "of something you decided," or "of your judgement."

﴿and submit with full submission﴾: that is, they yield to your command and accept it outwardly and inwardly, as the emphasis (*tawkid*) indicates. Perhaps the ruling of this verse remains until the Day of Resurrection, and it is not restricted to those who were in the time of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. For the judgement of his law, upon him be blessings and peace, is his judgement. It has been related from al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "If a people worshipped Allah, the Exalted, established prayer, paid zakat, fasted Ramadan, and performed the pilgrimage to the House, then said of something the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, did: 'Would that he had done other than what he did,' or found in themselves any discomfort, they would be polytheists." Then he recited this verse.

The occasion of its revelation, as al-Sha'bi and Mujahid said, is the story already mentioned of Bishr
**[p. 72]**
and the Jew, between whom Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, judged by what he judged.

Al-Bukhari and Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, and al-Bayhaqi related, by way of al-Zuhri, that Urwa ibn al-Zubayr told him: "from al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, that he disputed with a man of the Ansar before the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, concerning water-channels from the lava-field that both of them used to irrigate the palm trees. The Ansari said: 'Release the water so that it flows.' He refused. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: 'Irrigate, O Zubayr, then release the water to your neighbour.' The Ansari became angry and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, [did you rule so] because he is your paternal aunt's son?' The face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ changed colour. Then he said: 'Irrigate, O Zubayr, then hold back the water until it reaches the top of the bank (*al-jadr*), then release the water to your neighbour.'" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had given al-Zubayr his full right, and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, had previously suggested to al-Zubayr an opinion in which he intended ease for him and for the Ansari. When the Ansari provoked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, al-Zubayr was given his full right in the explicit ruling. Al-Zubayr said: "I do not think this verse was revealed except concerning that: ﴿So no, by your Lord﴾..." and so on.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 66:

﴿And if We had prescribed for them﴾, i.e., We made obligatory and required, ﴿that you kill yourselves﴾, i.e., as We commanded the Children of Israel. Interpreting it as referring to engaging in jihad is far-fetched. ﴿Or leave your homes﴾, as We also commanded the Children of Israel to leave Egypt.

The meaning is: We only prescribed for them obedience to the Messenger, submission to his judgment, and contentment with it. And if We had prescribed for them killing and leaving their homes, as We prescribed that for others, ﴿they would not have done it, except a few of them﴾. They are the sincere believers, such as Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him.

Ibn Abi Hatim related, from Amir ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "When this verse was revealed, Abu Bakr said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if you commanded me to kill myself, I would do it.' He said: 'You have spoken the truth, O Abu Bakr.'" And (the verse applies) to Abd Allah ibn Rawahah. He related from Shurayh ibn Ubayd: "When it was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) pointed at him with his hand and said: 'If Allah the Exalted had prescribed that, this man would be among those few.'" And (it applies) to Ibn Umm Abd. He related from Sufyan that the Prophet (ﷺ) said about him: "If it had been revealed, he would have been among them." He also related from al-Hasan who said: "When this verse was revealed, some of the Companions said: 'If our Lord had commanded it, we would have done it.' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Faith is firmer in the hearts of its people than the firm mountains.'" It was also narrated that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "By Allah, if we were commanded, we would have done it. Praise be to Allah who has spared us." This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "Indeed, among my nation are men whose faith is firmer in their hearts than the firm mountains."

In some reports, when al-Zubayr and his companion went out after the judgment from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they passed by al-Miqdad, who said: "Whose judgment was it?" The Ansari said: "The son of his paternal aunt," and twisted his cheek. A Jew who was with al-Miqdad noticed this and said: "May Allah fight these people! They testify that he is the Messenger of Allah, yet they accuse him concerning a judgment he passes between them. By Allah, we once sinned in the lifetime of Musa, peace be upon him, and he called us to repent of it, saying: ﴿kill yourselves﴾, so we did, and our dead reached seventy thousand, in obedience to our Lord, until He was pleased with us." Thabit ibn Qays then said: "Indeed, by Allah, Allah the Exalted knows my sincerity. If Muhammad (ﷺ) commanded me to kill myself, I would kill myself."

It is also narrated that the speaker of that was he (Thabit), together with Ibn Mas'ud and Ammar ibn Yasir, and that this reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning them, and he said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, indeed among my nation are men whose faith is firmer in their hearts than the firm mountains." And the verse was revealed concerning them.

In the narration of al-Baghawi, [it is limited] to Thabit ibn Qays. The connection of mentioning this verse with this report is clear. Perhaps for this reason the author of al-Kashshaf said regarding its meaning: "If We had made obligatory for them what We made obligatory for the Children of Israel, namely killing themselves or leaving their homes when they were ordered to repent of worshipping the calf, they would not have done it, except a few." Some of them said: the meaning is that We have lightened the burden for them, as we were content from them in their repentance with their making you judge and submitting to him. Had We made their repentance like the repentance of the Children of Israel, they would not have repented. What is understood from the implication of the reliable reports is that this writing has no connection with the ordering to repent. Perhaps the purpose of mentioning that is merely to draw attention to the deficiency of many people and the weakness of their Islam, after stating that their faith is not complete unless they submit completely.

The apparent meaning of what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, that the Children of Israel were commanded to leave their homes when they were ordered to repent, is hardly correct if by "homes" the Egyptian homes are meant. This is because the ordering to repent from worshipping the calf occurred only after they had left Egypt and after the splitting of the sea, and this is beyond doubt. Moreover, we do not accept that they were commanded to leave at any time as a repentance. Interpreting "humiliation" as leaving one's homes, because the humiliation of estrangement is a metaphor mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf will be overtaken by anger from their Lord and humiliation﴾, is not useful, since the verse does not indicate an order to that. And the dispute about it is also a dispute about whether this verse concerns those who repented from worshipping the calf.

Some verifiers have established that it concerns the Egyptians who persisted in worshipping it, as you will know, God willing. It is strange that the author of al-Kashf did not respond to the words of the author of al-Kashshaf with more than saying that it is not stated explicitly in the Qur'an, and then he quoted his words on the verse.

Furthermore, the discussion about "law" (lau) here is more famous than fire on a flag. Its rule, as they said, is that it should be followed by a verb. For this reason al-Tabarsi said: the estimate is: "If it had happened, We would have prescribed for them." Al-Zajjaj said: although that is its rule, the heavy "inna" (إنَّ) is placed after it, because it substitutes for the subject and predicate. We say: "I thought that you were knowledgeable," as we say: "I thought you knowledgeable," meaning: "I thought your knowledge established." So here it substitutes for the verb and the subject, just as there it substitutes for the subject and predicate.

The plural pronoun in ﴿upon them﴾ and what follows it was said to refer to the hypocrites, and it was attributed to Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. It is objected that the act of "a few of them" is inconceivable, since they are the hypocrites whose souls are not content with anything short of killing by many degrees, and everything short of death is easy. How then would they be content with killing and comply with the command to it?! It was answered that the meaning is: if We had prescribed that for the hypocrites, only a few of them would have done it, out of showing off and seeking reputation. Then the matter would have become difficult for them, and their disbelief would have been revealed. Since We did not do that to them, but imposed on them easy things, let them abandon hypocrisy and adhere to sincerity. This was attributed to al-Balkhi.

It is not hidden that his (ﷺ) saying about Abd Allah ibn Rawahah: "If Allah the Exalted had prescribed that, he would have been among them," and similarly the other earlier reports, refuse this interpretation most strongly, because they are given in praise. There is no praise in those mentioned being among the few who comply with the command out of showing off and seeking reputation; rather that is a great blame for them, and far be it from them. It was also said that the reference is to people in general, and the fewness is relative, because the intended "few" are the believers, who, although numerous, are few in comparison to others among the hypocrites, disbelievers and rebels: ﴿And most people, even if you were eager, are not believers﴾. In that case, it is not objected that it would follow from the verse that the Children of Israel were stronger in faith than the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since they complied with Allah's command to kill themselves until their dead reached seventy thousand, whereas if it were from the first generation, only a few would have complied.

Some people took the verse as an explanation of the perfection of gentleness toward this nation, since He does not accept killing from them except a few, because Allah the Exalted pardons them for a small killing, and does not leave them to kill a great deal as the Children of Israel did. This is not because they do not act as the Children of Israel did due to the fewness of the sincere among them and the abundance of the sincere among the Children of Israel, so that preference would follow.

It was said: it is possible that many of the Children of Israel were killed, because if they had not submitted, the punishment of Allah the Exalted would have destroyed them. This nation is safe until the Day of Resurrection, so they do not hasten as they hastened, due to the absence of fear of annihilation, not because they are inferior or because the Children of Israel were stronger in faith than them. You know that the verse is far from benefiting the perfection of gentleness, and neither the preceding context nor the subsequent context suggests this at all. The fear of annihilation and its absence is something that hardly occurs to the mind, as is not hidden to one who knows men by truth, not truth by men.

The pronoun in the accusative in ﴿they did it﴾ refers to what was written, which includes killing and leaving, because the verb indicates it. Or it refers to killing and leaving. And because of the conjunction with "or" the pronoun must be singular, since it refers to one of the two matters. The saying of Imam al-Razi, that the pronoun refers to both together by interpretation, is rejected by the grammatical rules. And "a few" (qalil) is a substitute for the raised pronoun in ﴿they did it﴾, because the sentence is non-affirmative.

Ibn Amir recited: ﴿except a few﴾ with the accusative (qalilan). Many scholars took it as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, and the exception is "emptied" (istithna' mufarragh), meaning: ﴿they did it not except a few deed﴾. In that case the "min" (مِن) in ﴿of them﴾ is for beginning, as in: "I did not strike him except a strike from you, severe."

Al-Tibi said: it is an explanation of the pronoun in "they did," like His saying: ﴿those who disbelieved among them will be touched﴾, in the manner of abstraction. This is not correct. What seems to have led them to this and to turning away from saying it is accusative as an exception is that the accusative in a non-affirmative sentence is not preferred, so the Qur'an should not be interpreted by it, as al-Zajjaj's words indicate, where he said: the accusative is permissible outside the Qur'an. But Ibn al-Hajib said: there is no distance in the least of the reciters being upon the stronger reading. Al-Himsi verified this. It was also said: rather, their consensus is evidence that this is the stronger, because they are the masters of the arts who take from the niche of prophethood, and the grammarians' explanation is not to be considered.

Some also preferred the accusative as an exception here, because there is agreement of the two readings in meaning, which is something to be concerned about, and because directing the sentence to the other reading involves artificiality and tenuousness. Abu Amr and Yaqub recited: ﴿ani qtulu﴾ with a kasra on the nun, according to the original rule of avoiding two consecutive unvocalized letters, and ﴿awi ukhruju﴾ with a damma on the waw for assimilation and resemblance to the plural waw in such as: ﴿and do not forget graciousness among yourselves﴾.

Hamzah and Asim recited both with a kasra, according to the original, and the rest with a damma on both, and this is clear. And "an" (أنْ), whatever its nun, is either explanatory of "that We wrote" in the sense of "commanded," and its transitivity by "upon" does no harm, because it has not left its meaning; and even if it left it, its transitivity according to its original meaning is permissible, as in "the situation spoke with such-and-such," where the verb is transitive with "bi," though they sometimes mean by it "indicated," which is transitive with "upon."

If you refuse this, and I do not think you will, we say it means "We revealed," and it is either a verbal (masdariyya) particle, which is the apparent meaning, and the disappearance of the command by the composition does no harm, because it is a command by estimation.

﴿And if they had done what﴾, i.e., what they are commanded to do, accompanied by promise and threat, namely following the Messenger (ﷺ) and submitting to his judgment outwardly and inwardly, ﴿it would have been better for them﴾ — their doing that — ﴿in the present and in the future﴾, ﴿and firmer in establishing them﴾ upon the truth and the right, and more protective of them from error, and further from doubts, as He the Glorified said: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾.

It was also said: its meaning is: more beneficial, because benefit from the truth endures and does not perish, since it is connected to the reward of the Hereafter, whereas benefit from falsehood perishes and vanishes, and is connected to the punishment of the Hereafter,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verses 67–68:

﴿And We would surely have given them﴾ — We would have given them ﴿from Us﴾, from Our presence, ﴿a great reward﴾, a great recompense, ﴿which no one knows the beginning of, nor reaches its end﴾. He mentioned ﴿from Us﴾ only for emphasis and exaggeration, and it is connected to ﴿We would have given them﴾.

It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of ﴿a reward﴾, and that the waw is for conjunction, and that ﴿We would have given them﴾ is verbally conjoined to ﴿it would have been better for them﴾, and that ﴿idhan﴾ (then) is inserted to indicate that this final recompense follows the sequence of the preceding consequence upon the antecedent. To show and confirm this, the muhaqqiqun said: it is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "And what would be for them after the firm adherence?" So it was said: ﴿idhan﴾ (then), if they had held firm, ﴿We would have given them﴾. Their meaning is not that it is an answer to a question that is implied verbally and in meaning, for otherwise its being joined with the waw would have had no justification. The appearance of ﴿law﴾ (if) is not because it is implied, but to confirm that this is an answer to the condition, though after considering its first answer. By the "answer" in their saying collectively that ﴿idhan﴾ is always a particle of answer, they mean that it occurs in a statement that is not initiated, but in a statement built upon something preceding it, either spoken or implied, whether it is a condition, the words of a questioner, or the like. Just as the answer it necessarily or usually requires is not meant except what is a recompense for the act of an agent, whether the questioner or another, and by this the objections raised in this context are dispelled.

Al-Tibi claimed that what we have pointed to of the implied supposition is an artificial construction in three respects, and that it is a delusion arising from heedlessness of the intended meaning, like what the Allama al-Thani claimed. So reflect upon it.

﴿And We would surely have guided them to a straight path﴾, and it is the stations after faith, which open their doors to those who act. Abu Nu'aym has related in al-Hilya, from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever acts upon what he knows, Allah will bequeath to him the knowledge of what he did not know." And al-Jubba'i said: the meaning is: and We would have guided them in the Hereafter to the path of Paradise.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verses 67–68:

﴿And We would surely have given them﴾ — We would have given them ﴿from Us﴾, from Our presence, ﴿a great reward﴾, a great recompense, ﴿which no one knows the beginning of, nor reaches its end﴾. He mentioned ﴿from Us﴾ only for emphasis and exaggeration, and it is connected to ﴿We would have given them﴾.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 69 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Whoever obeys God﴾ by submitting to His commands and prohibitions, ﴿and the Messenger﴾, who conveys what was revealed to him, by following his sharia and accepting his judgment. The statement is resumed (mustaʼnaf), and in it there is an abundance of encouragement to obedience and increased enticement toward it, by clarifying that its outcome is the highest goal that the aspirations of nations reach, the loftiest thing toward which their hopes extend and their gazes aspire through their resolve: being in the company of the greatest of creation in rank and the highest of them in standing. It also includes an explanation of what was left vague and a detailing of what was stated in summary in the answer to the preceding conditional clause.

"Man" (man) is a conditional particle. The singular pronoun in "yuti" (obeys) is in agreement with the wording, while the plural in His words, glorified is He, ﴿then those﴾, is in agreement with the meaning. That is, the obedient ones whose rank is elevated and whose station is far above in nobility and excellence.

﴿in the company of those whom God has blessed﴾ with what the expression falls short of detailing and explaining, ﴿from among the prophets﴾. This is an explanation of those who are blessed. It is a circumstantial clause (hal), either from "those" (alladhina), meaning "accompanying them while being from among the prophets," or from its pronoun. The specific mention of the prophets' companionship, without our Prophet (ﷺ) in particular, although the discussion concerns the ruling on obedience to him (ﷺ), is due to their being mentioned in the occasion of revelation, along with an indication that his obedience includes obedience to them.

Al-Tabarani, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Diya' al-Maqdisi reported it, and he graded it as good, saying: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of God, you are dearer to me than my own self, you are dearer to me than my children. I am in the house and I remember you, and I cannot be patient until I come and look at you. When I remember my death and your death, I know that when you enter Paradise you will be raised with the prophets, and that when I enter Paradise I fear I will not see you." The Prophet (ﷺ) did not answer him at all until Gabriel descended with this verse: ﴿Whoever obeys God﴾ etc. A similar report is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Kalbi said: "Thawban, the freed slave of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), had an intense love for him (ﷺ) and little patience in being apart from him. His body became emaciated and his color changed from fear of not seeing the Messenger of God (ﷺ) after death. He mentioned that to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and God revealed this verse."

From Masruq: "The companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: It is not fitting that we should part from you in this world, for when you part from us you will be raised above us. So this was revealed." He began with mention of the prophets because of the elevation of their rank and their height above all others.

Al-Sha'rani transmitted from our master, the Shaykh al-Akbar, may God sanctify his secret, that he said: "There was opened to me the measure of the eye of a needle of the station of prophethood, as a manifestation (tajalli), not as entry, and I nearly burned." Then, in descending order, He, glorified is He, added: ﴿and the truthful, and the martyrs, and the righteous﴾. The stations are four, some below others:

**The first:** the stations of the prophets, those who are supported by a divine power and accompanied by a soul at the highest levels of holiness (qudsiyya). Their likeness is that of one who sees a thing directly from near. For this reason, God Most High said in describing our Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾

**The second:** the stations of the truthful (siddiqin), those who lag behind the prophets (peace be upon them) in knowledge. Their likeness is that of one who sees a thing directly from afar. This is what 'Ali (may God honor his face) meant when it was said to him: "Have you seen God?" He replied: "I would not worship a Lord I had not seen." Then he said: "The eyes did not see Him through the evidences of direct sight, but the hearts saw Him through the realities of faith."

**The third:** the stations of the martyrs (shuhada'), those who know a thing through proofs. Their likeness is that of one who sees a thing in a mirror from a near place, like the one who said: "It is as if I see the Throne of my Lord manifest." This is what the Prophet (ﷺ) intended in his saying: "Worship God as if you see Him."

**The fourth:** the stations of the righteous (salihin), those who know a thing through firm acceptance (taqlid jazim). Their likeness is that of one who sees a thing from afar in a mirror. This is what the Prophet (ﷺ) intended in his saying: "If you do not see Him, then surely He sees you." Al-Raghib said this, and al-Tibi and others transmitted it.

Some of the disciples of our master, Shaykh Khalid al-Naqshbandi, may God sanctify his secret, transmitted that he once established that the ranks of the perfected (kummal) are four:

Prophethood, whose axis (qutb) is our Prophet (ﷺ); then siddiqiyya, whose axis is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may God be pleased with him); then shahada, whose axis is 'Umar al-Faruq (may God be pleased with him); then wilaya, whose axis is 'Ali (may God honor his face). He also held that the righteousness (salah) in the verse is an allusion to wilaya. Some of those present asked him about 'Uthman (may God be pleased with him): in which of the three ranks after prophethood is he? He replied: "He (may God be pleased with him) has attained a share of the rank of martyrdom and a share of the rank of wilaya. The meaning of his being 'the possessor of the two lights' (dhu al-nurayn) is that, according to the knowers (al-'arifin)." End of quotation.

I say, seeking help from God Most High and drawing from the people (may God sanctify their secrets): wilaya is the all-encompassing general sphere, the revolving orbit, and the great circle. The wali (friend of God) is one who stands upon clear evidence from his Lord in his state, so he knows what is his through the informing of the Truth to him in the manner by which affirmation occurs for him. It applies to many categories. However, the categories mentioned in this verse are four:

**The first category:** the prophets. What is meant by them here is the messengers, the people of sharia, whether they were sent or not sent, I mean in the sense of being obligatory upon them. There is no discussion for the people of God Most High regarding their stations and states, since they have no tasting of them. All of them acknowledge this, except that they say: prophethood is general and specific. The one for which they have no tasting is the specific, namely legislative prophethood (nubuwwat al-tashri'), and it is a specific station within wilaya.

As for general prophethood, it is continuous and flowing among the great men, not cut off in this world or the next. But the door of unrestricted application (al-itlaq) has been closed. On this basis, what al-Badr al-Tamasuki al-Baghdadi narrated from Shaykh Bashir, from the pole 'Abd al-Qadir al-Jili (may God sanctify his secret), is explained: that he said, "Assemblies of prophets, you were given the title, and we were given what you were not given." The meaning of his saying "you were given the title" is that the use of the term "Prophet" was forbidden to us, even though general prophethood is everlasting. His saying "and we were given what you were not given" is in the manner of the saying of Khidr to Moses (peace be upon him), though Khidr is superior to him: "O Moses, I have knowledge that God taught me which you do not know." This is another aspect, different from what we have previously mentioned before the explanation of this statement.

**The second category:** the truthful (al-siddiqun), those who believe in God Most High and His messengers on the word of the one who informs, not based on any proof other than the light of faith prepared in their hearts before the existence of what is believed in. This light prevents doubt or hesitation from entering their hearing of the informing messenger. Its real object is faith in the Messenger. Faith in God Most High is by way of drawing near (qurba), not by way of establishing His existence, since some of the truthful have had the existence of the Truth (al-Haqq) established for them by necessity or by reflection. But what was established is that it is a drawing near. There is no station between prophethood and siddiqiyya, as Hujjat al-Islam and others said. Whoever oversteps the necks of the truthful falls into prophethood, which is a closed door.

The Shaykh al-Akbar, may God sanctify his secret, established a station between them which he named the station of nearness (maqam al-qurba). It is the secret which settled in the heart of Abu Bakr (may God be pleased with him), alluded to in the hadith: "Between the Prophet (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr (may God be pleased with him) there is not a single man at all." This does not mean there is no station between siddiqiyya and prophethood. Siddiqiyya has parts equal in number to the branches of faith. Some explained it as a green light between two lights, through which is attained direct witnessing of the very thing the informer brought from behind the veil of the unseen, by the light of generosity. He explained this at length.

**The third category:** the martyrs. God took them as His own in martyrdom and made them among the drawn-near ones. They are among those who are present with God Most High upon the carpet of knowledge of Him. God, glorified is He, said: ﴿God bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels and those of knowledge﴾. Thus He joined them with the angels in the carpet of witnessing. They are monotheists by divine presence and eternal care. If God sends a messenger and they believe in him, then they are the believing scholars, and for them is the complete reward on the Day of Resurrection. Otherwise, they are not the martyrs who are blessed. Their faith after knowledge of what God, glorified is He, said is a drawing near to Him, from the standpoint that God, glorified is He, said it, or that the Messenger who came from Him said it. So He placed the truthful before the martyr, and placed him opposite the Prophet, for he is an intermediary between them, due to the connection of the light of faith with the light of messengership. The martyrs have the light of knowledge, which accompanies the light of the Messenger insofar as he is a witness to God Most High in His Oneness, not insofar as he is a messenger. It is not valid for them to be after him while accompanying him, lest it nullify it, nor for them to be with him because he is a messenger, while the witness is not in that. So they must be later.
