Thus there remains only that they be in the rank that follows siddiqiyya. For the truthful has a fuller light than him in siddiqiyya, because he is truthful from two aspects: the aspect of Oneness and the aspect of nearness. The martyr is truthful from the aspect of nearness only, because his monotheism is from knowledge, not from faith. So he falls below the truthful in the rank of faith, but he is above him in the rank of knowledge. Thus he is the one who precedes in the rank of knowledge and lags behind in the rank of faith and affirmation, because it is not valid for the knower to be a truthful. Knowledge precedes the rank of report. He knows that the one who conveys is truthful in God's Oneness when he conveys God's message. The truthful did not know this except by the light of faith prepared in his heart. So when the Messenger came, he followed him without any manifest proof.

**The fourth category:** the righteous (al-salihun). God took them as His own in righteousness. They are those in whose knowledge of God Most High and whose faith in Him and in what came from Him, glorified is He, no defect enters. If a defect enters it, their righteousness is nullified. Whoever has no defect entering his siddiqiyya is righteous, and in his martyrdom he is righteous, and in his repentance he is righteous. Everyone may pray for the attainment of righteousness for himself in the station in which he is, because a defect may enter upon him in his station. The matter is a divine particularization and not an essential attribute. So a defect may enter it and it may be lifted. Thus it is valid for the righteous one to pray that he be made among the righteous, that is, among those whose righteousness a defect may enter at some time.

It has been mentioned that every prophet either described himself as righteous, or prayed to be among the righteous, despite being a prophet. From here it was said that the rank of righteousness is more general than prophethood, and it may be attained by one who is neither a prophet, nor a truthful, nor a martyr.

This is what I have come to know of the words of these people, may God sanctify their secrets. I did not attain the detailed explanation that our master, the Shaykh, may God sanctify his secret, mentioned. So reflect.

Our formalist (rasmiyyun) colleagues have mentioned that "siddiq" is an intensive form of the pattern, like "sikkir" (one who drinks much), meaning one who is foremost in affirmation, who intensifies in truthfulness and sincerity in words and deeds. It is applied to each of the outstanding companions of the prophets (peace be upon them) and their eminent close followers, such as Abu Bakr (may God be pleased with him).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 69 (part 2 of 2):

And "the martyrs" (al-shuhada', plural of shahid) refers to those who gave up their lives in obedience to Allah the Exalted and in raising His word, and they are those slain by the sword of the disbelievers from among the Muslims. It has been said that what is meant here is something more general than that. Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'How do you count the martyr among you?' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, whoever is killed in the way of Allah the Exalted.' He said: 'The martyrs of my Ummah would then be few. Whoever is killed in the way of Allah the Exalted is a martyr, whoever dies of plague is a martyr, and whoever dies of a stomach ailment is a martyr.'" Some scholars have counted the martyrs to be far more than that. It has also been said: the shahid is the one who bears witness to the religion of Allah the Exalted, sometimes by proof and clear explanation, and at other times by the sword and the spear.

Al-Nisaburi claimed that it is far-fetched that this entire Ummah should be included among the martyrs, citing the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And thus We have made you a justly balanced nation, that you may be witnesses over the people﴾. But this is no argument, as is not hidden.

And "the righteous" are those who spend their lives in the obedience of Allah the Exalted and their wealth in seeking His pleasure, glory be to Him. It is said: the salih is the one whose condition is sound and whose way is upright. The muslih is the one who does what contains goodness. Al-Tabarsi said: For this reason it is permissible to say "muslih" with regard to Allah the Exalted, but not "salih."

The meaning of "companionship" is not the unity of rank nor mere general sharing in entering Paradise, but rather that they are in it in such a way that each one of them is able to see the other and visit him whenever he wishes, even if the distance between them is great.

Many have mentioned that there is no obstacle to the lower being raised to the station of the higher whenever He wills, as an honour for him, and then he returns; and it is not seen that he has a more pleasant life or more complete delight, lest it become a regret in his heart. Likewise, there is no obstacle to the higher descending to the station of the lower and then returning, without this being regarded as a deficiency in his dominion or a diminution of his rank.

It has been established in more than one hadith that the people of Paradise visit one another. Some have claimed that there is no visiting together with each seeing the other; this is because the world of lights has no obstruction or repulsion in it, so some of them reflect upon others like polished facing mirrors. To this is the allusion in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Brothers, on couches facing one another﴾. He claimed that this is the verification, but it is far from it; and even further from it by many stages is what has been said: it may be that the meaning is that the sense of the obedient one being with these is that he is with them in travelling the path of the Hereafter, so that he is safe from highwaymen, and his obedience is protected from plunder.

﴿And excellent is those as companions﴾ — i.e., as a friend. It is derived from rifq, which is gentleness of side and kindness in companionship, in speech and deed. The demonstrative "those" may refer to the prophets and those after them, and the sense of distance in it is as has passed many times. "Companion" (rafiqan) here is either a specifier (tamyiz) or a circumstantial accusative (hal), in the sense that they are described as excellent from the aspect of being companions to the obedient, or in the state of being companions to them. It is not pluralised, because fa'il is used for both the singular and others, or because the singular suffices for the plural in the case of the specifier since the meaning is understood; and what makes it good is its occurrence at the end of the verse, or because by interpretation each one of them is excellent, or because the intention is to explain the genus without regard to the species. It may also be that the demonstrative refers to "whoever obeys," and the plural is according to meaning; then "companion" is a specifier in the sense that they are described as excellent in companionship from among the four groups, not with excellence itself; so it is not permissible to introduce "min" before it, as it is permissible in the first aspect.

The sentence, on both possibilities, is a concluding statement confirming what precedes it, emphasising encouragement and eagerness. In al-Kashshaf: it carries the sense of wonder, as if it were said: "How excellent are those as companions!" Because it stands independently with the meaning of wonder, it was read as "wa-husnu" with a sukun on the sin, the speaker of wonder saying: "husnu al-wajhi wajhuka" with fatha, damma and with sukun. End of quote.

In al-Sihah it is said: "husuna al-shay'" (the thing became good); and if you wish, you may lighten the damma and say "husna al-shay'." The damma may be transferred to the ha', because it is a predicate. The transfer is permissible only when it carries the sense of praise or blame, because it is likened in permissibility of transfer to ni'ma and bi'sa, since originally in them it was ni'ima and bi'isa, the second being made sukun and its vowel transferred to what precedes it; and likewise everything that has their meaning. The poet said:

"People have not prevented from me what I wished, nor do I give them what they wished — hasuna dha adaban."

He intended "hasuna dha adaban," which was lightened and transferred. He intended that, since it was transferred to the form of an exclamation, it was fitting to change it as a signal to the place of transfer.

In al-Irtisaf: The form fa'ula transformed (into this pattern), al-Farisi and most grammarians went to attaching it only to the category of ni'ma and bi'sa, and applying their rulings to it; while al-Akhfash and al-Mubarrad went to attaching it to the category of wonder (ta'ajjub). Al-Akhfash related both usages from the Arabs. It is permissible in it to make the 'ayn damma or sukun and to transfer its vowel to the fa'. Its apparent sense indicates a difference between the two views.

In al-Tashil: it is of the category of ni'ma and bi'sa, and it carries the sense of wonder; this requires that there be no difference between them. The words of the two shaykhs incline to this, so understand.

Husn is an expression for everything delightful and desired, whether intellectually, by inclination, or by the senses. Most commonly in the common usage it is said of what is pleasing to the sight, and it has come in the Qur'an concerning it and concerning what is pleasing from the aspect of insight.

﴿That﴾ is an indication of what was established for the obedient from all that has preceded, or an indication of the bounty of these blessed ones and their excellence. It is the subject (mubtada'). His saying, glorified is He, ﴿the bounty﴾, is an attribute (sifah), and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from Allah﴾, is its predicate (khabar). The meaning is: that great bounty is from Allah, exalted is He, not from anyone else. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ﴿the bounty﴾ be the predicate, with (min Allah) related to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of it, and the element governing it is the sense of the indication. It is also permissible that it be a second predicate, meaning: that which has been mentioned, the bounty, is (كائِنًا أوْ كائِنٌ) from Allah, exalted is He, not that the deeds of the servants necessitate it.

﴿And sufficient is Allah as Knower﴾ of the reward of whoever obeys Him, and of the measures of bounty and the deserving of its people according to what the promise requires. So trust what He has informed you of, ﴿and none can inform you like one who is All-Aware﴾.

It was said: And sufficient is He, glorified is He, as Knower of the disobedient, the obedient, the hypocrites, and the sincere, and of who is fit to accompany these and who is not.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 71:

﴿O you who have believed, take your precaution﴾ meaning: your equipment of weapons. This is what Muqatil said, and it is also what is related from Abu Ja'far (may Allah be pleased with him). It is also said: al-hidhr (precaution) is a verbal noun like al-hadhar, which is guarding oneself against what is feared. In that case there is kinaya (metonymy) and takhyil (imaginative representation), by likening precaution to weapons and the means of protection. The taking is not a metaphor, so that there would be no combining of the literal and the metaphorical in His words, glorified is He: ﴿and let them take their precaution and their weapons﴾, since the figurative element lies in the act of applying (the verb).

The muhaqqiqun (verifying scholars) have affirmed the permissibility of combining the two meanings here. The sense is: prepare yourselves against your enemies, or be watchful, be on your guard against them, and do not let them gain access to you. ﴿Then go forth﴾ with the fa' vowelized with a kasra, and it has also been read with a damma, meaning: go out to fight your enemy and wage jihad alongside him when you set out. The original meaning of al-nafr is fright, like al-nafrah (aversion), and then it was used for what has been mentioned. ﴿in groups (thubat)﴾ is the plural of thubah, which is a group of men of more than ten; it is also said: more than two. It may also be applied to other than men, and from it is the saying of Amr ibn Kulthum:

"So when you fear for them on a day, our horses will become in the morning scattered companies (thubat)."

Its measure originally is fa'lah, like hatmah, its final radical was deleted, and the feminine ta' was substituted for it. It is uncertain whether it is from the waw of (tha·ba yathbu), like (ʿada yaʿdu), meaning it gathered, or from the ya' of (thabaytu), meaning I praised him by mentioning his good qualities. Regarding the plural of it there are two opinions.

Thubat al-hawd means its middle; it is waw-rooted, from thaba yathubu, meaning he returned. It has been pluralized in the sound feminine plural and inflected accordingly according to the eloquent dialect; in one dialect it is put in the accusative with a fatha. It has also been pluralized in the sound masculine plural, so one says thabun. This applies regularly to what has lost its final radical if it does not fulfil the conditions, as a compensation for it; and in its tha' at that point there are two dialects: damma and kasra. The plural here is in the position of a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: go forth in separate groups, one group after another.

﴿Or go forth all together﴾ meaning: gathered as one single group. An army, when it is gathered and not dispersed, is called katibah; a selected detached portion of it is called sariyyah. According to some, the sariyyah is the group that goes out at night and returns to it, and it is from one hundred to five hundred, or from five persons to three hundred and four hundred. What exceeds the sariyyah is called mansir (as in majlis and minbar) up to eight hundred. If it exceeds that, it is called jaysh up to four thousand. If it exceeds that, it is called jahfal, and the great army is called khamis. What separates from the sariyyah is called ba'th. The sariyyah may also be applied to any group in general.

Although the verse was revealed concerning war, it nonetheless contains an indication of encouragement to hasten to all good deeds, in whatever way is possible, before they are lost.

﴿And indeed among you is one who will certainly lag behind﴾: that is, he will certainly be sluggish and hold back from jihad. It is from *ba''ta* (بَطَّأ), in the sense of *abta'a* (أبطأ), like *ta''tama* (عَتَّمَ) in the sense of *a'tama* (أعتم), meaning he delayed. The address is to the army of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, both its believers and its hypocrites, and those who lag behind are the hypocrites among them. It is also permitted that the verb be transmitted both in form and in meaning from *ba'uda* (بَطُؤَ), like *thaqula* (ثَقُلَ) from *thaqqala* (ثَقَّلَ), so that the meaning would be: he will certainly cause someone else to lag behind and will discourage him from jihad, as Ibn Abi Nasa discouraged people on the day of Uhud. The latter reading is more suited to what follows.

The first *lam* (لَ) is the *lam al-ta'kid* (the emphatic lam, which enters the predicate of *inna* or its subject when the latter is postponed), and the second is the answer of an oath (*jawab qasam*). It has been said that it is extra (*za'idah*). The oath clause and its answer form the relative clause (*silat al-mawsul*) of the relative pronoun, and they are as one thing, so it is not objected that it contains a resumptive pronoun (*rabitah*) within the oath clause, just as it is not objected that the oath clause is non-declarative (*insha'iyyah*), which would make it unfit to serve as a relative clause, because what is intended is the answer, which is declarative and contains the returning pronoun. It would require supposing *aqsama* (أقسم) in the past tense so that its pronoun returns to the one who lags behind, but this is contrary to the apparent sense.

It is permitted to take (*man*, مَن) as a descriptive (*mawsufah*), and what is said regarding the relative clause applies to the descriptive phrase. This sentence has been said to be coordinated (*'atf*) with ﴿take your precautions﴾ as a coordination of one narrative upon another narrative. It has also been said that it is parenthetical (*mu'taridah*) up to His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿So let those fight﴾, and that this is coordinated with ﴿take﴾. It is also read as *layubt'in* (لَيُبْطِئْنَ) with lightening (*bi-l-takhfif*).

﴿But if a calamity strikes you﴾ from the enemy, such as killing and defeat, he (the one who lags behind) says, rejoicing at what he did and praising his own opinion: ﴿Allah has certainly bestowed a favor upon me﴾ by sitting out, ﴿in that I was not present with them as a witness﴾, that is, present with them in the battlefield, so that I would be struck by the like of what befell them of affliction and hardship. It has been said that the meaning may be: in that I was not a martyr (*shahid*) among their martyrs, or I was not with them in the position of martyrdom. Thus the favor is deliverance from being killed and fear of it, and it is expressed by "martyrdom" as mockery (*tahakkum*). Its remoteness is not hidden.

The *fa'* (فَ) in the conditional clause indicates the consequence of its content upon what precedes it, for mention of lagging behind entails mention of what follows from it, just as the very act of lagging behind calls for something that the one who lags behind awaits to occur.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 73:

﴿And if a bounty from Allah should befall you⁠—﴾ such as a conquest and spoils⁠—﴿from Allah﴾: this is connected to (asabakum, "befall you"), or to an omitted element that stands as a qualifier of (fadl, "bounty"). Attributing the bounty to the side of Allah the Exalted, while not attributing the calamity to Him, is a lesson in good manners toward Allah the Exalted, even though the calamity is in reality also a bounty. The conditional clause (al-shartiyyah al-ula, the first conditional) is placed first because its content suits their aim better, and the effect of their hypocrisy is more evident in it. ﴿He will surely say﴾: out of regret for his having held back, a grasping after the trappings of this world, and sorrow over having missed it. The emphasis on the statement indicates the extreme degree of grief understood from the speech. The first statement was not emphasized, and it was expressed in the past tense, either because its occurrence is certain and so does not need emphasis, or because the shift from the present tense to the past is itself an emphasis. Al-Hasan recited (layaqulunna) with a damma on the lam, taking into account the meaning of (man, "whoever"); this is common and permissible.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿as if there had never been between you and him any affection﴾, this is a parenthetical statement from the speech of Allah the Exalted, placed between the saying and its content, which is ﴿O, would that I had been with them, so I would have achieved a great achievement﴾. This is so that it is not imagined, from the opening of his speech, that his wish to be with them was for support and backing, as the affection between them would require. Rather, it is for greed after the trappings of this world, as its end reveals, for the great achievement he meant is that. The affirmation of affection between them is not by way of verification but by way of mockery. It is said: the comparative clause is a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the pronoun in (layaqulunna), meaning: he will surely say, being compared to one with whom there is no affection between you and him, since he did not wish for your support and backing. It is also said: it is from the speech of the one who holds back, included in the content like the clause of wishing, meaning: the one who holds back will say to whoever is discouraging him from among the hypocrites and weak believers, "as if there had never been between you and Muhammad (ﷺ) any affection, since he did not take you along with him in the campaign so that you could achieve what those taken along achieved," ﴿O, would that I had been with them﴾, etc. His aim is to sow enmity between them and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to reinforce it. Al-Jubba'i took this view. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi, al-Zajjaj, and al-Maturidi, following him, held that it is connected to the first sentence, namely "He said: 'Allah has blessed me'" etc., meaning he said that "as if there had not been" etc. Al-Raghib al-Isfahani rejected this, saying that if it were connected to the first sentence, then how could it be placed between the parts of the second sentence, and such a thing is considered objectionable. It was answered that their meaning is that it is a parenthetical clause between the parts of this sentence, and its meaning is explicitly connected to the first and implicitly to this one. (Ka'anna, "as if") is a lightened form of the heavy (inna), its subject is the pronoun of the matter, which is omitted. It is also said that it does not govern when it is lightened.

Ibn Kathir, Hafs from 'Asim, and Ruways from Ya'qub recited (takun) with a ta', because of the feminine form of the word (mawaddah, "affection"). The rest recited (yakun) with a ya', because of the separation, and because it means (al-wudd, "affection"). The addressed term in (ya laytani, "O, would that I had") is, according to the majority, omitted, meaning "O my people." Abu 'Ali says regarding such cases: there is no omitted addressee in the speech; rather, (ya, "O") enters specifically before the verb and the particle merely for the sake of alerting attention. (Fa-afawza, "so I would achieve") is in the accusative as an answer to the wish. From Yazid al-Nahwi and al-Hasan it is recited (fa-afuzu) in the nominative, on the estimate: "so I (would) achieve" at that time, or as a conjunction with the predicate of (layta, "would that"), in which case it falls within the wish.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 74:

﴿So let them fight in the way of Allah who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter.﴾ The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is the subject of the verb, and the non-explicit object (al-maf'ul al-ghayr al-sarih), namely the prepositional phrase, has been placed before it for emphasis on it. (Yashrun) is the present tense of shara, and it can mean "to sell," and "to buy" is among the words with contrary meanings (al-adad). If it means (yashtarun), "to buy," then the intended referent of the relative pronoun is the hypocrites, who were commanded to abandon hypocrisy and to strive alongside the believers. The fa' is for sequence (li-al-ta'qib), meaning: after what has proceeded from them of discouragement and hypocrisy, it is fitting that they abandon it and make up for what they missed of jihad afterward.

If it means (yabi'un), "to sell," then the intended referent is the believers, who abandoned this world and chose the Hereafter. They were commanded to remain steadfast in fighting and not to turn their attention to the discouragement of the laggards. The fa' is the response of an implied conditional clause (jawab shart muqaddar), meaning: if the hypocrites turn them away, then let them fight and not care.

﴿And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed or is victorious, We will give him a great reward.﴾ It is certain (wa-la budda). In the shift (al-iltifat) there is additional shift. ﴿A great reward⁠

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 75 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And what is [the matter] with you﴾ is an address to those commanded to fight, in the mode of iltifat (a shift in grammatical address), for the sake of emphasizing the urging and incitement to it. This is the purpose of the interrogative. The word "ma" (what) is the subject (mubtada'), and "lakum" (with you) is its predicate. The words of the Exalted, ﴿you do not fight in the way of Allah﴾, occupy the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the element governing it is either the stability (al-istiqrar) or the adverbial phrase, because it implies the meaning of a verb. The meaning is: "What is the matter with you, not fighting?" The intended sense is: you have no excuse for abandoning fighting. ﴿And the oppressed﴾ is either coordinated with the Majestic Name (i.e., "in the way of Allah"), meaning: "in the way of the oppressed," which is their rescue from captivity and their protection from the enemy. This is what is reported from Ibn Shihab (al-Zuhri), but it has been deemed remote on the grounds that rescuing them is the way of Allah the Exalted, not their way. It is answered that although the way of Allah, Mighty is His name, has a kind of particular connection to them, there is no obstacle to attributing it to them.

The possibility that the fighting in their way means fighting to open the route from Makkah to Madinah and to remove the obstruction the polytheists had placed in it, so that the departure of the oppressed could be made possible, is very far-fetched. Alternatively, it is coordinated with "the way" by omitting a noun in the genitive construction (idafa), and this is the view of al-Mubarrad (a grammarian). The meaning is: "and in the liberation of the oppressed." It is also permissible to read it in the accusative, by supposing "I mean" or "I specify." This is because the way of Allah the Exalted encompasses all doors of goodness, and the liberation of the oppressed from the hands of the polytheists is among the greatest and most specific of them. The meaning of "the oppressed" is those whose weakness and humiliation the polytheists sought, or the weak among them. The letter sin (in al-mustad'ifin) is for emphasis.

﴿Of the men and the women and the children﴾ is an explanation of "the oppressed," and they are the Muslims who remained in Makkah because the polytheists prevented them from emigrating, or because of their weakness with respect to the emigration. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: "I and my mother were among the oppressed." Among them were mentioned Salamah ibn Hisham, al-Walid ibn al-Walid, and Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl. The children are mentioned in order to complete the appeal to compassion, to draw attention to the extreme extent of the polytheists' oppression, to announce the answering of the following supplication, and the nearness of the time of deliverance. In this there is great emphasis on urging fighting.

From this it is known that the verse is not suitable as proof for the validity of the Islam of a child, on the basis that otherwise their rescue would not be obligatory. Moreover, there is room for doubt in restricting the obligation of rescue to the Muslim, because the child of a Muslim is expected to become Muslim, so it is not far-fetched that rescuing him is obligatory in order that he may attain the rank of the blessed. It has been said that the intended meaning of "the children" is slaves, male and female. According to the first view, the word is the plural of walid and walidah, meaning a boy and a girl. It has been said that it is the plural of walad, like warl and wirlal. According to the second view, it is likewise, except that walid and walidah mean slave (male) and slave (female).

In al-Sihah (a lexicon by al-Jawhari): al-walid is a boy and a slave, its plural is wildan, and al-walidah is a girl and a female slave, its plural is wala'id. So the expression "al-wildan" is used in the manner of taghlib (predominance of the masculine) to include both males and females.

﴿Who﴾ is in the genitive position as an adjective of "the oppressed," or of what is within the scope of the explanation. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative, by supposing a verb: "I mean" or "I specify" those who.

﴿who say: Our Lord, bring us out from this town whose people are wrongdoers﴾ through polytheism, which is a great wrong, and through harming the believers and preventing them from emigrating. The description is an attribute of "town" (qaryah). Its masculine form is due to the masculine form of what is attributed to it. When the active or passive participle is applied to something other than the one it belongs to, its masculinity or femininity follows the apparent noun that it governs. The wrong is not ascribed to it metaphorically, as in the words of the Exalted: "And how many a town exulted in its livelihood" and His words, glorified is He: ﴿And Allah presents an example: a town that was secure and tranquil﴾ up to His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿so it denied the favors of Allah﴾, because the intended town is Makkah, as Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, and others said. So it was honored by being spared the attribution of wrongdoing to it, as a mark of distinction, which Allah the Exalted bestowed upon it.

﴿And appoint for us from Yourself a protector﴾ who will take charge of our affair until he rescues us from the hands of the wrongdoers. Both prepositional phrases are connected to "appoint" (ij'al), because their meanings differ. Their placement before the direct object serves to show concern for them, and to highlight the desire for what is delayed by placing its circumstances first. The placement of "li" before "min" hastens to show that what is asked for is beneficial to them and desired by them. It is also permissible that "from Yourself" (min ladunka) be connected to an omitted element that falls as a circumstantial clause of "a protector." The same applies to the words of the Exalted:

﴿And appoint for us from Yourself a helper﴾, meaning: a firm proof. This is the view of 'Ikrimah and Mujahid. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: the meaning is: "Appoint over us a ruler from among the believers, who will take charge of us, look after our interests, protect our religion and our law for us, and help us against our enemies." Allah the Exalted indeed answered their supplication, for He facilitated for some of them the departure to Madinah, and made for those who remained among them the best of protectors and the most powerful of helpers. He opened Makkah at the hands of His Prophet (ﷺ), so He took charge of them in the best manner and gave them the finest support. Then He appointed over them 'Attab ibn Usayd, who was eighteen years old, and he protected them and supported them until they became the most honored people of that city. It has also been said that the meaning is: "Grant us from Yourself guardianship and support," that is, be You our protector and our helper. The repetition of the verb and its two complements serves to emphasize humble supplication and earnest entreaty.

* * *

Now, from the esoteric (ishari) allusions in the verses: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render the trusts to their owners﴾ is a command to the knowers (al-arifin) to reveal to their like the divine secrets that have been disclosed to them, and to conceal that from the ignorant. Or it means to render every right to its possessor, so that one gives the capacity (al-isti'dad) its due, and places each thing in its proper place. The last of the trusts to be rendered is the trust of existence. So let the servant render it back to his Master, glorified is He, and let him pass away in Him, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And when you judge between the people﴾ with guidance, which is not possible except after passing away (al-fana') and returning to subsistence (al-baqa'): ﴿then judge with justice﴾, which is overflowing (al-ifadah) according to the capacity.

﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah﴾ by purifying the Ka'bah of His manifestation, which is the heart, from the idols of other than Him. ﴿And obey the Messenger﴾ through striving (al-mujahadah) and exhausting the body by performing the rites of worship that He has prescribed for you. ﴿And those in authority among you﴾, who are the guiding shaykhs, by complying with their command in what they see as good for you and as refinement for your character.

It may be said: He, glorified is He, made obedience in three degrees, though in origin they return to one. Whoever is fit for the carpet of nearness and understands the address of the Real without intermediary, like the one who said: "You took your knowledge dead from dead, while we took it from the Living who does not die," then let him ask Allah the Exalted to reveal His intent, and let him picture what he has understood from Him. Whoever has not reached this degree, let him return to the explanation of the Great Intermediary, who is the Messenger (ﷺ), if he understands his explanation or is able to take from him, like some of the people of Allah. Let him obey him in what he commands and forbids. Whoever has not reached this degree, let him return to the great scholars of the community, and let him bind himself to one of the schools of law, and stop at its rulings in commands and prohibitions.

﴿And if you dispute over anything﴾, you and the shaykhs. This is at the beginning of the spiritual path, where the self is strong. ﴿Then refer it to Allah﴾ the Exalted ﴿and the Messenger﴾. Return to the Book and the Sunnah, for in them is what removes the dispute, whether by explicit expression or by allusion. Or if a ruling from the rulings of the unseen, which are ambiguous, befalls you, and the oppositions of trial appear in your inner selves, then return to the address of Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ), for in it are the oceans of the sciences of realities. Every thought that does not agree with the address of Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ) is rejected.

﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been revealed to you﴾ of the knowledge of tawhid (divine oneness) ﴿and what was revealed before you﴾ of the knowledge of origin and return. ﴿They desire to take their judgment to the false authority (taghut)﴾, which is the commanding self (al-nafs al-ammarah), which judges by what its thoughts lead to, not based on the Book and the Sunnah. ﴿And they had been commanded to reject it﴾ and to oppose it. ﴿Indeed, the self is one that commands evil, except that upon which my Lord has mercy.﴾

﴿And Satan desires﴾, who is the taghut, ﴿to lead them far astray﴾, which is deviation from the truth. ﴿So how will it be when disaster strikes them﴾, which is the disaster of bewilderment and loss of the path that leads [to Allah], ﴿for what their hands have put forward﴾, namely putting forward their corrupt thoughts, and not returning to you. ﴿Then they come to you swearing by Allah: "We intended only good﴾ toward ourselves, by training them to reflect until they have the faculty of drawing out secrets and subtleties from your expressions and allusions, ﴿and reconciliation﴾, meaning uniting reason and transmitted knowledge, or reconciling the two adversaries by what is close to their intellects, and we did not intend to oppose you. ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah knows what is in their hearts﴾ of the rust of doubts, so He will requite them for that on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿So turn away from them﴾ and do not accept their excuse. ﴿Admonish them and speak to them a far-reaching word in their selves﴾, an effective one, so that they may refrain; or speak to them according to the measure of their intellects and the limit of their capacity. ﴿And if they had, when they wronged themselves﴾ by occupying themselves with their own portions, ﴿come to you and asked forgiveness of Allah﴾, that is, asked Him to cover the attributes of their selves, which are the sources of those actions, ﴿and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them﴾ by supplying them with the lights of his attributes, ﴿they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance and Merciful﴾, purifying their selves and bestowing upon them the perfection fitting for them.

Ibn 'Ata' said regarding this verse: that is, if they had made you the means toward Me, they would have reached Me.

﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe until they make you judge in what is disputed among them, and then find within themselves no resistance to what you have decided, and submit in full submission.﴾ Some of them said: Allah the Exalted manifested in this verse, upon His beloved, a robe of honor from the robes of lordship. He made acceptance of His judgment, whether it pleased or displeased, a cause for the faith of believers, just as He made acceptance of His decree a cause for the certainty of the certain. So He removed from them the title of intermediary, because he (ﷺ) is characterized by the attributes of the Real and has taken on His character. Do you not see how Hassan said:

"He split for Him a name from His own name, to honor Him: the Lord of the Throne is Mahmud, and this is Muhammad."

Others said: Allah, glorified is He, blocked the way to Himself for all people except after faith in His beloved (ﷺ). Whoever does not walk beneath his domes has no share in Allah the Exalted at all. Then He, majestic is His affair, made it a condition of faith that opposition be completely removed. So the believer must receive destructions with a contented heart and a smiling face.

﴿And if We had decreed upon them: "Kill yourselves" by the sword of striving, so that you may live a good life, ﴿or "Leave your homes"﴾, which are the refuges to which you inclined, in which you pitched your tents, and upon which you were devoted; or if We had imposed upon them: "Suppress your desires," or "Depart from your stations by which you have been veiled from pure tawhid, such as patience and trust in God, for example," ﴿they would not have done it, except a few of them﴾, who are the people of success and high aspirations.

The second possibility is supported by what is related from some of the gnostics: that he asked Ibrahim ibn Adham about his state. Ibrahim said: "I wander in the deserts and roam in the wastelands, where there is no water, no tree, no meadow, and no rain. Is my state in trust (tawakkul) sound?" He said to him: "If you have spent your life in building your belly, then where is annihilation in tawhid?!"

Had they done what they were admonished with, it would have been better for them ﴿and more firmly establishing﴾ through steadfastness in the religion, for the good life it contains. ﴿And We would have given them from Us a great reward﴾, which is the unveiling of beauty. ﴿And We would have guided them to a straight path﴾, which is monotheism (tawhid). ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger, those are with the ones whom Allah has blessed﴾ with what does not enter the scope of thought: ﴿of the prophets﴾, the lords of legislation, who are elevated in rank, so their lofty station cannot be reached; ﴿the truthful﴾, whom their light led to casting off the various kinds of lordship and doubts, so they affirmed what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought without proof or hesitation; ﴿the martyrs﴾, the people of presence; ﴿and the righteous﴾, the people of steadfastness in the religion.

﴿O you who have believed, take your precaution﴾ against your own selves, for they are your most hostile enemy. ﴿Then go forth in small groups﴾: travel the path of Allah in groups, each group following the way of a perfect shaykh. ﴿Or go forth all together﴾ on the path of monotheism and Islam, and follow the actions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and take on his character. ﴿And indeed, among you is he who will surely lag behind﴾, meaning he will surely discourage the striving, disciplined mujahidin. ﴿So if a calamity afflicts you﴾, a hardship on the journey, ﴿he says, "Allah has certainly blessed me," in that I did not do as they did. ﴾ ﴿And if a bounty from Allah comes to you﴾, unseen gifts, divine knowledge, lofty stations of the Sunna, and acceptance among the elite and the common people, ﴿he will surely say, as if there had never been between you and him any affection,﴾ meaning out of envy toward you, ﴿"Oh, I wish I had been with them, so I would have achieved a great achievement,﴾ beyond them, ﴿and obtained that alone.﴾

﴿And whoever fights﴾ his own self ﴿in the cause of Allah and is killed﴾ by the sword of truthfulness, ﴿or overcomes﴾ it through victory, so that it submits at his hand, ﴿We will give him a great reward﴾, which is arriving at Us. ﴿And what is wrong with you that you do not fight in the cause of Allah﴾ and for the liberation of the oppressed ﴿men﴾, the intellects, ﴿and women﴾, the spirits, ﴿and children﴾, the spiritual faculties, ﴿who say, "Our Lord, bring us out of this city﴾, which is the city of the body, ﴿whose people are wrongdoers﴾, which is the commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammara). ﴿And appoint for us from Yourself a protector﴾ who will manage our affairs and guide us, ﴿and appoint for us from Yourself a helper﴾ who will support us against those who wronged us, and this is the Most Holy Emanation (al-fayd al-aqdas). We ask Allah the Exalted for this by His bounty and His generosity.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 76:

﴿Those who believe fight in the cause of Allah﴾ This is a resumptive statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), brought to encourage the believers and to incite them to jihad (struggle, including armed fighting in the way of God). That is: the believers only fight in the religion of Allah, the Exalted, which leads them to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, and for the exaltation of His word. Thus He is their Protector and their Helper without doubt.

﴿And those who disbelieve fight in the cause of al-Taghut﴾ [meaning] in that which leads them to Satan, which is disbelief; so there is no helper for them other than it. ﴿So fight﴾ O friends of Allah, the Exalted, if the matter is as such, ﴿the friends of Satan﴾ meaning all the disbelievers; for you will overcome them.

﴿Indeed, the plot of Satan has always been weak﴾ in itself. How much more so in comparison with the power of Allah, the Exalted, in whose cause they fight, and He, glory be to Him, is your Protector? He did not elaborate on the description of the strength of His majesty, the Exalted, as a notification of its manifestation. The function of (kana) is emphasis, by stating that His plot has been weak from the beginning. It is said: it carries the meaning of (sara), that is: it became weak through Islam. It is also said that it is superfluous (za'ida), but this is nothing.

[p. 85]

«﴿Have you not seen those who were told, "Restrain your hands"?﴾ It was revealed, as al-Kalbi said, concerning ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf al-Zuhri, al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad al-Kindi, Qudama ibn Maẓʿun al-Jumahi, and Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas. They were suffering severe harm from the polytheists while they were in Mecca before the Hijra (migration to Madina). They complained to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said, "O Messenger of God, permit us to fight these people, for they have harmed us." The Prophet (ﷺ) would say, "Restrain your hands and refrain from fighting, for I have not been commanded to do that." In another narration: "I have been commanded to pardon."»

﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾: occupy yourselves with what you have been commanded. Perhaps their being commanded to establish the prayer and to give zakat is an indication that jihad against the self (jihad al-nafs) takes precedence, since a Muslim who has not become firm in submitting to God's command to be generous with wealth can hardly be generous with his life, and generosity with one's life is the utmost degree of generosity. The phrase "it was said" is in the passive form, although the speaker is the Prophet (ﷺ), because what is intended and taken into account in the expression of wonder indicated at the beginning of the statement is only the completeness of their eagerness for fighting and their being in a state where they needed to be forbidden from it. The command to restrain the hands is mentioned within the relative clause only to confirm and depict it by way of kinaya (indirect expression), so no purpose is tied to clarifying the specific identity of the one who commanded. It has also been said that the passive form is to indicate that this is by the command of God, exalted is He.

﴿So when fighting was prescribed for them﴾, and they were commanded to it after they had migrated with the Messenger of God to Madina, ﴿behold, a party of them fear men﴾, that is, the disbelievers, that they would kill them, and this is fixed in human nature out of fear of destruction, ﴿as they fear God﴾, that is, as they would fear God, exalted is He, that His punishment might descend upon them. The fa' (then) is conjunctive, and what follows it is coordinated with ﴿it was said to them, "Restrain your hands"﴾ with regard to its indirect meaning, since in that case the difference between the two conjoined meanings is realized, and upon this the matter of wonder revolves, as if it were said: "Have you not seen those who were eager for fighting? When fighting was prescribed for them, a group of them disliked it, by the demand of human nature." Directing the wonder at all of them, though that dislike came only from some, indicates that it was not fitting for any of them to do what contradicts his earlier state. The particle idha (behold) is for sudden occurrence, and it is a locative adverb; it has been said to be temporal, but this is not correct. In it there is emphasis on the matter of wonder. Fariq (party) is the subject, minhum (of them) is its qualifier, and yakhshawna (they fear) is its predicate. It has been permitted that it be also a qualifier or a circumstantial clause. The predicate is idha, and kakhshyat Allah (as the fear of God) is in the position of a verbal noun, meaning: a fear like the fear of God. It has also been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the subject of yakhshawna, with an omitted noun governing it, meaning: in a state of being like the people of the fear of God, exalted is He, that is, resembling those who fear Him, glory be to Him. It has been said, and there is remoteness in this, that it is a circumstantial clause from a pronoun of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: men fear it as the fear of God. ﴿Or a fear even stronger﴾ is coordinated with it if you make it a circumstantial clause, meaning that they are more intensely fearful than the people of the fear of God, in the sense that their fear is more intense than their own fear. It may also be coordinated on it, taking the noun as a verbal noun, as has been said, on the basis that khashyatan (fear) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), and that the specification is the agent of the act, and that the noun governed by min of comparison corresponds to the described noun in the elative form. Thus the meaning becomes: their fear is more intense than the fear of others, which amounts to saying that the fear of their fear is more intense, and this is not sound, except according to the approach of "the grandfather of his grandfather," as held by Abu ʿAli and Ibn Jinni, and it would be like your saying: "Zayd is very diligent," with jiddan (very) in the accusative as a specification. But this is remote. Rather, it is coordinated with the noble Name, so it is in the genitive by the fatha because it is not declined. The meaning is: they fear men with a fear like the fear of God, or with a fear more intense than His, exalted is He, but this is on the basis of supposition, since there is no fear more intense among believers than the fear of God, exalted is He. This leads to preferring their fear over all other fears when each is distinguished one by one. Ibn al-Hajib mentioned that this coordination may be coordination of sentences, meaning: they fear men as the fear of

[p. 86]

men, or they fear with a more intense fear, with the first being a verbal noun and the second a circumstantial clause. It has been said against this that omitting the qualifier is easier than omitting the whole sentence, and more fitting to the requirement of contrast and the harmony of correspondence.

It has been permitted that khashyatan be in the accusative as a verbal noun, and ashadd (more intense) be a qualifier of what precedes it, so it is in the accusative in the circumstantial sense. Some have mentioned that the specification after the elative form may be the very thing from which it is accusative, as in: "God is better as a guardian (ḥāfiẓan)," since the guardian is God, exalted is He, just as if you said: "God is the best of guardians" in the genitive. In that case there is no obstacle to the fear itself being the described noun, and it does not follow that fear must have a fear, in the same way as saying: "most intense fear" in the genitive. The claim that this permission applies only when the specification is the described noun in concept and in wording is a matter open to examination, since the unity of the wording with the first being omitted does not involve any serious objection.

This is a strong objection against what has been said. Ibn al-Munir has transmitted from the Book (of Sibawayh) what supports it, so consider this carefully. As for ﴿or﴾ (aw), it has been said to be for variety (tanwiʿ), it has been said to be for obscuring matters to the listener, it has been said to be for choice (takhyir), it has been said to mean "and" (waw), and it has been said to mean "but" (bal).

﴿And they said﴾ is coordinated with the response of "when" (lamma), meaning: when fighting was prescribed for them, some of them were struck, either in their tongues or in their hearts. God, exalted is He, related this from them as a wish for lightening the burden, not as an objection to His ruling or a denial of its obligation, and for this reason they were not rebuked for it. ﴿Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us﴾ at this time?

﴿If only You had delayed us to a near term﴾, which is the appointed term, and it was described as near in order to move them to mercy, meaning that it is a small period that one should not be refused in the likes of it. The clause serves as an explanation of what precedes it, and for this reason it is not coordinated with it. It has been said that it was not coordinated with it only to indicate that the two are independent statements from them: sometimes they said the first clause, and sometimes the second. Had it been coordinated, it would have been understood that they said the two statements together, with the second coordinated to the first. ﴿Say﴾, that is, to make them disinclined toward what they hope for by remaining back from fighting and delaying until the appointed term, as the passing enjoyment, and to make them desirous of what they will obtain through fighting, the lasting bliss. ﴿The enjoyment of this world﴾, that is, all that is enjoyed and benefited from in this world, ﴿is little﴾ in itself, quick to pass away, and it is the least of little when compared to what is in the Hereafter. ﴿And the Hereafter﴾, that is, its reward which is tied to deeds, of which fighting is a part, ﴿is better﴾ for you than that little enjoyment, because of its abundance, its not ending, and its purity from turbidity. In the variation of style there is what is not hidden. God, glory be to Him, said ﴿for whoever fears God﴾ only to urge them and to encourage them to be mindful and not to neglect what the obligation requires. It has been said that the intended meaning is that the Hereafter itself is good, but it is for the God-fearing, since for the disbeliever and the sinner there are fires and terrors therein. For this reason it is said: "This world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever." It is not hidden that the first is more fitting to the context.

﴿And you will not be wronged a whit﴾ is coordinated with an omitted clause, meaning: you will be recompensed therein and not deprived of this small amount, let alone of what exceeds the reward of your deeds. So do not turn away from fighting, which is part of its delusion. Ibn Kathir and Kathir read: ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ with the yāʾ, referring the pronoun back to the apparent noun "man" (man).»

[Page 86]

﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you.﴾ It is possible that this is the beginning of a new statement coming from Him, the Exalted, by way of shifting the address (talwin al-khitab) and turning it away from the master of those addressed, ﷺ, to those mentioned first. This is done out of concern for binding them, through the Prophet's (ﷺ) explanation of the lowliness of this world and the grandeur of the Hereafter. In that case the sentence has no place in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis). It is also possible that it falls within the scope of the statement commanded to be said, in which case the sentence is in the accusative case (nasb). Several scholars held that what precedes is a reply to their first statement, and this is a reply to their second. So it is as if, when they said, ﹛Why have You prescribed fighting for us?﹜, they were answered by an explanation of the wisdom: it was prescribed for you so that your enjoyment would increase and your benefit would grow, because it brings about the enjoyment of the Hereafter. And when they said, ﹛Why did You not delay us...﹜ and so on, they were answered that ﹛wherever you may be﹜, whether on a journey or at home, ﹛death will overtake you﹜, because the appointed term is fixed.

[Page 87]

Therefore leaving to fight does not prevent it. The use of the verb "overtake" (idrak) implies that these people, because of their great distance from the causes of death, and the nearness of its time of arrival to them, with the passing of breaths and moments, are as if they were fleeing from it, while it is determined in pursuing them and does not slacken for a single breath in its approach to them.

Talhah ibn Sulayman read ﹛yudrikukum﹜ with a nominative ending (raf'). Its analysis has been disputed. It was said that it is by omitting the fa' (the particle of consequence), as in the verse Sibawayh cited:

Whoever does good deeds, God will reward them,
and evil with evil, in God's sight, is two-fold.

The apparent sense of al-Kashshaf is to be satisfied with supposing the fa'. Some scholars supposed an inceptive subject (mubtada') together with it, meaning: "So you, death overtakes you." It was also said that it is postponed from an earlier position, and the answer of the conditional (jawab al-shart) is omitted, meaning: "Death overtakes you wherever you may be, it overtakes you." This was objected to on the grounds that this is only good if what precedes the conditional requires it, as in the line:

O Aqra' ibn Habis, O Aqra'!
If your brother is struck down, you will be struck down.

Or if the particle is not a conditional noun. It was answered that the first condition, though it is reported from Sibawayh, is also reported from him in a general sense, and the second condition was not relied upon by the verifying scholars. It was also said that the nominative is due to the supposition that the conditional is in the past tense, for then the jussive (jazm) must appear in the answer. Since the particle's effect did not appear in the near case, it is not required to appear in the distant one. As for the objection that a past conditional with a present-tense answer is only good with the particle "an" (that), because it turns the past into the sense of the future, so "wherever you were, death would overtake you" would not be good except as a narration of the past, and the intention of making it present is open to question, yes, it does entail an extra difficulty (ta'assuf) at that point, because of the supposition, as Ibn al-Munir said, that what is supposed may be the original, or something so frequently used that it has become like the original, whereas what is supposed here is not like that.

It was also said that ﹛if death overtakes you﹜ is a separate statement, and ﹛wherever you may be﹜ is connected to ﹛you will not be wronged﹜. It was objected, as al-Shihab said, that this is not correct in meaning or in grammatical practice. As for the first, it does not fit being connected to what precedes, because ﹛you will not be wronged a thread﹜ refers to the Hereafter, so generalization does not fit it. As for the second, it would entail that what precedes the conditional noun works in it, which is not valid, since the conditional noun has the front position. It was answered regarding the first that there is no obstacle to generalizing ﹛you will not be wronged﹜ to this world and the Hereafter, or the meaning is that they will not be diminished by anything from the duration of the known term, not from the better (of the two), and with this the speech is coherent. Regarding the second, it was answered, as al-Halabi and al-Safaqisi said, that what is meant by connection to what precedes is connection to it in meaning, not in operation, on the basis that ﹛wherever you may be﹜ is a conditional whose answer is omitted, its supposition being ﹛you will not be wronged﹜, and what precedes is evidence of the answer.

You know that this analysis, even though one is obliged to defend it with what you have seen, goes against the apparent meaning that comes to mind. The best of the analyses is that it is by omitting the fa', which is what al-Mubarrad chose. The claim that omission is a necessity (darurah) is within the realm of prohibition.

﹛Even if you were in towers﹜, that is, in palaces, as Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Juraij said. And it is reported from al-Suddi and al-Rabi', may God be pleased with them, that they are palaces in the lowest heaven. It was also said that what is meant by them is the constellations (buruj) of the known heaven. And from Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i it is reported that they are the houses above the palaces. And from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that they are fortresses and castles. The word is a plural (jam'), its singular being (burj). Its root is from tabarruj, which is display, and from it: a woman "tabarrajat" when she displayed her beauty. ﹛Fortified﹜ (mushayyadah), that is, plastered with shid, which is lime plaster, as Ikrimah said, or lofty by height, as al-Zajjaj said, so it derives from shayyada al-bina' when he raised the building. Mujahid read (mashidah) with a fatha on the mim and a light ya', as in His words: ﹛and a lofty palace﹜ (qasr mashid). Abu Nu'aym ibn Maysarah read (mushayyidah) with a kasra on the ya', as a figurative usage, like ﹛a pleasant life﹜ (ishah radiyah) and ﹛a poem that is poetic﹜ (qasidah sha'irah). And the sentence conjoined to another like it, that is: "Even if you were not in towers, even if you were in them," and the omission has become common in such a case because the meaning is clear.

[Page 88]

﹛If good befalls them, they say, "This is from God"; and if evil befalls them, they say, "This is from you."﹜ It was revealed, as reported from al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd, concerning the Jews, because "they had been given abundant provision, and when the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina and invited them to faith, they disbelieved, and some of the provision was withheld from them. They said: 'We have continued to notice a decline in our fruits and our fields since this man came to us.'" So the meaning is: if blessing or ease befalls them, they attribute it to God, the Exalted; and if calamity befalls them, from drought and high prices, they attribute it to you, considering it an omen. This is like what is related of their forefathers in His words: ﹛If evil befalls them, they consider it an omen from Moses and those with him﹜. This is the view of al-Zajjaj, al-Farra', al-Balkhi and al-Jubba'i.

It was also said that it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, Ibn Ubayy and his companions, who stayed behind from fighting on the day of Uhud and said to those who were killed: ﹛If they had been with us, they would not have died or been killed﹜. So the meaning is: if spoils befall them, they say, "This is from God, the Exalted"; and if defeat befalls them, they say, "This is from the badness of your management." This is what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

It was also said that it was revealed concerning those mentioned before, but this is not the correct view. Several scholars affirmed that it was revealed concerning both the Jews and the hypocrites together, when they considered the Messenger of God (ﷺ) an omen when he came to Medina and they suffered drought. On this view, the immediate sense of "good" (hasanah) and "evil" (sayyi'ah) here is blessing and calamity. Their usage has, however, become common for obedience and disobedience, and many verifying scholars held this view. It is supported by the attribution of befalling (isabah) to both of them, and indeed the author of al-Kashf made it a clear proof for it, and because it is more suited to the context, since death and safety were mentioned before.

His words, the Exalted: ﹛Say: "All is from God"﹜ is a command to him (ﷺ) to refute their false claim and corrupt belief, and to guide them to the truth by explaining that the whole is attributed to Him, the Exalted, in general terms. That is, each of blessing and calamity is from God, the Exalted, in terms of creation and bringing into existence, without my having any part in the occurrence of any of them in any way, as you claim. Rather, the occurrence of the first is from Him directly by bounty, and the occurrence of the second is through the sins of the one afflicted, as punishment, as will be explained later.

This general answer is in the sense of what was said in refutation of the forefathers of the Jews, in His words: ﹛Their omen is with God﹜, that is: the cause of their good and evil is with God, the Exalted, not with anyone else, so that this is attributed to Him and they consider it an omen by Him. So said Shaykh al-Islam. From this it is known that the objection is dismissed which says that the people did not believe that the Prophet (ﷺ) was the doer of evil as they believed that God, the Exalted, was the doer of good, but rather they considered him an omen, and God forbid that of him, peace be upon him. How then could this be a refutation of them? There is no need for what the second 'Allamah answered, that the answer is not merely His words, ﹛Say: "All is from God"﹜, but extends to His words, the Glorified: ﹛Whatever misfortune befalls you is from yourself﹜, and so on.

His words, the Exalted: ﹛Then what is the matter with these people?﹜ that is, the Jews, the hypocrites and those who are contemptuous, ﹛that they can hardly understand﹜, that is, comprehend, ﹛a statement﹜. That is, a speech by which they would be admonished, which is the Qur'an, or any speech, or any matter that has happened and whose time is recent. The statement is from Him, the Exalted, interposed between the thing explained and its explanation, and it is given to rebuke them for ignorance, to condemn their condition, and to express wonder at the completeness of their dullness. The particle fa' indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes. The negated sentence is a circumstantial clause (hal), and what governs it is the sense of settledness (istiqrar) contained in the adverbial phrase, or the adverbial phrase itself. The meaning is: since the matter is so, what has happened to these people, while they are far from understanding the explicit texts of the Qur'an that state that everything overflows from God, the Exalted? Or while they are far from understanding "a statement" in any sense at all, so that they are counted like beasts that have no understanding? Or while they are far from grasping the vicissitudes of time and its change, so that they would know that He is its true doer, in whose hand is the whole of affairs, and no one has any part alongside Him?

[Page 89]

It is also permissible that the sentence be a new statement (isti'naf) founded on a question arising from the interrogative, which is evident. In both cases, the speech is expressed as an exaggeration of their lack of understanding, so it does not contradict their belief that the good is from God, the Exalted.

From some scholars' statements it is understood that what is meant by "statement" is what they had just uttered, since it entails a plurality of creators, which entails polytheism, which leads to corruption of the world. And the particle (ma) within the sphere of the command is a refutation of this consequence. It was placed first because it is more important. Then it was resumed with what is the true answer, namely His words, the Glorified: ﹛Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﹜. According to what we have mentioned, and perhaps it is the better view, this is an explanation of the general answer that was commanded, and the address in it, as al-Jubba'i said and as was reported from Qatadah, is general to everyone who reads it, not only to the Prophet (ﷺ), as in the line:

If you honour the noble, you will possess him,
and if you honour the base, he will rebel.

It includes those mentioned by primary inclusion. Placing the answer first on the tongue of the Prophet (ﷺ) and then the explanation coming from Him, the Exalted, in the second place, by way of shifting the address and turning (iltifat), indicates an increase in concern for it, and attention to refuting their false belief and corrupt claim, and an indication that its content is based on a subtle wisdom worthy of being explained by the Knower of the Unseen, the Mighty and Majestic. And turning away from addressing them all, as in His words: ﹛Whatever calamity befalls you is because of what your own hands have earned﹜, is for the sake of emphasis in establishing the matter, by cutting off the possibility that some of them are the cause of the punishment of others.

"Ma" here, as Abu al-Baqa' said, is a conditional particle, and (asaba) is in the sense of (yusibu). The good and evil here are what was meant by them earlier. That is: whatever blessing among the blessings befalls you, O human, is from God, the Exalted, directly, by bounty and kindness, without its being owed by you. How could it be otherwise, since every act of worship that the servant performs, which is hoped to be a means to the attainment of some blessing, is such that it can hardly repay even the blessing of existence, or the blessing of the capacity to perform it, for example, let alone deserve another blessing? For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said, as reported by the two Shaykhs from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "No one's deeds will admit him to Paradise." It was said: "Not even you, Messenger of God?" He said: "Not even I, unless God covers me with His mercy and grace."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 78 (part 2 of 2):

(Whatever affliction befalls you) of the afflictions, it is because of your own committing of sins and lapses that necessitate it, although from the standpoint of origination it is attributed to Him, the Exalted, descending from Him as a punishment. This is like His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your own hands have earned, and He pardons much﴾.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No servant is struck by a calamity, great or small, except because of a sin, and what Allah pardons is more."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said regarding the verse: "Whatever misfortune befalls you is because of your sin, and I (Allah) have decreed that upon you."

And from Abu Salih, the like of it.

Al-Zajjaj said: The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while the intended meaning is the Ummah. It was also said: it is addressed to him, peace and blessings be upon him, but not to describe his own state; rather, to describe the state of the disbelievers by way of depiction. Perhaps the shift away from addressing them is to show complete wrath and anger against them, and to indicate that, because of their extreme ignorance and dullness, they are far from deserving to be addressed, especially with such an elegant wisdom.

Then know that there is no proof for us, nor for the Mu'tazilah, in the matter of good and evil from these two verses; for one of them, by its apparent sense, is for us and the other for them, so interpretation (ta'wil) is necessary, and it is a shared obligation of argument. Also, the intended meaning of "good" (hasanah) and "evil" (sayyi'ah) is blessing and affliction, not obedience and disobedience, and the dispute concerns the latter. Nor is there any contradiction between them, since the difference of the aspects of negation and affirmation is evident.

Al-Imam al-Razi has greatly elaborated on this point, enumerating the opinions and preferences, and he chose to interpret "good" and "evil" in a way that encompasses blessings, acts of obedience, acts of disobedience, and afflictions.

Some of them said: It may be said that when the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And if good befalls them﴾, came after His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you﴾, it was fitting that the first good be taken to mean blessing and the evil to mean affliction,

* * *

and when the saying of the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿Whatever good befalls you﴾, was followed by what will come, it was fitting that these be taken to refer to what pertains to moral obligation, namely disobedience and obedience, as was narrated from Abu al-Aliyah. For this reason the style was changed, and the past tense was used after the present tense had been used. Then he (al-Alusi) quoted from al-Raghib that there is a distinction between your saying "This is from Allah, the Exalted" and your saying "This is from Allah, the Exalted," namely that "from the presence of Allah" (min 'inda Allah) is more general, in that it is said of what occurs by His pleasure and by His displeasure, and of what occurs while He has commanded it or forbidden it; whereas "from Allah" (min Allah) is said only of what occurs by His pleasure and by His command. On this basis, Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "If I am right, it is from Allah, and if I am wrong, it is from Satan." So reflect.

Abu Hayyan transmitted from a group of scholars that "Whatever affliction befalls you" and so on is under the assumption of a verb of saying, i.e., ﴿So what is wrong with these people that they can hardly understand any statement?﴾ They say: ﴿Whatever good befalls you﴾ and so on. The impetus for them toward this contrivance is the supposition of a contradiction. Others were moved to make the clause a substitute for ﴿statement﴾, in the sense that they do not understand this statement, namely ﴿Whatever affliction befalls you﴾ and so on, so they say it without shrinking from what it entails of multiplicity of creators. And others resorted to assuming an interrogative of denial, i.e., ﴿Then from yourself?﴾ and they claimed that it was read with this. You have learned that there is no contradiction at all, without any need to commit what sound taste scarcely allows.

Likewise, there is no proof for the Mu'tazilah in the Exalted's saying "statement" (hadithan) for the createdness of the Qur'an, because, as you know, it is not a text regarding the Qur'an; and even granting that it were a text, it would not indicate the origination of the inner speech, and the dispute concerns that.

Then the connection of these verses with what precedes them, as has been said, is that after He, glorified is He, related what He related about the Muslims and refuted them with what He refuted, He also related what He refuted of the disbelievers, and there is a connection between the two reported statements in that both involve attributing what is disliked to some matters and that the dislike is because of that; and this, as you see, is far-fetched.

In al-Kashshaf: the clause ﴿And if a misfortune befalls them﴾ is coordinated with the clause of His saying: ﴿If a misfortune befalls you﴾ and ﴿If a bounty comes to you﴾, indicating the confirmation of slowing and discouraging. As for the indication of the first two, there is no concealment in them; and as for the second, it is because when they believed in the one calling to jihad, ﴿ﷺ﴾, that false belief, they were certain that in following him, especially regarding what leads to what they counted as evil, there is corruption and ruin; and for this reason God turned it against them in His saying: ﴿Then from yourself?﴾ so that this would restrain them from discouragement toward encouragement; and He followed it with mention of what they are in of perversion regarding the one who is a mercy sent to mankind entirely, and He emphasized the matter of following him by making his obedience the obedience of Allah, the Exalted, together with the severe threat He added to it, contained in His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away﴾.

Then he said: It is not hidden that what came between the two coordinated clauses is not foreign, and that ﴿So let him fight﴾ is very closely tied to what precedes it. Since this arrangement necessitated dividing those addressed into a disbelieving slowpoke, a strong believer, and a weak believer, he took up their division once more in His, glorified is He, later saying: ﴿And they say﴾, i.e., the people addressed, one of whom is the first, the one who spends the night plotting, and the one who spreads it abroad is the third, and the one who refers it back is the second. This is the manner of the arrangement and connection between the preceding and following verses, end of quote. It is not devoid of goodness, but it is not definite, as is not hidden.

Furthermore, Abu Amr and al-Kisa'i, in one report from him, paused on the ﴿ma﴾ in the Exalted's saying ﴿So what is wrong with these people﴾, and a group paused on the lam of the genitive; and al-Samin criticized that by saying that neither of the two pauses should be permitted, since the first is a pause on the subject without its predicate and the second is a pause on the preposition without its genitive.

Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud, and Ibn Abbas read: ﴿Whatever evil befalls you is from yourself, and I have written it against you.﴾

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 79:

﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger.﴾ This is an explanation of the greatness of his station (ﷺ) and his standing with his Lord, the Exalted, after defending him in the most complete manner. It also contains a rebuttal of those who claimed that his (ﷺ) mission was restricted to the Arabs. The definite article in (lil-nas, "to mankind") is for totality (al-istighraq), and the prepositional phrase is connected to (rasulan, "as a messenger"), placed before it for restriction (li-l-ikhtisas), with attention to the qualifier of generality. That is: sent to all people, not merely to some of them as they claimed. (Rasulan) is an emphasizing circumstantial accusative (hal mu'akkidah) for its governing verb. It is also permitted that the prepositional phrase be connected to what precedes it, or that it be connected to a omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial accusative of (rasulan). It is also permitted that (rasulan) be an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), either as a verbal noun, as in the poet's words:

Indeed the slanderers have lied, I did not utter anything in their presence, nor did I send them with a messenger.

Or because the attributive form may be used in the sense of the verbal noun as an absolute object, as the poet used (kharijan) in the sense of (kharujan) in his words:

I have sworn an oath that I will never revile time as a Muslim, nor will a lying word of speech come out of my mouth.

Here he intended, as Sibawayh said: "and he does not go out (yakhruju) going out (khuruj)."

﴿And Allah suffices as a witness﴾ to your message, or to your truthfulness in everything you claim, since He established the miracles and sent down the clear signs. It has also been said that the meaning is: Allah, the Exalted, suffices as a witness over His servants for whatever good or evil they do. The shift to the third person (al-iltifat) is to cultivate reverence.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 80:

﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾ is an explanation of the rulings concerning his mission (risalah) ﷺ, following the explanation of its realisation. The reason it is so is that the one who commands and forbids in reality is the Truth, glorified is He, while the Messenger is only a conveyor (muballigh) of the command and the prohibition. Therefore obedience is not due to him in himself; it is due to the one who conveyed from Allah.

In some transmitted reports from Muqatil: "The Prophet ﷺ used to say: 'Whoever loves me has loved Allah, the Exalted, and whoever obeys me has obeyed Allah, the Exalted.' The hypocrites said: 'Do you not hear what this man says? He has committed shirk. He was forbidden to worship other than Allah, the Exalted. He only wants us to take him as a lord, just as the Christians took Jesus, peace be upon him.' So this verse was revealed."

The intended meaning of "the Messenger" is our Prophet ﷺ. Expressing him by this title and placing it in the position of a pronoun serves to indicate the causal link. It was said: the intended meaning is the category (jins) of messengers, and our Prophet ﷺ enters it in the primary sense. But the specification of address in the words of the Exalted, ﴿And whoever turns away, We have not sent you as a watcher over them﴾, rejects this, and making it a case of addressing an unspecified person is contrary to the apparent meaning. The word "man" (من) is conditional, and the answer of the condition is omitted; what is mentioned is a justification for it that stands in its place. That is: "And whoever turns away from obedience, then turn away from him, because We have sent you only as a messenger conveying, not as a watcher and guardian who keeps their deeds over them and calls them to account for them." It was said that the negation concerns his being a "ḥafīẓ" (one who guards intensively), not his being a "ḥāfiẓ" (a guard), because the messengership is never separated from guarding, since conveying the rulings is a kind of guarding against sins and wrongdoings. The word "watcher" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the kāf (in "arsalnāka"); making it a second object of "arsalnāka" by implying the meaning of "jaʿalnā" is unnecessary. "ʿAlayhim" is connected to it and was placed first for the sake of the rhyme (fāṣilah). In using the singular pronoun for the subject and the plural pronoun for the object there is consideration of the wording of "man" and its meaning. In shifting from the expected parallel "and whoever turns away, then he has disobeyed Him" to what is mentioned, there is a degree of emphasis that is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 81:

﴿ويَقُولُونَ﴾ The pronoun (ḍamīr) refers to the hypocrites (munafiqun), as narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him both) and al-Hasan and al-Suddi. It was also said that it refers to the Muslims of whom it is reported that they fear people as they fear Allah. That is: and they say, when you command them to something, ﴿obedience﴾, meaning our affair and our situation is obedience. This is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada') that must be omitted. The reading "your obedience is obedience" (taqdiruhu: ṭāʿatuka ṭāʿatun) goes against the apparent sense. Or the meaning is "with us or from us is obedience," where it is the subject (mubtada') and its predicate is omitted. Its original form was the accusative (naṣb), as the lover says: "We hear and obey" (samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan).
