However, in such constructions the nominative (rafʿ) is permissible, as Sibawayh explicitly stated, to indicate that this obedience is established for them before the answer.

﴿فَإذا بَرَزُوا مِن عِنْدِكَ﴾ That is: they went out from your assembly and left you. ﴿بَيَّتَ طائِفَةٌ﴾ That is: a group ﴿مِنهُمْ﴾ of them, namely their leaders, arranged (tabyit) at night. Tabyit is either from al-bayatah (spending the night), because it is the planning of an action at night and resolving upon it, and from it comes "tabyit the intention of fasting" (tabyit niyyat al-siyam), and it is said: "this is a matter that was planned (tabayyata) at night." Or it is from bayt al-shiʿr (a line of poetry), because the poet arranges and composes it. Or it is from the built house (al-bayt al-mabni), because it is arranged and planned. Yet this is remote, although al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) established it linguistically.

The intended meaning is: they devised and arranged (zawwarat wa-sawwat) ﴿غَيْرَ الَّذِي تَقُولُ﴾ that is: contrary to what you said to them, or to what they said to you of acceptance and pledging obedience. The shift from the past tense (al-madi) is for the purpose of indicating continuity. The attribution of the verb to a group of them indicates that they are the ones who directly undertake it, while the rest are followers of them in that, not because they are steadfast in obedience. The masculine form of the verb at first is because the feminine marking of the agent is not real (ghayr haqiqi). Abu ʿAmr and Hamzah read ﴿بَيَّتْ طائِفَةٌ﴾ with idgham (assimilation of consonants, i.e., merging of the two identical letters), because the two letters are close in articulation point (makhraj). Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) mentioned that idgham here is contrary to the original rule and analogy, and no mobile taʾ (ta' with a vowel) other than this one is assimilated.

﴿واللَّهُ يَكْتُبُ ما يُبَيِّتُونَ﴾ That is: He records it in their scrolls (ṣaḥaʾif) so as to requite them for it. Or it means: [He records it] in what He reveals to you, so that He informs you of their secrets and exposes them, as al-Zajjaj said. The purpose according to the first interpretation is to threaten them, and according to the second is to warn you.

﴿فَأعْرِضْ عَنْهُمْ﴾ That is: turn away from them, do not seek to take revenge upon them, or minimize your concern for them. The fa' (particle) indicates that what precedes is the cause of what follows. ﴿وتَوَكَّلْ عَلى اللَّهِ﴾ That is: entrust your affair to Him and trust in Him in all your affairs, especially regarding them.

The mention of the majestic name (Allah) here, rather than a pronoun, serves to indicate the reason for the ruling.

﴿وكَفى بِاللَّهِ وكِيلا﴾ Standing in charge of what has been entrusted to Him of management. So He will suffice you against their harm and will avenge you upon them. The explicit mention of the name is for what has preceded, and to announce that the sentence is self-standing and independent of everything else in every respect.

[Page 93]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 82:**

﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ This is perhaps the answer to a question that arose from God's making Him a witness (shahid). It is as if it were said: "God's testimony is free of doubt, but how is it known that what you have mentioned is God's testimony, reported from Him?" So He, glorified be He, answered with His words: "Do they not then reflect" (afala yatadabbarun). The root meaning of tadabbur (reflection, contemplation) is considering the backs of matters and their final outcomes. Then it was used for every kind of contemplation, whether it is a looking into the reality of a thing and its parts, its antecedents and causes, or its consequences and results. The fa' (then) here is for conjunction with an implied premise, meaning: "Do they doubt that what was mentioned is God's testimony, and so they do not reflect upon the Qur'an that was brought by this Prophet (ﷺ), to whom testimony was given, so that they would know that it is from God, and it would then be a proof? And what a proof it would be for the intended meaning!"

It has also been said: the meaning is, "Do they turn away from the Qur'an and so not contemplate it, so that they would know it is from God, the Exalted, by observing the signs within it, among which is this truthful revelation and the explicit text that exposes their hypocrisy, reported as it truly is?"

﴿Had it been (wa law kana)﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, ﴿from other than God﴾, as they claim, ﴿they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾, in that some of its unseen (ghaybi) reports, such as the report of what the hypocrites conceal, would not conform to reality. For the unseen is known only to God, the Exalted. Since truthfulness is consistent throughout it and that never happened at all, it is known that it is by His informing and from Him. To this the words of al-Asamm and al-Zajjaj point. In a narration from Ibn 'Abbas, the intended meaning is: "they would have found in it much contradiction." This is because human speech, when lengthy, by habit does not avoid contradiction, and what seems to be discrepancy, as in many verses, and of which what preceded just now is an example, is not discrepancy according to those who reflect. It has also been said, and this is not objectionable, contrary to the one who claims otherwise, that the meaning is: "much of it would have been discrepant and contradictory," its composition and eloquence differing. Some of it would reach the limit of inimitability (i'jaz), and some of it would fall short of that and could be matched; some of it would be reports of the unseen that agree with what they report, and some of it would be reports that disagree with what they report; some of it would indicate a correct meaning according to the scholars of semantics (al-ma'ani), and some of it would indicate a corrupt meaning that does not cohere. But since all of it answers with a supreme inimitable eloquence beyond the powers of the eloquent, and its meanings are sound and its reports true, it is known that it is none other than from One capable of what no other is capable of, knowing what no other knows. End of quotation.

[Page 93]

This is based on the premise that the aspect of inimitability (wajh al-i'jaz), according to the scholars of Arabic, is that the Qur'an is at the highest rank of eloquence, and that the purpose of the verse is to establish that the entire Qur'an and part of it are from God, the Exalted. In that case, it is impossible to describe the discrepancy as "much," because the discrepancy would then only be that some of it is inimitable and some of it is not, which is a single discrepancy. Therefore (wajadu) is made transitive to two objects, the first being (kathiran, "much") and the second (ikhtilafan, "discrepancy"), meaning "discrepant" (mukhtalafan). To this his words point: "much of it would have been discrepant." The necessary consequence, on the assumption that it were from other than God, the Exalted, was made to be that much of it would be discrepant, although it would necessarily follow that all of it would be discrepant, by limiting the statement to the lesser part, as in His words: ﴿Some of what He promises you will befall you﴾ (Q 40:28). This is an equitable (munsif) form of speech. By this, the objection is dispelled that "much" is an attribute of "discrepancy," and "discrepancy" is an attribute of the whole in composition, yet it has been made an attribute of "much," and "much" is an attribute of the "much" (i.e., of the part). For we do not accept that "much" is an attribute of "discrepancy." Rather, the two are the two objects of (wajadu). Likewise dispelled is the objection that it is understood from his words, "it would have been that some of it reaches the limit of inimitability," the existence of the power of someone other than God, the Exalted, over an inimitable speech, which is false. For we do not accept that, since the intended meaning is that the Qur'an, in its entirety and in part, is from God, the Exalted; that is, the part with which the challenge (tahaddi) occurred, which is the measure of the shortest surah of it. Had any part of its parts been from other than God, the Exalted, they would have found in it the discrepancy mentioned, namely that some of it would not reach the limit of inimitability. This was said by some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin).

Some have said: there is no escape from the last objection except by understanding the statement as a supposition and assumption, meaning: "Had there been the rank of inimitability in it, it would be only in part, on the condition that this measure is taken from the speech of God, the Exalted, as in quotation (iqtibas) and the like." However, its remoteness is not hidden. Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i also went to this interpretation, explaining discrepancy as variation in eloquence and lack of eloquence.

It is reported from al-Zamakhshari that the verse contains several benefits: the obligation of considering proofs and indications, the invalidity of taqlid (blind imitation), the invalidity of the view of one who says that religious knowledge is self-evident (darury), an indication of the validity of qiyas (analogy), and an indication that the acts of servants are not created by God, the Exalted, because of the contradiction found in them. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that its indication of the obligation of consideration in general and the invalidity of taqlid is correct for all of them. As for the view of one who says that all religious knowledge is self-evident, its indication is so as to validate qiyas according to the technical usage of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), which is not the case. As for the last point, according to what is verified in al-Kashf, it is because the necessary consequence is: "every discrepant thing is from other than God, the Exalted," according to their view, by the converse: "if not, then not"; and "if the acts of servants were of His creation, they would necessarily be from Him," and "the proposition is false"; or "some of the discrepant is from other than God, the Exalted," according to what Shaykh Ibn al-Hajib verified, and what is well known among the people of argumentation. Thus some acts of servants are not created by Him, the Exalted, and that suffices for the argument, since no one distinguishes between some and some when it is voluntary. He answered this by saying that the necessary consequence "every discrepant thing" is "a Qur'an from other than God, the Exalted," on the first reading, and in that case the argument is not complete.

It has been mentioned that the meaning of (had it been from other than God) according to the majority is: "had it subsisted in other than God, the Exalted." There is no room for creation in this implication. You know that this is not the apparent intention here. Likewise, the verse has been cited as evidence against the view of one who claims that the Qur'an cannot be understood except through the explanation of the Messenger (ﷺ) or the infallible Imam, as some Shi'a have said.

[Page 93]

﴿And when there comes to them﴾, i.e., the hypocrites, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and al-Dahhak and Abu Mu'adh; or the weak among the Muslims, as related from al-Hasan, and this is the view of most exegetes (mufassirun); or both groups, as transmitted by Ibn 'Atiyya. ﴿a matter of security or fear﴾, i.e., something that warrants security or fear. ﴿they spread it﴾, i.e., they disseminated it. The bi' (ب) in "adha'u bihi" is superfluous (mazidah). In al-Kashshaf it is said: "adha'a al-sharra" and "adha'a bihi" (both are used). It is also possible that the meaning is: they performed the act of dissemination (al-idha'ah) concerning it, and this is more emphatic than "adha'uhu," because it indicates that they are doing the very reality (of spreading), as in the phrase "Fulan yu'ti wa yamna'" (so-and-so gives and withholds), and because of the ambiguity and clarification it contains. It has also been said that the bi' is there to imply that idha'ah includes the meaning of "tahdith" (reporting), and that it is taken in the sense of "ma'a" (with), and the pronoun refers to the coming (al-maji'). But it is not appropriate to construe the noble speech of Allah the Exalted in this way.

The discourse is directed at explaining another offence among the offences of the hypocrites, or at explaining the offence of the weak following the explanation of the offence of the hypocrites. This is because when a military expedition (sariyyah) of the Muslims went out, people were informed about it, and they said: "The Muslims inflicted such-and-such on their enemy, and the enemy inflicted such-and-such on the Muslims." They then disseminated it among themselves without the Prophet (ﷺ) being the one who informed them of it, and this is hardly free of corruption (mafsadah). It has also been said: they used to stand, with respect to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the people in authority (ulu al-amr), in a state of security and confidence in victory over some enemies, or in a state of fear, and so they would spread it; it would then spread and reach the enemies, and the dissemination would thus become a corruption. It has also been said: the weak used to hear from the mouths of the hypocrites some report about the expeditions, which was conjectural and not of certain authenticity, and they would disseminate it before verifying it, and so that would turn out to be a calamity upon the believers. In this there is a rebuke for one who speaks of a matter before verifying it.

Muslim has transmitted from Abu Hurayra, as a marfu' report: "It is enough sin for a person that he narrates everything he hears." And the clause, according to the author of al-Kashshaf, is coordinated (ma'tufah) upon the words of the Exalted: ﴿And they say: obedience﴾.

The words of the Glorified: ﴿Will they not then reflect?﴾ form a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD), a warning to them against concealing (idmar) what contradicts the apparent meaning, for in reflecting upon the Qur'an there is a leading to obedience to the one to whom it was revealed, what a leading it is! It has also been said: the discourse is directed at averting what might be imagined in some matters of a semblance of contradiction, on the basis that they did not grasp the intended meaning; the explanation is that this is because they did not comprehend the meaning of the speech, not because its indication deviates from it. This is because some of the weak Muslims, who had no experience of the circumstances, used to disseminate, whenever the Prophet (ﷺ) informed them of what had been revealed to him of a promise of victory or a warning of the unbelievers, without understanding its meaning nor having precise grasp of its import, according to what they understood and the interpretations they gave it. And even assuming understanding, that might be conditional upon matters which are lost by dissemination, so its expected effect does not appear, and thus that becomes a source of imagining contradiction. This is not devoid of merit, but the transmissions of the early generations (al-salaf) are contrary to it.

Whatever the case, Allah the Exalted has censured them for that, saying: ﴿And if they had referred it﴾, i.e., that matter which came to them, ﴿to the Messenger﴾ (ﷺ) ﴿and to those in authority among them﴾, and they are the senior Companions (kibar al-sahabah), may Allah be pleased with them, the perceptive in affairs. This is the view taken by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and a great number of people.

Al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, and Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i said: what is meant by them are the commanders of the expeditions and the governors. The former view is the one relied upon. ﴿would have known it﴾, i.e., would have known the management of that matter which they were informed of; ﴿those who infer it from them﴾, i.e., they would extract its management by their acuteness, their experience, their knowledge of the affairs of war and its stratagems. Or: had they referred it to the Messenger (ﷺ) and those mentioned, and entrusted it to them, and acted as though they had not heard it, then those who infer its management would have known how to manage it and what to do and what to leave undone. Or: ﴿had they referred it to the Messenger﴾ (ﷺ), and to the great among his Companions, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them, and said: "We will remain silent until we hear it from them and know it," then they would have known whether it is of what should be disseminated or not, and whether its authenticity is established or not. These disseminators, who infer it from the Messenger and those in authority, that is, receive it from them and extract its knowledge from their side, or: had they presented it to his opinion, peace and blessings be upon him, seeking to uncover its meaning and what management befits it, and to the noble among his companions, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them, then those who refer it would have known its meaning and its management; and these are the ones who infer it and extract its knowledge and management from the side of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and whoever is honoured by being joined to him. The mention of "the Messenger" is because it is among the things that necessitate referral.

The word ﴿from﴾ (min) is either initial (ibtida'iyyah), with the adverbial phrase being a loose complement (laghw) attached to "yastanbitunahu"; or partitive (tab'idiyyah) or explicative (bayaniyyah, tajridiyyah), with the adverbial phrase being a circumstantial (hal). The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is placed in the position of the pronoun in the last two possibilities, to indicate that the aim of referral should be to seek out the meaning and clarify the import. Istinbat, in origin, is the extraction of a thing from its source, like water from a well, or a jewel from a mine; the extracted thing is called "nabat" (with a vowel on the ba'), and then it was used figuratively for every taking and receiving.

﴿And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾: this is an address to the group mentioned just before, on the basis that they are the weak among the believers, in the manner of the shift (iltifat). What is meant by grace and mercy is one thing, i.e., were it not for His grace upon you, glorified is He, and His mercy by guiding you to the path of right guidance, which is referral to the Messenger (ﷺ) and to those in authority, ﴿you would have followed Satan﴾, and acted according to your weak opinions, or taken on the opinions of the hypocrites in what you do and leave undone, and you would not have been guided to the direction of correctness ﴿except for a few﴾; and these are the people of authority whose minds are illuminated by the lights of firm faith, who stand upon the secrets, and who are firmly grounded in knowledge of the rulings through borrowing from the niche of prophethood. Thus the exception is discontinuous (munqati'), or the address is to the people in general, i.e., ﴿And were it not for the grace of Allah﴾, the Exalted, through the Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿and His mercy﴾, through the sending down of the Qur'an, as al-Suddi and al-Dahhak explained the two, and this is the choice of al-Jubba'i; and the reverse is not far-fetched. ﴿you would all have followed Satan﴾ and remained in unbelief and error, ﴿except for a few﴾ among you, upon whom was bestowed a sound intellect, so he was guided by it to the true path, and was safe from the abysses of error, and was preserved from following Satan without the sending of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the sending down of the Book, such as Qass ibn Sa'idah al-Iyadi, Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, Waraqah ibn Nawfal, and their like. Thus the exception is continuous (muttasil), and this is the view of al-Anbari.

Abu Muslim said: what is meant by the grace of Allah and His mercy is victory and help, time and again. The meaning is: were it not for the occurrence of victory and triumph for you in succession, ﴿you would have followed Satan﴾ in what he casts to you of whisperings and thoughts leading to cowardice, feebleness, inclination to error, and abandonment of the religion, ﴿except for a few﴾, and they are among the people of penetrating insight, firm resolve, and sincere intentions, among the excellent of the believers, who know that it is not a condition of the religion being true that worldly dominion be attained, nor of its being false that defeat and rout occur; rather, the matter of its being true or false rests upon the proof. It is not objected that making the exception from the sentence that precedes it entails the permissibility that a person may move from unbelief to faith, and from following Satan to disobeying him and being humiliated, and that Allah the Exalted has no grace in that. Far be it from Allah the Exalted that any Muslim monotheist, whether Sunni or Mu'tazili, should believe this. This is because "law" (lawla) is a particle indicating the prohibition of one thing because of the existence of another, and it has been shown that the non-following of Satan by the believers, in unbelief and otherwise, occurred only by the grace of Allah the Exalted upon them. Thus grace is the cause preventing the following of Satan. So if the exception is taken from what has been mentioned, you have negated the effect of Allah the Exalted's grace in preventing following for the excepted group, of necessity. And making them independently capable of faith and of disobeying Satan, who calls to unbelief, by themselves and not by the grace of Allah the Exalted, is unacceptable. Do you not see that when you say to one whom you remind of your right over him: "Had it not been for my assistance to you, you would have been stripped of your wealth, except for a little," you did not make your assistance have any effect in the preservation of the little for the addressee, but you bestowed favour upon him for the effect of your assistance in preserving most of his wealth and not all of it. This is because we say this only when the grace is general, not when it is specific, as we have indicated; for the non-following when it is not by this specific grace does not preclude its being by another grace. Yes, the apparent wording of al-Kashshaf in this context is problematic, in that it made the exception from the last clause and added the explanation (al-tawfiq) in the statement. It may also be said: he meant by it a specific tawfiq arising from what precedes it, and this is better than the unrestricted rendering, and removing the difficulty by saying that the absence of grace and mercy upon all does not necessarily entail its absence upon some, is forced (takalluf).

Some, to escape the objection, went to making the exception from the words of the Exalted: ﴿they spread it﴾. This was related from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the choice of al-Mubarrad, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Balkhi, al-Tabari. The Qadi Abu Bakr took the verse as evidence in refuting those who held that the exception, when there are multiple sentences, returns to the last one.

It is also reported from some people of language that the exception is from the words of the Glorified: ﴿they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾; and from most of them that it is from the words of the Exalted: ﴿those who infer it would have known it﴾. Al-Farra' and al-Mubarrad objected to this, saying: what is known through inference, the few know it and the many are ignorant of it, and directing the exception to what they have mentioned entails the opposite of that. al-Zajjaj responded to this by saying it is an error, because by this inference is not meant what is extracted by a fine inquiry and obscure reflection; it is rather the inference of news, and if that is the case, most people know it and none is ignorant of it except one who is extremely dull. This is open to scrutiny. Some have gone to making the exception an exception from the verbal noun (masdar), so that what follows "illa" is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), meaning: you would have followed it with every following except a few following, by remaining on the practice of unbelief and its traces, except for a small, rare remaining with respect to some, and that may be by mere disposition and custom. The best and closest of these aspects to verification, according to the Imam, is what Abu Muslim mentioned. The specification in what al-Anbari went to is supported by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger...﴾ etc., and the words of the Glorified: ﴿Will they not reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ both bear witness to it; and in what comes after it, that the words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And when there comes to them a matter of security or fear﴾ etc.

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 84:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So fight in the way of Allah; you are not burdened except with yourself﴾ is supported by what precedes it, and you know that the indication that it is restricted to these two matters is not evident. The fa' (فَ) in this verse is in response to an omitted condition (shart mahdhuf), which the noble composition implies. That is: if the matter is as has been related, namely the disobedience of the hypocrites and the shortcoming of the others in observing the rulings of Islam, then fight, you alone, without concern for what they have done.

Al-Tabarsi (al-Tabrisi) transmitted two views on how the verse is connected to what precedes it:

The first is that it is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed or triumphs, We will bring him a great reward﴾. The meaning is: if you desire the great reward, then fight. This is transmitted from al-Zajjaj.

The second is that it is connected to His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And what is [wrong] with you that you do not fight in the way of Allah﴾. The meaning is: if they do not fight in the way of Allah, then fight, you alone. It has also been said that it is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So fight the allies of Satan﴾. As for the meaning of ﴿you are not burdened except with yourself﴾, it means you are not burdened except with its doing, since there is no obligation imposed upon essences (adh-dhawat). This is an exception (istithna') that affirms what precedes it, for the restriction of his, upon him be blessings and peace, obligation to his own action is one of the necessary consequences of his, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, personally engaging in fighting. In it is an indication that what they did of discouragement and holding back does not harm him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and he is not held accountable for it.

Some of the scholars of verification (al-muhaqqiqin) held that the speech is figurative (majaz) or allusive (kinayah, metonymy) for that meaning. Therefore it is not objected that he was commanded to burden the people, for how can that be? And there is no need for what has been said. Rather, in its establishment, he said: he, upon him be blessings and peace, was commanded to fight alone at first. For this reason al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said regarding the people of apostasy: "I will fight them alone, and even if my right hand opposed me, I would fight them with my left."

Abu al-Baqa' made this clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the subject of (قاتِلْ), meaning: so fight, not burdened except with yourself.

It was read (لا تُكَلِّفْ) with the jussive, on the basis that (لا) is a prohibitive particle, and the verb is jussive due to it. That is: do not burden anyone with going out except yourself. It has also been said that it is jussive in response to the imperative, but this is far-fetched. (ولا نُكَلِّفُ) was read with the nun, on the basis of the active voice, so (نَفْسَكَ) is a second object with an implied genitive construction, and it is not in the position of the first object. That is: we do not burden you except with the action of yourself. It is not that we do not burden anyone except yourself. It has also been said that there is no impediment to this, meaning: we do not burden anyone with this burden except yourself, and the intended meaning of this burden is fighting alone.

﴿And urge the believers﴾ means: incite them to fighting, encourage them toward it, and admonish them, because they are sinful for having stayed behind, given that it was made obligatory upon them years before this. The original meaning of ta'rid (tahrid, urging) is removing the harad, which is what has no good in it and is not counted. So the form (taf'il) here indicates removal, like qadhaytuhu (I removed its speck) and jaladtuhu (I removed its skin). The object of urging was not mentioned because it is clearly evident.

﴿It may be that Allah will restrain the might﴾ (nikayah, the harm) of ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, among whom were the Quraysh. And (عَسى, it may be), from Allah, exalted is He, as al-Hasan and others said, is a certainty, and He, glorified is He, did what He promised. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, related: "After the battle of Uhud, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had promised Abu Sufyan a meeting at the lesser Badr season in Dhu al-Qa'dah. When the appointed time came, he called the people to go out, but some of them disliked it, so this verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, went out with a group of his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, until he reached the Badr season. Allah, glorified is He, restrained the might of the enemy from them, and Abu Sufyan did not meet them. Allah cast terror into his heart, and there was no fighting that day, and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, returned with those who were with him, safe."

﴿And Allah is mightier in might﴾ than those who disbelieved ﴿and more severe in punishment﴾, meaning in torment. Its original meaning is torment by nakl, which is a shackle, and it was generalized. The intended purpose of the sentence is threat and encouragement, and the manifestation of the glorious Name serves to instill awe, to give the reason for the ruling, to strengthen the independence of the sentence, and the emphatic form of the predicate serves to affirm the severity.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession will have a share of it﴾, meaning: a abundant portion, ﴿of it﴾, meaning: of its reward. This is a resumptive sentence (jumlah mustanifah), brought to explain that he, upon him be blessings and peace, through what he was commanded of urging the believers, has an ample portion of reward. Through this the verse is linked to what precedes it, as al-Qadi said.

'Ali ibn 'Isa said: when He, glorified is He, said: ﴿you are not burdened except with yourself﴾, indicating that he, upon him be blessings and peace, is not held accountable for the action of others, it may have given rise to the suspicion that just as he is not held accountable for others' actions, his deeds are not increased by others' deeds either. So what might be suspected by that was refuted. This is nothing, as is not hidden.

(Al-shafa'ah, intercession) is the mediation by speech in the attainment by a person, even if he is of higher rank than the intercessor, of some benefit, worldly or otherwise, or his deliverance from some harm of such kind. It derives from (al-shaf', even), the opposite of (al-witr, odd), as if the one interceded for was an odd number and the intercessor made him an even number. From it comes the (shafi') in ownership, because he joins the property of another to his own, or joins himself to the one who buys it and seeks it from him. (Al-hasanah, good) in it is what is in a legislated matter, by which the right of a Muslim is observed, seeking the face of Allah, exalted is He. Among it is supplication for the Muslims, for it is an intercession in meaning before Allah, exalted is He.

Muslim and others related from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "Whoever supplicates for his Muslim brother in his absence, it is answered for him, and the angel says: 'And for you is the like of that.'" In this is an explanation of the measure of the promised portion. I do not see it as proper to apply the term intercession to supplication for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; rather I can hardly permit it, even though there is benefit in it for him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, just as there is benefit for us according to the correct view.

Its interpretation as supplication, as transmitted from al-Jubba'i, or as reconciliation between two people, as al-Kalbi related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, is perhaps by way of example and not restriction. That the urging which he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did is of the category of intercession is evident, for the believers were freed by it from the harm of discouragement, the mockery of the enemy, and the risk of humiliation, and they succeeded in the immense reward stored up for them on the Day of Resurrection. They also gained great wealth because of that. It is related that when he, upon him be blessings and peace, arrived at Badr with his army and did not find any of the enemy there, he stayed eight nights. They had merchandise with them, so they sold it and gained much good.

Some people interpreted intercession here as a person becoming the partner (shaf') of his companion in obedience or disobedience, and the good intercession is that which is in obedience. Then the sentence is directed toward encouragement to jihad and warning against staying behind and holding back. The connection in this is evident, and there is no harm in it, though the majority hold otherwise.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 85:

Page 98
﴿And whoever intercedes with an evil intercession﴾: this is what is contrary to the good (ḥasanah). Among it is intercession concerning one of the ḥudūd (prescribed punishments) of God Most High. In a report (khabar): "Whoever's intercession comes between him and one of the ḥudūd of God Most High has indeed opposed God in His dominion, and whoever helps in a dispute without knowledge remains under the wrath of God Most High until he desists." Excepted from the ḥudūd is retaliation (qiṣāṣ), so interceding for its remission in exchange for blood money (diyah) is not forbidden. ﴿He will have a share (kifl) of it﴾, i.e., a portion of its burden (wizr). This is how al-Suddi, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd interpreted it, as did many of the people of lexicography (ahl al-lughah). The use of "share" (naṣīb) for the good intercession and "kifl" for the evil intercession is for variety of expression (tafannun). Some of the verifiers (muḥaqqiqin) distinguished between them by saying that naṣīb includes the increase, while kifl is the equal counterpart. So naṣīb is chosen first, because the reward of a good deed is multiplied, and kifl second, because whoever brings an evil deed is only recompensed with its equal. Thus the verse contains an indication of God Most High's gentleness toward His servants. Some said: although kifl means naṣīb, it has come to be predominantly used for evil, and rarely for anything else, as in the saying of God Most High: ﴿He will give you a double portion (kiflayn) of His mercy﴾. Therefore it was specified for the evil intercession, for the sake of praising (taṭriyah) and avoiding repetition.

﴿And God is ever Muqīt over all things﴾: i.e., Capable (muqtadir), as Ibn 'Abbas said when Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked him about it, and he cited the verse of Uhayhah al-Ansari:

"And one with rancor, I restrained myself from him, and I was over his ill-will (muqītan)."

This was also related from a group of the Successors (tabi'un).

In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, it means the Guardian (ḥafīẓ). Its derivation is from qūt (sustenance), for it strengthens the body and preserves it. And from al-Jubba'i it means the Recompenser (mujāzī), i.e., He recompenses for every thing, of good deeds and evil deeds. Its origin is muqwat, which was altered (u'illa) like muqīm. The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) confirming what precedes it according to all the other interpretations.

[p. 99]

﴿And when you are greeted with a greeting﴾: this is an encouragement, as Shaykh al-Islam said, toward a common instance of good intercession, after encouragement toward intercession in general and a warning against its opposite, evil intercession. The greeting of Islam from a Muslim is an intercession from him on behalf of his brother before Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This reading is more fitting to the context than what al-Tabarsi said: that since the meaning of peace (al-salam) is peaceful relations, which are the opposite of war, and since fighting had been mentioned earlier, the verse follows it to indicate restraint toward those who offer peace to the believers and greet them with the greeting of Islam.

The word tahiyyah is a verbal noun of ḥayya. Its original form was taḥiyyah, like tatmiyah and tazkiyah. The root of that was taḥiyyay with three yā's, the last of which was deleted and replaced by the feminine ending (tā' marbūṭah), the vowel of the first yā' was moved to the letter before it, and then the two were merged. Originally, as al-Rāghib said, it means invoking life and its length, and then it was used for every invocation. When the Arabs met one another they would say: "May Allah grant you life" (ḥayyāka Allāh taʿālā). Then the Sharia used it for greeting with peace, which is the greeting of Islam. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Their greeting on the day they meet Him will be, "Peace"﴾, and He, Glorified is He, said: ﴿So greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good﴾. It is said that this has an advantage over the phrase "May Allah grant you life," because it is an invocation for safety from calamities, which may entail a long life; and there is nothing in the other phrase but an invocation for a long life, or for that together with sovereignty. And many a life is such that death is better than it:

"Is there not a death that can be bought so I may buy it? For this life holds no good."

"Has the Guardian not had mercy on the soul of a free man who gave away his own death to his brother?"

Another poet said:

"He who has died and found rest is not a dead man; the dead one is the dead among the living.
The dead man is he who lives in grief, his affairs gloomy, with little hope."

Also, since al-Salam is among the names of Allah the Exalted, and beginning with mention of it is of undoubted merit and distinction, the meaning is: when peace is offered to you on behalf of the believers
[p. 99 continued]
as al-Hasan and ʿAṭāʾ said, or in general, as Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, and others reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both.

﴿then return it with something better than it﴾: that is, with a greeting better than the greeting with which you were greeted, by saying: "And upon you be peace and the mercy of Allah," if the Muslim has limited himself to the first part; or by adding "and His blessings," if the Muslim has combined both. This is the highest degree.

Al-Bayhaqi reported from ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr that a man greeted him saying: "Peace be upon you, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings." ʿUrwah said: "He has left us no excess; peace has come to its end with 'and His blessings.'" In the same sense, Imam Aḥmad and al-Ṭabarānī reported from Salmān al-Fārisī, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). This is because that greeting encompasses all the aims: safety from harms, attainment of benefits, their continuation and their growth. It is also said: the one greeted increases in dignity when the greeter combines all three for him.

Al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad reported from Salim, the freedman of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, who said: When Ibn ʿUmar was greeted by a single person, he would add to it. I came to him and said: "Peace be upon you." He said: "Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah." Then I came to him another time and said: "Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah and His blessings." He said: "Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah and His blessings and the goodness of His prayers."

The addition is not limited to what has been mentioned. A report narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Bayhaqi from Muʿadh includes the addition "and His forgiveness." So what is in al-Durr (that the intended meaning is that one should not add anything beyond "and His blessings") is not agreed upon.

﴿or return it﴾: that is, respond with its like. The "or" (aw) indicates a choice between adding and leaving it as it is. The apparent view is that the first option is the better one in replying. Indeed, if the greeter says more than "Peace be upon you," that is even better. Al-Bayhaqi reported from Sahl ibn Ḥunayf that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says, 'Peace be upon you,' Allah records for him ten good deeds. If he says, 'Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah,' Allah records for him twenty good deeds. If he says, 'Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah and His blessings,' Allah records for him thirty good deeds." Other reports with similar meaning have also come.

They have stated that responding to the recommended greeting is obligatory, and its obligation is collective (wājib kifāʾī, an obligation that is fulfilled by some and discharges the rest). The greeter's waiving of it does not affect this, because the right belongs to Allah the Exalted. The evidence for the collective obligation is the report of Abu Dawud, and in the same sense what al-Bayhaqi reported from Zayd ibn Aslam, without him declaring it weak: "It suffices on behalf of a group when they pass by that one of them greets, and it suffices on behalf of those sitting that one of them returns it." By this, the obligation is removed from the rest, and the reward is specific to the one who responds. If all of them respond, even in sequence, they are each rewarded with the reward of the obligatory act. In al-Mubtaghā it is said: the obligation is removed from the rest by the response of a child who understands, because he is among those who can establish the obligation to some extent, as evidenced by the permissibility of slaughter by him. It is said: No. The apparent view of al-Nihayah favors this, and the Shafiʿis hold it. They said: If a child responds, or does not hear them, it does not suffice, unlike the parallel case in the funeral prayer, because the purpose there is supplication, and that comes closer to being answered from him; here the purpose is security, and he is not of its people. Its implication is that the blessing of a child for a sneezer suffices on behalf of a group, because the purpose is blessing and supplication, like the funeral prayer. The obligation is also removed by the response of an elderly person.

Regarding the response of a young woman, there are two opinions, both among us (the Hanafis) and among the Shafiʿis. If a woman responds on behalf of a man, it suffices, provided it is legitimate to greet her and him. So it is not limited to an elderly woman. Rather, a mahram, and a man's female slave and wife are similar. In Tuhfatuhum it says: What is included in the recommended greeting is a woman's greeting to a woman, or to a relative within the prohibited degrees, or to her master, or to her husband; likewise to a non-mahram if she is an elderly woman who is not desired. In this case it is obligatory for her to return the greeting of a man. As for a desirable woman who has no other woman with her, it is forbidden for her to return the greeting of a non-mahram, and the same applies to initiating it. It is disliked for him to return her greeting, and likewise to initiate it. The difference is that her returning and her initiating greeting encourage him toward her more, unlike his initiating and returning. The hermaphrodite (khunthā), when with a man, is like a woman, and when with a woman, is like a man, in regard to gazing; so it is the same here. If greetings are offered to a group of women, it is obligatory to return the greeting of one of them, since temptation is not feared in that case. For this reason, seclusion with two women is permitted. The apparent view is that the matter here is like that of a man, both in initiating and in responding.

In al-Durr al-Mukhtar: If someone says, "Peace be upon you, O Zayd," the obligation is not discharged by someone else's response. But if he says, "O so-and-so," or gestures to a specific person, the obligation is discharged. If a group who are in sequence greet one person, and he responds once intending all of them, or if he responds without specifying, then according to the more correct views it suffices for him, so long as no harmful separation has occurred. In both initiating and responding, the voice must be raised to a degree that allows hearing in fact, even for one who is hard of hearing. However, if the one passing by quickly does not reach him with his voice, then the apparent view is that he must raise his voice as much as he can. The response should not be loud in a great degree. What is narrated from the Imam (Abu Hanifah), may Allah be pleased with him, perhaps applies to other than this case, not to running after him. It has been inferred that all of the phrasing must be heard both in initiating and in responding. The difference between this and answering the call to prayer when only part of it is heard is evident.

If a Jew, a Christian, or a Zoroastrian greets, there is no harm in responding, but one should not add anything to the reply beyond "and upon you" (wa-ʿalaykum), as in al-Khaniyyah. This has been narrated as a prophetic report in the Sahih. Non-Muslims should not be greeted first, because of the saying of the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace: "Do not initiate greetings to the Jews and the Christians. If you meet one of them on the road, force him to its narrowest part." Narrated by al-Bukhari.

Some Shafiʿis made it obligatory to answer the greeting of a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under protection) with "ʿalayka" alone, and this is what the Rawdah appears to require. However, al-Balqini, al-Adhraʿi, and al-Zarkashi said: it is recommended, not obligatory. From al-Hasan: it is permissible to say to a disbeliever, "And upon you be peace," but one should not say "and the mercy of Allah," for that is a request for forgiveness. From al-Shaʿbi: he said this to a Christian who had greeted him, and when he was asked about it, he said: "Does he not live within the mercy of Allah?"

Ibn al-Mundhir reported through Yunus ibn ʿUbayd, from al-Hasan, that he said about the verse: "Return with something better" is for Muslims, and "or return it" is for the People of the Book. Similar was reported from Qatadah. Some scholars permitted initiating greeting to them when there is a compelling need, and then it is rendered with "al-salam." From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he used to say to a dhimmi, and this is the apparent view when there is need: "al-Salam ʿalayka," while meaning, as Allah the Exalted said, "ʿalayka": that is, "he is your enemy."

In my view there is no objection, if it is not intended as such, to intend a supplication for him for safety, meaning remaining alive, so that he may become a Muslim, or give the jizyah (poll tax) in humility. In al-Ashbah, there is an explicit statement on this, regarding supplicating for him for a long life.

What remains is the disagreement about using the "wa" (and) when responding to him. Most of the hadith scholars, as al-Khattabi said, narrate it with the "wa" in the report, except Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah, who narrates it without "wa." It was deemed the correct version, because the "wa" implies joining with him and entering into what he said, while he may say "al-sam ʿalaykum" (death be upon you), as the report of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, indicates.

Al-ʿAllamah al-Tibi justified the retention of the "wa" by saying that what follows it may be separated from what it is joined to, to convey generality according to the requirement of the context, so it is estimated here as: "Upon you is curse or wrath," and "Upon you is what you have said." This is not very clear, even if he supported it with what he thought was a proof. The better view is what is in al-Kashshaf, that the narration of the majority is the correct one, and both share the nature of being supplications. However, the supplication of a Muslim against a disbeliever is answered, while the supplication of a disbeliever against him is not. It came in the Sahih from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when ʿĀʾishah said to a group of Jews who had said to him, upon him be prayers and peace, "al-sam ʿalayka" ("death be upon you"), "Rather, upon you is death and curse," he (ﷺ) said: "Do not be obscene." She said: "Did you not hear what they said?" He said: "I responded to them, so it is answered for me concerning them, and it is not answered for them concerning me."

When responding to a deaf person, it is obligatory to combine speech with a gesture, so that he may know, since knowledge is what matters. He is not obliged to respond unless the one greeting him combines both. A gesture suffices for a mute person, both in initiating and responding. It is obligatory to respond to a written greeting just as one responds to a spoken greeting.

According to the Shafiʿis, a written reply suffices. If he does not respond verbally, it is apparently obligatory to respond immediately, though the opposite is possible. If someone says to another, "Convey my greetings to so-and-so," the latter is obligated to convey them, and they reasoned that this is a trust (amanah) and its delivery is obligatory. It may be inferred that this applies when he has agreed to bear that trust. But if he refuses it, then no. Likewise, if he remains silent, based on the saying: "No statement is attributed to one who is silent."
[p. 101]
It is possible to distinguish between cases where there is an indication of consent or non-consent. If the obligation is affirmed, the apparent view for some is that the one entrusted need not intend the recipient specifically; rather, when he meets him and mentions it, he conveys it. Some researchers said: what is more appropriate is that he must intend its location, so long as there is no severe hardship by custom upon him, because the performance of a trust is obligatory as far as possible. Some distinguished between the sender saying: "Tell him, so-and-so says: Peace be upon you," and his saying to him: "Greet him for me." The apparent view is that there is no difference, in accordance with what was reported from al-Nawawi. So in both cases the response is obligatory, and it is recommended to respond to the one who conveys it and to begin, so one says: "And upon you and upon him be peace," based on the well-known report concerning this.

It is obligatory to return the greeting of a child, or of an insane person who has discernment (mumayyiz), and likewise of a drunk person who has discernment and did not sin by his drunkenness. The statement of the Majmu' (al-Nawawi): "It is not obligatory to return the greeting of an insane person or a drunk person," is to be understood as referring to one without discernment. The author of the Majmu' claimed that insanity and drunkenness negate discernment, through heedlessness of what the scholars have explicitly stated, namely that they do not negate it. It is not obligatory to return the greeting of a sinner (fasiq) or an innovator (mubtadi'), as a rebuke to him or to others, although it is legislated to greet him. Likewise, it is not obligatory to return the greeting of a beggar (sa'il), because his greeting is not for the purpose of greeting but in order to be given something. Nor is it obligatory to return the greeting of one who is exiting the prayer (mutahallil min al-salah), if the one present with him intends it, according to the more correct view, because what matters to him is the exit from prayer, and the one present is intended by it so that its blessing may return to him, and that is achieved even if he does not return it. The one who swears not to speak or greet is made to break his oath only by that, because in both cases the criterion is the truth of the designation alone, and the scholars of the Shafi'is have stated this explicitly. I have not seen from our companions (the Hanafis) anything besides the explicit statement that one breaks his oath regarding one who swears not to speak to Zayd, and then greets a group in which he is present. As for an explicit statement on this specific issue, I have not seen it. In al-Diya' (Diya' al-Din al-Maqdisi's work), it is explicitly stated that the return is not obligatory if the greeter says "al-salamu 'alaykum" with the mim vowelled with a jazm (sukun). It seems, according to what is in our Tuhfa (Tuhfat al-Muluk / the Hanafi text cited), that this is because it contravenes the Sunnah. Accordingly, if he raises the mim without tanwin and without definite article, it is like the jazm of the mim in not making the return obligatory, because it likewise contravenes the Sunnah.

And a number of the Shafi'is have affirmed decisively that the formula of greeting, both at the beginning and in reply, is "'alayka al-salam" and its reverse, and that it is permissible to make its word indefinite (tankir) even if the tanwin is omitted, and that "salaman 'alaykum" suffices, and likewise "salamu Allah ta'ala" (the peace of God Most High), and even "salami 'alayka" and its reverse. And [al-Ramli / some scholars] inferred the sufficiency of "sallamtu 'alayka" (I have greeted you) and "ana musallimun 'alayka" (I am greeting you) and the like, drawing from what they mentioned, that it suffices in the tashahhud: "Salla Allahu ta'ala 'ala Muhammad" (may God Most High bless Muhammad), and "al-Salatu 'ala Muhammad ﷺ," and the like. There is no harm in what they have said, in my view. Perhaps the interpretation of "tahiyya" in the verse is so that it encompasses all these formulas.

Some of the scholars (of the community) said: "al-Salam" with the definite article is the greeting of the living, and "salam" indefinite is the greeting of the dead, and they related a report regarding this. The Shi'a deny this entirely, and they deny it.

It has come from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Abu Hurayrah, and Anas, that "al-Salam" in "al-Salam" (the greeting) is one of the names of God Most High. This requires the preference of the definite article as well, so understand.

The better way of replying is to prefix it with "wa" (and), and it suffices without it according to the sound view. In initiating, it is harmful, as is limiting oneself in one of the two (greeting and reply) to one of the two halves of the sentence, even if he intends to imply the other. The Kashf contains what supports this. The report in which the reply "wa 'alayka" is sufficient is not meant to suffice with this word alone; rather, what is meant is that the Prophet ﷺ replied with the same as what was used to greet him, and did not add to it, as its ending indicates.

Al-Tahawi mentioned that it is recommended to return the greeting while in a state of purity (tahara) or dry ablution (tayammum). For al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others narrated from Abu al-Jahm, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ came from the place of relieving himself, and a man met him and greeted him, but the Messenger of God ﷺ did not return the greeting to him, until he came to a wall, placed his hand on it, then wiped his face and his hands, and then returned the greeting to the man." The apparent position is that there is no difference between returning and initiating in this regard. The greeting is recommended (sunnah) as an individual obligation for one person, and as a collective obligation (kifayah) for a group, as we have indicated, when initiating it upon arriving and departing, based on the sound and good report: "Indeed, the people closest to God Most High are the one who initiates the greeting to them." The difference between returning and initiating is that the sense of alienation and fear in not returning is greater than in not initiating.

Some have issued a fatwa that initiating is better, just as remitting a debt for the insolvent is better than granting him a delay. From their saying "initiating" (ibtida'an) it is taken that if he does it after speaking, it is not counted. Yes, it may be considered if the speech was out of forgetfulness or ignorance, and he is excused, because the initiation is not lost, so the reply to it is obligatory. Similar to this, and even more so, is speech for seeking permission (al-istidhan), since it is legislated, for they have explicitly stated that when one comes to a person's house, he must seek permission before greeting. It is recommended to show cheerfulness in his presence, for al-Bayhaqi narrated from al-Hasan who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Indeed, among charity is that you greet the people while your face is open and cheerful." And from 'Umar: "When two believers meet, and each of them greets the other and they shake hands, the one of them who is most beloved to God Most High is the one who is most cheerful toward his companion."

It is recommended that one say "'alaykum" (to a group) even if in some reports the singular is used, out of regard for the angels who are with him, and he intends them so that they reply to him and he attains the blessing of their supplication. If he enters a house and sees no one, he says: "al-salamu 'alayna wa 'ala 'ibad Allah al-salihin" (peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God), for the inhabitants (jinn) will return it to him. In al-Akam (a work): Indeed in every house there are inhabitants from the jinn. It is recommended at meeting that a younger person greet an older person, a walker greet one standing or reclining, and a rider greet those on foot, a rider on a horse greet a rider on a donkey, and fewer greet more, because the one approaching (the walker) fears from the one approaching on the mount, and to increase the status of the elder over the younger. By "meeting" is excluded the one sitting, standing, or reclining; so whoever arrives upon one of them greets him unconditionally. If each greets the other: if they are sequenced, the second is a reply, that is, as long as it is not intended as an initiation alone, as it has been said; otherwise it would be obligatory on each to reply.

Our companions (Hanafis) disliked greeting in certain situations. In al-Nahr from Sadr al-Din al-Ghuzzi:

Your greeting is disliked for whoever you greet, and after it is shown, it is recommended and legislated:
the one praying, reciting, remembering, speaking, the preacher, and whoever listens to them and hears;
the one repeating jurisprudence, sitting for its judgment, and those who discuss jurisprudence, leave them so they may benefit;
the muezzin as well as the one who is standing for the iqama, the teacher; likewise foreign young women, I prohibit them;
the players of chess and those resembling them in their creation, and whoever is with his family enjoying himself;
leave also the disbeliever and the one whose private parts are exposed, and whoever is in the state of defecating is more repulsive;
leave the one eating, unless you are hungry, and you know from him that he will not prevent you;
likewise the teacher who sings, who is dancing; this is the conclusion, and additions are beneficial.

If one greets these people, then according to some of them he does not deserve a reply, and some made the reply obligatory in some of these cases. The Shafi'is mentioned that the listener to the preacher must return the greeting. With us (the Hanafis), it is prohibited, like all other speech, without distinction between near and far, according to the more correct view. They disliked it for one who is relieving himself and the like, like one having intercourse, and they made it recommended for one eating, like the sunnah of greeting him after swallowing and before placing the morsel in the mouth, and it becomes obligatory for him to reply then. And for one in the bathhouse and the like, it is by speech.

They preferred that one greets the one in the slaughterhouse, and that it being the abode of devils does not prevent this; the marketplace is likewise, and greeting those in it is legislated, even if they are occupied with haggling or transactions; and a praying person or a muezzin is greeted by gesture. Otherwise, after finishing, if the interval is short. They prohibited replying to one who greets someone like an apostate or an enemy combatant. Some recommended greeting the reciter even if he is occupied with reflection (tadabbur), and made it obligatory to reply to him. Its locus is the one reflecting whose reflection does not overwhelm his heart; otherwise greeting is not recommended, whether as initiation or reply, like one absorbed in supplication, because he is now in the position of one without discernment. Rather, it should be that the ruling for one whom worry has overwhelmed is likewise. They also explicitly stated that one should not greet a sinner (fasiq), and it is recommended to abstain from greeting one who openly displays his sinfulness, one who commits a grave sin and has not repented of it, an innovator, except for an excuse or fear of harm; and one who is saying the talbiyah (pilgrim's chant), one who is prostrating, one who is drowsy, and litigants before a judge.

Some issued a fatwa on the disliking of bowing the back (hanyi al-zahr), and many said it is prohibited, due to the good hadith that the Prophet ﷺ forbade it, and forbade embracing others and kissing them, and he commanded shaking hands, as long as the person is not a dhimmi. Otherwise, shaking hands with him is disliked for the Muslim; rather he disbelieves if he intends veneration, just as he disbelieves by greeting him in the same manner.

Some also issued a fatwa on the disliking of bowing the head, and kissing the head, a hand, or a foot, especially for a rich person, due to the hadith: "Whoever humbles himself before a rich man has lost two-thirds of his religion." It is recommended for one of piety, knowledge, or nobility, because Abu 'Ubaydah kissed the hand of 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both.

The phrase "sabbahaka Allahu bil-khayr" (may God greet you in the morning with goodness) or "qawwaka Allahu" (may God strengthen you) is not counted as a greeting (tahiyya), and one who begins with it does not deserve a reply. Supplicating for him with its equivalent is good, unless by neglecting it one intends to discipline him for abandoning the sunnah of greeting. "Marhaban" (welcome) is similar in this regard.

It has been mentioned that if the greeter says: "al-salamu 'alayka wa rahmatu Allahi wa barakatuh," and the one replying says only "'alayka al-salam," it suffices him, but it is contrary to what is preferable. The apparent meaning of the verse is contrary to this, for the command in it revolves between replying with the better and replying with the same, and what has been mentioned is neither of them.

Interpreting "tahiyya" as greeting (al-salam) is the view of most of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) and imams of the religion. It has been said that what is meant by it is gift and bestowal, and the one who said this made compensation or return to the recipient obligatory. This is an ancient view of al-Shafi'i, and it has also been attributed to our great imam (Abu Hanifah), may God be pleased with him. Some justified this by saying that the greeting has already occurred, so it is not returned in its exact form, and therefore it is interpreted as a gift; and its use for gift has come. It was answered that this is a metaphor, like the saying of al-Mutanabbi:

"Stop, the first glance from the eyelid will cost my eye the second, and the one who destroys a thing is liable for it."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Uyaynah that he said regarding the verse: Do you see this as only about greeting? This applies to everything. Whoever does good to you, do good to him and reward him; if you cannot find anything, pray for him, and praise him before his brothers. Perhaps his intention, may God Most High have mercy on him, was to analogize other kinds of kindness to greeting, because what is meant by "tahiyya" is that which encompasses greeting and other things, due to its obscurity. Perhaps whoever intended the more general meaning explained it as what is bestowed upon a person by which his life is made pleasant.

﴿Indeed God is ever, over all things, a Reckoner.﴾ So He will hold you accountable for every one of your deeds, and this includes what they were commanded regarding greeting, by primary inclusion.

Furthermore, from the door of allusion (ishara) in these verses: ﴿Those who believe fight﴾ their souls ﴿in the way of God﴾, so they destroy them by the swords of striving (mujahadah) in order to reach Him, may His glory be exalted; ﴿and those who disbelieve fight﴾ their intellects and contend with them ﴿in the way of﴾ the tyrant (taghut) of their souls, so that they may obtain pleasures and seize in this transient abode the commodities of desires; ﴿so fight the allies of Satan﴾, which are the carnal faculties, or the soul and its faculties; ﴿indeed, the plot of Satan has ever been weak﴾, so his ally is weak, having sought refuge in a "qarmala" (a weak, feeble thing).

[p. 104]

Have you not considered those who were told, ﴿Restrain your hands﴾, meaning: the observers said to them, ﴿restrain your hands﴾ from harming souls now, before the performance of the rites of worship, ﴿and establish the prayer﴾, by which is meant wearying the body through performing bodily worship, ﴿and give zakat﴾, by which is meant wearying the heart through performing financial worship. Once you have accomplished that, turn to fighting the self (nafs), for fighting it before that is without weapons, since these formal acts of worship are the weapon of the wayfarers (salikin). The refinement of the inner self is not completed for anyone before the reform of the outer self.

﴿When fighting was prescribed for them﴾, at the time they were performing what they had been commanded to perform, ﴿behold, a group of them﴾, because of the weakness of their readiness, ﴿fear people as they fear God, or with even greater fear﴾. So they cannot abandon them, nor commit what humiliates their souls, out of fear of their objection to them or their turning away from them. ﴿And they say﴾ with the tongue of their state, ﴿"Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us?"﴾ now, ﴿"If only You had delayed us to a near term"﴾, which is natural death. Death is either death or disgrace. This is the condition of many of the ascetics (nasikin), who turn away from the path and from bearing its hardships, which involve the humbling and degradation of their souls, out of fear of blame and of people's objections to them. So they remain in the veil of their own works, thinking that they are doing good, while ﴿how evil is what they used to do﴾.

﴿Say: The enjoyment of this world is little﴾, [p. 105 follows]

So they should not heed people in abandoning it, nor pay attention to them. ﴿And the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful of God﴾, so they should bear blame in pursuing it. ﴿And you will not be wronged even as much as the thread of a date-stone﴾ in what has been prescribed for you. Therefore, one should not fear anyone other than God, the Exalted.

﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you﴾ and you will part from what you fear parting from, inevitably. If you travel the path, then part from them by traveling it, which is voluntary death, before you part from them through destruction, which is involuntary death. ﴿And even if you were in towers built high﴾, meaning strong bodies. As one poet said:

"Whoever has a sturdy, firm bone hopes by it
to break the stick of time, but time is its breaker."

﴿And if good befalls them﴾, meaning, if something suits their natures reach them, ﴿they say, "This is from God"﴾, attributing it to God, the Exalted, out of the joy of the soul and the pleasure of desire, if they had followed knowledge and love. ﴿And if evil befalls them﴾, meaning, something their natures recoil from, even if the reality is otherwise, ﴿they say﴾, out of the constriction of their souls, ﴿"This is from you"﴾, attributing it to other than Him, the Exalted, and returning to secondary causes, because true faith has not taken root in their hearts. ﴿Say, "All is from God"﴾. This is a call to them to affirm the unity of actions, to deny the influence of others, and to acknowledge that He, glorified is He, is the creator of good and evil.

﴿What is wrong with these people﴾, the veiled ones, ﴿that they can hardly understand any statement?﴾ Because they argue by the attributes of the souls, and because the ears of their hearts, which are the vessels of hearing and understanding, are in need. Then God, glorified is He, further clarified by saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God﴾, whether small or great, ﴿and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾, whether slight or grave. That is, it comes from the self, because of the acquired readiness caused by the self's manifestation through attributes and acts that veil the heart and cloud its essence, until it needs polishing through calamities, misfortunes, trials and afflictions. It does not come from the Messenger (ﷺ) or anyone else. ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾, so you are a mercy to them, and nothing evil comes from you to them. ﴿And God suffices as a witness﴾ to that. ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God﴾, because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is the mirror of the Truth, through which He manifests Himself to creation. Some of the knowers (arifin) said: the inner meaning of this verse points to the "unity of union" (ayn al-jam').

﴿Do they not reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ so that it may guide them to the fact that you are the Messenger of God, the Exalted, and that obeying you is obeying Him, glorified is He, since it contains both distinction (farq) and union (jam'). It has also been said: Will they not reflect upon it, so that they may be admonished by its noble exhortations and follow the excellence of its commands? Or: will they not reflect upon it so that they may know that God, majestic is His station, has manifested Himself to them in it?

﴿Had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much inconsistency﴾, meaning they would have found much of it varying in eloquence and lacking it, so that it would be like the speech of created beings. Then they would have had a pretext to deny it and to refuse to accept its testimony, or to claim that it is not fit to be a locus of manifestation of God, the Exalted.

﴿And when there comes to them some news of security or fear, they spread it﴾. This is a report about those at the beginnings of the path. That is, when something from the traces of beauty (jamal) or majesty (jalal) comes upon them, they divulge and broadcast it. ﴿But if they had referred it﴾, meaning presented it, ﴿to the Messenger﴾, to what is known of his states and what he was upon, ﴿and to those in authority among them﴾, namely the perfect guides who attained the station of Muhammadan inheritance, ﴿those who [can] investigate it would have known it﴾, meaning they would have known its outcome, and whether it is something to be divulged or not, ﴿those who deduce it from them﴾ and receive it from them, that is, from their side and through the intermediary of their emanations. What is meant by the relative clause is the ones who refer it themselves. The upshot is that when something from the traces of beauty or majesty appears to the aspirant (murid) in the course of his journey and path, he should not disclose it to anyone before presenting it to his shaykh, who will inform him of the reality of the state, for disclosing it before that causes much harm.

﴿Had it not been for the grace of God upon you﴾, O people, through the great intermediary, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), ﴿and His mercy﴾ through the guiding heirs, ﴿you would have followed Satan﴾, and the self, which is his greatest army, if you were not he, ﴿except for a few﴾. They are the wayfarers who travel by means of a divine light poured upon them, by which they became self-sufficient, like some of the people of the interval (ahl al-fatra). It has been said that they are on the footing of the Friend (al-Khalil), upon him be blessings and peace.

﴿So fight in the way of God; you are not held responsible except for yourself﴾, meaning: fight whoever opposes you alone. ﴿And urge the believers﴾ to fight those who stand between them and their Lord. ﴿Perhaps God will restrain the might of those who disbelieve﴾, meaning those who concealed the attributes of Lordship. ﴿And God is stronger in might﴾ than them, meaning in punishment, ﴿and stronger in punishment﴾, meaning in torment.

﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession﴾, meaning whoever accompanies his soul in acts of obedience, ﴿will have a share of it﴾, meaning an abundant portion of its reward. ﴿And whoever intercedes with an evil intercession﴾, meaning whoever accompanies his soul in disobedience, ﴿will have a portion of it﴾, meaning an equal share of its punishment. ﴿And God is ever Keeper over all things﴾, so He delivers reward and punishment to those deserving of them.

﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with a better one or return it﴾. This is instruction in a kind of noble character and excellent conduct. It has also been said that the meaning is: when God, the Exalted, bestows a gift upon you, then give out the best of His gifts, or give in charity what He has given you, and return it to God, the Exalted, through the hands of those who deserve it. And God, the Exalted, is the best of those who grant success.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 87:**

﴿Allahu la ilaha illa Huwa﴾ is a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate). His saying, glorified is He, ﴿He will surely gather you unto the Day of Resurrection﴾ is the answer to an implied oath, meaning: "By Allah, He will surely gather you." The sentence is either a new, independent sentence with no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis), or a second khabar, or the khabar itself, with ﴿la ilaha illa Huwa﴾ being a parenthetical insertion. That it could be a khabar after a khabar of kana is far-fetched, as is the view that the sentence ﴿Allahu la ilaha illa Huwa﴾ is a parenthetical insertion emphasizing a threat intended by what precedes and follows it. Then, although the khabar is indeed the oath and its answer, in reality it is the answer. So there is no objection about a performative utterance (inshā') occurring as a khabar, nor that the answer to an oath is among the sentences with no place in i'rab, for how could it then be a khabar? There is no impossibility in considering a place in i'rab and its absence from two different standpoints.

The verb jama' (to gather) here means hashr (to assemble for judgment). For this reason it takes the preposition ila (to), just as hashr takes it in His saying, ﴿Unto Allah you will be gathered (tuhsharun)﴾. It is said that it takes ila because it is construed with the meaning of ifdā' (to lead to, to bring to), which takes ila: that is, "He will surely raise you from your graves to the reckoning of the Day of Resurrection," or "leading to it." It is also said that ila here means fi (in), as the grammarians have established: that is, "He will surely gather you on that Day."

﴿There is no doubt concerning it﴾: that is, concerning the Day of Resurrection, or concerning the gathering. The sentence is either a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) describing the Day, or a descriptive clause (ṣifa) of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: "a gathering, there is no doubt concerning it." The word al-qiyāma (the Resurrection) is derived from qiyām (standing up). The tā' (feminine ending) was added to it for emphasis, as in ʿallāma (very learned) and nassāba (very skilled in genealogy). That Day was named thus because people stand up on it for the reckoning, together with the severity of the terror that occurs in it.

The connection of the verse with what precedes it is evident: when He mentioned ﴿Indeed Allah is ever, over all things, a Reckoner﴾, He followed it with informing of His oneness, glorified is He, and of the gathering and the resurrection from the graves for reckoning before Him.

Al-Tabarsi said: The arrangement (wajh al-naẓm) is that when He, glorified is He, previously commanded and forbade, He then made clear that none deserves worship besides Him, so that they would know in accordance with what He obligated upon them. He also indicated that this action has a reward, by stating its time, which is the Day of Resurrection, so that they would strive in it, desire it, and fear it.

﴿And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾ The interrogative is one of denial. The comparative form is with respect to quantity in true reports, not quality, since there is no conceivable variation in them, because truthfulness (ṣidq) is conformity to reality, and this may increase. So one does not say of a particular statement that it is "more truthful" than another, except by interpretation and figurative usage. The meaning is: no one is more truthful than Him, exalted is He, in His promise and in all His reports. It also conveys the negation of equality, as in the saying: "There is no one in the city more knowledgeable than Zayd." It is so only because it is impossible to attribute lying to Him, glorified is He, in any way whatsoever. No disagreement is known among those who acknowledge that Allah, exalted is He, speaks with speech, regarding this impossibility, although their sources of proof differ.

The Mu'tazila have argued for the impossibility of lying in the speech of the Lord, exalted is He, on the grounds that speech is among His acts, exalted is He, and lying is ugly in itself, and Allah, exalted is He, does not do what is ugly. This is founded on their doctrine of the intrinsic goodness and ugliness (of acts), and their obligating Him to observe what is best for the servants (ri'āyat al-ṣalāḥ wa'l-aṣlaḥ). As for the Ash'ari, they have—as al-Amidi said—two approaches in demonstrating the impossibility of lying in His eternal, inner speech, exalted is He:

*Page 106*

The first is rational (ʿaqlī) and the second is scriptural (samʿī). As for the first approach: truthfulness and falsehood in a report belong to eternal inner speech not by their own essence, but by reference to what the report concerns of the thing reported. If it has been connected to the thing as it actually is, the report is true; if it is contrary to that, it is false. In that case, if the speech of the Lord, glorified is He, which subsists in Him, were to be connected to something contrary to what it actually is, then it would either be with knowledge of that, or without knowledge. The second is not possible, for it would entail ignorance, which is impossible for Him, glorified is He, in many respects. If it is the first, then one who knows a thing cannot possibly fail to have the report about it subsist in him in accordance with what it actually is. This is known necessarily.
