Hence, if the report about it subsisted in the self contrary to what it actually is, while he knew it and reported about it as it actually is, then a true report and a false report would subsist in the self with reference to one and the same thing from one and the same aspect, and its falsity is known necessarily.

It has been objected: we know necessarily from ourselves that when we know a thing, we are able to report a false report, and we know that we are lying. If we did not know the thing reported, the knowledge that we are lying could not be conceived. The answer is: the report by which we know ourselves to be lying is only the verbal report (lisānī). As for the inner report (nafsānī), we do not concede the soundness of our knowledge of its falsity at the moment of asserting it.

As for the second approach: it has been established that the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) is shown by the decisive miracle (muʿjiza) in that matter in which he is a messenger, as explained in its proper place.

It has been transmitted from him by mutawātir report (a report transmitted by so many that it cannot be fabricated) that the speech of Allah, exalted is He, is truthful, and that lying about Him, glorified is He, is impossible. Al-Amidi examined this, saying: One may say: the validity of scripture depends on the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ), and his truthfulness depends on the impossibility of lying about Allah, exalted is He, insofar as the manifestation of the miracle in accordance with his challenge to prophethood is tantamount to Allah's confirmation, glorified is He, of his claim. So if lying were permissible for Him—majestic is His rank—it would be possible that He lies in confirming him, and then the Messenger would not be truthful. And if each of the two depends on the other, that is circular reasoning (dawr).

It may be said: establishing the prophethood does not depend on the impossibility of lying about Allah, exalted is He, so as to be circular. For establishing the prophethood does not depend on the announcement that he is a messenger, such that truth and falsehood would enter into it, but rather on the manifestation of the miracle in accordance with his challenge. This is treated as performative speech (inshā'), and establishing the prophethood and making him a messenger in the present is like the saying of one who says: "I have appointed you as my agent in my affairs, and I have made you my deputy in my matters." That does not require confirmation or denial. For it may be said then: if the miracle appeared at the hand of a person who had not previously made a challenge, then—on the basis of the neighbouring of this (idea) with the principles of the Community (al-Jamāʿa)—the miracle would not be, by consensus, indicative of the establishment of his prophethood. And if the manifestation of the miracle at his hand were treated as performative speech establishing his prophethood, it would necessarily follow that he be an obeyed messenger after its appearance, and that is not the case. And the notion that performative speech is conditioned by the challenge is far-fetched, considering the ruling on performative utterances. And even granting that it is so, the most that follows is that prophethood is established by way of performative speech, and it does not follow from this that the Messenger is truthful in everything he reports without a rational proof showing his truthfulness in what he reports, or Allah's confirmation of him in that. And there is no rational proof showing that. And Allah's confirmation of him depends on the truthfulness of his report, which brings back what preceded. So it is fitting that this scriptural approach be used to demonstrate the impossibility of verbal speech, and it is sound in that respect.

The objection that arises there is cut off here. For the truthfulness of verbal speech, although it depends on the truthfulness of the Messenger, the truthfulness of the Messenger does not depend on the truthfulness of verbal speech, but on verbal speech itself. So the forbidden circularity is avoided.

In al-Mawaqif: the argument for the impossibility of lying about Allah, exalted is He, according to the People of the Sunna, is by three aspects:

The first: that it is a deficiency, and deficiency is prohibited by consensus. Furthermore, it would entail that we are more perfect than Him, glorified is He, at some times, namely the time of our truthfulness in our speech.

The second: that if He were characterized by lying, glorified is He, it would be an eternal lie, since what is originated cannot subsist in His essence, exalted is He. It would then follow that truthfulness is impossible for Him. For what has been established as eternal is impossible to cease to be. But the consequent is false, for we know necessarily that whoever knows something is able to report about it as it actually is. These two aspects only indicate that the inner speech, which is an attribute subsisting in His essence, exalted is He, is truthful.

Then he brought the third aspect as proof of the impossibility of lying in both verbal and inner speech, in the manner of what is in the second approach. You have known what al-Amidi has said about it, so reflect upon all of that, so that the truth may become clear to you.

﴿Fa-ma lakum﴾ is a subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar). The interrogative is for denial (inkar), and the negation and address are directed to all the believers, while what it contains of rebuke (tawbikh) is directed at some of them. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿fi al-munafiqin﴾ ("regarding the hypocrites"), may, as al-Samin said, be taken in three ways. It may be connected to what is indicated by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿fi'atayn﴾ ("two groups"), meaning: "Why do you split into factions regarding the hypocrites?" It may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from "fi'atayn," meaning: "two groups divided regarding the hypocrites," and when it was placed first, it was put in the accusative as a circumstantial. It may also be connected to what the predicate is connected to, meaning: "What is it that exists for you regarding their affair and their condition?" In that case the genitive noun (al-mudaf) has been omitted and the genitive complement (al-mudaf ilayh) has been put in its place.

Regarding the accusative case of "fi'atayn," there are two views, as in al-Durr al-Masun:

The first is that it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of "lakum" in the genitive, and its governing element is the stability (al-istiqrar) or the adverbial phrase standing in for it. This circumstantial is obligatory, and the sentence is not complete without it. This is the view of the Basran grammarians regarding this construction and what resembles it.

The second, which is the view of the Kufan grammarians, is that it is the predicate of an implied "kana" (was/were), meaning: "What do you have regarding their affair? You were two groups." This was rejected on the ground that its indefiniteness is obligatory in their usage, as in His saying: ﴿Fa-ma lahum 'ani al-tadhkirati mu'ridin﴾ ("Why, then, are they turning away from the reminder?").

As for what was said against the first view, that the circumstantial's bearer (dhu al-hal) being a part of its governing element is strange and scarcely valid according to most scholars, so it cannot be an object of it, and that it is not permissible for the governing element to differ between the circumstantial and its bearer, this belongs to the philosophy of grammar (falsafat al-nahw), as al-Shihab said. The intended meaning is the denial that the addressees have anything that justifies their disagreement regarding the affair of the hypocrites, and the explanation that it is obligatory to rule definitively that they are disbelievers and to treat them in the same way as open (mujahirin) enemies in all rulings. Their being mentioned under the title of hypocrisy is based on their previously described attribute.

Abd ibn Humayd related from Mujahid, who said: "They are a people who came out of Makkah until they reached Madinah, claiming that they were emigrants (muhajirin). Then they apostatized after that, and they asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to go to Makkah to bring their goods with which they traded. The Muslims disagreed about them: one said, 'They are hypocrites,' and another said, 'They are believers.' So God, exalted is He, made their hypocrisy clear and revealed this verse, and He commanded that they be killed."

Ibn Jarir related from al-Dahhak, who said: "They are people who stayed behind from the Messenger of God ﷺ and remained in Makkah. They professed faith but did not emigrate. The companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ disagreed about them: some befriended them, and others disassociated from their friendship, saying: 'They stayed behind from the Messenger of God ﷺ and did not emigrate.' So God, exalted is He, named them hypocrites, absolved the believers of their friendship, and commanded them not to befriend them until they emigrate."

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim), al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ahmad, and others related from Zayd ibn Thabit, that "the Messenger of God ﷺ went out to Uhud, and some people who had gone out with him returned. The companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ were divided concerning them into two groups (fi'atayn): one group said, 'Let us kill them,' and another group said, 'No.' So God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Fa-ma lakum fi al-munafiqin﴾, the whole verse."

What makes this problematic is what will come shortly, God willing, namely making their emigration the limit (ghayah) for the prohibition against befriending them, unless it is turned away from its apparent meaning, as you will learn.

It was also said that they are the 'Uraniyyun, who raided the herd and seized Yasar, the shepherd of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and mutilated him: they cut off his hands and feet, drove thorns into his tongue and eyes until he died. This is refuted, as Shaykh al-Islam said, by what will come, God willing, of the verses that speak of how they were to be treated in peace and in war. These [the 'Uraniyyun] were already seized, and what was done to them of mutilation and killing was carried out, and no disagreement of the Muslims concerning their affair is reported. Other views were also stated.

Page 108

﴿Wallahu arkasahum bima kasabu﴾ ("And God has returned them to [disbelief] because of what they earned") is a circumstantial clause from "al-munafiqin," serving to emphasize the preceding denial. It was also said that it is a circumstantial from the pronoun of the addressees, with the connecting element being the waw. It was also said that it is a new independent sentence (mustaʼnafa), and the "ba'" is causal, and "ma" is either a verbal-noun (masdariyya) or a relative (mawsulah).

"Arkasa" and "rakasa" have the same meaning. Scholars differed about the lexical meaning of "al-raks." It was said that it means "to return," as was said in the verse of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt:

"So they were returned into the fire of Hell, because they were sinners, and they uttered falsehood and lies."

This is the version related by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. The meaning then is: God, exalted is He, returned them to disbelief after faith because of what they earned by apostasy and joining the polytheists, or something similar, or because of their earning. It was also said that it is close to "naks" (overturning), and its essence is that He, exalted is He, cast them down head first, and casting someone down head first is more emphatic than making them head-down, because one who is thrown head-down into a pit rarely escapes from it. The meaning is that He, glorified is He, by their earning disbelief, or by what they earned of it, turned their state upside down and cast them into pits of fire.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi that he interpreted "arkasahum" as "adallahum" (led them astray), and "al-irkas" has come with the meaning of misguidance, and from it is the line:

"And it returned me from the path of guidance, and made me an example for enemies."

al-Tasti related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said: the meaning is that He imprisoned them in Jahannam. Al-Bukhari related from him that the meaning is "babbadahum," that is, He scattered them and split their gathering. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah: "He destroyed them." These meanings are perhaps all returning to one root. It is also reported from Abd Allah and Ubayy that they read "rukisu" without an alif, and it has also been read as "rakkasahum" with a shaddah.

﴿Atureedun an tahdu man adalla Allah?﴾ ("Do you wish to guide one whom God has led astray?") is a rebuke (tawbikh) directed at the group who claimed the faith of those hypocrites on the basis of their claim, and an indication that this leads to an attempt at the impossible, namely guiding one whom God, exalted is He, has led astray. That is because ruling that they are believers and asserting that they are guided, while they are far from that, is an effort toward their guidance and a desire for it. So the intended referent of the relative pronoun is "the hypocrites," except that it was placed in the position of their pronoun to intensify the denial and emphasize the impossibility of guidance because of what was mentioned in the relative clause. Taking it in a general sense, with those previously mentioned falling within it by primary inclusion (dukhul awwali), as Abu Hayyan claimed, is nothing.

The denial was directed at the desire itself rather than at its object, to exaggerate its denial by showing that desiring it is something impossible, let alone its being possible in itself. The verse is clear in support of the view of the majority (al-jama'ah), and interpreting guidance and misguidance as a ruling of them is contrary to the apparent meaning. What weakens that is His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Wa man yudlili Allahu fa-lan tajida lahu sabila﴾ ("And whomever God leaves astray, you will never find for him a way"). The understanding from it is creation, meaning: whoever has misguidance created in him, whoever he may be, and this includes here those mentioned earlier by primary inclusion. "Fa-lan tajida lahu sabilan" means that you will not find for him any of the ways, let alone that you guide him to it. The address in "tajida" is either to an unspecified person or to each one of the addressees, to indicate the absence of finding for each individually. Negating the finding of a way is more emphatic than negating a guide. Interpreting His misguiding as His ruling and decree of misguidance undermines the fine correspondence between the condition and the consequence, and making "sabil" mean "proof" (hujjah), so that the meaning is: whomever God makes misguided by His ruling, you will not find for him any proof in his misguidance, as Ja'far ibn Harb said, is nothing, as is not hidden.

The sentence is either a closing parenthetical statement (i'tiraD tadhyeeli) that confirms the preceding denial and emphasizes the impossibility of guidance, or a circumstantial clause from the subject of "tureedun" or "tahdu," with the connecting element being the waw.

﴿They wish that you would disbelieve﴾ is an explanation of their extremity and persistence in disbelief, and of their eagerness to lead others astray, following the explanation of their disbelief and misguidance within themselves. The word ﴿لَوْ﴾ (law) is a verbal particle (masdariyya) with no answer clause. The meaning is: they wish that you would disbelieve. The words ﴿as they disbelieved﴾ are a qualifier (na't) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), and ﴿ما﴾ (ma) is a verbal particle. The meaning is: a disbelief like their disbelief. Alternatively, it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of that verbal noun, as is the view of Sibawayh. There is no indication in attributing disbelief to them that it is created by them independently, with no role for Allah the Exalted in it, so that this verse would be evidence for turning what came before away from its apparent meaning, as Ibn Harb claimed. This is because the actions of servants have an attribution to Allah the Exalted in terms of creation (khalq), and an attribution to the servants in terms of acquisition (kasb), in the sense we verified earlier.

The words ﴿so that you would be alike﴾ are coordinated with ﴿that you would disbelieve﴾ and fall under the same wish. The meaning is: they wish that you would disbelieve, so that you would be equal in disbelief and misguidance. It is also permitted that the word ﴿لَوْ﴾ retains its own function, with an omitted answer clause, like the object of "wadda" (to wish). The meaning is: they wish your disbelief, if you were to disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be alike, and they would rejoice at that.

﴿So do not take from among them allies﴾: the particle ﴿فَ﴾ (fa) is an explanatory particle (fasiha). The word ﴿allies﴾ is plural in consideration of the plural of those addressed, since what is intended is a prohibition to each of those addressed from taking each of the hypocrites as an ally. The meaning is: if their state is as mentioned, namely their wish, then do not befriend them.

﴿until they emigrate in the way of Allah﴾: that is, until they believe, and realize their belief through an emigration (hijra) that is for Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ), not for some worldly purpose. The root meaning of "sabil" (way) is path, and it is used frequently for the path that leads to Allah the Exalted, which is carrying out the commands and avoiding the prohibitions. The verse clearly indicates the obligation of emigration.

It is explicitly stated in al-Taysir that it was an obligation in the early period of Islam. Emigration (hijra) has three uses:

First: leaving the land of disbelief for the land of Islam, which is the well-known usage.

Second: abandoning what is forbidden.

Third: going out to fight. On this basis, whoever said that the verse was revealed concerning those who turned back on the day of Uhud, as related by the report of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), understood emigration in this sense, and al-Khazin affirmed it.

﴿But if they turn away﴾: that is, they turn away from emigration in the way of Allah the Exalted, as Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said. ﴿Then seize them﴾ wherever you have power over them, ﴿and kill them wherever you find them﴾, within the sacred area and outside it, for their ruling is the ruling of all other polytheists regarding capture and killing. It was also said: what is intended is killing only, but the command to seize is mentioned because seizing usually comes before killing.

﴿And do not take from among them an ally or a helper﴾: that is, keep away from them completely, and never accept from them guardianship or support. This is indicated by the present tense verb, which denotes continuity or repetition, serving emphasis.

[Page 109]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 90:

﴿Except those who join a people between whom and you there is a covenant﴾ is an exception from the pronoun in His words, glorified is He: ﴿so seize them and kill them﴾. That is: except those who reach and join a people who have made a covenant with you and who have not fought against you, and they are the Banu Mudlij.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and others narrated from al-Hasan that Suraqah ibn Malik al-Mudlaji related to them, saying: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prevailed over the people of Badr and Uhud, and those around them embraced Islam, Suraqah said: 'It has reached me that he (peace be upon him) intends to send Khalid ibn al-Walid to my people, the Banu Mudlij. So I came to him and said: "I implore you by the favour (of kinship)." They said: "Enough!" He said: "Leave him. What do you want?" I said: "It has reached me that you intend to send (someone) to my people, and I want you to make a truce with them. If your people embrace Islam, they will embrace it too, and if they do not, you will not fear for the hearts of your people concerning them." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took Khalid's hand and said: "Go with him and do what he wishes." Khalid then made a treaty with them, that they would not assist anyone against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; and if Quraysh embraced Islam, they would embrace it with them; and whoever joined them among the people would be on the same covenant as they.'" Then Allah the Exalted revealed ﴿They wish﴾ up to ﴿except those who join﴾, so whoever joined them was with them under their covenant.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the chain of Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the verse was revealed concerning Hilal ibn Uwaymir al-Aslami, Suraqah ibn Malik al-Mudlaji, and the Banu Jadhimah ibn Amir.

Page 110
It is not permissible that it be an exception from the pronoun in (do not take), even though it is closer, because taking a protector from among them is forbidden absolutely.

﴿Or those who come to you﴾ is a conjunction upon the relative clause (ṣilah), meaning: and those who (come to you) restraining themselves from fighting you and fighting their people. Thus two groups are excepted from those commanded to be seized and killed: one who abandons the combatants and joins the covenanted, and one who comes to the believers and refrains from fighting both groups. Or it is a conjunction upon the attribute of the people, as if it were said: except those who join a people covenanted, or a people restraining from fighting you and against you.

The first is preferred both in transmission (riwayah) and in understanding (dirayah), since upon it there are two causes for withholding from fighting: connection with the covenanted and connection with those who restrain. Upon the second, the two causes would be: connection with the covenanted and connection with those who restrain; but the later words of His, exalted is He, ﴿then if they withdraw from you﴾ etc., establish that one of the two causes is restraint from fighting; for the consequent is caused by the condition, so it requires conjunction upon the relative clause, since if it were conjoined upon the attribute, one of the two causes would be connection with those who restrain, not restraint from fighting. If it is said: if it were conjoined upon the attribute, the suitability would also be realized, because the cause of withholding from harming them would then be connection with the covenanted and connection with those who restrain, and connection with these and those is a cause for entering into their ruling; and His words, glorified is He, ﴿then if they withdraw from you﴾ clarify the ruling of those who restrain, since the ruling of those connected to them precedes. It is answered: that is permissible, but the first is more evident and is applied to the style of Arabic speech, because when they make an exception they clarify the ruling of the excepted item, by way of affirmation and emphasis.

Al-Imam said: making restraint from fighting a cause for abstaining from harm is better than making connection with one who restrains from fighting a cause for abstaining from harm, because that is a remote cause; moreover, those connected to the covenanted are not themselves covenanted, but they have their ruling; unlike those connected to the restraining, for if they restrain, they are they, and otherwise there is no effect for it.

Ubayy read (came to you) without (or), as a resumptive statement occurring as an answer to a question, as if it were said: How was the covenant between you and them? So it was said: (they came to you), etc. It was also said: the question is assumed: How did they reach the covenanted, and from where was that known? But this is nothing. Or it is an attribute after an attribute of (a people), or an explanation of (join), or a substitute for it. Abu Hayyan weakened the explanation on the ground that it does not occur with verbs, and the substitute on the ground that it is neither it, nor part of it, nor comprising it. It is answered: reaching the covenanted and joining them amounts to restraint from fighting, so it is correct to make their coming to the Muslims in this manner and with this resolve an explanation of their connection with the covenanted, or a substitute for it, wholly, partly, or by inclusion; and that this does not apply to verbs is not held by the scholars of meanings. It was also said: it is conjoined by omitting the conjunction.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿their breasts constrained﴾ is a circumstantial clause with a hidden (qad). The reading of al-Hasan supports this: (their breast is constrained), and likewise the readings (constrained) and (constraining). The possibility that it is an attributive for (a people) by way of causation is remote, since the accusative and genitive are equal in it.

It was also said: it is an attribute of a omitted noun which is a circumstantial clause of the subject of (came), meaning: they came to you as a people whose breasts were constrained; there is then no need to assume (qad). What is said, that the intended circumstantial sense is description, because it is a preparatory circumstance and therefore must have (qad), especially when the noun is omitted, is an unestablished obligation of adding a hidden element without necessity.

It was also said: it is an explanation of (came to you), and that is like al-Tibi's view, since their coming without fighting and (their breasts constrained that they fight you) have one meaning. The second scholar said: from the aspect that the intended meaning of coming is connection and abandonment of opposition and fighting, not literal coming; or from the aspect that it is an explanation of the manner of coming. It was also said: the inclusion of (those who came to you) indicates it, since coming includes constraint and other things. It was also said: it is a supplicatory sentence, and this was rejected, since there is no sense in invoking against the unbelievers that they not fight their people, but rather that discord and killing occur among them. And (constriction), with two fatha, means narrowness and contraction.

﴿that they fight you or fight their people﴾: that is, from fighting you, or because, or out of dislike that they should.

﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have given them power over you﴾
Page 111
by strengthening their hearts, expanding their breasts, and removing terror from them, ﴿so they would have fought you﴾ right after that, and not held back from you. The lam is a response-lam, as it is conjoined to the answer; there is no need to assume (law). Makki and Abu al-Baqa named it the lam of conditional response and pairing, and this is a strange designation. Repetition indicates that it is an independent answer, and the intended purpose of this is to bestow favour upon the believers.

It is also read (so they would have slain you) with light and heavy forms. ﴿Then if they withdraw from you﴾ and do not oppose you, ﴿and do not fight you﴾, despite what you know of their capacity for that by Allah's will, exalted is He; ﴿and offer you peace﴾, that is, reconciliation, so they submit and surrender. The casting of peace is a metaphor, since whoever hands over something casts it and throws it before the one to whom it is handed. It is also read with sukun on the lam, with fatha and kasra on the sin. ﴿Then Allah has not made for you any way against them﴾: that is, He has not permitted you to seize or kill them. In the negation of making a way there is emphasis on not harming them, since one who does not pass by a thing how can he harm it?

These verses have their ruling abrogated by the verse of Bara'ah: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾, and this has been narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 91:

﴿You will find others who wish to be secure from you and secure from their own people.﴾ They are people who used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and embrace Islam out of show (riya'), then return to Quraysh and relapse into idols, seeking by this to be secure from the Prophet of Allah, may Allah exalt him (ﷺ), and secure from their people. So Allah the Exalted refused this for them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. It is also said that the verse concerns the hypocrites. ﴿Whenever they are returned to temptation﴾ i.e., they are called to polytheism, as narrated from al-Suddi. It is also said: to fight the Muslims. ﴿They are plunged back into it﴾ i.e., they are turned over in it in the most abominable and vile manner.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that a man's people would say to him: "With what have you believed? With this monkey, scorpion and beetle?" ﴿So if they do not withdraw from you﴾ by refraining from confronting you in any way ﴿and offer you peace﴾ i.e., and do not offer you reconciliation and truce ﴿and restrain their hands﴾ i.e., and do not restrain themselves from fighting you.

﴿Then seize them and kill them wherever you find them﴾ i.e., wherever you come upon them and reach them, or wherever you are able to overpower them. It is related from some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin): this verse is the counterpart of the first verse, and between them there is opposition, either by affirmation and negation or by absence and possession, since one is negative and the other positive; there is neither opposition of contrariety (tadadd) nor opposition of correlation (tadayuf), because, as they have established, these two do not exist except between two positive matters. So His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So if they do not withdraw from you﴾ is the counterpart of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if they withdraw from you﴾; and His saying, majestic is His majesty: ﴿and offer you peace﴾ is the counterpart of His saying, mighty is His glory: ﴿and cast peace to you﴾; and His saying, majestic is His splendor: ﴿and restrain their hands﴾ is the counterpart of His saying, mighty is the One who speaks: ﴿so they do not fight you﴾. The waw does not require sequence, so the antecedent in the two verses is composed of three parts. In the first verse these are withdrawal, non-fighting and casting peace; with these parts the condition is complete, and its consequence is non-interference with them by seizing and killing, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿Allah has not given you any way against them.﴾ In the second verse these are non-withdrawal, non-casting of peace and non-restraint from fighting; with these three parts the condition is complete, and its consequence is seizing and killing, expressed by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Then seize them and kill them.﴾

From this it is known that (wa-yakuffu) [and they restrain] means (lam yakuffu) [they did not restrain], and is coordinated with the negated clause, not with the negation itself, as indicated by the dropping of the nun, which is the sign of the jussive (jazm). Coordinating it with the negation while the jussive is governed by (in) the conditional particle is not valid, because it entails contradiction: the meaning of ﴿So if they do not withdraw from you﴾ is "if they do not restrain," and if (yakuffu) were coordinated with the negation, it would entail the simultaneous occurrence of non-restraint and restraint, which is far removed from the speech of Allah. Likewise it is not valid for His saying, glorified is He: (wa-yakuffu) to be a circumstantial clause (hal), or a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'nafiyya bayaniyya), or a grammatical clause (nahwiyya), since each of these entails contradiction; moreover, it would require the nun to be present in (yakuffu), as is usual in such constructions. Abu Hayyan made the consequent in the first verse dependent on two things and in the second on three, and the secret of this is to indicate the greater wickedness of these others. The words of the Allamah al-Baydawi, may Allah whiten the brightness of his states, in this context are not free from complexity, and perhaps no sound interpretation can be found for them except after effort and strain. So reflect deeply. ﴿And those (are they)﴾ are those described by the abominable attributes mentioned.

﴿We have given you against them a manifest authority﴾ i.e., a clear proof concerning what We have commanded you regarding them, because of the evident nature of their enmity and the clarity of their disbelief and vileness; or a domination without any obscurity, since We have permitted you to seize them and kill them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 92:

﴿And it is not for a believer﴾ This begins an explanation of the state of the believers after the explanation of the state of the disbelievers and the hypocrites. It has also been said: when Allah, glorified is He, encouraged fighting the disbelievers, He mentioned right after it what relates to warfare in general. That is, it is not proper for him, nor is it of his nature, ﴿to kill﴾ without right ﴿a believer﴾, for faith restrains one from that, ﴿except by mistake﴾, for that is something that cannot be entirely avoided, and a fighter rarely is free of it. Its grammatical position (intiṣāb) is either as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning: it is not for him to kill a believer in any circumstance except in the circumstance of error; or as an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu), meaning: it is not for him to kill him for any cause except error; or as an adjectival qualifier of the verbal noun, meaning: except a killing by error. So the exception in all of these is "mufarragh" (an exception from a general/absent object), and it is an "muttaṣil" (connected) exception according to what the words of some of the verifiers imply. It does not necessitate that killing by error is permissible in the Sharia, since the meaning is: it is part of the nature of the believer that he does not kill except by error.

Some of them said: the exception in the verse is "munqaṭi'" (disconnected), meaning: but if he kills him by mistake, then his recompense is what is mentioned. It has also been said: "illa" (except) is in the sense of "wa-la" (and not), and the estimate is: "It is not for a believer to kill a believer, either intentionally or by mistake." It has also been said: the exception is from "believer", meaning: except one who errs. The preferred reading, despite the long separation in such a construction, is the accusative. Error (khaṭa') is that which is not accompanied by an intention toward the act or the person, or that which is not generally intended to cause the departure of the soul, or that which is not intended as a forbidden act, such as shooting a Muslim among the ranks of the disbelievers while unaware of his Islam. It was also read as (khaṭā') with a long vowel, and as (khaṭa) on the pattern of (ʿaman), with the hamza lightened.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Suddi that: "ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿa al-Makhzumi, who was a brother of Abu Jahl and al-Harith ibn Hisham through their mother, accepted Islam and emigrated to the Prophet ﷺ. He was the most beloved of his mother's children to her, so that grieved her, and she swore that no roof would shade her until she saw him. Abu Jahl and al-Harith came until they reached Medina and informed ʿAyyash of what his mother had suffered, and asked him to return with them so that she might look at him, and they would not prevent him from returning. They gave him a covenant that they would release him after his mother saw him. He set out with them, and when they had left Medina, they deliberately bound him and flogged him about a hundred lashes, and a man from the Banu Kinana helped them in that. ʿAyyash swore that he would surely kill the Kinani if he could. They brought him to Mecca, and he remained imprisoned until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ conquered Mecca. ʿAyyash went out and met the Kinani, who had accepted Islam, while ʿAyyash did not know of his Islam, and he struck him until he killed him. Afterward he was informed, so he came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and told him the story, and the verse was revealed." Similar was narrated from Mujahid and ʿIkrima.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Zayd that it was revealed concerning a man killed by Abu al-Darda', who was in a military expedition. Abu al-Darda' turned aside to a ravine seeking a need of his, and found a man of the people with his sheep, so he struck him with the sword, and the man said: "There is no god but Allah," but he was struck down. Then he brought his sheep to the people, then he found something in himself, so he came to the Prophet ﷺ and mentioned that to him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Did you not split open his heart, when he had informed you with his tongue, and you did not believe him!" He said: "How about me, O Messenger of Allah?" He ﷺ said, peace and blessings be upon him: "And how about 'There is no god but Allah'!" This was repeated. Abu al-Darda' said: "I wished that day was the beginning of my Islam," then the Qur'an was revealed.

﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake, then [he must free] a neck﴾ meaning: upon him, that is, his obligation is the freeing of a neck. Liberation (taḥrīr) is manumission, and its original meaning is: making him free, that is, noble, because every honored thing is called "free" (ḥurr), and from it come "ḥurr al-wajh" (the noble-faced, i.e., the cheek) and "aḥrār al-ṭayr" (the free birds), and likewise "taḥrīr al-kitāb" (writing/editing a book) comes from this as well.

The intended meaning of "neck" (raqaba) is "a soul" (nasama), an expression of the whole by a part. Al-Raghib said: in common usage it is for slaves, just as "head" and "back" are used to express a mount, so one says: "So-and-so keeps such-and-such a head, and such-and-such a back."

﴿believing﴾ means one judged to be a believer, even if young. This was the view of ʿAṭa'. It was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Sha'bi, Ibrahim, and al-Hasan: a child or a disbeliever does not suffice for the expiation of killing.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated from Qatada that he said: in the reading of Ubayy: "[the freeing of] a believing neck, in which a child does not suffice." In the verse there is a refutation of those who claim the freeing of a young People of the Book, or an adult or young Magian, is permissible. It has also been used as evidence that half a neck plus half another neck does not suffice.

﴿and a compensation (diya) delivered to his family﴾ meaning: paid to the heirs of the slain, who divide it among themselves according to the inheritance. Indeed, the authors of the four Sunan narrated from al-Dahhak ibn Sufyan al-Kilabi who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ wrote to me ordering me to give the wife of Ashyam al-Dhababi a share of the blood-money of her husband." It is paid from it, the debt is settled from it, and the bequest is carried out, and there is no distinction between it and the rest of the estate. But Sharik said: no debt is paid from the blood-money, and no bequest is carried out.

From Rabi'a: the ghurra (the indemnity for a fetus) belongs to the mother of the unborn child alone, and this contradicts the view of the majority. The freeing of the neck is required from the killer's property, while the blood-money is borne on his behalf by the ʿaqila (paternal kin); if there is none, it is from the public treasury (bayt al-mal); if there is none, then from his own property.

﴿unless they remit it as charity﴾ meaning: his family give it up as charity to him, and He named forgiving it "charity" to urge it. Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from the Prophet ﷺ: "Every good deed is charity." This phrase is connected to the "upon him" estimated before, or to "delivered" (musallamatun): meaning, upon him is the blood-money, or he delivers it at all times except when his family give it up as charity, in which case it falls, and its delivery is not required. There is not in it, as has been said, an indication that the freeing falls away, so that another estimate would be needed before His words "and a compensation delivered"; rather the phrase in the accusative position is an exception.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the phrase in the accusative position is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the killer, or the family, or as an adverbial. Abu Hayyan criticized him, saying both of these analyses are wrong, because "an" with the verb cannot be a circumstantial clause or accusative as an adverb of time, as the grammarians have stated. It is mentioned that some cited, as evidence for "an" with its clause occurring in the position of a time adverb, the verse:

"I said to her: do not marry him, for he is for the first arrow to meet a gathering."

That is: at the first arrow, at the time of its meeting. Ibn Malik, as al-Saffaqsi said, estimates in the verse and the line a prepositional particle, that is, "bi-an yaṣṣaddaqū" (by their giving as charity) and "bi-an yulāqiya" (by its meeting). Ubayy read: "illa an yataṣaddaqū."

﴿But if he was﴾ that is, the one killed by error ﴿from a people hostile to you﴾ meaning disbelievers who wage war against you ﴿and he was a believer﴾, and the killer did not know of it, because he was among his people, either because he came to them after having accepted Islam for some important matter, or because he accepted Islam among them and did not separate from them. The verse was revealed, as Ibn Jubayr said, concerning Mirdas ibn ʿAmr when Usama ibn Zayd killed him by mistake: ﴿then [he must free] a believing neck﴾, meaning: upon his killer is the expiation and not the blood-money, since there is no inheritance between him and his family.

﴿And if he was﴾ that is, the believing slain, as narrated from Jabir ibn Zayd, ﴿from a people﴾ of disbelievers ﴿between you and them is a covenant﴾ meaning a treaty, either temporary or permanent, ﴿then a compensation﴾ meaning: upon his killer is blood-money ﴿delivered to his family﴾ from the Muslim family if they are found, and it is not delivered to his relatives among the disbelievers, even if they are covenanted; since a disbeliever does not inherit from a Muslim. Perhaps the mention of this ruling first, with the delay of its counterpart earlier, as has been said, is to signal haste in delivering the blood-money, to avoid any suspicion of breaking the covenant. ﴿And [he must free] a believing neck﴾, as is the ruling for all Muslims. Perhaps singling it out for mention, as has also been said, although it is included in the ruling of what came before in His words, glorified is He, "And whoever kills a believer by mistake" etc., is to clarify that its occurring among covenanted people does not prevent the obligation of blood-money, as its occurring among warring people prevented it.

It has been said: the intended slain here is one of those covenanted people, so his killer must free a neck and pay the blood-money to his polytheist family, due to the covenant between us and them. This was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Sha'bi, and Abu Malik. It has been used as evidence that the blood-money of a Muslim and of a protected dhimmi is equal, since He, exalted is He, mentioned in each the expiation and the blood-money, so their blood-money must be equal, just as the expiation for both is equal.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Shihab who said: We have been informed that the blood-money of a covenanted person was like the blood-money of a Muslim, then it was later reduced at the end of time, so it was made like half the blood-money of a Muslim.

Abu Dawud narrated from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that "the blood-money of the People of the Book during the time of the Prophet ﷺ was half the blood-money of the Muslims," and Malik acted upon this.

From al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him: the blood-money of a Jew or a Christian is half the blood-money of a Muslim, and the blood-money of a Magian is two-thirds of a tenth of it. Some claimed that blood-money is also obligatory where the slain is from a hostile people of ours and is a believer, due to the general wording of the first verse, and that silence about blood-money in its verse does not negate it; it was only omitted because there is no blood-money due there to be delivered to his family, since they are disbelievers; rather it goes to the public treasury, so by silence He intended to show that his family deserves nothing.

Others said: blood-money is obligatory for a believer when he is from a covenanted people, and it is delivered to his disbelieving family, who have the greater right to his blood-money because of their covenant. Perhaps these do not count it as inheritance, since a disbeliever, even if covenanted, does not inherit from a Muslim, as has been proven.

﴿But whoever does not find﴾ a neck to free, meaning he does not own it, nor the price by which he could reach it ﴿then fasting﴾ meaning: upon him is fasting ﴿two consecutive months﴾. Mujahid said: he must not break it, nor interrupt its fasting; if he does so, without illness or excuse, he must begin the fast of both months anew. If an illness or excuse befalls him, he fasts what remains of them. If he dies without having fasted, sixty needy persons are fed on his behalf, a mudd for each needy person. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it.

It was also narrated from him that he said: whoever does not find blood-money or manumission, upon him is fasting, and by this view was taken by those who said that fasting for one who lacks both blood-money and a neck suffices for both. Restricting the neck alone as the object is the view narrated from the majority. Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak that he said: fasting is for one who does not find a neck; as for the blood-money, it is obligatory and nothing nullifies it. Then he said: and this is the correct view, because in killing by error the blood-money is on the ʿaqila and the expiation is on the killer, so one fasting does not suffice for what is owed by another from his property.

Those who used the verse said: there is no feeding in this expiation. And whoever said: one moves to it upon inability to fast, analogized it to the zihar (pre-Islamic divorce formula), and this is one of al-Shafi'i's two opinions, may Allah have mercy on him. From the mention of expiation in error but not in intentional killing, some said: there is no expiation for intentional killing; while al-Shafi'i says: it is more deserving of it than error.

﴿A repentance﴾ is in the accusative as an object of purpose, meaning: this was prescribed for you as a repentance, that is, an acceptance of it, from "Allah accepted his repentance" when He accepts his repentance. In it is an indication of shortcoming by abandoning caution.

It has been said: "repentance" means lightening, meaning: this was prescribed for you as a lightening upon you. It has also been said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "upon him", with an omitted modifier, meaning: upon him is fasting two months in the state of being one with repentance. It has also been said: it is in the verbal noun position, meaning: He accepted your repentance with a repentance.

His words, glorified is He, ﴿from Allah﴾ are connected to an omitted element that stands as a qualifier of the indefinite noun, meaning: a repentance coming from Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing﴾ of all things, of which the state of this killer is part, ﴿Wise﴾ in all that He prescribed and decreed of rulings, of which what He prescribed and decreed concerning his case is part.

﴿Whoever deliberately kills a believer﴾ by intending to kill him with something that separates the parts of the body, or with something he cannot possibly survive, while knowing that he is a believer. The phrase is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the subject of (yaqtul).

It is narrated from al-Kisa'i that he read the (tā') with sukūn, apparently to avoid a sequence of vowels. ﴿Then his recompense﴾ is what he deserves for his crime: ﴿Hell, to abide therein﴾, that is, remaining forever, or remaining for a long time, for as long as Allah the Exalted wills. This is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) with the sense of a future state, referring back to the subject of an implied verb required by the context, as if it were said: his recompense is that he enters Hell to abide therein.

Abu'l-Baqa' said: it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the nominative or accusative in (yujziha), which is implied. It was also said: it is from the accusative pronoun only, and the verb is taken to be (jazahu). This is supported by the claim that it is more appropriate for what follows to be coordinated with it, since it agrees with it in form. It was prohibited to make it a circumstantial clause from the genitive pronoun in (fa-jaza'uhu), for two reasons:

First, that it would be a circumstantial clause from the genitive noun attached to the pronoun.

Second, that the circumstantial clause and its owner would be separated by the predicate of the subject.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is angry with him﴾ are coordinated with an implied clause, which the conditional structure clearly indicates, as if it were said by way of resumption, confirming its content: Allah the Exalted has decreed that his recompense is that, ﴿and He is angry with him﴾, that is, He takes vengeance upon him, according to the view of the Ash'arites (the Ash'ariyyah, a school of Islamic theology). ﴿And He curses him﴾, that is, He removes him from His mercy by making his recompense what has been mentioned. It was also said: this and what follows it are coordinated with the predicate, with (an) implied, and the past tense is taken in the sense of the future, that is: his recompense is Hell, and that Allah the Exalted will be angry with him, etc.

﴿And He has prepared for him a great punishment﴾, whose extent cannot be measured.

The verse is as Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn Jubayr: "It was revealed concerning Miqyas ibn Dhubaba al-Kinani, that he embraced Islam together with his brother Hisham, and they were in Madina. One day Miqyas found his brother Hisham killed among the Ansar, in the clan of Banu'n-Najjar. So he went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of that. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a man from Quraysh, from Banu Fihr, and Miqyas went with him to Banu'n-Najjar, whose dwellings at that time were in Quba'. (He said): Hand over to Miqyas the killer of his brother, if you know who it is; otherwise, pay him the blood-money. When the messenger came to them, they said: We hear and obey Allah the Exalted and the Messenger (ﷺ). By Allah the Exalted, we do not know who the killer is, but we will pay the blood-money. So they gave Miqyas one hundred camels as the blood-money of his brother. When Miqyas and the Fihri were returning from Quba' to Madina, and there was an hour between them, Miqyas set upon the Fihri, the messenger of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and killed him, and he apostatized from Islam."

In another narration, he struck him against the ground, crushed his head between two stones, mounted a camel from the blood-money, drove the rest of it with him, and joined Makkah, saying in a poem of his:

"I killed for him Fihr, and I carried his blood-money,
the chiefs of Banu'n-Najjar, lords of Fari'.
I have obtained my vengeance and lain down cushioned,
and I was the first to return to the idols."

Then this verse was revealed, containing thunder, lightning, severe threat and distancing. It is also confirmed by other reports from the Master of Mankind (ﷺ).

Ahmad and al-Nasa'i recorded from Mu'awiya: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Every sin, Allah the Exalted may forgive, except a man who dies as a disbeliever, or a man who deliberately kills a believer."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded, from Abu'd-Darda', the like of it.

Ibn 'Adi and al-Bayhaqi recorded from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever helps in the shedding of the blood of a Muslim man even with half a word, will come on the Day of Resurrection with the words 'despairing of the mercy of Allah' written between his eyes."

Both of them recorded from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The passing away of this world and all that is in it is less significant before Allah the Exalted than the killing of a believer. And if the people of His heavens and the people of His earth were to share in the blood of one believer, Allah the Exalted would cause them all to enter the Fire."

In the narration of al-Isbahani, from Ibn 'Umar, that he (may the prayers and peace be upon him) said: "If the two weights (humans and jinn) were to gather to kill one believer, Allah the Exalted would overturn them on their faces into the Fire. And Allah the Exalted has forbidden Paradise to the killer and the one who orders it."

The Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites, a school of theology) argued by this and similar severe texts that whoever deliberately kills a believer will abide forever in the Fire. Some of the verifiers answered that this comes in the form of strong emphasis in deterrence, especially this verse, since the structure of the verse requires it, like the words of the Exalted: ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ in the verse of Hajj, and like the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) to al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, as in the two Sahihs, when he asked him about killing one of the disbelievers who had embraced Islam after cutting off his hand in battle: "Do not kill him; for if you kill him, he will be in your position before you kill him, and you will be in his position before he uttered the word that he uttered."

On this basis is understood what 'Abd ibn Humayd recorded from al-Hasan, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I pleaded with my Lord concerning the killer of a believer, that He make repentance possible for him, but He refused me."

And what he recorded from Sa'id ibn 'Aynā, that he said: "I was sitting beside Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him) when a man came to him and asked him about the killer of a believer: Is there repentance for him? He said: No, by Him besides whom there is no god, he will not enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle."

The saying denying repentance for him is widely reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and many have recorded it from him, and it is to be understood in the sense we have mentioned.

This is supported by what Ibn Humayd and al-Nahhas recorded from Sa'id ibn 'Ubayda, that Ibn 'Abbas used to say: "For the one who kills a believer there is repentance." A man came to him and asked: Is there repentance for the one who kills a believer? He said: "No, only the Fire." When the man stood up, his companions said to him: You were not thus giving fatwas to us; you used to give us fatwa that there is accepted repentance for the one who kills a believer. So what is the matter with this day? He said: I think he is an angry man who wants to kill a believer. So they sent after him and found him to be just so.

This was also the position of other elders. Sufyan said: When the people of knowledge were asked, they would say: There is no repentance for him. But when a man was tested, they would say to him: Repent.

Others answered that what is meant by abiding (khulūd) in the verse is a long stay, not perpetuity, because the texts are manifestly clear that the punishment of the disobedient believers does not last forever.

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded, from 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah, that he said: ﴿Then his recompense is Hell﴾ if He recompenses him. The like of this was narrated with a weak chain from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), raised to the Prophet (ﷺ). It was said: This is like when a person says to someone whom he is restraining from a matter: If you do it, your recompense is killing and beating; then if he does not punish him, that is not a lie on his part. The basis of this, as al-Wahidi said, is that Allah the Exalted, may He be glorified, may break a threat, though it is impossible for Him to break a promise. And the Sunnah has come with this.

In the hadith of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever Allah the Exalted promises a reward for his deed, He will certainly fulfil it for him; and whoever He threatens with punishment for his deed, then it is up to Him."

From the supplications of the truthful Imams (may Allah be pleased with them): "O You who, when You promise, fulfil, and when You threaten, pardon." The Arabs boasted of breaking a threat and did not regard it as a deficiency, as his words indicate:

"And when I threaten him, or promise him,
I break my threat and fulfil my promise."

It was objected that the threat is a type of report, and if breaking it is permissible, which is a lie for the sake of showing generosity, then why would it not be permissible in narratives and reports for some purpose? Opening that door leads to undermining all the laws.

Those who hold that some of those threatened may be pardoned include some who claimed that the verses of threat are performative (inshā'), and some who said they are reports, but with an implied conditional clause for intimidation, so there is no breaking of a promise of pardon in them. Shaykh al-Islam said: The verification is that there is no need to derive what we are discussing from the basic principle, because it is a report from Him, the Exalted, that his recompense is that, not that He will recompense him. How could it be otherwise, when He, the Mighty and Majestic, has said: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾? If this were a report that He, may He be glorified, recompenses every evil with its like, it would be contradicted by His saying, may His majesty be exalted: ﴿and He pardons much﴾. This is taken from the words of Abu Salih and Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah. Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i objected to it, saying: What is not done is not called a recompense. Do you not see that when a hired worker deserves his wage, the dirhams that are with his employer are not called a recompense until they are given to him and reach him?

al-Tabarsi criticized this, saying: This is not correct, because recompense is an expression for what is deserved, whether it is done or not. That is why it is said: The recompense of the good-doer is goodness, and the recompense of the wrongdoer is wrongdoing, even if the good-doer and the wrongdoer are not specified, so that it is said: that was done to them both, or was not done. It is also said of one who killed another: The recompense of this is that he be killed. That is a true statement even if the killing has not been carried out. What is not said of the dirhams is that they are the recompense of the worker, because the worker is entitled to the wage as a debt, not to the specific dirhams; so the employer may give him from them or from others.

It was objected: We grant that recompense does not necessarily have to be carried out; yet many verses, such as His words: ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ and ﴿and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾, indicate that He, the Exalted, definitely conveys the recompense to those who deserve it; and the verse contains an indication of this. But there is no hiding what is wrong with this, because the verses in which He, the Exalted, conveys the recompense to its deserving object are all in the category of verses of threat, and pardon in them is permissible, so there is no sense in asserting definiteness. Hence it was said that the verse is not fit to serve as evidence for the Mu'tazilah together with His words: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾.

al-Bayhaqi recorded from Quraysh ibn Anas, who said: "I was with 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd in his house, when he began to recite a poem: I will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and set before Allah the Exalted, and He will say to me: Why did you say that the killer is in the Fire?! I will say: You said it. Then he recited this verse: ﴿And whoever kills a believer﴾, etc. I said to him: There was nothing in the house smaller than me: What do you think if He says to you: I have said, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that a partner be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾; so how do you know that I do not will to forgive this one? He said: So he could not answer me with anything."

This is supported by what Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Isma'il ibn Thawban, who said: "I used to sit with the people before the Great Calamity in the Great Mosque, and I heard them saying: When the verse ﴿And whoever kills a believer﴾ was revealed, the Muhajirun and the Ansar said: The Fire is certain for whoever does this, until the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that a partner be associated with Him﴾, etc. Then the Muhajirun and the Ansar said: Allah the Exalted does whatever He wills."

By the verse of forgiveness, Ibn Sirin answered whoever held fast to the verse of abiding, and became angry with him and expelled him from his presence. That the verse of abiding was revealed after that verse by six months or four months, as reported from Zayd ibn Thabit, does not add anything; and the claim of abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of one ruling by a later one) in such a matter is hardly valid, as is not hidden.

Some scholars answered that the ruling of the verse applies only to the killer who regards it as permissible (al-mustahill), and that his disbelief is beyond doubt, so this is not a point of dispute. This is supported by the fact that the verse was revealed concerning al-Kinani, as its narration has already been related. It has also been reported from ʿIkrimah, Ibn Jurayj, and a group [of scholars] that they interpreted "intentionally" (muta'ammidan) as "regarding it as permissible" (mustahillan).

This was objected to on the grounds that what counts is the general wording of the expression, not the specific occasion of revelation (al-sabab al-khass). It was also objected that interpreting "intentionally" as "regarding it as permissible" is hardly acceptable, since this is not its meaning either linguistically or in the Shariah. If it is claimed to be a metaphor, there is no evidence for it. And the occasion of revelation cannot serve as evidence for what you have now learned. Moreover, the contrast between this killing mentioned in this verse and the killing mentioned in the preceding verse, which is pure accidental killing (al-khata' al-sirf), would be lost.

It has also been said that permissibility is understood from attaching the killing to "a believer" (mu'min), because it is a derived term (mushtaqq), and attaching a ruling to a derived term indicates that the basis of the derivation is the cause (ʿillah). Thus it is as if it were said: "Whoever kills a believer for the sake of his faith" — and there is no doubt that whoever kills him for that reason can only be one who regards it as permissible — so he can only be a disbeliever. This killer therefore falls outside the point of dispute, even if the occasion of revelation is not taken into account.

This was objected to on the grounds that "believer," although derived in origin, has been treated as if it were a fixed noun (jamid). Do you not see that your saying "I spoke to a believer," for example, is not understood as meaning that you spoke to him because of his faith? If attaching the ruling to "a believer" indicated causation, then striking a believer, withholding greeting from him, or failing to stand for him would be like killing him, making one a disbeliever, and no one holds this. And treating derivation as valid at one time and not valid at another is outside the bounds of sound reasoning, so let this be understood.

Then, Glorified is He, here He mentioned the ruling of the intentional killing in the Hereafter, and did not mention its worldly ruling, being content with what was stated earlier in the verse of al-Baqarah.

[p. 119]

﴿O you who believe﴾: the beginning of a warning against what would lead to regret, namely killing someone who should not be killed.

﴿When you go forth in the cause of God﴾: that is, when you travel for raiding (ghazw), as indicated by the preceding and following context. ﴿Then investigate﴾: that is, seek clarity about the matter in everything you do or refrain from, and do not act in it without reflection and deliberation.

Hamzah, 'Ali and Khalaf read (fa-tathabbatu), "then seek firmness," meaning: seek the establishment of the matter and do not hasten in it. The two meanings are close. The form tafa''ala here carries the sense of seeking (istiqbal). The fa' (fa-) has entered because (idha) contains the meaning of a conditional, as if it were said: "If you go forth to raid, then investigate."

﴿And do not say to one who offers you peace﴾: that is, who greets you with the greeting of Islam. Its counterpart is the greeting of the Jahiliyyah, such as "may your morning be pleasant" (an'ama sabahan) and "may God greet you" (hayyaka Allah ta'ala).

Hamzah, Khalaf and the people of Syria read (al-salam) without an alif. In some transmissions from 'Asim, he read (al-silm) with a kasrah on the sin and a fathah on the lam. The meaning in both readings is submission and compliance, and some have interpreted al-salam in the well-known reading in this sense as well. The lam, according to al-Samin, is for communication (li-l-tabligh), the past tense has the sense of the present, and (man) is either a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun. The intended meaning is a prohibition against what results from neglecting the commanded action, and the specifying of a significant matter among those in which clarification and verification are required. The restriction of this to travel is because the lack of clarification occurred there, not because it is required only there. The meaning is: do not say to one who has shown you what indicates his Islam, ﴿you are not a believer﴾, and that he only did so out of fear of being killed. Rather, accept from him what he has shown and deal with him according to its requirement.

It is narrated from 'Ali, may God honour his face, and Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir, may God be pleased with them both, and Abu Ja'far al-Qari', that they read (mu'ammanan) with a fathah on the second mim, meaning: granted safety to you. ﴿Seeking the goods of the worldly life﴾: that is, seeking its wealth, which is a fleeting trinket that soon vanishes. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the subject of (taqulu), indicating what drives them to haste. The prohibition refers to both the condition and the conditioned.

God's words, ﴿with God are many spoils﴾, are a reason for the prohibition against the condition, containing an implicit promise, as if it were said: do not seek that paltry, passing trinket, for with Him, glorified is He, and within His power are ﴿many spoils﴾, which He will grant you as booty, thereby sufficing you without it.

God's words, glorified is He, ﴿so were you before, then God bestowed favour upon you﴾, are a reason for the prohibition against the conditioned, on the basis that what is meant by it is the rejection of the faith of the one who offers greeting, because they thought that the saving faith is only that whose possessor shows signs that his tongue and heart agree. The demonstrative (dhalika) refers to the relative pronoun by virtue of its being characterised by what is in its relative clause. The fa' in (fa-manna) is for conjunction with (kuntum), and its predicate has been placed first for the sake of restriction, which conveys the emphasis of resemblance. As if it were said: do not reject the faith of one who greets you with the greeting of Islam, and do not say that it is not a saving faith, and that one characterised by it is not a protected believer, because you think that agreement of tongue and heart is a condition for protection, and mere greeting does not indicate it. For you yourselves, at the beginning of your Islam, were like this one who offered greeting, in that nothing appeared to people from you except what appeared from him to you of greeting and the like, and nothing appeared from you that you consider a condition, such as what indicates agreement.

[p. 120]

And the mere fact that entry into Islam did not happen under the shade of swords does not indicate that. So God bestowed favour upon you by accepting that from you, and did not command an inquiry into the agreement of your tongues and hearts, and thereby He protected your blood and your property. When the matter is thus, then investigate this matter and do not hasten, and deliberate, so that it may become clear to you that the apparent state is sufficient for saving faith, since it sufficed for you before. This reason, it is said, was placed last because it contains a kind of detail which, if placed first, might disrupt the coherence of the parts of the noble text, along with the consideration of the comparison between the earlier reason and what is given as a reason here. Or because placing the first one first indicates some inclination of the people toward that trinket, and that their joy in it is stronger, so placing it first would hasten their delight, and that involves a kind of disparagement of them. May God exalt their rank, and may the Lord, mighty is His majesty, be pleased with them. Or because the latter reason is clearer in explanation and comes to mind more readily than the former. Perhaps one of the two reasons was not conjoined to the other so that it would not be thought that they are reasons for one thing, or that their combination is a single cause. It is also said: [they were left unconjoined] in conformity with what is given as a reason for them, namely the condition and the conditioned, since they are not distinguished by conjunction. And it is said: it was not conjoined because the first is a reason for the second prohibition by a promise of an otherworldly matter, since the meaning is: do not seek the goods of the worldly life, because with Him, glorified is He, there is great reward in the Hereafter, which He has prepared for those who do not seek that. He expressed the reward by "spoils," fitting the context. The second reason for the first prohibition is not like this. Al-Zamakhshari and others mentioned in the verse what Shaykh al-Islam rejected, with what bears the marks of verification.

Some people have said regarding it: the meaning is that just as this one whom you killed was concealing his religion among his people out of fear for himself from them, so you were concealing your religion out of fear of your people for yourselves. Then God bestowed favour upon you by making His religion manifest and strengthening its adherents, until you openly professed Islam after you had been concealing it from the people of polytheism. ﴿Then investigate﴾ the blessing of God upon you, or ﴿investigate﴾ the affair of the one you are killing. It is not hidden that this, although part of it is related from Ibn Jubayr, does not fully fulfil the intended meaning.

Moreover, the claim that the addressees were concealing their religion out of fear of their people is open to objection, unless it is said that the fact that some of them were concealing was sufficient for the address. It is also said that God's words, glorified is He, ﴿then God bestowed favour upon you﴾, are disconnected from what precedes it, because when He forbade the people from killing the one mentioned, He informed them afterward that He had bestowed favour upon them by accepting their repentance from that reprehensible act. Then He repeated the command to investigate, for emphasis in warning. Or He commanded them to make clear the blessing of God, glorified is He, in thanks for what He had bestowed upon them. And this, as you see, is weak.

There is a difference concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of the verse. Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as hasan, and Ibn Humayd, who graded it as sahih, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: "A man of the Banu Sulaym passed by some companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was driving his sheep. He greeted them with salam. They said: 'He only greeted us so that he might seek refuge from us.' So they set upon him and killed him, and brought his sheep to the Prophet ﷺ, and then [the verse] was revealed."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ sent a expedition under the command of Usama ibn Zayd against the Banu Dhamrah. They met a man from them called Mirdas ibn Nahik, who had with him a little flock and a red camel. He took refuge in a mountain cave, and Usama pursued him. When Mirdas reached the cave he placed his flock in it, then turned toward them and said: 'Peace be upon you. I testify that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God.' Usama rushed at him and killed him for the sake of his camel and his little flock. The Prophet ﷺ, whenever he sent Usama, wished to praise him well and ask about his companions. When they returned he did not ask them about him. The people began to tell the Prophet ﷺ and say: 'O Messenger of God, if only you had seen Usama when a man met him and said: there is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and he rushed at him and killed him, while he was turning away from them.' When they insisted upon it, he raised his head toward Usama and said: 'How will you be with "there is no god but God"?!' He said: 'O Messenger of God, he only said it seeking refuge by it.' He ﷺ said: 'Why did you not split open his heart and look into it?!' Then the verse was revealed."

[p. 121 is not included in this passage]

Narrated from Ibn Zayd that it was revealed concerning a man whom Abu al-Darda' killed, and he mentioned of his story something like what was mentioned of Usama's story. Restricting the mention to the greeting of Islam in this case, although it was accompanied by the word of testimony, is for the sake of intensifying the prohibition and rebuke, and for drawing attention to the full clarity of their error, by showing that the greeting was [a sign of] peace and of abstaining from harming its bearer. How much more so when it is accompanied by that good word.

The verse and its context have been cited as evidence for the validity of the faith of one under compulsion, that the mujtahid may err, and that his error is excusable. The mode of inference for the first is that, although the killers thought that the Islam of the one mentioned was out of fear of being killed, which is a kind of compulsion in meaning, He rebuked them for killing him. Had his Islam not been valid, He would not have rebuked them. The mode of inference for the second is that He commanded in it the making clear, which indicates that haste is an error. The mode of inference for the third is taken from the context and from the absence of a threat for abandoning investigation. Some have held that there is no excuse for abandoning verification in such matters, and that the one who errs is sinful, and they argued for this with what Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from al-Hasan: "Some companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ set out to make raids, and they met some enemy people, and they charged against them and defeated them. A man from among them pursued a man intending to seize his goods. When he reached him with his spear, the man said: 'I am a Muslim, I am a Muslim.' He thrust him with the spear and killed him and took his goods. This was reported to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he said to the killer, peace be upon him: 'Did you kill him after he said: I am a Muslim?!' He said: 'O Messenger of God, he only said it seeking refuge.' He said: 'Did you not split open his heart?' He said: 'Why, O Messenger of God?' He said: 'So that you would know whether he is truthful or a liar.' He said: 'Was I to know that, O Messenger of God?' He, peace be upon him, said: 'His tongue only expresses what is in him, his tongue only speaks for him.'" He said: "The killer did not remain long before he died. His companions dug a grave for him, and in the morning he was cast out by the earth. They returned and dug for him again, and in the morning he was cast out by the earth beside his grave." Al-Hasan said: "I do not know how many times the companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ said: we buried him, twice or three times, every time the earth would not accept him. When we saw that the earth would not accept him, we took hold of his foot and threw him into one of those ravines." Then God, glorified is He, revealed His words: ﴿O you who believe﴾, the verse.

In the narration of 'Abd al-Razzaq, from Qatadah, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed the earth refused to accept him, so throw him into a cave of the caves." The mode of inference here regarding sin is clear. It is answered that this killer perhaps did not do that because the one killed was unacceptable in Islam in his view, but for another reason, and he excused himself with what he excused, lying before the Messenger of God ﷺ. This is supported by what Ahmad, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and a group narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Hadrad al-Aslami, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ sent us to Idam. I went out with a group of Muslims, among them Abu Qatadah al-Harith ibn Ribi, and Muhallim ibn Jathamah ibn Qays al-Laythi. We went out until, when we were in the valley of Idam, 'Amir ibn al-Adbat al-Ashja'i passed by us on a riding camel, with his little flock and a skin of milk. When he passed us he greeted us with the greeting of Islam. We withheld from him. Muhallim ibn Jathamah attacked him because of something that was between them, and killed him and took his little flock. When we came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and informed him of the news, the Qur'an was revealed concerning us: ﴿O you who believe﴾, etc."

The apparent reading is that the unnamed man in the report of al-Hasan is this same man who is named in this report. This indicates that the killing was due to something that was in the heart from old grudges. We said this is the apparent reading because of the report of Ibn 'Umar: "When Muhallam ibn Jaththama returned, he came to the Prophet ﷺ wearing two garments, and sat before him - upon him be prayer and peace - so that he might ask forgiveness for him. He said: 'May Allah the Exalted forgive you.' So he stood up, while he was wiping his tears with his two garments. Not an hour had passed before he died. They buried him, but the earth cast him out. They came to the Prophet ﷺ and mentioned that to him, and he said: 'Indeed the earth accepts one who is worse than your companion, but Allah the Exalted wished to admonish you.' Then they threw him between two rocks of a mountain and cast stones upon him." What the heart inclines toward is the unity of the story.

It was objected to the acceptance [of this view] on account of the absence of a threat that the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾ [4:94] imply a threat. That is, He, glorified is He, has always been and still is aware of all the deeds you do, the apparent and the hidden, and their manners, and this includes the act of verification and its abandonment, with an initial entry and most complete awareness, so He will recompense you according to that: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil. The clause is a causal explanation by way of resumption. It was also read with the fath of (أنَّ), as a object of (تَبَيَّنُوا) or with the deletion of the lam of causation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 4, verse 95:
