﴿Those who sit back [from jihad] are not equal﴾. This begins an exhortation to jihad, so that they will be ashamed to abandon it and will be eager to avoid what would cause a defect in it. By "those who sit back" is meant those who were given permission to remain behind from jihad, on the basis that others would suffice. Al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they are "those who sat back from Badr," and this is the apparent meaning, which accords with history, as has been said.

Abu Hamza said: they are those who stayed behind from Tabuk. It is related that the verse was revealed concerning Ka'b ibn Malik from Banu Salima, Murara ibn al-Rabi' from Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf, al-Rabi', and Hilal ibn Umayya from Banu Waqif, when they remained behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on that expedition.

﴿from among the believers﴾: this is a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier, a term for an accusative describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) of "those who sit back." It is also permitted that it be a *hal* of the concealed pronoun within it. The benefit of this is to announce from the outset that sitting back from jihad does not expel them from faith, and to indicate the cause of their deserving what will be mentioned later of the best reward. That is: those who remain behind from jihad are not equal to those who strive, while being among the believers.

﴿other than those with a harm﴾: this is in the nominative, as a *sifa* (qualifying adjective) of "those who sit back." Although it is definite, and *ghayr* (غَيْرُ) does not become definite in such a position, what is intended is not particular individuals who sit back but the category as a whole, so it resembles a generic noun, and thus its being described by it is valid.

'Isam al-Din claimed that *ghayr* (غَيْرُ) here is definite, and that *ghayr ulī al-ḍarar* (غَيْرُ أُولِي الضَّرَرِ) means "one who has no harm." This was reported from al-Radi, and on the basis of it what was previously stated was judged weak, namely that the indefinite article-marked noun (المُعَرَّفُ بِاللّامِ المُبْهَمُ) even though it has the ruling of an indefinite noun, is not described by what an indefinite noun is described by; rather, its qualifier must necessarily be a verbal clause whose verb is in the present tense, as in his saying:

*And indeed I pass by the base man who abuses me,*
*So I turn away, then say, "It does not concern me."*

Some have preferred to make it a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for "those who sit back," because the *al* (ال) in it is relative (مَوْصُولَةٌ), whereas the known usage for the definite with *al* is to denote the category; and between them there is a difference. Al-Zajjaj permitted the nominative reading as an exception (*istithna'*), and al-Wahidi followed him in this. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read it in the accusative, as a *hal*, in which case it is indefinite and not definite, or as an exception, in which case the grammatical case of what follows it is made apparent by it.

It was also read in the genitive, as a *sifa* of "the believers," or as a *badal* of it. That an indefinite noun is not substituted for a definite noun except when it is described is a majority rule, not a universal one.

*al-ḍarar* (الضَّرَرِ): illness and infirmities that leave no way to participate in jihad. In the same sense, or included within it, is inability to obtain the necessary equipment. The verse was revealed without the phrase "other than those with a harm," and then it was revealed afterwards.

For Malik narrated from al-Zuhri, from Kharija ibn Zayd, who said: Zayd ibn Thabit said: "I was writing before the Prophet (ﷺ) on a shoulder-blade: *Those who sit back from among the believers are not equal to those who strive*, and Ibn Umm Maktum was with the Prophet (ﷺ). He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, Allah has revealed what He has revealed concerning the excellence of jihad, and I am a blind man, so is there any concession for me?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'I do not know.' Zayd said: My pen was still wet and had not dried when the revelation overtook the Prophet (ﷺ), and his thigh came to rest upon my thigh, so that my thigh nearly broke from the weight of the revelation. Then it was lifted from him, and he said to me: 'Write, O Zayd: *other than those with a harm*.'"

﴿and those who strive in the way of Allah﴾: in His religious path. ﴿with their wealth﴾: by spending in what weakens the schemes of the enemies. ﴿and their lives﴾: by bringing them to bear in close combat at the encounter. Both prepositional phrases are linked to "those who strive." They were mentioned under this heading rather than the heading of going out (*al-khurūj*), which is the counterpart of the description of the one joined to them, and it was qualified in the manner it was, to praise them and to indicate the cause of their deserving elevated rank, together with the appropriateness of the word "path" (*sabil*) in contrast to "sitting back," as has been said.

It has been said: they were mentioned under the heading of jihad only to indicate that sitting back was from it, but the explicit statement of this was omitted there out of consideration for them in general. "Those who sit back" was placed before "those who strive" and was not placed after them, so that the explicit statement of their preference over them would follow directly. It has also been said: this is to announce from the outset that the deficiency indicated by non-equality is on the side of those who sit back and not on the side of their counterparts. For the concept of non-equality between two things that differ in excess and deficiency, although it is permissible to consider it in terms of the excess of the one who exceeds, the more immediate sense is to consider it in terms of the deficiency of the one who is deficient. On this basis is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Are the blind and the seeing equal, or are darknesses and light equal?﴾, and so on.

As for His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Are those who know and those who do not know equal?﴾, perhaps the precedence of the superior in it is because its attribute (*silah*) is a faculty (*malaka*) that is the attribute of the inferior.

You know that there is no conflict among the subtle rhetorical points, and that in a single matter there may be an aspect of precedence and an aspect of posteriority, so that this one is considered at one time and that one at another. Here, the Exalted has placed the mention of wealth before the lives, while in His saying, exalted be His majesty: ﴿Indeed Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth﴾ He reversed it, because the self is nobler than wealth. He placed the lives first as the purchased item, to alert that the desire for them is more intense, and delayed the seller, to alert that holding on to them is more intense, so one does not give them up except for a benefit. In the same pattern comes His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Allah has preferred those who strive in His way with their wealth and their lives over those who sit back﴾ from among the believers (other than those with a harm) ﴿by a degree﴾ whose measure cannot be estimated and whose reality cannot be reached. This is an explicit statement of what the negation of equality implied, for it entails preference. However, it did not suffice with what was understood, out of concern for it and so that it might be more firmly established. And because the sentence explains and clarifies what preceded it, it was not joined to it by a conjunction. It was also permitted that it be an answer to a question that the discourse leads to, as if it were said: "How did that preference occur?" and so it was said: "Allah preferred..." and so on. The *al* (ال), as we have indicated, in both plurals is for prior reference (*ahd*), and it is not precluded by its complement being a descriptive clause, as has been said, since *al* (ال) often occurs in it for definiteness, as the grammarians have explicitly stated.

﴿by a degree﴾ (*darajatan*, دَرَجَةً) is in the accusative as a *masdar* (verbal noun, a cognate accusative), because it includes the sense of preference, for it is a station and a rank, and these occur in ascent and superiority. So it occupies the position of a verbal noun, as if it were said: "He preferred them with a preference," like the expression "I struck him with a whip," meaning "a strike." It has also been said that it is in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier), meaning "possessors of a degree." It has been said that it is a *tamyiz* (specification, an accusative clarifying what is vague), and it has been said that it is by omission of the preposition, meaning "by a degree," and it has been said that it occupies the position of an adverb of place, meaning "in a degree and a station."

His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And to each﴾: *kullan* (كُلا) is the first object of what follows it, and it was placed before it to affirm restriction (*qasr*), as an emphasis of the promise. Its tanwin (التنوين) is a substitute for the omitted genitive complement, meaning: each one of the two groups, those who strive and those who sit back. ﴿Allah has promised﴾ the reward ﴿the best﴾, which is Paradise, as Qatada and others said, not just one of the two alone.

al-Hasan read *wa-kullun* (وكُلٌّ) in the nominative, as a subject, in which case the first object, which is the returning pronoun in the predicate clause, is omitted, meaning: His promise. The obligation of the accusative in the widely transmitted reading seems to be because a verbal clause precedes it. With this it differs from what is in al-Hadid. And "the best" (*al-husna*, الحُسْنى) in both readings is the second object. The clause is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*), brought in to correct what might suggest that preferring one of the two groups over the other entails deprivation of the inferior one.

His saying, glorified be He: ﴿And Allah has preferred those who strive over those who sit back﴾ is a conjunction with what precedes it. The *al* (ال) sufficed in place of mentioning what was omitted by way of gradual reduction of the restrictions. The gradualness was not considered in omitting what was mentioned with those who sit back at first, namely by omitting "from among the believers" alone and mentioning "other than those with a harm" in the first verse, and omitting both together in the second verse. Rather, it omitted both at once at the first intention of gradualness. It has been said that the restriction "other than those with a harm" was after the question, as the occasion of revelation indicates. In some reports it is related that when the verse was revealed, Ibn Umm Maktum began to say: "O Lord, where is my excuse? O Lord: where is my excuse?" Then that was revealed, so the door of need for him was closed, and the questioner was content with its mention once, so it was dropped together with what accompanied it, dropped at once for that purpose. This is not the case with what was mentioned with those who strive, for its inclusion was out of pure grace and benevolence without any prior question. So when the door of dropping was opened, gradualness was considered in it, to distinguish between the two situations.

His saying, exalted be He: ﴿a great reward﴾ is a *masdar mu'akkid* (emphatic verbal noun) for "preferred." It is, although it means "bestowed excellence," and excellence is more general than reward, because reward is what is given in return for a deed, yet here what is intended is the more specific sense, because it stands in contrast to jihad. It is also permissible that it retain its general meaning. "A reward" (*ajran*, أجرًا) is a direct object, and because it includes the sense of giving, it took the object in the accusative, meaning: He gave them an increase over those who sit back, a great reward. It has been said that it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, meaning: He preferred them with a reward.

Making it a description of His saying, exalted be He:

[p. 122] [p. 123]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 4, verse 96:**

﴿Darajat (degrees)﴾ is placed before its verb and is therefore in the accusative as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative). Since it is originally a *maṣdar* (verbal noun), which is used in the same form for the singular and the plural, it is permissible for it to qualify a plural. This is far-fetched.

It is also permitted that *darajat* be a *badal al-kull* (substitution of the whole, *badal al-kull*) for ﴿ajran (a reward)﴾, clarifying the quantity of the favour. It is also permitted that it be a *ḥāl*, meaning "possessors of degrees", or that it occupy the position of an *ẓarf* (adverb of place), meaning "in degrees".

The words of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿minhu (from Him)﴾ are connected to an omitted element that functions as an adjective of *darajat*, indicating its magnificence and the elevation of its rank.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd transmitted from Ibn Muḥayriz that he said: "They are seventy degrees, the distance between each two degrees being the running of a swift, well-trained horse for seventy years."

Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i transmitted from Abu Sa'id that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is pleased with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) as Messenger, Paradise becomes obligatory for him." Abu Sa'id was amazed by it and said: "Repeat it to me, O Messenger of Allah." So he repeated it to him. Then he (ﷺ) said: "And another (deed) by which Allah raises the servant a hundred degrees in Paradise, the distance between each two degrees being like the distance between the heaven and the earth." He said: "And what is it, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Jihad in the way of Allah."

It is also transmitted from al-Suddi that they are seven hundred.

It is also permitted that the accusative of *darajat* be a *maṣdariyya* (verbal-noun accusative), as in your saying: "I struck him with whips (*aswāṭan*)", meaning "strokes", as if it were said: "He preferred them with preferences." The paucity plural here stands in place of the plurality of abundance (*jam' al-kathra*), and it has been said that it remains in its original usage.

By *darajat* is meant what is mentioned in the verse of Surat Bara'a (al-Tawba): ﴿It was not for the people of Madina and the Bedouins around them to remain behind from the Messenger of Allah, nor to prefer their own selves over his self. That is because they are not afflicted by thirst, nor fatigue, nor hunger in the way of Allah, nor do they tread upon a place that enrages the disbelievers, nor do they gain anything from an enemy except that a righteous deed is recorded for them because of it.﴾ up to His words, glorified is He: ﴿so that Allah may reward them with the best of what they used to do﴾. This is attributed to ʿAbd Allah ibn Zayd.

As for His words, mighty is His rank: ﴿wa maghfiratan (and forgiveness)﴾, it is a conjunction (*ʿaṭf*) upon *darajat*, which itself is a *badal al-kull* for *ajran*, except that this is a *badal al-baʿḍ* (partial substitution) from it, because part of the reward is not of the category of forgiveness. That is, (there is) great forgiveness for what they commit of sins, which the rest of the good deeds that those who stayed behind perform do not expiate. Therefore it is counted among their distinguishing features. His exalted words: ﴿wa raḥmatan (and mercy)﴾ are also a conjunction upon it, and it is a *badal al-kull* from *ajran*. It is also permitted that both be in the accusative by means of an implied verb, meaning: He forgave them a forgiveness, and had mercy upon them with mercy.

This, and perhaps the repetition of the preference by way of conjunction, which indicates difference, and its restriction at one time with "a degree" (*darajatan*) and at another with "degrees" (*darajat*), while the preferred and the preferred-over are the same, as the apparent sense requires, is either to treat the difference in description between the two preferences and between "degree" and "degrees" as if it were an essential difference, as a preparation for following the path of vagueness and then explanation; or it is for greater confirmation and affirmation, indicating that the merit of the strivers is in a station that the green birds of thought cannot reach. Since this may almost be taken to imply the deprivation of those who stay behind, He, glorified is He, took care to remove this by His saying, mighty is He: ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best﴾. Then He, majestic is His rank, wished to explain what the indefiniteness had conveyed by way of vagueness, in a manner that cuts off the possibility that it refers to a single unit, so He said what He said and closed the door of possibility.

There is no concealing what there is in the vagueness and the explanation of conjunction. As for what has been said about the singular "degree" being used first because the intended meaning there is the preference of each striver, and the plural being used second because the intended meaning there is the preference of the group, so that in "degrees" there is a correspondence of plural to plural, with each striver having a degree, and the outcome of the two expressions being one, and the difference being a variation of style: this belongs to spoken speech, not to the Preserved Tablet.

Or it is for the essential difference between the two preferences and between "degree" and "degrees". Al-Raghib favoured this, and al-Tibi considered it good, on the basis that the intended meaning of the first preference is what Allah granted them promptly in this world of spoils, victory and true good remembrance, by being a single degree; and the intended meaning of the second preference is what He, glorified is He, has stored up for them of lofty degrees and exalted ranks, beyond counting. This is indicated by the first being placed first and the second being placed last, and by the promise of Paradise being placed between them, as if it were said: He preferred them in this world by one degree, and in the Next by degrees beyond counting. He placed between them in the mention what is intermediate between them in existence, namely the promise of Paradise, to clarify their condition and to hasten to console the one who is preferred-over. This is how the esteemed Mawlana Shaykh al-Islam established it.

It has also been said: the intended meaning of the first preference is the pleasure of Allah and His spiritual bliss, and the intended meaning of the second preference is the sensory bliss of Paradise. But in this, the conjunction of forgiveness and mercy makes this specification unlikely. It has also been said: the intended meaning of the first strivers is those who fought the disbelievers, and the intended meaning of the other strivers is those who struggled against their own selves, and they were increased in reward for their greater merit, as His saying, peace and blessings be upon him, indicates: "We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad." But in this, the context and the occasion of revelation refuse this, and the hadith he mentioned has no basis, as the scholars of hadith have said.

It has also been said: the intended meaning of those who stay behind in the first is the disabled, and in the second others, as Ibn Jurayj said, and Ibn Jarir transmitted it from him. But in this there is a dislocation of the arrangement that is not hidden.

It remains that the verse does not explicitly indicate the ruling concerning those with harm (*ulī al-ḍarar*), according to the interpretation accepted by us. Yes, in some hadiths there is what indicates their equality with the strivers. It has been authentically transmitted from the hadith of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from the expedition of Tabuk and drew near to Madina, he said: "Indeed, in Madina there are people; you have not travelled any journey nor crossed any valley except that they were with you in it." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, and they are in Madina?!" He said: "Yes, and they are in Madina; excuse has held them back." The implication of the descriptive qualification and the exception in ﴿other than those with harm (ghayr ulī al-ḍarar)﴾ indicates this. It is transmitted from al-Zajjaj that he said: "Except those with harm, for they are equal to the strivers." It is also transmitted from some of them that this equality is conditioned by another condition other than harm, which was mentioned in His saying, mighty is He: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick﴾ up to His words, glorified is He: ﴿when they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger﴾. What testimony from transmission and reason supports is that the disabled are superior to others in rank, just as they are below the strivers in worldly rank. As for whether they are equal to them in the rank of the Hereafter, there is no certainty about it. The verse, according to what Ibn Jurayj said, indicates that they are below them in this as well.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted, through the chain of Thabit, from ʿAbd al-Raḥman ibn Abi Layla, that Ibn Umm Maktum, after the revelation of the verse, used to fight and say: "Hand me the banner and place me between the two lines, for I will not flee."

Ibn Mansur transmitted from Anas ibn Malik that he said: "I saw Ibn Umm Maktum after that in some of the battlefields of the Muslims, and with him was the banner."

From the negation of equality in the beginning of the verse, which implies the preference explicitly stated afterwards between the striver with wealth and self and the one who stays behind, it is known that its negation is between the striver with one of the two and the one who stays behind. The possibility that the verse intends the negation of equality between the one who stays behind from jihad with wealth and the striver with it, and between the one who stays behind from jihad with the self and the striver with it, by making the intended meaning of "strivers in the way of Allah with their wealth and selves" those who strive therein with their wealth and those who strive therein with their selves, and by "those who stay behind" also both kinds of those who stay behind, with the intended meaning being the negation of equality between each kind of those who stay behind and its counterpart, is very far-fetched.

Ibn al-Ghars said that it was used as evidence by those who prefer wealth over poverty, on the basis that Allah, glorified is He, preferred the striver with his wealth over the striver without his wealth. There is no doubt that the extra degree of merit for the striver with his wealth is only from the aspect of wealth. They also used it as evidence for the preference of the striver with his own wealth over the striver with wealth given to him from the public treasury (*dīwān*) or the like.

﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a *tadhyīl* (concluding appendage) confirming what He, glorified is He, promised before.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 97:**

﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death﴾ is an explanation of the state of those who stayed behind from emigration (hijra), following the explanation of those who stayed behind from jihad. Alternatively, it explains the state of the hypocrites who stayed behind from supporting the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and from fighting alongside him, following the explanation of the state of the believers who stayed behind. The verb (tawaffahum) may be a past tense, and the feminine marker has been omitted because of the separation (between the verb and its subject) and because the subject is not a truly feminine noun. It may also be an imperfect (mudari') whose original form was (tatawaffahum), with one of the two tas deleted for lightness. In that case it recounts a past situation. The first reading is supported by the reading of the one who reads (tawaffathum), and the second by the reading of Ibrahim, (tuwaffahum), with a dammah on the tā', as an imperfect of (wafaytu). The meaning is that God Most High causes the angels to fulfil their souls, so they fulfil them, that is, He enables them to complete the taking of them. Ibn Jinni pointed to this. By "taking in death" is meant the seizing of the soul, and this is the apparent meaning, which Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, adopted.

It is reported from al-Hasan that the intended meaning is the gathering (hashr) to Hell. The "angels" here are the Angel of Death and his assistants. According to al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's Al-Bahr al-Muhit), they are six: three for the souls of believers and three for the souls of unbelievers. It is reported from the majority of scholars (al-jumhur) that the intended meaning is the Angel of Death alone, and this is an use of the plural to mean the singular, in order to magnify him and exalt his rank. It is not hidden that using the plural for the singular is not free from remoteness. The verified position is that there is no obstacle to attributing the taking in death to God Most High, to the Angel of Death, and to his assistants. The reasoning is that God Most High is the One who commands, indeed He is the true Agent, while the assistants are those who undertake to draw the soul out from the veins, the arteries and the sinews, and who sever its attachment to them. The Angel is the one who seizes it directly, taking it once it has been prepared. In the Qur'an there is: ﴿God takes the souls﴾, and ﴿The Angel of Death who has been entrusted with you will take you﴾, and ﴿Our messengers took him in death﴾. Similar to this is ﴿The angels take them in death while they are wronging themselves﴾, by abandoning emigration and choosing to dwell among the unbelievers, which necessarily leads to neglect of the matters of religion. Or (they wrong themselves) by their hypocrisy and their holding back from supporting the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and by their assisting the disbelievers.

Al-Tabarani reported from Ibn 'Abbas that there were people in Makkah who had embraced Islam. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) emigrated, they disliked emigrating and feared, so God Most High revealed this verse concerning them.

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Dahhak: "These are people from among the hypocrites who remained behind from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in Makkah and did not go out with him to Madinah. They went out with the polytheists of Quraysh to Badr, and they were struck among those who were struck. So God revealed this verse concerning them."

It is related from Ikrimah: "The verse was revealed concerning Qays ibn al-Fakih ibn al-Mughirah, al-Harith ibn Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad, Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Abu al-As ibn Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj, and Ali ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf. They had embraced Islam, but they gathered at Badr with the polytheists of Quraysh, and they were killed there as unbelievers." This was narrated by Abu al-Jarud, from Abu Ja'far, may God be pleased with him.

"Zalimi" (wronging) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun of the object in (tawaffahum). Its annexation is verbal (lafziyyah), so it does not give it definiteness. The original form is (zalimina anfusahum), "wronging themselves."

﴿They said﴾, that is, the angels, peace be upon them, said to those who were taken in death, as a rebuke for their shortcoming in showing their Islam and in establishing its rulings and rites. Or they said, as a reproach and censure for what they were engaged in: aiding the disbelievers, increasing their numbers, being absorbed into their army, and holding back from supporting the Messenger of God (ﷺ). ﴿What was your condition?﴾ That is, in what matter of your religion were you? The alif of the interrogative (ma) when it is in the genitive has been dropped, for conformity with the rule, and it is written joined to the preceding word, treating them as a single word. For this reason, (ila, ala, hatta) are written as (ilam, ala ma, hatta ma) with an alif, when they are not pausal, whereas when pausal (with the ha') they are written differently.

Page 126

In (fi ilam, wa ala ma, wa hatta ma) with an alif, as long as it is not stopped upon with the ha'.

However, as you know, the question is matched by the answer in the words of God Most High: ﴿They said, "We were oppressed on the earth."﴾ Otherwise, the expected answer would be "We were in such-and-such" or "We were in nothing." The sentence is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) built upon a question arising from the narrated question of the angels, as if it were said: "Then what did those who were taken in death answer?" So it was said: they answered: "We were oppressed in the land of Makkah, among the polytheists who were our kinsmen."

What is meant is that they offered excuses for their shortcoming in showing Islam, and for their introducing a defect into it through weakness and inability to carry out the duties of the religion among the people of Makkah. Therefore they sat and slept, or they made excuses for not going out with them, and for being absorbed into that assembled mass, by claiming that they were overpowered under their hands and that they did this unwillingly. In either case, the angels did not accept this from them, as His words, glorified be He, indicate: ﴿They said﴾, that is, the angels: ﴿Was not the earth of God spacious, so that you could have emigrated therein?﴾ That is, your excuse for that shortcoming, by settling among the people of that land, is colder than the zamharir (the bitter cold). For you could resolve the knot of this matter which has harmed your religion by migrating to another region of the earth, where you could establish the affairs of religion, as did the one who emigrated to Abyssinia and to Madinah. Or, your excuse for holding back from going out with the enemies of God Most High, in a way that angers His Messenger (ﷺ), by claiming that you are overpowered among those peoples, is not acceptable, because you have a way to escape their domination, and you are able to emigrate from their neighbourhood and to come out from under their hands. ﴿Those, then﴾, whose dreadful state has been described, ﴿their refuge﴾, that is, their dwelling in the Hereafter, ﴿is Hell﴾, because they abandoned the obligatory duty, for emigration was obligatory in the early period of Islam.

It is reported from al-Suddi that he used to say: whoever embraces Islam but does not emigrate is a disbeliever until he emigrates. The first view is more sound. Or (they are Hell-bound) because of their hypocrisy, their disbelief, and their support of the enemies of God Most High over the chief of His beloved ones, upon him be the best of blessings and peace. The absence of the qualification "except those who are made to suffer" (from the verse) is not an explicit text concerning disobedience short of disbelief; rather, the explicit text is the qualification by its absence. The demonstrative (ism al-isharah) is the first subject, (mawahum) is the second subject, and (jahannam) is the predicate of the second, and the two together are the predicate of the first. The connecting element is the genitive pronoun. The whole is the predicate of (inna), and the fa' is because its subject includes the meaning of a conditional. God's words, glorified be He, (They said: What was your condition?) occupy the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the angels, and (qad) with it is presumed according to the well-known view. To make it a circumstantial clause from the object pronoun with (qad) presumed at the beginning and (lahum) at the end is remote. Or (the clause "They said...") is the predicate, and its connecting element is omitted, that is, (lahum, for them). The sentence introduced by the fa' is conjoined to it, derived from it and from what is in its predicate. It is not correct to make any of the second and third (utterances of "they said") a predicate, because it is an answer and a rejoinder. Whoever says that if (qala, they said) were made a second predicate there would be no need to presume a connecting element has erred. It has also been said that the predicate is omitted, its estimate being "they perished" or something similar. (Tuhajiru, you emigrate) is in the accusative as the answer to the interrogative. God's words, Most High: (And evil is the destination) follow the pattern of (ni'ma, bi'sa), that is, (bi'sat masiran, evil is the destination), and the entity praised or blamed is implied, that is, "their destination" or "Jahannam."

Some scholars have used the verse as evidence for the obligation to emigrate from a place where a man cannot establish his religion. This is the position of Imam Malik. Ibn al-Arabi reported that emigration is also obligatory from plague-stricken lands. In the book Al-Nasikh wa al-Mansukh (on naskh, abrogation), it is stated that emigration was an obligation in the early period of Islam, then it was abrogated (naskh), and its recommendation remained.

Al-Tha'labi reported from the hadith of al-Hasan, as a mursal (a report lacking the Companion): "Whoever flees with his religion from one land to another land, even if it is a span of land, Paradise becomes due for him, and he will be the companion of his father Ibrahim and of his Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ)."

We have already presented to you what benefits you here, so remember.

[Page 127]

﴿Except the oppressed﴾ is a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*, an exception not belonging to the same category as what precedes it), because the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*, "those who") and its pronouns, and the demonstrative "those" (*ulaika*) referring to it, apply to "those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves." So the oppressed mentioned here are not included among them. It was also said that it is a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*), with the excepted-from being ﴿their refuge is Hell﴾, but this is not correct. That is: except those who were unable to emigrate and were weak, ﴿among the men﴾ such as Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, Salamah ibn Hisham, and al-Walid ibn al-Walid, ﴿and the women﴾ such as Umm al-Fadl Lubabah bint al-Harith, the mother of Abdullah ibn Abbas, and others, ﴿and the children﴾ such as the Abdullah mentioned, and others, may Allah be pleased with them. The prepositional phrase ("from these") is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *al-mustad'afin*, or from the implicit pronoun within it, meaning: being among these. The mention of children serves to emphasize the strictness of the obligation of emigration and the command to undertake it, to the point that it is as if it were something children are also obligated to do. Or it may be said that their being obligated means the obligation of their guardians to bring them out of the lands of disbelief, and that by "children" are meant those approaching puberty, or those whose childhood is recent, used metaphorically as in the case of orphans (*al-yatama*). Or the intended meaning is to equate these groups in being free from sin and obligation, or that their incapacity should be like the incapacity of children. Or the intended ones are slaves and female slaves.

﴿They cannot devise a plan﴾ means: they do not find the means and beginnings of emigration. ﴿Nor are they guided to a way﴾ means: nor do they know the route to the place to which one emigrates, either by themselves or by a guide. This clause is a description (*sifah*) of what follows "from" (*min*), or of *al-mustad'afin*, because the intended meaning is the category, whether the *alif-lam* is a relative pronoun or the definite article; in meaning it is like an indefinite noun. Or it is a circumstantial clause from it, or from the implicit pronoun within it. It is also permitted that it be a resumed sentence (*mustaʾnafah*) explaining the meaning of weakness intended here.

Then (as for) "those" — i.e., the oppressed (mustad'afun) — ﴿It may be that Allah will pardon them﴾. In this there is an indication (iidhan) that abandoning emigration (hijrah) is a grave matter, to the extent that the one compelled who has been established as not obligated to it should nonetheless regard leaving it as a sin, not feel secure, watch for the opportunity, and attach his heart to it.

﴿And Allah is ever Pardoning, Forgiving﴾ — a concluding statement (tadhyil) that confirms what came before in the most complete manner.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 100 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And whoever emigrates in the cause of Allah will find in the earth many a place of refuge and abundance.﴾ This is an encouragement to emigration (hijrah) and a consolation for it. By *muraghaman* (a place of escape, or a place of humbling the enemy) is meant the place to which one moves and emigrates, as this was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Qatadah and others. It is thus a noun of place, and it was expressed in this way to emphasise the encouragement, because it implies that the place to which the emigrant moves is one that becomes a cause for the humbling of the noses of the people he left. From Mujahid: the meaning is that he will find in it someone who has moved away from what he dislikes. It was also said: a wide space, relative to the narrowness he suffered from the polytheists. It was also said: a path by whose travel he humbles his people, i.e., he separates from them in spite of their noses (in defiance of them). *Al-raghm* is humiliation and disgrace, and its origin is the sticking of the nose to *al-righam*, which is dust. It was read as *murghaman* (with a different vowelling). ﴿And abundance﴾, i.e., of provision, and this is the view of the majority; from Malik: abundance of lands.

﴿And whoever leaves his house as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger, then death overtakes him﴾: i.e., death descends upon him before he reaches the destination and lays down the saddle of travel. Even if that happens outside his door, as the choice of the phrase "leaving his house" over "emigrating" suggests. The *thumma* (then) does not preclude this, as you will come to know shortly, Allah willing. The clause is coordinated with the conditional verb (*fi'l al-shart*). It was also read as *yudrikuhu* with *raf'* (nominative vowelling). Ibn Jinni (d. 392 AH) explained it, as al-Samin said, as a present verb in the nominative because it is free of any governing or jussive particle, with *al-mawt* (death) as its subject, and the clause as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "then he, death overtakes him." In this case the nominal clause is coordinated with the conditional verbal clause. Yunus (al-Akhfash?) interpreted on this basis the verse of al-A'sha:

*In tarkabu fa-rukubu al-khayli 'adatuna*
*aw tanzilun fa-inna ma'sharun nuzulu*

Meaning: "If you ride, riding horses is our custom; or if you dismount, we are a people who dismount." That is, "or you yourselves dismount." The nominal clause in that case, as some verifiers said, is in a place of *jazm* (apocopation), even though it cannot validly occur as a conditional, because they are lenient with the following element. They only posited the omitted subject so that its *raf'* (nominative) could be correct alongside coordination with the imperfect conditional.

Isam al-Milla said: It should be known that on the assumption of an omitted subject, *man* must be taken as a relative pronoun, because a conditional cannot be a nominal clause, and *yakhruj* would also be nominative. It would then follow that there is no need to posit an omitted subject. So it is better that the *raf'* is based on the assumption of the nominative of *yakhruj*, since the context is one of the places where the relative is expected. It is not hidden that this is confusion and heedlessness regarding what they mentioned.

It was also said: the *damma* on the *kaf* is transferred from the *ha'* (the pronominal suffix), as if he intended to pause on it, then moved its vowel to the *kaf*, as in the saying:

*'ajibtu wa-al-dahru kathirun 'ajabuhu*
*min 'anzi yasubbuni lam adribuhu*

Meaning: "I was amazed, and time is full of its wonders, at a goat that insults me; I did not strike it."

This, as in *al-Kashf*, is very weak, because it treats the connected reading as the pause, and also the transfer, then the vowelling of the *ha'* after transfer with *damma*, and treating the attached pronoun as part of the word. The verse has only the transfer and the treatment of the pronoun as part of the word.

al-Hasan read *yudrikahu* with *nasb* (accusative), and many explained it as being with an implied *an* (that), similar to what Sibawayh cited:

*sa-atruku manzili libani Tamimin*
*wa-alhaqu bi-al-Hijazi fa-astarihа*

Meaning: "I will leave my dwelling for the Banu Tamim, and I will join the Hijaz, and rest." Its aspect in this is that *sa-atruku* is a future that is desired, so it functions like an imperative and the like. The verse, because its intended purpose is urging departure, and the conditional, which bears a strong resemblance to a non-affirmative (*ghayr al-mujab*), precedes, is stronger than the verse of poetry.

Some verifiers mentioned that the *nasb* in the verse was permitted by the Kufans, because the verb falling between the conditional and the answer may take *raf'*, *nasb* and *jazm* in their view when it comes after *wa* or *fa*, as in the saying:

*wa-man la yuqaddim rijlahu mutma'innatan*
*fa-yuthbitaha fi mustawa al-qa'i yazlaqi*

They analogised on these two there, but what is mentioned in the verse is not the same as the verse. It was also said: it is coordination of a supposed verbal noun (*masdar mutawahham*) on a supposed verbal noun, like "Honour me and I will honour you," i.e., let there be honouring from you and from me. The meaning is: whoever has departure from his house and death overtakes him.

﴿Then his reward has fallen upon Allah﴾, i.e., it became obligatory by the requirement of His promise and bounty. This is the answer to the conditional. In the juxtaposition of this conditional with the previous conditional there is an indication that the emigrant has one of the two good outcomes: either he humbles the noses of the enemies of Allah and abases them by his separation from them and his connection with good and abundance; or death overtakes him and he reaches true happiness and everlasting bliss.

In the verse there is what is not hidden of exaggeration in encouragement. It was said: the apparent expectation would have been "Whoever emigrates to Allah and His Messenger and dies, He will reward him," but "Whoever leaves his house as an emigrant" was chosen over "Whoever emigrates," for the reason we pointed out just now. The placement of "death overtakes him" in the place of "dies" is an indication of greater pleasure from Allah the Exalted, and that death is like a gift from Him, glorified is He, to him, because it is a cause of arriving at lasting bliss, which is not attained except through death. *Thumma* (then) was used in place of *wa* (and) to complete this subtlety, and that the rank of departure is below this rank. The phrase ﴿then his reward has fallen upon Allah﴾ was put in the place of "He will reward him," because it indicates necessity and permanence, and because the reward is great, its measure cannot be estimated nor its essence grasped, since it is from the Most Holy Essence named by that all-encompassing name.

From al-Zamakhshari: the benefit of "then death overtakes him" is to explain that the reward is only established if death does not nullify the deed.

It was disputed about who the verse was revealed concerning. Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) narrated from Ibn Jubayr that it was revealed concerning Jundub ibn Damrah. He had heard the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves...﴾ (4:97), the verse, while he was in Mecca, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent it to its Muslims. He said to his sons: "Carry me, for I am not one of the oppressed, and indeed I am guided to the path, and indeed I will not spend the night in Mecca." They carried him on a litter facing Medina, and he was a very old man. He died at al-Tan'im. When death overtook him he began to clap his right hand onto his left and say: "O Allah, this is for You and this is for Your Messenger (ﷺ); I pledge allegiance to You on what Your Messenger (ﷺ) pledged allegiance on." When news of his death reached the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, they said: "Would that he had died in Medina." So the verse was revealed.

al-Sha'bi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it was revealed concerning Aktham ibn Sayfi, when he embraced Islam and died while being an emigrant.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated, by way of Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father al-Zubayr, that it was revealed concerning Khalid ibn Hizam, who had emigrated to Abyssinia, and a snake bit him on the road and he died.

Other than these has been narrated. In any case, the intended meaning is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion. Many have also mentioned that whoever travels for a matter in which there is reward, such as seeking knowledge, pilgrimage, earning lawful income, or visiting a righteous and truthful person, and dies before reaching the destination, his ruling is the same.

Abu Ya'la and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever sets out for pilgrimage and dies, there is written for him the reward of the pilgrim until the Day of Resurrection; whoever sets out for 'umrah and dies, there is written for him the reward of the one performing 'umrah until the Day of Resurrection; and whoever sets out as a warrior in the way of Allah the Exalted and dies, there is written for him the reward of the warrior until the Day of Resurrection."

The people of Medina used the verse as evidence that if a warrior dies on the road, his share of the spoils becomes due. The correct view is that only the otherworldly reward is established.

﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving﴾, exceeding in forgiveness, so He forgives him what he neglected of sins, among which is sitting back from emigration until the time of departure. ﴿Merciful﴾, exceeding in mercy, so He, glorified is He, shows him mercy by completing the reward of his emigration and his intention.

* * *

From the way of allusion (*al-isharah*) in some of the verses previously mentioned: ﴿It is not for a believer﴾, i.e., it is not fitting for a believer of the spirit (*min al-ruh*) ﴿to kill a believer﴾, who is a believer of the heart, except by error. That only happens when the spirit is freed from the veils of human attributes. When it wishes to turn the lights of the soul towards the self in order to kill it, its manifestation falls upon the heart, and it falls unconscious from that manifestation, and the mountain of the self is crumbled to dust. So its killing is by error, because it was not intended. ﴿And whoever kills﴾ a heart ﴿a believer﴾ by error ﴿then [the freeing of] a believing slave﴾, which is the slave of the innermost spiritual secret, and its freeing is its release from the bondage of created things. ﴿And a compensation (diyah) delivered to his family﴾: the blood-money is delivered by the 'aqilah (the paternal kin who pay), which is the divine subtleties (al-alutaf al-ilahiyyah), to the spiritual powers, so each of the two has a share of the divine morals. ﴿Unless they forgo it (yassaddaquu)﴾, and that is at the time of their annihilation (fana') in Allah the Exalted. ﴿If he was﴾ the one killed by manifestation ﴿from a people hostile to you﴾, in that he was from the powers of the commanding self (al-nafs al-ammarah) ﴿and he was a believer, then [the freeing of] a believing slave﴾, which is the slave of the heart, so it frees him from the bonds of the slavery of love of this world and inclination toward it. There is no blood-money in this case for the family of the slain. ﴿And if he was from a people between you and them is a covenant﴾, in that he was from the powers of the self that are receptive to the legal rulings outwardly and to the truce with the heart, ﴿then a compensation delivered﴾, obligatory upon the 'aqilah of mercy, ﴿to his family﴾, i.e., the family of that self from the other attributes, ﴿and [the freeing of] a believing slave﴾, which is the slave of the spirit, and its freeing is its annihilation and release from all the restrictions. ﴿So whoever does not find﴾ such a slave, in that his spirit was previously freed, ﴿then fasting two consecutive months﴾, i.e., upon him is abstaining from habitual things and leaving off what is customary for sixty days, which is the measure of the Mosaic appointed time (al-miqat al-musawi), and half of it, in hope that subsistence after annihilation will be attained for him.

﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell﴾: an indication that when the self kills the heart and dominates it, it remains tormented by the fires of nature, distanced from mercy, a manifestation of the wrath of Allah the Exalted. ﴿O you who have believed, when you travel in the cause of Allah﴾ to guide His servants, ﴿investigate﴾ the state of the seeker in rejection and acceptance. ﴿And do not say to one who gives you [the sign of] peace, "You are not a believer," seeking the goods of worldly life﴾, i.e., do not repel the one who has surrendered to you and submitted his self into your hands so that you may guide him, lest you say to him, "You are not a sincere believer because your heart is attached to this world; so hand over what you have of its trash, so that your heart may be empty for your Lord and fit to travel the path." ﴿For with Allah are many spoils﴾ for those journeying to Him. When the traveller attains them, he leaves for them what is in his hand of this world, and his heart turns away from that. ﴿Thus were you before, and Allah conferred favour upon you, so investigate﴾, i.e., like this seeker you were at the beginnings of your seeking and surrendering your selves to the shaykhs, when you had an attachment to the world. ﴿Then Allah conferred favour upon you﴾ after your journeying with those many spoils that He has, so He made you forget all that was in your hands, and weaned your hearts from the world entirely. So measure the state of one who surrenders his self to you by your state, so that you know that Allah, glorified is He, by the requirement of what He has accustomed those who turn to Him and seek Him, will bestow upon these the same favour He bestowed upon you, and will remove the love of this world from their hearts in the best manner, as He removed it from your hearts.

The summary is that it should not be said to one of the people of this world who wishes to turn toward the Truth, exalted is He, at the beginning of the matter: "Leave your worldly life and set out on the path." For that would repel him and close the door of turning toward Him upon him, because of the severity of abandoning what he loves all at once. Rather, he is commanded to set out on the path and is charged with deeds that remove that love from his heart, but gradually. ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾ means that they withhold the self from its rights, which its preparedness (istidad) requires, from the words deposited within it. ﴿They will say, "In what were you engaged?"﴾ That is, why did you sit back from striving, neglect the side of God, Exalted, and fall short of reaching the perfection to which you were called? ﴿They will say, "We were oppressed in the land."﴾ That is, the land of preparedness, through the domination of the powers of the commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammarah) and the overwhelming authority of desire and the devil of illusion (wahm). They say, ﴿Was not the earth of Allah spacious enough for you to emigrate therein?﴾ That is: was not the breadth of your preparedness such that you could have emigrated within it, from the beginning of your natural disposition (fitrah) to the end of your perfection? That is a vast field. So if you had moved and traveled by the light of your natural disposition, even small steps, such that some of the veils were lifted from you, you would have been freed from the captivity of the powers, and delivered from the bonds of desire, and gone out from the town whose people are wrongdoers, which is the Mecca of the commanding soul, to the good city, which is the city of the heart. The reason that Glorified and Exalted He attributed the taking in death here to the angels is that taking in death, which is the complete extraction of the spirit from the body by seizing it from the body, occurs in three ways: the taking of the angels, the taking of the Angel of Death, and the taking of Allah, Exalted. As for the taking of the angels, it is for the people of the souls, who are either happy or wretched. As for the taking of the Angel of Death, it is for the people of hearts who have emerged from the veil of the soul to the station of the heart. As for the taking of Allah, Exalted, it is for the monotheists (muwahhidun) who have been raised beyond the station of the heart to the place of witnessing (shuhud). So there remains no veil between them and their Lord, and He, Glorified, takes their spirits Himself and gathers them to Himself, Mighty and Majestic. Since the wrongdoers were not of either of the last two categories, He, Glorified, attributed their taking to the angels and restricted it to the state of their wronging themselves. ﴿Then their refuge will be Hell﴾ which is the nature (al-tabi'ah), ﴿and evil is it as a destination﴾, because the fire of distance and veiling is kindled therein. ﴿Except for the oppressed among men﴾ who are, as some of the knowers (arifin) said, those of strong preparedness, whose appetitive and irascible powers are strong together with the strength of their preparedness, so they were not able to subdue them in the course of the path of truth, and they did not submit to their imaginative and estimative powers, so their preparedness is nullified by corrupt beliefs under the captivity of their bodily powers, despite the kindling of their preparedness with the light of knowledge, and their inability to travel the path by removing the bonds. ﴿And the women﴾ that is, those deficient in preparedness to attain scientific perfection and to travel the path of realization, weak in powers. It has been said they are the simpletons (bulh) mentioned in the report: "Most of the people of Paradise are the simpletons." ﴿And the children﴾ that is, those who fall short of reaching the degree of perfection because of a period that overtakes them from the qualities of the soul. ﴿Who are unable to devise a plan﴾ because of their lack of ability and their inability to break the soul and subdue desire. ﴿Nor are they guided to a way﴾ because they do not know how to travel. ﴿For those, it is expected that Allah will pardon them﴾ by erasing those dark conditions, because they have not become firmly established and their beliefs are sound. ﴿And ever is Allah Pardoning﴾ of sins so long as the natural disposition is not altered, ﴿Forgiving﴾, who covers by the light of His purity the qualities of souls that are receptive to that. ﴿And whoever emigrates in the way of Allah﴾ from the familiar dwelling places of the soul ﴿will find on the earth many forsaken places﴾ that is, the earth of his preparedness, ﴿and abundance﴾ that is, expansion of the breast, due to deliverance from the straits of the qualities of the soul and the captivity of desire. ﴿And whoever leaves his home emigrating to Allah﴾ that is, his station in which he is, ﴿and His Messenger﴾ by turning toward the affirmation of the Essence's oneness, and by turning toward seeking uprightness in the oneness of the Attributes, ﴿then death overtakes him﴾ that is, cessation, ﴿his reward has already become due from Allah﴾ according to what he turned toward. ﴿And ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾, so He covers with His attributes the attributes of the one who turned toward Him, and shows mercy to the one who ceased before reaching, by what he deserves. And Allah, Exalted, is the Guide to the straight path.

[p. 131]

Then, after He had commanded jihad and encouraged emigration (hijrah), He followed that with an explanation of how to pray in situations of necessity, a lightening of the burden that reinforces resolve in that matter. So He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And when you travel through the land﴾ — meaning, you journey on whatever journey it may be. For this reason it was not restricted by the conditions that were attached to hijrah. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, restricts travel to the permissible (mubah), such as trade travel, and to acts of obedience, such as travel for Hajj, and excludes travel of disobedience, such as highway robbery and running away (ibaq), so the ruling that follows does not apply to it, because it is a concession (rukhsah), and concessions are established only as a lightening, and what is of this nature is not connected to what necessitates strictness, because attaching a ruling to an attribute that implies its opposite is a flaw in the formulation (fasad fi al-wad'). Our (Hanafi) argument is the unrestricted wording of the texts, together with an indication in some of them that points to the intended unrestricted sense, and the addition of the condition of not being in disobedience has been abrogated (nusikh), as is known in its proper place. Also, travel itself is not an act of disobedience, since it is a term for a lengthy departure, and there is nothing of disobedience in this. Disobedience is rather what occurs after it, as in theft, or what accompanies it, as in running away. Thus, in its essence, travel is a fitting subject of the concession, and it is not the place of the disengagement from what accompanies it. This is like when one usurps a leather sock and wears it: it is permissible for him to wipe over it, because what is required is the covering of the foot, and there is no prohibition in that; the prohibition lies in what accompanies it, which is the attribute of its being usurped. Its full treatment is in the books of usul (legal theory).

The word "land" (al-ard) here includes both land and sea, and the intention is generality: when you travel in any place in which travel takes place, whether by land or by sea. ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾ — that is, no hardship or sin — ﴿in shortening﴾ — that is, in that you shorten (an-taqsuru). Qasr is the opposite of madd (extension). It is said: "qassartu al-shay'" when you make a thing short by removing some of its parts or attributes. The object of qasr is therefore the thing itself, not a part of it, since a part is the object of removal (hadhf), not of qasr. Accordingly, His words ﴿from the prayer﴾ should, on this basis, be an object of (taqsuru), with (min) being extra (za'idah), as Abu al-Baqa' relayed from al-Akhfash, who held that it may be extra in affirmative sentences. As for taking it to be partitive (tab'idiyyah), with the object omitted and the prepositional phrase in the position of a qualifier — as the aforementioned scholar relayed from Sibawayh — meaning "some of the prayer," then the part must be described with the attribute of the whole. Alternatively, qasr may be taken to mean confinement (habs), as in His words ﴿Restrained (maqsuratun) in pavilions﴾. Or "prayer" may be taken as a genus, so that the intended object is a portion of it, namely the four-rak'ah prayers, meaning: there is no blame upon you in shortening some of the prayer by halving it. It is also read as (tuqsiru) from aqsara, whose verbal noun is al-iqsar. Al-Zuhri read (tuqassiru) with doubling, whose verbal noun is al-taqsir. All of these have the same meaning.

The shortest duration of travel to which shortening applies, according to what is well known from Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, is three days and nights at the pace of camels and walking on foot at a moderate speed on land, and the sailing of a ship in the sea when the wind is moderate. In mountainous terrain, this distance is also measured by the average pace along the mountain path. In a narration from him, may Allah be pleased with him, the measure is given in stages (marahil), which is close to the well-known opinion.

Abu Yusuf set it at two days and most of a third day. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, in one opinion set it at one day and night. Most of the shaykhs measured it in farsakhs, then they differed: some said twenty-one farsakhs, others said eighteen, and others fifteen. The correct view is that it is not to be measured at all. Probably everyone who set a measure among those mentioned believed that it equals three days and nights of travel. The evidence for this duration is what is authentically established from the saying of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: "The resident wipes for a full day and night, and the traveller for three days and nights." Because the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, generalized the concession to the category, and its necessary consequence is the generality of the measure. The view that three days is a time-frame (zarf) for the traveller and not for (yamsahu) is refuted by the fact that the context serves only to explain the quantity of the traveller's wiping, not to state it absolutely. And if it were a time-frame for the traveller, then (yumsah) would be unrestricted and not the intended point. Also, this view is invalidated by the fact that the resident would wipe for a day and night, which would imply that the rulings of travel and residence coincide in some cases, namely the case of a traveller of one day and night, since he would then wipe for one day and night; this is clearly invalid, since the Shari'ah is known to distinguish between traveller and resident. Furthermore, the time-frame of (three) for the traveller requires the time-frame of the day for the resident, so that the two parts of the hadith correspond. In that case, it would hardly be attributed to the most eloquent of those who spoke Arabic, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. Some have cited for shortening in less than three days what is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "O people of Makkah, do not shorten (the prayer) for a distance less than four barids from Makkah to 'Usfan." This indicates shortening for four barids, which are covered in less than three days. It is answered that the narrator of this hadith is 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn Mujahid, who is extremely weak according to the transmitters, to the point that Sufyan used to accuse him of lying. So let this be understood.

Imam al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, argued from the apparent wording of the noble verse that shortening is not obligatory and that completing (the prayer) is preferable. This is supported by what Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bazzar and al-Daraqutni narrated from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that "the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, used to shorten in travel and also complete." And by what al-Nasa'i and al-Daraqutni (who graded it good) and al-Bayhaqi (who graded it sound) narrated: that 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, "when she performed 'umrah with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: O Messenger of Allah, I shortened and completed, and I fasted and broke the fast. He said: You did well, O 'A'ishah." And by what is narrated from 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, that "he used to complete and shorten."

According to us, shortening is obligatory without doubt, except that some of our shaykhs called it a firm obligation ('azimah), and some called it a concession of dropping (rukhsat isqat), in the sense that there is no room for completing, not a concession of choice (rukhsat tawfiyah), since there is no meaning in offering a choice between the lighter and the heavier. This is the view of 'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jabir, and all the People of the House (ahl al-bayt), may Allah be pleased with them all. It was also the view of al-Hasan, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-‘Aziz, Qatadah, and it is the view of Malik.

al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The prayer of travel is two rak'ahs, complete and not shortened, according to the tongue of your Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace."

al-Shaykhan narrated from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "The first prayer that Allah prescribed was two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs; then it was confirmed for travel and increased for residence." As for what is narrated from her about completing, she excused herself from it, saying: "I am the Mother of the Believers; wherever I dwell, that is my home," just as 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, excused his completing by saying that he had married in Makkah and resolved to reside there, as narrated from al-Zuhri. So it is not objected that she, may Allah be pleased with her, acted against her own narration, since if a narrator acts against his narration in a matter, his narration is not to be acted upon in that matter. The claim that her hadith is not marfu' (traced to the Prophet) because she did not witness the prescription of prayer is not accepted, since it is possible that she heard it from the Prophet, peace be upon him. Yes, some of the Shafi'is mentioned that the report should be interpreted as meaning that "prescribed" in her words "it was prescribed as two rak'ahs" carries the sense of "explained," and this sense has come in such usage as ﴿Allah has ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾.

al-Tabari said: its meaning is that it was prescribed for whoever among the travellers chose it, and this is like what is said of the pilgrim: that he has the option to leave on the second or third day, and whichever he does, he has fulfilled the obligation and it is correct.

al-Nawawi said: the meaning is that it was prescribed as two rak'ahs for one who wishes to limit himself to them; then two rak'ahs were added in residence as a binding requirement, while the prayer of travel remained permissible to complete. Where the evidences for completion are established, it becomes necessary to turn to that, in order to reconcile the evidences.

Ibn Hajar, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What appears to me in reconciling the evidences is that the prayer was prescribed on the night of the Isra' as two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs, except for the maghrib; then it was increased after the Hijrah, except for the Subh, as narrated by Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban and al-Bayhaqi from 'A'ishah, and in it: "the Fajr was left as it was for its lengthy recitation, and the Maghrib because it is the witr of the day." Then, after the four-rak'ah prayers became fixed, it was lightened for travel at the revelation of the verse. This is supported by the statement of Ibn al-Athir that shortening was in the fourth year after the Hijrah, which is derived from another's saying that the revelation of the verse of fear was in it. It has also been said that shortening was in Rabi' al-Akhir of the second year, as mentioned by al-Dulabi, and al-Suhayli said it was a year or so after the Hijrah, and it has been said it was forty days after the Hijrah. On this basis, the words of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, "the prayer of travel was confirmed," mean in terms of what the matter ultimately became of lightening, not that it continued from the time it was prescribed. Therefore it does not follow from this that shortening is a firm obligation. End of quote.

This combination was judged unlikely, because if the prayer had been two rak'ahs before the Hijrah, that would have been well known. Others among them said: the verse is explicit in denying the obligation of completing, and what was mentioned is a single report (khabar wahid), which does not oppose an explicit text. Moreover, it is specific to other than Fajr and Maghrib, and the authority of a general text that has been specified is disputed. Our scholars mentioned that the abundance of reports, and the practice of a great multitude of the Companions, the Successors, and the whole 'Itrah (family of the Prophet), may Allah be pleased with them all, strengthen the view of obligation. The wording of the verse with the removal of blame is because they were accustomed to completing, so they were likely to think that there was a deficiency upon them in shortening. Therefore it explicitly removed blame from them so that their hearts would be at ease and reassured by it, as in His words: ﴿Whoever performs Hajj to the House or makes 'umrah, there is no blame upon him in going around between them﴾, although that circumambulation is obligatory according to us, and a pillar (rukn) according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. It is reported from Abu Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, that he recited this verse to one who considered the obligation unlikely because of the removal of blame.

﴿If you fear that those who disbelieve will afflict you﴾ — its answer (jawab) is omitted, being indicated by what precedes it. That is: if you fear that they will confront you with what you dislike, of fighting or otherwise, ﴿then there is no blame upon you﴾, etc. Some have taken the apparent sense of this condition and restricted shortening to the situation of fear.

Ibn Jarir narrated from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her... but what the imams hold is that shortening is also legislated in security, and reports to this effect are abundant. al-Nasa'i and al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "We prayed with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, between Makkah and Madinah while we were secure, fearing nothing, two rak'ahs."

al-Shaykhan and others from the authors of the Sunan narrated from Haritha ibn Wahb al-Khuza'i that he said: "I prayed with the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, the Dhuhr and the 'Asr at Mina, when the people were most numerous and most secure, two rak'ahs," and so on.

It should not be imagined that this contradicts the Book, because restriction by a condition, according to us, only indicates the establishment of the ruling when the condition exists. As for its absence when the condition is absent, it is silent about it; if evidence for that is found, the ruling is established there too, and otherwise it remains as it is, because the evidence for it is not established, not because the evidence for its absence is established.

Moreover, consider what you have heard of the clear proofs. As for those who hold the doctrine of the mafhum (implicit meaning), the reason is that it only indicates the negation of the ruling when the condition is absent if there is no other benefit in it; and here the condition has come out in the manner of what is most common, as has been said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you fear that they may twist (your words) ... there is no blame upon them for what she ransoms herself with﴾. Rather, it is said that the noble verse is general (mujmal) regarding the extent and manner of the shortening, regarding what is connected to it of the prayers, and regarding the length of the travelling that the shortening was tied to. So whatever came from the Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, of shortening in a state of security, and restricting it to the four-rak'a prayers by way of halving, and to travelling for the specified duration, is an explanation of the generality of the Book, as the Shaykh al-Islam (Shaykh al-Islam) has said.

Some of them said: the shortening in the verse is to be understood as shortening of the states (conditions): by gesturing (in prayer), lightening the glorification (tasbih), and facing in whatever direction one can. In that case the condition remains on the apparent sense of its implied meaning that comes readily to minds. This is attributed to Tawus and al-Dahhak.

Ibn Jarir related, from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said concerning the verse: "The shortening of the prayer, if you meet the enemy and the time has come, is that you glorify God and lower your head in gesture, riding or walking." It was also said that His saying, exalted is He, "if you fear..." and so on, is connected to what follows it concerning the prayer of fear, and is separate from what precedes it.

Ibn Jarir related from 'Ali, may God ennoble his face, who said: "A people of the merchants asked the Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, and they said: 'O Messenger of God, we travel in the land, so how should we pray?' So God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And when you travel in the land, there is no blame upon you that you shorten the prayer﴾. Then the revelation ceased. Then, after a year, the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, went on a campaign and prayed the midday prayer, and the polytheists said: 'Muhammad and his companions have had their backs exposed to you; why did you not press upon them?' One of them said: 'Indeed they have another prayer after it, which is like it.' So God revealed between the two prayers: ﴿If you fear that those who disbelieve will attack you﴾ up to His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Indeed God has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾, and the prayer of fear was revealed."

Perhaps the answer of the condition in this case is also omitted, in the manner mentioned before. Al-Tabarsi related from some of them that the shortening in the verse means combining the two prayers, but this is not a thing at all. Ubayy recited, as Ibn al-Mundhir said: "So shorten from the prayer, lest they tempt you," and it is well known that, like 'Abd Allah, he dropped only "if you fear."

In any case, "that they may tempt you" (an yaftinakum) is in the position of an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), by means of an implied genitive: as if it was said, "That was legislated for you out of dislike that they might tempt you," for the continuation of occupation with the prayer is a likely cause for the disbelievers' ability to bring about temptation.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed the disbelievers have been to you an open enemy﴾ is either a reason for that with regard to its being motivated by what was mentioned, or a reason for what is understood from the speech, namely that their temptation is expected, for complete enmity is among the things that necessitate attacking with harm. And "enemy" (ʿaduwwan), as Abu al-Baqa' said, is in the position of "enemies" (aʿdaʾ). It was also said that it is a verbal noun on the pattern fa'ul, like al-walul and al-qabul, and "to you" (lakum) is either a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of it or is connected to "was" (kana).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 102 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when you are among them﴾ is an explanation of what precedes it, namely the general text on the legitimacy of shortening (qasr) the prayer, by way of a derivation (tafri'), and a depiction of how it is to be performed in cases of complete necessity. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ by way of abstraction (tajrid). Those who restricted the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf) to his presence, peace and blessings be upon him, have clung to its outward meaning, such as al-Hasan ibn Zayd. This is also attributed to Abu Yusuf, and al-Jassas transmitted it in his book Ahkam al-Qur'an, and al-Nawawi in al-Muhadhdhab. But the majority of jurists hold otherwise, for the imams after him, peace and blessings be upon him, are his deputies and those who carry on what he used to do, so the ruling of the address directed to him includes them, as in the saying of God Most High: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾.

Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban and others narrated, on the authority of Tha'labah ibn Zahdam, who said: "We were with Sa'id ibn al-'As in Tabaristan, and he said: 'Which of you prayed the prayer of fear with the Messenger of God ﷺ?' Hudhayfah said: 'I did.' Then he described it to him, and they prayed as he described, and they did not make it up. This took place in the presence of the Companions, may God be pleased with them, and none of them denied it, and they are those who 'do not fear the blame of any blamer in the cause of God Most High.'" This stands in the place of consensus (ijma'), and it also refutes what al-Muzani claimed of abrogation (naskh).

﴿So when you establish the prayer for them﴾, i.e., you intend to lead them in the prayer, ﴿let a party of them stand with you﴾ after you have divided them into two groups, ﴿and let the other party stand before the enemy for guard duty.﴾

Because it is evident, the phrase ﴿and let them take﴾ has been omitted, i.e., the party mentioned that stands with you should take their weapons, those that do not hinder prayer, such as the sword and the dagger.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the one who takes (the weapons) is the party on guard, so there is then no need for the restriction, except that this is contrary to the apparent meaning. The meaning of "taking" is not putting down, and it has been expressed in this way to signal concern for keeping the weapons with oneself, as though they were taking them from the outset. ﴿Then when they have prostrated﴾, i.e., those standing with you, that is, when they have finished the prostration and completed the rak'ah, as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. ﴿Then let them go behind you﴾, i.e., let them withdraw to guard against the enemy.

﴿And let another party come who have not prayed﴾ yet, and they are the ones who were on guard. He indefinitely referred to them (nakkaraha) because they had not been mentioned before. ﴿Let them pray with you﴾ the remaining rak'ah of your prayer. The feminine and masculine forms are used in accordance with the wording and the meaning. The noble verse does not specify the status of the remaining rak'ah for each of the two parties, but this has been explained by the Sunnah.

Al-Shaykhan, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and others narrated, on the authority of Salim, from his father, regarding His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So when you establish the prayer for them﴾, that it is the prayer of fear: the Messenger of God ﷺ prayed with one of the two parties one rak'ah, while the other party was facing the enemy. Then the party that prayed with the Prophet ﷺ departed and took the place of those (on guard), facing the enemy, and the other party, which had been facing the enemy, came forward, and the Messenger of God ﷺ prayed with them another rak'ah, then he gave them the salam. Then each party stood and prayed one rak'ah each. Thus the Messenger of God ﷺ had two rak'ahs, and each of the two parties had two rak'ahs: one rak'ah with the Messenger of God ﷺ and one rak'ah after his salam.

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud: "When the Prophet ﷺ prayed the prayer of fear, he prayed with the first party one rak'ah, and with the second party one rak'ah, as in the verse. Then the first party came and went to face the enemy, until the first party completed the second rak'ah without recitation, and they gave the salam. Then the other party came and completed the first rak'ah with recitation, until each party had two rak'ahs."

This is what Imam Abu Hanifah, may God be pleased with him, held.
