The recitation was dropped from the first party in their second rak'ah after the salam of the Messenger of God ﷺ because they, although during his second rak'ah, peace and blessings be upon him, were facing the enemy, were nonetheless in the prayer and in the status of following (muta'abah), so the recitation of the imam stood in place of their recitation, as is the rule of following (iqtida'). This is not the case with the other party, because they followed the imam in the second rak'ah, and the imam completed his prayer, so they had to recite in their second rak'ah, since they were not following the imam at that time.

Some held that the prayer of fear described in the verse is one rak'ah, and this is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas and others.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Nahhas narrated from him, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "God Most High prescribed through the tongue of your Prophet ﷺ four rak'ahs in residence, two rak'ahs in travel, and one rak'ah in fear."

The first two, along with Ibn Abi Hatim, narrated on the authority of Yazid al-Faqir, who said: "I asked Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah about the two rak'ahs in travel: are they shortened? He said: 'The two rak'ahs in travel are complete; the shortening is only one rak'ah at the time of fighting. While we were with the Messenger of God ﷺ in a battle, the prayer was called, and the Messenger of God ﷺ stood, and one party lined up, and another party with their faces towards the enemy. He prayed with them one rak'ah and prostrated with them two prostrations. Then they went to those others and stood behind the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he prayed with them one rak'ah and prostrated with them two prostrations. Then the Messenger of God ﷺ sat and gave the salam, and those behind him gave the salam, and the first ones gave the salam. So the Messenger of God ﷺ had two rak'ahs, and the people had one rak'ah each.' Then he recited the verse."

Imam Malik, may God be pleased with him, held that the manner of the prayer of fear is that the imam prays with one party one rak'ah; when he rises for the second, they separate from him and complete their prayer, and go to face the enemy, and the others who were facing the enemy come, and they follow him, and he prays with them the second rak'ah. When he sits for the tashahhud, they stand and complete their second rak'ah, and catch up with him, and he gives them the salam.

This is the prayer of the Prophet ﷺ at Dhat al-Riqa', as narrated by al-Shaykhan, and it is one of the forms that al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, chose, and it was made problematic out of sixteen forms. It is possible to apply the verse to it, and "prostration" would mean the prayer, the meaning being: "When they have finished the prayer, (then let them be) etc." This is supported by the fact that there is no deficiency in the explanation according to it, and that the apparent meaning of His saying, glorified is He: "(let them pray with you)" is that the last party completes the prayer with the imam, and there is no indication in it of guarding them a second time while they are in the prayer at all. The verse may admit, indeed it has been said that it is clearly so, that the imam prays twice, each time with a group, and this is the prayer of the Messenger of God ﷺ as al-Shaykhan also narrated at Batn Nakhl. Its admitting the form that the Messenger of God ﷺ performed at 'Usfan is very far-fetched, because he, peace and blessings be upon him, as Ibn 'Abbas said and as Ahmad, Abu Dawud and others narrated from him: "He arranged the people behind him in two rows, then he bowed and they all bowed, then he prostrated with the row next to him, while the others stood guarding them. When they prostrated and stood, the others sat, and they prostrated in their place. Then these advanced to the positions of those, and those to the positions of these. Then he bowed, peace and blessings be upon him, and they all bowed. Then he raised himself and they raised themselves. Then he prostrated, he and the row next to him, while the others stood guarding them. When they sat, the others sat and prostrated. Then he gave them the salam, then he departed, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace." The complete discussion is to be sought in its proper place.

﴿And let them take﴾, i.e., the other party, ﴿their precaution﴾, i.e., their caution. He likened it to what one protects oneself with of instruments, and therefore attributed the taking to it figuratively (takhyil). Otherwise it is a non-physical matter that cannot be taken. The conjunction of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and their weapons﴾ to it does no harm, since combining the literal and the figurative is permissible; for on the correct view the figurative element lies in the predication and attribution, not in the terms. Something like this is not objectionable in combination, as in the saying of God Most High: ﴿who had settled in the abode and in faith﴾.

Some verifiers said: this and similar cases are a kind of "ishtibah" (correspondence) to what necessarily follows from metonymy (kinayah), namely the explicit mention of both its terms. It may be countered that the likened item is more general than what is mentioned, and if "caution" is explained as that by which one is protected, then there is no objection. Perhaps the increase in the command to take caution, as Shaykh al-Islam said, on this occasion is because it is a likely time for the disbelievers to notice that the party standing with the Prophet ﷺ is occupied with an absorbing task, whereas before it they might think them standing merely with their weapons.

﴿The disbelievers wish that you would neglect your weapons and your belongings, and they would turn upon you in a single attack.﴾ This is an explanation of the reason for which they were commanded to take up arms. The address to both groups is by way of iltifat (shift of address), i.e., they wished to gain an opening against you in your prayer, so that they might charge upon you all at once. By "belongings" is meant what one uses in war, not everything in general. It is read as "amti'atikum" (your goods). The command is for obligation, due to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And there is no blame upon you if you put down your weapons because of rain or because you are ill﴾, where He granted them permission to lay them down when carrying and keeping them became burdensome for them because of rain or illness. After that they were commanded to be vigilant and cautious, so He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And take your precaution﴾, i.e., after laying down the weapons for the excuse, lest the enemy fall upon you unawares.

Some Shafi'i scholars chose that the command is recommended (nadb), and they restricted it to the case where one does not fear a harm that would permit tayammum by leaving off carrying. But if one fears, carrying becomes obligatory according to the more likely view, even if the weapon is impure and prevents prostration. In the commentary on al-Minhaj by the scholar Ibn Hajar: "If the fear of harm is absent and carrying it harms others, it is disliked if the harm is light, such as when it is customarily borne; otherwise it is forbidden." By this the general statement of its being disliked and the general statement of its being forbidden are reconciled.

The verse, as al-Bukhari and others narrated on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, who was wounded.

Abu Damrah mentioned, and al-Kalbi narrated, on the authority of Abu Salih, that "the Messenger of God ﷺ

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, commentary on Surah 4, verse 102 (part 2 of 2):

"He (the Prophet) fought against Muharib and Banu Anmar, and Allah defeated them, and He granted (the Muslims) their women and children and wealth. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Muslims alighted, and they did not see a single enemy. So they laid down their weapons, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out for a need of his, having put down his weapon, until he crossed the valley while the sky was sprinkling rain. The valley came between him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and his companions. He sat in the shade of a samurah tree, and Ghawrath ibn al-Harith al-Muharibi saw him and said: 'May Allah destroy me if I do not kill him!' He descended from the mountain with his sword. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not notice him until he was standing over his head with the sword drawn from its sheath. He said: 'O Muhammad, who will protect you from me now?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Allah, Mighty and Majestic.' Then he said: 'O Allah, suffice me against Ghawrath ibn al-Harith in whatever way You wish.' The enemy of Allah fell on his face, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up and took his sword and said: 'O Ghawrath, who will prevent you from me now?' He said: 'No one.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Do you testify that there is no god but Allah, and that I am the servant and Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'No, but I pledge to you that I will never fight against you, nor will I help any enemy against you.' So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave him back his sword. Ghawrath said to him: 'You are better than me.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'I am more deserving of that.'" Ghawrath returned to his companions, and they said: "O Ghawrath, we saw you standing over his head with the sword; what prevented you from him?" He said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic. I swung the sword at him to strike him, but I do not know who pushed me between my shoulders, so I fell on my face, and my sword fell, and Muhammad, upon whom be prayers and peace, preceded me to it and took it, and he completed the story for them. Some of them believed, and the valley did not stay long before it calmed. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went to his companions and informed them of the news, and he recited the verse to them."

﴿Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾ This is a justification for the command to take precaution, i.e., He has prepared for them a degrading punishment, which is the punishment of being defeated by you and of your victory over them. So attend to your affairs and do not neglect to take the means, so that He may punish them by your hands. It was also said: since the command to be wary of the enemy might suggest their domination and might, He negated that suggestion by promising victory and the humiliation of the enemy, so that the hearts of those addressed would be strengthened, and they would know that taking precaution is itself an act of worship, just as the prohibition against casting oneself into destruction is for this reason, not to prevent engaging in battle. It was also said: it is not far-fetched that the humiliating punishment refers to the legislation of the prayer of fear, in which case ending the verse with it has complete relevance; but its remoteness is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 103:

﴿When you have completed the prayer﴾ meaning: when you have performed the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf) in the manner described and have finished it, ﴿then remember Allah, standing, sitting, and on your sides﴾ meaning: persist in remembering Him, glorified is He, in all circumstances, even during the time of fighting, of engaging in close combat, and of shooting arrows. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that after explaining it he said: "Allah has not excused anyone from abandoning His remembrance except the one whose mind has been overcome." It has also been said: the meaning is: when you intend to perform the prayer and the fear intensifies or the fighting becomes engaged, then pray however you can. This is consistent with the school of al-Shafi'i regarding the obligation to pray during combat and the impermissibility of delaying it beyond its time. In that state the one praying is excused for not facing the qiblah for the sake of the needs of the fighting, but not for something like a runaway animal, and if the separation is prolonged. Likewise, many actions are excused if needed, according to the more sound view, but not shouting or speaking without need. If the need calls for it, such as alerting someone who is feared to be about to fall into destruction, or driving away horses, or announcing that he is so-and-so, the famous one for bravery, because such need is rare, then there is no obligation to make up the prayer after safety is restored. However, if they prayed in this manner because they thought they saw a dark mass (sawad), even if on the report of a trustworthy person, that the enemy was there, and then it became clear that there was no enemy, and that between them and it there was something preventing its reaching them, such as a trench, or that near them there was customarily a fortress in which they could take refuge without being besieged in it, then according to the more apparent view they must make up the prayer. It is not hidden that interpreting the verse in that way is extremely far-fetched.

﴿When you are secure﴾ meaning: when you have settled, as Qatadah and Mujahid said, and this refers back to His statement, may He be exalted: Page 138
﴿and when you travel through the land﴾. Since striking (dharb) implies movement, and it was used as a metaphor for travel, it is fitting that settling (itmi'nan) be used as a metaphor for residence, and its original sense is stillness and tranquility, meaning: when you have become settled from the journeying and travel in your cities ﴿then establish the prayer﴾ meaning: perform the prayer whose time has come, complete it, make its pillars balanced, observe its conditions, and guard its limits.

It has also been said: the meaning is: when you are secure, then complete the prayer, meaning its kind, with balanced pillars, and do not pray it while walking or riding or sitting. This is what is narrated from Ibn Zayd. It has also been said: the meaning is: when you are generally at peace, then make up what you prayed in those states which are states of unrest and disturbance. This is attributed to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, but it is not correct, because of what you know of his school (and none informs you like one who is all-aware).

﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers as a decree﴾ meaning: written and obligatory, ﴿within specified times﴾ meaning: with fixed times, so it is not permissible to delay it from its times in any circumstance. Therefore it must be established even while traveling. It has also been said: the meaning is: it was an obligation prescribed upon them, determined in residence as four rak'ahs and in travel as two rak'ahs, so it must be performed at every time as prescribed for that time. Whoever took the remembrance mentioned earlier to refer to prayer, and made it obligatory during fighting, has used this verse as evidence, contrary to what Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, held.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 104:

﴿And do not falter in pursuit of the people.﴾ That is: do not be weak or slack in seeking out the disbelievers with fighting.

﴿If you suffer pain, then indeed they suffer pain just as you suffer pain, and you hope from Allah for what they do not hope.﴾ This is a reason for the prohibition and an encouragement to them. That is: what befalls you of pains is not specific to you alone; rather the matter is shared between you and them. Then they endure that, so why do you not endure? Even though you are more deserving of patience than they are, since you hope and aspire from Allah the Exalted for what does not occur to them: the manifestation of your true religion over all the false religions, and the abundant reward and everlasting bliss in the Hereafter.

It is also permissible to interpret "hope" as "fear." The meaning would then be: pain should not prevent you, because you have a fear of Allah the Exalted which should be guarded against more than the guarding against pain; whereas they have no fear that compels them to pain, yet they choose it for the exaltation of their false religion. So what is wrong with you that you should feel weakness? This interpretation is not free from remoteness.

Even more remote is what has been said: the meaning is that pain is a shared lot, and that you worship the God who is Knowing, Powerful, All-Hearing, All-Seeing, from whom good can be hoped, whereas they worship idols, whose good is not hoped for and whose harm is not feared.

Abu Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj read (أنْ تَكُونُوا, "that you suffer") with a fatha on the hamza, meaning: do not falter because you suffer pain. His words ﴿فَإنَّهُمْ﴾ ("for indeed they...") are a reason for the prohibition against weakness on account of it. It was also read (تَئْلِمُونَ كَما يَئْلِمُونَ) with a kasra on the prefixed letter of the imperfect (the letter ta' / ya' of the present tense). It is said that the verse was revealed concerning the going out to Badr al-Sughra for the appointment of Abu Sufyan, and it is said that it was revealed on the day of Uhud concerning the pursuit of Abu Sufyan and his army to Hamra' al-Asad; this is narrated from Ikrimah.

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing﴾ exceedingly in knowledge, so He knows your interests and your deeds, what you display of them and what you conceal, ﴿Wise﴾ in what He commands and forbids. So strive in complying with that, for in it are praiseworthy outcomes and success in attaining the sought-after goal.

[Page 139]

﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾. Ghayr wahid (many) narrated from Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "There was a household among us called the Banu Ubayriq: Bishr, Bushayr and Mubashshir. Bishr was a hypocrite who composed poetry, satirizing the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and then attributed it to some of the Arabs, saying, 'So-and-so said such-and-such, and so-and-so said such-and-such.' When the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) heard that poetry, they would say, 'By Allah, none but this wicked man composes this poetry.' [Bishr] then said:

Whenever men compose a qasidah, they conceal it, and say, 'Ibn al-Ubayriq composed it.'

They were a people of need and poverty in the Jahiliyyah and in Islam. The food of the people in Madinah was dates and barley. Whenever a man had means and a caravan of foodstuffs arrived from Syria, bearing fine wheat flour (al-darmak), he would buy from it and reserve it for himself. A caravan arrived, and my uncle Rifa'ah ibn Zayd bought a load of fine flour and placed it in his storeroom (mashrubah). In the storeroom were his weapons: two coats of mail, two swords and their accessories. A thief named Ubayd came in the night, breached the storeroom, and took the food and the weapons. When morning came, my uncle Rifa'ah came to me and said, 'Nephew, you know that we were robbed last night, our storeroom was breached, and our food and weapons were taken.' We searched the house and asked around, and we were told, 'We saw the Banu Ubayriq kindle a fire this night, and we think nothing but that it was from some of your food.' The Banu Ubayriq said, 'We too have been asking around the house. By Allah, we do not think your companion (the thief) is anyone but Lubayd ibn Sahl, a man of us who has piety and Islam.' When Lubayd heard this, he drew his sword, came to the Banu Ubayriq and said, 'I am a thief! By Allah, this sword will touch you, or you will make this theft clear!' They said, 'Get away from us, O man! By Allah, you are not its perpetrator.' We kept searching the house until we had no doubt that they were its perpetrators.

My uncle said to me, 'Nephew, if you went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and mentioned this to him...' So I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said, 'O Messenger of Allah, a household among us are people of rudeness. They targeted my uncle Rifa'ah, breached his storeroom, and took his weapons and food. Let them return our weapons to us; as for the food, we have no need of it.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'I will look into this.' When the Banu Ubayriq heard, they went to a man among them called Usayr ibn 'Urwah and spoke with him about this. A group of people from the household gathered around him, and they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said, 'O Messenger of Allah, Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man and his uncle have targeted a household of ours, a household of Islam and righteousness, accusing them of theft without evidence or proof.' Qatadah said, 'I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and spoke with him, and he said, "You have targeted a household among whom Islam and righteousness are mentioned, accusing them of theft without evidence or proof."' So I returned, and I wished I had lost some of my property rather than having spoken to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this.'

Then my uncle Rifa'ah came to me and said, 'Nephew, what have you done?' I told him what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had said to me. He said, 'Allah is the One sought for help.' We had not waited long before the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book﴾, and so on. When it was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent for the weapons and returned them to Rifa'ah. When I brought the weapons to my uncle — he was an old man who had gone blind in the Jahiliyyah, and I used to see his Islam as being tainted — he said, 'Nephew, it is in the way of Allah.' I then knew that his Islam was sound. Then Bushayr joined the polytheists, and he stayed with Sulafah daughter of Sa'd. Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger﴾, the verse. Then Hassan ibn Thabit, may Allah be pleased with him, satirized Sulafah, saying:

She has harboured him, the daughter of Sa'd, and she has become one who contends with him, and he with her, over the skin of her backside.

You thought that what you did would remain hidden, while among us is a Prophet whose revelation is his witness.

When Sulafah heard that, she carried his baggage on her head and threw it down at al-Abtah, and said, 'You have brought me the poetry of Hassan! You never brought me anything good.'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi, and al-Tabari chose this: "A Jew deposited a coat of mail with Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq. He took it to his house and the Jew dug a hole and buried it. Tu'mah went to it, dug it up and took it. When the Jew came seeking his coat of mail, Tu'mah denied it. The Jew went to some people of his tribe from among the Jews and said, 'Come with me, for I know where the coat of mail is.' When Tu'mah learned of this, he took the coat of mail and threw it into the house of Abu Mulayk al-Ansari. When the Jews came seeking the coat of mail, they could not find it, and Tu'mah and some people of his folk clashed with them and reviled them. Tu'mah said, 'Are you accusing me?' They went searching for it in his house, and they came to the house of Abu Mulayk, and there they found the coat of mail. Tu'mah said, 'Abu Mulayk took it.' The Ansar argued on behalf of Abu Mulayk against Tu'mah. Tu'mah said to them, 'Come with me to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and say to him that he should defend me and refute the argument of the Jews.' They came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was inclined to do so, but Allah the Exalted revealed the verse. When Allah exposed Tu'mah through the Qur'an, he fled until he came to Makkah, where he apostatized after his Islam and stayed with al-Hajjaj ibn 'Ilat al-Sulami. He breached his house and intended to steal from him. Al-Hajjaj heard a rustling in his house and the clatter of hides that were there. He looked and there was Tu'mah. He said, 'My guest and my cousin, do you want to steal from me?' He expelled him, and he died in the lava-field of the Banu Sulaym as a disbeliever. Allah the Exalted revealed about him: ﴿And whoever opposes﴾, and so on."

And from 'Ikrimah: "When the Qur'an was revealed about Tu'mah, he joined the Quraysh and turned back from his religion. He attacked a storeroom of al-Hajjaj, and a stone fell on him and he was lamed. In the morning they expelled him from Makkah, and he went out. He met a caravan from Qudha'ah and presented himself to them. They said, 'A stranded traveller.' They carried him, but when night fell he attacked them and stole from them, then went off. They went back in pursuit of him, caught up with him, and pelted him with stones until he died."

And from Ibn Zayd: after he joined Makkah, he breached a house to steal from it, and Allah the Exalted caused it to collapse upon him, killing him. It was also said: he was expelled and boarded a ship to Jeddah, where he stole a purse containing dinars; he was caught and thrown into the sea.

Furthermore, the emphasis on the ruling indicates attention to its importance, as in the attribution of the sending down to the pronoun of majesty, glorifying the matter attributed, and the fronting of the indirect object for emphasis and to arouse interest.

His saying, glorified is He, ﴿in truth﴾ (bil-haqq) is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), meaning: We have sent down to you the Qur'an clothed in truth, ﴿so that you may judge among the people﴾, the righteous and the wicked among them, ﴿by what Allah has shown you﴾, i.e., by what He has made you know and revealed to you. Here "ma" (ما, a relative pronoun) is a relative, and its returning pronoun is omitted, which is the first object of "arā" (to show). It is from ra'ā meaning "to know", which takes one object, but it can take two with the hamzah (causative). It was also said that it is from ra'y (opinion), as in the saying "the opinion of al-Shafi'i is such-and-such". To make it a verb of knowledge would require it to take three objects with two of them omitted, meaning "by what Allah has shown you as truth", which is far-fetched. As for taking it as from the visual ra'ā metaphorically, there is no need for that.

﴿And do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾, namely the Banu Ubayriq, or Tu'mah and whoever supports him, or he and whoever follows his way. The lam is for causation. It was also said that it means "on behalf of" (ʿan), i.e., do not be on their behalf, or about them. ﴿Disputing﴾ means contending on behalf of the innocent. The prohibition is coordinated with an implied clause which the noble text presupposes, as if it were said: "We have sent down to you the Book, so judge by it, and do not be..." etc.

It was also said that it is coordinated with "We have sent down" with the implied "We said", and it was permitted to coordinate it with "the Book" because it is sent down. But it is very clearly contrary to the apparent meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 106:

﴿And seek forgiveness from God﴾ for what you said to Qatadah (Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man), or for what you intended regarding the matter of Tu'mah (Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq) and his innocence, according to the apparent state of affairs. And [it is also for] what the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Qatadah. Likewise, the intention to do something, especially when it is thought to be the truth, is not a sin for which one must seek forgiveness. However, due to the greatness of the Prophet (ﷺ), God's protection (ʿiṣmah) of him, and His purifying him from anything that would give the impression of deficiency - far be it from him - He commanded him to seek forgiveness, in order to increase his reward, and to guide him to deliberation (taathbut), and [to show] that what is not a sin, which for others might almost be counted as a good deed, when it proceeds from him - upon him be prayers and peace - is, in relation to his greatness and his praiseworthy station, close to being like a sin. Therefore there is no basis in the command to seek forgiveness for denying infallibility (ʿiṣmah), as some have claimed. It has also been said: it is possible that what is meant is "and seek forgiveness" for those people who exonerated that traitor.

﴿Indeed, God is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾, exceeding in forgiveness and mercy toward whoever seeks His forgiveness. It has also been said: toward whoever seeks forgiveness for him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 4, verse 107:

﴿And do not dispute on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾. That is: who betray their own souls. The betrayal of others is treated as betrayal of themselves, because its burden and harm return to them. It is also possible that sin is called betrayal, so the meaning of "they betray themselves" is: they wrong themselves by committing sins and perpetrating transgressions. It has been said that betrayal here is a metaphor for harm, and there is no difficulty in this.

The relative clause may refer either to the thief, or to the depositor who denies a deposit, and those like them, or to whoever assists them, for he is a partner in the sin and the betrayal. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he, upon him be blessings and peace, is the intended target of the prohibition. A prohibition concerning something presupposes that the one prohibited has committed what is forbidden. It may be said that this is of the same category as ﴿If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely be lost﴾ (39:65). From here it has been said: the meaning is, "Do not dispute, O human being."

﴿Indeed, Allah does not love one who is habitually a betrayer﴾, meaning one who is abundant in betrayal and excessive in it, ﴿sinful﴾, meaning one immersed in sin. The negation of love, which is intended to mean hatred and wrath, is expressed in the form of an intensive. It is not meant to restrict it, but to show the excess of the Banu Ubayriq and their people in betrayal and sin.

Abu Hayyan said: the intensive form is used for both of them so as to exclude one who committed sin or betrayal only once, and one for whom that proceeded from him through heedlessness and lack of intent. But this is not correct.

As for the pairing of "betrayer" with "sinful," it has been said that it is for emphasis. It has also been said that the first refers to theft or denial of a deposit, and the second refers to accusing the innocent. This was narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father). The attribute of betrayal is mentioned before the attribute of sin because it is its cause, or because their occurrence was in that order, or for the harmony of the verse-endings (*fawasil*), as has been said.

[Page 141]

They seek concealment from people (yastakhfūna min al-nās), that is, they hide themselves from them out of shame and fear of their harm. The root meaning of this is seeking to be hidden. The plural pronoun refers, according to the more apparent view, to those who act treacherously (yakhtānūn). The clause is resumed (mustanʾafah) and has no place in i'rab. It was also said that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from (min) and "and they do not seek concealment from Allah" (wa lā yastakhfūna min Allāh), that is, they are not ashamed before Him, glorified be He, though He is more worthy that one feel shame before Him and fear His punishment. The seeking of concealment from the Exalted was interpreted as shame only because hiding oneself from Him, exalted be His dignity, is impossible, so there is no benefit in negating it, and there is no sense in reproaching its absence.

Some verifying scholars (al-muḥaqqiqīn) mentioned that the expression in this way is by way of mushākalah (matching of expression). "And He is with them" (wa huwa maʿahum) in the manner befitting His own essence, glorified be He. It was also said that the meaning is: the Exalted knows them and their states, so there is no way to conceal oneself from the Exalted except by abandoning what would bring one to account. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (yastakhiffūn).

"When they plot by night" (idh yubayyitūn), that is, they devise (yudabbirūn). Since most planning is done by night, the verb was used for it. The adverbial phrase (ẓarf) is connected to what the preceding phrase is connected to. It was also said that it is connected to (yastakhiffūn).

"What He does not approve of in speech" (mā lā yarḍā min al-qawl): such as slandering the innocent and giving false testimony. Al-Naysaburi said: calling planning, which is a meaning within the soul, "speech" is unproblematic according to those who hold the doctrine of inner speech (al-kalām al-nafsī). As for others, it is metaphorical. Or perhaps they gathered at night and arranged the manner of their deceit, so Allah, the Exalted, named their talk that as "speech planned by night" which He, glorified be He, does not approve. You have already been given in the Introductions (al-Muqaddimāt) what will benefit you here, so recall it.

"And Allah is ever, of what they do" (wa kāna Allāh bi-mā yaʿmalūn), that is, of their deed, or of what they do of actions, apparent and hidden, "encompassing" (muḥīṭan), that is, watchful (ḥafīẓan), as al-Ḥasan said, or knowing, nothing escapes Him and nothing eludes Him, as others said. On both views, the encompassing here is metaphorical. Some have placed it among the ambiguous (mutashābih) verses.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 109:

﴿Here you are, you who argued on their behalf in the life of this world﴾ is an address to the defenders, implying that enumerating their crimes necessitates addressing them directly with rebuke and reproach. The phrase is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar). His words, exalted is He: ﴿argued on their behalf in the life of this world﴾ form a clause explaining that (ula'i) is the predicate, so it means "those who argue" (al-mujadilin), and the meaning is complete with it. It is also permissible for (ula'i) to be a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), as is the view of some grammarians regarding every demonstrative noun (ism ishara), with (jadaltum) as its relative clause (silah). The connection is then clear. Al-mujadalah (contention, or disputation) is the most intense form of hostile dispute (al-mukhasamah), and its root is from al-jadal, which means the intensity of a strong grip (shiddat al-qatl), and from it the falcon is called ajdal (the "strong-gripping" one). The meaning is: suppose you exerted your effort in disputing on behalf of those whom the reports point to in this world.

Page 142
﴿So who will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ That is: who will dispute with Him, exalted is He, on their behalf on the Day when they cannot conceal any statement, and nothing from the punishment of Allah, exalted is He, will avail them? ﴿Or who will be their guardian (wakil)?﴾ on that Day, meaning: a protector and defender from the might and punishment of Allah, exalted is He. The original meaning of wakil is the person to whom affairs are entrusted and attributed. Interpreting it as protector and defender is a metaphor, through the use of a thing for its necessary meaning (isti'mal al-shay' fi lazim ma'nah).

The (am) here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), as al-Samin said, and it was said that it is conjunctive (ati'ah), as transmitted in al-Durr al-Masun. The interrogation, as al-Karkhi said, in both places is for negation, meaning: no one argues on their behalf, and no one will be their guardian.

﴿Whoever does evil﴾, that is, something that harms another, as Bushayr did to Rifa'a, or Tu'mah did to the Jew. ﴿Or wrongs himself﴾ by that which affects only him, such as denial (inkar). It was said: "evil" (su') is what falls short of shirk (associating partners with God), and "wrong" (zulm) is shirk. It was also said: "evil" is a minor sin (saghirah), and "wrong" is a major sin (kabirah).

﴿Then seeks forgiveness from God﴾ through sincere repentance (tawbah), even if shortly before death, ﴿will find God Forgiving﴾ of whatever he sought forgiveness for, whatever it may be, ﴿Merciful﴾, bestowing favour upon him. In this there is an encouragement, for those among the sinners concerning whom the verse was revealed, to repent and seek forgiveness. It was said: it is also a warning, by implication (mafhum), to whoever does not seek forgiveness and does not repent, for it indicates that whoever does not seek forgiveness is deprived of God's mercy, and is afflicted with His wrath.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 111:

﴿And whoever earns﴾ i.e., does, ﴿a sin﴾, a sin among the sins, ﴿then he earns it only against himself﴾ in such a way that its harm does not extend to others. So let him guard against exposing others to punishment and calamity. ﴿And Allah is ever Knowing﴾ of everything, including the earning, ﴿Wise﴾ in everything He decrees and ordains, and of this is: ﴿no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾. It has been said: (Knowing) of the thief, (Wise) in prescribing the cutting of his hand. But the first is preferable.

And whoever earns a fault (*khati'ah*), that is, a minor sin, or whatever among sins is not deliberate. Mu'adh ibn Jabal recited *yakissib* (ﷺ-less), with a kasra on the kaf and a doubled sin, and its origin is *yaktasib*. And whoever earns a sin (*ithm*), that is, a major sin, or whatever is committed deliberately. It was said: *khati'ah* is shirk, and *ithm* is what falls short of it.

In *al-Kashshaf*: *ithm* is the sin for which its doer deserves punishment, and the hamza in it is a substitute for a waw, as if it were *yathim al-a'mal*, meaning it breaks deeds by nullifying them. In *al-Kashf*: "It is as if this was its origin, then it was used for sin in general," as in His saying, "the major sins of sin" (﻿“كَبائِرُ الإثم”). From this it is known that what the author of *al-Qil* mentioned is weak.

﴿Then he throws it﴾, that is, casts it and attributes it, and the pronoun is singular because it refers to one of the two matters specifically, as if it was said: then he throws one of the two matters. It was said that it refers to *ithman* (sin), because for two items joined by *aw* (or), the pronoun after them may refer to the first item of the conjunction, as in His saying: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion, they scatter toward it﴾, and to the second item, as in: ﴿Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them﴾.

It was said that it refers to the earning (*kasb*), in the manner of: ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾. It was said that there is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: he throws with it and with him. And *thumma* (then) indicates a delay in rank. It was read with both (pronouns). ﴿Innocent﴾ of what he attributed to him, so that he may burden him with the punishment of the immediate world, as did the one who had the coat of mail with Lubayd ibn Sahl, or with Abu Mulayk. ﴿Then he has borne﴾ by what he did of throwing the innocent, and his intention of loading his offence upon him. It is more emphatic than (*hamala*, he carried). It was said: *ifta'ala* is in the sense of *fa'ala*, so *iqtadara* and *qadara* (both mean to be able).

﴿A slander﴾, which is lying against another by what makes him be astonished and bewildered upon hearing it because of its grossness. It was said: it is the lie in whose magnitude one is bewildered. The past tense is *baha* like *mana'a*, and for the verbal noun it is said *bahtan*, *bahatan* and *buhtan*. ﴿And a manifest sin﴾, that is, clear, with no doubt or obscurity in it, and it is an attribute of *ithman*. The emphatic indefiniteness was sufficient to show the magnitude of the slander, on the basis that describing the sin with what has been mentioned is equivalent to describing the slander with it, because both are an expression of one matter, which is throwing the innocent with the crime of one's own self.

[Page 143]

He expressed it with both in order to magnify its affair and to make its state appear repugnant. So the basis of the magnitude and grandeur is that the thing thrown belongs to the thrower. For throwing an innocent with a crime, whether it be a fault or a sin, is slander and a sin in itself. As for it being slander, that is obvious. As for it being a sin, that is because the sin being a fault in relation to the one who committed it does not necessarily make it so in relation to the one who attributes it to the innocent, rather it is definitively impermissible, since it is a lie forbidden in all religions. So it is in itself slander and a sin without doubt. By the crime belonging to the thrower, this increases in severity and grows in ugliness, but not by the joining of his own earned crime to the throwing of the innocent, for otherwise throwing with a crime other than his would be equal to it in magnitude, nor merely by its including the clearing of his own erring self, for otherwise throwing with a crime other than his, together with clearing his own self, would be equal to it in magnitude. Rather it is because it includes the intention of loading his crime upon the innocent and making its punishment fall upon him, as is indicated by the preference of *al-ihtimal* (bearing) over *al-iktisab* (earning) and the like, because of what it contains of the notification of reversing his assessment, along with what it contains of the suggestion of the weight of the burden and the difficulty of the matter, according to what the apparent form of the *ifti'al* pattern requires.

Yes, with what has been mentioned, the joining of his earning and the clearing of his own self to the throwing of the innocent increases the crime in ugliness. But that increase is an attribute of the whole, not of the sin alone. So said Shaykh al-Islam. It is not hidden that this is more appropriate than what is understood from the apparent speech of *al-Kashshaf*, that in the revelation there is *laff wa nashr* (a rhetorical device of enumeration then correspondence) that is not in order (*ghayr murattab*) where he said after His saying ﴿then he has borne﴾, etc.: "for by his earning the sin he is sinful, and by his throwing the innocent he is a slanderer, so he combines both matters, because he is free of what would bind him." Even if an answer is given to it, so understand.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 113:

﴿And had it not been for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy﴾ by informing you, through revelation, of what they were planning, and by alerting you to the truth. It was also said: "Had it not been for His bounty through prophethood and His mercy through protection (ʿişmah, freedom from sin)." It was also said: "Had it not been for His bounty through prophethood and His mercy through revelation." It was also said: what is meant is "Had it not been for His guarding you and His watching over you."

﴿A group of them would have resolved﴾, that is, of those "who betray" (yakhtanun). The intended people are Usayr ibn ʿUrwah and his companions, or those who defended Ṭuʿmah, who were aware of the details of the affair and knew its reality. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to people in general, and the intended "group" would then be those who defended the thief, or the treacherous depositary. It was also said that the intended people are the delegation of Thaqif. It has been narrated from Jarir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, we have come to pledge allegiance to you on condition that we do not break our idols with our own hands, and that we may enjoy (al-ʿUzza) for a year.' The Prophet (ﷺ) did not answer them, and Allah protected him from that, and so this was revealed."

It is narrated from Abu Muslim that they were the hypocrites, who "resolved upon what they could not attain" of destroying the Prophet (ﷺ), but Allah protected him from them and guarded him with the eye of His care.

﴿To lead you astray﴾, that is: by leading you astray from judging with the truth, or from following what came to you regarding the matter of the idols, or by destroying you. Misguidance (al-ıḍlal) has come in this sense, and it is said that among its uses is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And they say: "Will we, when we have gone astray in the earth...?"﴾. The clause is the answer to "had it not been". Their resolve is negated, although what is negated is only its effect, as an indication that its effect is entirely absent. It was also said that what is meant is an effective resolve, and there is no doubt that it is absent in reality.

Al-Raghib said: the people were Muslims, and they did not resolve at all to mislead him (ﷺ); rather, that was right in their view and in their opinion. Abu al-Baqaʾ permitted that the answer be omitted, and the meaning would be: "And had it not been for Allah's bounty upon you and His mercy, they would have led you astray." Then he resumed with His words, glorified is He: (they resolved), that is: they had indeed resolved upon that. ﴿But they lead none astray except themselves﴾, that is: they remove no one from the truth except themselves, or they destroy no one except themselves, because the consequence and harm of that return upon them. The clause is parenthetical.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Nor can they harm you in any way﴾ are coordinated with what precedes, and its coordination with (to lead you astray) is a pure error. (min) is additional, and the governed noun is in the accusative position as a verbal noun, meaning: "nor can they harm you with any harm, because He, exalted is He, protects you from deviation in judgment."

As for what occurred to your mind, it was an action on your part based on outward circumstances, trusting the statements of those who spoke, without it occurring to you that the reality was otherwise. Or it was because He, glorified is He, protects you from compromise and from inclining toward the opinions of the heretics, when the matter is contrary to what Allah has sent down to you. Or it was because He, exalted is His majesty, promised you protection from people and kept them from being able to reach you.

﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and the wisdom﴾, that is: the Qur'an, which combines both titles. It was also said that what is meant by "wisdom" is the Sunnah (the Prophetic tradition), and the discussion of verifying that has already preceded. The clause, according to what al-Ajhuri said, is in the position of giving the reason for what comes before it, and al-Tabarsi pointed to this, but it is not accepted according to what Abu Muslim held.

﴿And taught you﴾ through various kinds of revelation ﴿what you did not know﴾, that is: that which you did not know of hidden matters and the secrets of hearts. Among them are the ways of nullifying the schemes of schemers, or matters of this world and the rulings of the Sharia, as was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, or the good and evil, as al-Dahhak said, or reports of the earlier and later peoples, as it was said, or all of what has been mentioned, as is said.

Among the people is one who interpreted the relative pronoun as referring to the secrets of the Book and wisdom, meaning: He, glorified is He, sent that down to you, informed you of its secrets, and made you aware of its realities. In that case the second clause serves as a completion of the first clause. Al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) preferred the generality of the meaning.

﴿And the bounty of Allah upon you has been immense﴾, which no expression can contain, and no allusion can encompass. Among it is general prophethood, complete leadership, and the great intercession on the Day of Resurrection.

[p. 144]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 114:

﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk﴾ That is: those who commit treachery (yakhtanun). A group has chosen that the pronoun refers to people in general, and the words of Mujahid point to this. And "najwa" (secret talk) in the language, as al-Zajjaj said, is what a group or two people discuss privately. Is it a condition that it be secret or not? There are two opinions. It may mean "private conversation" (tanajji), and it may also be applied to the people conversing privately, as in ﴿when they are in secret talk﴾. This is either of the pattern of "rajul 'adl" (a just man), or it is the plural of "najiy," as al-Kirmani transmitted.

The first adverbial phrase is the predicate of "la" (there is no), and the second is in the position of a qualifier for the indefinite noun, meaning: existing in their secret talk. ﴿Except for one who enjoins﴾, that is: except in the secret talk of one who enjoins ﴿charity﴾. So the speech is elliptical with an omitted genitive (muḍāf), and by this the exception connects. Likewise, if "secret talk" is taken to mean the people conversing, according to one of the two considerations, there is no need for that estimation. For the validity of the connection, it suffices that inclusion is valid, even if it is not affirmed. So what 'Isam al-Din imagined does not apply: that "a large number of men came to me except Zayd" does not admit connection because it is not certain that Zayd is included in the large number, nor disconnection because it is not certain that he is excluded. There is no need for the strained answer that the meaning is: there is no good in much of the secret talk of any one of them except the secret talk of one who enjoins, etc., for in much of his secret talk there is good, since this, for all its merits, cannot be paralleled under the possibility of the plural reading.

May God Most High have mercy on him, he permitted, indeed claimed, that it is preferable to make "except one who enjoins" dependent on that to which the secret talk is attributed, by exception or by substitution. It is not hidden that, if it is granted that it has a meaning, it is contrary to the apparent sense.

Many have permitted that the exception be disjunctive (munqati'), in the sense: but rather, one who enjoins charity, however small, has good in his secret talk. ﴿Or kindness﴾, which is everything that the Sharia has recognized and deemed good, and so it includes all categories of righteousness, such as lending, aiding the distressed, guiding the lost, and other things. Here it is intended to mean what is other than charity and other than what is indicated by the words of the Exalted: ﴿or reconciliation between people﴾. Restricting it to lending, aiding the distressed, and voluntary charity, and restricting charity in the preceding to obligatory charity, is something for which there is no reason, and it has no support on which one may rely.

The Exalted singled out charity and reconciliation between people
Page 145
for mention from among what this general term includes, to signal their importance: in the first is the spending of wealth, which is the twin of the soul, and in the second is the removal of corruption in relations, which is the destroyer of religion, as in the report.

He placed charity before reconciliation because enjoining it is more difficult, for it involves imposing the giving of what is beloved, and the soul recoils from one who imposes that on it, whereas this is not the case with enjoining reconciliation.

Imam al-Razi mentioned that the reason for singling out these three categories is that doing good that extends to people is either to convey benefit or to repel harm, and benefit is either physical, like giving wealth, to which the words of the Exalted refer: ﴿except one who enjoins charity﴾; or spiritual, to which the enjoining of what is right refers. As for removing harm, it is indicated by the words of the Exalted: ﴿or reconciliation between people﴾. What is in this is not hidden. By reconciliation between people is meant bringing them together in affection when they have fallen into discord, without going beyond the bounds of the noble Sharia.

Indeed, lying is permitted for this purpose. Al-Shaykhan and Abu Dawud related from Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqba that she heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "The liar is not one who reconciles between people, so that he improves (good) or says good." She said: "I did not hear him grant permission in anything of what people say except in three: in war, in reconciliation between people, and in a man's speech to his wife and a woman's speech to her husband."

Many have counted reconciliation as a form of charity, and this is supported by what al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Ayyub, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "O Abu Ayyub, shall I not guide you to a charity whose place God and His Messenger are pleased with?" He said: "Yes." He said: "You reconcile between people when they have become corrupt, and you bring them close when they have become estranged."

And from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The best charity is the reconciliation of relations between people." This report clearly indicates that reconciliation is better than charity with wealth.

Similar to it is what Ahmad, Abu Dawud, and al-Tirmidhi related, and he graded it sound, from Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of something better in rank than fasting, prayer, and charity?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Reconciliation of relations between people." It is not hidden that this and the like are phrased as encouragement, and its apparent sense is not what is meant; for there is no doubt that obligatory fasting, obligatory prayer, and charity of that kind are better than reconciliation, except where reconciliation is such that its neglect entails great evil and grave corruption among people.

﴿And whoever does that﴾, that is: the aforementioned charity and its two companions. The statement is a concluding clause (tadhyil) following the exception. The apparent wording would have been "whoever enjoins" that, to match what is concluded; but He attached the promise to the act immediately after explaining the superiority of the one who enjoins, since the purpose is to encourage the act, and the explanation of the superiority of one who enjoins it serves to indicate its superiority all the more.

It is also permitted that the enjoining is expressed by the act, since the act is used as a metaphor for all things, as when one says: "I swore to Zayd and honoured him, and so-and-so," and you reply: "How well you have done!" Perhaps the point of shifting from "yamur" (enjoins) to "yaf'al" (does) in this case is to indicate that causing another to act, in charity, reconciliation, or good of any kind, is sufficient for the reward to be bestowed, and this does not depend on the wording. It is also permissible to take that as referring to the enjoining, so that "man amara" and "man yaf'al al-amr" have the same meaning.

It has been said: there is no need to make it a concluding clause, which would require interpretation in order to achieve correspondence; rather, when He mentioned the one who enjoins, He digressed to mention the one who complies with his command, as if it were said: "and whoever complies."

﴿Seeking the pleasure of God﴾, that is: for the sake of seeking God's good pleasure. ﴿Then We shall give him﴾ with the plural of majesty, by way of iltifat (shift of person). Abu 'Amr, Hamza, Qutayba from al-Kisa'i, Sahl and Khalaf read it with the yā' (third person). ﴿A great reward﴾, which no bounds of description can encompass. It has been said: the act is restricted to the aforementioned seeking only because actions are by intentions, and whoever does good for other than this purpose deserves nothing but deprivation. It is not hidden that this apparently indicates that showing-off (riya') totally nullifies the reward of deeds, and this is what Ibn 'Abd al-Salam and al-Nawawi stated explicitly.

Page 146
al-Ghazali said: if sincerity prevails, he is rewarded, otherwise not. It was also said: he is rewarded whether sincerity prevails or not, in proportion to the sincerity. Yet in the verse's indication that one who is not sincere deserves nothing but deprivation there is room for scrutiny, because He, glory be to Him, affirmed in it a great reward for the sincere, and that does not preclude that others may have something less than it. And that the greatness is relative to worldly matters is contrary to the apparent sense.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 4, verse 115:**

﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger﴾ means: contradicts him. It is derived from *al-shiqq* (side), because each of two opponents is on a side other than the side of the other. Because the separation between the Messenger and his opponent is evident, the idgham (assimilation of the doubled letter) is undone (*fakk*) here. In His saying, exalted is He, in Surah al-Anfal, ﴿And whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger﴾, the form is kept with idgham, out of consideration for the conjoined noun. It was not undone in His saying, exalted is He, in al-Hashr: ﴿And whoever opposes Allah﴾.

Al-Khatib said regarding the wisdom of undoing and not undoing the doubling: the *(Al)* (ال) in the noble name (Allah) is obligatory, unlike its presence in (al-Rasul). Obligatoriness requires heaviness, so the doubling was lightened by idgham where the divine name accompanies it, unlike where the word "Messenger" accompanies it. In the verse of al-Anfal, the conjoined and the thing conjoined to became like one thing. What we have mentioned is more preferable. The mention of the title of messengerhood serves to show the full ugliness of what they dared to do of opposition and defiance, and to give the reason for the ruling that follows. The verse was revealed, as we mentioned earlier, concerning the thief of the coat of mail or the one who had deposited it. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the people of Tu'mah when they apostatized after having embraced Islam. In any case, the lesson is drawn from the generality of the wording, not from the specificity of the occasion of revelation, so that this and others among those who oppose are included in it.

﴿From after the guidance had become clear to him﴾ means: the truth became manifest to him regarding what the Prophet (ﷺ) judged, or regarding what he claims, peace and blessings be upon him, through witnessing the miracles that prove his prophethood. ﴿And follows a path other than that of the believers﴾ means: other than that to which they persist in belief and practice, so it encompasses the fundamentals and the subsidiaries, the whole and the part. ﴿We shall leave him to what he has turned to﴾ means: We shall make him a guardian (*wali*) over what he has taken up of error. This leads to the meaning that We cause him to go astray. It was also said: its meaning is that We leave him between himself and what he has chosen for himself. It was also said: We shall leave him in the Hereafter to what he relied upon and was supported by in this world of idols. ﴿And We shall burn him in Hell﴾ means: We shall make him enter it, and this has been discussed before. It was also read with a fatha on the nun, from (*sallahu*).

﴿And evil is it as a destination﴾ means: Hell, or the turning away. Imam al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, derived the authority of consensus (*ijma'*) from this verse. It is reported from al-Muzani that he said: I was with al-Shafi'i one day when an old man came to him, wearing woolen clothing and holding a staff. When he saw that he had dignity, he sat up straight, for he had been leaning against a pillar, and he straightened his clothes. He said to him: What is the proof in the religion of Allah, exalted is He? He said: His Book. He said: And what else? He said: The Sunnah of His Prophet (ﷺ). He said: And what else? He said: The consensus of the community. He said: From where is this last one? Is it in the Book of Allah, exalted is He? Al-Shafi'i reflected silently for a while. The old man said to him: I give you three days and nights; if you bring a verse, well and good, otherwise withdraw from people. He remained for three days without going out. On the third day he came out between noon and afternoon, his complexion changed. The old man came to him, greeted him, sat down, and said: What is your need? He said: Yes. I seek refuge in Allah, exalted is He, from Satan the accursed. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after the guidance has become clear to him﴾ until the end. Whoever opposes the believers, Hell will not reach him unless following them is obligatory. He said: You are right, and he rose and left. It is also reported from him that he said: I recited the Qur'an every day and every night three times until I attained it.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) reported from him that he was asked about a verse from the Book of Allah, exalted is He, that indicates that consensus is authoritative, so he recited the Qur'an three hundred times until he found this verse.

Al-Raghib objected to this, saying: the path of the believers is faith itself, just as when it is said: follow the path of those who fast and those who pray, meaning in fasting and prayer. Therefore there is no indication in the verse for the authority of consensus and the obligation to follow the believers in anything other than faith.

(Page 147)

Al-Kashf refuted this, saying: it is a restriction by what the first condition (the conditional clause "after the guidance had become clear") refutes. Furthermore, if the customary practice of those who fast is seclusion (*i'tikaf*), for example, the command to follow them includes that as well. Likewise it includes what is required by faith in the matter under discussion. So the path of the believers here is general in the sense we have indicated.

It was objected that the conjoined (the path of the believers) is restricted by (after the guidance became clear, *tabayyana al-huda*), so the same restriction must apply to the conjoined. Then, if consensus has no benefit, because guidance is general to all guidance, and among it is the proof of consensus, and once the proof is established the thing proven has no benefit. It was answered: the restriction does not necessarily apply to the conjoined. And even on assuming it does, the meaning of guidance is the proof for monotheism and prophethood, so the verse indicates that opposing the believers after the proof of monotheism and prophethood is forbidden. Consensus is then beneficial regarding the subsidiary rulings after the fundamentals have become clear.

The judge (al-Baydawi) clarified the way of deriving from it the authority of consensus and the prohibition of opposing it: God, exalted is He, attached in it a severe threat to opposition and to following other than the path of the believers. This is either because each one of the two is forbidden, or one of them, or the combination of both. The second is invalid, for it would be ugly to say: whoever drinks wine and eats bread deserves the prescribed punishment. The third is likewise invalid, because opposition is forbidden whether or not something else is added to it. And if following other than their path is forbidden, then following their path is obligatory, because abandoning the following of their path, for one who knows their path, is following other than their path.

If it is said: We do not grant that abandoning the following of the path of the believers is truly described as following other than the path of the believers, because it is not impossible that the path of the believers is not followed and neither is the path other than that of the believers. It is answered: following means performing the same act as another. When it is the nature of non-believers not to imitate the believers in their actions, then whoever among the believers does not follow the path of the believers has performed the act of non-believers and trodden in their footsteps, so he must be following them.

In other words: abandoning the following of the path of the believers is following other than the path of the believers, because the responsible person cannot be free of following some path whatsoever.

It was also objected that this proof is not conclusive, because "other than the path of the believers" may have several possible restrictions: it may mean their path in following the Messenger, or in supporting him, or in emulating him, peace and blessings be upon him, or in that by which they became believers. When such possibility exists, its best outcome is apparentness (*zuhur*), and holding to the apparent meaning is established only through consensus. Without it, one would be obliged to act on the proofs that forbid following conjecture (*zann*). So this would be establishing consensus by something whose authority is established only by consensus, and this becomes circular (*dawr*), and escaping from it was found difficult. Ibn al-Hajib mentioned this in al-Mukhtasar, and close to it is the statement of al-Isfahani: when following their path is open to what has been mentioned and other things, it becomes general, and its indication of one of its individual instances is not decisive, because it may be restricted by something that excludes it, along with the circularity involved.

He answered the circularity by saying: it arises only if no other proof has been established for it, and there is another proof for it, which is that it is a probable (*maznun*) matter that must be acted upon. For if we do not act on it alone, then either we act on it together with its opposite, or we act on neither of the two, or we act on its opposite. On the first, there is the combination of contradictories; on the second, the elimination of both; on the third, acting on the less probable while the more probable exists. All of these are invalid, so it is necessary to act on it with certainty.

It was also objected that the prohibition of following other than the path of the believers is not absolute, but conditional upon opposition. The proponents answered this with arguments that are not free of weakness, and with the claim that the derivation depends on restricting "the believers" to the people who loose and bind (*ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd*) in every age, and the indication of this is not evident, along with other matters mentioned by al-Amidi, al-Tilimsani and others, and they answered what they answered from them.

In sum, this derivation hardly escapes the disputes of "he said, and he said," and the authority of consensus does not depend on it, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 116:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with, but He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills.﴾ Its interpretation has already passed in what preceded, and it is repeated for emphasis. This place is singled out for it so that it may serve as a completion of the story of those mentioned before, by mentioning the promise after the mention of the threat within the preceding verses. So it does no harm after the covenant. Or, because the verse has another occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), al-Tha'labi related on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "an old man from the Arabs came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'I am an old man immersed in sins, but I have never associated anything with Allah, the Exalted, since I knew Him and believed in Him, and I have not taken any protector besides Him, and I have not committed sins out of audacity, and I have not imagined for the blink of an eye that I could escape Allah, the Exalted, by fleeing. Indeed I am regretful and repentant. So what do you think my state is with Allah, the Exalted?'" So it was revealed.

﴿And whoever associates with Allah anything﴾ — of association (shirk), or any one of the creation. And included in the meaning of associating with Allah, the Exalted, is the denial of the Creator (al-sani'), and it is not far-fetched that it is one of its instances.

﴿Then he has certainly strayed far astray﴾ — from the truth, or from being among those who have any minimal intellect. The recompense has been stated here as "then he has strayed" (faqad dalla) and so on, whereas in what preceded it was ﴿then he has certainly invented a great sin﴾, because those earlier verses concerned the People of the Book, who, from their own scriptures, were aware of what they doubted regarding the truth of the Messenger ﷺ, the obligation to follow his law, and what he called to of belief in Allah, the Exalted. Despite that, they associated partners with Allah and disbelieved, so that this became fabrication, deviation, and a great audacity against Allah, the Exalted. This verse, however, concerned people who had not known any scripture and had not previously recognized any revelation, and there had come to them none but the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with guidance and the religion of truth. Yet they associated partners with Allah, the Exalted, and disbelieved, and went astray despite the clarity of the proof and the brilliance of the evidence. So their straying was far (ba'idan). For this reason, after that verse came: ﴿Have you not seen those who justify themselves?﴾ and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Look how they invent lies against Allah.﴾

Following it, in the commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 117:

Its statement, exalted is He, follows: ﴿They call upon none besides Him but females﴾. That is, "What they worship, or what they call upon for their needs, besides Allah, the Exalted, is only idols." The clause explains the reason for what precedes it, which is why it is not joined to it by a conjunction. The idols are described as "females" because of what is narrated from al-Hasan (al-Basri): that every tribe of the Arabs had an idol that they worshipped, and they called it "the female of Banu so-and-so," because they put jewelry and various adornments on it, as they do with women. Or it is because their names are feminine, as has been said. They call whatever has a feminine name a "female," as in the verse:

*"And every male, if it grows large, becomes a female, of tight grip, having no molars."*

He meant the tick, which, while small, is called a *qurad*, and when it grows it is called *halama*, like a *thamara* (date).

It has been objected that some idols have masculine names, such as Hubal, Wadd, Suwa', and Dhu al-Khalasa. The claim that this is by the majority is not conceded. It has also been said that they are inanimate objects, and inanimate objects are often made feminine because they resemble females in being acted upon (*infi'al*). So describing them with this name alerts to the extreme of their ignorance and the excess of their foolishness, in that they call upon what is acted upon, and abandon the Doer (*fa'"al*) of what He wills.

It has also been said that the intended meaning of "females" is "dead ones." Ibn Jarir and others narrated from al-Hasan: "The *unthā* is every dead thing that has no spirit, like a dry piece of wood or a dry stone." In using this expression rather than "idols," the same alert noted above is also present. However, describing the idols as dead is a metaphor (*majaz*).

It has also been said: Allah named them females because of their weakness, the scarcity of their good, and their failure to help. It has been said: because of the lowliness of their rank and the baseness of their station, based on the fact that the Arabs use "female" for anything whose rank is low, of whatever kind it may be.

It has also been said: in every idol there was a female devil (*shaytana*) who appeared to the keepers (*sadana*) and sometimes spoke to them. Therefore He, glorified be He, informed that they worship none besides Him but females. This is narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the angels, because of their saying, "The angels are the daughters of Allah, exalted is His name." This is narrated from al-Dahhak. *Inath* is the plural of *unthā*, like *rabab* and *ruba* in the dialect of those who vowel the *ra'* with a kasra.

It has been recited as *illā unthā* in the singular, and as *illā unuthā* with two dammas, like *rusul* (messengers). This may be a single adjective, like *imra'a junub*. Or it may be a plural of *anīth*, like *qalīb* and *qulub*; and it has come: *ḥadīd anīth*. Or it may be a plural of *inath*, like *thimār* and *thamar*.

It has been recited as *wathanan* and *athanan*, with lightening and with doubling, and with the *tha'* placed before the *nun*, as the plural of *wathan*, like your saying *asad*, *usd*, *usud*, and *wusd*. The *waw* was changed to an *alif*, like *ujūh* for *wujūh*.

Ibn Jarir narrated that in the codex (*mushaf*) of 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, it was: *illā awthānan*.

﴿And they call upon none but﴾, that is, they worship with the worship of those idols, ﴿none but a rebellious devil﴾. For it is he who commanded them to worship them and incited them, so their obedience to him became worship. Thus the statement is taken figuratively, and does not contradict the restriction (*ḥasr*) mentioned earlier. It has also been said: the intended meaning is that whoever they call upon, they obey, so there is no contradiction either.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sufyan that he said: "There is no idol except that in it is a devil." The apparent meaning of "the devil" here is Iblis, and this is what is narrated from Muqatil and others.

*Marid*, *marid*, and *mutamarrid* mean: the defiant one who exits obedience. The root *m-r-d* originally denotes smoothness and bareness, and from it comes ﴿a palace made smooth﴾ (27:44), and *shajara marda'* for a tree whose leaves have fallen off. The devil is described with this either because he is stripped bare for evil, or because he is likened to the smooth thing to which nothing clings. It has also been said: because his evil is manifest, like the manifest chin of a beardless youth, and the manifest branches of the bare tree.

﴿لَعَنَهُ اللَّهُ﴾ أي: طَرَدَهُ وأبعَدَهُ عن رحمتِهِ. وقيل: المرادُ باللعنةِ فِعلُ ما يَستحِقُّها به من الاستكبارِ عن السجود، كقولِهم: "أبَيْتَ اللَّعْنَ"، أي: ما فعلتَ ما تستحقُّه به. والجملةُ في موضعِ نصبٍ صفةٍ ثانيةٍ لـ﴿شَيْطانًا﴾.

وجوَّزَ أبو البقاءِ أن تكونَ مستأنفةً على الدعاءِ، فلا موضعَ لها من الإعرابِ (*i'rab*: التحليلُ النحويُّ لبيانِ وظيفةِ الكلمةِ في الجملة).

﴿وقالَ لَأَتَّخِذَنَّ مِن عِبادِكَ نَصِيبًا مَفْرُوضًا﴾ عطفٌ على الجملةِ المتقدمةِ، والمرادُ شيطانًا مريدًا جامعًا بين لعنةِ اللهِ تعالى وهذا القولِ الشنيعِ الصادرِ منه عند اللعنِ. وجُوِّزَ أن تكونَ في موضعِ الحالِ بتقديرِ (قَدْ)، أي: وقد قال، وأن تكونَ مستأنفةً مستطردةً، كما أنَّ ما قبلها اعتراضيةٌ في رأيٍ. والجارُّ والمجرورُ إمّا متعلقٌ بالفعلِ، وإمّا حالٌ مما بعده، واختارَه البعضُ.

والاتخاذُ أخذُ الشيءِ على وجهِ الاختصاصِ، وأصلُ معنى الفَرْضِ القطعُ، وأُطلِقَ هنا على المقدارِ المعيَّنِ لاقتطاعِهِ عمّا سواه، وهو كما أخرجَ ابنُ أبي حاتمٍ عن الضحّاكِ، وابنُ المنذرِ عن الربيعِ: «من كلِّ ألفٍ تسعُمِائةٍ وتسعةٌ وتسعونَ».

والظاهرُ أنَّ هذا القولَ وقعَ نُطقًا من اللعينِ، وكأنه، عليه اللعنةُ، لمّا نالَ من آدمَ عليه السلامُ ما نالَ طمِعَ في ولدِه، وقالَ ذلك ظنًّا، وأُيِّدَ بقولِه تعالى: ﴿وَلَقَدْ صَدَّقَ عَلَيْهِمْ إِبْلِيسُ ظَنَّهُ﴾. وقيل: إنه فهِمَ طاعةَ الكثيرِ له مما فهِمَتْ منه الملائكةُ حين قالوا: ﴿أَتَجْعَلُ فِيهَا مَن يُفْسِدُ فِيهَا وَيَسْفِكُ الدِّمَاءَ﴾.

وادّعى بعضُهم أنَّ هذا القولَ حاليٌّ، كما في قولِه:

امْتَلَأَ الحَوْضُ وقالَ قِطْنِي مَهْلًا رُوَيْدًا قَدْ مَلَأْتَ بِطْنِي

Translation: The basin is full and it says: "Enough, my dear, gently, slowly, you have filled my belly."

وفي هذه الجملِ ما يُنادي على جهلِ المشركينَ، وغايةِ انحطاطِ درجتِهم عن الانخراطِ في سلكِ العقلاءِ على أتمِّ وجهٍ وأكملِه، وفيها توبيخٌ لهم كما لا يخفى.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 4, verse 119:**

﴿And I will surely mislead them﴾ from the truth, ﴿and I will surely lead them on with false hopes﴾, and I will say to them: "There is no resurrection for you, no raising up, no Paradise, no Fire, no reward, and no punishment, so do whatever you wish." It was also said: "I will lead them on with long life in this world, so they will postpone their deeds." And it was said: "I will lead them on with false desires that call to disobedience. I will beautify for them the lusts and the adornments of this world, and I will call each of them to whatever his nature inclines toward, thereby turning him away from obedience." The first interpretation was related from al-Kalbi.

﴿And I will surely command them﴾ to cut (the ears), as Abu Hayyan said, or to lead them into error, as others said, ﴿so they will surely slit the ears of the cattle﴾. That is, they will surely cut them off at their roots, as was related from Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him. Or they will split them, as al-Zajjaj said, in accordance with My command, without hesitation or delay, as the particle "fa" (so) indicates. This refers to what the pre-Islamic Arabs (al-Jahiliyyah) used to do: they would slit the ear of a she-camel when she had borne five offspring and the fifth was a male, and they would forbid riding her, burdening her, and all other forms of benefit from her. ﴿And I will surely command them﴾, so that they will ﴿surely alter the creation of Allah﴾, obeying without delay, ﴿from its course﴾, whether in form or in attribute. This includes what is done by gouging out the eye of a stallion camel when it has stayed for a long time (in service) until it has produced offspring of offspring, and this is called the "hami"; castrating slaves; tattooing (al-washm); filing the teeth (al-washr); sodomy (al-liwat); lesbianism (al-sihaq); and similar practices; and worshipping the sun, the moon, fire, or stones, for example; and changing the fitrah (natural disposition) of Allah the Exalted, which is Islam; and using the limbs and faculties in what does not bring perfection to the self nor earn it nearness to Allah, glory be to Him.

It has been reported from the early generation (al-Salaf) that they limited the verse to some of the things mentioned, while the general wording would forbid castration in all cases. It is also related that a group of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, forbade it.

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade the castration of horses and animals." 'Ikrimah claimed that the verse was revealed concerning this, and some scholars permitted it for animals.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Urwah that he castrated a mule of his; and from Tawus that he castrated a camel; and from Muhammad ibn Sirin that he was asked about castrating stallions and said: "There is no harm in it." The same was reported from al-Hasan. And from 'Ata' that he was asked about castrating a stallion, and he saw no harm in it when it was aggressive and of bad temper.

Al-Nawawi said: "It is not permissible to castrate an animal that is not eaten, either in its youth or in its adulthood. It is permissible to castrate an edible animal in its youth, because there is a benefit in it, which is the goodness of its meat, but it is not permissible in its adulthood."

Castration of human beings is forbidden according to the general consensus of the early and later scholars (al-Salaf wa al-Khalaf). According to Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, it is disliked to buy eunuchs, to employ them, or to keep them, because the desire for them leads to their castration.

Circumcision (al-khitan), tattooing for a need, dyeing the beard, and trimming what exceeds the Sunnah (in the beard and similar matters) are excepted from the alteration of the creation of Allah the Exalted, and similar things.

It is related from Qatadah that he recited the verse and then said: "What is wrong with people, ignorant people, who alter the dye (sibghah) and the color of Allah the Exalted, glory be to Him!" It is hardly accepted from him if he meant to include the recommended dyeing, such as dyeing with henna, and even with katam (indigo) for the purpose of frightening the enemy.
