It is authentically reported from a group of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, that they did this, among them Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. The hadith forbidding it is to be understood as referring to something other than this.

﴿And whoever takes Satan as a guardian instead of Allah﴾, by preferring what he calls to over what Allah the Exalted has commanded, and by transgressing obedience to Allah the Exalted in favor of obedience to him. The qualifier "instead of Allah" is to clarify that following him contradicts following the command of Allah the Exalted, and it is not a restrictive qualifier (ihtiraziyy) as is supposed. As for what is said, that there is not a creature of Allah the Exalted except that you have a guardianship over it if you knew it, and a benefit in its existence if you sought it, and that for this reason guardianship was restricted to being "instead of Allah the Exalted", this arises from heedlessness regarding the realization of the meaning of guardianship. So understand.

﴿Then he has surely suffered a manifest loss﴾, that is, a clear one. And what loss is greater than exchanging Paradise for the Fire? And what transaction is more losing than forfeiting the pleasure of the Most Merciful for the pleasure of Satan?

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 120:

﴿Yaʿiduhum﴾: [He promises them] what He hardly fulfils. It is also said: [the promise is of] victory and safety. And it is said: [it is of] poverty and need, if they spend [in charity]. Al-A'mash read (yaʿidhum) with a sukun on the dal, which is a lightening [of the word] because of the many vowel movements.

﴿Wa-yumanniihim﴾: [He arouses in them] vain wishes. It is also said: [it means] long life in this world and the continuance of its bliss. It is permissible that the meaning of the two clauses is: He makes the promise for them and He makes the wishing for them, in the manner of the saying: "So-and-so gives and withholds." The pronoun of the plural object in (yaʿiduhum wa-yumanniihim) refers back to (man) according to its meaning, just as the singular pronoun of the nominative in (yattakhidh) and (khasira) refers back to it according to its wording. God, glorified is He, informed of the occurrence of the promise and the wishing, along with the occurrence of other things that the accursed one also swore to, because they are among the hidden matters and the strongest causes of misguidance and the snares of deception.

﴿Wa-ma yaʿiduhumu sh-shaytanu illa ghurura﴾: [Ghurur] is causing one to imagine benefit in what contains harm. In my view, this promise and command are of the same kind, either through corrupt thoughts or through the tongue of his allies. The possibility that he takes the form of a human and does what he does is remote. (Ghurura) is either a second object of the verb (promises), or an object of purpose, or an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a promise that is deceptive, or a deceiving one, or it is a verbal noun not from its own verb form, because (yaʿiduhum) is in the sense of "he deceives them with his promise," as al-Samin said. The clause is parenthetical. The wishing is not mentioned because it falls under the category of promise. In al-Bahr: the two are close in meaning, so the first of them was sufficient.

﴿Ulā'ika﴾ (Those) is a demonstrative referring to those who took Satan as a protector, taking into account his meaning (the plural sense of the word for the group). The distance implied in it indicates the remoteness of their station in loss. ﴿Ma'wāhum﴾ (their abode) and their resting place, all of them, ﴿is Jahannam (Hell), and they will find no escape (maḥīṣ) from it﴾. That is, no way of deviation (ma'dal) and no refuge (maharab). It is either a noun of place (ism makān) or a mimi verbal noun (maṣdar mīmī, a verbal noun beginning with mīm) from ḥāṣa, yaḥīṣu, meaning to deviate and turn away. It is said maḥīṣ and maḥāṣ. The original meaning of the root, as has been said, is evasion (al-rawaghān). From it come the expressions "they fell into ḥayṣ bayṣ" and "ḥāṣa bāṣa," meaning they were in a matter from which it is difficult to get free. It is also said ḥāṣa yaḥūṣu, and ḥawṣan and ḥiyāṣan. The phrase (ʿanhā), "from it," is dependent on an omitted element that occupies the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) modifying (maḥīṣan).

They did not allow it to be dependent on (yajidūna), "they find," because (yajidūna) does not take (ʿan) as its complement. Nor (is it dependent) on (maḥīṣan), because if it is a noun of place, it does not govern, since it is assimilated to the invariable nouns (mulḥaq bil-jawāmid). If it is a verbal noun, then the object of a verbal noun (maʿmūl al-maṣdar) may not precede it. Whoever permitted its preceding when it is an adverbial phrase or a prepositional phrase permitted it here.

﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is His words, exalted is He: ﴿We will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the relative clause (al-mawsul) be in the accusative position, governed by a deleted verb that the following words explain. Its weakness is not hidden. This is a promise to the believers following the threat against the disbelievers. Glorified and exalted is He, He joined the two together to add to the joy of His beloved ones and the grief of His enemies. ﴿A promise of Allah, in truth﴾: that is, He promised them a promise and made it true (ahaqqahu haqqan). The first (wa'd Allah) is an emphatic (mu'akkid) for its own content (mu'akkid li-nafsihi), in the sense customary in usage, since the content of the preceding sentence admits of nothing other than it, for a promise is nothing but the report of the conveyance of benefits before they occur.

The second (haqqan) is an emphatic for something else (mu'akkid li-ghayrihi), like your saying "Zayd is standing, in truth." The declarative sentence, considered in itself and apart from its speaker, admits of truth and falsehood, of what is真 and what is false. It is also permitted that wa'dan be in the accusative as an absolute object (masdar) of ﴿We will admit them﴾, according to what Abu al-Baqa' said, without its own verb form, since it carries the meaning of "We promise them the admission into gardens." Then haqqan would be a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of it.

﴿And who is more truthful than Allah in speech?﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to the preceding discourse, emphasizing it. The waw is parenthetical (i'tiradiyya), and al-qil is a verbal noun (masdar) of qala, and al-qal is similar to it.

It is reported from Ibn al-Sikkit that they are two nouns, not verbal nouns, and their accusative is as a specifier (tamyiz). The rhetorical force of the interrogation, the specification of the all-comprehensive divine name, the form of the elative (af'al), and the placing of speech as a specifier are not hidden as expressions of intensification. The intended meaning is to counter the false promises of Satan to his companions, by which they were deceived until they deserved the threat, with the true promise of Allah to His friends, which brings them to the supreme felicity. For this reason He, glorified is He, emphasized and stressed it, urging its attainment and encouraging it.

Some of them claimed that the waw is conjunctive (atifa), and the sentence is conjoined to a deleted element, that is: "Allah has spoken truly," ﴿and who is more truthful than Allah in speech?﴾, meaning: He spoke truly, and none is more truthful than Him. This is not hidden as an artificial construction that is unnecessary, and it seems that what prompted it was heedlessness of the rule of the waw that enters upon the concluding sentence. And the permission that the sentence be a quoted statement of a deleted verb, that is: "and saying: who is more truthful than Allah in speech?", so that it would be a conjunction to "abiding" (khalidin), is more grievous and more bitter.

The Kufan reader other than 'Asim, and Warsh, read the ṣad with the ishmam toward the zay (i.e., pronounced with a partial sound of the zay).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 123:**

﴿It is not by your wishful thinking, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book.﴾ The address is to the believers. *Al-amani* (الأمانِيُّ), whether read with shaddah or without (both readings are attested), is the plural of *umniyyah* (أُمْنِيَّةٌ), on the pattern *uf'uluh* (أُفْعُولَةٌ). As al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, it is "the image formed in the soul from wishing for a thing," that is, its estimation and depiction within the soul. It is said, "*manna lahu al-manni*," meaning the one who decrees has decreed for him, and from this comes the word *maniyyah* (مَنِيَّةٌ), meaning "decreed." *Tamanni* (التَّمَنِّي, wishing or wishful thinking) is often applied to imagining something that has no reality, and from this it is used to express falsehood (الكَذِبِ), because it is the imagining of what has been mentioned and its expression in words. Thus wishing is regarded as its source, which is why it is validly used to express it. From this is the saying of Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him): "I have neither wished nor engaged in *tamanni* since I embraced Islam."

The *ba'* (الباءُ) in (بِأمانِيِّكُمْ) is like the *ba'* in (زَيْدٌ بِالبابِ, "Zayd is at the door"), and it is not superfluous. Superfluity is a possibility, though some scholars rejected it. The subject of (لَيْسَ, "is not") is a pronoun concealed within it, referring to the promise in its verbal sense or to the thing promised. This is *istikhdam* (اسْتِخْدامٌ, a rhetorical device in which one term is used with two referents), as al-Sa'd (al-Sa'd al-Taftazani) said. It has also been said that it refers to the promised reward included in the operative phrase (وَعْدَ اللَّهِ, "the promise of Allah"), or to entry into Paradise, or to righteous deeds. It has been said that it refers to faith (الإيمانِ) understood from (الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا, "those who believed"). It has also been said that it refers to the matter under dispute, supported by the context of the revelation (سَبَبُ النُّزُولِ).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, who said: "Some Muslims, Jews and Christians met. The Jews said to the Muslims: 'We are better than you. Our religion came before your religion, our Book before your Book, and our prophet before your prophet, and we are upon the religion of Ibrahim (Abraham). (And none will enter Paradise except those who are Jews.)' The Christians said the same. The Muslims said: 'Our Book came after your Book, our prophet (ﷺ) after your prophet, and our religion after your religion. You have been commanded to follow us and abandon your affairs. So we are better than you. We are upon the religion of Ibrahim, Isma'il and Ishaq, and none will enter Paradise except those who are upon our religion.' Then Allah revealed: (It is not by your wishful thinking)."

His saying, may He be glorified: ﴿And who is better in religion...﴾ and so on, means: the promise of Allah, or what He promised of reward, or entry into Paradise, or righteous deeds, or faith, or what you disputed about, is not attained merely by your wishful thinking, O Muslims, or by the wishful thinking of the Jews and Christians. It is attained only through striving and exerting oneself (التَّشْمِيرِ عَنْ ساقِ الجِدِّ) in obeying the command. The return of the pronoun to faith understood from what precedes is supported by what Ibn Abi Shaybah related from al-Hasan as a *mawquf* (مَوْقُوفًا, a report ending with a Companion or Successor, not the Prophet ﷺ): "Faith is not by wishful thinking, but it is what settles in the heart and is confirmed by action. Some people were distracted by wishful thinking about forgiveness until they left this world with no good deeds. They said, 'We think well of Allah,' and they lied. Had they thought well of Allah, they would have done good deeds."

Al-Bukhari, in his *Tarikh* (تارِيخِهِ, *History*), related from Anas as a *marfu'* (مَرْفُوعًا, a report traced to the Prophet ﷺ): "Faith is not by wishful thinking nor by adornment, but it is what settles in the heart. As for knowledge of the heart, it is beneficial knowledge, and knowledge of the tongue is a proof against the children of Adam."

It is related from Mujahid and Ibn Zayd that the address is to the polytheists, for they said, "We will not be resurrected and we will not be punished," just as the People of the Book said, (none will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians). This is supported by the fact that there was no mention of the Muslims in the context of wishful thinking, whereas there was mention of the polytheists in that regard. The meaning is: the matter is not by the wishful thinking of the polytheists and their saying that there is no resurrection and no punishment, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book and what they said. Allah, may He be glorified, established this with His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾, whether in this world or in the Hereafter.

Al-Tirmidhi and others related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) when this verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O Abu Bakr, shall I recite to you a verse that was revealed to me?' I said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah,' and he recited it to me. I felt a snapping in my back, so that I stretched myself because of it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'What is the matter with you, O Abu Bakr?' I said: 'May my father and mother be sacrificed for you, O Messenger of Allah! Which of us has not done evil, and will we not be recompensed for every evil we have done?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'As for you, O Abu Bakr, and your companions who are believers, you will be recompensed for it in this world, until you meet Allah with no sins upon you. As for the others, it will be gathered for them until they are recompensed on the Day of Resurrection.'"

Muslim and others related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When this verse was revealed, it grieved the Muslims greatly, and it affected them to the extent that Allah willed. They complained of this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Be steadfast and aim for moderation, for everything that afflicts a Muslim is an expiation, even the thorn that pricks him or the setback that befalls him.'"

The hadiths with this meaning are too numerous to count. For this reason, the majority of scholars agreed that illnesses, diseases, the calamities of this world and its worries, even if their hardship is slight, are by which Allah expiates sins.

The majority also hold that they raise a person's ranks, and that good deeds are recorded by them. This is the sound view on which reliance is placed, for it is authentically reported through more than one chain: "No Muslim is pricked by a thorn or anything more than it, except that a rank is recorded for him by it and a sin is erased from him by it."

The judge (al-Qadi) related from some scholars that these only expiate sins and do not raise any rank. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud: "Pain does not earn a reward, but sins are expiated by it." This view relied on the hadiths that mention only expiation, and it did not reach them, the authentic hadiths that explicitly state the raising of ranks and the recording of good deeds.

The matter remains as to whether these expiate major sins (al-kaba'ir, الكَبائِرُ) or not. The apparent meaning of the hadiths, including the report of Abu Bakr, is that they do expiate them. A sound report from Aisha has come: "Indeed, the servant comes out of his sins by means of this, as red gold comes out of the furnace."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi related from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Headache and fever will not cease to afflict the Muslim person until they leave him like white silver." And there are other reports to this effect.

It is not hidden that keeping this on its apparent meaning is something their statement rejects. Some of them restricted the recompense to the Hereafter, and restricted (مَن, "whoever") to the polytheists and the People of the Book.

This was related from al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd, who said: "This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do We recompense anyone except the ungrateful?﴾" It has also been said that the intended meaning of evil here is polytheism (الشِّرْكُ). Ibn Jurayj related this from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) and Ibn Jubayr. Both views contradict the apparent meaning.

In the verse there is a refutation of the Murji'ah (المُرْجِئَةُ, a theological school holding that sin does not harm faith), who said: "Disobedience does not harm alongside faith, just as obedience does not benefit alongside disbelief."

﴿And he will not find for himself, besides Allah, a protector (وَلِيًّا)﴾, meaning one who goes beyond the guardianship and support of Allah, ﴿who would take charge of his affairs and defend him, and repel what descends upon him of the punishment of Allah, nor a helper (نَصِيرًا)﴾, meaning one who would help him and save him from the punishment of Allah when it befalls him.

There is no evidence in the verse for those who deny forgiveness to the disobedient, since the generality in it is specified by the repentant, by consensus. And once the door of specification is opened, there is no barrier to specifying it also by those whom Allah, may He be exalted, graciously pardons, in accordance with what other evidences indicate.

﴿Whoever does﴾ of the deeds ﴿righteous ones﴾, meaning some of them and a portion of them, because no one can do all righteous deeds, and many a person who is accountable has no obligation of Hajj, no zakat, and no jihad. So ﴿مِن﴾ (min) is partitive (tab'iḍiyyah, indicating a part of a whole). It has been said that it is superfluous (za'idah), and al-Tabarsi chose this view, but it is weak. Restricting ﴿الصالحات﴾ (al-salihat, the righteous deeds) to the obligatory duties, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, is contrary to the apparent meaning.

His saying, glorified is He, ﴿مِن ذَكَرٍ أَوْ أُنثَى﴾ (min dhakarin aw unthā, "whether male or female"), is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿يَعْمَلْ﴾ (ya'mal, "does"), and ﴿مِن﴾ (min) is explicative (bayaniyyah).

It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from ﴿الصالحات﴾ (al-salihat), with ﴿مِن﴾ being initial (ibtida'iyyah), meaning "originating from a male," and so on. This has been objected to as not sound in meaning. Nevertheless, the more evident is to estimate ﴿كائِنًا﴾ (ka'inan, masculine) rather than ﴿كائِنَةً﴾ (ka'inatan, feminine), because it is a circumstantial clause from ﴿شَيْئًا﴾ (shay'an, "something") of them.

That the meaning be "the righteous deeds issuing from males and females" is of no benefit, due to the awkwardness in that. Perhaps the specifying of the doer as male or female is to rebuke the polytheists for their killing of their daughters and for depriving them of inheritance.

His exalted saying, ﴿وَهُوَ مُؤْمِنٌ﴾ (wa huwa mu'min, "while he is a believer"), is also a circumstantial clause. The condition that the deed be accompanied by faith in order to earn the reward mentioned in what follows is an indication that no account is taken of it without faith. It also serves to repel the supposition that a righteous deed benefits the disbeliever, since it is paired with mention of the evil deed, which harms both believer and disbeliever. The masculine form is used to give precedence to the male over the female, as has been said. You have already been given, shortly before, what benefits you, so reflect on it.

﴿فَأُولَئِكَ﴾ (fa-ulā'ika, "those") refers back to ﴿مَن﴾ (man, "whoever") under the description of its being characterized by righteous deeds and faith. The plural is used in consideration of its meaning, just as the earlier singular was used in consideration of its wording. The sense of distance in it (the use of ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ rather than a proximate demonstrative) has been explained more than once.

﴿يَدْخُلُونَ الْجَنَّةَ﴾ (yadkhulūna al-jannah, "they will enter Paradise") as a reward for their deeds. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Abu Ja'far read ﴿يُدْخَلُونَ﴾ (yudkhalūna) in the passive voice, from the causative (al-id'khal).

Page 154

﴿وَلَا يُظْلَمُونَ نَقِيرًا﴾ (wa lā yuẓlamūna naqīran, "and they will not be wronged even a naqir") means they will not be deprived of anything, however small, of the reward of their deeds. The naqir is a term for the smallest and most insignificant amount, and its origin is a small hollow in the back of a date pit, from which the palm tree sprouts. From the negation of diminishing the reward of the obedient, the negation of increasing the punishment of the disobedient follows a fortiori, because the harm in increasing punishment is greater than in diminishing reward. If He does not accept the first, while He is the Most Merciful of the merciful, how would He accept the second? This is the secret of specifying the absence of diminution of reward in the statement, rather than mentioning the absence of an increase in punishment, although the context is one of encouragement to righteous deeds, so only this fits it. The sentence is a concluding summary (tadhyil) of what precedes it, or a coordinated clause (\'atf) upon it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 125:**

[p. 155]

﴿Who is better in religion than one who submits his face to God﴾. That is: who sincerely devotes himself to Him, the Exalted, recognising no lord for himself other than Him. It is also said: who sincerely directs his attention to Him, glorified is He. And it is said: who offers his face to Him, mighty and majestic is He, in prostration. The interrogative (al-istifham) is one of denial (inkari), and it carries the sense of negation. The intended meaning is to praise the one who does this in the most perfect manner. The word *dinan* ("in religion") is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of *ahsanu* ("better"), transferred from the subject. The underlying sense is: "And who has a religion better than the religion of one who submitted…", and so the statement comes to mean the preference of one religion over another. In this there is an indication that the servant turning himself entirely to God, the Exalted, is the highest rank that human capacity can attain. The phrase *mimman* ("than one who") is connected to *ahsanu*, and so is the august Name (God). It has also been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from *wajhahu* ("his face").

﴿while he is a doer of good﴾. That is: one who performs good deeds and abstains from evil deeds. Or: one who performs righteous deeds in the proper manner, which is their descriptive goodness, entailing their intrinsic goodness. It is authentically reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about *ihsan* (excellence), and he (ﷺ) said: "That you worship God as though you see Him; and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you." It has also been said: the more apparent view is that it means "while he is a doer of good in his belief," and this is what is meant by the one who said: "that is, while he is a monotheist (muwahhid)." On this basis, it is better to interpret submitting one's face to God as yielding to Him, glorified is He, through deeds. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of *aslama* ("submitted").

﴿and follows the religion of Abraham﴾, the one that is consistent with the religion of Islam, agreed upon as sound. This is a conjunction (atf) upon *aslama*. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿as a hanif﴾, that is, inclining away from the deviant religions, is a circumstantial clause from "Abraham." It has also been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the subject of *ittaba'a* ("followed").

﴿And God took Abraham as a khalil﴾. This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) brought to encourage following his religion, peace be upon him, and to announce that it is the pinnacle of goodness. The mention of his name, peace be upon him, is for exalting him and explicitly stating that he is the one praised. It is not permissible to make it a conjunction upon "who is better" etc., contrary to the view of someone who claimed this, whether it is a digression (istitrad) or a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh). Its purpose is to affirm the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds﴾, and to clarify what the righteous deeds are and who the believer is, since there is no fitting connection. The conjunction between the conjoined and the conjoining element achieves what it achieves of emphasis and clarification. It is also not a relative clause (silat) of *man* ("one who"), since it is unsuitable for that. That its conjunction upon ﴿and he is a doer of good﴾ is invalid is clearer than needing elaboration. Making the clause circumstantial with an implied *qad* is contrary to the apparent sense. A conjunction upon ﴿as a hanif﴾ is valid only with artifice. The word *khalil* is derived from *khullah*, with a *damma* on the *kha'*. It is either from *khilal*, with a *kasra* on the *kha'*, for it is an affection that permeates the soul and mingles with it in an inward mixing. So the khalil is one whose affection has reached this rank, as the poet said:

*You have penetrated the path of the spirit within me, and for this reason the khalil is called khalil.*
*When I speak, you are my speech; and when I am silent, you are my anguish.*

Or it is from *khalal*, as has been said, in the sense that each of the two friends repairs the other's deficiency. Or it is from *khall* with a *fatha*, which is a path in the sand, because they agree upon one way. Or it is from *khallah* with a *fatha* on the *kha'*, meaning a trait or disposition, because they agree in qualities and characters. It has come in a report: "A person is upon the religion of his close friend, so let each of you look at whom he befriends." Or it is in the sense of poverty and need, because each of them needs the other's connection and is not self-sufficient. As for its application to Abraham, peace be upon him, it has been said: because the love of God has permeated his soul and mingled with it completely. Or because he took on the character of God, exalted is He. From this it is that he used to honour the guest and be good to him, even if he were an unbeliever, for among the attributes of God, exalted is He, is goodness to both the righteous and the wicked. In some reports, of which I am not certain of the authenticity: "A guest from outside his community came to him, and he said to him: 'Affirm the oneness of God, that I may host you and be good to you.' He said: 'O Abraham, for the sake of a morsel I would abandon my religion and the religion of my fathers.' So he departed from him. God, exalted is He, revealed to him: 'O Abraham, he has spoken the truth! I have been providing for him for seventy years while he associates others with Me, and you want him to abandon his religion and the religion of his fathers for the sake of a morsel?' So Abraham, peace be upon him, caught up with him and asked him to return so that he could host him, and apologised to him. The polytheist said to him: 'O Abraham, what has changed for you?' He said: 'My Lord has rebuked me concerning you, and said: "I have been providing for him for seventy years despite his disbelief in Me, and you want him to abandon his religion and the religion of his fathers for the sake of a morsel?!"' The polytheist said: 'Has this really happened? Such a One ought to be worshipped!' So he embraced Islam and returned with Abraham, peace be upon him, to his home."

Then afterwards His generosity embraced the creation of God from every arrival who came to him. When it was said to him about this, he said: "I learned generosity from my Lord. I saw Him not neglecting His enemies, so I will not neglect them either." God revealed to him: "You are truly My khalil."

Al-Bayhaqi related in (al-Shu'ab) from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O Gabriel, why did God take Abraham as a khalil?" He said: "For his feeding of food, O Muhammad." It has also been said, and al-Balkhi and al-Farra' preferred it, that it was for his display of poverty and need before God, his devotion to Him, and his not turning towards anyone else, as his saying to Gabriel, peace be upon him, when he said to him on the day he was thrown into the fire, indicates: "Do you have any need?" He said: "As for you, no." Then he said: "God is sufficient for me, and He is the best Guardian." Other explanations have been given for the reason he, peace be upon him, was called the khalil of God. The well-known view is that the khalil is below the habib (beloved).

It is supported by what al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: "Some of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) were sitting waiting for him, and he came out until, when he drew near to them, he heard them discussing. He heard their conversation, and one of them was saying: 'God has taken a khalil from among His creation: Abraham is His khalil.' Another said: 'What is more marvellous than that God spoke to Moses directly?' Another said: 'Jesus is the Spirit of God and His Word.' Another said: 'Adam, God chose him.' So he came out to them and greeted them, and said: 'I have heard your speech and your wonder. Indeed Abraham is the khalil of God, and so he is. Moses is His interlocutor, and Jesus is His Spirit and His Word, and so he is. Adam, God chose him, and so he is. Yet know that I am the habib of God, and I say this without boasting. I am the first intercessor and the first whose intercession is accepted, and I say this without boasting. I am the first to move the rings of Paradise, and God opens it for me, and the poor among the believers enter with me, and I say this without boasting. I am the most honoured of the first and the last on the Day of Resurrection, and I say this without boasting.'"

Al-Tirmidhi related in (Nawadir al-Usul), and al-Bayhaqi in (al-Shu'ab), though he weakened it, and Ibn Asakir and al-Daylami, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God took Abraham as a khalil, and Moses as one who converses intimately (najiy), and He took me as a habib. Then He said: 'By My might, I will certainly prefer My habib over My khalil and My intimate.'" The apparent sense from the words of the researchers is that khullah is a rank among the ranks of love, that love has a wider circle, that among its ranks is what the aspiration of the khalil, peace be upon him, does not reach, and this is the rank established for him (ﷺ). And that our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, has attained of the station of khullah what his father Abraham, peace be upon him, did not attain. The branch contains what the root contains and more. What guides you to this is that conforming to the character of God, exalted is He, which is one of the effects of khullah, is more apparent and more complete in our Prophet (ﷺ) than in Abraham, peace be upon him, for it is authentically reported that his character was the Qur'an. And it came from him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, that he said: "I was sent to perfect noble character." And God, exalted is He, testified to him with His saying: ﴿And indeed you are of a tremendous character﴾. The source of honouring the guest is mercy, and the all-encompassing throne of that mercy is the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾. For this reason he, peace and blessings be upon him, was the Seal.

Al-Hakim related and authenticated from Jundub that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say before he died: "God has taken me as a khalil, just as He took Abraham as a khalil." The comparison is in the manner of ﴿Fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you﴾, in one opinion. It has been said that the word *yutawaffa* ("he dies") does not indicate that the station of khullah came after the station of love, as is not hidden.

In the wording of love and khullah there is enough for the knower to see the difference between them, and it guides him to know which of the two circles is wider. Some eminent scholars held that the verse is an allegorical metaphor (isti'ara tamthiliyya), to declare God free of having a companion or a friend, and that the meaning is that He chose him and specified him with an honour resembling the honour of a khalil with his khalil. As for the khalil alone, it is an explicit metaphor (isti'ara tasrihiyya), as al-Shihab stated. Yet afterwards it became a proper name for Abraham, peace be upon him.

Some claimed that there is no barrier to describing Abraham, peace be upon him, as khalil literally, in the sense of the sincere one, or one who has purified and perfected affection, or something similar. The fact that the term khalil is not applied to anyone else, peace be upon him, although the station of khullah in the well-known sense among the knowers is not specific to him, since every prophet is a khalil of God, is either because that station was established for him in a way not established for others, as has been said, or because of the increase of honour and exaltation, as we say. Some Christians objected: if it is permissible to apply the term khalil to a human as an honour, why is it not permissible to apply the term son (ibn) to another for that same reason? It is answered that khullah does not entail sameness of kind, unlike sonship, which definitely entails it. God, exalted is He, is far removed from resemblance to created things.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 126 (part 1 of 2):

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ This may be connected to His saying, ﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits himself to Allah while being a doer of good?﴾ and what lies between them is an interjection, meaning: all the existing things in the heights and the depths belong to Allah, the Exalted, in creation and in ownership, and nothing of them goes out of His dominion. So He recompenses each one according to what its deeds require: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil. It may also be connected to His saying, glorified is His majesty, ﴿And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend﴾, on the basis that its meaning is "chose him and selected him." That is, He owns all His creation, so He chooses whomever He wills of them, such as Abraham, peace be upon him. Thus it is to show that his selection, peace be upon him, was by the sheer will of Allah, the Exalted.

It was also said: it is to show that Allah's taking Abraham, peace be upon him, as a khalil (intimate friend) is not because He needs anything of His own matters, as is the habit of created beings, since the basis of their friendship is the need of some of them for others in their interests. Rather, it is merely for the sake of His honouring and ennobling him. Also in it is an indication that his intimacy, peace be upon him, does not take him out of servitude to Allah, the Exalted.

﴿And Allah is ever encompassing of all things﴾: encompassment of knowledge and power. This is on the basis that the true meaning of encompassment (ihatah) applies to bodies, so Allah is not described with it, and therefore interpretation (ta'wil) and recourse to figurative usage (majaz) is necessary, as the later scholars (al-Khalaf) held. The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyil) confirming what precedes it according to all its aspects.

* * *

This, and from the allusive (ishari) interpretation of the verses: ﴿And when you travel through the earth﴾, that is, you journey in the land of readiness (isti'dad) to fight the enemy of the self, or to attain the states of perfections. ﴿There is no blame upon you if you shorten the prayer﴾, that is, reduce the bodily acts [p. 157] ﴿if you fear that those who disbelieved will harm you﴾, that is, those veiled from the truth by the faculties of imagination and fancy. The essence of this is a concession to the people of the path: when they fear the trial of the faculties, they may reduce the bodily acts and increase the acts of the heart, such as thought and remembrance, so that the heart becomes clear and its light shines upon the faculties, and their harm lessens. Then the bodily acts become pure. But according to the people of special attainment, it is not permissible to abandon the obligations for this reason, as some ignorant people claimed.

﴿And when you are among them﴾, and you are not absent from them by your journeying into the depths of the Unseen and the majesty of witnessing, swimming in the seas of "For me with Allah there is a time when neither a close angel nor a sent prophet can contain me." ﴿and you establish the prayer for them﴾, that is, the bodily acts. ﴿Let a group of them stand with you﴾, and let them do as you do. ﴿And let them take their weapons﴾ from the faculties of the spirit, and let them gather their senses, so that resemblance to you may be possible for them, or so that they may comprehend the secrets in your action and the whisperings will not mislead them. ﴿When they have prostrated﴾, and reached the goal in knowing what you have established for them, and performed it in its proper manner, ﴿then let them be behind you﴾, repelling from you the objections of the ignorant, or attending to your necessary needs. ﴿And let another group come who have not prayed﴾ yet ﴿and let them pray with you﴾, and let them do as you do. ﴿And let them take their precaution and their weapons﴾, as the first group took their weapons. He commanded these to take precaution as well only to urge them to greater caution, lest they fall short in it, relying on those who took first from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to take afterward.

The summary of this allusion is that teaching the laws and etiquettes to the seekers should be given to one group after another among them, so that it takes firmer root in them. It was said: the first group is an allusion to the elite, and the second to the common people. For this reason, in the first only the command to take weapons was given, while in the second the command to take precaution was also added. ﴿Those who disbelieved wish that you would be heedless of your weapons﴾, and they are the faculties of the commanding self (nafs ammarah), ﴿and your goods﴾, which are the divine knowledges, ﴿so that they could come down upon you in one charge﴾, and strike you with the arrows of calamities and doubts and destroy you. ﴿And there is no blame upon you if rain has caused you discomfort﴾, namely a downpour ﴿of rain﴾, meaning the rain of the clouds of manifestations, ﴿or if you are ill﴾ with the fever of longing and passion, and you are unable to perform the acts of the spiritual faculties, ﴿to lay down your weapons﴾ and abandon the acts of those faculties until those clouds clear, the rain ceases, the ground of your hearts is stirred by the flowers of the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, and the fever of longing is extinguished by the waters of nearness. ﴿And take your precaution﴾ when laying down your weapons, and guard your hearts from turning to anything other than Allah, the Exalted. ﴿Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers﴾ from the soul's faculties ﴿a humiliating punishment﴾, that is, one that degrades them. This happens when the heart is guarded and the spirit's oven is kindled.

﴿And when you have completed the prayer﴾, that is, performed it, ﴿then remember Allah﴾ in all states, ﴿standing﴾ in the station of the spirit through witnessing, ﴿and sitting﴾ in the place of the heart through unveiling, ﴿and on your sides﴾, that is, your turnings in the place of the self through striving. ﴿And when you become secure﴾, and reach the place of permanence, ﴿then establish the prayer﴾, perform it in its most complete form, because the heart is then free from the self's whisperings, which are like ritual impurity (hadath) according to the people of special attainment. ﴿Indeed, prayer has been enjoined upon the believers at fixed times﴾, so it does not drop from them as long as the intellect and life remain. ﴿And do not weaken in pursuit of the people﴾ who fight against you, and they are the self and its faculties, ﴿for indeed they suffer as you suffer﴾ from them, because you prevent them from their desires, ﴿and you hope from Allah﴾, that is, you hope from Him, glorified is He, ﴿that which they do not hope﴾, because you hope to enjoy the garden of nearness and witnessing, and that does not occur to them at all. Or you fear separation, while they do not fear it. ﴿And Allah is ever Knowing﴾, so He knows your states and theirs, ﴿Wise﴾, so He bestows upon the receptive ones according to their receptivities.

﴿Indeed We have sent down to you the Book﴾, that is, the knowledge of the details of the attributes and the rulings of their manifestations, ﴿in truth﴾, you being clothed with that Book in truthfulness, or you standing by the truth not by yourself. ﴿That you may judge between the people﴾, the elite among them and the common among them, ﴿by what Allah has shown you﴾, that is, by what Allah, glorified is He, has taught you of wisdom. [p. 158] ﴿And do not be a pleader for the treacherous﴾, those who did not fulfil the trust of Allah, the Exalted, which was deposited with them from eternity, of what was mentioned in their readiness, namely the possibility of obeying Him and complying with His command. ﴿Disputant﴾, defending them from punishment, and giving the creatures power over them in humiliation and disgrace. Or it means you say to Allah, the Exalted: "O Lord, why did You forsake them and subdue them, for they are wrongdoers?" Yet Allah, the Exalted, has the conclusive proof against them.

﴿And seek forgiveness from Allah﴾ for the natural inclination that the mercy which encompassed you required. ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾, so He does what you ask of Him and more. ﴿And do not argue﴾ on behalf of anyone from ﴿those who betray themselves﴾ by squandering the rights of their souls. ﴿Indeed Allah does not love one who is a habitual betrayer﴾ of his own self, ﴿sinful﴾, one who commits sin, inclining toward the desires.

﴿They hide from people﴾ by concealing their vices and the attributes of their souls, ﴿but they cannot hide from Allah﴾ by removing and uprooting them, ﴿while He is with them﴾, encompassing their outward and inward states, ﴿when they plot by night﴾, that is, they devise in the darkness of the world of the self and nature, ﴿what He does not approve of in speech﴾, of imaginings and corrupt fancies. ﴿And Allah is ever encompassing of what they do﴾, so He will recompense them according to their deeds.

﴿And whoever does evil﴾ by the manifestation of an attribute of his self, ﴿or wrongs himself﴾ by the lack of some of its perfections, ﴿then seeks forgiveness from Allah﴾, and asks Him to cover that by turning to Him and humbling himself before Him, ﴿he will find Allah Forgiving, Merciful﴾, so He covers and gives what the readiness requires. ﴿And whoever earns a sin﴾ by displaying some vices, ﴿or a sin﴾ by erasing what is in the readiness, ﴿then throws it upon an innocent﴾, by saying: "Allah made me do it," or "So-and-so made me do it." ﴿He has indeed borne a slander and a manifest sin﴾, since he did the act and attributed his action to another. Had he not been ready for that and seeking it by the tongue of readiness from eternity, it would not have been bestowed upon him nor would it have come forth into the courtyard of existence. For this reason the accursed Iblis silenced his followers with what Allah, the Exalted, related to us of his saying: ﴿Indeed Allah promised you the promise of truth﴾ until he said: ﴿So do not blame me, but blame yourselves.﴾ (Translator's note: the source closes the quotation here with an unbalanced bracket.)

﴿And were it not for the grace of Allah upon you﴾, that is, His enabling and support for travelling His path, and His mercy, since He bestowed upon you absolute perfection, ﴿a group of them would have resolved to mislead you, but they mislead none but themselves﴾, because its harm returns to them, and because He guards you in the fortresses of your readiness from anything of that reaching you. ﴿And He sent down upon you the Book﴾ comprehending the details of knowledge and wisdom, which are the rulings of those details together with action, ﴿and wisdom﴾, ﴿and taught you what you did not know﴾ of the knowledge of the outcomes of creation and the knowledge of what was and what will be. ﴿And the grace of Allah upon you has been immense﴾, since He made you fit for the station of ﴿two bow-lengths or closer﴾ and graced you with what none but the scope of existence can encompass.

﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk﴾, which is what belongs to the category of idle matters that do not concern anyone, except (illa) the secret talk of ﴿one who enjoins charity﴾ and guides to the virtue of generosity arising from chastity, ﴿or kindness﴾, verbal, such as teaching knowledge, or practical, such as relieving the distressed, ﴿or reconciliation between people﴾, which belongs to the category of justice. ﴿And whoever does that﴾ and combines the perfections ﴿seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾, not for show and reputation, from everything by which virtue returns to being vice, ﴿We will give him a great reward﴾ from Allah, the Exalted, and He will admit him into the gardens of attributes.

﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger﴾, that is, contradicts what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought, or the intellect, which they call the "self-messenger," ﴿and follows other than the way of the believers﴾, that is, other than what the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and those who followed their path among the righteous held, or the spiritual faculties, ﴿We will leave him to what he has turned to and drive him into Hell﴾ of deprivation, ﴿and evil is it as a destination﴾ for whoever burns in it.

﴿They call upon none besides Him except females﴾, which are the idols called by the names of the selves, since everyone who worships other than Allah, the Exalted, is in fact worshipping his own self, obeying its desires. Or the intended meaning of "females" is the contingent beings (mumkinat), since every contingent being is in need, deficient in terms of its contingency, passive and affected when determined, so it is the most like every thing to the female. ﴿And they call upon none but a rebellious devil﴾, namely the devil of fancy, since they accepted his seduction and obeyed him. ﴿Allah has cursed him﴾, that is, removed him far from the gardens of His nearness. ﴿And he said: "I will surely take from among Your servants a determined portion,"﴾ namely those who are not sincere, who were excepted in another verse, ﴿and I will mislead them﴾ from the true path, ﴿and I will arouse in them false desires﴾, from seeking fleeting pleasures, ﴿and I will command them so they will cut off the ears of cattle﴾, that is, they will cut off the ears of their souls from hearing what benefits them, ﴿and I will command them so they will alter the creation of Allah﴾, which is the natural disposition (fitrah) upon which Allah created people, of monotheism. ﴿But those who believe﴾, and affirmed the oneness of Allah, did good deeds, and remained steadfast, ﴿We will admit them into gardens﴾, the garden of actions, the garden of attributes, and the garden of the Essence.

﴿It is not by your wishful thinking, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book﴾, that is, the attainment of what is promised is not by wishes; rather, striving in what it requires is necessary. There is a saying: "Wishing is the capital of the bankrupt." ﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah﴾, that is, better in condition, ﴿surrenders himself to Him and is annihilated in Him﴾, ﴿while being a doer of good﴾, witnessing all in the very view of preference, following the path of excellence through steadfastness in deeds, ﴿and follows the religion of Abraham﴾ in monotheism, ﴿as a ḥanīf﴾, inclining away from all besides Him. ﴿And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend (khalil)﴾, since knowledge permeated all his parts insofar as he was composite, so no single atom remained but that the knowledge of his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, had dwelt in it. Thus he knows Him with every part of himself. From here it was said: when the blood of al-Hallaj fell upon the earth, it was inscribed with every drop of it: "Allah." And he recited:

Not a limb has been severed from me, nor a joint, but in it there is a remembrance for you.

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ Because everything that comes into existence is one of His affairs, glorified is He. ﴿And Allah is ever, of all things, Encompassing.﴾ In that He is the One who bestows generosity upon it, and He is the Lord of bounty and munificence. There is no lord besides Him, and none is hoped for except His good.

**Page 160**

﴿They ask you for a ruling concerning women.﴾ That is, they ask you to clarify the difficult rulings concerning women, those that are obligatory for them and upon them, in general. The Prophet ﷺ was asked about many rulings related to them. What had been explained earlier is referred back to what has been revealed about it in the Book, and what had not yet been explained is explained here. Many scholars have said that the intended meaning is: "They ask you about their inheritance." The indication of this is the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul). Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jubayr that he said: "No one inherited except a man who had reached the age of standing up to deal with property and working with it. A child did not inherit, nor did a woman, anything. When the inheritance verses in Surat al-Nisa' were revealed, this was difficult for people, and they said: 'Shall a child who cannot deal with property inherit, and a woman who is likewise, so that both inherit as a man inherits?!' They hoped that some event would come from heaven concerning this, so they waited. When they saw that no event came, they said: 'If this is established, it is indeed obligatory and there is no escape from it.' Then they said: 'Ask the Prophet ﷺ.' So Allah Most High revealed this verse."

Abd ibn Humayd related from Mujahid that he said: "The people of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period) did not give women or children any inheritance. They used to say: 'They do not fight, nor do they acquire any good (spoils).' So this verse was revealed."

al-Hakim related it and authenticated it from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, something similar. Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Abi al-Sharif?) inclined to the first view.

﴿Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning them.﴾ That is, He clarifies for you His ruling concerning them. Ifta' (giving a legal ruling) means making the difficulty clear to the questioner. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) it is said: one says "aftahu ifta'an, wa futya, wa fatwa" (he gave him a ruling), and "aftaytu fulanan ru'yah" means "I interpreted his dream for him."

﴿And what is recited to you in the Book﴾. There are three possibilities for the word Arabic *ma* (what): nominative, accusative, and genitive.

On the first (nominative): it may be a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence) with the khabar (predicate) omitted, meaning: "And what is recited to you in the Qur'an gives you a ruling and makes clear to you." The use of the imperfect form (yutla, "is recited") indicates the continuity and perpetuity of recitation. The phrase *fi al-kitab* ("in the Book") is connected to *yutla* or to an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the pronoun within it, meaning: "recited, being in the Book." Or it may be a mubtada' with *fi al-kitab* as its khabar; in that case "the Book" means the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), since if it meant its apparent sense, there would be no benefit unless it is forced. The sentence is then parenthetical, given to explain the great status of what is recited ("and what is recited"), encompassing what has been recited and what will be recited.

Or it may be conjoined to the hidden pronoun in *yuftikum* ("gives you a ruling"), and this is valid because of the separation and the combination of the literal and the metaphorical. Rational metonymy (al-majaz al-'aqli) is common and acceptable, so it is not objected that Allah Most High is the true agent of the verb while what is recited is a metaphorical agent, and attributing it to it is of the kind of attributing an act to its cause, so the conjunction would not be valid. A similar example is: "Zayd and his gift enriched me." Or it may be conjoined to the Exalted Name (Allah), and this objection also does not apply. However, it is more apparent that this conjunction is of a singular noun conjoined to a singular noun, and the singular form of the pronoun distances this, as is clear.

On the second (accusative): it is the object (maf'ul) of an omitted verb, meaning: "And He clarifies for you what is recited." The sentence is either conjoined to the sentence *yuftikum*, or parenthetical.

On the third (genitive): it may be in the position of the genitive by the oath which indicates the exalting and magnifying of the one sworn by, as if it were said: "Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and He swears by what is recited to you in the Book." Or it may be conjoined to the genitive pronoun, as transmitted from Muhammad ibn Abi Musa. But what the Basrans hold is not revelation so that it must be followed. Yes, there is a meaningful defect in this that is hard to remove. Or it may be conjoined to *al-nisa'* ("women"), as al-Tabarsi transmitted from some of them, and what is wrong with it is not hidden.

Allah's words, ﴿concerning the orphan women﴾ (*fi yatama al-nisa'*), are connected to *yutla* ("is recited") in most of the possibilities, meaning: "what is recited to you concerning their affair." They prohibited this when *ma* is a mubtada' with *fi al-kitab* as its khabar, because it would require separating the parts of the relative clause (sila) by the predicate. Likewise on the assumption of the oath, since there is no sense in restricting the recited matter to this in an apparent way. They also allowed that it be a badal (apposition) of *fihinna* ("concerning them"), and that it be another sila of *yuftikum*. When two prepositions are required to be connected to one thing without conjunction, this is resolved by holding that they do not have the same meaning, and what is prohibited is their being so connected when they have one and the same meaning.

In the second (fi), here there is a causal sense, as in the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat." So the sentence is like: "I came to you on Friday concerning the matter of Zayd," meaning: because of it. The idafa (construct) of "orphans" to "women" is in the sense of *min* (of), since it is the idafa of a thing to its kind. Abu Hayyan made it in the sense of *li* (for), meaning specification, and claimed that this is more apparent, but it is nothing, as al-Halabi and others said.

It was read as *yayama* with two yas (yayama), taking it as the plural of *ayyim* (widow/unmarried woman), and the Arabs often change the hamza into ya.

﴿Those to whom you do not give what is prescribed for them﴾. That is, what has been prescribed for them of inheritance and other things, according to what Shaykh al-Islam chose; or what has been prescribed for them of inheritance only, according to what is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid, may Allah be pleased with him, and which al-Tabari chose; or what has become due to them of dowry, according to what is reported from ʿA'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and which al-Jubba'i chose. It was also said: what has been prescribed for them of marriage, since the guardians used to prevent them from marrying. This is reported from al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Suddi and Ibrahim.

﴿and you desire to marry them﴾ is conjoined to the sila (relative clause) of *allati* ("those whom"), or to the negated verb alone. It is also allowed that it be a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the subject of *tu'tunahunna* ("you give them"). If we hold that a present circumstantial clause may be joined with the conjunction *wa*, then it is obvious. If we hold that it is not permitted, then one must assume an omitted subject, meaning: "while you desire..."

﴿to marry them﴾, that is, concerning marrying them. As is reported in more than one tradition, the guardians of orphans used to desire them if they were beautiful, and they would consume their property; otherwise they would withhold them, out of greed for their inheritance. Omitting the preposition here is not considered ambiguity but generality, so each of the two prepositions is intended alternately. Some of our companions (Hanafi scholars) used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of marrying an orphan girl, since it mentions desire for marrying her, which implies that it is permitted. The Shafi'is say that it mentions what the Jahiliyyah used to do, in the manner of censure, so there is no proof in it for that. Moreover, desire to marry her does not necessarily entail doing so while she is young. This disagreement concerns other than the father and the grandfather; as for them, it is permitted for them to marry off a minor without any disagreement.

﴿and the weak among the children﴾
**Page 161**

This is conjoined to ﴿orphan women﴾, and they used not to give them inheritance, just as they did not give it to women, as mentioned just before.

﴿and that you stand for the orphans with justice﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it. If *fi yatama* is taken as a badal, then the accusative is the appropriate form in this part; and *al-mustad'afin* (the weak) is conjoined to the position of *fihinna* (in the genitive position). They prohibited conjunction to the badal, on the basis that the intended meaning of "the weak" is children in general, those whom they prevented from inheritance even if they were male. If it were conjoined to the badal, it would be a badal, and the only valid kind would be badal al-ghalat (the apposition of error), which does not occur in eloquent speech. It was also allowed for *an taqumu* ("that you stand") to be in the nominative, as a mubtada' with an omitted khabar, meaning: "is good" or the like; and in the accusative, by an omitted verb, meaning: "and He commands you that you stand." This is an address to the rulers, that they look after them and secure their rights, or to the guardians and executors, to be just toward them.

﴿And whatever good you do﴾ concerning the rights of those mentioned, ﴿as you are commanded﴾, or whatever good you do in general, which includes what concerns these people as a primary inclusion.

﴿Indeed Allah is ever Knowing of it﴾, so He will reward you for it. He limited it to good because it is what He encourages. In this there is an indication that evil is something that should not occur from them, nor even cross their minds.

And if a woman fears (this begins an explanation of rulings that were not explained before).

Al-Tirmidhi related it and graded it hasan, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Sawda (may Allah be pleased with her) feared that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would divorce her, so she said: 'O Messenger of Allah, do not divorce me, and give my day to 'A'isha.' So he did, and this verse was revealed."

Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) related from Ibn al-Musayyib: "The daughter of Muhammad ibn Maslama was married to Rafi' ibn Khadij, and he disliked something in her, either her age or something else, so he wanted to divorce her. She said: 'Do not divorce me, and allot to me whatever you wish.' So they agreed upon a settlement, and the sunna went by that, and the Qur'an was revealed."

Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid that it was revealed concerning Abu al-Sa'ib.

That is: "And if a woman fears" (khafat). This is an instance of ishtighal (the construction in which the verb is occupied with a pronoun referring back to the noun that precedes it). The Kufans claimed that "imra'a" (woman) is the mubtada' (subject) and what follows is the khabar (predicate), but this view is not the accepted one. Some scholars estimated here "kanat" (was), on the basis of the frequent deletion of kana after in, and did not regard this as ishtighal; this contradicts the well-known view of the majority.

The fear is either in its literal sense, or in the sense of expectation, meaning: "And if a woman expects, due to the signs that appeared to her," ﴿from her husband﴾, i.e. her spouse. This phrase is connected either to "khafat," or to a deleted element that serves as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the words ﴿nushuzan﴾ (ill-treatment). Nushuz means haughtiness and rising up, when a man raises himself above his wife toward another for some reason; the term applies to the conduct of either spouse. ﴿Or aversion﴾ means turning away, either with his face or with some of the benefits she used to receive from him. In al-Bahr it is said: nushuz is that he distances himself from her, by withholding himself, his maintenance, and the affection between them, or by harming her with abuse or beating, for example. I'rad (aversion) is that he reduces his conversation and companionship with her, due to disparagement of her age, plainness, a defect in her form or character, boredom, an eye drawn to another woman, or other such reasons; and it is lighter than nushuz. ﴿Then there is no blame﴾, i.e. there is no hardship and no sin, ﴿upon them both﴾, i.e. upon the woman and her husband in that case.

﴿That they make a settlement between themselves, a settlement﴾, i.e. in making a settlement between them, by the woman giving up her day to him, as Sawda (may Allah be pleased with her) did with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); or by remitting to him some of what is due to her in maintenance or clothing; or by giving him her dower, or part of it; or by giving him money so that she may win his favour and continue to remain in his care. The statement begins with the negation of blame to deny what might be supposed, namely that what is taken in this way is like a bribe and therefore unlawful.

The readers other than the people of Kufa read (yaṣṣālaḥā) with a fatḥah on the yā', a shaddah on the ṣād, and an alif after it; its original form is (yatasālaḥā), in which the tā' was changed to ṣād and assimilated. Al-Jahdari read (yaṣṣallaḥā) with a fatḥah and shaddah without an alif; its original form is (yaṣṭalliḥā), which was lightened by changing the ṭā', which had replaced the tā' of the iftiʿāl form, into a ṣād, and the first letter was assimilated into it. This does not mean that the tā' was first changed to ṣād and then assimilated, as Abu al-Baqa' said; because the tā' of iftiʿāl must be changed to ṭā' after the four letters.

(Yaṣṭaliḥā) has also been read, and it is clear. ﴿A settlement﴾ (ṣulḥan), in the reading of the people of Kufa, is either a direct object, in the sense of "they bring about the settlement," or an object through a preposition, meaning "they make peace," where what is meant is that by which peace is made. ﴿Between them﴾ is an adverbial of place, mentioned to indicate that the people should not be informed of what is between them, but that the spouses should conceal it from others. Or it is a circumstantial qualifier of ﴿ṣulḥan﴾, meaning "existing between them." It may also be an infinitive with its additional letters omitted, or of the type of "Allah caused it to grow as a growing." ﴿Between them﴾ is then the object, since it is a noun in the sense of mutual disagreement and opposition; or it is an extended use of the adverbial, not meaning "what is between them," as has been said.

It is also possible that ﴿between them﴾ is an adverbial of place and the object is omitted, meaning "their condition and the like." In the reading of the others, it may stand in the place of (taṣāliḥā) and (iṣṭilāḥan), or it may be governed by a verb that follows from what was mentioned, meaning "so he makes their condition right with a settlement." This possibility is remote in the first reading. It has also been allowed that ﴿ṣulḥan﴾ is in the accusative by dropping the preposition, meaning (yaṣṣālaḥā) or (yaṣṣallaḥā) "with a settlement," i.e. with something by which reconciliation is brought about.

﴿And settlement is better﴾, i.e. than separation and bad companionship, or than enmity. The lam here is for the known (ʿahd), and affirming superiority to the one compared against is by way of supposition. The meaning is: if there is any good in it, then this is better than it; otherwise there is no goodness in what has been mentioned. It is also permissible that ﴿khayr﴾ does not mean comparative superiority, but is used as a verbal noun or an adjective, meaning that it is a good among goods; the lam is then for the class. It has been said that the lam, in both interpretations, may indicate either the known or the class. The sentence is parenthetical, and likewise the words of the Exalted: ﴿And souls are made present to avarice﴾. For this reason the lack of similarity between the two sentences is excused, since the first is nominal and the second verbal, and there is no meaningful connection between them. The benefit of the first is to encourage reconciliation, and the second prepares the excuse for holding on to the marriage and for the difficulty in it, as has been said.

(Ḥaḍara) is transitive with one object, while (aḥḍara) is transitive with two. The first object is (al-anfus), which takes the place of the subject, and the second is (al-shuḥḥ). The meaning is: Allah made souls present to avarice, which is stinginess together with greed. It is also possible that the one taking the place of the subject is the second, meaning that avarice has been made present to them, never absent from them; or that they have been made present to it, inclined toward it by nature, so that a woman hardly yields any of her rights to men, and a man hardly gives freely of maintenance and good companionship, for example, to the one he does not desire.

Shaykh al-Islam mentioned that this includes the establishment and confirmation of settlement, urging each of the spouses toward it; not by looking at one's own condition, for that would lead to prolonging discord, but by looking at the condition of the other. If the man is avaricious and his inclination does not turn from its natural state without being won over, this may compel the woman to give up some of her rights to him in order to win him over; and likewise, if she is avaricious with her rights, this may compel the man to be content with something small from her and not to demand much of her. Thus the settlement that is good is realised.

﴿And if you do good﴾ in companionship with women, ﴿and guard against﴾ ill-treatment and aversion, even if the causes that call to them come together, and you are patient in that, and do not compel them to lose anything of their rights or to give up what is dear to them.

﴿Indeed Allah is ever, of what you do﴾ of good and of guarding, or of all that you do, which includes what has been mentioned by primary inclusion, ﴿Acquainted﴾; so He will reward you and recompense you for it. Glory be to Him, He has made His being knowing and fully aware of their deeds stand in the place of recompensing and rewarding them for those deeds, which in reality is the answer to the condition, by putting the cause in the place of the effect. It is not hidden what there is in addressing the husbands by way of the shift of address (iltifat), in expressing the observance of their wives' rights as good conduct, in the word "taqwa," which indicates that ill-treatment and aversion are things to be guarded against, and in ordering the gracious promise upon that. All of this is of the gentleness of winning over and encouragement toward good treatment.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 129:**

﴿And you will never be able to be equitable between wives﴾. That is: you will absolutely not be able to achieve justice among them, such that no inclination at all falls toward one side

[Page 163]

in any of the matters, such as division (of nights), maintenance, attentiveness, looking after them, attention, companionable conversation, playfulness, and friendly company, and others besides these, the enumeration of which cannot be exhausted.

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from ʿUbaydah that he said: "﴿And you will never be able to be equitable﴾ refers to love and intercourse."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Masʿud that he said: "It refers to intercourse."

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from al-Hasan, and Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, that both of them said: "It refers to affection."

Both (Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir) narrated from Abu Mulaykah that the verse was revealed concerning ʿA'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) loved her more than others.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and others narrated from her (ʿA'ishah) that she said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to divide (his time) among his wives equitably, and then he would say: 'O Allah, this is my division in what I control, so do not blame me for what You control and I do not control.'" By "what You control," the Prophet (ﷺ) meant love and the inclination of the heart that is not within one's choice.

﴿And even if you are eager﴾ to establish that and you strive hard for it, ﴿do not incline completely﴾, that is: do not be unjust toward the one you are averse to in every way, so that you withhold from her her right without her consent. Rather, be equitable as far as you are able, for your inability to attain true justice does not prevent your being obligated to what is less than it, from the levels that you are able to achieve. The word (كُلَّ, kulla, "all/completely") is in the accusative as a verbal noun (مَصْدَرِيَّة), for it has been established that it takes its case according to what is annexed to it, whether a verbal noun, an adverb of time or place, or something else. ﴿So you leave her﴾, that is: so you leave the one toward whom you have inclined, ﴿as if suspended﴾. It is, as Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said, the one who is neither divorced nor has a husband. Ubayy recited (كَالْمَسْجُونَةِ, ka-l-masjūnah, "like one imprisoned"), and Qatadah explained (al-Muʿallaqah, "the suspended") accordingly. The prepositional phrase (الجارُّ والمَجْرُورُ, "the preposition and its object") is connected to an omitted element and functions as a circumstantial clause (حال) from the pronoun in the accusative within (تَذَرُوها, tadharūhā, "you leave her").

Al-Samin permitted that it could be in the position of the second object of (تَذَرُ, tadhar, "to leave"), in the sense of (تَصِيرُ, taṣīr, "to become"). The deletion of the nūn in (تَذَرُوها, tadharūhā) is either due to the accusative particle, which is the implied (أنِ, an, "that") after a prohibition in response, or due to the jussive particle, on the basis that it is conjoined with the verb before it. There is in the verse a kind of rebuke.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has two wives and inclines toward one of them will come on the Day of Resurrection with one of his sides fallen."

Others than one narrated from Jabir ibn Zayd that he said: "I had two wives, and I was truly equitable between them, to the point that I would count the kisses."

It is narrated from Mujahid that he said: "They used to recommend that co-wives be treated equally even in perfume, so that one applies perfume for this one just as one applies it for that one."

It is narrated from Ibn Sirin concerning a man who has two wives that it is disliked for him to perform ablution in the house of one of them and not the other.

﴿And if you set things right﴾ in what you were corrupting of their affairs, ﴿and you guard yourselves﴾ against the inclination that Allah, the Exalted, has forbidden you from in the future, ﴿then indeed Allah is ever Forgiving﴾, so He will forgive you what has passed of the injustice, ﴿Merciful﴾, so He will bestow upon you His favor through His mercy.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 130:**

﴿And if they separate﴾, i.e., the woman and her husband. It is also read (yatafaraqa), meaning: and if they do not reconcile, and no agreement of any kind is reached between them, whether by way of reconciliation or otherwise, and separation occurs between them by divorce. ﴿Allah will enrich each﴾ of them, i.e., He will make him or her independent of the other and will suffice him for what concerns him. It is said: He will enrich the husband with another wife, and the woman with another husband. ﴿From His abundance﴾, i.e., from His wealth and His power. In this there is consolation for each of the two spouses after the divorce. It is also said: it is a deterrent to them against separation. In whatever way it is understood, it is restricted by the will of Allah, exalted is He. ﴿And Allah is ever All-Encompassing﴾, i.e., Rich and Sufficient for creation, or Capable, or Knowing. ﴿All-Wise﴾, i.e., perfect in His acts and His rulings.

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ Thus it is not difficult for Him to grant independence after separation, nor companionship after loneliness, nor [no]... nor. In this there is a clear reminder of the perfection of His vastness and the greatness of His power. The sentence is a new (*mustaʾnafa*, an independent resumptive clause) that was brought, as is said, for this purpose.

﴿We have certainly enjoined those who were given the Book before you﴾, that is: We commanded them in the most eloquent manner. By them are meant the Jews, the Christians, and those nations before them. "The Book" is general, covering the divine scriptures, and there is no necessity to restrict the relative pronoun to the Jews or "the Book" to the Torah. Rather, it may be claimed that generalization is more suited to the purpose for which the discourse was delivered, which is the emphasis on the command to sincerity.

The phrase (مِن) is connected either to (وصَّيْنا, "We enjoined") or to (أُوتُوا, "were given"). (وإيّاكُمْ, "and you") is conjoined to the relative pronoun. The rule for a conjoined pronoun is that it be detached (independent), and it was not placed first so that it would remain connected, in observance of the natural order (*al-tartib al-wujudi*, the order of existence). ﴿That fear Allah﴾, that is: We enjoined each of them and you with (أنِ, "that") "fear Allah, the Exalted." Here (أنْ) is a verbal (*maṣdariyya*) particle with an implied preposition, and its position is in the accusative, or in the genitive according to the two schools. Its connection to an imperative, like a prohibition and the like, is permissible, as Sibawayh explicitly stated. It may also be an explanatory (*mufassira*) particle for the enjoining, because it contains the sense of saying.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you disbelieve, then indeed to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is conjoined to (وصَّيْنا, "We enjoined") with an implied (قُلْنا, "We said"), meaning: We enjoined and said to you and to them: If you disbelieve, then know that He, glorified is He, is the Owner of dominion and sovereignty. Your disbelief and disobedience do not harm Him, just as your gratitude and piety do not benefit Him. He enjoined you and them only out of His mercy, not out of His need.

In the discourse there is *taghlib* (prevalence of the addressees over the absent parties). The apparent sense of some scholars' words suggests that the conjunction is to (اتَّقُوا اللَّهَ, "fear Allah"). It was objected that the conditional (الشَّرْطِيَّةَ) cannot occur after the verbal (أنِ) or the explanatory (أنِ) particle, so it is not correct to conjoin it to what follows them, whether it is an imperative or a declarative, and whether the verb is (وصَّيْنا, "We enjoined") or (أمَرْنا, "We commanded") or other. It was also said that the aforementioned conjunction is of the type of:

*"I fed her straw, and cold water."*

Abu Hayyan permitted that it be a new sentence addressed to this community alone, or together with those who were given the Book.

﴿And Allah is ever Self-Sufficient﴾, in His essential self-sufficiency (*al-ghina al-dhati*) from the creation and their worship, ﴿Praiseworthy﴾, that is: praised in His essence, whether they praise Him or do not. The sentence is a concluding appendix (*tadhyil*, a closing clause that confirms what precedes it). It was said that the words of His, exalted is He:
