Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 132:

﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾ and so on, is a warning against disbelief, meaning: He, exalted is He, is able to punish you however He wills, and there is no escape from His punishment, for all that is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him. His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And Allah is ever Rich and Praiseworthy﴾ is to indicate that He, Majestic and Exalted is He, is not harmed by their disbelief.

His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ may be an independent statement addressed to the audience, as a preparation for what follows of the conditional clause, meaning: to Him, glorified is He, belongs whatever creatures are in them, by creation and dominion; He disposes of that however He wills, bringing into existence and annihilating, giving life and causing death. It may also be like a completion of the concluding remark (tadhyil) by explaining the proof, for all created beings indicate, by their need and their inherent poverty, His self-sufficiency, and by what He, glorified is He, has bestowed upon them of existence, attributes and perfections, His being (ḥamīdan) [Praiseworthy].

﴿And Allah suffices as Disposer of affairs (wakīl)﴾ is a concluding remark (tadhyil) to what precedes it. The wakīl is the one who maintains and undertakes the matter entrusted to him. In absolute terms this is Allah, exalted is He. In an-Nihayah it is said: "Fulan entrusted (wakkala) Fulan" when he asks him to take care of his affair, out of trust or inability to handle his own affairs. Among the names of Allah, al-Wakil is the one who provides for the sustenance of His servants. Its reality is that He independently carries out the matter entrusted to Him. It is not hidden that restricting it to sustenance is deficient, so it was generalized. (And put your trust in Allah, exalted is He.)

Al-Baydawi, may Allah whiten the face of his states, claimed that this sentence refers back to His saying: ﴿Allah will make each of them independent from His abundance﴾, for if you rely on Him and entrust yourself to Him, He is the Self-Sufficient, because whoever relies on Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, is sufficed by Him. Since what lies between them serves as an affirmation of it, it is not counted as a separation. It is not hidden that, despite its remoteness, there is no need for it.

﴿If He wills﴾, i.e., if He intends to remove you and bring about others, ﴿He will remove you﴾, i.e., He will annihilate you and destroy you, ﴿O people, and bring others﴾, i.e., He will at once bring into existence in your place a different people from mankind. So the address is to a category of people.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Jarir narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him) that: "When the saying of the Exalted was revealed: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people﴾, the Prophet (ﷺ) struck the back of Salman al-Farisi (may Allah be pleased with him) with his hand and said: 'They are the people of this one.'" In this there is a kind of confirmation of what has been mentioned concerning this verse. As for what is reported from al-Iraqi, that the striking took place at the time of its revelation, then what has been mentioned is necessarily a lapse (sahw), according to what Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti explicitly stated.

Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, and their followers permitted that the intended meaning is "other creatures" (khalqan akhariyn), i.e., a kind other than the kind of humanity. Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying it is an error. As for it being a figurative usage (majaz), as has been said, this does not complete the intended meaning, because it contradicts the usage of the Arabs. For ghayr (غَيْرًا) is applied to something different in kind or in attribute, whereas akhar (آخَرُ) is applied only to a difference between parts of one and the same kind.

In Durrat al-Ghawwas fi Awham al-Khawass (The Pearl of the Diver on the Errors of the Elite), it is stated that people say: "I bought a male slave and another female slave (jariya ukhra)," and they are mistaken in this, because the Arabs did not describe with the words akhar (آخَرَ) and ukhra (أُخْرى) and their plural forms except what is of the same kind as what was mentioned before. As Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other (al-ukhra)?﴾ And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it; and whoever is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days (ayyam ukhar)﴾. So He described Manat as "the other" (al-ukhra) because she is of the same kind as al-'Uzza, and He described the days as "other" (ukhar) because they are of the same kind as the month. And the female slave (ama) is not of the same kind as the male slave ('abd), because she is feminine and he is masculine. Therefore it is not permissible for her to be described by the word ukhra, just as one does not say: "Hind came, and a man (rajul) other (akhar)." The principle in this is that akhar is of the type of af'al which is accompanied by min, and it matches what is mentioned after it. This is shown by the fact that when you say: "Qala al-Findu al-Zimmani, and qala akhar," the sense of the sentence is: "and qala akhar min al-shu'ara'" (and another of the poets said). The word min is omitted only because the meaning indicates it and because akhar is frequently used in speech.

In al-Durr al-Masun: this is not agreed upon. Rather, many grammarians and lexicographers adopted it, and al-Radi, Najm al-A'imma, approved it. However, he objects to al-Zamakhshari and those with him that akhariyn is an attribute of a omitted noun (mawsuf mahdhuf), and an attribute does not take the place of its qualified noun except if it is specific (khassa), as in: "marartu bi-katib" (I passed by a scribe), or if evidence indicates the specification of the qualified noun. Here the attribute is not specific, so it must be of the same kind as the first (noun), so that it indicates the omitted noun.

Ibn Ya'sun, al-Siqilli, and a group said: the Arabs do not say "marartu bi-rajulayn wa-akhar" (I passed by two men and another), because akhar corresponds only to what is of its own kind, dual, plural, or singular. Ibn Hisham said: this is not correct, due to the saying of Rabi'a ibn Mukaddam:

"And indeed I interceded for the two of them with another, a third, and my generosity refused to flee until morning."

And Abu Hayya al-Numayri said:

"I used to walk upright on two, and I became walking on another (ukhra) of the trees."

By their saying that it is of the same kind as what precedes it, they mean that the name of the qualified noun must be akhar in wording, or the estimate must allow its application to the earlier item which it is matched with, by way of common application (tawatu'). For this reason, if you say: "Jaa'ani Zayd wa-akhar" (Zayd came to me and another), it is acceptable, because the estimate is: "wa-rajul akhar" (and another man). Likewise: "Jaa'ani Zayd wa-ukhra," intending "nasama ukhra" (another soul). Likewise: "ishtaraytu farasan wa-markuban akhar" (I bought a horse and another mount) is acceptable, even if the other mount is a camel, because the term "mount" applies to both by common application. But if the application of the name to both is by way of pure homonymy (ishtirak mahd), then if their reality is one, the matter is permissible, as in: "qama ahad al-Zaydayn wa-qa'ada al-akhar" (one of the two Zayds stood up and the other sat down). If their reality is not one, it is not permissible, because it is not matched with what is of its own kind, as in: "ra'aytu al-mushtari wa-al-mushtari al-akhar" (I saw the buyer and the other buyer), intending by one of them the star and by the other the counterpart of the seller.

Is agreement in masculinity and femininity a condition along with common application? There is a difference of opinion on this. Al-Mubarrad held that it is not a condition, so it is permissible to say: "Jaa'atni jariyatuka wa-insan akhar" (your slave-girl came to me and another human, masculine). Ibn Jinni made it a condition. The correct view is that of al-Mubarrad, on the evidence of the saying of 'Antara:

"And the horses plunge into the dust, frowning, from between one clad in armour and another who clothes (himself)."

Page 166

What has been mentioned, that akhar is matched with what precedes it of its own kind, is the preferred view. Otherwise, they may use it without anything of its kind preceding it. Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash) claimed that this is permissible only in poetry. So if you say: "Jaa'ani akhar" (another came to me) without having first spoken of anything of its kind, it is not permissible. And if you say: "akaltu raghifan wa-hadha qamis akhar" (I ate a loaf and this is another shirt), it is not good.

As for the saying of the poet:

"May the Compassionate send blessings upon 'Azza and her daughter, and Layla, and upon her neighbours, the others (al-akhar)."

It is to be understood that he made her daughter a neighbour of hers, so that the other would be of her kind. Had it not been for this estimate, it would not have been proper to follow the mention of the daughter with neighbours; rather he would have said: "wa-sallaa 'ala banatiha al-akhar" (and upon her other daughters). In the verse, akhar, which is plural, has also been matched with ibnatiha, which is singular.

Al-Suhayli claimed that ukhra in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And Manat, the third, the other (al-ukhra)﴾ was used without anything of its kind preceding it, because she is other than Manat the tyrant, whom they used to invoke at Qudayd, so He made her the third after al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and "the other" (ukhra) for Manat, whom 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh and others of his people worshipped, although no mention of her had preceded. The correct view is that He made her "the other" with reference to al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and this was permissible because the thing described as "the other," namely the third, can be applied to al-Lat and al-'Uzza. Do you not see that each of them is a third with reference to her companion? This is directed at what Abu al-Hasan mentioned, that the use of akhar and ukhra without their kind preceding them is not permissible except in poetry. End of quotation.

This is an excellent investigation, but, if Allah the Exalted wills, the detailed discussion of the verse he cited will come later.

In al-Masa'il al-Sughra of al-Akhfash, in a chapter he devoted to establishing this matter, he states that the Arabs do not use akhar except for what is of the same type as what precedes it. So if you say: "Atani sadiq laka wa-'aduww laka akhar" (a friend of yours came to me and an enemy of yours, another), it is not good, because it is nonsensical speech. It resembles sa'ir (سائِرَ, "all the rest"), baqiyya (بَقِيَّةَ, "remainder"), and ba'd (بَعْضَ, "some") in that it is used only with its own kind. So if you say: "darabtu rajulan wa-taraktu sa'ir al-nisa'" (I struck a man and left all the other women), it is not a proper sentence. Yet what is prohibited may be permitted through interpretation, as in: "ra'aytu faraswan wa-himaran akhar" (I saw a horse and another donkey), considering that both are beasts. Imru' al-Qays said:

"When I say: 'This is my companion,' and I am pleased with him, and both eyes are cooled by him, I have been replaced by another."

In a hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) felt lightness in his illness, so he said: 'Look for someone to lean upon.' Then Barira and another man came, and he leaned upon them both."

The conclusion of this is that a thing is not described as akhar except when it is of the same kind as what precedes it, so that its difference may be clear in a place where its unity might be suspected, even by interpretation. In that case, what al-Zamakhshari stated is not a definite error, and the contradiction of Arab usage, on which the majority rely, is what counts.

﴿And Allah is, over that﴾, i.e., over the complete annihilation of you and the bringing of others, ﴿Capable﴾, i.e., of far-reaching power. However, He, glorified is He, did not do so, and He left you upon what you are upon of disobedience, because His will was not directed to it, for a wisdom that required it, not because of any incapacity on His part, exalted is He above that by a great exaltation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 134:

﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world﴾ — like the warrior who, in his jihad, desires booty and worldly benefits — ﴿with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter﴾. The apodosis (jaza' al-shart, the answer of the conditional clause) is understood with the implied sense of informing and telling, i.e.: (whoever desires the reward of this world), then inform him and tell him that with Allah, Exalted is He, is the reward of both abodes. So why does he not seek that, like one who says: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good﴾? Or [the verse means] he seeks what is more noble, namely the reward of the Hereafter. For whoever fights, for example, purely for the sake of Allah, Exalted is He, the worldly benefits will not escape him, and in the Hereafter he will have [rewards] compared to which they are as nothing.

In the Musnad of Ahmad, on the authority of Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever has the Hereafter as his greatest concern, Allah, Exalted is He, will gather his affairs together, place his richness in his heart, and the world will come to him humbled. And whoever has the world as his intention, Allah, Exalted is He, will scatter his affairs, place his poverty before his eyes, and he will not obtain from the world except what has been written for him."

It is also permissible that the apodosis be understood as being of the kind of loss, so that it is said: whoever desires only the reward of this world has indeed lost and perished; with Allah, Exalted is He, is the reward of both this world and the Hereafter for him, if he desires it.

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "The first of people to be judged on the Day of Resurrection will be a man who was martyred. He will be brought forward, and Allah will make him recognize His blessings, and he will recognize them. [Allah] will say: 'What did you do with them?' He will say: 'I fought for You until I was martyred.' He will say: 'You lie, rather you fought so that it would be said, "He is brave," and it has been said.' Then he will be ordered, and he will be dragged on his face until he is thrown into the Fire.

And a man who learned knowledge and taught it, and recited the Qur'an, will be brought forward, and He will make him recognize His blessings, and he will recognize them. [Allah] will say: 'What did you do with them?' He will say: 'I learned knowledge and taught it, and I recited the Qur'an for Your sake.' He will say: 'You lie, rather you learned so that it would be said, "He is a scholar," and you recited so that it would be said, "He is a reciter," and it has been said.' Then he will be ordered, and he will be dragged on his face until he is thrown into the Fire.

And a man whom Allah made wealthy and gave him all kinds of wealth, will be brought forward, and He will make him recognize His blessings, and he will recognize them. [Allah] will say: 'What did you do with them?' He will say: 'I did not leave any path in which You would like money to be spent except that I spent in it.' He will say: 'You lie, rather you did it so that it would be said, "He is generous," and it has been said.' Then he will be ordered, and he will be dragged on his face until he is thrown into the Fire."

It has been said: the apodosis is indeed "with Allah is the reward," but it is interpreted as something arranged upon the condition, because its outcome is that he is blamed and reproached for leaving the more important and more exalted [aim], which encompasses what he desired together with an addition. However, whoever requires the returning pronoun in the apodosis will supply it as we have indicated.

It has also been said: the meaning is that with Allah, Exalted is He, is the reward of both abodes, so He gives each one what he desires, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter, We increase for him in his harvest﴾, and so on.

﴿And Allah is ever Hearing, Seeing﴾ — a concluding remark (tadhyil) supporting the sense of reproach, i.e.: how does the one who shows off show off? And that Allah, Exalted is He, is (Hearing, samee') of what passes through his mind and what his impulses command, (Seeing, baseer) of all his states, outward and inward, so He will recompense him for that. It may be said that it is appended with this because the desire for reward is either by supplication or by striving; the first is heard, and the second is seen. It has also been said: hearing and seeing are two expressions for His, Exalted is He, awareness of the purpose of the one who desires this world or the Hereafter, and that is an expression for the recompense. It is not hidden that this, although it is not without merit, nevertheless gives the impression of reducing the attribute of hearing and seeing to knowledge, which contradicts what is established in theology (kalam).

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 4, verse 135:

﴿O you who have believed, be persistent in upholding justice﴾. That is: be constant in establishing justice in all matters, striving in that with every effort, and let nothing turn you away from it.

From al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) it is reported that by the word *al-qawwamin* (persistent) He, glorified is He, drew attention to the fact that upholding justice once or twice is not sufficient; rather, it must be constant. Religious matters have no standing unless they are continuous and lasting, and whoever is just once or twice is not truly just; that is, it is not appropriate that this term be applied to him. ﴿Witnesses﴾ [*shuhada'*] ﴿in justice﴾ [*bil-qist*] ﴿for Allah﴾ [*lillah*], by your giving your testimony for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, and not for any worldly purpose. The accusative of *shuhada'* is that it is a second predicate (*khabar thani*) of *kunu* (be), and the excellence of placing the first predicate first is not hidden.

It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun concealed within it. This is supported by what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said regarding the meaning of the verse: that is, be those who speak the truth in testimony, whether it is against someone or for someone, whether they are near or far.

It has also been said that it is an attribute (*sifah*) of *qawwamin*, and it has been said that it is the predicate of *kunu*, with *qawwamin* being a circumstantial clause.

﴿Even if it be against yourselves﴾: that is, even if the testimony is against yourselves. The word "testimony" is interpreted figuratively (*majazan*) as "declaration of the truth," so that it includes the acknowledgment (*iqrar*) intended here and the testimony in its literal sense (*al-haqiqi*) intended afterwards, and thus there is no need to combine the literal and the figurative meanings. It has also been said that the statement is in the mode of exaggeration (*mukhraj al-mubalaghah*), and what is intended is not its literal meaning; therefore there is no need to say that the figurative usage is general so as to include acknowledgment, since a person giving testimony against himself is not customary.

The prepositional phrase, as has been indicated, is a settled adverbial phrase (*zarf mustaqirr*) that occurs as the predicate of an omitted *kana*, although originally it is a complement (*silah*); because the complement of a verbal noun (*masdar*) may be made a predicate of it, and so it becomes settled, like *al-hamdu lillah* (praise belongs to Allah). This does not apply to the active participle (*ism al-fa'il*) or the like. It is also permitted that it be a free adverbial phrase (*zarf laghw*) related to an omitted predicate, that is: "even if the testimony were a burden upon yourselves."

Abu al-Baqa' linked it to a verb indicated by *shuhada'*, that is: "even if you testify against yourselves." It is permitted that it be related to *qawwamin*, but this is remote. *Wa-law* (even if) is either in its original sense or with the meaning of *in* (if), and it is concessive (*wasliyyah*). It has been said that its apodosis is omitted, that is: "it would be obligatory that you bear witness against it."

﴿Or [against] parents and relatives﴾: that is, even if it is against your parents and the nearest of people to you, or your kinsfolk. The first is joined by *aw* (or) because it corresponds to "selves," and the second is joined to it by *wa* (and) because there is no correspondence.

﴿Whether he be rich﴾ [*in yakun*]: that is, the one being testified against, who is expected in custom and feared; ﴿or poor﴾, who is generally pitied and shown compassion. 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) recited *in yakun ghaniyyun aw faqirun* with the nominative, on the basis that *kana* is complete (*tammah*). The apodosis of the condition is omitted, indicated by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿then Allah is more worthy of both﴾: that is, do not refrain from testifying against the rich in seeking his pleasure, or against the poor out of compassion for him, because Allah, the Exalted, is more worthy of both categories and more solicitous of them than all other people. Were it not that the right of testimony is a benefit for them both, He would not have prescribed it. So observe the command of Allah, for He knows the interests of His servants better than you do.

Ubayy recited *fa-llahu awla bihim* with the plural pronoun, and this is evidence that the intended referents are the two categories, the rich and the poor, and that the dual pronoun does not refer to the rich and the poor as mentioned, because the rule for a pronoun referring to a noun joined by *aw* is singular, as has been said, since *aw* is for one of two things or of things. It has also been said that *aw* has the meaning of *wa* (and), and the pronoun refers to those mentioned; this is reported from al-Akhfash. It has been said that *aw* retains its own sense, and here it serves to detail what was left vague in the utterance. This rests on the basis that testimony covers both testimony for a person and testimony against him, so that each of the one testified for and the one testified against may be rich or poor: they may both be rich, they may both be poor, or one may be poor and the other rich. Since the categories were not mentioned, *aw* is used to indicate this. Thus the dual pronoun refers to the one testified for and the one testified against, in whatever condition each of them is. It has been said other than this.

Al-Radi (al-Radi al-Astarabadi) said: a pronoun referring back to a plural mentioned noun some of whose members are joined to others by *aw* may be singular or may agree with the plural, and this depends on intention. Thus it is permitted to say: "Zayd or 'Amr came to me, and he left," or "and they both are going to the mosque." On this basis there is no need for explanation, since the dual is not invalid, and the singular is not obligatory for this kind of pronoun. Yes, it has been said that the apparent (*zahir*) form is the singular rather than the dual, and although each is permissible, departing from the apparent requires a reason (*nukhtah*).

Some have claimed that the purpose is to generalize the priority and to prevent the misconception that it is restricted to one party. So reflect.

﴿So do not follow [your] desire﴾: that is, the desire of your souls ﴿lest you deviate﴾ [*an ta'dilu*], from *'udul* (deviation) and inclination away from the truth, or from *'adl* (justice), the opposite of injustice. It occupies the position of an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), either for the following that is forbidden or for the prohibition. The possibilities are four:

The first: that it has the meaning of deviation, and it is the cause of what is forbidden, so there is no need for an elision.

The second: that it has the meaning of justice, and it is the cause of what is forbidden, so an element is elided: that is, "lest you dislike to be just."

The third: that it has the meaning of deviation, and it is the cause of the prohibition, so it requires elision as in the second possibility: that is, "I forbid you from following desire out of dislike for deviating from the truth."

The fourth: that it has the meaning of justice, and it is the cause of the prohibition, so it does not require elision as in the first possibility: that is, "I forbid you from following desire for the sake of justice and the avoidance of injustice."

﴿And if you distort﴾ [*wa-in talwu*] your tongues from testimony, by giving it in a manner other than the form it deserves. This is reported from Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak. It is reported from Abu Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, and this is the apparent meaning. It has been said: *al-lay* is procrastination in its delivery, and it is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them.

﴿Or you refuse﴾ [*aw tu'ridu*]: that is, you leave off establishing it entirely. This address is to the witnesses. It has been said that the address is to the judges, and *al-lay* is judging falsely, and refusal is not paying attention to either of the two disputants. This is attributed to al-Suddi, and it is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. Hamzah recited *wa-in talu* with a *damma* on the *lam* and a silent *waw*, and this is from *wilayah* in the sense of directly undertaking the testimony. It has been said that its original form is *talwu* with two *waws*, and the *damma* of the *waw* was moved to the preceding letter after the *waw* was changed to a hamzah or from the beginning, then it was elided because of the meeting of two silent letters. On this basis the two readings have the same meaning.

﴿Indeed Allah is ever, of what you do﴾ of distortion and refusal, or of all deeds, of which this is one, ﴿Acquainted﴾ [*khabiran*]: knowing and aware, so He will reward you for that. This is a pure threat according to the first reading. According to the last reading it may be a threat, and it may contain a promise as well.

The verse, as Ibn Jarir reported from al-Suddi, was revealed concerning the Prophet ﷺ: "Two men, one rich and one poor, came to dispute before him. His disposition was toward the poor, for he considered that the poor man would not wrong the rich man. But Allah, the Exalted, refused except that he should establish justice regarding both the rich and the poor." It includes testimony against those whom Allah, the Exalted, has mentioned, and it does not explicitly address testimony in their favour, as is the apparent meaning. Some have taken it to cover both kinds.

This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, as we have indicated. According to him, the testimony of a child for his parent, and of a parent for his child, is permissible.

It is reported from Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri that he said: "The predecessors of the Muslims acted on this until people displayed matters that led the rulers to suspect them, and so the testimony of those who were suspected was abandoned." It is not hidden that applying the verse to this is very remote, and far more remote, indeed not to be considered even as an indication, is that its meaning is: "Be witnesses for Allah" in His oneness, the perfection of His attributes, and the truth of His rulings, even if that is harmful to yourselves or to your parents and kinsfolk, such that the testimony would bring about the loss of their lives or their property or something else.

﴿If he be rich﴾ [*in yakun*]: that is, the witness, whose testimony harms him by his wealth, ﴿or poor﴾, whose testimony closes off for him the door of relieving need ﴿then Allah﴾, the Exalted, ﴿is more worthy of both﴾ than they are of themselves, so they should prefer Allah, the Exalted, over themselves.

The verse has been cited as evidence that a slave has no role in testimony, since he is not a guardian (*qawwam*) in that matter because he is prevented from going out to the judge; and as evidence that the judge must treat both disputants equally, which is apparent according to one opinion.

As for its connection with what precedes, according to *al-Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit* of Abu Hayyan): when the Exalted mentioned women, disobedience, and reconciliation, He followed it with standing up to render rights, and testimony involves rights. Or, because He, glorified is He, showed that the one who seeks the world is blameworthy and indicated that the one who seeks both (the world and the Hereafter), or the better of the two, is the one who is praised, He explained that the perfection of this is that a person's speech and action be for the Exalted. Or, because He, exalted is His majesty, in this surah mentioned ﴿And if you fear that you will not deal justly with orphans﴾, and the calling of witnesses when handing their property over to them, and commanded the spending of self and wealth in the way of Allah, the Exalted, and mentioned the story of the traitor and the gathering of his people upon falsehood and false testimony, and urged reconciliation, He followed that by commanding His believing servants to stand firmly with justice and to bear witness for the sake of Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 136:

﴿O you who have believed﴾ is an address to the Muslims in general. So the meaning of His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger and the Book which He has sent down upon His Messenger and the Book which He sent down before﴾ is: remain steadfast in faith in that, and persist in it.

This is narrated from al-Hasan, and al-Jubba'i (al-Jubba'i, a Mu'tazili scholar) chose it. It was also said: the address is to them, and the intended meaning is: increase in faith in tranquility and certainty; or (believe) in what has been mentioned in detail, on the basis that the faith of some of them is general (ijmali). In either case, there is no requirement of obtaining what is already obtained. It was also said: the address is to the hypocrites who outwardly appear as believers, so the meaning of (believe) is: make your faith sincere. This was chosen by al-Zajjaj and others.

It was also said: it is specifically for the believing Jews. This is supported by what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that "'Abdullah ibn Salam, Asad and Usayd, the two sons of Ka'b, Tha'labah ibn Qays, the son of the sister of 'Abdullah ibn Salam, and Yamin ibn Yamin came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'We believe in you and in your Book, and in Musa and the Torah and 'Uzayr, and we disbelieve in what is other than that of the books and messengers?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Rather, believe in Allah, exalted is He, and Muhammad ﷺ and his Book, the Qur'an, and in every Book that came before it.' They said: 'We will not do that.' So it was revealed, and they all believed."

It was also said: it is for the believers among the People of the Two Books. This was narrated from al-Dahhak.

It was also said: it is for the polytheist believers in al-Lat and al-'Uzza.

It was also said: it is for all creation, because of their faith on the day of the taking of the covenant, when He, glorified is He, said to them: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said: ﴿Yes﴾.

The first Book is the Qur'an, and what is meant by the second Book is the genus that encompasses all heavenly books, and this is indicated by His saying afterward: (His books). What is meant by faith in them is faith in them within the framework of faith in the Book sent down upon the Messenger ﷺ, in the sense that faith in each one of them is included under faith in that Book, and that the rulings of each of them were true and established, obligatory to be acted upon until the arrival of what abrogated them, and that what has not been abrogated of them up to now, of laws and rulings, is established insofar as they are among the rulings of that Book about which there is no doubt and no alteration that can befall it.

From here it is known that the command to the believers among the People of the Book to believe in their Book, on the basis that the address is to them, does not mean steadfastness, because this kind of faith is not already obtained by them, and it is the intended meaning. And there is no need to say that the actual object of the command is faith in what is other than it, as if it were said: believe in all of it and do not single out part of it.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu 'Amr read (nuzzila) and (unzila) in the passive voice, and the use of (nazzala) first and (anzala) second is because the Qur'an was revealed in installments by consensus, and its completion took twenty-three years according to the correct view, which is not so for the other Books. So reflect.

﴿And whoever disbelieves in Allah and His angels and His books and His messengers and the Last Day﴾ means: in any one of those. For the ruling attached to items joined by the conjunction "and" (waw), as the second scholar (al-'Allamah al-Thani) said, may refer to each one, and may refer to the whole, and reliance is on the contextual indicators. Here the indicator has shown the first, because belief in all is obligatory, and the whole is negated by the negation of a part. Such a case is not one of making the waw mean "or" in any way. Some scholars allowed its reference to be to the whole, to describe the error with the utmost remoteness in His saying: ﴿then he has certainly strayed far astray﴾.

It is derived from this that disbelief in any one part is an error characterized by (remoteness), and the well-known view is that what is meant by "far astray" is the error far from the goal, such that the one characterized by it can hardly return to its path. It is also permissible that what is meant is (far astray) from reaching it. The conditional sentence serves as a concluding statement to the preceding discourse and an emphasis upon it.

The mention of the angels and the Last Day on the side of disbelief, according to what Shaykh al-Islam mentioned, is because by disbelieving in either of them faith is not realized at all. The plural of Books and Messengers is because disbelief in one book or messenger is disbelief in all. The mention of the Messenger earlier, in relation to the Book, is in the aspect of its being sent down upon him, and the mention of the angels and the Books before the Messengers is because they are intermediaries between Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and the Messengers in the sending down of the Books. It was also said: the difference in order in the two places is a matter of variety in styles, and the addition in the second is merely for emphasis. And it was read: (bi-kitabihi), with the intention of the genus.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verses 137–138:

﴿Indeed, those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, then increased in disbelief﴾. They are a people among whom apostasy was repeated, who persisted in disbelief, and who increased in persistent transgression in error. And it is narrated from Mujahid and Ibn Zayd that they are hypocrites (munafiqun) who showed faith, then apostatized, then showed it again, then apostatized, and then died upon their disbelief.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, took it to be general for every hypocrite in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, on land and sea.

And it is narrated from al-Hasan that they were a group from the People of the Book who wished to create doubt among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. They would profess faith in their presence, then say: "A doubt has presented itself to us," and so they would disbelieve; then they would profess faith again, then say: "Another doubt has presented itself to us," and so they would disbelieve, and they would continue in disbelief until death. This is the meaning of His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And a group of the People of the Book said: "Believe in what has been revealed to those who believed at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end, that perhaps they may return."﴾

It has also been said: they are the Jews, who believed in Musa (peace be upon him), then disbelieved by worshipping the calf when he was absent from them, then believed upon his return to them, then disbelieved in 'Isa (peace be upon him), then increased in disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ. This is narrated from Qatadah.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: they believed in Musa (peace be upon him), then disbelieved after him, then believed in 'Uzair, then disbelieved in 'Isa (peace be upon him), then increased in disbelief in our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.

An objection to this is that those who increased in disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ were not believers in Musa (peace be upon him) and then disbelievers by worshipping the calf or something else, then believers in his return to them, or in 'Uzair, and then disbelievers in 'Isa (peace be upon him). Rather, they are either believers in Musa (peace be upon him) and others, or disbelievers because of their disbelief in 'Isa (peace be upon him) and the Injil.

It is answered that a specific people is not meant by this; rather, the category is meant, and the rebuke falls upon the Jews present, by way of attributing to them what was done by some of them, as though it had come from all of them.

What the heart inclines to is that the intended meaning is a people among whom apostasy was repeated, whether they were hypocrites or others. This is supported by what Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said concerning the apostate: "I would ask him to repent three times," and then recited this verse. Some of the imams followed the opinion of Imam 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, saying: the apostate is killed at the fourth time and is not asked to repent. It seems he meant that there is no benefit in asking him to repent, since there is no gain in it. Based on this, the meaning of His, glory be to Him, statement: ﴿Allah would never forgive them, nor guide them to a way﴾ is that He, glory be to Him, does not do that at all, even if they repent. According to the well-known view, which the majority hold, the negation of forgiveness and guidance means the negation of what necessitates them, namely firm true faith. The meaning of its negation is the improbability of its occurrence, for those among whom apostasy and increase in disbelief and persistence upon it have repeated come to the state where their hearts have been struck with disbelief and accustomed to apostasy, and faith has become for them the least and most insignificant thing, so they scarcely come within an inch of it so as to become worthy of forgiveness and of being guided to the path of Paradise. It does not mean that, even if they sincerely believed, it would not be accepted from them or they would not be forgiven.

Some restricted the non-requirement of repentance to the one who mocks and treats religion lightly, when there is evidence for that. The predicate of (kana) in such places is omitted, and the lam is connected to it, as the Basrans held, meaning: Allah, exalted is He, was not willing to forgive them. Negating the will to do an act is more emphatic than negating the act itself.

The Kufans held that the lam is extra (za'idah) and the predicate is the verb itself. It was judged weak, because what follows it is in the accusative; if the accusative is by the lam itself, then it is not extra, and if it is by (an), then it is invalid because it involves predicating a verbal noun of the essence. It is answered by choosing the first part, that there is no obstacle to governing together with the extra particle, as with the extra prepositions; and by choosing the second part, that predicating a verbal noun of the essence is impermissible because it does not signify, by its form, an agent or a particular time, whereas the verb introduced by (an) signifies both, so predicating it is permissible, though the verbal noun itself is not. But there is no hiding what is in this, for the predication here is with the verb, not with the verbal noun, and even if the verbal noun is interpreted as an active participle, it is not with it either. So understand.

Some chose, regarding the people, what Mujahid held, and this is supported by His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Give glad tidings to the hypocrites that for them is a painful punishment﴾, where (bashshir) is placed in the position of (andhir), as mockery of them. So in the speech there is a mocking metaphor (isti'arah tahakkumiyyah). It was also said that it is in the position of (akhbir), so there is a mocking metonymy (majaz mursal tahakkumi).
