It has also been said: they are the Jews, who believed in Musa (peace be upon him), then disbelieved by worshipping the calf when he was absent from them, then believed upon his return to them, then disbelieved in 'Isa (peace be upon him), then increased in disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ. This is narrated from Qatadah.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: they believed in Musa (peace be upon him), then disbelieved after him, then believed in 'Uzair, then disbelieved in 'Isa (peace be upon him), then increased in disbelief in our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.

An objection to this is that those who increased in disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ were not believers in Musa (peace be upon him) and then disbelievers by worshipping the calf or something else, then believers in his return to them, or in 'Uzair, and then disbelievers in 'Isa (peace be upon him). Rather, they are either believers in Musa (peace be upon him) and others, or disbelievers because of their disbelief in 'Isa (peace be upon him) and the Injil.

It is answered that a specific people is not meant by this; rather, the category is meant, and the rebuke falls upon the Jews present, by way of attributing to them what was done by some of them, as though it had come from all of them.

What the heart inclines to is that the intended meaning is a people among whom apostasy was repeated, whether they were hypocrites or others. This is supported by what Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said concerning the apostate: "I would ask him to repent three times," and then recited this verse. Some of the imams followed the opinion of Imam 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, saying: the apostate is killed at the fourth time and is not asked to repent. It seems he meant that there is no benefit in asking him to repent, since there is no gain in it. Based on this, the meaning of His, glory be to Him, statement: ﴿Allah would never forgive them, nor guide them to a way﴾ is that He, glory be to Him, does not do that at all, even if they repent. According to the well-known view, which the majority hold, the negation of forgiveness and guidance means the negation of what necessitates them, namely firm true faith. The meaning of its negation is the improbability of its occurrence, for those among whom apostasy and increase in disbelief and persistence upon it have repeated come to the state where their hearts have been struck with disbelief and accustomed to apostasy, and faith has become for them the least and most insignificant thing, so they scarcely come within an inch of it so as to become worthy of forgiveness and of being guided to the path of Paradise. It does not mean that, even if they sincerely believed, it would not be accepted from them or they would not be forgiven.

Some restricted the non-requirement of repentance to the one who mocks and treats religion lightly, when there is evidence for that. The predicate of (kana) in such places is omitted, and the lam is connected to it, as the Basrans held, meaning: Allah, exalted is He, was not willing to forgive them. Negating the will to do an act is more emphatic than negating the act itself.

The Kufans held that the lam is extra (za'idah) and the predicate is the verb itself. It was judged weak, because what follows it is in the accusative; if the accusative is by the lam itself, then it is not extra, and if it is by (an), then it is invalid because it involves predicating a verbal noun of the essence. It is answered by choosing the first part, that there is no obstacle to governing together with the extra particle, as with the extra prepositions; and by choosing the second part, that predicating a verbal noun of the essence is impermissible because it does not signify, by its form, an agent or a particular time, whereas the verb introduced by (an) signifies both, so predicating it is permissible, though the verbal noun itself is not. But there is no hiding what is in this, for the predication here is with the verb, not with the verbal noun, and even if the verbal noun is interpreted as an active participle, it is not with it either. So understand.

Some chose, regarding the people, what Mujahid held, and this is supported by His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Give glad tidings to the hypocrites that for them is a painful punishment﴾, where (bashshir) is placed in the position of (andhir), as mockery of them. So in the speech there is a mocking metaphor (isti'arah tahakkumiyyah). It was also said that it is in the position of (akhbir), so there is a mocking metonymy (majaz mursal tahakkumi).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 139:

Page 172

﴿Those who take the disbelievers as allies﴾ is in a position of nasb (accusative) or raf' (nominative) by way of censure (dhamm), meaning: "What is intended by them is those who..." or "They are those who..." It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative by way of being an apposition (ittiba') to "the hypocrites" (al-munafiqin), and the presence of the intervening element (al-fasil) does not prevent this, for the Arabs permitted it. As for "the disbelievers" (al-kafirin), it is said that they are the Jews; it is said that they are the polytheists of the Arabs; and it is said that the term encompasses both of these and the Christians. The first view is supported by what is narrated: that some of them would say to others, "The matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) will not be completed," so they allied themselves with the Jews.

﴿Apart from the believers﴾, i.e., going beyond the allegiance of the believers. This phrase is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the doer of (yattakhidhun). ﴿Do they seek honour﴾, i.e., the hypocrites, ﴿with them﴾, i.e., with the disbelievers, ﴿honour (al-'izzah)﴾, i.e., strength and protection. Its root meaning is hardness, and from it comes the term 'azaz for hard ground. The interrogative is for denial (inkar), and the sentence is a parenthetical clause (mu'tarida) confirming what precedes it. It is also said that the interrogative is for mockery (tahakkum), and it is said that it is for wonder (ta'ajjub).

﴿Indeed, honour belongs to Allah entirely﴾, i.e., it is exclusive to Him, the Exalted; He grants it to whomever He wills. He, glorified is He, has prescribed it for His allies, so He, mighty is His majesty, says: ﴿And honour belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾. The sentence is a justification (ta'lil) for what the denying interrogative implies, namely the invalidity of their opinion and the frustration of their hopes.

It is also said: it is an explanation of the aspect of the mockery or the wonder. And it is said: it is the answer to an omitted conditional clause, meaning: "If they seek honour from these, then indeed honour..." etc. In this estimation, it stands in the place of the answer, not that it is literally the answer. As for (jami'an, "entirely"), it is said to be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase, because it relies on the subject. There is no omitted noun in the statement, i.e., "for the allies," as some have claimed.

This is the commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 140:

His saying, glorified be He: ﴿And it has already been revealed to you﴾ is an address to the hypocrites by way of iltifat (the shift from third person to second person), which conveys intensified reproach, the kind demanded by the enumeration of their misdeeds.

Those who read (nuzzila) with the passive form, for what has not been named as its doer (that is, all readers except ʿĀṣim and Yaʿqūb), make the clause a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relating to the pronoun in ﴿they take﴾. It also conveys the complete ugliness of their condition, by showing that they did what they did, namely taking the enemies of God as allies, even though there was something that should have prevented them from it: the prohibition against sitting with them, which necessarily implies a prohibition against taking them as allies, expressed in the most emphatic and eloquent way, right after the explanation of the absence of what would have prompted them to it, by way of the interposed clause. It is as if it were said: "Would you take them as allies?" While the situation is that God, exalted is He, ﴿has revealed to you﴾ before this, in Mecca, ﴿in the Book﴾, that is, the Qur'an of great stature.

﴿That when you hear the verses of God being disbelieved in and mocked, do not sit with them until they engage in a discourse other than it﴾. This is His saying: ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them﴾, up to the end of the verse. This requires refraining from sitting with them in that ugly state, so how much more so from allying with them and seeking strength through them?

(An) here is the light form (al-mukhaffafa) of the heavy (an) (al-thaqīla), and its noun is an implied dhamīr al-shaʾn (pronoun of the matter), meaning: that when you hear. Some have taken its implied noun to be the pronoun of the addressees, meaning: that you. As for the light (an) not governing anything except the pronoun of the matter except out of necessity, as Abū Ḥayyān said, it is within the realm of prohibition, but a number of scholars have affirmed its permissibility without necessity. The conditional clause is a predicate (khabar), and predicates of this kind occur in the speech of the Arabs. The phrase (an) and what follows it is in the accusative position, as a direct object of (nazzala), which is the substitute for the doer according to the second reading. The possibility that the substitute for the doer could be (ʿalaykum), with (an) being explanatory (mufassira), is not taken into account, because revelation carries the meaning of saying. The phrase (yukfaru bihā wa-yustahzaʾu) is in the position of a circumstantial clause relating to the verses. These two were brought in to restrict the prohibition against sitting, for a restriction of a restriction is itself a restriction. The meaning is: do not sit with them at the time of their disbelief and mockery of the verses. The attribution of the verses to the Glorious Name is to honour them, to make clear their importance, and to magnify the gravity of disbelief in them. The pronoun in (maʿahum) refers to the disbelievers implied by (yukfaru) and (yustahzaʾu). The pronoun in (ghayrihi) refers to their discourse of disbelief and mockery. It has been said that it refers to "the disbelief and the mockery," because the two are in the status of one thing.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you would then be like them﴾ is a reason for the prohibition, not included under the revelation. (Idhan) is nullified (mulghāh), because the condition for its government of the verb in the accusative is that it stand at the beginning of the sentence, and therefore no verb has come after it. (Mithl) is the predicate of the plural pronoun, and it is valid with its singular form because it is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar), which applies equally to the singular, masculine and others. It has been said that it is like a verbal noun in applying to the few and the many, or because it is attached to a plural, so it is general. It may also agree with what precedes it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then they would not be like you﴾. The majority read it in the nominative, and it was read, irregularly, in the accusative. It has been said that it is accusative as an adverb of place, because the meaning of your saying "Zayd is like ʿAmr" in that he is in the state of his likeness. It has also been said that when it is attached to an indeclinable noun it takes on indeclinability, and this is not restricted to (mā) as a verbal particle, as is supposed, but occurs with it, as in ﴿Just as you speak﴾, and with other than it, as in the verse of poetry:

So they became, God having restored their blessing to them, since they are Quraysh, and there is no human like them.

Ibn Mālik stipulates for the acquisition of indeclinability that the attached noun not accept the dual or plural forms, like (dūna, ghayr, bayn). He did not validate this for (mithl), and he parsed it as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the implied pronoun in (ḥaqq) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is the truth, just as you speak﴾.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, God will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers together in Hell, all of them﴾ is a reason for their being like them in disbelief, by explaining what it entails of their sharing with them in the punishment. The intended meaning of "the hypocrites" is either the addressees, and the apparent noun was put in place of the pronoun to record their hypocrisy and to give the reason for the ruling by way of its derivation; or it is the genus, and they are included in it by primary inclusion. Its placement first is to intensify the threat against the addressees, and its being in the accusative as a circumstantial clause follows the pattern of what has passed.

It has been raised as an objection that the address is to the hypocrites, since they are like the disbelievers in disbelief without any causal link to sitting with them, so there is no basis for making the recompense follow the condition. And the shift from the likeness in disbelief to the likeness in openly declaring it does not fit with the clause "Indeed, God..." etc. being a reason for their likeness by that likeness in the way mentioned. Also, those who were forbidden from sitting with the disbelievers and the mockers in Mecca were the believers who were sincere, not the hypocrites, because the sprouting of hypocrisy only appeared in Medina, so how can the hypocrites be mentioned in it by a prohibition that was revealed in Mecca before they existed?

This has been answered: if it is granted that what was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, even though it was addressed to him specifically, was revealed to the community, both its sincere and its hypocritical members, until the Hour, then the inclusion of the hypocrites is valid even if they were not present at the time of revelation. If this is not granted, then if it is claimed that it is restricted to the Prophet ﷺ, the sincere believers would not be included either. If it is claimed that they are included but not the hypocrites, who are believers outwardly, then there is no evidence for this. How, when all the rulings are attached to the believers however they may be? We are not charged with probing the hearts of the servants; rather, we have the outward, and God, exalted is He, takes charge of the hidden things. Moreover, evidence has been established that the legal rulings which were at the beginning of Islam and were not abrogated are addressed to whoever has uttered the good word and whom it has reached before the Hour, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿That I may warn you thereby, and whoever it reaches﴾. Because of this subtle point, some of the verifiers said: the intended address here is the truthful believers, and what is meant by "those who disbelieve and mock" is more general than the hypocrites and the disbelievers.

The pronoun in (maʿahum) refers to what is understood from the two verbs. This is supported by what is transmitted from al-Wāḥidī, that he said: the hypocrites used to sit with the rabbis of the Jews and mock the Qur'an, so God, exalted is He, forbade sitting with them. What is meant by the parity in the recompense is parity in sin, because they are able to turn away and deny, not unable as in Mecca; or parity in disbelief, in the sense of: if you are pleased with that. This is based on the principle that being pleased with another's disbelief is itself disbelief without detail. It is a narration from Abū Ḥanīfa, may God be pleased with him, which the author of al-Dhakhīra came across.

Shaykh al-Islam Khawahrzada said: being pleased with another's disbelief is only disbelief if one considers disbelief permissible or finds it good. As for when one is not like that, but loves death or killing for the disbeliever who harms him, until God takes vengeance upon him, this is not disbelief. Whoever reflects on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth﴾, up to the end of the verse, will see the soundness of this claim, and this is what is transmitted from al-Māturīdī.

As for the saying of some that whoever a disbeliever comes to in order to become Muslim, and he says, "Wait until I perform ablution," or delays him, becomes a disbeliever because of his being pleased with that disbelief at the time, this agrees with what was narrated from the Imam, but what contradicts it is what is narrated in the authentic hadith about the conquest of Mecca: that Ibn Abī Sarḥ was brought by ʿUthmān, may God be pleased with him, to the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: "O Messenger of God, accept his allegiance," so the Prophet ﷺ withheld his hand and looked at him three times. This is well known in the biographies, and it indicates by its outward meaning that hesitation in general is not, as they claimed, disbelief.

Some have used the verse as evidence for the prohibition of sitting with the wicked (fussāq) and innovators (mubtadiʿīn) of any kind. This is the view of Ibn Masʿūd, Ibrāhīm, and Abū Wāʾil, and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said the same. Hishām ibn ʿUrwa narrated from him that he struck a man who was fasting, who had been sitting with a people who drink wine; when he was asked about that, he recited the verse. It is the basis for what the authors do of referring to what was mentioned in another place, drawing attention to it, and relying on the meaning.

From here it has been said: the basis for turning away from those who engage in what does not please God, exalted is He, is knowledge of their engaging in it, and therefore it is expressed sometimes by seeing and sometimes by hearing; and that what is meant by turning away is showing opposition by rising from their company, not turning away in the heart or the face alone.

It is reported from al-Jubbā'ī that the thing forbidden is sitting with them without showing displeasure at what one hears or sees. According to this view, which some verifiers adopted, it is possible that what is meant by "the hypocrites and the disbelievers" in the clause of reasoning is what was meant by the pronoun in (maʿahum), and this title was stated explicitly for the reason we indicated earlier.

It is also possible that what is meant is the genus, and that (ulāʾika) is included in it by primary inclusion,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 141:

The address in His words, ﴿Those who wait in ambush for you﴾, is to the sincere believers, without any disagreement. The relative clause (al-mawsul) is either a substitution (badal) for ﴿those who take﴾, or a qualifier (sifah) for the hypocrites alone, since they are the ones who wait (al-mutarabbisun), not the disbelievers.

Abu al-Baqa' and others allowed that it be a qualifier for both groups, or that it be in the nominative or accusative case by way of censure (dhamm). Making it a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the conditional clause is not free from artificiality. Al-tarabbus (waiting, al-intizar) is, according to the apparent sense of some scholars' words, a verb whose object is omitted, and the prepositional phrase is attached to it, meaning: they await the occurrence of some matter befalling you. The words of al-Raghib imply that it is transitive with the preposition "bi" (ba'), since it is from (intazara bi-al-sil‘ah ghala' al-si‘r), "he waited with the goods for the rise of prices."

The fa' in His words, ﴿If there comes to you a victory from Allah﴾, indicates the sequence of its content upon what precedes it, for the report of their waiting entails the report of what occurs after it. That is: if victory and triumph over the enemies happen to befall you, ﴿they say﴾, that is, to you, ﴿Were we not with you?﴾, fighting your enemy, so give us a share of the spoils. ﴿And if there is a share for the disbelievers﴾, that is, a portion of the war, for it is a matter of alternation (sijal), ﴿they say﴾, that is, the hypocrites say to the disbelievers, ﴿Did we not gain mastery over you?﴾, that is: did we not overcome you and gain the ability to kill and capture you, and yet we spared you? Or: did we not overcome you by [our] favour, and inform you of the secrets of Muhammad, ṣallā Allāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallam, and his companions, and write to you with their news, until you prevailed over them? ﴿And prevent you from the believers﴾, that is, we repelled from you the assault of the believers by discouraging them, weakening them, falling short in supporting them, and casting into their hearts what weakened them against fighting you. So recognise this right of ours over you, and bring us our share of what you have obtained. It has also been said that the meaning is: did we not overcome you in your opinion by [our] loyalty to you, and [did we not] prevent you from entering the body of the believers? This is contrary to the apparent sense.

The origin of al-istihwadh is al-istila' (seizure, domination). Its analogical form would have been istaḥāza yastaḥīzu istiḥāzatan with the ḥā' (of the root ḥ-w-dh being treated like the root of a heart condition), but the wāw remained sound in it and this became common in it and in similar forms, until it was assimilated to the regular pattern and was deemed eloquent. Abu Zayd said that it is regular (qiyasi). In any case, it cannot be objected to regarding the eloquence of the Qur'an, as has been verified in its proper place.

It has been read (wa-namna‘akum) with the accusative, by implying "an" (that), and the sense is: there was not from us seizure and prevention, like your saying: "Do not eat the fish and drink the milk." The victory of the Muslims was called fath, and what the disbelievers had was called only a share (naṣīb), to magnify the status of the Muslims and to belittle the portion of the disbelievers. It has also been said: the first was called fath as an indication that it is among the entrances to the opening of the abode of Islam, unlike what the disbelievers have, for there is no victory for them in their domination, but rather the light of what they gained will be extinguished.

﴿So Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection﴾, rewarding His beloved and punishing His enemies. As for in this world, you and they are equal in inviolability (al-‘ismah), according to His words, ṣallā Allāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallam: "When they say it, they have protected from me their blood and their property." It has been said that in the phrase there is a figure of speech (taghlib), and it has been said that there is an ellipsis (hadhf), that is: between you and between them.

﴿And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾, that is: on the Day of Resurrection and at the time of judgement, just as that may be granted in this world as a trial and a respite. This has been related from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, and Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Or [it refers] to this world, that is: He has not given them a complete authority over the believers by extermination, nor a clear proof against them that silences them. This has been reported from al-Suddi. It is also permissible to leave the statement on its general sense, so that it includes this world and the Hereafter, and this is perhaps the better view.

The Shafi'is argued from the verse for the invalidity of a disbeliever's purchase of a Muslim slave, because if it were valid, he would have a hand and a way over him through owning him. We say: it is valid, but he is prevented from employing him and disposing of him except by selling him and removing him from his ownership, so he obtains no way over him.

Some of our companions (the Hanafis) argued by its apparent sense that separation between spouses occurs through the apostasy of the husband, because the contract of marriage establishes for the husband a way over her in keeping her in his house, disciplining her, and preventing her from going out, and it is incumbent upon her to obey him in what the marriage contract requires. The words "the believers and the disbelievers" include females. Likewise, if a disbeliever's wife becomes Muslim. This was judged weak on the ground that apostasy does not negate that the marriage, if he returns to faith before the waiting period expires, remains. It was objected that at the time of disbelief he has no way over her, and the negation of the way is through the occurrence of separation, and after separation occurs, the bond needs a cause for its renewal, which is evident. If the return is considered as apostasy being like a revocable divorce, and the return like the revocation, then there is no weakness in it.

You know that if the negation of the way refers to the Hereafter, or to this world by extermination, or the way means proof, then there is no basis in the verse for our companions nor for the Shafi'is, so do not be heedless.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 142:

﴿Indeed, the hypocrites try to deceive Allah﴾. That is, they do what a deceiver does: they display faith while concealing its opposite.

It is related from al-Hasan, and al-Zajjaj preferred this view, that the meaning is: they deceive the Prophet (ﷺ), in the manner of ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you pledge allegiance only to Allah﴾ and ﴿And He is their Deceiver﴾. That is, He treats them in the way that the one who prevails in deception acts: He left them in this world with their lives and property protected, and prepared for them in the Hereafter the lowest level of the Fire. It has also been said: Allah's deception of them is that He gives them a light on the Day of Resurrection by which they walk with the believers, then He takes that light away from them and sets a wall between them.

This was also related from al-Hasan, and from al-Suddi, and a group of exegetes chose it. The verification of this has already passed, and all praise is due to Allah.

The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or it is coordinated with the predicate of (inna), or it is a new independent clause like the first.

﴿And when they stand up to prayer, they stand up lazily﴾. That is, sluggish and slow, without energy or desire, like one compelled to an act, because they do not believe in any reward for performing it or any punishment for abandoning it. It is also read with a fatḥah on the kāf (kasālā), and both forms are plurals of (kaslān).

﴿They show off to the people﴾ so that they may think them believers. The murā'āh (showing off) is a form of mufā'ala derived from ru'yah (seeing). It may be in the sense of tafʿīl, because fā'ala is used in their speech in the sense of fa'ila, like naʿima and nā'ama; the reading of ʿAbdullah and Ishaq (yurūna) supports this. Or it is for reciprocity: because of their act in a witnessed setting, they see the people and the people see them, and they intend that their deeds be seen while the people approve of them. So the mufāʿala in seeing is unified, and the difference lies only in the object of the showing. Thus this division is not objected to on the grounds that mufāʿala in its true sense requires the unity of the act and its object. The clause is either a resumptive statement built upon a question arising from the speech, as if it were said: "What do they intend by this standing?" and it is answered: "They show off," etc.; or it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (qāmū) or from the pronoun in (kusālā).

﴿And they remember Allah only a little﴾ is coordinated with (yurāʾūna). It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause from its subject; that is, they do not remember Him, glorified is He, at all except for a little time, or except a little remembrance, since the showy person acts only in the presence of the one he shows off to, and that is the least of his states. Or because their remembrance with the tongue is little in comparison with remembrance by the heart. It has also been said that they are described as having little (remembrance) only because it is not accepted, and whatever Allah does not accept is little even if it is much. This was related from Qatadah, and al-Bayhaqi and others related something similar from al-Hasan.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: "No deed is small when accompanied by piety, and how could that be small which is accepted?!" It has also been said that the remembrance meant is the remembrance occurring in prayer, such as takbīr and tasbīḥ, and al-Jubba'i held this view.

This is supported by what Muslim and Abu Dawud related from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "That is the prayer of the hypocrite: he sits watching the sun until, when it is between the two horns of Satan, he rises and pecks four times, remembering Allah in it only a little."

It has also been said that remembrance here means prayer, because speech is involved in it, not in its ordinary sense. It was allowed that by "little" is meant "none," but the exception then raises a difficulty regarding its construction.

It was answered that the meaning is: "They do not remember Allah" (exalted is He) "except" a remembrance that is reckoned as nothing, because it does not benefit them, so there is no difficulty. But what is in this is not hidden, for "little" in the sense of "none" is a metaphor, and making "none" refer to what has no benefit is another metaphor; and besides, there is nothing in the speech that indicates it. Some verifiers said, in explaining the statement on that assumption: the meaning then is that, if it were valid to count the absence of remembrance as remembrance, then their remembrance is in the manner of his saying:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords are notched from the clashing of the battalions."

And in this, though it is easier than the first, there is what there is. The verse has been used as evidence for the recommendation of entering prayer with energy, and for the disliking of a person saying "I am lazy (kasiltu)."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he disliked a man saying: "I am lazy (kaslān)," and he would interpret this verse accordingly.

﴿Mudhabdhabīna bayna dhālik﴾ (wavering between that) is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative, a state of the subject) of the subject of ﴿yurāūna﴾ (they show off), or of the subject of ﴿yadhkurūna﴾ (they remember). It is also permissible that it be a *ḥāl* of the subject of ﴿qāmū﴾ (they stand), or that it be in the accusative of dispraise (*naṣb ʿalā al-dhamm*) by a verb that is implied. ﴿Dhālik﴾ refers to belief and disbelief, which are implied by the mention of the believers and the disbelievers. For this reason ﴿bayna﴾ is prefixed to it. This was narrated from Ibn Zayd. It is also valid that ﴿dhālik﴾ refers to the believers and the disbelievers, so that what follows it is an explanation of it, in the manner of the poet's words:

"The man of keen insight, who suspects you of a suspicion as if he had seen and heard."

The meaning is: wavering between them, bewildered, Satan having unsettled them. The root of *dhabdhabah* (unsettling, wavering), as al-Rāghib (al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī) said, is the sound of movement of a hanging thing; then it was borrowed for every agitation, movement, or hesitation between two things. The second *dhāl* is original according to the Basrans (the grammarians of Basra), and is substituted from a *bāʾ* according to the Kufans (the grammarians of Kufa). This is a well-known disagreement among them.

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read ﴿mudhabdhibīna﴾ with a *kasra* on the second *dhāl*. Its object, on this reading, is omitted, meaning: unsettling their hearts, or their religion, or their opinion. It is also possible to make it intransitive, with *faʿlala* in the sense of *tafaʿlala*, as ﴿ṣalṣala﴾ came in the sense of *taṣalṣala* (to ring/clang). That is: wavering. This is supported by what is in the codex (*muṣḥaf*) of Ibn Masʿūd: ﴿mutadhabdhibīna﴾.

It was also read with an unpointed *dāl* (*dabdaba*), which is derived from *al-dubbah* with a *ḍamma* on the *dāl* and a *shadda* on the *bāʾ*, meaning path or way. As in the *Nihāyah* (of Ibn al-Athīr): it is said, "He is on my *dubbah*," meaning my path and my manner. In the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās: "Follow the *dubbah* of Quraysh, and do not separate from the community." The meaning then is that they were taken by them, at one time one way, and at another time another way.

﴿Lā ilā hāʾulāʾi wa lā ilā hāʾulāʾi﴾ (neither to these nor to those): that is, not counted as belonging to the believers in truth, because of their concealing disbelief, nor to the disbelievers, because of their showing belief. Or: not arriving at the former nor at the latter. Its position is accusative, being a *ḥāl* from the pronoun in ﴿mudhabdhabīna﴾, or being a *badal* (substitute) for it. It is also possible that it is an explanation and elaboration of it.

﴿Wa man yuḍlili Allāh﴾ (and whomever Allah sends astray), because of his lack of readiness for guidance and success, ﴿fa-lan tajida lahu sabīlan﴾ (you will not find for him a way): a path connecting him to the truth and rightness, let alone your guiding him to it. The address is to everyone who is fit for it, and this is more emphatic in censure.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 144:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers.﴾ This is a prohibition addressed to the sincere believers against allying with the disbelievers, [meaning] the Jews only, as has been said, or [meaning] what includes them and others, as is apparent after the description of the state of the hypocrites. That is: do not take them as allies, for that is the habit and religion of the hypocrites, so do not imitate them. It has also been said that what is meant by "those who have believed" is the hypocrites, and by "the believers" the sincere ones; the verse then is a prohibition to the hypocrites against allying with the disbelievers, not to the sincere ones. It has also been said that what is meant by the relative pronoun is the sincere ones and by "the disbelievers" the hypocrites, as if it were said: "I have already made clear to you the characteristics of these hypocrites, so do not take them as allies." al-Qaffal went to this view, but both opinions are far-fetched.

﴿Do you wish to give Allah a clear proof against yourselves?﴾ That is: a manifest argument for punishment. This implies that Allah, by the requirement of His wisdom, does not punish anyone except after the establishment of proof against him, and many verses indicate this. It has also been said: do you wish by this to give Him, exalted is He, a clear proof that you are in agreement [with them]? For allying with the disbelievers is the clearest evidence of hypocrisy.

Some people kept "sultan" in its well-known meaning. However, Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Every sultan in the Qur'an is a proof." It is one of the words that may be used with both masculine and feminine forms by consensus; its masculine form is taken in view of "the proof" or in view of its well-known meaning, and the feminine form in view of "the argument." The feminine is more common among eloquent speakers, according to what al-Farra' said, but it was not considered here, and the masculine was taken so that the closing word (fasilah) would be fitting.

Ibn 'Atiyyah claimed that the masculine is more well known, and it is the language of the Qur'an wherever it occurs. "Against yourselves" (ʿalaykum) may be connected to "giving," or to a omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial state (hal) of "sultan." The direction of the rebuke toward the wish itself, rather than toward its object, by saying "Do you make...?" and so on, is for the sake of emphasizing its denunciation and magnifying its gravity, by making clear that it is something that a rational person would not even wish, let alone actually do.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 145:

﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire.﴾ That is: in its lowest level, which is its bottom. The Fire has seven levels. The first is called, as it is said, (Jahannam); the second (Laza); the third (al-Hutamah); the fourth (al-Sa'ir); the fifth (Saqar); the sixth (al-Jahim); and the seventh (al-Hawiyah). The Fire as a whole may be called by the name of the first level, and some of the levels by the names of others, because the word "Fire" encompasses them all. These levels are called darak (depths) because they follow one another in succession, one beneath another. The (darak) (depth) is like (daraj) (degree), except that (darak) is used with regard to descent, while (daraj) is used with regard to ascent. The fact that the hypocrite is (in the lowest depth) indicates the severity of his punishment.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya related from al-Ahwas, from Ibn Mas'ud: "The hypocrite will be placed in a coffin of iron, which will be locked shut upon him, and then he will be placed in the lowest depth." He was punished more severely than other disbelievers because he added to shared disbelief the mocking of Islam
Page 178
and the deception of its adherents.

As for what is related in the two Sahihs from the saying of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: "Whoever has four qualities is a pure hypocrite, and whoever has one of them has a quality of hypocrisy until he abandons it: when he is entrusted, he betrays; when he speaks, he lies; when he promises, he breaks it; and when he disputes, he acts wickedly." The scholars of hadith have said about this that it is specific to his time, peace be upon him, because through the light of revelation he knew the inner states of those who possessed these traits. So he, peace be upon him, informed his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, of their signs so that they might guard against them, but he did not name them out of fear of strife, of their apostasy, and of their joining the warriors against Muslims.

It has been said: it is not specific, but it is to be interpreted as referring to one who considers that permissible, or the meaning is that whoever has these traits resembles the pure hypocrites. The Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, applied this designation to him as a severe warning and threat. This applies to one who habitually does so, not to one who does it occasionally. Or he is a hypocrite in matters of religion by customary usage, and in custom "hypocrite" is applied to anyone who conceals the opposite of what he displays in a way that causes harm, even if it is not a matter of belief and disbelief. It seems to be derived from (al-nafiqa'), and the intention is not restriction. This statement was issued by the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, according to the requirements of the occasion, which is why some narrations say "three" and others "four."

The Kufans read (al-darki) with a sukun on the ra', which is a dialect form like (al-satr) and (al-satar). The fath (vowel) is more common and more eloquent, because its plural is attested as (af'al), and (af'al) for the pattern (fa'al) with a vowel is common and regular, while its occurrence with a sukun is rare, like (farkh, afrakh) and (zand, azna'd). That one of the two forms is dispensed with by the plural of the other is permissible, but it is contrary to the apparent, so the preference is not refuted by it. The statement is taken in its literal sense.

Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi claimed that there are no levels in the Fire, and that this is a report of reaching the utmost in punishment, as one says: "The sultan brought so-and-so down to the lowest ground and so-and-so up to the throne," meaning the lowness or height of rank, not distance. It is not hidden that this contradicts what the transmitted reports have brought.

(min al-nar) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), and there are two possibilities regarding its referent:

One: it is (al-darak), and the governing element is the stability (istiqrar).

The second: it is the concealed pronoun in (al-asfal), since it is an adjective, so it may carry the pronoun, meaning: the state of that being from the Fire.

﴿And you will not find for them any helper.﴾ One who will take them out of it, or who will lighten for them what they are in on the Day of Resurrection, when they are in the lowest depth. That the meaning is (and you will not find for them any helper) in this world, so that the verse would be a description of them as having lost both this world and the Hereafter, is of no account, as is not hidden. The address is to everyone who is fit for it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 146:

﴿Except those who repent﴾ from hypocrisy. This is an exception from the hypocrites, or from their pronoun in the predicate, or from the pronoun in the genitive (lahum). It is said that it is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is what follows the fa' (the particle "then"), and the fa' entered because of the meaning of the condition in the speech.

﴿And make amends﴾ for what they corrupted of their intentions and states during the time of hypocrisy. It is said that it means they remained steadfast in repentance in the future, but the first is preferable. ﴿And hold fast to Allah﴾, that is, they held firmly to His Book or trusted in Him. ﴿And are sincere in their religion for Allah﴾, meaning they do not intend by their obedience except His face and His good pleasure, glory be to Him, not the show-off of people or the averting of harm, as in hypocrisy.

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from Abu Thumama, who said: The disciples (al-hawariyyun) said to Isa, peace be upon him: "O Spirit of Allah, who is the one sincere to Allah?" He said: "The one who acts for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, and does not like that people praise him for it."

Then ﴿those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the relative pronoun in terms of its being characterized by what is in the place of the attribute, and what it contains of the meaning of distance, as has passed more than once. ﴿With the believers﴾, that is, the known believers, those from whom hypocrisy never proceeded at all since they believed. The intended meaning is that they are with them in the high ranks of Paradise, or that they are counted among them in this world and the Hereafter.

﴿And Allah will soon give the believers a great reward﴾, a reward whose measure cannot be estimated, so they will share in it and divide it with them.

Page 179
Abu Hayyan interpreted the great reward as eternal abiding (khulud). Generalization is preferable, and the intended meaning of "the believers" here is what was intended by it in what came before. Considering the sharing was followed by more than one scholar, and were it not for interpreting the verse this way, there would be no clear meaning in its mention of the states of those who repented from hypocrisy.

Some scholars went to not considering it, and the intended meaning is the announcement of increased reward for one who never had hypocrisy at all. Some believers are generalized to include one who had no prior hypocrisy and one who had hypocrisy earlier and repented from it. The apparent meaning is what we have mentioned. (يُؤْتِ) is written without a yā', and it is a present-tense verb in the nominative, so its yā' by right should be written both in pronunciation and in script, but it was dropped in pronunciation because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, and the script followed the pronunciation. The readers pause on it without the yā' following the script, except Ya'qub, who pauses with the yā', looking to the original form; this is also narrated from al-Kisa'i, Hamza and Nafi'. Al-Samin claimed that the better course is to follow the script, because word-endings have frequently been elided.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 147 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe?﴾ This is addressed to the hypocrites. It has also been said that it is addressed to the believers, but this view is weak. The verse is set down to show that the basis for their punishment, both its existence and its non-existence, is only their disbelief and nothing else. Thus the sentence confirms what precedes it, namely their steadfastness upon repentance. The *ma* (what) is interrogative, implying negation in the most emphatic and forceful manner. It has also been said that *ma* is negating, the *ba'* (with) is causal, and it has been said that the *ba'* is superfluous. The meaning is: What thing does Allah, glorified is He, do by means of your punishment? Does He thereby find relief from rage? Does He attain vengeance by it? Does He draw benefit to Himself? Or does He ward off harm by it? This would be the case with kings, but He is the Absolutely Rich, exalted above the like of such things. Rather, it is a matter required by the sickness of your disbelief and hypocrisy. So if you guard yourselves against hypocrisy and purify your souls with the draught of faith and gratitude in this world, you will be healed and safe. Otherwise, you will perish an inescapable perishing through eternal abiding in the Fire. The gratitude was placed first, although the apparent order would place it later, because it is not counted as valid except after faith, since it is a path leading to faith at the first of its stages.

The knower (*al-'arif*) Abu Isma'il al-Ansari has mentioned that gratitude, in origin, is a name for the recognition of a blessing, because a blessing is the way to recognising the Benefactor. It has three degrees. When one considers a blessing such as provision or creation, a longing to recognise the Benefactor arises within him. This movement is called *al-yaqaza* (awakening), *al-shukr al-qalbi* (gratitude of the heart), and *al-shukr al-mubham* (undetermined gratitude), because his Benefactor has not become clear to him in identity; he only knows that there is a Benefactor since he is one upon whom favour is bestowed. When he awakens to this, he is granted success in a greater blessing than it, which is the knowledge that the one who bestows favour upon him is the Eternal Refuge, Vast in mercy, the Rewarder, the Punisher. Then his limbs move to glorify Him, and he adds to the gratitude of the heart the gratitude of the members, and then he proclaims this beauty with his tongue, saying:

*Three have bestowed blessings upon you from me: my hand, my tongue, and the veiled inner conscience.*

Thus what is mentioned in the verse is undetermined gratitude, and it precedes faith. So there is no need for what the Imam (al-Razi) claimed, that the speech is in terms of inversion, i.e., "you believed and you were grateful." As for the view that this objection applies only on the assumption that the *wa* (and) denotes sequence, and that if it does not denote sequence there is no objection, this is something that one who has even a slight taste of the science of eloquence and rhetoric should not utter. For the *wa*, even if it does not denote sequence, yet placing forward what is not meant to be placed forward is not befitting eloquent speech, let alone inimitable speech. For this reason you see them mentioning a reason and a subtle point for whatever contradicts it.

Al-Naysaburi mentioned another reason for the placement, but he based it on the *wa* denoting sequence. He said: Perhaps the reason for this is that the verse is addressed concerning the hypocrites, and there is no dispute about their faith outwardly. The dispute is only concerning their inner states and their actions, which come from them not in conformity with their tongue's speech. So placing gratitude first here was more important, because it is an expression for directing all that Allah, Exalted, has bestowed toward that for which it was created, so that their actions and speech are upon the path of rectitude and the ways of uprightness. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that he did not take the gratitude in the verse to mean undetermined gratitude, and this is not without merit.

[p. 180]

More clear and more pleasing than this is what has stirred in my breast. Then I saw the great scholar al-Tibi, may God have mercy on him, state it explicitly: What the outstanding composition requires is that this address is with the hypocrites, and that His saying, glorified is He, ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment﴾ is connected to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire, and you will not find for them a helper﴾, and so on. It is also a warning to them that what caused them to fall into that predicament was their ingratitude for the blessings of Allah, Exalted is He, their negligence in thanking for what they were given, and their forfeiting for themselves, through their hypocrisy, the supreme aim, which is the felicity of companionship with the best of creation, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and joining the company of those whose description is ﴿in the Torah and their description in the Gospel﴾. So when they repent, amend, hold fast to Allah, Exalted is He, and make their religion sincerely for Him, then their ruling is that they should be included among those felicitous believers, after they had been deserving of the lowest ranks of the Fires. Then He turned, by way of allusion to them, that this punishment was from them and because of their negligence and their ingratitude for that exalted blessing, and their forfeiting for themselves that lofty opportunity. Otherwise, Allah is absolutely Rich, free of their punishment, let alone that He would cast them into those perils.

So His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿if you are grateful﴾ is a summary (*fadhlaka*) of the meaning of turning back from corruption on earth to reform therein, and from seeking refuge in creation to holding fast to Allah, Exalted is He, and from showing off in religion to sincerity therein. Then His saying, Mighty is the Speaker: ﴿and believe﴾ is an explanation of it and an affirmation of its meaning, i.e., and you believe the faith which contains those virtuous qualities and gathers those complete attributes. Thus placing gratitude before faith, when its proper place is after it, is an announcement that the speech is concerning it, and that the preceding verse is directed toward explaining the ingratitude for Allah's great blessing, while disbelief is a consequence. So if gratitude is delayed, these secrets and subtleties are neglected. For this reason, glorified is He, concluded the verse by way of causal explanation with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is Appreciative﴾, i.e., rewarding for gratitude, ﴿Knowing﴾ of all particulars and universals, so that nothing escapes His knowledge. Thus He delivers the reward in full to the grateful. This is the view the Imam took.

Others said: *al-Shakir* (the Appreciative) and likewise *al-Shakur* (the Most Appreciative) are among His names, Exalted is He, and it means the one who rewards small acts of obedience with many degrees, and who gives blessings in the Hereafter that are unlimited in exchange for deeds done in a few days. Under both interpretations it refers to an active attribute. It has also been said that its meaning is the one who praises those who hold fast to His obedience, and so it refers to an attribute of speech.

\* \* \*

This, and from the way of allusion in the verses:

As for His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And they ask you concerning women﴾ up to His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And Allah is ever Expansive and Wise﴾, al-Naysaburi said concerning it: The soul (*nafs*) relative to the spirit (*ruh*) is like the mirror relative to the bride. ﴿The orphan women﴾ are the attributes of the souls, and ﴿what has been prescribed for them﴾ is what Allah, Exalted is He, has made obligatory of rights. The sum of the meaning is: Your soul is your mount, so be gentle with it. To this the Exalted refers in His saying: ﴿And reconciliation is best﴾, and ﴿Souls have been made present with stinginess﴾. The spirit is stingy about abandoning the rights of Allah, Exalted is He, and the soul is stingy about abandoning its shares. ﴿Do not incline completely﴾ in rejecting the shares of the soul. It has come in a report: "Indeed your soul has a right over you." ﴿So you leave her as if suspended﴾ between the upper world and the lower world. ﴿And if they separate﴾, i.e., the spirit and the soul, ﴿Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾. The spirit draws with a pull: "Leave your soul and come to Me, to the vastness of the wealth of Allah, Exalted is He, in a world I have desired," so it is made independent of the vehicle of the soul by reaching the goal. The soul is drawn by a pull: ﴿Return to your Lord﴾, to the vastness of the wealth of Allah, Exalted is He, in the world of ﴿Enter among My servants﴾ and ﴿Enter My Paradise﴾. End of quotation. It is not hidden that the door of interpretation is wide, and what he mentioned is not definitive; it is possible that the verse be taken as concerning the shaykh and the disciple.

As for His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, be [persistently standing firm in justice]﴾, and so on, we say: Indeed He, glorified is He, commanded the believers, who are seeking the reward of both abodes and who hold to scientific monotheism, to be firm in the station of justice, which is the most noble of virtues, ﴿maintaining it﴾ with its rights, such that it becomes a firmly rooted disposition in them, with which no injustice is possible in anything, nor the appearance of a trait of the self following desire for worldly gain or for the removal of a similar harm.

[p. 181]

Then Mighty and Majestic He said: ﴿O you who have believed﴾ — from the standpoint of proof, ﴿believe﴾ — from the standpoint of clarification, until you believe from the standpoint of direct vision. Or: O you who have believed by traditional faith, believe with the faith of the eye. Or the meaning is: O you who claim to strip faith for Me without intermediary, there is no way for you to reach the pure stripping except by accepting the intermediaries. So the verse is an allusion to the distinction after the union.

﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ by imitation, ﴿then disbelieved﴾ since imitation had no root, ﴿then believed﴾ by rational inference, ﴿then disbelieved﴾ since their intellects were not illuminated by the Divine light, ﴿then increased in disbelief﴾ through doubts and objections. This may be an allusion to the description of those who waver in following the path of the friends of Allah, Exalted is He, and in believing in their states, when their desire for leadership over the people was stirred. When the night of striving enveloped them, they could not bear it and they denied, and they returned to the portions of their souls. When they saw the end of the great ones, and thought they could catch up with them if they remained upright and believed, but when they did not attain any of the stations and honours of the people because of their lack of sincerity and the poor state of their preparedness, they apostatised and became deniers of them and of their stations, and increased in denial when they returned to pleasures and desires, and preferred this world over the Hereafter. They began saying to people: Indeed these are not upon the truth, for we have followed what they followed and entered what they entered, but we found nothing but a mirage in a desert plain. This is the state of many evil scholars who deny the people, may God sanctify their secrets.

﴿Allah would not forgive them﴾ because of the veil of doubt, the corruption of the core of the heart, and the disappearance of readiness; ﴿nor would He guide them to a way﴾ toward truth, nor toward perfection, because they do not accept that. ﴿Those who take the disbelievers as allies﴾ because of their affinity with them, and the like is drawn toward its like, ﴿instead of the believers﴾ because of the absence of kinship. ﴿Do they seek with them honour?﴾, i.e., they seek to be strengthened by them, and to gain strength through their wealth and their position in this world. ﴿Indeed, honour belongs entirely to Allah﴾; thus there is no path for them to it except from Him, glorified is He, Mighty and Majestic.

Then glorified is He mentioned from the description of the hypocrites that ﴿when they stand up for prayer, they stand lazily﴾, because they have no desire to attend and they are averse to it, due to their lack of readiness and the domination of desire over them. ﴿They show off to the people﴾ because they hide behind them from seeing Allah, Exalted is He. ﴿And they do not remember Allah except a little﴾, because they remember Him only with the tongue and only in the presence of people. This is unlike the sincere believers, who when they stand for prayer fly to it on the wings of longing and awe. Rather, they yearn for its times:

*Like the yearning of a Bedouin woman who longs for the ruins of Najd, which she has left, and for its acacia.*

From here it is reported that the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, used to say to Bilal: "Give us rest, O Bilal" — meaning, as he, upon him be blessings and peace, intended: establish the prayer for us so that we may pray and find rest in it, not rest from it. Whoever supposes the latter about the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has committed disbelief, God forbid. And when they worship, they see none but Allah, Exalted is He, and what is the worth of other than Him in their eyes that they should show off to it? Indeed every part of them remembers Allah, Exalted is He. Yes, they may occupy themselves with something else instead of Him, and then remembrance is not attainable for them there. The knowers have counted remembrance for the people of witnessing as a sin, and for this one of them said:

*By the remembrance of Allah, sins increase, and vices and faults are exposed.*

*And abandoning remembrance is better than everything, and the sun of the Essence has no setting.*

But some of them have said that the servant does not reach that station except through abundant remembrance, and one who said the following pointed to a lofty station:

*None abandons remembrance except one who witnesses Him, and one who does not remember Him does not witness Him.*

*Remembrance is a veil over the One Remembered, and when one remembers Him in the state, it conceals Him.*

*So I will not cease to make Him witnessed in states, and I will not cease to remember Him with every breath.*

[p. 182]

﴿O you who have believed, do not take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers﴾, lest the darkness of their disbelief spread to you. ﴿Do you want to give Allah a clear authority against you?﴾ A manifest proof for your punishment, by the firm establishment of the disposition (al-hay'ah) through which you incline toward their alliance. ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire﴾, because of their bewilderment, through the weakness of their readiness (isti'dad). ﴿And you will not find for them a helper﴾, one who could help them against the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, because their connection is severed and their love for the people of Allah, the Exalted, has been lifted. ﴿Except for those who repent﴾, who return to Allah, the Exalted, by the remnant of the light of readiness and by accepting the extent of success (tawfiq). ﴿And reform﴾ what they corrupted of their readiness, by suppressing desire, breaking the qualities of the self (nafs), and lifting the veil of the faculties. ﴿And hold fast to Allah﴾ by adhering to His commands and turning toward Him, glorified is He. ﴿And make their religion sincerely for Allah﴾ by removing the hidden traces of polytheism and turning away from everything other than Him. ﴿Then those will be with the believers﴾, the truthful ones. ﴿And Allah will give the believers a great reward﴾, from witnessing the manifestations of the Attributes (tajalliyat al-sifat) and the gardens of the Acts (jannat al-af'al). ﴿Why would Allah punish you if you are grateful﴾ through repentance, reforming what was corrupted, holding fast to the rope of the commands, turning toward Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and making the religion sincerely for Him, glorified is He, ﴿and you believe﴾, with the faith that merits all of that. ﴿And Allah is Ever Grateful and All-Knowing﴾, so He rewards and conveys the reward in full. And Allah, the Exalted, says the truth, and He guides to the way.

[Page 2]

In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Allah does not love the public utterance of evil speech﴾. His, glory be to Him, not loving something is a metaphor for His anger. The letter *bāʾ* (with) is connected to *al-jahr* (public utterance), and the prepositional phrase in which it occurs is in the accusative or nominative position. *Min* (from) is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) describing *al-sūʾ* (evil). *Al-jahr bi-l-shayʾ* means to announce or make something manifest, as is understood from the *Qāmūs* (the lexicon of al-Fayrūzābādī). In the *Ṣiḥāḥ* (of al-Jawharī), it says: "Jahara bi-l-qawl" means he raised his voice with it. Perhaps the intended meaning here is manifestation, even if it does not involve raising the voice. That is: Allah, glory be to Him, does not love that anyone announce evil speech of any kind.

﴿Except one who has been wronged﴾, meaning: except the public utterance of one who has been wronged, for this is not displeasing to Him, exalted is He. This is by praying against his oppressor, or by complaining about him and reminding him of the evil that is in him.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it means: praying against one who has wronged him.

And from Mujāhid, the meaning is: Allah, glory be to Him, does not love that anyone should censure another or complain about him, ﴿except one who has been wronged﴾, so it is permissible for him to complain of his oppressor, make his matter known, and remind him of the evil he has done.

And from al-Ḥasan and al-Suddī, and this is also narrated from Abū Jaʿfar, may Allah be pleased with him, the meaning is: Allah does not love reviling in retaliation, ﴿except one who has been wronged﴾, so there is no harm for him to retaliate against the one who wronged him by means that retaliation is permitted by in the religion.

Al-Ḥasan permitted that when a man is told, "O adulterer!", he may respond to the one who said it with the same.

Ibn Jarīr (al-Ṭabarī) transmitted from Mujāhid that a man was a guest of a people who did not feed him, so he complained about them and was punished for it, and then this verse was revealed. You know that the lesson is drawn from the generality of the wording, not from the specific occasion of revelation (sabab).

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, and from Ubayy, Ibn Jubayr, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and ʿAṭāʾ, that they recited (*illā man ẓalama*) in the active voice (*ʿalā al-bināʾ li-l-fāʿil*). Then the exception is disjunctive (*munqaṭiʿ*), and the meaning is: "But the wrongdoer, He loves him," or "But he does what Allah, exalted is He, does not love, so he publicly utters evil." The relative clause is in the accusative position. Al-Zamakhsharī permitted that it be in the nominative position as a substitute (*badal*) for the subject of *yuḥibbu*, as if it were said: "None loves the public utterance of evil except the wrongdoer," according to the dialect of one who says: *mā jāʾanī Zaydun illā ʿAmrun* (no one came to me except ʿAmr), with the meaning *mā jāʾanī illā ʿAmrun* (none came to me but ʿAmr). From this is the verse: ﴿None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾. This is a Tamimi dialect, and upon it the poet says:

*ʿAshiyyata mā tughnī al-ryimāḥu makānahā*
*wa-lā al-nabla illā al-mashrafiyyu al-muṣammimu*

(On the evening when spears cannot take their place, nor arrows, except the keen Indian sword.)

Sībawayh transmitted this dialect, and some denied it. The transmission of the master of the discipline (*shaykh al-ṣināʿa*) is sufficient support for the one who affirms it. It is reported from Abū Ḥayyān that the verse of poetry is not like the example, because in it one may imagine generality in the sense of weapons, whereas with Zayd no generality is imagined. It cannot be made correct except on the basis that its original form is: *mā jāʾanī Zaydun wa-lā ghayruhu* (no one came to me, Zayd or any other), so the coordinated element is omitted because the exception indicates it. The same applies to the verse that was mentioned. It was refuted, as al-Shihāb (al-Khafājī) said, on the grounds that if the estimated sense were what was mentioned in the example, the exception would be connected (*muttaṣil*), whereas the premise is the opposite. And it was refuted that the meaning, as al-Ṭībī's words imply, is to make the replaced element (*mubdal minhu*) equivalent to what is not mentioned, so that the exception is effectively "exception of the whole" (*mufarragh*) and the negation is general, except that he explicitly negated some individual members of the general class to add emphasis to the negation regarding that, or because it is a likely occasion for the illusion of affirmation. They say: *mā jāʾanī Zaydun illā ʿAmrun*, and the meaning is: *mā jāʾanī illā ʿAmrun*. Similarly here the meaning is: "None loves the public utterance of evil except the wrongdoer." Thus the word *Allāh* is introduced as an emphasis on the negation of

[Page 3]

His love, exalted is He. That is, for Allah, glory be to Him, there is exclusivity in the non-love, which belongs to no one other than Him.

If it is said: "Then what follows *illā* (except) at that point cannot be the subject, which is evident, so the substitution is determined, and it is an error?" It is answered: It would be an error only if this specific element were not in the position of the general, and the meaning were not: "None came to me except ʿAmr."

If it is said: "Then the word *Allāh* would be a metaphor for someone, and there is no way to that?" It is answered: "*Lā yuḥibbu Allāh*" (Allah does not love) is interpreted as "*lā yuḥibbu aḥad*" (no one loves), occurring in its place without any figurative use in the word *Allāh*. Thus it is said.

Al-Shihāb objected to this, saying: when the excepted-from element is general, it is either by estimating a word, as Abū Ḥayyān mentioned, or by figurative use in the word for knowledge (*al-ʿilm*), and both have problems. There is no other way to generality. So what the respondent mentioned requires explaining its method. Unless it is said that the exception from knowledge is conditioned on its subject being more deserving of the ruling, such that when it is negated from him, its negation from others is known by a stronger means without estimation or figurative use. It would be said here, for example: when Allah, glory be to Him, does not love the public utterance of evil, He being the One free of all needs, others do not love it by any means. You know that this does not satisfy, because the stated condition is something for which no proof has been established. Moreover, the claim that the negation of love for public utterance of evil from Him, exalted is He, implies its negation from others by a stronger means is most obscure. The better position is what he mentioned afterward, namely that it is said: what was mentioned is estimated in the speech, but the exception is counted as disjunctive according to what is apparent and the outward reading.

It was permitted, according to the reading in the active voice (*qirāʾat al-maʿlūm*), that the phrase be connected to *al-sūʾ* (evil), that is: "except the evil of one who has been wronged, so the public utterance of it is loved and accepted." It was said that it is connected to the statement of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe?﴾ It is narrated from al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim that he used to say this with inversion of order, meaning: "What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe, except one who has been wronged." He used to recite it that way. This hardly is accepted in interpreting the words of Allah, the Mighty.

﴿And Allah is ever Hearing﴾ of all things heard, so the speech of the wronged and the wrongdoer is included in it, ﴿Knowing﴾ of all things known, among which is the condition of the wronged and the wrongdoer. The sentence is a concluding statement (*tadhyīl*) confirming what the exception conveys, and that generality does not conflict with this, as was supposed.

As for the connection of this verse with what precedes it, according to what the scholar al-Ṭībī stated: when He, glory be to Him, finished explaining the sending down of His mercy and affirming the manifestation of His compassion, He brought this statement, exalted is His majesty, "Allah does not love the public utterance of evil," as a completion of that, and as instruction for the servants to adopt His attributes, exalted is His majesty. In this there is: this is something that yields no benefit, and the connection is not completed by it. He claimed that the first verse also contains an indication of teaching adopting noble character traits, as ʿIṣām al-Milla established, and he hoped that it would be among the inspired insights. In that case both would share that each includes the aforementioned instruction, which is nothing, as is not hidden.

Similar to this is what ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā mentioned regarding the connection, namely that when He, exalted is His dignity, mentioned the hypocrites, who are those who display the opposite of what they conceal, He, exalted is He, clarified that what is in the soul includes what is permissible to conceal and what is permissible to display. Al-Shihāb al-Dīn said: the apparent point is that when gratitude was mentioned in a way from which His pleasure with it and His love for its manifestation were known, He, glory be to Him, completed it by mentioning its opposite, as if it were said: He loves gratitude and its public proclamation, and He dislikes evil and its public proclamation. In this there is an elegant *iḥtibāk* (interlocking of opposites).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 149:

﴿If you disclose good⦆ — that is, you make it manifest — ﴿any good⦆, whatever it may be, of words and deeds. It has also been said: the intended meaning is, "If you disclose" a beautiful and good word concerning one who has done you a kindness, thanking him for his favour upon you. It has also been said: the intended meaning of "good" is wealth, and the meaning is: if you make charity manifest, ﴿or conceal it﴾ — that is, do it secretly. It has also been said: "or resolve upon doing it." ﴿Or pardon an evil⦆ — that is, you overlook one who has wronged you, despite the fact that you were permitted to hold him to account and were authorised to do so. The explicit mention of this, despite its being included in the beginning of good and its concealment according to one of the opinions, is for the sake of giving it weight, drawing attention to its rank, and showing that it is among the greatest of goods. The mention of disclosing good and concealing it serves as a preparation and introduction to it, as the words of the Exalted indicate:

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning and Competent﴾. The placing of pardon in the position of the answer to the condition indicates that the principal matter is pardon together with power. Had disclosing good and concealing it also been intended by the condition, it would not have been apt to limit the response to Allah being (ʿAfuwwan Qadīran), that is, He greatly pardons the disobedient while having complete power to hold them to account. Al-Hasan said: He pardons the wrongdoer while being able to take revenge, so you should follow the practice of Allah the Exalted. Al-Kalbi said: He is more capable of pardoning your sins than you are of pardoning the sins of one who wronged you. It has also been said: (ʿAfuwwan) toward the one who pardons, (Qadīran) upon bestowing reward upon him. This was related by al-Naysaburi and others.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 150–151:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers﴾ That is, according to what their creed leads to and what their opinions require, not that they explicitly declare it, as His words indicate: ﴿and they want to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers﴾ in belief, by believing in Him—Mighty and Majestic—and disbelieving in His messengers—upon them be prayers and peace. But they do not explicitly declare belief in Him Most High and disbelief in them altogether; rather, it is by way of necessary implication, as His words indicate: ﴿and they say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others"﴾. That is, we believe in some of the prophets—upon them be prayers and peace—and disbelieve in some of them, as the People of the Book did. And this is nothing but disbelief in Allah Most High and a distinction between Allah Most High and His messengers; for He—Mighty and Majestic—has commanded them to believe in all the prophets—upon them be prayers and peace—and there is no prophet who did not inform his people of the truth of the religion of our Prophet—may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace. So whoever disbelieves in one of them has disbelieved in all of them, and in Allah Most High as well, without realizing it. ﴿And they intend﴾ by this statement ﴿to take a way between that﴾, i.e., between belief and disbelief, ﴿a path﴾, i.e., a road they travel, although there is certainly no intermediate between them, since the truth does not vary. (And what is there after the truth but error?)

This is what some have said in the interpretation of the verse, and it is what the reports support:

For ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarir related from Qatada that he said regarding it: "Those are the enemies of Allah Most High, the Jews and the Christians. The Jews believed in the Torah and Moses, and disbelieved in the Gospel and Jesus—peace be upon him. The Christians believed in the Gospel and Jesus—peace be upon him—and disbelieved in the Qur'an and Muhammad—may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace. So they adopted Judaism and Christianity, and these are two innovations, not from Allah—Mighty and Majestic—and they abandoned Islam, which is the religion of Allah Most High with which He sent His messengers."

Ibn Jarir related the same from al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj.

Some said: Those who disbelieve in Allah Most High and His messengers—upon them be prayers and peace—are those whose disbelief is pure in its entirety, so they negate the Creator, for example, and deny prophethood. And those who make a distinction between Him Most High and His messengers—upon them be prayers and peace—are those who believe in Allah Most High and disbelieve in His messengers—upon them be prayers and peace—and not the reverse. And if it is said that this can be imagined among the Christians, for their belief in Jesus—peace be upon him—and their disbelief in Allah Most High, since they said: "He is the third of three," and disbelief in Allah—glory be to Him—includes both association and denial, (the matter is clear enough) — and those who believe in some and disbelieve in others are those who believed in some prophets—peace be upon them—and disbelieved in some of them, like the Jews. These are opposite categories, and the apparent expectation would be that they be joined by "or," but "and" has been used in their place, so it has the same meaning. And it has been said: the relative pronoun is implied, based on the permissibility of omitting it while its clause remains. And it has been said: His words—Most High—"and they want to make a distinction" etc., are an explanatory conjunction to His words—Glorified be He—"who disbelieve," because this desire is itself disbelief in Allah Most High, since whoever disbelieves in the messengers of Allah—Glorified be He—has disbelieved in Allah Most High, like the Brahmins.

As for His words—Majestic and Exalted be He—"and they say, 'We believe in some'" etc., it is a conjunction to the relative clause, and the "and" carries the meaning of "or" of classification. So the first group made a distinction between belief in Allah Most High and His messenger, and the latter group made a distinction between the messengers of Allah Most High—peace be upon them—so they believed in some and disbelieved in others, like the Jews. In every case, the predicate of "indeed" is His words Most High: ﴿Those﴾, i.e., those described with the ugly qualities, ﴿are the disbelievers﴾, the complete ones in disbelief; there is no regard for what they claim and call belief at all. ﴿Truly﴾ is a verbal noun emphasizing something other than itself, its governing verb being omitted, i.e., "that is established," that is, their being complete in disbelief is truly established. It is also permissible that it be an adjective of the verbal noun of "the disbelievers," i.e., they are those who disbelieved a true disbelief, that is, there is no doubt or uncertainty in it. Then the governing verb is mentioned, and "truly" has the sense of the passive participle, not the sense of the opposite of falsehood; for this reason its occurrence as an adjective is correct both grammatically and semantically. The possibility of its being a circumstantial clause, as Abu al-Baqa' claimed, is remote. And the verse, according to what some have claimed, is connected to His words Most High: "O you who believe" etc., as though it were a justification for it; and what intervenes between the cause and the effect of sentences and verses is, upon close reflection, either parenthetical or digressive. ﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers﴾, i.e., for them. The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun to draw attention to the abominable quality of disbelief, which indicates causation. It may also be intended to include all disbelievers, who enter it in the first instance.

﴿a humiliating punishment﴾ that will humiliate and degrade them, as recompense for their disbelief, through which they supposed they had honor.
