﴿a humiliating punishment﴾ that will humiliate and degrade them, as recompense for their disbelief, through which they supposed they had honor.

﴿Those who believe in God and His messengers, and do not make any distinction between any of them﴾, by believing in some and disbelieving in others as the disbelievers did. The use of (بين) with أحد (aḥad, "any one") has already been discussed. The relative construction (al-mawṣūl, "the relative pronoun") is the subject (mubtada', "subject of the nominal sentence"), and its predicate (khabar, "predicate") is the clause of His saying: ﴿those﴾, i.e. those described by these sublime attributes, ﴿He will give them﴾, i.e. God, exalted is He, ﴿their rewards﴾, those promised to them. The genitive (idafa, "construct phrase") here is for a known referent (al-'ahd, "the specific, known").

Some claimed that the predicate is omitted, meaning "their opposites and counterparts." The use of (سوف, "sawfa") is to emphasize the promise, which is the giving, and to indicate that it will certainly occur even if delayed, not to inform that it is delayed for a time. Al-Zamakhshari said that (يفعل, "yafʿalu"), which denotes the future, is by its form put to the meaning of the future. When (سوف) enters upon it, what it is put to, namely the affirmation of the act in the future, is emphasized, not that it is given something that is not in its origin. So (سوف) corresponds to (لن, "lan"), and its relation to (يفعل) is like the relation of (لن) to (لا يفعل, "lā yafʿalu"), because (لا) is for negating the future. When (لن) is placed in its position, the established meaning, which is the negation of the future, is emphasized. Thus each of (لن) and (سوف) is in essence emphasis. For this reason Sibawayh said: "لن يفعل" is the negation of "سوف يفعل." It seems that He, glory be to Him, was content with stating what these believers have, rather than saying: ﴿those are truly the believers﴾, while the meaning of opposition is understood from what indicates it. In the verse there is an iltifat (shift, "a change of grammatical person") from first-person speech to third-person absence.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Kathir read ﴿We will give them﴾ with nūn (the first-person plural), so there is no shift. ﴿And God is ever Forgiving﴾ toward those whose attribute this is, for the sins and transgressions that preceded in their past, ﴿Merciful﴾ to them, so He multiplies their good deeds and increases them beyond what they were promised.

[p. 6]

﴿They ask you﴾, O Muhammad, ﴿the People of the Book﴾, those who divided the Messengers, ﴿to bring down for them a Book from heaven﴾. They said: Musa (peace be upon him) brought the tablets from Allah, the Exalted, so bring us tablets from Him, the Exalted. They demanded that what is sent down be all at once, and that it be written in a heavenly script. This was narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi and al-Suddi.

It is also narrated from Qatadah that they asked Him to send down a book specifically for them. Close to this is what Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) reported from Ibn Jurayj, who said: The Jews said to Muhammad (ﷺ): "We will not pledge allegiance to you in what you call us to until you bring us a book from Allah: from Allah to so-and-so, that you are the Messenger of Allah, and to so-and-so, that you are the Messenger of Allah." Their purpose in this was nothing but to dictate terms and to be obstinate.

Al-Hasan said: Even if they had asked this seeking guidance and not out of stubbornness, He would have given them what they asked. ﴿So they had asked Musa﴾ (peace be upon him) ﴿for something greater than that﴾, or ﴿a greater request﴾ than the one mentioned and more serious. The fa' (the "so") is in response to an implied conditional clause, and the response is interpreted so that the sequence makes sense. That is: if you consider this to be great, and you know what they were upon, it will become clear to you how deeply rooted their disbelief is. It has also been said that the fa' is causal, and the meaning is: Do not be concerned and do not consider it great, for they had asked Musa (peace be upon him) for what was greater. Although this request came from their forefathers, since they followed the same path in everything they did and did not do, it was attributed to them. Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) regarded this as an instance of attributing to the effect what belongs to its cause. It is also permissible that this is an attribution of the act of some to all, on the basis of the complete unity of the people, as in the verse of poetry:

*My people are they who killed Umaym, my brother; so when I shoot, my arrow strikes me.*

In that case the pronoun in (they asked) refers to all the People of the Book, since the request came from some of them. The term "People of the Book" may also refer to all of them, and then the attribution of (asks you) to the People of the Book belongs to this same kind of attribution. It may also refer to this category (genus) of people, and the purpose would then be to describe the ugly qualities of this group. In that case there is no strain or figurative extension, either in the pronoun or in its referent.

You know that attributing the act of some to all is common in the Noble Book and occurs in about a thousand places.

Al-Hasan read (akthara) ("greater") with a thaa' (with three dots). ﴿Then they said: Show us Allah﴾, the One who sent you, ﴿openly﴾, meaning openly and visibly seen. It is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, a word describing the state of another noun at the time of the action) from the first object, as Abu al-Baqa' said. It may also be a ḥāl of the second object, meaning seen by the eyes, in the passive form. There is no ambiguity in this, since each of the two implies the other. So it should not be said that it must be a ḥāl of the second object because it is closer to it.

It is also permissible that it is an adjective (ṣifah) of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar) which is the seeing (ru'yah), not the showing (ira'ah), because in the lexicographical works, jahrah (openly) is an adjective of the first object, not the second. So the implied meaning is: (Show us) so that we see Him with an open seeing. It has also been said that the verbal noun being described is an implied question, that is, a question openly; or it has been said that it is a statement, that is, an openly stated statement. This is supported by what Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), that he said about the verse: "When they see Him, they have seen Him." They only said (openly) (show us Allah), so the order is inverted; but this is far-fetched. The fa' here is explanatory.

﴿Then the thunderbolt seized them﴾, that is, destroyed them because they asked Him and said what they said. The thunderbolt (al-ṣā'iqah) is fire that came from the sky.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj that he said: "The thunderbolt" is death. Allah caused them to die before their appointed times as a punishment for their statement, then He resurrected them. The authenticity of this report is doubtful.

Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) read (al-ṣa'qah) ("the blast"). ﴿For their wrongdoing﴾, that is, because of their wrongdoing, which is their obstinacy and their request for what is impossible in that state they were in. Rejecting the disbelievers' request to see Allah out of obstinacy does not imply that seeing Him is impossible absolutely.

Al-Zamakhshari used the verse as evidence for absolute impossibility. He based this on the claim that the wrongdoing attributed to them was nothing but the mere fact that they requested the seeing. Then he said: If they had requested something permissible, they would not have been called wrongdoers, and the thunderbolt would not have seized them, just as Ibrahim (peace be upon him) asked for the revival of the dead, yet He did not call him a wrongdoer, nor did He strike him with thunderbolts. Then (Allah) thundered and lightning flashed and He invoked a curse upon the claimant that seeing Him is permissible, with what he deserves more.

You know that this man was overcome by his desires, so he overlooked the fact that the Jews asked only out of obstinacy, and they did not take into account the miracle as such, even though miracles are equal in their power to show proof. Their asking for a miracle is enough to make them wrongdoers. Comparing it to the request of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is an extraordinary wonder, as is not hidden from people of understanding.

﴿Then they took the calf﴾ and worshipped it

[p. 7]

﴿after the clear signs had come to them﴾, that is, the miracles He showed to Pharaoh: the staff, the white hand, the splitting of the sea, and others; or the clear proofs indicating His divinity and His oneness. It does not mean the Torah, because it was revealed to them only after the taking of the calf. ﴿Then We pardoned that﴾ taking, when they repented. It has been said that this implies an invitation to them to the Torah, as if it were said: Those who committed the crime repented, so We pardoned them; so you too repent, so that We may pardon you.

﴿And We gave Musa a manifest authority﴾, that is, an evident dominion over them when He commanded them to kill themselves as repentance for their taking of the calf. It has been said: Although this was before the pardon, the command to kill was before the repentance, since accepting the killing was a repentance for them. But the conjunction (wa) does not imply sequence. It has been suggested that this authority should not be considered the same as that dominion, but rather a dominion after the pardon, in that they submitted to him and were not able after that to oppose him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 154:

﴿And We raised above them the mount (al-Tur)﴾. This is what is related from Qatadah: it was a mountain, and they stood at its base, and Allah raised it and placed it above them as if it were a canopy. Its extent was about the size of their encampment, one farsakh by one farsakh. It was not, as is said in al-Bahr, the mountain known as Tur Sinai. The adverbial phrase is connected to (raised). It has also been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) of al-Tur, meaning: We raised the mount while it was above them ﴿with their covenant﴾, i.e., because of their covenant, so that they would accept it. This is according to what is related, that they refused to accept the law of the Torah, so the mountain was raised over them and they accepted it. Or (it was raised) so that they would fear and not break the covenant, according to what is related, that they intended to break it, so the mountain was raised over them, they became afraid, and they desisted from breaking it. It is said: this is the more appropriate reading in light of His words, exalted is He, afterward: ﴿And We took from them a firm covenant﴾.

Al-Jubba'i claimed that the meaning of the breaking of their covenant, which was taken from them, was that they would act in accordance with what is in the Torah, and they broke it by worshipping the calf. In response: the Torah was revealed only after their worship of the calf, as was mentioned just before, so this cannot be the case. Abu Muslim said: Allah, exalted is He, only raised the mountain above them to shade them from the sun, as a reward for their covenant and as an honour to them. It is not hidden that this is a violation of the consensus of the exegetes, and it has no foundation whatsoever.

﴿And We said to them﴾ through the tongue of Yusha' (peace be upon him), after the passing of the period of wandering (al-tih): ﴿Enter the gate﴾. Qatadah said, as related by Ibn al-Mundhir and others from him: "We used to say that it was a gate of the gates of Bayt al-Maqdis." It was also said: it is Iliya', and it was said: Ariha', and it was said: it is the name of a village. Or (the words "And We said to them") were through the tongue of Musa (peace be upon him), while the mount was shading them, (Enter the gate) mentioned, when you come out of the wandering; or it is the gate of the dome toward which they used to pray, because they did not come out of the wandering during his lifetime, peace be upon him.

The apparent meaning is that there is no restriction. ﴿Prostrating﴾: humbling oneself and submitting. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it means bowing (ruku'). It was also said: prostrating upon your foreheads in gratitude to Allah, exalted is He. ﴿And We said to them﴾ through the tongue of Dawud (peace be upon him): ﴿Do not transgress﴾, i.e., do not exceed what has been permitted to you, or do not wrong by hunting fish ﴿on the Sabbath﴾.

It is possible—as al-Qadi said, may Allah whiten the forehead of his states—that it refers to the tongue of Musa (peace be upon him) at the time the mountain shaded them, for the Sabbath was then legislated; but the transgression in it and the transformation (into apes) occurred in the time of Dawud (peace be upon him). Warsh, from Nafi', recited (la ta'addu) with a fatha on the 'ayn and a shadda on the dal. It is related from Qalun that at times the 'ayn is pure sukun, and at times the fatha of the 'ayn is hidden (ikhfa'). As for the first, its origin is (ta'taddu), according to His words, exalted is He: ﴿who transgressed among you on the Sabbath﴾, for this indicates that it is from transgression (i'tida'), which is the form ifti'al from 'udwan. The intention was to assimilate its ta' into the dal; its vowel was transferred to the 'ayn, it was changed into a dal, and assimilated. As for pure sukun, it is something the grammarians consider objectionable, because it joins two sukun in a manner beyond its limits. As for ikhfa' and ikhtilas, it is lighter than that, because it is close to producing some vowel. Al-A'mash recited (ta'taddu) in its original form. The original of (ta'addaw) in the well-known reading is ta'addawu with two waws: the first is the waw of the root, and the second is the pronoun of the subject. The damma was felt heavy on the lam of the root, so it was dropped; two sakin met, so the first, which is the first waw, was dropped, and the pronoun of the subject remained.

﴿And We took from them a firm covenant﴾: a solid, emphasized pledge, that they would comply with the commands of Allah, exalted is He, and refrain from His prohibitions. It is said: it is their saying: ("We hear and we obey"). That it is a covenant is evident; that it is "firm" is derived from the expression in the past tense, or from the conjunction of obedience with hearing, on the basis of interpreting it thus. In deriving that from what was mentioned there is an obscurity, which is not hidden. It is related that after they accepted what they had been charged with of the religion, they were given a covenant that if they intended to turn back from it, Allah, exalted is He, would punish them with whatever kinds of punishment He wished. If this is sound, the strength of the covenant is most evident. Some claimed that this covenant is the covenant which Allah, exalted is He, took from the Prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, to confirm and believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), which is mentioned in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets: whatever I have given you of the Book and wisdom...﴾ to the end of the verse. That it is "firm" is in regard to His taking it from each prophet, and each one taking it from his own community, so it is a covenant emphasized and repeated. It is not hidden that this is contrary to the apparent meaning that the context requires.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 155:**

﴿Then, because of their breaking their covenant﴾. There is an implied element in the sentence. The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) is linked to another implied element too. The particle *ba'* (bi) indicates causation (sababiyyah), and *ma* is an additional particle (mazidah) used for emphasis. This indicates that the causation is strong. The context may also indicate exclusivity (hasr), as an inversion (taqdim) before the governing word (al-'amil) does, if that is required here. It is also permitted that *ma* be an indefinite complete noun (nakirah tammah), with *naqdihim* (their breaking) in apposition (badal) to it. The meaning would then be: they opposed and broke [the covenant], so We did to them what We did because of their breaking. If you wish, you may delay the governing word.

Abu Hayyan, may Allah have mercy on him, preferred the implied element to be "We cursed them" placed after, because it appears explicitly in that way in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Then, because of their breaking their covenant, We cursed them﴾. Many scholars permitted the prepositional phrase to be linked to "We forbade" (harramna) which comes later, with the words of Allah the Exalted ﴿then, because of wrongdoing﴾ being an apposition (badal) to His words ﴿then, because of their breaking﴾. This view was taken by al-Zajjaj. Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr criticised it, saying that it is remote because of the many intervening elements between the apposition and what it substitutes for, and because what is conjoined to a cause is also a cause. This would require that part of the cause for the prohibition be delayed beyond the prohibition, so it cannot be part of a cause or a cause except by a remote interpretation. The explanation is that their saying ﴿against Mary a tremendous slander﴾ and their saying ﴿We killed the Messiah﴾ come later in time than the prohibition of the good things upon them. Al-Safaqsi approved this, then said: it may be strained to resolve it by saying that the continuance of the prohibition at every time is like its beginning, but this is open to discussion.

The Allamah (al-Allama al-Thani) made the *fa'* in ﴿then, because of wrongdoing﴾ on this interpretation a repetition of the *fa'* in ﴿then, because of their breaking﴾, conjoined to ﴿We took from them﴾, or the answer to an implied condition. He also considered this remote for two reasons, one verbal and one semantic. He explained the first by the long separation, and by the substitution of a prepositional phrase together with a conjunctive particle or the answer to a condition, while it is certain that the governed element is only the prepositional phrase. He explained the second by its indication that the prohibition of some good things is caused by and follows from such great crimes. He then said: If *fa'* were made conjunctive to ﴿then, because of their breaking﴾, as in your saying: "I was captivated by Zayd and by his beauty" (or "and then by his beauty", or "then by his beauty"), then there would be no need to make it an apposition.

Abu al-Baqa' and others permitted that it be linked to an omitted element indicated by the words of Allah the Exalted ﴿Rather, Allah has sealed their hearts because of their disbelief﴾. This was rejected, because this cannot serve as an explanation (mufassir) nor as an indicator (qarinah) of the omitted element. As for the first, it is because it is linked to another statement, since it is a rejection and denial of their saying ﴿Our hearts are uncircumcised﴾. As for the second, it is because it is a digression (istitrad) and the speech is complete without it, while being an indicator of what is the core of the speech requires that the speech not be complete without it.

The conclusion is that an indicator must have a semantic link to what precedes it in order to be suitable for that role. From this it is known that there is no basis for the objection that the two sealings are compatible in their accidents, one by disbelief and the other by breaking the covenant. It was also said that it is linked to ﴿they do not believe﴾, with the *fa'* being superfluous. It was also said that it is linked to what it indicates. The rejection of this is not hidden.

﴿and their disbelief in the signs of Allah﴾, that is, His proofs indicating the truthfulness of His prophets, peace be upon them, and the Qur'an, or what is in their scripture, by distorting it, denying it, and not acting upon it. ﴿and their killing of the prophets without right﴾, like Zechariah and John, peace be upon them both. ﴿and their saying: "Our hearts are uncircumcised (ghulf)"﴾. *Ghulf* is the plural of *ghilaf* (covering/sheath) in the sense of a container, and its origin is *ghulaf* with two dammas, which was lightened. The meaning is: they are receptacles for knowledge, so we are self-sufficient with what is in them and have no need of anything else. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and by 'Ata'. Al-Kalbi said: they mean that our hearts are such that nothing reaches them without their retaining it, and if there were anything in your speech they would retain it too. It is also possible that it is the plural of *aghlaf* (having covers), meaning: they are covered with natural veils, so that what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought hardly reaches them. This is like the words of Allah the Exalted ﴿and they said: "Our hearts are in coverings from what you call us to"﴾.

﴿Rather, Allah has sealed them because of their disbelief﴾ is a parenthetical statement placed between the two conjoined elements, brought in as a digression, hastening to refute their corrupt claim. The meaning is: the matter is not as you claim, that they are receptacles of knowledge. Rather, they are sealed, veiled from knowledge, and nothing of it has reached them, like a locked house sealed upon. The *ba'* here indicates causation, and it is also permitted that it indicates instrument. It is also possible that the meaning is: the non-arrival of the truth to your hearts is not because they are in natural coverings and veils, as you claim, but because Allah the Exalted has sealed them because of your acquired disbelief. This sealing means abandonment and the prevention of the success needed to reflect on the signs and be admonished by the exhortations, according to many. According to some, *taba'a* (sealed) is literal, and this is supported by what al-Bazzar narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The seal is hung from the pillar of the Throne. When the sanctity is violated, sins are committed, and one becomes bold against Allah the Exalted, Allah the Exalted sends the seal, and it seals his heart, so he does not understand anything after that." Al-Bayhaqi also narrated it in *al-Shu'ab*, but he declared it weak.

﴿So they do not believe except a little﴾. It is in the accusative because it is an adjective (na't) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: except a little belief. So it is like belief in the prophethood of Musa, peace be upon him, and this is not beneficial, because disbelief in part is disbelief in the whole, as has passed. Or it is an adjective of an omitted time, meaning: a little time. Or it is in the accusative as an exception from the pronoun in "they do not believe", meaning: except a few of them, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his like. Al-Samin rejected this, saying that the pronoun refers to those sealed upon their hearts, and whoever is sealed upon the heart with disbelief cannot have faith proceed from him. It was answered that what has passed, ascribing to all what belongs to some, is meant by considering the majority.

'Isam al-Millah said: just as it is necessary to make an exception of the few from the non-belief that follows from the sealing upon their hearts, it is necessary to make an exception of a few hearts from their hearts. So it is as if the meaning is: "Rather, Allah the Exalted has sealed upon most of them." So let this be understood.

[p. 9]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 156:

﴿And because of their disbelief﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "because of their disbelief" that precedes it. It should not be supposed that this is the conjoining of a thing to itself, nor that it is without benefit; for the disbelief meant by the conjoined phrase is disbelief in ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, while the disbelief meant by the phrase conjoined to is either disbelief in general, or disbelief in Muḥammad, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, because it is linked with the words of God the Exalted: ﴿Our hearts are uncovered﴾. God the Exalted has related this saying of theirs concerning them in their confrontation with him, peace and blessings be upon him, in several places. Thus the conjunction indicates that each of the two disbeliefs is fit to be a cause.

It may also be considered that the conjoined phrase is plural, and the difference from the singular phrase it is conjoined to is evident. Or it is a conjunction to ﴿because of their breaking of their covenant﴾. It is permissible to regard the conjoining of the plural of this and what is conjoined to it as conjoined to the plural of what precedes it, and the prohibited consequence is not supposed, even if we say that the disbelief is one and the same, since the plural differs from the plural even if some of its parts do not differ from one another. It may also be said that the disbelief differs across the three places, by taking it in the latter two as what we have indicated, and in the first as disbelief in Mūsā, peace be upon him, because it is linked with breaking the covenant.

Already mentioned is the matter of the enemy regarding the Sabbath. ﴿And their saying against Mary a great slander﴾: its magnitude cannot be measured, since they attributed to her — far be it from her — what she is, in herself, a thousand thousand stations removed from, and they persisted in this, unconcerned by the miracle (of the infant's speech) that established her innocence. Buhtān (slander) is the lie that one is bewildered by because of its severity and enormity. It is in the accusative as the direct object of "their saying." It is also permitted that it be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., "a slanderous saying." It has also been said that it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative, i.e., "while confounding (them)."

[Commentary of al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 4, verses 157–158]

﴿And their saying﴾ in a spirit of boasting.

﴿Indeed, we killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the Messenger of Allah﴾ They called him by the title of messenger in mockery and derision, as in His saying, exalted is He, quoting the disbelievers: ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down﴾ etc. It is possible that they said this on the basis of his (ﷺ) saying, peace be upon him, even though they did not believe it. It has also been said that they described him with other attributes of blame, and these were changed in the quotation, so that this is part of the quotation and not part of what is quoted. It has also been said that it is a new statement from Allah, praising him, peace be upon him, elevating his status, and showing the extent of their audacity in undertaking to kill him and the height of their insolence in their boasting. ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or a parenthetical clause (i'tirāḍ). ﴿But it was made to appear so to them﴾ It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that a group of Jews insulted him, peace be upon him, and his mother, so he invoked a curse upon them and they were transformed into apes and swine. This reached Yahudha (Judas), the head of the Jews, and he feared, so he gathered the Jews, and they agreed to kill him. They set out toward him to kill him, but Jibril, peace be upon him, placed him in a house and lifted him from it to the heaven, and they did not perceive this. Then Tityanus (Titus) entered upon him to kill him, but did not find him, and he delayed with them. Allah, exalted is He, cast upon him the likeness of Jesus, peace be upon him. When he came out, they killed him and crucified him.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said, in a lengthy report transmitted from him by Ibn al-Mundhir: "Jesus, peace be upon him, came with twenty-seven of the disciples into a house, and they surrounded them. When they entered upon them, Allah, exalted is He, transformed them all into the form of Jesus, peace be upon him. They said to them: 'You have bewitched us. Let Jesus, peace be upon him, come forth to us, or we shall kill you all.' Jesus said to his companions: 'Who among you will sell his soul today for Paradise?' A man among them said: 'I will.' So he went out to them and said: 'I am Jesus.' They killed him and crucified him, and Allah, exalted is He, raised Jesus, peace be upon him."

Qatada, al-Suddi, Mujahid and Ibn Ishaq said likewise, although they differed regarding the number of the disciples. No one other than Wahb mentioned that his likeness, peace be upon him, was cast upon all of them; rather, they said that his likeness was cast upon one, and Jesus, peace be upon him, was raised from among them.

Al-Tabari preferred the view of Wahb and said: "It is the most resembling (to what is correct)." Abu Ali al-Jubba'i said: The chiefs of the Jews seized a man, killed him and crucified him at a high place, and did not allow anyone to approach him, so his features changed. They said: "We have killed Jesus," in order to deceive their common people, because they had surrounded the house in which Jesus, peace be upon him, was, and when they entered it they did not find him. They feared that this would become a cause for the belief of the Jews, so they did what they did.

It has also been said that one of the disciples was a hypocrite toward Jesus, peace be upon him. When they wanted to kill him, he said: "I will show you where he is," and he took thirty dirhams for that. He entered the house of Jesus, peace be upon him, and Jesus, peace be upon him, was raised, and the likeness of him was cast upon the hypocrite. They entered upon him and killed him, thinking that he was Jesus, peace be upon him. It has been said other than this.

The verb (shubbiha) is attributed to the prepositional phrase (lahum, "to them"), and the meaning is that a resemblance occurred to them between Jesus, peace be upon him, and the one who was crucified; or, in the matter, according to the view of al-Jubba'i. Or it is attributed to the pronoun of the one killed, which is indicated by (inna qatalnā, "we killed"), meaning: the one whom they killed was made to resemble Jesus, peace be upon him, for them. Or the pronoun refers to the matter, and (shubbiha) is from (shubha, doubt), meaning: the matter became confused for them on the basis of that statement. The subject of the verb is not the pronoun of the Messiah, peace be upon him, because he is the one likened to, not the one likened.

﴿And indeed, those who differed concerning him﴾ meaning concerning the affair of Jesus, peace be upon him. When that event occurred, people differed. Some of them said: "He was an impostor, so we have killed him in truth." Others hesitated, and some of them said: "If this is Jesus, where is our companion? And if this is our companion, where is Jesus?" Some of them said: "The face is the face of Jesus, and the body is the body of our companion." And one who had heard from him said: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, will raise me up to the heaven" — he was raised to the heaven. The Christians who claim his divinity, peace be upon him, said: "The humanity (nāsūt) was crucified, and the divinity (lāhūt) ascended." For this reason they do not consider the killing a deficiency, since they did not attribute it to the divinity. These (other) people reply that this is impossible according to the Jacobites (al-Ya'qūbiyya), who hold that the Messiah became, by union, one single nature, since in a single nature no humanity remains distinct from divinity, and one single thing is not said to have died and not died, or to have been humiliated and not humiliated.

As for the Romans (al-Rūm, here Byzantine Christians), who hold that the Messiah after the union remained in two natures, it is said to them: Did the divinity separate from his humanity at the time of the killing? If they say: "It separated from it," then they have nullified their religion, for the Messiah did not deserve lordship (rubūbiyya) in their view except through the union. If they say: "It did not separate from it," then they are committed to what applies to the Jacobites, namely the killing of the divinity together with the humanity. If they interpret the union as (tadarru', "wearing as a covering"), meaning that God made him a dwelling and a house and then separated from him when what befell the humanity befell him, they have nullified his divinity in that state. We say to them: Was he not humiliated? This amount suffices to establish deficiency, since the divinity did not disdain that its dwelling be touched by these deficiencies. If it was able to ward them off, then it has treated its neighbour badly and accepted its deficiency, and this returns deficiency upon it in itself. If it was not able, then that is further removed from the majesty of lordship. These people deny the casting of the likeness and say: "That is not permitted, for it is misguidance." Its refutation is clearer than to be hidden. It suffices to establish it that if it were not established, the Messiah would have been falsified, and his prophethood nullified, and indeed all the prophethoods. Moreover, their statement in the (Fasl) that the crucified one said: "My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?" contradicts contentment with the bitter decree and conflicts with submission to the rulings of the All-Wise. And that he complained of thirst and asked for water. And the Gospel clearly states that the Messiah used to fast for forty days and nights — and other things besides, in which they have, if authentic, what proclaims that the one crucified was the likeness, as is not hidden.

So what is meant by the relative pronoun (alladhīna) is what includes the Jews and the Christians all together. ﴿Certainly they are in doubt concerning it﴾ meaning: certainly they are in hesitation. The origin of (shakk, doubt) is that it be used for the equality of the two sides, and it may be used for its necessary meaning, which is hesitation in general, even if neither of its sides is preponderant. This is what is meant here, and therefore He emphasized it by negating knowledge that encompasses that as well, by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾. The exception is disjunctive (munqaṭi'), meaning: rather, they follow assumption.

It is permitted to interpret doubt as ignorance, and knowledge as belief in which the soul rests, whether certain or otherwise; then the exception is connected (muttaṣil), and Ibn Atiyya followed this, although it contradicts the well-known view. As for what has been said, that following assumption is certainly not from knowledge, so connection to it cannot be conceived, it is refuted by the fact that whoever said this made it mean followed assumption. ﴿And they did not kill him with certainty﴾ The pronoun refers to Jesus, peace be upon him, as is apparent. That is: they did not kill him with a certain killing, or as those who were certain. It is not objected that negating a certain killing requires the affirmation of a doubtful killing, because it is negation of the qualifier, and there is no obstacle to his having been killed in their supposition, for that implies that it was not so in reality. So there is no need to commit to making (yaqīnan, "with certainty") an absolute object of an omitted verb, the sense being: they were certain of that with certainty. It has been said that it refers to knowledge, and this is the view of al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba, meaning: they did not kill knowledge (with certainty), from the saying of them: "I killed knowledge and opinion," and "I killed such-and-such knowledge" when your knowledge of it has been thorough. This is a metaphor, as in al-Asās (of al-Zamakhshari), and the meaning is: they did not know it with certainty. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the assumption, meaning: they did not settle the assumption with certainty. This is transmitted from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and al-Suddi. Ibn al-Anbari related that in the sentence there is a transposition, and that (yaqīnan) is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, Allah raised him﴾, meaning: rather, He raised him to Himself (with certainty). Abu Hayyan refuted this in al-Bahr, saying that al-Khalil explicitly stated that what follows (bal) does not operate on what precedes it. The statement is a rejection and denial of his killing and an affirmation of his being raised, peace be upon him. In it, according to Abu Hayyan, there is an omitted modifier, meaning: to His heaven. He said: "He is alive in the second heaven, as is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of the Night Journey (mi'raj). He remains there until he descends to the earth, kills the Dajjal (Antichrist), and fills it with justice as it was filled with injustice. Then he lives in it forty years, or their completion from the age at which he was raised — and he was then thirty-three years old — and he dies as humans die, and he is buried in the chamber of the Prophet (ﷺ) or in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem)."

Qatada said: Allah, exalted is He, raised Jesus, peace be upon him, to Himself, and clothed him with feathers, and dressed him with light, and cut off from him the pleasure of food and drink. So he flew with the angels, and he is with them around the Throne. Thus he became human, angelic, heavenly and earthly. This raising, according to the preferred view, took place before the crucifixion of the likeness, and the Gospel of Luke supports this.

As for the vision of some of the disciples of him, peace be upon him, after the crucifixion, it is from the category of the spirit's manifestation (tatawwur al-rūḥ), for the saints (qiddisiyyūn) have the power of manifestation in this world, even if their spirits are raised to the most exalted station. Manifestation has occurred to many of the friends of Allah (awliyā') of this community, and their accounts concerning that are too many for the scope of enumeration.

﴿And Allah is ever Mighty﴾ not overcome in what He wills, ﴿Wise﴾ in all His acts. So it includes His arrangements, glorified is He, concerning the affair of Jesus, peace be upon him, and the casting of the likeness upon the one on whom it was cast, as an initial inclusion.

[Commentary of al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 4, verses 157–158]

﴿And their saying﴾ in a spirit of boasting.

﴿Indeed, we killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the Messenger of Allah﴾ They called him by the title of messenger in mockery and derision, as in His saying, exalted is He, quoting the disbelievers: ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down﴾ etc. It is possible that they said this on the basis of his (ﷺ) saying, peace be upon him, even though they did not believe it. It has also been said that they described him with other attributes of blame, and these were changed in the quotation, so that this is part of the quotation and not part of what is quoted. It has also been said that it is a new statement from Allah, praising him, peace be upon him, elevating his status, and showing the extent of their audacity in undertaking to kill him and the height of their insolence in their boasting. ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or a parenthetical clause (i'tirāḍ). ﴿But it was made to appear so to them﴾ It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that a group of Jews insulted him, peace be upon him, and his mother, so he invoked a curse upon them and they were transformed into apes and swine. This reached Yahudha (Judas), the head of the Jews, and he feared, so he gathered the Jews, and they agreed to kill him. They set out toward him to kill him, but Jibril, peace be upon him, placed him in a house and lifted him from it to the heaven, and they did not perceive this. Then Tityanus (Titus) entered upon him to kill him, but did not find him, and he delayed with them. Allah, exalted is He, cast upon him the likeness of Jesus, peace be upon him. When he came out, they killed him and crucified him.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said, in a lengthy report transmitted from him by Ibn al-Mundhir: "Jesus, peace be upon him, came with twenty-seven of the disciples into a house, and they surrounded them. When they entered upon them, Allah, exalted is He, transformed them all into the form of Jesus, peace be upon him. They said to them: 'You have bewitched us. Let Jesus, peace be upon him, come forth to us, or we shall kill you all.' Jesus said to his companions: 'Who among you will sell his soul today for Paradise?' A man among them said: 'I will.' So he went out to them and said: 'I am Jesus.' They killed him and crucified him, and Allah, exalted is He, raised Jesus, peace be upon him."

Qatada, al-Suddi, Mujahid and Ibn Ishaq said likewise, although they differed regarding the number of the disciples. No one other than Wahb mentioned that his likeness, peace be upon him, was cast upon all of them; rather, they said that his likeness was cast upon one, and Jesus, peace be upon him, was raised from among them.

Al-Tabari preferred the view of Wahb and said: "It is the most resembling (to what is correct)." Abu Ali al-Jubba'i said: The chiefs of the Jews seized a man, killed him and crucified him at a high place, and did not allow anyone to approach him, so his features changed. They said: "We have killed Jesus," in order to deceive their common people, because they had surrounded the house in which Jesus, peace be upon him, was, and when they entered it they did not find him. They feared that this would become a cause for the belief of the Jews, so they did what they did.

It has also been said that one of the disciples was a hypocrite toward Jesus, peace be upon him. When they wanted to kill him, he said: "I will show you where he is," and he took thirty dirhams for that. He entered the house of Jesus, peace be upon him, and Jesus, peace be upon him, was raised, and the likeness of him was cast upon the hypocrite. They entered upon him and killed him, thinking that he was Jesus, peace be upon him. It has been said other than this.

The verb (shubbiha) is attributed to the prepositional phrase (lahum, "to them"), and the meaning is that a resemblance occurred to them between Jesus, peace be upon him, and the one who was crucified; or, in the matter, according to the view of al-Jubba'i. Or it is attributed to the pronoun of the one killed, which is indicated by (inna qatalnā, "we killed"), meaning: the one whom they killed was made to resemble Jesus, peace be upon him, for them. Or the pronoun refers to the matter, and (shubbiha) is from (shubha, doubt), meaning: the matter became confused for them on the basis of that statement. The subject of the verb is not the pronoun of the Messiah, peace be upon him, because he is the one likened to, not the one likened.

﴿And indeed, those who differed concerning him﴾ meaning concerning the affair of Jesus, peace be upon him. When that event occurred, people differed. Some of them said: "He was an impostor, so we have killed him in truth." Others hesitated, and some of them said: "If this is Jesus, where is our companion? And if this is our companion, where is Jesus?" Some of them said: "The face is the face of Jesus, and the body is the body of our companion." And one who had heard from him said: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, will raise me up to the heaven" — he was raised to the heaven. The Christians who claim his divinity, peace be upon him, said: "The humanity (nāsūt) was crucified, and the divinity (lāhūt) ascended." For this reason they do not consider the killing a deficiency, since they did not attribute it to the divinity. These (other) people reply that this is impossible according to the Jacobites (al-Ya'qūbiyya), who hold that the Messiah became, by union, one single nature, since in a single nature no humanity remains distinct from divinity, and one single thing is not said to have died and not died, or to have been humiliated and not humiliated.

As for the Romans (al-Rūm, here Byzantine Christians), who hold that the Messiah after the union remained in two natures, it is said to them: Did the divinity separate from his humanity at the time of the killing? If they say: "It separated from it," then they have nullified their religion, for the Messiah did not deserve lordship (rubūbiyya) in their view except through the union. If they say: "It did not separate from it," then they are committed to what applies to the Jacobites, namely the killing of the divinity together with the humanity. If they interpret the union as (tadarru', "wearing as a covering"), meaning that God made him a dwelling and a house and then separated from him when what befell the humanity befell him, they have nullified his divinity in that state. We say to them: Was he not humiliated? This amount suffices to establish deficiency, since the divinity did not disdain that its dwelling be touched by these deficiencies. If it was able to ward them off, then it has treated its neighbour badly and accepted its deficiency, and this returns deficiency upon it in itself. If it was not able, then that is further removed from the majesty of lordship. These people deny the casting of the likeness and say: "That is not permitted, for it is misguidance." Its refutation is clearer than to be hidden. It suffices to establish it that if it were not established, the Messiah would have been falsified, and his prophethood nullified, and indeed all the prophethoods. Moreover, their statement in the (Fasl) that the crucified one said: "My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?" contradicts contentment with the bitter decree and conflicts with submission to the rulings of the All-Wise. And that he complained of thirst and asked for water. And the Gospel clearly states that the Messiah used to fast for forty days and nights — and other things besides, in which they have, if authentic, what proclaims that the one crucified was the likeness, as is not hidden.

So what is meant by the relative pronoun (alladhīna) is what includes the Jews and the Christians all together. ﴿Certainly they are in doubt concerning it﴾ meaning: certainly they are in hesitation. The origin of (shakk, doubt) is that it be used for the equality of the two sides, and it may be used for its necessary meaning, which is hesitation in general, even if neither of its sides is preponderant. This is what is meant here, and therefore He emphasized it by negating knowledge that encompasses that as well, by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾. The exception is disjunctive (munqaṭi'), meaning: rather, they follow assumption.

It is permitted to interpret doubt as ignorance, and knowledge as belief in which the soul rests, whether certain or otherwise; then the exception is connected (muttaṣil), and Ibn Atiyya followed this, although it contradicts the well-known view. As for what has been said, that following assumption is certainly not from knowledge, so connection to it cannot be conceived, it is refuted by the fact that whoever said this made it mean followed assumption. ﴿And they did not kill him with certainty﴾ The pronoun refers to Jesus, peace be upon him, as is apparent. That is: they did not kill him with a certain killing, or as those who were certain. It is not objected that negating a certain killing requires the affirmation of a doubtful killing, because it is negation of the qualifier, and there is no obstacle to his having been killed in their supposition, for that implies that it was not so in reality. So there is no need to commit to making (yaqīnan, "with certainty") an absolute object of an omitted verb, the sense being: they were certain of that with certainty. It has been said that it refers to knowledge, and this is the view of al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba, meaning: they did not kill knowledge (with certainty), from the saying of them: "I killed knowledge and opinion," and "I killed such-and-such knowledge" when your knowledge of it has been thorough. This is a metaphor, as in al-Asās (of al-Zamakhshari), and the meaning is: they did not know it with certainty. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the assumption, meaning: they did not settle the assumption with certainty. This is transmitted from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and al-Suddi. Ibn al-Anbari related that in the sentence there is a transposition, and that (yaqīnan) is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, Allah raised him﴾, meaning: rather, He raised him to Himself (with certainty). Abu Hayyan refuted this in al-Bahr, saying that al-Khalil explicitly stated that what follows (bal) does not operate on what precedes it. The statement is a rejection and denial of his killing and an affirmation of his being raised, peace be upon him. In it, according to Abu Hayyan, there is an omitted modifier, meaning: to His heaven. He said: "He is alive in the second heaven, as is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of the Night Journey (mi'raj). He remains there until he descends to the earth, kills the Dajjal (Antichrist), and fills it with justice as it was filled with injustice. Then he lives in it forty years, or their completion from the age at which he was raised — and he was then thirty-three years old — and he dies as humans die, and he is buried in the chamber of the Prophet (ﷺ) or in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem)."

Qatada said: Allah, exalted is He, raised Jesus, peace be upon him, to Himself, and clothed him with feathers, and dressed him with light, and cut off from him the pleasure of food and drink. So he flew with the angels, and he is with them around the Throne. Thus he became human, angelic, heavenly and earthly. This raising, according to the preferred view, took place before the crucifixion of the likeness, and the Gospel of Luke supports this.

As for the vision of some of the disciples of him, peace be upon him, after the crucifixion, it is from the category of the spirit's manifestation (tatawwur al-rūḥ), for the saints (qiddisiyyūn) have the power of manifestation in this world, even if their spirits are raised to the most exalted station. Manifestation has occurred to many of the friends of Allah (awliyā') of this community, and their accounts concerning that are too many for the scope of enumeration.

﴿And Allah is ever Mighty﴾ not overcome in what He wills, ﴿Wise﴾ in all His acts. So it includes His arrangements, glorified is He, concerning the affair of Jesus, peace be upon him, and the casting of the likeness upon the one on whom it was cast, as an initial inclusion.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 159:

﴿And there is none of the People of the Book﴾, meaning the Jews specifically, as Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both; or they and the Christians, as many exegetes have held. Here ﴿in﴾ (إنْ) is negative, meaning "ma" (not). Regarding the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa'l-majrur) there are two possibilities. The first is that it is a qualifier (sifah) of a deleted subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject). The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿except that they will surely believe in him before their death﴾, form a sworn clause (jumlah qasamiyyah), and the oath together with its answer is the predicate (khabar) of the subject. It is not objected that an oath is an expressive utterance (insha'), because what is meant by the predicate is its answer, which is a statement emphasized by an oath. Nor does it conflict with the fact that the answer to an oath has no grammatical position (la mahalla lahu), because that is so only in terms of its being an answer, so there is no barrier to its having a grammatical position from another standpoint, if it is granted that the predicate is not the whole thing. The sense is: "There is not any one of the People of the Book except that by Allah he will surely believe in him." The second possibility is that the phrase is connected to a deleted element that serves as the predicate of that subject, and the oath clause is a qualifier of it, not a predicate. The sense is: "There is not any one, except that he will surely believe in him, being one of the People of the Book." Its meaning is: every man of the People of the Book will believe in him before his death. This is a complete and meaningful statement. Therefore the objection to this second possibility, that a noun (ahad) and a prepositional phrase do not form a complete predication (lā yantazim min ahad wa'l-jar wa'l-majrur isnad, because it does not convey a benefit), does not hold, since the benefit is undoubtedly achieved. Yes, the meaning on the first possibility is: every man of the People of the Book will believe in him before his death. The apparent intention is this, and it is more complete in benefit. The exception (istithna') is an incomplete exception (mufarragh) from the most general of the descriptions. The Kufan grammarians posit a relative pronoun (mawsul) after "illa", while the Basran grammarians prohibit deleting the relative pronoun while leaving its complement (silah). The second pronoun refers to the deleted subject, namely "ahad" (anyone), while the first refers to Jesus, peace be upon him.

The meaning of the verse, then, is that every Jew and Christian will believe in Jesus, peace be upon him, before his soul departs, that he is the servant of Allah the Exalted and His messenger. His faith will not benefit him at that time, because that time, being joined to the barzakh (the intermediate state), in which the truth becomes manifest to everyone, is a time when obligation (taklif) ends. This is supported by the fact that Ubayy read ﴿they will surely believe in him before their death﴾ (لَيُؤْمِنُنَّ بِهِ قَبْلَ مَوْتِهِمْ) with a dammah on the nun. The return of the plural pronoun to "ahad" is clear, because it has the sense of a plural, whereas its return to Jesus, peace be upon him, is not apparent.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he explained the verse in this way. He was asked: "What do you say if he falls from the top of a house?" He said: "He speaks it in the air." It was said: "What if his neck is struck?" He said: "His tongue stammers with it."

Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: al-Hajjaj said to me, "O Shahr, I have never recited a verse from the Book of Allah the Exalted without some doubt arising in my mind about it: Allah the Exalted says, (﴿And there is none of the People of the Book except that he will surely believe in him before his death﴾), yet I am brought prisoners and I strike off their necks, and I do not hear them say anything?" I said: "It has been presented to you in a way other than its intended sense. When a Christian's soul departs," i.e., when its departure draws near, as another report from him indicates, "the angels strike him from his front and his back and say: 'O wretch, the Messiah whom you claimed to be Allah the Exalted, and that he is the son of Allah, glory be to Him, and that he is the third of three, is the servant of Allah and His spirit and His word,' so he believes in him at a time when his faith will not benefit him. As for the Jew, when his soul departs, the angels strike him from his front and back and say: 'O wretch, the Messiah whom you claimed you killed is the servant of Allah and His spirit,' so he believes in him at a time when faith will not benefit him. When Jesus descends, their living will believe in him just as their dead believed in him." He said: "From where did you take this?" I said: "From Muhammad ibn 'Ali." He said: "You have taken it from its source." Shahr said: "By Allah, it was only Umm Salamah who related it to me, but I wanted to anger him."

The informing of their state in this way is a threat to them and an incitement to hasten to faith in him before they are compelled to it, at a time when it will be of no use.

It has also been said that both pronouns refer to Jesus, peace be upon him. This was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and from Abu Malik, al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd, and al-Tabarani chose it. The meaning is that none of the People of the Book who are alive at the descent of Jesus, peace be upon him, will remain except that he will surely believe in him before he dies, and all religions will become one religion.

Ahmad narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Jesus son of Mary will descend, and he will kill the pig, and he will efface the cross, and prayer will be gathered for him, and he will give wealth until it is not accepted, and he will lay down the kharaj (land tax), and he will alight at al-Rawha, and from there he will perform Hajj or 'Umrah or join them both." He said: Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, then recited: (﴿And there is none of the People of the Book except that he will surely believe in him before his death﴾).

It has also been said that the first pronoun refers to Allah the Exalted, but its remoteness is not hidden. Even more remote is the view that it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), which was narrated from 'Ikrimah. What weakens this is that no mention of him (peace and blessings be upon him) has preceded here, and there is no necessity that requires returning the pronoun to him. Nor is it as al-Tabari claimed, that if this were correct it would not be permissible to apply the rulings concerning disbelievers to the People of the Book after their deaths, because that faith occurs at the point when obligation has ceased, so it is not counted.

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection he will be﴾, i.e., Jesus, peace be upon him, ﴿against them﴾, i.e., the People of the Book, ﴿a witness﴾. He will bear witness against the Jews for their denial of him, and against the Christians for their saying about him that he is the son of Allah the Exalted. The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is connected to (shahidan, "a witness"). Its being placed first indicates the permissibility of placing the predicate of "kana" (to be) before it in general, or when it is an adverbial phrase or a prepositional phrase, because a complement (ma'mul) may be placed first only where its governing element (amil) may be placed first. Abu'l-Baqa' permitted that the governing element of the phrase be (yakunu, "he will be").

[Page 14]

**﴿Because of the wrongdoing of those who became Jews﴾**, meaning: those who repented of worshipping the calf. Describing them by this title signals the extreme gravity of their wrongdoing, since it occurred after that great repentance. Its gravity was already stated by the magnifying indefinite *tanwin* (*al-tanwin al-tafkhimi*, the tanwin of magnification) in the phrase *ẓulmin* ("wrongdoing"). The meaning is: because of a great wrongdoing, one that exceeds the limits of ordinary things and their equivalents, and that proceeded from them. **﴿We forbade them good things which had been made lawful for them﴾**, and for those before them, and not for any other reason as they claimed. Whenever they committed one of the sins they perpetrated, some kind of good things that had been lawful for them and for their forefathers before them would be forbidden to them, as a punishment. Despite this, they used to fabricate lies against Allah, the Exalted, and say: "We are not the first to whom these were forbidden. They were forbidden to Noah, Abraham and those after them, peace be upon them, until the matter came down to us." So Allah, the Exalted, refuted them in many places and rebuked them with His words, glorified be He: **﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel﴾**, and so on, whose discussion has already been presented. Some exegetes held that what was forbidden to them is what will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, in (*al-An'am*) in detail.

[Page 14]

It has been raised as an objection that the prohibition was in the Torah, and at that time there was no disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ) and Jesus (peace be upon him), nor what is indicated by the words of Allah, the Exalted: **﴿and their barring many from the way of Allah﴾**, meaning: many people, or a barring, or a long period of time. It has been said in reply that the intended meaning is the continuation of the prohibition. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

This clause is coordinated (*ma'tuf*) with the wrongdoing (*al-zulm*) and its causative element, and likewise what is coordinated with it in *al-Kashshaf* as an explanation of it. This, as some verifiers have said, is to counter what may be said: that coordinating with a fronted complement (*al-ma'mul al-muqaddam*) contradicts restriction (*al-hasr*). Whoever takes *al-zulm* in its literal sense and makes **بِصَدِّهِمْ** (*bi-saddihim*, "by their barring") dependent on an omitted verb has no difficulty with it. From this it is known that the rhetoricians' (*ahl al-ma'ani*, the scholars of meaning) statement that it contradicts restriction is restricted to the case where the second item is not an explanation of the first, as when you say: "I struck Zayd for a sin and for his bad manners," where what is meant is: not for no sin. Likewise they restricted this to the case where restriction is not derived from fronting. The preposition **بِ** (*bi-*) is repeated here, but it is not repeated in His words, Exalted be He: **﴿and their taking of usury though they had been forbidden from it﴾**, because the coordinated item and what it is coordinated with were separated by something that is not a complement of the item coordinated with. Since it was separated by its own complement, it was not repeated. The clause **وقَدْ نُهُوا** (*wa-qad nuhu*, "though they had been forbidden") is a circumstantial clause (*hali*).

The verse indicates that usury was forbidden to them just as it is forbidden to us, and that the prohibition indicates the prohibition of what is prohibited. Otherwise He, glorified be He, would not have threatened punishment for opposing it. **﴿and their consuming the wealth of people by falsehood﴾**, by bribery and all other forbidden means. **﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them﴾**, meaning: for those who persist in disbelief, not for those among them who repented and believed, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his like, **﴿a painful punishment﴾**, which they will taste in the Hereafter just as they tasted in this world the punishment of prohibition.

It is mentioned in *al-Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) that the prohibition was general, applying to the wrongdoer and others, and that it belongs to the category of **﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have done wrong﴾**, but not to the punishment. For this reason He, glorified be He, said **لِلْكافِرِينَ** (*li-l-kafirin*, "for the disbelievers") rather than **لَهُمْ** (*lahum*, "for them"). Al-Jubba'i (*al-Jubba'i*) also took this view. So reflect.
