﴿But those firm in knowledge among them﴾ is a corrective exception (istidrak) to His words, exalted is He, "And We have prepared" etc., and it clarifies that some of them are contrary to that condition, in this world and the next. "Among them" (minhum) is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), meaning: but those who are firm, well-grounded in knowledge among them, who have insight into it, not following conjecture like those ignorant ones. By them are meant ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, Usayd, Thaʿlaba and their likes. The verse was revealed concerning those mentioned, as al-Bayhaqi related in al-Dalail from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. ﴿And the believers﴾ means: among them. The words of Qatada point to this. They are described as believers after being described with what entails firmness in knowledge, by way of conjunction (ʿatf) based on the difference between the two conjoined items, treating the difference in designation as if it were a difference in essence, as has passed.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿who believe in what has been sent down to you﴾ of the Qur'an ﴿and what was sent down before you﴾ of the scriptures to the prophets and messengers, is a circumstantial phrase (hal) from "the believers," explaining the manner of their faith. It has been said that it is a parenthetical clause (iʿtiraḍ) emphasizing what precedes it. His words, exalted is He: ﴿and those who establish the prayer﴾. Sibawayh and the rest of the Basran grammarians said it is in the accusative (naṣb) by way of praise (madḥ). al-Kisa'i objected to this, saying that the accusative of praise occurs only after the completion of the sentence, and here it is not so, since the predicate (khabar) will come later. It was answered that there is no evidence that it is impermissible to insert a parenthetical clause between the subject (mubtada') and its predicate.

Ibn ʿAtiyya related from a group that they prohibited its accusative by way of severance (qaṭʿ) because of the conjunction particle, since severance does not occur in conjunction but only in qualifiers (nuʿut). Whoever claims that this is a case of severance in conjunction relies on what Sibawayh cited as an example of severance with a conjunction particle, the verse:

*And he resorts to women, bare and disheveled, nursing infants like the ghouls.*

al-Kisa'i said: it is in the genitive (majrur) by conjunction with "what was sent down to you," on the basis that the intended people are the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace.

It is said: according to this, the intended meaning of establishing the prayer is not its performance, but its public manifestation and its prescription, so that it becomes a distinctive attribute. It has been said: the intended "those who establish" are the angels, based on His words, exalted is He: ﴿They glorify Him night and day, never tiring﴾. It has been said: the Muslims, with an elided noun, that is: and by the religion of those who establish. Some said it is conjoined to the pronoun in "minhum," and it has been said to the pronoun in "ilayka," and it has been said to the pronoun in "qablika."

The Basrans do not permit these three possibilities, because they involve conjoining to a pronoun in the genitive without repeating the preposition, and this matter has already been discussed. Some later scholars claimed that the more plausible reading is its accusative by way of wahm (mistaken assimilation), since the preceding word stands in place of the heavy "lakinna," and the light "lakin" was placed in its position. There is no hiding what is problematic in this. In sum, no attention should be paid to one who claims that this is a grammatical error (laḥn) in the Qur'an, and that the correct reading is "wal-muqimūna" with a waw, as in the codex of ʿAbd Allah, and this is the reading of Malik ibn Dinar, al-Jahdari and ʿIsa al-Thaqafi, since there is no doubt about the transmission of the text by mass transmission (tawatur), so error in it is not permissible at all.

As for what is reported, that when the codex was completed it was brought to ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, and he said: "You have done well and beautifully. I see some error which the Arabs will correct with their tongues. Had the dictator been from Hudhayl and the scribe from Quraysh, this would not have been found in it." al-Sakhawi said: it is weak, and its chain of transmission has irregularity (idtirab) and disconnection (inqita'), for ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, appointed for the people an imam to follow. How then would he see error in it and leave it for the Arabs to correct with their tongues? He wrote several codices, and there is no difference in them at all except in what concerns the variant readings (wujuh al-qira'at). If he did not correct it, nor those who undertook the compilation, and they are who they are, how could others correct it?

Some interpreted the error in his speech, on the assumption that it is authentically related from him, as meaning allusion and indication, as in the verse:

*An eloquent speech, and you speak with allusion at times, and the best speech is that which is allusive.*

That is, what is intended is allusion, by omitting some letters in writing, such as the alif of "al-sabirin," which the readers recognize when they see it, and likewise adding some letters. We have already presented to you what is useful here, so remember.

Then, the apparent meaning is that "those who establish," according to the nominative reading, is conjoined to what precedes it, and the difference in designation also takes the place of the difference in essence. Conjoining to the pronoun in "yu'minūn" is nothing. The same applies to His words, exalted is He: ﴿and those who give zakat and those who believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾, for the intended meaning of all of them is the believers among the People of the Book. They were first described as firmly grounded in the knowledge of the Book, not troubled by doubt, and not shaken by doubts, signifying that this is what entails faith, and that those other than them only remained persistent because they were not firmly grounded in it. Rather, they are like a feather in the wilderness of error, tossed by the gusts of doubts and illusions. Then they are described as believing in all that was sent down of the Book to the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace, then as acting upon its rulings. Among them, only the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakat are mentioned, as these two entail all the bodily and financial acts of worship.

Because in establishing the prayer properly there is standing before the Truth, may His majesty be exalted, and severance from other than Him and turning toward the Master, the ones who establish were clothed in the garment of the accusative, so that the accusative would be made easy for them, and their severance from dependence (on the preceding word). How delightful is this severance, which points to connection with the highest ranks!

Then He described them as those who have knowledge of the origin and the return, confirming their possession of faith in its two aspects, and their encompassing it from both sides, and as an implicit reproach that those other than them among the People of the Book are not truly believers in either of them, since they have mixed honey with poison and have become, away from following pure truth, blind and deaf. ﴿Those﴾ is a reference to those described with the previous noble qualities, firm in structure. It is the subject (mubtada'), and His words, exalted is He: ﴿We will give them a great reward﴾ is its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of the subject which is "those firm," and the "sin" is for emphasizing the promise, as we have mentioned, and the indefiniteness of "reward" is for magnification, as has passed more than once. There is no hiding the complete correspondence in this between the two sides of the corrective exception, in that the first were threatened with a painful punishment, and the latter were promised a great reward.

Some exegetes allowed that the predicate of the first subject is the clause "yu'minūn," and understood the believers as the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) from among those other than the People of the Book. The correspondence on this view is not complete.

Some held that the corrective exception is only from His words, exalted is He: "The People of the Book ask you" etc., as if it were said: But these do not ask you what those ignorant ones ask of you, namely sending down a book from the sky, because they know the truth of what you say in what they read from the books sent down to the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace, and the obligation of following you upon them. So they have no need to ask you for another miracle, since they know from your affair, through the knowledge firmly rooted in their hearts, what suffices them in that regard.

This was related from Qatada, and the correspondence of the two sides of the corrective exception on it is more complete than on the view of the majority.

Hamza read "sa-yu'tihim" with the yā' (third person), in consideration of the apparent sense of His words, exalted is He: "the believers in Allah."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 163:

﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him.﴾ This is an answer to the People of the Book regarding their demand that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) bring down a book from heaven, and an argument against them: his situation in revelation is like that of all the other prophets (peace be upon them), whose prophethood is beyond doubt. It has also been said that this is a justification (ta'lil) for the statement of Allah, the Exalted: (those firmly grounded in knowledge).

Ibn Ishaq and others narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: Sukayn and Adi ibn Zayd said: "O Muhammad, we do not know that Allah the Exalted has sent down anything to a human being after Moses (peace be upon him)." So Allah the Exalted sent down this verse.

The kaf (ك, "like") is in the accusative position, either as a qualifier (na't) of a deleted verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: a revelation like Our revelation to Noah (peace be upon him); or as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of that verbal noun when it is definite, as is the view of Sibawayh, meaning: We have revealed the revealing, made similar to Our revealing, and so on. In both cases, ma (ما) is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya).

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a relative particle (mawsulah), in which case the kaf is the direct object, meaning: We have revealed to you the like of what We revealed to Noah, of monotheism and other things. But this is not the preferred view. And (min ba'dihi, "after him") is connected to (awhayna, "We revealed"). They did not permit it to be a circumstantial clause of (al-nabiyyin, "the prophets"), because adverbs of time cannot function as circumstantial clauses for bodies.

Allah, glorified is He, began with Noah (peace be upon him) as a warning to them, because he was the first prophet whose people were punished. It has also been said that it is because he was the first to whom Allah prescribed laws and rulings through his tongue, but this has been objected to. It has also been said that it is because of his resemblance to our Prophet (ﷺ) in the universality of his call to all the people of the earth. This is not free from scrutiny, because the universality of the call of Noah (peace be upon him) was incidental, not intended; and the universality of the call, if one holds that view (and its verification will come, Allah willing), is not definitively indicative of that, as is not hidden.

﴿And We revealed to Abraham﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with (We revealed to Noah) and falls under the same rule of comparison, meaning: as We revealed to Abraham ﴿and Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the tribes (al-asbat)﴾. These are, according to the well-known view, the sons of Jacob (peace be upon him). Others said: the tribes (asbat) among the descendants of Isaac are like the clans among the descendants of Ishmael, and a number of messengers were sent from among them. So it is possible that Allah, glorified is He, meant by revelation to them the revelation to the prophets among them, as you would say: "I sent to the Banu Tamim," meaning: I sent to their notables.

It is not established that the tribes who were the brothers of Joseph (peace be upon him) were prophets; rather, what is established according to me (and al-Jalal al-Suyuti wrote a treatise on it) is the opposite. ﴿And Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron and Solomon﴾ are mentioned although their inclusion in the thread of the prophets is evident, in order to honour them and to show their excellence, in accordance with the well-known practice of mentioning the specific after the general in this kind of context. The repetition of the verb reinforces the emphasis on revelation and draws attention to the fact that they are a distinct group, specially characterised by a particular kind of revelation.

Abraham was mentioned after the repetition for his greater honour; and because he is the third father of the prophets (peace be upon them), as stated explicitly by al-Ajhuri and others. Jesus (peace be upon him) was placed before those after him, to affirm his prophethood and to cut off what the Jews thought about him. It has also been said that this is so that the start is with one of the Ulu al-Azm (the steadfast messengers), after the change in the description of the coordinated items, both in the singular and in the plural.

All these names, according to what Abu al-Baqa' mentioned, are non-Arabic (a'jamiyyah), except for (al-asbat). There is a well-known disagreement about this. For (Yunus, "Jonah") there are several dialectal forms; the most eloquent of them is with a dammah on the nun without a hamzah, and it is permissible to vocalise it with a fatha or a kasra, with or without the hamzah.

﴿And We gave David the Zabur﴾ is coordinated with (awhayna, "We revealed") and falls under its rule, because the giving of the Zabur is a form of revelation. And as We gave David the Zabur, and the choice of it over (awhayna to David), is because the likeness is confirmed in a specific matter, which is the giving of a scripture, after it has been confirmed in the general matter of revelation. The Zabur, with a fatha on the zay, according to the majority, is on the pattern fa'ul in the sense of maf'ul (passive), like (halub, "milked") and (rakub, "ridden"), as Abu al-Baqa' explicitly stated.

Hamzah and Khalaf read (zuburan) with a dammah on the zay wherever it occurs. It is the plural of (zibr), with a kasra and then a sukun, in the sense of (mazbur, "written"), i.e., written; or (zabr), with a fatha and a sukun, like (fals) and (fulus); it has also been said that it is a verbal noun, like (qu'ud) and (julus); it has also been said that it is the plural of (zabur) with the extra letters removed. By custom, it became the name of the book sent down to David (peace be upon him). His receiving it was in portions (munajjaman), and by this the obligation (ilzam) is achieved.

It contained, as al-Qurtubi said, one hundred and fifty surahs, none of which contained a ruling of the rulings of the law, but were only wise sayings and admonitions, and the praise and glorification of Allah, the Exalted, and His praise.

**[Commentary of al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 4, verse 164]**

﴿And messengers﴾ is in the accusative case, governed by an implied verb: "We sent messengers." The indication of this implied verb is His saying, exalted be He, "We revealed" (*awhaynā*), which precedes it, since revelation necessarily entails sending. The phrase ﴿And messengers﴾ is conjoined to that verb and is included with it in the ruling of comparison. It has also been said that the indication is His saying, exalted be He, ﴿We have related them to you﴾, not that it is accusative governed by "We related" (*qaṣaṣnā*) with an elided genitive, meaning "We related the accounts of messengers." Nor is it accusative by removal of the preposition, meaning "as We revealed to Noah and to messengers," as has been said, because the first interpretation is free of what it establishes: the precise parallel between his (ﷺ) situation and the situations of the prophets whose prophethood they acknowledge, in general revelation, then in the giving of the Book, then in sending. For His saying, exalted be He, "We have revealed to you" (*innā awhaynā ilayka*) necessarily encompasses the meaning of "We gave you" (*ātaynāka*) and "We sent you." It is as if it were said: "We have revealed to you as We revealed to so-and-so and so-and-so, and We have given you the like of what We gave so-and-so, and We have sent you like what We sent the messengers whom We have related to you and others. There is no difference between you and them in the reality of revelation and sending. So why do they ask you for something that none of these messengers, upon them be prayers and peace, was given?" The meaning of relating them to him (ﷺ), upon him be prayers and peace, is the narration of their accounts to him and the explanation of their circumstances and affairs.

﴿From before﴾ means: from before this surah, or from before today. It has been said: He related them to him (ﷺ) in Mecca in Surah al-An'am and elsewhere. Some have said: Allah, glorified be He, related them to him (ﷺ) through revelation outside the Qur'an, and then related them to him afterward in the Qur'an. ﴿And messengers We have not related to you﴾ means: before this. Therefore the verse does not contradict what has been reported in the report that "the messengers number three hundred and thirteen, and the prophets number one hundred and twenty-four thousand," and what is reported from Ka'b (that they number one million, four hundred thousand, and twenty-four thousand). This is because the negation of their being related before does not entail the negation of their being related at all. The negation of the particular does not entail the negation of the general. It is possible that He related them to him (ﷺ) afterward, so he learned of them and reported what he reported, since the implication is understood from the speech even if it is not in the statement. This is because *lam*, according to the well-known view, when it enters on the present tense, turns its meaning into the past. Moreover, relating means mentioning accounts. The negation of mentioning their accounts to him (ﷺ) does not entail the negation of mentioning their number on its own, detached from mention of accounts and narratives. It is therefore possible to say: He, glorified be He, did not mention to him (ﷺ) their accounts at all, but He mentioned to him, may His majesty be exalted, that they were such-and-such a number of men. Thus is dismissed what some contemporary writers imagined, namely that the verse is explicit in his (ﷺ) lack of knowledge of the number of the messengers, upon them be prayers and peace, and therefore they accept it and reject the hadith. It seems that what led them into this illusion was the words of some verifiers. The better course is not to limit oneself to the number in the verse; otherwise one errs in understanding and dies entangled in blind imitation. We ask Allah, exalted be He, for well-being.

﴿And Allah spoke to Moses﴾ is read with the word Allah in the nominative and Moses in the accusative. It is reported from Ibrahim and Yahya ibn Wassab that they read it with inversion (*qalb*): Allah in the accusative and Moses in the nominative.

﴿speaking﴾ is an emphatic verbal noun that removes the possibility of metaphor, according to what many have mentioned. Al-Shihab considered this and said: it emphasizes the verb, so it removes metaphor from the verb. As for its removing metaphor from the attribution, namely that the speaker is His messengers from among the angels, as one says, "The caliph said such-and-such," when it was said by his vizier, this is not so, even though it emphasizes the verb, and the intended meaning is figurative. This is like the saying of Hind bint al-Nu'man about her husband Rawh ibn Zinba', vizier of Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan:

*The silk wept because of Rawh, and denied his skin,*
*and the garments of Judham cried out in a loud cry.*

She emphasized "cried out," although it is a metaphor, because garments do not cry out. What is reported from al-Farra' is that the Arabs call whatever reaches a person "speech," by whatever way it reaches him, so long as it is not emphasized with a verbal noun. But if it is emphasized, it is nothing but the literal reality of speech, which does not fulfill the purpose, since the most that it does is remove metaphor from the verb in this material, and it does not address removing metaphor from the attribution. So the opponent may say: "Speaking is literal, but its attribution to Allah, exalted be He, is metaphorical," and the verse is not a proof against him unless that possibility is negated. Yes, it is evident in what the People of the Sunnah have maintained.

The sentence is either conjoined to His saying, exalted be He, "We have revealed to you," as a conjunction of narrative to narrative, not conjoined to "We gave" and what is conjoined to it. Or it is a circumstantial clause with *qad* implied, as the change of style through the shift (*iltifāt*) indicates. The meaning is that speech without intermediary is the highest and most exalted of the ranks of revelation, and it was specific to Moses, peace be upon him, among the prophets whose prophethood you acknowledge. That did not detract from them at all. So how could it be imagined that the descent of the Torah upon him all at once detracts from the prophethood of one to whom the Book was sent down in detail, given the evident wisdom of that?

Furthermore, you have already been told the manner in which Moses, peace be upon him, heard the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic be He. Speech also occurred for our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) during the Isra' (Night Journey), with additional elevation. Indeed, there is no miracle of any of the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace, except that our Prophet (ﷺ) has its like, with additional honor for him, which Allah has exalted. Indeed, there is no particle of light that has shone among the worlds except that the sun of his essence (ﷺ) has given it in charity. How excellent is al-Busiri, may Allah be glorified, when he says:

*Every sign the noble messengers brought*
*is only connected to them from his light.*

So may Allah, exalted be He, bless him (ﷺ) and grant him abundant peace.

﴿Rusulan mubashshirina wa-mundhirin﴾ is in the accusative (nusiba) either as a laudatory accusative (nasb 'ala al-madh), or by supposing a verb (bi-idmar) (arsalna, "We sent"), or as a circumstantial accusative (ḥal) from "rusulan" which precedes it, or from its pronoun. It is then an anticipatory circumstantial (ḥal muwatiʼa), and the intended meaning is its description. This was held to be weak, because in that case there is no point in separating the circumstantial from the one it modifies. It was also permitted that it be in the accusative as an appositive (badal) of the first "rusulan," but this was held weak, because the identity of the appositive and the word it replaces in form is remote. Nevertheless, the reliable view regarding the appositive is the description, i.e., (mubashshirin) those who believed and obeyed, with Paradise and reward, and (mundhirin) those who disbelieved and disobeyed, with the Fire and punishment. ﴿So that mankind will have no argument against God﴾, i.e., no excuse with which they may plead, saying: "Why did You not send us a messenger, so that he would explain Your laws to us and teach us what we did not know of Your rulings," because of the limitation of human faculties in grasping the particular details of benefits, and the inability of most people to grasp their universal principles. Therefore the verse clearly shows that there is necessarily a revealed law (shar') and the sending of messengers, and that reason alone does not suffice in place of this.

The Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) claimed that reason is sufficient, and that the sending of messengers is only to alert people from the slumber of heedlessness that overtakes a person without choice. So the meaning of the verse according to them is: so that there will not remain for people an argument against God. The refutation of this will come, God willing, together with the verification of this topic.

The naming of what is said when messengers are not sent an "argument" (ḥujja), while it is impossible that anyone could have an argument against Him, glorified is He, is a metaphor (majāz), by treating the excuse, in terms of its acceptance with Him, exalted is He, according to the requirement of His generosity and kindness, as the status of a decisive argument that cannot be repelled. Thus the statement of the Ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni community) is not invalidated, that no one has any objection against God, exalted is He, regarding any of His acts; rather, He, glorified is He, may do to whomever He wills whatever He wills.

The lam is connected to the supposed (muqaddar) "arsalna," or to "mubashshirin wa-mundhirin" by way of tanāzuʻ (competition between two verbs for one complement). It was also permitted that it be connected to what the two words indicate. "Ḥujja" is the subject of "kāna," and its predicate is "lil-nās"; "ʻalā Allāh" is a circumstantial from "ḥujja." It is also permissible that the predicate be "ʻalā Allāh," and "lil-nās" a circumstantial. It is not permissible for "ʻalā" to be connected to "ḥujja," because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) and its complement does not precede it. Whoever permitted this with the adverbial complement permits it here too.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿after the messengers﴾, i.e., after their sending and the conveying of the law through their tongues, is an adverbial complement of "ḥujja." It was also permitted that it be a qualifier of it, because a temporal adverb may be used to describe verbal nouns, just as it is used to predicate them. ﴿And God is ever Mighty﴾, whom none overcomes in a matter He wills, ﴿Wise﴾ in all His acts. From the requirement of this is the refraining from answering the demand of those who seek to confound, and the cutting off of argument by sending messengers, the diversity of revelation to them, and the miraculous (iʻjāz).

It has been said: "Mighty" in punishing the disbelievers, "Wise" in giving excuse after warning has preceded, as if they had asked for the sending down of the Book of God, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 166 (part 1 of 2):

﴿But Allah bears witness﴾ with the nun lightened and the divine name (al-jalalah) in the nominative case.

al-Sulaymi read it with the nun doubled and the divine name in the accusative (انصب). This is an istidrak (a corrective "but" that qualifies what precedes it) on the implied meaning of what came before. It is as if they had asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to send down a book from heaven and had been obstinate, and so he was answered by the words of God Most High: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you﴾, and so on. It was said: they do not bear witness, but Allah bears witness.

The sum of this is: if they do not accept the proof and bear witness for you, then Allah Most High bears witness. It was also said: when He, glory be to Him, compared the revelation made to the Prophet (ﷺ) with the revelation made to the prophets, peace be upon them, that comparison might suggest that revelation to them was of equal distinction. So He corrected this by stating that revelation to you has the distinction of Allah's own witness.

﴿with what He has sent down to you﴾: that is, with the truth of what He sent down to you, which is the Qur'an. The prepositional phrase is connected to (bears witness), and the bi (با) is a particle of connection (صلة). The thing witnessed to is the truth (al-haqqiyyah). It is also permissible for the thing witnessed to to be prophethood, and then (with what He has sent down) is connected as a means (تعلق الآلية): that is, He bears witness to your prophethood by means of what He has sent down to you, since its miraculous nature indicates your truthfulness and prophethood. The ultimate meaning may well be one and the same, for His witnessing, glory be to Him, to the truth of what He has sent down of the Qur'an, by manifesting the inimitable miracle which is intended to establish His Prophet's prophethood (ﷺ).

al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and others, related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: "A group of Jews entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said to them: 'By Allah, I know that you know that I am the Messenger of Allah.' They said: 'We do not know that.' Then (But Allah bears witness) was revealed."

In the narration of Ibn Jarir from him: "When ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you﴾ was revealed, they said: 'We do not bear witness for you.' Then ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you﴾ was revealed."

It was read (أُنزِل) in the passive voice. ﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾. Four aspects have been mentioned regarding this:

The first: the meaning is "He has sent it down" with His own special knowledge, which no one else possesses, glory be to Him, namely its composition in an arrangement and style which every eloquent person and master of expression is unable to match. A group of exegetes chose this.

The second: the meaning is "He has sent it down" while knowing that you are worthy of its being sent down to you, because of your upholding of the truth in it and your calling people to it. al-Tabarsi chose this.

The third: the meaning is "He has sent it down" with what He knows of the welfare of the servants, comprising it.

The fourth: the meaning is "He has sent it down" while knowing it and watching over it, protecting it from the devils through a guard of angels.

As for knowledge in the first aspect, it was said to mean the known (المعلوم), and what is intended by it is the composition and the particular arrangement. It is not that knowledge is used figuratively for that. If it were taken as knowledge in its verbal-noun sense (المعنى المصدري), and the bi is for accompaniment (الملابسة), and its composition is a clarification of His being accompanied by it rather than of knowledge itself, that would be valid. However, there is a figurative extension here, since composition is not the same as the accompaniment but its effect. On this basis, it is also possible that the bi is for instrumentality (الآلية), as one says: "He did it with his knowledge," when he has mastered it and done it as it should be. Then it would be a description of the Qur'an with perfect beauty and eloquence.

As for the second and third aspects, knowledge is in its verbal-noun sense, or in the third aspect it means the known. The adverbial phrase is a circumstantial element (حال) from the subject or the object. The object of knowledge differs: it is that you are worthy of its being sent down, or the welfare of the servants.

The apparent sense of some speakers' words is that in the second aspect it is a circumstantial element from the subject, and in the third from the object. It was also permitted that it be an absolute object (مفعول مطلق): that is, a sending down accompanied by His knowledge. The placement of the clause in the first aspect is that of an explanatory clause, since it is a clarification of the witnessing, as the Zamakhshari explicitly stated. In both aspects, its placement is that of confirmation and clarification of the relative clause. It was also said that in the three aspects it is like an explanation of (He has sent down to you), since it clarifies its being sent down in a particular manner.

As for the fourth aspect, knowledge has been construed to mean watching over and protecting. The adverbial phrase is a circumstantial element from the subject, and (He has sent it down) is a repetition so that what is attached to it may be attached. Or, as it was said, some people did not regard this aspect as valid, since it has no connection to this context. It was also said that it contains a glorification of the matter of the Qur'an by protecting it from the devils of the jinn, which also implies its protection from the devils of mankind. In that case the clause is, at that point, like an explanation of the witnessing as well.

It was also read (نزّله) with an intensive form.

﴿And the angels bear witness﴾ likewise, to what Allah Most High bore witness to, because they follow Him, glory be to Him, in witnessing. The clause is coordinated with what precedes it. It was also said: it is a circumstantial element from the object of (He has sent it down): that is, He has sent it down while the angels bear witness to its truthfulness and its reality. Some people have also made the angels' witness to his truthfulness (ﷺ) in his claim consist of their coming to aid him (ﷺ) in battle, appearing in view, as occurred at the Battle of Badr. In any case, (they bear witness) is from witnessing, and it has been mentioned that on the fourth aspect it is from witnessing in the sense of watching over.

﴿And Allah suffices as a witness﴾ to what He has witnessed to for you, since He set up the proof, made the way clear, removed doubts, and exaggerated in that in a manner that needs no testimony of anyone else, mighty and majestic is He.

* * *

Furthermore, among the allusive (إشارة) interpretations of the verses:

(﴿Allah does not love the public utterance of evil speech﴾) that is: Allah does not love that the servant should expose His cover when a lapse has issued from him, or a stumble has befallen him. (﴿except by one who has been wronged﴾) that is: except the public utterance of one whose own soul has wronged him through the firm establishment of wicked dispositions in him. He is permitted to make public what is in him of those dispositions and to present them to physicians of the hearts, so that they may prescribe a remedy for him.

It was said: Allah Most High does not love the disclosure of the secret of lordship and the manifestation of the gifts of divinity, or the unveiling of the veil from the hidden treasures and the protected mysteries of the mystery of mysteries (﴿except by one who has been wronged﴾) by the overwhelming of states and the successive cups of majesty and beauty, so that he is compelled to speech and says, with the enduring tongue and not the perishing tongue: "I am the Truth, and glory be to me, how great is my affair!" In calling that overwhelming state "wronging" there is an obscurity that is not hidden.

In the apparent meaning of the verse there is a great good news for sinners, since He, glory be to Him, has made clear that He is not pleased with the exposure of the cover except by the one who has been wronged. How, then, would He, glory be to Him, be pleased with Himself that He should expose the cover of the disobedient, when they have not wronged Him, exalted is His majesty? They have only wronged their own souls, as the Book has declared: (﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers, and wish to differentiate between Allah and His messengers, and say: "We believe in some and disbelieve in others"﴾). These are a people who have veiled themselves by plurality from detail. They denied the messengers, because they imagined a unity incompatible with multiplicity and a totality contrary to differentiation. From here they nullified the sacred laws, permitted what is forbidden, and abandoned the prayers. (﴿And wish to adopt a way between that﴾), that is: belief in the whole, both in totality and in detail, and disbelief in the whole, (﴿a way﴾), that is: a path. (﴿Those are the disbelievers﴾), the veiled, (﴿truly﴾) in their essences and their attributes, since their knowledge is an illusion and an error, and their monotheism is heresy and misguidance. The killing of one of them is more beneficial than the killing of a thousand combatants, according to what Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali, may his secret be sanctified, indicated.

(﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers, and do not differentiate between any of them﴾) these are the believers in both totality and detail, whom totality does not veil from detail, nor detail from totality, like the true masters of the people of unity. (﴿Those, He will soon give them their rewards﴾) from the three gardens. (﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving﴾) who covers their essences and their attributes (﴿Merciful﴾) who shows them mercy with the bestowed existence of truth and the everlasting subsistence.

(﴿The People of the Scripture ask you to bring down to them a book from heaven﴾) that is: certain knowledge through unveiling, from the heaven of the spirit. (﴿For they asked Moses for greater than that, and said, "Show us Allah plainly"﴾) that is: they sought direct vision, and there is no doubt that it is greater and higher than unveiling. (﴿So the thunderbolt seized them﴾) that is: the fire of egoism overcame them and destroyed their readiness through their wrongdoing, which is their seeking of direct vision while their own essences remained. (﴿Then they took the calf﴾) that is: the calf of appetites, which the Samiri of the commanding soul fashioned. (﴿After the clear proofs had come to them﴾) which were a deterrent to them from that. (﴿And We gave Moses a manifest authority﴾) and that is the radiance of the light of manifestation from his face, to the point that he needed to cover his face with a veil, out of mercy for the bats of his community. (﴿And We raised the Mount above them﴾) that is: We made it dominant over them. (﴿For their covenant﴾) that is: because they were required to give the covenant. The mountain is taken as an allusion to Moses, peace be upon him, or to the intellect. Raising it above them is its strengthening by divine lights. (﴿And We said to them: enter the gate﴾) that is: the gate of journeying and spiritual wayfaring which leads to the court of holiness and the kingdom of kings. (﴿prostrating﴾) humbling themselves, abased.

And His saying, exalted is He: (﴿Nay, Allah raised him up to Himself﴾). By it is alluded, according to what some of the people have mentioned, and the responsibility for it lies with them, to the connection of his spirit, peace be upon him, with the higher world at the moment of his departure from the lower world. That elevation, in their view, is to the fourth heaven, because the source of the outpouring of his spirit, peace be upon him, is the spiritual nature of the sphere of the sun, which is in the position of the heart of the world. Since he did not attain the true perfection, which is the degree of love, he had no choice but to descend again in a bodily form, following the Muhammadan religion, in order to attain that lofty degree. At that time everyone will recognize him, and the People of the Book, that is, the people of knowledge who know the origin and the return, all of them without exception, will believe in him (﴿before his death﴾), peace be upon him, through annihilation in Allah, mighty and majestic is He. When they believe in him, it will be the Day of Resurrection, that is, the day of their emergence from the physical veils and their awakening from the sleep of heedlessness (﴿a witness﴾). That will be by the Truth manifesting to them in His form.

(﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who judaized﴾) which is their worship of the calf of appetites, their taking it as a god, their refusal to enter the gate of the court of holiness, their transgression on the Sabbath by violating the Law, which is the greatest manifestation, their veiling from the unveiling of the oneness of actions, their breaking of Allah's covenant, their veiling from the oneness of attributes, which is disbelief in the signs of Allah Most High, and other such faults, along with their like:

"Their equals, if they were divided among the women, would not be dowered except by divorce."

(﴿We forbade them good things﴾) great and glorious, namely what is in the three gardens (﴿which had been made lawful for them﴾) according to their readiness, were it not for these barriers (﴿and for their hindering from the way of Allah﴾) that is, the path leading to Him, glory be to Him (﴿much﴾), that is: a great many creatures, which are the spiritual faculties. (﴿And their taking of usury﴾), which is the surplus of formal, disputational knowledge, which is like a tree of disagreement with no fruit, like bodily pleasures and the appetites of the soul. (﴿And they were forbidden it﴾), because it is the great veil. (﴿And their devouring of people's wealth in falsehood﴾), that is: using the knowledge of the spiritual faculties to obtain base worldly things, or taking what is in the hands of the servants through the vile trait of greed and covetousness.

(﴿But those firm in knowledge﴾) who are upright in the particular hearing from Allah, glory be to Him, without the opposition of the souls and the disturbance of the secrets, (﴿and the believers﴾) with the eyewitness faith, while (﴿they believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you﴾) of the legal rulings and the divine secrets.

[p. 20]

(﴿And those who establish prayer﴾) in the most complete manner; (﴿and those who give zakat﴾) by expending their very selves (qawam) in the various kinds of obedience; (﴿and those who believe in God and the Last Day﴾) that is, in the Originating Principle (mabda') and the Return (ma'ad). What is meant by these conjoined terms is one single group, as we have previously stated. (﴿Those – We shall give them a great reward﴾) whose measure cannot be estimated, in the gardens that have been prepared for them.

(﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah﴾) and so on. The comparison is in the manner of the comparison in His, exalted is He, saying: (﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you﴾), according to the saying of God: (﴿messengers as bearers of good news﴾) with the manifestations of gentleness (lutf), (﴿and as warners﴾) with the manifestations of severity (qahr), (﴿so that people will have no argument against God after the messengers﴾). That is, so that they would have no dominion or authority after that has been effaced through the support of the messengers. (﴿And God is ever Mighty﴾) so He effaces their attributes and annihilates their essences; (﴿Wise﴾) so He bestows upon them of His attributes and preserves them in His essence, as wisdom requires. (﴿But God bears witness to what He has sent down to you﴾) because of His manifestation in it, exalted is He, (﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾), that is, accompanied by His all-encompassing knowledge, from which not an atom's weight escapes Him in the heavens or on the earth. From this, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, knew what has been and what will be. (﴿And the angels﴾) who are the possessors of holy souls (al-nufus al-qudsiyya) (﴿bear witness﴾) likewise, because they are not veiled. (﴿And sufficient is God as a witness﴾), for He is the All-Comprehensive, and there is no existent other than Him. And God, exalted is He, is the Granter of success to what is right.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 167:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ in what has been sent down to you, or in everything that faith in it is obligatory, and this includes it as a primary inclusion. The intended people are the Jews. It seems that the sentence is to explain the judgment of Allah, glorified is He, concerning them after explaining their condition and their obstinacy (﴿and who averted [others] from the way of Allah﴾), that is, from the religion of Islam, those who wished to follow it, by their denial of the description of the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, and their saying: "We do not recognize him in our Book," and that the law of Musa, peace be upon him, is not abrogated, and that prophets only come from the descendants of Harun and Dawud, peace be upon them both.

It was also read as ﴿ṣuddū﴾ in the passive voice. ﴿They have certainly gone astray﴾ through disbelief and averting, ﴿a far-reaching straying﴾, because they combined going astray and leading others astray, and because the one who leads astray is stronger, more deeply immersed in error, and further from being extricated from it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 168–169:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ in what has been mentioned just before, ﴿and do wrong﴾ — wronging Muhammad (ﷺ) by denying his prophethood and concealing his glorious attributes, or wronging people by barring them from the Straight Path. The meaning is that those who combine disbelief with this kind of wrongdoing ﴿Allah will not forgive them﴾, because forgiveness cannot apply to a disbeliever. The verse, according to the sound view, refers to the Jews; it was also said that it refers to the polytheists, while what precedes it refers to the Jews. Some scholars claimed that wrongdoing here means something other than disbelief, such as the other major sins, and they interpreted the verse to mean: those among them who were disbelievers and those who were wrongdoers, people of major sins, ( ﴿Allah will not⦆ ) etc. It is not hidden that this is a departure from the apparent meaning, prompted only by the belief that sinners abide forever in Hell as disbelievers do, whereas the verse runs counter to this belief. For both verbs have been made relative clauses of the relative pronoun, so that both actions necessarily occur from each individual member of the group. Do you not see that when you say "the Zaydun stood," you have attributed standing to each individual of the plural? Likewise, if you join another verb to it by conjunction, that meaning necessarily applies to it as well. The context of the verse also rejects that meaning. But the habit of the Mu'tazilah has always been to follow their desires, so they do not care into what valley they fall.

﴿Nor will He guide them to any path﴾ ﴿except the path of Hell﴾, because they are not prepared for guidance to the truth and to righteous deeds, which is the path of Paradise. The guidance understood from the exception, by way of implication, as many have said, is His creating their evil deeds, which lead them to Hell according to their preparation; or His driving them to Hell on the Day of Resurrection through the angels. Some have mentioned that the expression "guidance" is sarcastic if it is not meant as mere indication, and the "path" is general, and the exception is contiguous, as Abu al-Baqa' and others chose. Al-Samin permitted that "path" refers to a specific thing, namely righteous deeds, and that the exception is disconnected. ﴿Abiding therein﴾ is a circumstantial clause of the pronoun in the accusative, because abiding occurs after their being brought to Hell; had it been construed as ("they remain abiding"), it would not fit. It was said that one may dispense with taking it as a prospective circumstantial clause by saying that this is a guidance that leads to Hell, or guidance to a path that leads to it, so it is a circumstance relating to the object in terms of conveying, not guiding; so reflect.

And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿forever﴾ is in the accusative of time, removing the possibility that abiding means a long stay. ﴿And that is﴾ — i.e., the absence of His forgiveness and guidance of them, and casting them into the Fire for eternity — ﴿for Allah, easy﴾, simple, with nothing to divert Him from it. This is a belittling of their affair, and an explanation that He, exalted is He, does not regard them nor care about them.
