Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 4, verse 170:

﴿O mankind﴾ is an address to all who are morally responsible. This comes after Allah, glorified is He, had related to His Messenger (ﷺ) the Jews' pretexts with falsehoods and their demand for baseless things out of obstinacy. He, exalted is His majesty, answered them with what He answered and confirmed that with what He confirmed. Directing the address to them, and commanding them to believe while coupling this with promise and warning, serves as a reminder that the path has become clear and the proof has become binding, so no one has any excuse left for not accepting.

It has been said that the address is to the people of Makkah, because the address ﴿O mankind﴾ wherever it occurs is directed to them. But it is not hidden that generality is preferable, and what was mentioned falls within the scope of inference. What has been related from some of the early generation is the predominant view. It has also been said that it is addressed to the disbelievers absolutely, keeping the command on its apparent meaning, and there is no need to interpret it as covering both those who are new to the matter and those who are steadfast.

﴿The Messenger has certainly come to you﴾ means Muhammad (ﷺ). Mentioning him with the title of messengership, peace be upon him, serves to emphasize the obligation of obeying him. ﴿With the truth﴾ means, in a state of being clothed with it. It has been explained as the Qur'an, as the religion of Islam, and as the testimony of monotheism. It is also permissible that the particle *bi* (with) be for transitivity (*li-l-ta'diyah*) or for causation (*li-l-sababiyyah*), connected to *jā'a* (came), meaning: he came to you because of the establishment of the truth.

His, glorified is He, saying ﴿from your Lord﴾ is connected either also to the verb, or to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) of *al-ḥaqq* (the truth), meaning: he came to you with it from Allah, exalted is He, or being from Him, glorified is He. The use of the title of lordship together with the attachment to the pronoun of the addressees indicates that this is for their upbringing and conveying them to their fitting perfection, encouraging them to comply with what follows of the command. Likewise, mentioning the sentence serves as a preparation for what follows from that.

It has been said that it is a repetition of the testimony, an affirmation of what is testified to, and a preparation for what is mentioned: ﴿so believe﴾, that is, in the Messenger (ﷺ) and in what he brought of the truth. The *fa'* (so) indicates that what precedes it necessitates what follows it.

His, glorified is He, saying ﴿better for you﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an omitted verb that is obligatory in its omission, its estimate being: *wa-if'alū* (and do) or *i'tū* (bring about) better for you. This is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh. Al-Farra' held that it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a better faith for you. It was objected to this that it implies that faith is divided into better and otherwise. The reply is that it is an emphasizing attribute, and that the concept of an attribute may not be taken into account. Even on the view that it is taken into account, it may be said that mentioning it is an allusion to the People of the Book, for they have faith in some of what must be believed in, such as the Last Day for example, but it is not better, since it was not in the approved manner.

Al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubayd held that it is the predicate of a hidden *kāna* (was), the estimate being: let faith be better for you. This was rejected on the grounds that *kāna* is not omitted together with its subject without its predicate except in certain positions that call for it, and that what is estimated is the answer of an omitted conditional clause, so that it would require omitting the condition together with its answer, since the estimate would be: if you believe, let faith be better. It was answered that restricting the omission of *kāna* and its subject to certain positions is not accepted by this objector, and that the necessity of omitting the condition together with its answer is based on the view that the jussive is governed by an estimated condition. If we say that it is governed by the imperative itself and its sister forms, as is the view of some grammarians, that objection does not arise.

Makki related from some of the Kufans that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, but this is far-fetched.

﴿And if you disbelieve, then to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ means: of the existing things, whether they are within their very essence, by which the state of the two themselves is known in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, or outside them but residing in them, of rational beings and others. The addressees enter into this by primary inclusion. That is, all of that belongs to Him, exalted is He, in creation, ownership, and disposal, and not a particle or less than that departs from His dominion and power. The sentence is an indication of the answer, put in its place, because its content was already established before their disbelief, so it is not suitable to be the answer. The estimate is: and if you disbelieve, then He, glorified is He, is able to punish you for your disbelief, because to Him, exalted is His majesty, belongs what is in the heavens and the earth; or else: then He is independent of you and is not harmed by your disbelief just as He does not benefit from your belief. Some said: the estimate is: ﴿and if you disbelieve﴾ then you have certainly flouted your intellects, ﴿then to Allah﴾ glorified is He, belongs what He has, of what indicates what contradicts your state and belief, so how could disbelief in Him occur along with that? It has been said: the estimate is: ﴿and if you disbelieve﴾ then the servants other than you do not disbelieve, but rather worship Him and submit to His command. This is not free from distance.

﴿And Allah has always been Knowing﴾ of the condition of each, and their disbelief enters into this by primary inclusion, ﴿Wise﴾ in all His sayings and arrangements, and the punishment of whoever disbelieves enters into this likewise.

[Page 25]

**O People of the Book** is a direct address that is restricted and specified to the Christians, to rebuke them for the far-reaching error they were in. This is the view of Abu Ali al-Jubba'i, Abu Muslim, and a group of exegetes. It is also reported from al-Hasan that the address is to them and to the Jews, because excess (*ghuluw*), meaning going beyond the limit and exaggeration, which is forbidden in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Do not exceed the limits in your religion﴾, occurred among all of them. As for the Christians, some of them said that Jesus, peace be upon him, is the son of God, Mighty and Majestic; others said that he is God, Glorified be He; and others said that he is the third of three. As for the Jews, they said that he, peace be upon him, was born out of wedlock. The view held by the majority was preferred, because the statement of the Jews has already been condemned in what precedes, and because it fits better with what follows.

﴿And do not say about God except the truth﴾. That is: do not mention or believe anything except the true statement, not the statement that implies the claim of incarnation (*ittihad*), indwelling (*hulul*), taking a consort, or having a son. The exception is an exhaustive exception (*istithna' mufarragh*), and according to most scholars it is a connected exception (*muttasil*).

Some claimed that the meaning of "the truth" here is His transcendence above having a consort or a son. The more fitting reading of the exception is that it is disconnected (*munqati'*), because transcendence is not something that is said *about* someone; rather it is said *of* Him and *for* Him. This is because the meaning of "he said about it" (*qala 'alayhi*) is "he fabricated." This view contradicts what the majority holds regarding the exhaustive exception, so understand this.

﴿The Messiah﴾ is pronounced with a light (*takhfif*) pronunciation, and its meaning has already been explained. It is also read as *al-Missih*, with a kasra on the *mim* and a shadda on the *sin*, like *al-Sikkit*. It is the subject (*mubtada'*). The word ﴿Isa﴾ is either a substitute (*badal*) for it or an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*), as Abu al-Baqa' and others said.

The phrase ﴿son of Mary﴾ is an attribute of it, which indicates the falsity of what they claim about him, that he is the son of God, Mighty and Majestic. The phrase ﴿Messenger of God﴾ is the predicate of the subject, and the sentence is a resumptive sentence (*mustaanifah*) given to explain the prohibition against the false statement, which implies the command to its opposite. That is: he, peace be upon him, is confined to the rank of messengership and does not transcend it to what you say.

﴿And His word﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) on ﴿Messenger of God﴾. The meaning of his being a "word" is that he came into being by the word "Be" without any customary material. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatada.

Al-Ghazali, may God sanctify his secret, said: every child has a near cause and a distant cause. The first is the semen, and the second is the word "Be." Since evidence establishes that there was no near cause in the case of Jesus, peace be upon him, the distant cause was attributed to him, which is the word "Be," as an indication of the absence of the near cause. He clarified this with His saying, Glorified be He: ﴿which He conveyed to Mary﴾, that is: He delivered it to her and placed it in her. He made it like the semen that is cast into the womb, so this is a metaphor. It was also said that the meaning is that he is guided by it, just as one is guided by the speech of God, Exalted is He. This was reported from Abu Ali al-Jubba'i. It was also said that the meaning is the glad tidings of God, Exalted is He, with which He gave good news to Mary, peace be upon her, through the angels, as He, Glorified be He, said: ﴿When the angels said: O Mary, God gives you glad tidings of a word﴾.

The clause ﴿which He conveyed﴾ is, according to what has been said, a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in ﴿His word﴾, with the implicit *qad*. The governing element in it is the meaning of the genitive construction (*idafah*). The estimated meaning is: "His word, having cast it." It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause from his pronoun, peace be upon him, which is hidden in what is indicated by ﴿His word﴾, from the meaning of the derivative noun (*mushtaqq*) that governs it. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "was" (*kana*), understood with *idh*, which is connected to the word in the sense that what is meant by it is the thing brought into being. The estimated meaning is: "when he was: ﴿He conveyed it to Mary﴾."

﴿And a spirit from Him﴾ is coordinated on what precedes it. He, peace be upon him, was called a spirit because he came into being from the breath of Gabriel, peace be upon him, into the garment of Mary, peace be upon her, by the command of Glorified be He. The use of the term "spirit" for breath is found in their speech, and from it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah about fire:

*"And revive it with your spirit."*

The preposition ﴿from﴾ is connected to an omitted element that is in the position of an attribute of ﴿spirit﴾. It denotes the starting point of the origin in a metaphorical sense, not partitive, as the Christians claim.

It is related that a skilled Christian physician of al-Rashid debated with Ali ibn al-Husayn al-Waqidi al-Marwazi one day. He said to him: "In your book there is something that indicates that Jesus, peace be upon him, is a part of Him, Exalted is He," and he recited this verse. Al-Waqidi then recited His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, all of it from Him﴾. He said: "Then it follows that all things are a part of Him, Glorified be He, Exalted high above that by a great exaltation." The Christian was silenced and became a Muslim, al-Rashid rejoiced greatly, and he gave al-Waqidi a splendid reward.

It was also said that he was called a spirit because people live by him, just as they live by spirits. Al-Jubba'i took this view. It was also said that "spirit" here means mercy, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He strengthened them with a spirit from Him﴾, in one sense. It was also said that what is meant by "spirit" is the revelation that was revealed to Mary, peace be upon her, in the glad tidings. It was also said that it is customary, when they wish to describe something as extremely pure and clean, to say: "it is a spirit." So when Jesus, peace be upon him, was formed from breath and not from a drop of semen, he was described as a spirit. It was also said that what is meant by "spirit" is the secret, as one says: "the spirit of this matter is such-and-such," meaning that he, peace be upon him, is a secret of the secrets of God, Exalted is He, and a sign of His signs, Glorified be He. It was also said that what is meant is "one possessing a spirit," by omitting the modified noun or by using "spirit" in the sense of "one possessing a spirit." The attribution to God, Exalted is He, is for honor. A parallel to this is what is in the Torah: "Moses, peace be upon him, is the man of God, his staff is the rod of God, and Jerusalem is the house of God."

It was also said that what is meant by the spirit is Gabriel, peace be upon him, and the coordination is on the hidden pronoun in ﴿He conveyed it﴾. The meaning is: God, Exalted is He, and Gabriel conveyed it to Mary. Its distance is not hidden.

In any case, there is no proof for the Christians in anything they claim regarding the honoring of Jesus, peace be upon him, through attributing the spirit to him, since others besides him, peace be upon him, share this with him. In the Gospel of Luke it says: Jesus said to his disciples: "Your heavenly Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him." In the Gospel of Matthew: "John the Baptist was filled with the Holy Spirit while he was in his mother's womb." In the Torah: God, Exalted is He, said to Moses, peace be upon him: "Choose seventy of your people, so that I may pour upon them of the spirit that is upon you, and they will bear with you the burden of this charge." He did so, and He poured upon them of His spirit, and they immediately prophesied. In it also, concerning Joseph, peace be upon him: "The king says: Have you seen anyone like this youth, in whom the spirit of God, Mighty and Majestic, dwells?" Also in it: "The spirit of God dwelt in Daniel," and other such things.

Perhaps the spirit in all of this is a sacred matter and a divine secret, which God, Exalted is He, bestows upon whomever He wills of His servants, as He wills, and at whatever time He wills. The application of this term to Jesus, peace be upon him, is by way of hyperbole, in the manner said of "Zayd is justice." It is not intended that it is the spirit by which life exists at all. This may appear in a form, as the Qur'an appears in the form of a pale man, and death in the form of a ram. This is supported, in general terms, by what is in the Gospel of Matthew in the account of the baptism of Jesus, peace be upon him: "When Jesus was baptized and came up out of the water, the heavens were opened for him, and he saw the spirit of God coming upon him in the form of a dove. And behold, a voice from heaven said: This is my beloved son in whom my soul delights." This, if it is authentic, demolishes what the Christians claim, that he, peace be upon him, was incarnated with the Holy Spirit in his mother's womb. The answer regarding what contains his description, peace be upon him, as a prophet will come, God willing, Exalted is He.

[Page 26]

﴿So believe in God﴾, and single Him out for divinity, ﴿and His messengers﴾ all of them, and do not exclude any of them from what it is impossible to attribute to them of divinity. ﴿And do not say: Three﴾, that is: the gods are three: God, Glorified be He, the Messiah, and Mary, as His saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿Did you say to the people: Take me and my mother as two gods besides God?﴾ Its meaning is two gods other than God, Exalted is He, so they would be three together with Him. This estimation was reported from al-Zajjaj.

Or it means: God, Glorified be He, is one of three, if it is authentically reported from them that they say: God, Exalted is He, is one substance (*jawhar*) with three hypostases (*aqanim*): the hypostasis of the Father, the hypostasis of the Son, and the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit. They mean by the first the essence or the existence, by the second knowledge, that is the Word, and by the third life. Thus it has been said.

The detailed explanation of this matter, according to what some scholars have mentioned, is that the Christians agreed that God, Exalted is He, is a substance, in the sense of: self-subsisting, not localized, not confined to a direction, not measured by a measure, does not receive accidents in His essence, and origination and non-existence cannot be conceived of Him. He is one in substance and three in hypostasis. The hypostases are attributes of the eternal substance, and they are existence, knowledge, and life. They expressed existence by the Father, life by the Holy Spirit, and knowledge by the Word.

Then they differed. The Melkites, the followers of Melka who appeared among the Romans and took control of them, held that the hypostases are other than the eternal substance, that each one of them is a god, and they explicitly affirmed the Trinity. They said: God is the third of three, Glorified be He, High above what they associate with Him. They said that the Word was united with the body of the Messiah, clothed itself in his humanity (*nasut*), and mingled with him like water mixed with wine, and plurality turned into unity. They said the Messiah is a universal humanity, not a particular one, and that it is eternal and without beginning. They said Mary bore an eternal God. They differed about Mary, whether she was a universal or a particular human, but they agreed that the union of divinity (*lahut*) was with the Messiah and not with Mary. They agreed that the killing and crucifixion fell upon both the humanity and the divinity together. They applied the name "Father" to God, Exalted is He, and "Son" to Jesus, peace be upon him.

Nestor the Wise, in the time of al-Ma'mun, held that God, Exalted is He, is one, and that the three hypostases are neither other than His essence nor the very essence of Him. He said that the Word was united with the body of the Messiah, not in the sense of mixing but in the sense of illumination, that is, it shone upon him like the sun's light through a niche upon crystal.

Among the Nestorians there was one who said that each of the three hypostases is living, speaking, and existing. They explicitly affirmed the Trinity like the Melkites. Some of them forbade this, and some affirmed other attributes such as power, will, and the like, but they did not make them hypostases. They claimed that the Son has never ceased to be begotten of the Father, and that his incarnation and his union with the body of the Messiah occurred when he was born. The origination (*huduth*) returns to the humanity. Thus the Messiah is a complete God and a complete human, and these two are eternal and originated. The union does not invalidate the eternity of the eternal nor the origination of the originated. They said that the crucifixion fell upon the humanity and not upon the divinity.

Some of the Jacobites held that the Word was transformed into flesh and blood, so the God became the Messiah. They said that God is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary. They related from John the Evangelist that he said at the beginning of his Gospel: "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us," and he said: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God is the Word."

Among them there was one who said: the divinity appeared in the humanity, to the extent that it became identical with it. This is like the appearance of the angel in the form referred to in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then he appeared to her as a man in every respect﴾.

Among them there was one who said: the substance of the eternal God and the substance of originated man were combined like the combination of the rational soul with the body, and they became one substance, which is the Messiah, and he is God. They say: God became a human, though the human did not become God, just as it is said of a coal thrown into fire: it became fire, but one does not say: the fire became coal.

Ruh al-Ma'ani: [Commentary of al-Alusi on surah 4, verse 171, part 2 of 5]

They say: the union of the divinity (al-lahut) with the particular human (al-insan al-juz'i), not the universal, and that Mary bore a god, and that the killing and crucifixion befell both the divinity and the humanity (al-nasut) together; for if it had befallen one of the two, the union would be void.

Among them are those who said: the Messiah, with the unity of his substance, is eternal in one respect and created in another.

Among the Jacobites (al-Ya'qubiyya) are those who said: the Word (al-Kalima) took nothing from Mary; rather it passed through her as water passes through a gutter.

Among them are those who claimed that the Word would penetrate the body of the Messiah, so that the signs that appeared from him would proceed from him, and it would depart from him at times, so that afflictions and pains would befall him.

Among the Christians are those who claimed that the meaning of the union of the divinity with the humanity is the manifestation of the divinity upon the humanity, even though nothing transfers from the divinity to the humanity nor does it indwell it. This is like the impression of a seal's design on wax, or a visible image in a mirror.

Among them are those who said: Being (al-wujud) and the Word are eternal, while life (al-hayah) is created.

Among them are those who said: God the Exalted is one, and He named Himself Father, and the Messiah is the Word of God the Exalted and His Son by way of adoption (al-istifa'), and he was created before the world, and he is the creator of all things.

The historians and transmitters relate that Arius (Aryus), one of the great Christians, believed, he and his sect, in the unity of the Creator, not associating anyone with Him, and did not hold concerning the Messiah what the Christians hold; rather he believed in his prophethood and that he was created in body and spirit. His doctrine spread among the Christians, so they corresponded and gathered at the city of Nicaea (Niqiya) before King Constantine (Qustantin), and they debated. Arius explained his doctrine, and Alexander (al-Iksidurus), patriarch of Alexandria, refuted him and denounced his doctrine before the king. Then they debated at length in their disputes, so the king marvelled at the spread of their doctrine and the multiplicity of their disagreements. The patriarch (al-Batrak) stood up for them and commanded them to search for the acceptable doctrine. Their opinion agreed upon something, which they wrote down and named the Creed (al-Amana), and most of them today hold to it. It reads: We believe in God the Exalted, the one Father, maker of all things, owner of all things, maker of what is seen and what is not seen; and in the one Lord, the Messiah, Son of God the Exalted, the one, firstborn of all creation, who was begotten of his Father before all worlds, not made, true God from true God, of the substance of his Father, by whose hand the worlds were perfected and all things were created; who for us men and for our salvation came down from heaven, and was incarnate of the Holy Spirit and Mary, and became man, and was conceived, and was born of the virgin Mary, and suffered, and was crucified under Pilate, and was buried, and rose on the third day as it is written, and ascended into heaven, and sat at the right hand of his Father, and he is prepared to come again at another time to judge between the dead and the living; and we believe in the one Holy Spirit, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from his Father, and in one baptism for the forgiveness of sins, and the Church is one, holy, catholic, and in everlasting life forever and ever. End of quotation.

This is the sum of the sayings, and of the falsehoods these infidels hold. These, together with their contradiction of reason and their clashing with the foundations, have no support, and they have no reliance in them except imitation of their predecessors and grasping at the outward wording of expressions which they do not comprehend. Moreover, what they call the Creed has no basis in the law of the Gospel, nor is it derived from the words of the Messiah or from the sayings of his disciples; and it is, besides, confused, self-contradictory, and incoherent, some of it refuting, opposing and contradicting the rest. Having known this, listen to what is recited to you in refutation of them, to complete the benefit and to confirm the nullification of those corrupt doctrines.

As for their saying that God the Exalted is a substance in the sense mentioned, we have no dispute with them concerning it in terms of meaning; rather the dispute is over the verbal application by way of revelation, and the matter there is light. As for their restriction of the hypostases (al-aqanim) to three, namely the attribute of being (sifat al-wujud), the attribute of life (sifat al-hayah), and the attribute of knowledge (sifat al-'ilm), this is invalid; for even granting that the attribute of being is additional, if they were asked for proof of the restriction they would find no way to it except their saying: "We investigated and found nothing other than what we have mentioned," and this is not certain, as is not hidden. Furthermore it is invalid by what has been established in its proper place concerning the necessity of the attributes of power, will, hearing, sight and speech. If they say: the hypostases are the properties of the substance and attributes of its essence, and it is of their nature that they be necessary to the substance and not pass beyond it to another, and this is realised in being and life, since the existence of the eternal essence and its life have no relation to anything else; and likewise knowledge, since knowledge is specific to the substance insofar as it is known by it; and this is unlike power and will, for neither of them is specific to the eternal essence, but they relate to other things which are capable and willed, while the eternal essence is neither capable nor willed; and also, life does not suffice in place of power and will, insofar as the living does not lack them, unlike knowledge, for it may lack it; and because it is impossible for life to suffice in place of knowledge, since life is specific to not admitting intensification and preference, unlike knowledge. We say:

As for their saying that being and life are specific to the essence of the Eternal and have no relation to other than it, this we grant; but it follows from this that knowledge is not a hypostasis, since it relates to other than the essence of the Eternal, for it is known by it. If they say: knowledge is a hypostasis only insofar as it relates to the essence of the Eternal, not insofar as it relates to other things, then it follows for them that sight would be a hypostasis, since it relates to the essence of the Eternal insofar as it sees itself; and they have not said this. And it follows for them that the subsistence (al-baqa') of the essence of God the Exalted would be a hypostasis, since subsistence is specific to itself and does not relate to other, as in being and life. If they say: subsistence is the very being, then it follows that what exists at the time of its coming into being would be subsistent, and this is impossible.

As for their saying that will suffices in place of power and will: either they mean that power and will are the very life, or that they are external to it and necessary to it and never separate from it. If the first, then they have overturned their own doctrine, since they said that life is a hypostasis by its specificity to the substance of the Eternal, while power and will are not specific to the essence of the Eternal, Exalted; and this indicates difference, and there is no union with them. If they say they are necessary to it with difference, this is denied, for just as it is permissible for the living to lack knowledge, so also it is permissible for it to lack power and will, as in the state of sleep and fainting, for example.

As for their saying that it is impossible for life to suffice in place of knowledge, since knowledge is specific to intensification and preference, it follows from this that life is not sufficient in place of power either, since power is specific to this kind of intensification and preference.

As for their saying that the Word indwelt the Messiah and clothed itself with him, this is invalid in two respects:

The first: it has been established that it is impossible for the attribute of the Eternal to indwell other than the essence of God the Exalted.

The second: the claim that the Word indwells is no more apt than the claim that the Spirit indwells, which is life. And if they say: we inferred the indwelling of knowledge in him because he was specific to knowledge that no other shares with him, we say:

Firstly, we do not grant that; for the Christians themselves relate that he, peace be upon him, was asked about the Resurrection and did not answer, and said: "None knows it but God alone."

Secondly, we grant it, but he was specific, according to you, to raising the dead, healing the blind and the leper, and to matters which no other created being can accomplish by your claim; and power, in your view, is in the position of life, either in the sense that it is the very same or that it is necessarily attached to it; so it would be necessary to say that life indwelt him, and you have not said so.

As for the saying of the Melkites (al-Malkaniyya) concerning the Trinity in the divinities, and that each hypostasis is a god: they must either say that each one is characterised by the attributes of the God the Exalted, such as being, life, knowledge, power and other attributes, or not say so. If they say so, it contradicts their own principle, and it is in any case impossible, because the proofs establish the impossibility of two gods.

Also, they must either say that the substance of the Eternal is also a god, or not say so. If the first, they have overturned their own doctrine, for they all agree on the Trinity, and by this saying it would follow that there is a Quaternity. If the second, they find no way to distinguish, although the substance of the Eternal is the root and the hypostases are following attributes, so it would be more fitting that it be a god. If they say the second, the upshot returns to a verbal dispute, whose resolution rests on the revealed law permitting such an application.

As for their saying that the Word mingled with the body of the Messiah, it is refuted by the impossibility of the attributes of the Eternal indwelling anything other than the essence of God the Exalted; and their claim of union is impossible both by way of demonstration and by way of implication. As for the first: when the two are united, it must be said either that both remain,

صفحة 29 (continued)
or that neither remains, or that one remains and the other does not. If both remain, they are two as they were; if neither, the existing one is other than both; and if the third, then there is no union, given duality and the absence of one of them. As for the second supposition, it is from four aspects:

First: if the union of the hypostasis of the eternal substance with the created is permissible, what prevents the union of the attribute of the created with the eternal substance? If they say: what prevents it is that the union of the attribute of the created with the eternal substance entails its deficiency, which is impossible, while the union of the attribute of the Eternal with the created entails its honour, and the honour of the created through the Eternal is not impossible, we say: just as the essence of the Eternal would be diminished by the union of the attribute of the created with it, so the eternal hypostasis is diminished by its union with the created humanity; let this too be impossible.

Second: there is agreement on the impossibility of the union of the hypostasis of the eternal substance with other than the humanity of the Messiah; so what is the difference between one humanity and another? If they say: it united only with the universal humanity and not the particular, we refute this by what you will know shortly, God willing.

Third: their doctrine is that the hypostases are additional to the essence of the eternal substance, while being specific to it; and their subsistence in it did not entail union. Thus it is more fitting that the union of the hypostasis with the humanity not entail it.

Fourth: there is consensus that the hypostasis of the eternal substance differs from the humanity, just as the attribute of the essence of the substance differs from the essence of the accident, and the attribute of the essence of the accident differs from the substance. If they say it is permissible for the attribute of the substance to unite with the accident, or the attribute of the accident with the substance, so that the substance comes to be in the state of an accident and the accident in the state of a substance, they have committed themselves to something contrary to their principles. And if they say that the union of the attribute of the essence of the substance with the accident, and the essence of the accident with the substance, is impossible, though the accident and the substance are more susceptible to change and alteration, then it is more impossible in the case of the Eternal and the created.

As for their saying that the Messiah is a universal human, it is false in four respects:

The first point: the universal human (al-insan al-kulli, the human nature considered in general) is not specific to any one individual among people. The Christians agree that the Messiah was born of Mary, peace be upon them both. In that case, either it is said that Mary's humanity is also universal, as has been reported of some of them, or it is particular. If it is universal, then either it is the very same humanity as the Messiah's, or it is other than his. If it is the very same, then a thing would be born from itself, which is impossible. Furthermore, it would follow that the Messiah is Mary and Mary is the Messiah, and no one has said this. If it is other than his, then the universal human is that which is general and shared among all, and its nature is part of the meaning of every human. It would follow from this that the humanity of the Messiah, by its nature, is part of the concept of the humanity of Mary, and vice versa, which is impossible. If Mary's humanity is particular, then, since the Messiah must have been born of her, the universal, which is suitable for being shared by many, would be restricted to the particular, which is not suitable in itself, and this is impossible.

The second point: the Christians are unanimous that the Messiah was visible and could be pointed to, whereas the universal is not like this.

The third point: they say that the Word (al-Kalima) indwelt the Messiah, either by way of union (ittihad) or not by way of union. If the Messiah were a universal human, he would not be specifically related to some individuals of humankind rather than others, and the one born of Mary would not be specifically the locus of the indwelling of the Word rather than others. They have not said this.

The fourth point: the Melkites agree that the killing fell upon both the divinity (lahut) and the humanity (nasut). If the Messiah's humanity were universal, the occurrence of a particular upon it could not be conceived.

As for what Nestorius (Nusturus) held, namely that the hypostases (aqanim) are three, the discussion with him concerns the restriction in the same manner as previously stated.

As for his saying: "[the attributes] are neither the very essence of Him nor other than His essence." If he means by this what al-Ash'ari meant in his saying that the attributes are neither identical nor other, then it is true. If he means something other than this, then it is not an intelligible meaning. As for his interpretation of knowledge as the Word, the dispute with him over this expression is verbal. Then it is either that he intends by the Word the inner speech (al-kalam al-nafsi) or the spoken speech (al-kalam al-lisani), and the discussion on this is well known.

As for his saying: "the Word was united with the Messiah in the sense that it shone upon him," this has no real meaning. For either he intends by the shining of the Word upon him, peace be upon him, what is understood from its example
[p. 30]
namely that he is a receptacle for its rays upon him, or he intends that it is connected to him like the connection of eternal knowledge to the objects of knowledge, or he intends something other than that. If the first, it would follow that it is something with rays, and in a direction from the place of its rays, and from this it would follow that it is a body, and that it is not an attribute of the eternal essence, and this is impossible. If the second, then it is true, except that the connection of the hypostasis to the Messiah in this interpretation would not be exclusive. If the third, then it must be depicted so that one can speak about it.

As for the saying of some Nestorians, that each of the three hypostases is a living, speaking God, it is false by the proofs refuting the Trinity.

As for those among them who affirm for God, exalted is He, other attributes such as power, will, and the like, they are correct. Except that the claim of excluding them from being hypostases, while they share with them in being attributes, is pure arbitrariness, and the distinction on which they rely is false, as you have come to know.

As for their saying: "The Messiah is a complete human and a complete God, and these are two substances, eternal and originated," the method of refuting it is from two aspects:

The first: addressing the refutation of the claim that the hypostasis united with the body of the Messiah is God. This is done by saying: either they say that what was united with the body of the Messiah is God alone, or that every hypostasis is God, as the Melkites held. If the first, it is impossible because of the lack of priority. If the second, it is also impossible for what has preceded.

The second: that if the Messiah comprises the hypostasis and the originated humanity, then either they say that there is union, or the indwelling of the hypostasis in the humanity, or the indwelling of the humanity in the hypostasis, or that there is no indwelling of either in the other. If the first, it is false by what preceded in the refutation of union. If the second, it is false by what refutes the indwelling of an eternal attribute in other than the essence of God exalted, and the indwelling of the originated in the eternal. If the third, then either it is said that they are adjacent and connected, or not. If it is said the first, then either it is said that the eternal hypostasis is separated from the originated substance, or it is not said. If it is said separation, it is impossible for two reasons: the first is what shows the refutation of the transfer of an attribute from its subject; the second is that it would entail the subsistence of an attribute by itself at the time of its adjacency to the humanity, and this is impossible. If one does not say that the hypostasis is separated from the eternal substance, it would entail that the essence of the eternal substance is connected to the body of the Messiah, necessarily, since its hypostasis is connected to it. In that case, the union of the hypostasis with the humanity is no more preferable than the union of the eternal substance with it, and they have not said this. And if one does not say that they are adjacent and connected, then there is no meaning to union with the body of the Messiah, and the claim of union without connection with the body of the Messiah is no more preferable than the reverse.

As for the saying of whoever among them says: "God is one, the Messiah was born of Mary, he is a righteous created servant, except that God, exalted is He, honored him by naming him a son," then this is what the monotheists (al-muwahhidun) say, and there is no disagreement with them except regarding the application of the name "son."

As for the saying of some Jacobites (Ya'qubiyya), that the Word turned into flesh and blood, and God became the Messiah, it is more evidently false than what preceded. Its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: if it were permissible for the hypostasis to transform into flesh and blood despite the difference of their realities, then it would be permissible for the impossible to become possible, the possible to become impossible, the necessary to become possible or impossible, the possible or impossible to become necessary. No one would remain confident in any of the self-evident propositions, and it would be permissible for substance to become accident and accident to become substance, flesh and blood to become a hypostasis, a hypostasis to become an essence, an essence to become a hypostasis, the eternal to become originated, and the originated to become eternal. No one of the intelligent has said this.

The second: if the hypostasis were transformed into flesh and blood, then either it would be the very same as the blood and flesh that the Messiah had, or it would be additional to them, joined to them. The first is manifestly corrupt, and the second they have not said.

As for what has been transmitted from John (Yuhanna), his saying: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word," it is among what he alone reported. It is not found in any of the Gospels. Apparently it is a lie, for it is like the saying of one who says: "The dinar is with a money-changer, and the money-changer is the dinar," which no intelligent person would utter. Likewise his saying: "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" is not established as authentic. Even if it is granted, it admits of a reading with inversion:
[p. 31]
That is: the flesh which became, by naming, a Word, dwelt among us. He meant by that flesh Jesus, peace be upon him. It is also possible that he pointed by this to Peter (Butrus), the chief of the disciples and the executor of the Messiah's will, for he stood after him, peace be upon him, in managing his religion, and the Christians used to resort to him, as their books testify. So it is as if he were saying: if the Word, i.e., Jesus whom God, exalted is He, named thus, has departed from among us, then it has not departed until it became flesh and dwelt among us, meaning that its management is present in a body among us, and that is Peter.

Some people have interpreted his speech by dropping the interrogative hamza when translating it from Hebrew into the Arabic tongue, and the meaning would be: "has it become?" but this is distant.

Among the most astonishing wonders is that John mentioned that the Messiah said to his disciples: "Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, there is no life for you after me; for my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink; whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me and I in him." When his disciples heard this word, they said: "How hard is it! Who can bear to hear it?" Many of them then turned away from his companionship. This, together with his saying that God, exalted is He, is the Word, and that the Word became flesh, is in extreme difficulty, since it involves the command of the originated to eat and drink of God, the eternal, the pre-eternal. The truth is that neither of these two statements is established, so we do not bear the burden of interpretation.

As for their saying: "the divinity (lahut) appeared in the humanity (nasut) and so became it," they either mean by it that the divinity became the very essence of the humanity, as their saying "became it" clearly indicates, which returns to permitting the inversion of realities, and this is impossible, as you have known. Or they mean that the divinity was characterized by the humanity, and this too is impossible, because of what has been established regarding the impossibility of the indwelling of the originated in the eternal. Or they mean that the humanity was characterized by the divinity, and this too is impossible, because of the impossibility of the indwelling of the eternal in the originated.

As for whoever among them says: that the substance of the eternal God and the substance of the originated human were composed and became one substance, which is the Messiah, this is false for two reasons:

The first is what has been mentioned of the refutation of union.

The second is that it is no more preferable to make the humanity divinity through its composition with the divinity, than to make the divinity humanity through its composition with the humanity. They have not said this. As for the substance of a coal when thrown into fire, we do not grant that it became the very substance of the fire; rather, it became adjacent to the substance of the fire. Its extent is that some of the attributes and accidents of the substance of the coal were nullified by the adjacency of the substance of the fire, but that the substance of one of them became the substance of the other, that is not so.

As for their saying: that union with the particular humanity and not the universal is impossible, because of the proofs refuting union and the indwelling of the eternal in the originated, and by this their saying that Mary bore a God is nullified, as is their saying that the killing fell upon both the divinity and the humanity together, since this entails the death of God, which is self-evidently false.

As for the saying of whoever says: that the Messiah, with the union of his substance, is eternal in one respect and originated in another respect, this is false. For if the substance of the Messiah is united with no plurality in it, then the origination is either for the very same thing which was said to be eternal, or for something else. If the first, it is impossible, otherwise the one thing would be eternal without a beginning and originated with a beginning, which is contradictory. If the second, it is contrary to what was assumed.

As for the saying of whoever says: that the Word passed through Mary like the passage of water through a gutter, it would entail the transfer of the Word, which is impossible, as is not hidden. By this is nullified the saying of whoever says that the Word used to enter the body of the Messiah at times and depart from it at other times.

And their saying: that what appeared of the image of the Messiah in the humanity was not a body but an illusion, like the image seen in a mirror, is false. For it is among their principles that the Messiah only brought the dead to life and healed the blind and the leper by what was in him of the divinity. Thus, if what appeared in him of the divinity had no reality, but was pure illusion, it would not be suitable for the origination of what originated from God through it.

And the claim that the hypostasis of life is created and originated is not so, because of the proofs establishing the eternity of the attributes. It is eternal and everlasting. How could it be otherwise? For if it were originated, God would have been non-living before it! And whoever is not living is not knowing nor speaking.

And the saying of whoever says: that the Messiah was created before the world, and he is the creator of every
[p. 32]
thing, is false, because of the proofs establishing that God, exalted is He, was, and there was nothing other than Him.

As for the creed by which they draw near to God and in which they worship, the demonstration of its instability, its contradiction, and its incoherence is from several aspects:

The first: their saying "We believe in the One God, the Father, the Creator of all things" contradicts their saying "and in the one Lord, the Messiah," etc., a contradiction that is hardly hidden.

**Second**, their saying that Jesus the Messiah, the son of God, the firstborn of all creation, implies that the Messiah is created. There is no sense in his being the son of God except that he came after Him, since the father and the son cannot exist together. Their co-existence is impossible by the self-evident judgment of reason, because the father cannot be other than one of two cases: either he begot a son who has always existed, or he did not. If they say, "He begot a son who has always existed," we reply: then he did not beget anything, since the son has always existed. And if he begot something that did not exist before, then the son is originated and created. This contradicts their saying: "God of God, true God of true God, of the substance of His Father," and that He perfected the worlds with His hand and created everything.

**Third**, their saying: "true God of true God, of the substance of His Father," is contradicted by the words of the Messiah in the Gospel, when he was asked about the Day of Resurrection. He said: "I do not know it, and no one knows it except the Father alone." If he were of the substance of the Father, he would know what the Father knows. Moreover, if it were permissible for there to be a second god from a first god, it would be permissible for there to be a third god from a second god, and the matter would not stop at any limit, which is impossible.

**Fourth**, their saying that Jesus perfected the worlds with his hand and created everything is false and contradicts what is in the Gospel. Matthew says: "This is the birth of Jesus Christ, son of David." Also, the Creator of the world must necessarily be prior to it, so how can the Messiah be prior when Mary bore him? Also, in the Gospel, Satan said to the Messiah: "Bow down to me and I will give you all the world, and I will make you king over everything." Satan kept dragging him from place to place and preventing him from achieving his aim, and he hoped to make him worship him. How then can the Creator of the world be confined within the hand of some of the world? We seek refuge in God from error.

**Fifth**, their saying: "The Messiah is the true God who descended from heaven for the salvation of mankind, and was incarnate of the Holy Spirit, became a man, was conceived and born in her," entails several corruptions:

Among them: the Messiah does not refer merely to the Word, nor merely to the body, but is a name that refers to this body which Mary, peace be upon her, bore. The Word was not Messiah from eternity, so it is invalid that it is He who descended from heaven.

Among them: he who descended from heaven is either the Word or the human nature (*nasut*, the human nature; *lahut*, the divine nature). If they claim that the one who descended was the human nature, that is a plain lie, because his human nature is from Mary. If they claim that it was the divine nature, then it is said: it is either the Essence, or the knowledge expressed by the Word. If it is the first, then it entails the attachment of deficiencies to the Creator, may His name be exalted. If it is the second, then it entails the transfer of an attribute and the Creator remaining without knowledge, and that is invalid.

Among them: their saying that He descended only for the salvation of the human race means that when Adam, peace be upon him, disobeyed, he bound all his descendants in the snare of Satan and made it obligatory for them to abide forever in the Fire. Their salvation therefore came through the killing of the Messiah, his crucifixion and his torment. This is a claim for which there is no evidence. Grant that we accept it for them. Still, it is said: tell us, from what is this salvation for which the Eternal God toiled, and did to Himself what He did for its sake? Why did He save you? From whom did He save you? How did He alone undertake your salvation without the Father and the Spirit, when lordship is shared among them? And how was He humiliated and abased in your salvation without the Father and the Spirit? If they claim that the salvation is from the burdens and cares of this world, sense refutes them. If it is from the legal obligations of the Law, and that prayer and fasting, for example, have been lifted from them, then the Messiah and the apostles refute them by what they imposed upon them of obligations. If they claim that they have been freed from the judgments of the Hereafter, so that whoever among them commits a forbidden act is not held accountable, then the Gospel and the prophecies refute them. For the Messiah says in the Gospel: "I will set the people on my right and on my left on the Day of Resurrection, and I will say to those on the right: 'You did such and such; go to the bliss prepared for you before the foundation of the world.' And I will say to those on the left:

(Page 33)

'You did such and such; go to the punishment prepared for you before the foundation of the world.'"

**Sixth**, their saying "and was incarnate of the Holy Spirit" is false according to the text of the Gospel. Matthew says in the second chapter of it: when John the Baptist baptized the Messiah, the Holy Spirit came down to him from heaven in the form of a dove, and that was after he had reached thirty years of age.

**Seventh**, their saying that the Messiah descended from heaven, that Mary conceived him, and that he dwelt in her womb, is contradicted by the words of Luke the Evangelist, who says in the account of the Apostles, in the fourteenth chapter: God Most High is the Creator of the world and all that is in it, and He is the Lord of heaven and earth. He does not dwell in temples, nor is He touched by the hands of men, nor does He need anything at all, because He is the One who gave men life; our existence, our life and our movements are from Him. Thus Luke bore witness that the Creator and His attributes do not dwell in temples, and that men cannot touch Him with their hands. This contradicts the Word dwelling in the temple of Mary and being transformed into the temple of the Messiah.

**Eighth**, their saying that after he was killed and crucified he rose from among the dead, ascended to heaven, and sat at the right hand of his Father, is a gross lie that entails originatedness.

**Ninth**, their saying that this Jesus, the Lord who was crucified and killed, is prepared to come again at another time to decide the judgment between the dead and the living, is like the saying of the poet:

*I will surely find you after death, lamenting me,*
*while in my life you did not provide me with provision.*

For they claim that in the first time he was unable to save himself, until what was done to him by his enemies was completed. How then can he be able to save all of them in the second time?

**Tenth**, their saying: "We believe in one baptism for the forgiveness of sins," contradicts their own principles. This is because the belief of the Christians is that their sins were not forgiven without the killing of the Messiah, and for this reason they called him "the camel of God, Most High," which bears the sins, and they called him "the Savior of the world from sin." If they believe that the one baptism is what forgives their sins and frees them from their wrongdoings, then they have declared that there is no need for the killing of the Messiah, since baptism alone suffices for salvation and forgiveness. If baptism is sufficient for forgiveness, then they have acknowledged that the crucifixion was pointless. If forgiveness is only obtained by killing him, then what is the benefit of baptism, and what is this faith?!

Thus these are ten complete aspects in refuting that trust (*amanah*), and in showing the treachery they contain. Whoever examines it closely will refute it many times over. Abu al-Fadl al-Maliki said, after some discourse:

*Their trust has been nullified; from its content*
*its treachery has appeared through the lines of its pages.*

*They began with the oneness of God, then associated*
*Isa with Him, so there is contradiction in its expression.*

*They said: their God is Isa, who*
*scattered existence over all creation.*

*He created his mother before indwelling in her womb;*
*how far was his essence from needing her kind!*

*Was he in need of drinking her milk,*
*or of being raised in the lap of her bosom?*

*They made him a lord, a substance of a substance,*
*and went to what the people of intellect do not accept.*

*They said: there came from heaven, as a favor,*
*for the salvation of Adam from its blaze and heat.*

*Adam had repented an accepted repentance,*
*but their misguidance made the ransom by other than it.*

*Even if he came in the shade of the clouds, and around him*
*the angels of heaven, all of them, in honor...*

*And He ransomed Him who with His two hands fashioned His clay*
*by pardoning all matters and covering them.*

*Then He chose him, beloved and favored,*
*and protected him from the error of souls and their evil.*

(Page 34)

*You made God a station for your*
*own selves, in what your souls see of their association.*

*Without His needing in his deliverance*
*that all creation should bear its harm.*

*The enemies disparage Him with what He does not approve,*
*from their scheming and from what their deception brought.*

*This is their trust, and this is its explanation:*
*God is greater than the meanings of its disbelief.*

Then know that the Christians who hold the doctrine of the Trinity have no proof from what is narrated from Matthew the disciple, that he said: when the Messiah bade them farewell, he said: "Go and baptize the nations in the name of the Lord, the Son, and the Holy Spirit." From here they made that the opening of the Gospel, just as the opening of the Qur'an is ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. The words of some of us may give the impression that this formula descended from heaven, like the basmala in our view. For we say, assuming the narration is sound, and without it there is only thorny difficulty: it is possible that by "the Father" is meant the origin (*mabda'*), for the ancients used to call the origins "fathers," and by "the Son" is meant the Messenger, and he was so called as an honor and a dignity, just as Abraham, peace be upon him, was called "the Friend" (*khalil*). Or it is by consideration that they call effects "sons." They also narrated from the Messiah, peace be upon him, that he said: "I am going to my Father and your Father," and he said: "Do not give your charity in front of people to be seen by them, for you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven."

It may also be said that "the Son" means the beloved or something similar. What points to this is what they narrated, that he, peace be upon him, said after a charge he gave to the apostles: "So that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, and that you may be perfect as your Father who is in heaven is perfect." By "the Holy Spirit" is meant Gabriel, peace be upon him, and the meaning is: baptize by the blessing of God Most High and His Messenger, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace, and by the angel who supports the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, in conveying the commands of their Lord.

In *Kashf al-Ghayn 'an al-Farq bayna al-Basmalatayn* by Shaykh 'Abd al-Ghani al-Nabulusi, may his secret be sanctified, it is stated that the basmala of the Christians points to three divine presences of the One, Unique, Absolute Hidden Reality. The Father is an indication of the Spirit, which is the first creature of God Most High, as in the report, and which is called the Intellect, the Pen, and the Muhammadan Reality (*al-Haqiqa al-Muhammadiyya*). It is attributed to God Most High, so it is said "the Spirit of God Most High," for honor and magnification, like "the she-camel of God Most High." The Holy Spirit is also an indication of it, in consideration of its manifestation in the form of a perfectly formed human who breathed into the garment of Mary, peace be upon her. The Son is an indication of Jesus, peace be upon him, and he is a son of that Spirit in consideration of the fact that his coming into being was by means of its breathing. The Father is the Son, and the Son is the Holy Spirit in reality. The Absolute Hidden Reality is exalted and sanctified above the three, for He, glory be to Him, in His essence, there is nothing with Him, and it is not possible that anything be with Him. So the basmala of the Gospel belongs to the station of the divine attributes and the lordly names, not to the station of the most holy Essence.

Then let no one imagine that the words of our Sufi masters, may God sanctify their secrets, revolve around the words of the Christians, as one claims who has no knowledge of the verification of their speech and no taste for their path. This is because these people, may God Most High benefit us through them, are free from what those veiled from the truth have attributed to them of belief in anthropomorphism (*tajsim*), the doctrine of identity with God (*'ayniyya*), union (*ittihad*), and indwelling (*hulul*).

As for the claim that they did not hold anthropomorphism, this is because it has been established among them that the Truth, glory be to Him, is pure Existence, existing by Himself, subsisting by Himself, determined by Himself. Every body is a form in the extended Existence over the realities, expressed as "the cloud" ('ama'), determined by the requirement of the readiness of a non-existent quiddity. Nothing of the bare Existence, which is determined by its own essence, is in the form determined within the extended Existence by the requirement of the non-existent quiddity. So nothing of the body is bare existence that is determined by its own essence. This is reversed to: nothing of bare existence that is free of quiddity and determined by its own essence, and this is what was to be proved.

[Page 35]

As for their not holding the doctrine of *'aynlyya* (identity of the Creator with creation), this is because the Real, exalted is He, is what you know of as pure existence (*al-wujud al-mahd*), and so on. The created is the apparent form within existence, spread over the realities, determined according to its nonexistent quiddity (*mahiyya*). Nothing that is abstracted from quiddity, determined by its own essence, is the same as what is conjoined with quiddity and determined according to it. Among what bears witness to this is the saying of the Greatest Shaykh (Ibn al-'Arabi), may God sanctify his secret, in the 558th chapter of the *Futuhat* (*al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya*), in the presence of the Originator (*hadrat al-Badi'*), after an exposition: "This shows you that the world is not the very essence of the Real. It only appeared in the Real's existence. For if it were the very essence of the Real, it would not be correct for it to be originated (*badi'*)."

His saying in this same chapter, regarding God's words ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He﴾, is: He, glory be to Him, alone knows them and denied knowledge of them to everything else. Thus He established you in this verse and informed you that you are not He. For if you were He, you would know the keys of the unseen through your own essence, and what you know only through a station (*mawqif*), you are not the very station. Likewise have said more than one. The Shaykh Sharaf al-Din Isma'il ibn Sudkin said in his commentary on the *Tajalliyat*, quoting the Shaykh, may God sanctify his secret, also: "When the possibilities (*al-mumkinat*) appeared through God's manifesting them to them, and this became so firmly established that the possible can never remove this reality, it remained humble before God's greatness and submissive to Him. This is the prostration of eternity, and it is an expression for the servant's knowledge of his own reality."

From here the reality of His saying, glory be to Him: "I was his hearing and his sight," (the hadith) and so on, becomes known. When some of the weak received a glimpse of this vision and said, "I am the Real," he became intoxicated and cried out, and did not realize it, because he was absent from his own reality. End of quotation.

As for their not holding the doctrine of *ittihad* (unification of essences), this is because unification is either by the pure, abstracted existence, determined by its own essence, becoming an existence conjoined with a nonexistent quiddity and determined according to it, or the reverse. This is impossible in both respects, because abstraction from quiddity is essential to the Real, exalted is He, and conjunction with quiddity is essential to the possible, and what is by essence does not cease.

In the *Kitab al-Ma'rifa* of the Greatest Shaykh, may God sanctify his secret: "If unification makes two essences one, it is impossible. For if each of the two is existent in the state of unification as its own essence, then they are two essences. And if one essence is annihilated while the other remains, then it is only one."

He said in the *Kitab al-Ya'* (which is the *Kitab al-Hu'*): "Unification is impossible," and he went on with the discourse until he said: "There is absolutely no unification, neither by way of meaning nor by way of form."

He said in the fifth chapter of the *Futuhat*, as an address from the Real, exalted is He, to the Universal Spirit: "I have veiled you from knowing the manner of My support for you with the divine secrets, since you have no capacity to bear witnessing them. For if you knew them, the 'I-ness' (*al-aniyya*) would not occur, and the unification of 'I-ness' is impossible. So your witnessing of that is impossible. Does the 'I-ness' of the composite return to the 'I-ness' of the simple? There is no way to reverse realities."

As for their not holding the doctrine of *hulul* (indwelling), this is because they have explained *hulul* sometimes as "attainment by way of dependence," and sometimes as "a thing's being in a locus and subsisting in it." It is known that the Necessary Being, exalted is He, who is pure existence subsisting by His own essence and determined as such, cannot subsist in anything other than Himself.

The Greatest Shaykh, may God sanctify his secret, said in the 292nd chapter of the *Futuhat*: "When the light of the sun manifests in the full moon, it gives forth wisdoms that it does not give forth without the moon. There is no doubt of that. Likewise, when divine power (*al-iqtidar al-ilahi*) manifests in the servant, it brings forth actions from the creation. So although it is by divine power, the judgment differs, because it is through this manifested locus, which is like a mirror for His manifestation. And as is known by reason, the moon in itself has nothing of the sun's light in it, and the sun did not move into it by its own essence, but it had a place of manifestation. Likewise the servant has nothing of his Creator in him, and He did not indwell in him, but he is a locus of manifestation for Him, a particularity, and a place of appearing of Him." End of quotation.

This is an explicit text in denying *hulul*. The source of the error of the veiled deniers is their failure to understand the words of these masters, may God benefit us through them, in their proper sense, and their failure to distinguish between *hulul* and *tajalli* (divine manifestation). They did not realize that a thing being the locus of manifestation of another is not the same as its being the locus of indwelling of it. For the image that appears in a mirror is clearly external to the mirror in its essence, unlike what indwells in a place, which is present within it. So manifestation is other than indwelling,

[Page 36]

for the manifestation of the Vast, the Holy (*al-Wasi' al-Quddus*) in the loci of manifestation is compatible with transcendence (*tanzih*), unlike indwelling. Yes, there occurred in their speech the expression of indwelling, while by it they meant manifestation. Among this is the saying of one of them:

"O my qibla, let me be, with prostration, for I have seen a person prostrating to a person within me.
His divinity (*lahut*) indwelt my humanity (*nasut*), so it sanctified me. I am amazed that someone like me is not worshipped."

It would have been better, outwardly, not to use such expressions. But these people have states and stations that our understandings do not reach, and perhaps their excuse is clear to the fair-minded.

Having known this and verified the disagreement of the Christians in their beliefs, know that He, glory be to Him, only related in some verses the saying of some of them, and in others the saying of others. The relation of their claim of the divinity of Mary, peace be upon her, like their claim of the divinity of Jesus, peace be upon him, is among what the Qur'an has spoken of, though it was not clearly spread from them. But it necessarily follows for them according to what Imam al-Razi, may God have mercy on him, established.

And the Christians today deny it, and God is the truest of speakers. It may be said that those who explicitly claimed her divinity, peace be upon her, were a group among them who perished long ago, like the Jewish sect who say "Uzayr is the son of God," as it is said. Then He, glory be to Him, was emphatic in reproving the speakers, so He followed the prohibition with His words, Mighty is the Speaker: ﴿Desist﴾ from saying the Trinity, ﴿it is better for you﴾. The discussion of the grammatical possibilities of its accusative status has already passed. ﴿God is but one God﴾, that is, in essence, transcendent above plurality in any respect. ﴿Glory be to Him that He should have a son﴾, that is: I glorify Him with a glorification from, or from His having a son, or glorify Him from that. For a son resembles the father and is like him, and God, exalted is He, is transcendent above likeness and similitude. Also, a son is only sought so that he may stand in the place of his father when the father is absent, and for this reason there is procreation. But God, exalted is He, is everlasting, and extinction does not touch His lofty sanctuary. So He has no need of a son, and no wisdom requires it. You have known what led the Christians to their belief that Jesus, peace be upon him, is the son of God, exalted is He.

Among the strange coincidences is what our master Raghib Pasha, may God have mercy on him, quoted, summarized from the definitions of Abu al-Baqa. He said: The erudite Imam Muhammad ibn Sa'id, known as al-Busiri, may God illuminate his tomb, said: "Some of the Christians championed their religion and derived from the noble basmalah (the invocation "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate") a proof for strengthening their belief in the Messiah, peace be upon him, and the soundness of their certainty about him. So he transposed its letters, denied what was known in it, separated what was familiar in it, placed first and last in it, reflected and planned, and was killed for how he planned. Then he frowned and scowled, then he turned his back and became arrogant, and said: 'From the basmalah the Son of God has been set free.' I said to him: Since you have accepted the basmalah between us and you as an arbiter, and have taken from it rulings and judgment, then the basmalah will surely support us, the good against the wicked, and will surely prefer the people of Paradise over the people of the Fire. For the basmalah has said to you in the language of its state: 'God is only the Lord of the Messiah, the Merciful to the sacrifice (al-nahr); the Messiah has no lord.' 'God has not ceased to be merciful to the Muslims. Ask the son of Mary: the unlawful was made lawful for him; the Messiah is not the Son of God, set free.' 'There is no mercy for the base, the sons of sorcerers,' mercy to a free Muslim who turned to God. 'For God there is a Prophet, a Muslim; wine is forbidden; the capital of the word of faith has profited.' If you say: 'He, peace be upon him, is a Messenger,' I have believed you."

And she said: "Eel sent mercy with flesh (lahm)." "Eel" is one of the names of God, exalted is He, in the language of their books, and "lahm" translated is "Bethlehem" (Bayt Lahm), which is the place where Jesus, peace be upon him, was born. And there is more of that which indicates the refutation of the doctrine of the Christians.

Then look at the basmalah: it informs that behind its solution are horses and lions, and without its shade are torrents and rains. You may think I found your cold word pleasing and wove upon its pattern, and matched the one with ten like it. Rather, I have brought you what will suffice you and astonish you, and make you hear what deafens you from answering and silences you. So you will know that this basmalah is a resting place for all the sciences and arts, and a repository for the jewel of its hidden secret. Do you not see that the basmalah,

[Page 37]

when you sum its letters, the number is seven hundred and eighty-six, which agrees with its sentences: "Indeed the likeness of Jesus is like Adam's" (Q 3:59), "There is no partner with God" by the reckoning of the alif that comes after the lams of the divine name (Allah), and "I do not associate anyone with my Lord" (Q 72:20), "God guides by His light whom He wills" (Q 24:35), by dropping the alif of the divine name. Thus the basmalah has answered you with what you did not encompass in knowledge, and what came to you that you could not bear patiently." End of quotation.

Something like this has already passed in the remainder after removing the repeated letters from the alphabet at the beginnings of the surahs, where the Shi'i arranged from them what he thought would strengthen what he held, namely: "The path of 'Ali is truly what we hold fast to." We answered him with what would confound him, arranged from these same letters as well. So reflect.

Al-Hasan read ﴿in yakun﴾ (إنْ يَكُونَ) with a kasra on the hamza and a raf' on the nun, meaning: Glory be to Him; there is not for Him a son, so that the speech is two sentences.

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth﴾ is a resumed sentence, brought to give the reason for transcendence. Its explanation: He, glory be to Him, is the owner of all existent things, the high and the low. Nothing of them goes out from His dominion. And if He had a son, the son would be like Him in ownership, and so He would not be the owner of all of them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God suffices as Guardian﴾ is an indication of another proof, because the guardian (*wakil*) means the preserver. So when He, glory be to Him and exalted is He, is self-sufficient in preservation, He has no need of a son. For a son helps his father in his lifetime and stands in his place after his death. God, exalted is He, is transcendent above all of this. So a son cannot be conceived for Him by reason, and to claim one for Him would be foolishness and ignorance.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 172 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The Messiah will never disdain﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf muqarrir) confirming what preceded of the declaration of God's transcendence (tanzih). It is related that the delegation of Najran said to our Prophet (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, why do you revile our companion?" He said: "And who is your companion?" They said: "Jesus (peace be upon him)." He said: "And what should I say about him?" They said: "You should say that he is the servant of God and His messenger." Then this was revealed.

Al-istinkaf (disdain) is an form of istif'al derived from al-nakf. Its origin, as al-Raghib said, is from "nakaftu al-shay'," meaning "I moved it away," and its origin is the moving away of tears from the cheek with a finger. They said: "a sea that cannot be nakf," i.e., cannot be drained. From this is his saying:

"They departed, and had it not been for what they recalled of them from the oath, the tear would not have been held back from your two eyes."

It was also said: al-nakf is evil speech. One says: "There is no nakf or wakf for him in this matter." Istaf'ala here denotes privation (salb), as stated by al-Mubarrad. In al-Asas: istankafa and nakafa mean he refrained and withdrew out of pride and zeal (anafan wa hamiyatan).

Al-Zajjaj said: al-istinkaf is arrogance in refusing out of a sense of honour (anafa), and it is not in al-istikbar (haughtiness). The meaning: he will not feel honour-offended and will not refuse.

From Ibn Abbas (may God be pleased with him): "The Messiah will not be arrogant (la yastakbir al-Masih) ﴿to be a servant of God﴾," i.e., "from" or "from being a servant of God Most High, persisting in His worship and obedience, as is the duty of servanthood. How could it be otherwise, since that is the highest rank of honour?" Qadi Iyad alluded to the honour of servanthood in his saying:

"What has increased my wonder and pride, and I was about to tread the Pleiades with my toes,
is my entering under Your saying, 'O My servants,' and Your making me the best of Your creation as a prophet."

The avoidance of mentioning his (peace be upon him) not disdaining this, although it is his custom (sha'n) to take pride in it, as his states indicate and his sayings disclose, is because it occurs in the place of responding to what the disbelievers said, as you have just learned. This is also the reason for making the object of disdain his being a servant of Him, rather than saying "from the worship of God" or similar, together with what it conveys, as has been said, of a great benefit: the complete purity of his (peace be upon him) from disdain altogether, since this attribute persists and entails the attribute of servanthood. Thus not disdaining the attribute implies not disdaining what it entails, unlike the attribute of worship, which is a renewed state not necessarily implying permanence; it suffices for its bearer to be characterized by it once. Therefore not disdaining worship does not imply not disdaining its continuance.
