Among the things in Christian books that indicate his servanthood (peace be upon him) is that Clement said in his second epistle: "Look at this Messenger, the chief of our rabbis, Jesus, entrusted from the One who created him, like Moses (peace be upon him) in all his states, except that he is better than Moses, peace be upon him."

Mark said in his Gospel: Jesus said: "My soul is sorrowful unto death." Then he fell on his face, praying to God Most High, and said: "O Father, all things by Your power, take this cup from me; but not as I will, but as You will." Then he fell on his face, praying to God Most High.

The indication in this is clear, for he is a supplicant, God Most High is the one supplicated, he is a worshipper, and God Most High is the one worshipped. What servanthood could exceed this? The texts of the Gospels speak of his servanthood (peace be upon him) in more than one place. And God Most High's excellence is evident in Abu al-Fadl when he says of him:

"He is a near servant, a prophet, and a messenger whom his Lord has specially chosen.
God purified his essence and bestowed upon him, then brought him His revelation and guidance.
And by 'Be' He created him; the Word of God came to Mary the virgin, and created him.
Such is the manner of his Lord, the Creator of creation by 'Be', who created them; how excellent is the God!
The Gospels bear witness, and from him: God is his Lord, and none other.
He was humble to God, submissive, desiring, fearing, hoping for His pleasure.

It suffices to establish his servanthood (peace be upon him) what God Most High indicated by His saying: ﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, is but a messenger; messengers have passed away before him, and his mother was a truthful woman﴾ and ﴿They both used to eat food﴾. And in the expression "the Messiah" there is also an indication of servanthood.

﴿Nor the angels brought near﴾ is a conjunction (atf) upon "the Messiah," as is apparent, i.e., the angels brought near do not disdain to be servants of God Most High. It was said that it is a conjunction upon the concealed pronoun in (yakun) or ('abdan), since it is a description, but this is not correct. Estimating the complement of the verb is necessary according to the majority.

It was said: by "the angels" is meant each one of them, so there is no need for an estimate. Some claimed that it is a conjunction of sentences, and they insisted on estimating the verb, but as you see, it is unsound.

Al-Qadi Abu Bakr, al-Halimi, and the Mu'tazilah used the verse as evidence that the angels are superior to the prophets (peace be upon them), because what the context and the rules of meaning and the speech of the Arabs require is ascent from the lesser to the greater. So the meaning is: the Messiah will not disdain, nor will whoever is above him, as one says: "The minister will not disdain this matter, nor the sultan," not the reverse. It was answered that the sequence of the verse, although it is a refutation of the Christians, has incorporated into it a refutation of the worshippers of angels, who share with them in raising some created beings from the rank of servanthood to the rank of divinity, and claim their kinship with God Most High through what is among the traits of divinity. "Those brought near" was specified because they used to worship them over others. This answer was rejected: this does not negate the superiority of the second, as the requirement of the science of meanings indicates.

It was said: there is no objection to it, because it is known from the context that it is repelled, since the primary intent is the matter of the Messiah, so he was placed first. And even if it be granted that it does not negate superiority, it does not establish it, as when you say: "Zayd did not do this, nor 'Amr," and this suffices to repel the opponent's argument. As for the claim that the sequence and context contradict it, this is nothing, because the answerer said: it is incorporation and digression (idmaj wa istitrad). It was also answered, granting that the refutation is specific to the Christians, that "the angels brought near" is a plural form that encompasses the totality of angels, so this conjunction requires that the totality of angels be superior to the Messiah, and it does not follow that each one of them be superior to the Messiah.

Al-Taftazani (in al-Intisaf) said: There is a point to consider here, for if its subject is built on the basis that the Messiah is superior to each one of the individual angels, it may be said that it entails that he is superior to all of them, just as the Prophet (ﷺ), since he is superior to each one of the prophets (peace be upon them all), is superior to all of them. And none of those who wrote on this subject distinguished between superiority over each and superiority over the whole.

It had escaped some contemporary imams that he distinguished between the two superiorities, and the claim that superiority over each does not necessarily entail superiority over the whole has not been established from him. And even if he said it, it is rejected by a subtle argument: the superiority intended is mainly indicated by the raising of the rank of the superior in Paradise, and the hadiths are widely transmitted on that. In that case, either the rank of one of the lesser ones is raised above the one who is in fact superior to each of them, or the rank of none of them is raised above him. The first is impossible, because it entails raising the lesser above the superior, so the second is determined, namely that the rank of the superior is raised above the ranks of the whole necessarily; thus his superiority over the whole follows from his superiority over each of them, with certainty. End of quote.

I say: what is widely known of the disagreement between the Hanafis and the Shafi'is about whether the Prophet (ﷺ) is superior to the whole just as he is superior to all, or whether he is superior to all only and not to the whole, is not in its proper place on this basis, so reflect.

It was said in response: the most that the verse indicates is the superiority of the angels brought near, who are the Cherubim around the Throne, or those who are higher in rank than them, among the angels, over the Messiah among the prophets (peace be upon them). That does not entail the superiority of one of the two kinds over the other absolutely, and that is the point in dispute. It was rejected: the claim is that in such a statement, the requirement of the rules of meaning is ascent from the lower to the higher, not the reverse, or equality. It is known that the ruling for the definite plural (al-jam' al-muhallā bi-al) applies to the individuals, and the claim is nothing but that the speech indicates that the brought-near angel is superior to Jesus (peace be upon him). This suffices to nullify the claim that the elite of humans are superior to the elite of the angel.

Some claimed that the conjunction of the angels upon the Messiah with the particle "wa" (and) does not require sequence, and that the examples cited for the second being of higher rank than the first are countered by examples that do not require that, such as the saying of one who says: "Zayd and 'Amr did not help me in this matter," and your saying: "Do not harm a Muslim or a dhimmi." Rather, if you reversed in this example and made the higher the second, you would depart from the limit of speech and the canon of eloquence, as al-Taftazani said. Then he said in it: But the truth is more fitting than the intended meaning, and there is no contradiction between the two examples.

We will prepare a preface to remove the confusion and uncover the veil, and we say: the point of the order in the two examples which are thought to contradict each other is one, and it requires in some places placing the higher first and in others placing it later. That point is that the requirement of eloquence is distance from repetition and safety from descent. When you adopt this understanding, it leads to your last speech being a descent in relation to the first, or the last being included in the first, already conveyed by it, so that you need not the last. So turn away from that toward what is an ascent from the lower to the higher, and a resumption for a benefit that the first did not contain. An example is the verse mentioned: for if you went in it to the view that the Messiah is superior to the angels and higher in rank, the mention of the angels after him would be as if dispensable. For if the superior, who is the Messiah under this assumption, is a servant not disdaining servanthood, it follows that whatever is below him in virtue is more fitting not to disdain being a servant of God Most High, and these are the angels under this assumption. Thus nothing new is added by His saying ﴿nor the angels brought near﴾ beyond what preceded at the beginning of the speech. But if you suppose the Messiah inferior in relation to the angels, it is as if you ascended from magnifying God Most High, by saying that the inferior does not disdain being His servant, to saying that the superior does not disdain that either, and it does not follow from the non-disdain of the inferior the non-disdain of the superior. So the need for mentioning the angels is compelling, since the first does not entail the last. Thus the speech under this assumption becomes renewed in benefit and increasing in it, and whenever it is so, it is determined that the Noble Book should be interpreted accordingly, for it is the ultimate in eloquence.

Therefore, with this same subtle point, you must say: "Do not harm a Muslim or a dhimmi (non-Muslim under protection)," placing the lesser before the greater, contrary to the order in the verse. For if you forbid him from harming the Muslim, it may be said: that is among his special privileges, out of respect for the religion of Islam; so it does not follow from that the prohibition of harming the disbeliever, from whom this special privilege is withheld. Thus, when you say "or a dhimmi," you have introduced a benefit that was not in the first, and you have ascended from the prohibition of some kinds of harm to the prohibition of more than that. And if you arranged this example in the order of the verse, saying "Do not harm a dhimmi," the one addressed would understand that harming the Muslim is more included in the prohibition, since he shares with the dhimmi the cause of obligation, which is humanity for example, and is distinguished from him by a cause that is nobler and greater, which is Islam. So this prohibition convinces him of a further prohibition against harming the Muslim. But if you say "or a Muslim," you have not introduced a new benefit, and you have not informed him of anything other than what you informed him of first. Thus you know that it is a single point which sometimes requires placing the higher first and sometimes placing it later, and only the context distinguishes this for you. I have no doubt that the context of the verse requires placing the lesser first and the higher later.

Among the eloquence that follows from this point is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾, dispensing with a prohibition of striking them or worse, by placing the lesser first. It would not befit the eloquence of the Mighty Book to intend a prohibition of something higher than mere "uff" and reproach; since that is already dispensed with, and the one who reflects upon the verses of the Qur'an, with confirmation, needs no other witness besides them. And since fairness required acknowledging that the verse implies the preference of the angels, while the view that the prophets are preferred (peace be upon them) is the belief of most of Ahl al-Sunnah and the Shi'ah, it was necessary to interpret the preference in the verse as applying to a matter other than the point of disagreement, namely the preference of the angels in strength, severity of force, and breadth of capacity and power.

This kind of virtue is the one suited to the context of the verse, because the aim is to refute the Christians in their belief in the divinity of Jesus (peace be upon him), basing it on the fact that he raised the dead, healed the blind and the leper, and extraordinary great signs occurred at his hands. So it fits to say: he at whose hands these marvels occurred does not disdain the worship of God Most High; rather, there are those who perform greater marvels and show more manifest effects, such as the angels brought near, among whom is Jibril (peace be upon him), whose strength and the power God gave him reached the point that he uprooted cities, carried them on a feather of his wing, and overturned them upside down. So the preference of the angels in this sense is established, and there is no dispute that they are stronger and more forceful, and that their marvels are greater; the dispute concerns preference in terms of greater reward, honours and elevation of ranks in the abode of recompense, and the verse contains no proof of that.

It may also be said: since most of what was confused for the Christians regarding the divinity of Jesus (peace be upon him) was that he existed without a father, God informed them that this one who came into being without a father does not disdain the worship of God Most High, nor do the angels, who came into being without father or mother. The mention of them is therefore delayed because their creation is more wondrous than the creation of Jesus (peace be upon him). This is supported by the fact that God Most High compared Jesus with Adam (peace be upon them both); He likened the strange to the stranger, and the marvel among the signs of His power to the more marvelous, since Jesus was created from Adam (peace be upon them both), and Adam (peace be upon him) was created without father or mother. For this reason He, glorified is He, said: ﴿He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was.﴾ The core of this discussion rests on the point that has been indicated; so whenever the inclusion of the second mention is shown to contain a benefit not contained in the first, by whatever way, whether of preference or of another benefit, it conforms to the form of the verse. End of quotation.

Summary of the matter: the question is one resting on transmitted evidence (sam'iyyah), and the detailed proofs and positions on it fill the books of kalam, while a definitive ruling depends on a text admitting no interpretation, which is rare to find.

Al-Amidi in Abkar al-Afkar, after extensive discussion, argued and refuted, stated that this question is speculative (zanniyyah), with no room for certainty in affirmation or negation, and its basis is the transmitted proofs rather than rational proofs.

The most excellent of the later scholars, Salih Afandi al-Mawsili (may God cover him with His mercy), said in his glosses on al-Baydawi: "In my view, the better course regarding this question, with respect to other than our Prophet (may God's peace and blessings be upon him), is to suspend judgment, since there is no certainty that indicates a ruling on it, and knowing it is not what we were charged with. The matter is weighty and one should not rush into it; so suspension is safer, and God knows best."

﴿And whoever disdains His worship﴾, i.e., His obedience, so it includes all disbelievers, for their not obeying Him, exalted is He. The thing disdained here is stated as His worship, not what preceded, as Shaykh al-Islam said, in order to attach the threat to the attribute that is manifestly established for the disbelievers, since their not obeying Him is something they cannot deny they are characterized by. God expressed their not obeying Him by "disdain" although their doing so was by way of denying that the command came from Him, not by way of disdain; for they used to disdain obeying the Messenger of God (may God's peace and blessings be upon him), and this is disdain of obeying God Most High, since the Prophet (may God's peace and blessings be upon him) has no command apart from the command of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God﴾.

It has been said: the expression "disdain" is by way of mushakalah (correspondence in wording): ﴿and is proud (yastakbir)﴾, i.e., regarding that. The root of istikbar (pride) is seeking greatness without entitlement, not in the sense of seeking to attain it while believing it is not attained, but in the sense of counting oneself great and believing so. It was expressed by what indicates seeking only to signal that its outcome is pure seeking without attaining what is sought. A parallel to this, as has been said, is His saying: ﴿They bar from the way of God and seek it crooked﴾. Istikbar, as al-Zajjaj indicated and as was mentioned earlier, is other than istinkaf.

A hadith from him (may God's peace and blessings be upon him) has come: "The one in whose heart is an atom's weight of pride will not enter Paradise." A man said: "O Messenger of God, a man loves that his garment be fine and his sandal fine?" He said: "God is beautiful and loves beauty. Pride is rejecting the truth and looking down on people."

Scholars have various interpretations of this hadith, which Imam al-Nawawi mentioned in his commentary on Muslim, among them: that the pride preventing entry into Paradise is pride in refusing faith. Our most excellent contemporary chose this, then said: "On this reading, what is negated is the very entry, as is the apparent and immediate meaning. The indefinite 'pride' is for the kind, and the definite at the end of the hadith is the genus of pride, not this specific type; although it is common in repeating an indefinite as definite to intend the same first thing. The Prophet (may God's peace and blessings be upon him) specified the ruling of that type by explanation so that it would be more forceful in warning against pride, for a genus some of whose kinds bring their possessor to such a dreadful end and evil outcome, namely perpetual wretchedness, deserves to be guarded against with utmost care. Then the Prophet (may God's peace and blessings be upon him) defined pride by what he defined, lest one imagine that blameworthy pride is restricted to the type mentioned."

By this explanation, the objection of al-Nawawi (may God Most High have mercy on him) to this interpretation is dispelled: that the hadith came in the context of warning against well-known pride, which is denying the truth and despising people, so restricting pride to that alone departs from the tenor of speech. The way its objection is dispelled is not hidden from people of understanding. End of quotation. Apparently, what is in the hadith is a definition by a concomitant of the linguistic meaning.

﴿So He will gather them to Himself all together﴾, i.e., the disdainers and their counterparts, indicated by mention of the non-disdain of the Messiah and the angels brought near (peace be upon them). The mention of one of the two groups was left out in the detailed part, relying on the detail to reveal it, and confident that the requirement of gathering one with the other is evident, since gathering is general to all creation, just as the mention of one of the two groups was left out in the detailed part at His saying: ﴿As for those who believed in God and held fast to Him﴾, despite the address including both, relying on the same. So it should not be said that the detail does not correspond to what is detailed, since it includes both groups while the detailed part covers one group.

It has been said regarding justifying the correspondence: the purpose of gathering is recompense, and His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 173:

﴿So as for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full﴾ and so on, as a detailing of the recompense. It is as if it were said: "And whoever disdains His worship, he will be punished with regret when he sees the rewards of the doers and what befalls him of the punishment of Allah, the Exalted." Thus the pronoun refers to those who disdain and are arrogant, and no others, and the wording of (man) (whoever) and its meaning have both been taken into account.

Al-Allama al-Taftazani (d. 792 AH) criticised this, saying: "It is not correct, because (amma) (as for) enters upon the two groups, not upon the two divisions of the recompense. Moreover, this group is mentioned by the description of faith and righteous deeds, not by the description of not disdaining, which would suit what comes before and after it, in order to draw attention to the fact that it is the one that brings about what follows of its fruits." The meaning of "giving them their rewards in full" is granting them those rewards without any reduction whatsoever. It was also read as (fa-sayahshuruhum) (He will gather them) with a kasra on the shin, which is a dialectal form, and it was read as (fa-sanahshuruhum) (We will gather them) with the royal plural "nun," and in this there is a shift (iltifat) in person.

﴿And He will increase them from His bounty﴾ by multiplying their rewards manifold, and by giving them what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human being.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and al-Isma'ili in his Mu'jam recorded, with a weak chain, from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "{He will give them their rewards in full:} He will admit them to Paradise. {And He will increase them from His bounty:} intercession for those for whom the Fire has become due, from among those to whom good was done in this world."

﴿And as for those who disdained﴾ the worship of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿and were arrogant﴾ toward it, ﴿He will punish them﴾ because of that ﴿with a painful punishment﴾ which description cannot encompass. ﴿And they will not find for themselves, besides Allah, a protector﴾ who would manage their affairs and arrange their interests, ﴿nor a helper﴾ who would help them against His might, or deliver them from His punishment, glory be to Him.

O mankind (﴿يا أيُّها النّاسُ﴾): this is an address to all those who are legally accountable, coming after the demonstration of the falsehood of the various forms of disbelief and error held by the disbelievers, and after binding them with what would make the solid mountains crumble. It also alerts them that the proof has been fully established, so that no excuse remains for one who makes excuses and no pretext for one who offers pretexts.

﴿There has certainly come to you﴾ (قَدْ جاءَكُمْ): it has reached you and arrived at you, ﴿a proof from your Lord﴾ (بُرْهانٌ مِن رَبِّكُمْ): i.e., a decisive argument. It is said that what is meant by it is the miracles (al-mu'jizat).

Ibn 'Asakir reported, from Sufyan al-Thawri, from his father, from a man whose name he does not remember, that the intended meaning of "the proof" (al-burhan) is the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was referred to by this term because of the miracles he possessed, which bear witness to his truthfulness, peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ). It has also been said that what is meant by it is the true religion (din al-haqq) which the Prophet (ﷺ) brought. The nunation (al-tanwin, the sound "n" added to the end of a noun) is for exaltation (lil-tafkhim), and "min" (from) is for the starting point of the end (li-ibtida' al-ghayah) in a figurative sense. It is connected either to "jaa'" (has come) or to an omitted element that functions as a qualifying attribute (sifah) conferring honour upon "burhan," reinforcing what the nunation conveys.

It is also permitted that it be partitive (tab'idiyyah), with the omission of a governed noun, i.e., "one of the proofs of your Lord." The mention of the title of Lordship (al-Rububiyyah) together with the attachment to the pronoun of those addressed serves to show kindness toward them and to indicate that the coming of this is for their nurture and perfection.

﴿And We have sent down to you﴾ (وأنْزَلْنا إلَيْكُمْ): through the intermediary of the Prophet (ﷺ). The omission of mention of the intermediary shows the completeness of the kindness toward them and an emphasis on removing their excuses. ﴿a clear light﴾ (نُورًا مُبِينًا): this is the Qur'an, as Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Suddi said. The possibility that the earlier scriptures, which indicate his prophethood (peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ)), are intended is extremely remote.

If what is meant by "the proof" is also the Qur'an, then it has been treated with a conjunction (al-'atf) based on the difference between the two terms. This is to treat the difference in designation as if it were a difference in essence. The term "proof" is applied to it because it is the strongest evidence for the truthfulness of the one who brought it. The term "clear light" is applied to it because it is evident in itself, self-sufficient in establishing its truth and its being from Allah, Exalted, through its inimitability (i'jaz), not needing anything else. It makes clear other things, distinguishing truth from falsehood, and guides creation by bringing them out from the darknesses of disbelief into the light of faith. Its connection to those addressed is expressed at one time with "coming" (al-majī'), attributed to it, which indicates the perfection of its strength as a proof, as if it comes by itself, establishing what it establishes without anyone bringing it, and coming against the disbelievers' doubts by refuting them. At another time it is expressed with "sending down" (al-inzal), directed toward it, which suits the aspect of its being light, as a means of honouring it, each of its two designations being given its fitting portion.

The attribution of its sending down to Allah, Exalted, through the shift of grammatical person (al-iltifat), is for the perfection of its honour, as stated by our master Shaykh al-Islam. The matter under any other reckoning is straightforward.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 175:

﴿As for those who believed in Allah﴾ in accordance with what the proof that came to them requires. ﴿and held fast to Him﴾, meaning they protected themselves through Him, glorified is He, from what would destroy them, such as the deviation caused by Satan and other things.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) and others narrated from Ibn Jurayj that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, namely the manifest light, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. ﴿He will admit them into mercy from Him﴾, meaning a great reward whose worth is commensurate with their faith and their deeds, a mercy from Him, glorified is He, not a settlement of an obligatory right.

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, it is narrated that the intended meaning of "mercy" is Paradise. According to the first view, there is a figurative usage in the word "in" (fi), by likening the comprehensiveness and inclusiveness of the reward to the comprehensiveness of the container. According to the second view, the figurative usage is in the genitive noun and not in the preposition. This is what al-Shihab stated, and the discussion on this is well known. ﴿From Him﴾ is connected to an omitted element and functions as a qualifying adjective of "mercy", ennobling it. ﴿And bounty﴾, meaning a favour whose extent cannot be measured, in addition to that.

﴿And He will guide them to Him﴾, meaning to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The commonly accepted meaning is guidance to His worship, glorified is He. It has been said that the pronoun refers to everything mentioned before it, in terms of it being a promise, and it has been said that it refers to the bounty. ﴿a straight path﴾ is Islam and obedience in this world, and the way to Paradise in the next. The mention of the promise of admission into mercy, meaning the reward or Paradise, is placed before the promise of this guidance in order to hasten the announcement of what is the primary purpose.

Regarding the grammatical case of "ṣirāṭan" (صِراطًا), there are several views. It has been said that it is a second object (mafʿūl thānī) of an omitted verb, meaning "He will make them know a path" (يُعَرِّفُهم صِراطًا). It has been said that it is a second object of "yahdīhim" (يَهْدِيهِمْ) on the basis of tadmin (the verb being given the sense of another verb), so that it carries the meaning of "yuʿarrifuhum" (يُعَرِّفُهم). It has been said that it is a second object of it on the basis that guidance transitively takes two objects in its literal use.

Some people made "ilayhi" (إلَيْهِ) connected to an omitted element, meaning "brought close to Him" (مُقَرَّبِينَ إلَيْهِ), or "bringing them close to Him" (مُقَرِّبًا إيّاهم إلَيْهِ), on the basis that it is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the subject or the object. Others made it a circumstantial qualifier of "ṣirāṭan", then said: our saying "yahdīhim" (He guides them) to the path of Islam leading to His worship does not carry great meaning. Therefore, the more appropriate view is that "ṣirāṭan" be made a substitute (badal) for "ilayhi". ʿIṣam al-Millah wa al-Din objected to this, saying: our saying "yahdīhim" (He guides them) to the path of Islam, leading to His worship, has a clear meaning, and there is no justification for "ṣirāṭan" to be a substitute for the preposition and its object. So understand this.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 4, verse 176 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿They ask you for a ruling﴾: that is, concerning the *kalalah* (a deceased person who leaves neither ascendants nor descendants). The word is omitted because it occurs in His saying: ﴿Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning the kalalah﴾. The prepositional phrase is connected to *yuftikum* (gives you a ruling). The Kufans said it is connected to *yastaftunaka* (they ask you). Abu al-Baqa' rejected this view, arguing that if it were so, it would have said: *yuftikum fiha fi al-kalalah*. The explanation of *kalalah* has already passed at the beginning of the surah. The verse was revealed concerning Jabir ibn Abdullah, as related from him by Ibn Abi Hatim and others.

[Page 44]

The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and a great many others related from him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon me while I was ill and unable to think. He performed ablution, then poured (the water) over me, and I regained my senses. I said: 'Only a kalalah inherits from me, so how is the inheritance (to be divided)?' Then the verse of the shares was revealed." It is the last verse to be revealed.

Al-Bukhari and others related from al-Bara' who said: "The last complete surah to be revealed was Bara'ah (Surat al-Tawbah), and the last verse to be revealed was the conclusion of Surat al-Nisa'." What is meant by the verses here is those related to legal rulings, as the scholars who verify such matters have stated; the detailed discussion of this will come, if Allah wills. It is called *Ayat al-Sayf* (the Verse of Summer).

Malik and Muslim related from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "I did not ask the Prophet (ﷺ) about anything more often than I asked him about the kalalah, until he struck my chest with his finger and said: 'The verse of summer in the end of Surat al-Nisa' is sufficient for you.'"

﴿If a man dies﴾: this is a clarifying resumption (*isti'naf*) explaining the ruling. *Imru'un* (a man) is in the nominative by a verb implied by the mentioned word, according to the well-known view. His saying ﴿who has no child﴾ is a qualifier of it, and the separation by the explaining element does no harm, since it is an emphasis. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to it, but this was objected to on the grounds that it is indefinite, and a circumstantial clause coming from an indefinite word is contrary to the apparent sense, since what is understood in clauses following indefinite nouns is that they are qualifiers. Al-Halabi said it is valid for it to be a circumstantial clause relating to it, with *halaka* (died) as the qualifier of it. Abu al-Baqa' made it a circumstantial clause of the concealed pronoun in *halaka*. It has been objected to this that the explaining element is not intended, to the extent that some claimed there is no pronoun in it, since it is an explanation of the verb alone without a pronoun. This is rejected by His saying: ﴿Say: If you possessed the treasures of my Lord﴾ (where the explanation has a pronoun).

Abu Hayyan said: "What the structure requires is that this is impermissible, because the subject in reality is only the noun governed by the omitted verb. It is that which should not be qualified. As for the pronoun, it is in an explanatory clause which has no place in the grammatical analysis (*i'rab*), so it is like a reinforcement of what preceded. When following (*ittiba'*) and qualification revolve between a reinforcer and a reinforced element, the correct view is that it applies to the reinforced element (in the accusative case, *al-mu'akkad bi-l-fath*), since it is the basis of the original predication." Al-Halabi agreed with him. Al-Sifaqsi said: "The more apparent view is that this is a preference, not a requirement."

What is meant by "child," according to what some have chosen, is the male, since that is what is immediately understood. Also, although a sister inherits alongside a daughter according to other than Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) and the Imamiyya, she does not inherit half by way of a fixed share (*fardiyya*). Some verifying scholars criticized this, preferring the general sense, arguing that it is specification without a specifier. The explanation that a son excludes the sister but a daughter does not is not sound, because the ruling is the designation of a half. This (half-share) is established when there is neither son nor daughter, and not established when either of them exists. As for the son, he excludes the sister. As for the daughter, she makes the sister an agnatic residuary (*'asabah*), so no fixed share is determined for her.

Yes, her share alongside a single daughter is half by way of agnatic residuary status, not by a fixed share. So there is no need to interpret "child" as "son," neither explicitly nor implicitly.

Also, the discussion concerns the kalalah, which is one who has no child at all, and likewise one who has no parent. However, mention was limited to "child," relying on the matter being clear. The word "child" is a general term in negative context, so it includes all, and specification requires a specifier, and where is it?! So let this be understood.

His saying ﴿and he has a sister﴾ is coordinated with ﴿who has no child﴾, and it may be a circumstantial clause. By "sister" is meant a sister from both parents (full sister), the mother and the father, because a sister from the mother only has a fixed share of one-sixth, and its explanation has passed at the beginning of the honored surah.

﴿then she receives half of what he left﴾: that is, by fixed share, and the remainder goes to the agnatic residuaries, or to her by return (*radd*) if he has no agnatic residuaries. The *fa'* (then) is in the answer to the conditional. ﴿And he inherits from her﴾: that is, from his sister who is entitled to a fixed share, if it is assumed that she dies while he survives. The clause is resumptive and has no place in grammatical analysis. As Abu al-Baqa' said, it takes the place of the answer to the condition in His saying ﴿if she has no child﴾, whether male or female. So his inheriting from her means taking all her property entirely, since that is conditioned on the complete absence of a child, and not that he inherits from her in part,

[Page 45]

for that is realized even when her daughter exists. The verse, just as it does not indicate that siblings are excluded by anything other than a child, also does not indicate that they are not excluded by a child. The Sunnah (the Prophetic tradition) has indicated that they do not inherit alongside the father, since it is authentically related from him (ﷺ): "Give the fixed shares to their rightful heirs, and what remains goes to the nearest male agnate." There is no doubt that the father is closer than the brother. This is not the first of two rulings, one of which is explained by the Book and the other by the Sunnah.

﴿If there are two (females), then for them is two-thirds of what he left﴾: this is coordinated with the first conditional. The pronoun refers to those who inherit by siblingship, and its dual form is treated according to the meaning. The ruling for more than two is the same as for two. The reference of the dual pronoun to "two" was regarded as problematic, because the predicate must convey something different from what the subject conveys, which is why "the master of the slave-girl is her owner" is not valid. The dual pronoun already indicates two, so the predicate about it conveys nothing. It was answered that "two" indicates mere plurality without restriction to age, or other attributes, so it is as if it were said: they deserve what is mentioned by mere plurality without considering any other matter, and this is informative. This was the view of al-Akhfash, but it was rejected on the grounds that the dual pronoun also indicates that, so the problem returns.

Makki related from him that he answered that this was taken according to the meaning of "the one who inherits," and that the original structure and its intended meaning is: "If the one who inherits by siblingship is two," and "if the one who inherits is males and females in what follows." It was said "they were" (*kanatā*) and "they were" (*kānū*) to match the predicate, as it is said "whoever your mother was" (*man kanat ummuka*). But this was rejected on the grounds that it is not correct and not analogous to the example, because in that example "whoever" is explicitly mentioned, and it has both a form and a meaning, so whoever made it feminine observed the meaning, which is "mother," and did not make it feminine for the sake of the predicate. The meaning of the predicate there differs from the meaning of the noun, unlike what we have here, where their meaning is the same.

Abu Hayyan mentioned two ways of parsing the verse:

The first: the pronoun in "they were" does not refer to the two sisters but to the heirs, and there is an omitted qualifier for "two." The qualifier together with the qualified is the predicate, and the meaning is: "If they (the female heirs) were two" from among the sisters, so the predicate in that case conveys what the noun does not convey. Omitting the qualifier is permissible when the meaning is understood.

The second: the pronoun refers to the two sisters as they (the scholars) mentioned, and the predicate of *kāna* is omitted, as indicated by the meaning, though its omission is rare. "Two" is then an emphatic circumstantial clause, and the meaning is: "If they (the two sisters) were his," that is, belonging to the dead man, and the omission of "his" is indicated by "and he has a sister."

﴿And if they are siblings, men and women, then for the male is the equivalent of the share of two females﴾: its original form is: "and if they are brothers and sisters," so the masculine was given precedence through its companion "men and women," which occurs in apposition. It was also said that there is ellipsis (*iktifa'*) in it. ﴿Allah makes clear to you﴾: the ruling of the kalalah, or its rulings and laws, of which its ruling is one. This is the view of Abu Muslim. ﴿That you may not go astray﴾: that is, lest you go astray regarding it. This is the view of the Basrans, and al-Mubarrad stated it explicitly.

Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and other Kufans held that there is an implied *lam* (in order that) and *la* (not) at both ends of *an* (that): that is, "so that you do not go astray." It was also said: there is no omission or implication here, but rather the *an*-clause is the object of *yubayyin* (makes clear): that is, He makes your error clear to you. This was preferred because it is a fine conclusion and a return to the beginning of the surah, which is: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾. He commanded them to be pious and made clear to them what they were upon in the pre-Islamic age. When its detail was complete, He said to them, Mighty and Majestic is He: "I have made clear to you your error, so fear Me as I commanded you, for when evil is recognized it is avoided, and when good is recognized it is practiced."

It was objected that what is explicitly made clear is the truth, and error is known by comparison, so the apparent wording would be: "He makes clear to you the truth." Unless it is said: the clarification of the truth is evident, while the clarification of error is hidden, so it was necessary to draw attention to it. There is room for reflection in this.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned that the fine conclusion of this surah is that it ends with the verse of the shares, and in it are the rulings of

[Page 46]

death, which is the last matter of every living thing, and it is also the last of the rulings to be revealed. ﴿And Allah, of all things﴾, among the things of which are your affairs connected with your living and your dying, ﴿is Knowing﴾: intensively knowing, so He makes clear to you what contains your benefit and your advantage.

* * *

Furthermore, among the allusive interpretations (*al-isharah*) of the verses: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved﴾: they concealed what their readiness (*isti'dad*) required. ﴿And obstructed﴾: and prevented others ﴿from﴾ treading ﴿the way of Allah﴾: that is, the path that leads to Him. ﴿They have certainly strayed far astray﴾: because they deprived themselves and others of what contains salvation. ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and wronged﴾: they blocked their readiness from its rights of perfection by committing vices. ﴿Allah would never forgive them﴾: because their readiness has become void. ﴿Nor will He guide them to a path﴾: because of their compound ignorance and corrupt belief. ﴿Except the path of Hell﴾: which is the fires of the longings of their wicked souls. ﴿And that is ever for Allah easy﴾: because they are naturally drawn toward it.

﴿O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion﴾: this is a prohibition addressed, according to most of our masters, to the Jews and the Christians, and both groups have exaggerated in their religion. As for the Jews, they went to extremes in the outward and denied the inward, so they degraded Jesus (peace be upon him) from the rank of prophethood and from being characterized by the attributes of Allah the Exalted. As for the Christians, they went to extremes in the inward and denied the outward, so they raised Jesus (peace be upon him) to the rank of divinity.

﴿And do not say about Allah except the truth﴾: by combining the outward and the inward, and the multiplicity and the distinction, as is the Muhammadan monotheism (*al-tawhid al-Muhammadi*). ﴿The Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, was but a messenger of Allah﴾: who calls to it. ﴿And His word which He directed to Mary﴾: that is, a reality from among His realities that indicate Him. ﴿And a spirit from Him﴾: that is, a holy matter, transcendent above all imperfections.

Al-Shaykh al-Akbar (may his secret be sanctified) mentioned that the reason 'Isa (peace be upon him) was singled out with this description is that the one who breathed into him, in terms of the Jibrili form, is none other than the Exalted Truth. Thereby he became a complete spirit, manifesting the Name of Allah Most High, emanating from a essential Name (ism dhati), and not emanating from the subsidiary Names (al-asma' al-far'iyya) as others did. Between him and Allah Most High there were no intermediaries, as there were for the spirits of the other prophets, peace be upon them all. For their spirits, although they are from the presence of the Name of Allah Most High, are nonetheless through the mediation of many theophanies from the rest of the Names' presences. 'Isa was called the Spirit of Allah Most High and His Word only because he came into being from the inner unity of the collective Divine Presence. For this reason, acts specific to Allah Most High proceeded from him: the raising of the dead, the creation of birds, and his influence over the high and the low kinds. His call was to the inner and the holy world, for the Word is indeed from the inner dimension of the Name of Allah Most High and His unseen Identity. For this reason Allah Most High purified his body from natural impurities, for he is a spirit embodied in an imaginal, spiritual body, and so on to the end of what Imam al-Sha'rani mentioned in al-Jawahir wa'l-Durar.

(﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers﴾) with both the collective and the detailed view. (﴿And do not say: "Three"﴾) because that contradicts true monotheism. And 'Isa, peace be upon him, in reality, since his existence is by the existence of Allah Most High, his life by His life, exalted is He, and his knowledge by His knowledge, glorified is He. (﴿Allah is only one God﴾), who is the Absolute Existence, even beyond the restriction of absoluteness. (﴿Glory be to Him; [He is exalted above] having a son﴾), meaning: I declare Him far above there being any existent other than Him, begotten of Him, sharing existence with Him. (﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾), meaning: what is in the heavens of spirits and the earth of bodies, for they are the manifestations of His Names and Attributes, exalted is His majesty.

(﴿The Messiah will never disdain to be a servant of Allah﴾) in the station of detail, since everything that appears is contingent, and the contingent has no existence of its own, so it is a servant, needy, humbled, dependent, not disdaining the humiliation of servanthood. (﴿Nor will the angels brought near﴾), who are pure spirits and purely holy lights. As for the station of collectivity, there is neither 'Isa, nor an angel, nor nearness, nor distance, nor... nor....

(﴿And whoever disdains His worship﴾) by the manifestation of his selfhood (ananiyya), (﴿and is arrogant﴾) by his transgression in manifesting through his attributes (﴿He will gather them to Himself all together﴾)
Page 47
by the manifestation of the light of His Face and His theophany in the attribute of subjugation, until they completely pass away in the very essence of the collectivity.

(﴿As for those who believed﴾) with true faith, by effacing attributes and obliterating the essence (﴿and did righteous deeds﴾) and observed the details of the attributes and their theophanies (﴿He will give them their rewards in full﴾) from the gardens of His attributes (﴿and increase them from His bounty﴾) with the existence bestowed on them after annihilation (﴿But as for those who disdained and were arrogant﴾) and manifested selfhood (ananiyya) (﴿He will punish them with a painful punishment﴾) through their veiling and deprivation, as one of them said: "I am your Most High Lord," while seeing himself.

(﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you a proof from your Lord﴾), which is the essential Oneness (al-tawhid al-dhati) (﴿and We have sent down to you a clear light﴾), which is the detail within the collectivity. The first refers to the Qur'an, and the second to the Furqan.

(﴿As for those who believed in Allah and held fast to Him﴾) and did not turn to the others insofar as they are others (﴿He will admit them to mercy from Him﴾), which are the gardens of acts (﴿and bounty﴾), which are the gardens of attributes (﴿and guide them to Himself on a straight path﴾), which is annihilation in the Essence. Or: mercy is the gardens of attributes, bounty is the gardens of the Essence, and guidance to Him on a straight path is steadfastness upon the Oneness amid the details of multiplicity. There is no restriction upon the people of spiritual taste, for the Book of Allah Most High is a sea that buckets cannot drain, and Allah Most High is the Guide to the right path. We ask Him for success in understanding His speech, and for the expansion of our breasts with the bounties of His goodness and the feasts of His favor. There is no lord but Him, and none is hoped for except His good.
